title: Minimum Description Length Unsupervisedly Separates Law-Grade from Statistical-Grade Knowledge in a Self-Improving Science Agent - and Reveals 86% of Its Own Discoveries Are Statistical
description:
arXiv:2610.32245v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: AI systems that discover scientific relations now generate candidate "laws" at scale, but the bottleneck has shifted from generation to vetting: which candidates deserve belief? We show that a deployed self-improving science agent - one that has admitted 252 relations through held-out prediction courts - already computes the quantity that answers this question: the Minimum Description Length compression ratio used for model selection doubles, when read under discrete accounting, as an unsupervised epistemic grader. The compression-ranked top band of the agent's ledger recovers exactly the canonical laws among its discoveries (vis-viva across seven planets, Balmer/Rydberg) plus cross-measurement identities - enrichment $p=3.6\times10^{-12}$ under a hypergeometric test - with zero counterexamples and physically coherent band structure. The same lens retroactively reveals that 86% of the ledger compresses nothing ($\mathrm{cr}\approx 1$): the agent had been recording statistical regularities, including a learned predictor with held-out $R^2=0.541$ admitted through the prediction gate, under a narrative of compression as the unified value of knowledge - a narrative that was never true for them. We formalize the resulting dual-axis bookkeeping - prediction value ($R^2$) and compression value (cr) as nearly decoupled axes of knowledge - demonstrate its robustness to quantization, and register forward falsifiable predictions. The episode is, to our knowledge, the first measured instance of a discovery agent auditing its own knowledge ledger by an internal measure and finding itself over-claiming.

title: Automated Nucleus Segmentation in Histology Images: An Attention U-Net Approach with Comprehensive Preprocessing and Inference Pipelines
description:
arXiv:2610.31902v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Objectives: In the area of digital pathology, nucleus segmentation is an essential step for quantitative analysis; however, high nuclear density and staining heterogeneity in histology images pose a great challenge.
  Methods: This study implements a lightweight Attention U-Net model on the MoNuSeg 2018 dataset to overcome these challenges. The proposed pipeline integrates comprehensive image and mask preprocessing, including stain deconvolution and multi-pass mask smoothing, with a high-fidelity overlapping patch-stitching strategy during inference on high-resolution images.
  Results: The model achieved an Intersection over Union (IoU) score of 0.8745 on full-resolution, unseen test images. This result demonstrates the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in enhancing feature localization and validates the stitching methodology for generating seamless and accurate segmentation maps.
  Conclusion: Attention U-Net is an effective and competitive method for automated, scalable nucleus delineation in challenging clinical contexts.

title: Lifelong Context Adaptation through Bidirectional Memory-Skill Learning
description:
arXiv:2610.32295v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lifelong LLM agents must learn from an expanding history of interactions while making each decision within a bounded context window. Memory makes past experience available, but the agent may still need to infer how to solve each new task from the retrieved records. Skills provide reusable procedures, yet may omit the task-specific facts needed to apply them. Because retrieved memory and skills shape the agent's behavior, they also influence the experience available for future learning. We introduce MemCryst, a framework for lifelong context adaptation through bidirectional learning of memory and skills with a frozen language model. Recurring episodes stored in memory support skill creation and revision, and the interactions guided by those skills supply new memory for subsequent learning. Facts retrieved from memory and learned skills jointly form the agent's context, while task outcomes adjust the future retrieval influence of the records actually served without rewriting their content. Across ten settings spanning embodied control, long-document reading, conversation, mathematics, and code, MemCryst leads seven reported comparisons. On ALFWorld, joint serving achieves 63.17% success, compared with 59.83% for memory-only and 50.50% for skill-only serving. Code is available at https://github.com/tianyi0216/Memcryst.git

title: How to Scrape Mastodon with Go: Profiles, Posts, Hashtags Across Servers, and Trends (2026)
description:
Scraping Mastodon is unusual in a good way: you don't need to parse HTML at all. Every Mastodon server exposes the same public REST API, and most read endpoints answer without a token. The hard part isn't getting data. It's that there is no single "Mastodon". There are thousands of servers, each with its own partial view of the network, its own rate limits, and its own settings.

In this post I'll build a small Mastodon scraper in Go, standard library only, that:

  1. Looks up a profile on the account's home server
  2. Pages through a user's original posts for the last N days and computes engagement
  3. Collects a hashtag from several servers and de-duplicates the results
  4. Reads trending hashtags per server
  5. Writes everything to CSV

Everything below was run on October 26, 2026, and the output is real.

Before you start: read the server's rules and terms, keep request rates low, and respect people's choices. Mastodon accounts can set noindex (opt out of search engines) and indexable flags; the code below skips noindex accounts. Don't build profiles of individual people, and don't republish their posts out of context.

How the Mastodon API looks from a scraper's point of view

All the endpoints in this post are plain GET requests that return JSON:

What Endpoint (on any server) Auth?
Profile by handle /api/v1/accounts/lookup?acct=user No
A user's posts /api/v1/accounts/:id/statuses No
Hashtag timeline /api/v1/timelines/tag/:tag Usually no
Trending tags /api/v1/trends/tags No
Public/federated timeline /api/v1/timelines/public Often yes
Full-text post search /api/v2/search?type=statuses Yes

The last two rows are the first surprise. On mastodon.social, the public timeline answers HTTP 422 with {"error":"This method requires an authenticated user"}, and status search returns an empty statuses array when you're logged out. Server admins can turn these on or off, so check them on each server you target.

Pagination isn't in the JSON body. It's in the Link response header, like GitHub's API:

Link: <https://mastodon.social/api/v1/accounts/1/statuses?max_id=115...>; rel="next", <...>; rel="prev"

Rate limits are in headers too. Unauthenticated requests on mastodon.social got x-ratelimit-limit: 300 per five-minute window, with x-ratelimit-remaining and an x-ratelimit-reset timestamp.

Step 1: A polite HTTP helper 

mkdir mastoscraper && cd mastoscraper
go mod init mastoscraper

The helper sends a real User-Agent (put your own contact URL in it), retries on network errors and 5xx, sleeps until the reset time on a 429, and slows down on its own when fewer than 20 requests are left in the window. It returns the response headers, because we need Link for pagination.

package main

import (
    "encoding/csv"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "flag"
    "fmt"
    "html"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "regexp"
    "sort"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const userAgent = "mastoscraper/0.1 (+https://example.com/contact)"

var client = &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}

// getJSON fetches a URL, decodes JSON into out, and returns the response
// headers so callers can read Link (pagination) and X-RateLimit-*.
func getJSON(u string, out any) (http.Header, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", u, nil)
        req.Header.Set("User-Agent", userAgent)
        req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt+1) * 2 * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode == 429 {
            wait := untilReset(res.Header)
            fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "429 from %s, sleeping %s\n", res.Request.URL.Host, wait)
            res.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode >= 500 {
            res.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(attempt+1) * 3 * time.Second)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode != 200 {
            res.Body.Close()
            return res.Header, fmt.Errorf("GET %s: HTTP %d", u, res.StatusCode)
        }
        err = json.NewDecoder(res.Body).Decode(out)
        res.Body.Close()
        // Be polite even when we have budget left.
        if rem, _ := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("X-RateLimit-Remaining")); rem > 0 && rem < 20 {
            time.Sleep(untilReset(res.Header))
        }
        return res.Header, err
    }
    return nil, errors.New("gave up after retries: " + u)
}

func untilReset(h http.Header) time.Duration {
    if t, err := time.Parse(time.RFC3339Nano, h.Get("X-RateLimit-Reset")); err == nil {
        if d := time.Until(t); d > 0 {
            return d + time.Second
        }
    }
    return 30 * time.Second
}

// nextURL pulls the rel="next" URL out of a Link header like
// <https://host/api/v1/...?max_id=123>; rel="next", <...>; rel="prev"
var linkNext = regexp.MustCompile(`<([^>]+)>;\s*rel="next"`)

func nextURL(h http.Header) string {
    m := linkNext.FindStringSubmatch(h.Get("Link"))
    if m == nil {
        return ""
    }
    return m[1]
}

Step 2: Types and small helpers

Mastodon returns post bodies as HTML (<p>, links, mention spans), so plainText strips tags and unescapes entities. splitHandle accepts @user@server, user@server, or a profile URL.

type Account struct {
    ID             string `json:"id"`
    Acct           string `json:"acct"`
    DisplayName    string `json:"display_name"`
    URL            string `json:"url"`
    FollowersCount int    `json:"followers_count"`
    FollowingCount int    `json:"following_count"`
    StatusesCount  int    `json:"statuses_count"`
    LastStatusAt   string `json:"last_status_at"`
    Bot            bool   `json:"bot"`
    Indexable      *bool  `json:"indexable"`
    Noindex        *bool  `json:"noindex"`
}

type Status struct {
    ID              string    `json:"id"`
    URI             string    `json:"uri"`
    URL             string    `json:"url"`
    CreatedAt       time.Time `json:"created_at"`
    Content         string    `json:"content"`
    Language        string    `json:"language"`
    RepliesCount    int       `json:"replies_count"`
    ReblogsCount    int       `json:"reblogs_count"`
    FavouritesCount int       `json:"favourites_count"`
    Account         Account   `json:"account"`
    Reblog          *Status   `json:"reblog"`
    Tags            []struct {
        Name string `json:"name"`
    } `json:"tags"`
}

var tagRe = regexp.MustCompile(`<[^>]+>`)

func plainText(h string) string {
    h = strings.ReplaceAll(h, "</p><p>", "\n\n")
    h = strings.ReplaceAll(h, "<br />", "\n")
    return strings.TrimSpace(html.UnescapeString(tagRe.ReplaceAllString(h, "")))
}

// splitHandle turns "@user@server", "user@server" or a profile URL into (user, server).
func splitHandle(handle string) (string, string, error) {
    if strings.HasPrefix(handle, "https://") {
        u, err := url.Parse(handle)
        if err != nil {
            return "", "", err
        }
        return strings.TrimPrefix(strings.Trim(u.Path, "/"), "@"), u.Host, nil
    }
    parts := strings.Split(strings.TrimPrefix(handle, "@"), "@")
    if len(parts) != 2 {
        return "", "", fmt.Errorf("want user@server, got %q", handle)
    }
    return parts[0], parts[1], nil
}

Step 3: Profiles and posts, from the home server

Any server can look up any account it knows about. mastodon.social will happily answer lookup?acct=golang@hachyderm.io. But that answer is mastodon.social's cached copy, and it's only as fresh as the last time mastodon.social refreshed it. In my checks today the numbers matched, but nothing guarantees that, and copies of posts on other servers definitely lag behind on favourites and boosts. So the code asks the account's own server.

exclude_replies=true&exclude_reblogs=true keeps only original posts, limit=40 is the maximum page size, and the loop stops when posts get older than the cutoff. Posts come back newest first, so it can stop early instead of paging through years of history.

// lookup asks the account's HOME server, not mastodon.social, so the counts are authoritative.
func lookup(handle string) (Account, string, error) {
    user, server, err := splitHandle(handle)
    if err != nil {
        return Account{}, "", err
    }
    var a Account
    _, err = getJSON(fmt.Sprintf("https://%s/api/v1/accounts/lookup?acct=%s", server, url.QueryEscape(user)), &a)
    return a, server, err
}

func userPosts(handle string, maxPages int, since time.Time) ([]Status, error) {
    a, server, err := lookup(handle)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    if a.Noindex != nil && *a.Noindex {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s has opted out of search indexing (noindex); skipping", handle)
    }
    next := fmt.Sprintf("https://%s/api/v1/accounts/%s/statuses?limit=40&exclude_replies=true&exclude_reblogs=true", server, a.ID)
    var all []Status
    for page := 0; next != "" && page < maxPages; page++ {
        var batch []Status
        h, err := getJSON(next, &batch)
        if err != nil {
            return all, err
        }
        stop := false
        for _, s := range batch {
            if s.CreatedAt.Before(since) {
                stop = true
                break
            }
            all = append(all, s)
        }
        if stop || len(batch) == 0 {
            break
        }
        next = nextURL(h)
    }
    return all, nil
}

$ ./mastoscraper profile @Gargron@mastodon.social
Eugen Rochko (Gargron) on mastodon.social
  followers 383376 · following 764 · posts 82664 · last post 2026-10-26 · bot=false

$ ./mastoscraper posts -days 30 -pages 3 @Gargron@mastodon.social
34 original posts in the last 30 days
avg favourites 184.7 · avg boosts 61.3
  1012 ★ 451 ⟳  Heh. I misremembered the date--thought it was today, but loo…
   961 ★ 450 ⟳  "AI" is a failed technology, in the sense that it's neither …
   468 ★  95 ⟳  #SilentSunday

Note that last_status_at is a date, not a timestamp. Mastodon rounds it on purpose.

Step 4: One hashtag, several servers, no duplicates

This is where federation matters. A hashtag timeline on a server only contains posts that server has seen: posts by its own users, plus posts from accounts someone on that server follows. #golang on mastodon.social, fosstodon.org, and hachyderm.io are three different, overlapping lists.

So the code reads the tag from each server and de-duplicates by uri. The uri is the post's canonical ActivityPub id, and it's the same on every server. The id field is not: each server assigns its own local id to its copy of a post. When the same post shows up more than once, it keeps the copy with the highest counts, since remote copies are the ones that lag.

// tagAcrossServers reads the same hashtag from several servers and de-duplicates by URI,
// because each server only sees the posts that federated to it.
func tagAcrossServers(tag string, servers []string, maxPages int) (map[string]Status, map[string]int) {
    seen := map[string]Status{}
    perServer := map[string]int{}
    for _, srv := range servers {
        next := fmt.Sprintf("https://%s/api/v1/timelines/tag/%s?limit=40", srv, url.PathEscape(tag))
        for page := 0; next != "" && page < maxPages; page++ {
            var batch []Status
            h, err := getJSON(next, &batch)
            if err != nil {
                fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "%s: %v\n", srv, err)
                break
            }
            for _, s := range batch {
                perServer[srv]++
                prev, ok := seen[s.URI]
                // Keep the copy with the highest counts; remote copies lag behind.
                if !ok || s.FavouritesCount+s.ReblogsCount > prev.FavouritesCount+prev.ReblogsCount {
                    seen[s.URI] = s
                }
            }
            if len(batch) == 0 {
                break
            }
            next = nextURL(h)
        }
    }
    return seen, perServer
}

The acct field has its own trap. It's relative to the server you asked: an account local to hachyderm.io shows up as plain golang when you ask hachyderm.io, and as golang@hachyderm.io everywhere else. If you mix servers, normalize it:

// fullAcct makes "user" (local to whichever server we asked) into "user@server".
func fullAcct(a Account) string {
    if strings.Contains(a.Acct, "@") {
        return a.Acct
    }
    if u, err := url.Parse(a.URL); err == nil {
        return a.Acct + "@" + u.Host
    }
    return a.Acct
}

func short(s string, n int) string {
    s = strings.ReplaceAll(s, "\n", " ")
    if r := []rune(s); len(r) > n {
        return string(r[:n]) + "…"
    }
    return s
}

$ ./mastoscraper tag -pages 2 -out golang.csv golang
  mastodon.social  80 posts
  fosstodon.org    80 posts
  hachyderm.io     80 posts
240 posts fetched, 106 unique after de-duplicating by URI
    34 ★ resetreboot@masto.astropirad… Bueno, mastodones. Hoy por sorpresa y sin dar ni l…
    27 ★ golang@hachyderm.io          🥳 Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 are released!  🔏 Security:…
     7 ★ omkar_foss@mastodon.social   Dear #fediverse,  Introducing gracias, a #noai cli…
     6 ★ skybert@hachyderm.io         Lock down your website to a dedicated few browsers…
     5 ★ haitchfive@oldbytes.space    The Bathroom  Originally by Matthew Smith.  #zenpl…

240 posts fetched, 106 unique. More than half of what you download from a second and third server is stuff you already have. That's normal, and it's why de-duplicating by uri isn't optional. Also notice that the top post is in Spanish and not really about Go: hashtags are free text, so filter by language and your own keywords if you need precision.

Step 5: Trending hashtags per server

/api/v1/trends/tags returns each tag with a history array of daily uses and accounts. The first trap: history[0] is today, which is still being counted. My first run printed #tatort (0) and #FineArtAPlaceOrDestination (218) from today's partial numbers; switching to history[1] (yesterday, a complete day) gives comparable numbers. A tag can also trend today and still show 0 for yesterday, as you'll see below.

type TrendTag struct {
    Name    string `json:"name"`
    History []struct {
        Day      string `json:"day"`
        Uses     string `json:"uses"`
        Accounts string `json:"accounts"`
    } `json:"history"`
}

$ ./mastoscraper trends
mastodon.social  #SilentSunday (884), #audi (189), #OppositesAMovie (713), #FineArtAPlaceOrDestination (0), #tatort (72)
fosstodon.org    #SilentSunday (696), #Monsterdon (25), #Serbia (179), #CrispSandwichDay (51), #Tatort (31)
hachyderm.io     #silentsunday (717), #OppositesAMovie (641), #audi (113), #FineArtAPlaceOrDestination (0), #my9albums (45)

Trends are per server and moderated: admins review tags before they can trend. So "trending on mastodon.social" isn't "trending on Mastodon", and case varies (#SilentSunday vs #silentsunday). Lowercase tag names before you compare servers.

Step 6: CSV output and the CLI 

func writeCSV(path string, posts []Status) error {
    f, err := os.Create(path)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer f.Close()
    w := csv.NewWriter(f)
    w.Write([]string{"created_at", "author", "url", "favourites", "boosts", "replies", "language", "text"})
    for _, s := range posts {
        w.Write([]string{
            s.CreatedAt.Format(time.RFC3339), fullAcct(s.Account), s.URL,
            strconv.Itoa(s.FavouritesCount), strconv.Itoa(s.ReblogsCount), strconv.Itoa(s.RepliesCount),
            s.Language, plainText(s.Content),
        })
    }
    w.Flush()
    return w.Error()
}

func main() {
    if len(os.Args) < 2 {
        fmt.Println("usage: mastoscraper profile|posts|tag|trends ...")
        os.Exit(1)
    }
    cmd := os.Args[1]
    fs := flag.NewFlagSet(cmd, flag.ExitOnError)
    pages := fs.Int("pages", 3, "max pages per source")
    days := fs.Int("days", 30, "only posts from the last N days")
    servers := fs.String("servers", "mastodon.social,fosstodon.org,hachyderm.io", "comma-separated servers")
    out := fs.String("out", "", "write CSV here")
    fs.Parse(os.Args[2:])
    arg := fs.Arg(0)

    switch cmd {
    case "profile":
        a, server, err := lookup(arg)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
            os.Exit(1)
        }
        fmt.Printf("%s (%s) on %s\n  followers %d · following %d · posts %d · last post %s · bot=%v\n",
            a.DisplayName, a.Acct, server, a.FollowersCount, a.FollowingCount, a.StatusesCount, a.LastStatusAt, a.Bot)
    case "posts":
        since := time.Now().AddDate(0, 0, -*days)
        posts, err := userPosts(arg, *pages, since)
        if err != nil {
            fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        }
        var fav, boost int
        for _, p := range posts {
            fav += p.FavouritesCount
            boost += p.ReblogsCount
        }
        fmt.Printf("%d original posts in the last %d days\n", len(posts), *days)
        if len(posts) > 0 {
            fmt.Printf("avg favourites %.1f · avg boosts %.1f\n", float64(fav)/float64(len(posts)), float64(boost)/float64(len(posts)))
            sort.Slice(posts, func(i, j int) bool { return posts[i].FavouritesCount > posts[j].FavouritesCount })
            for _, p := range posts[:min(3, len(posts))] {
                fmt.Printf("  %4d ★ %3d ⟳  %s\n", p.FavouritesCount, p.ReblogsCount, short(plainText(p.Content), 60))
            }
        }
        if *out != "" {
            writeCSV(*out, posts)
        }
    case "tag":
        seen, per := tagAcrossServers(strings.TrimPrefix(arg, "#"), strings.Split(*servers, ","), *pages)
        total := 0
        for srv, n := range per {
            fmt.Printf("  %-16s %d posts\n", srv, n)
            total += n
        }
        fmt.Printf("%d posts fetched, %d unique after de-duplicating by URI\n", total, len(seen))
        var list []Status
        for _, s := range seen {
            list = append(list, s)
        }
        sort.Slice(list, func(i, j int) bool { return list[i].FavouritesCount > list[j].FavouritesCount })
        for _, p := range list[:min(5, len(list))] {
            fmt.Printf("  %4d ★ %-28s %s\n", p.FavouritesCount, short(fullAcct(p.Account), 28), short(plainText(p.Content), 50))
        }
        if *out != "" {
            writeCSV(*out, list)
        }
    case "trends":
        for _, srv := range strings.Split(*servers, ",") {
            var tags []TrendTag
            if _, err := getJSON("https://"+srv+"/api/v1/trends/tags?limit=5", &tags); err != nil {
                fmt.Printf("%s: %v\n", srv, err)
                continue
            }
            names := []string{}
            for _, t := range tags {
                uses := "?"
                // History[0] is today (still counting); History[1] is yesterday, a full day.
                if len(t.History) > 1 {
                    uses = t.History[1].Uses
                }
                names = append(names, "#"+t.Name+" ("+uses+")")
            }
            fmt.Printf("%-16s %s\n", srv, strings.Join(names, ", "))
        }
    }
}

go build -o mastoscraper .
./mastoscraper posts -days 30 -out gargron.csv @Gargron@mastodon.social
./mastoscraper tag -servers mastodon.social,fosstodon.org -pages 2 -out golang.csv golang

Pitfalls, in one place

  • The public timeline and status search need auth on mastodon.social (422 and empty results when logged out). Server admins decide this.
  • Pagination lives in the Link header. If you only read the JSON body, you'll get one page and think you're done.
  • id is per server, uri is global. De-duplicate on uri.
  • acct is relative to the server you asked. Normalize to user@host.
  • Remote copies lag. Ask the home server for profiles, and keep the highest counts when merging posts.
  • Content is HTML. Strip it, and expect custom emoji shortcodes like :blobcat: in the text.
  • Trends history[0] is today, still counting.
  • Rate limits are per server and per IP (300 requests per 5 minutes unauthenticated on mastodon.social). Reading many servers spreads load, but be polite on each one.
  • Not every fediverse account is Mastodon. Misskey, Pleroma, and others federate with Mastodon but have different APIs. The lookup above only works on Mastodon-compatible servers.

When you don't want to manage servers yourself

If you'd rather not juggle per-server rate limits, Link headers, and federated copies, I also run ScrapeAtlas*, which has Mastodon endpoints that wrap the same public API. For example, /v1/mastodon/hashtag takes a tag and an optional server, and /v1/mastodon/user/posts takes a handle with filter=original and a since date:

req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", "https://api.scrapeatlas.com/v1/mastodon/user/posts?handle=Gargron@mastodon.social&filter=original&since=2026-09-26", nil)
req.Header.Set("x-api-key", os.Getenv("SCRAPEATLAS_API_KEY"))
// The JSON has "posts" (same fields as Mastodon's API), a "cursor" for the next page,
// and "coverage.warnings" that tell you when results are partial.

There are also /v1/mastodon/profile, /post, /post/replies, /post/interactions, /user/connections, /search, /trends, and /server. But honestly, for Mastodon the DIY route above is very workable. The API is open, documented, and stable.

Wrapping up

  • Mastodon has a real public API. No HTML parsing, no headless browser.
  • Think in servers. Every server has a partial view; read several and de-duplicate by uri.
  • Go to the source for profiles and fresh counts.
  • Read the headers: Link for pages, X-RateLimit-* for pacing.
  • Respect opt-outs like noindex, and don't collect more than you need.

Which server-specific quirk have you hit while scraping the fediverse? Tell me in the comments and I'll add it to the list.

*I build it.

title: Your Users Save and Still See Old Data: Laravel 13.38 Fixes Read Replica Lag, Except in 3 Places
description:
Originally published at hafiz.dev

I changed a post title to "Q4 pricing update", got the green "Saved" banner, and the heading right under it still said "Q3 pricing update". The debug line on the same page said the request had read from the primary. That was Laravel 13.38.0, with the new PreventStaleDatabaseReads middleware installed exactly the way the docs show it.

The middleware is a good idea. Jack Bayliss wrote it after seeing his replicas lag 0 to 1 seconds on average and up to 15 seconds under some workloads. That's long enough for a user to edit a title, refresh, see the old one, and file a bug report. It shipped in v13.38.0 on 20 October.

To see what it covers, I set up a MySQL 8.4 primary and a replica in Docker, held the replica 5 seconds behind with delayed replication (SOURCE_DELAY=5), and pointed a clean Laravel 13.38.0 project at both. Five seconds is slow for a healthy replica. That's the point. It makes every gap reproducible on a laptop. All output below is real.

The documented setup needs one extra call before it protects the most common kind of page. And three things the middleware never touches still read stale data after you fix it. API routes, queued jobs, and the database cache store, which is where your rate limiter keeps its counts.

What sticky already did, and what 13.38 adds

Laravel has split reads and writes for years. You give the connection a read and a write server, and set sticky so a request that writes also reads its own writes:

'mysql' => [
    'driver' => 'mysql',
    'read' => ['port' => env('DB_READ_PORT', '3306')],
    'write' => ['port' => env('DB_WRITE_PORT', '3306')],
    'sticky' => true,
    // host, database, credentials...
],

Both of my servers run on 127.0.0.1, so only the port differs. In production you'd override host instead.

But sticky only lasts for one request. Save a form, redirect, and the GET that follows is a new request on a clean connection. It reads the replica.

PreventStaleDatabaseReads carries the write across requests through the session. This is the core of it, from the framework source:

$connection->useWriteConnectionWhenReading(
    $request->session()->get('_database_modified_at', 0) >= Date::now()->subSeconds((int) $seconds)->getTimestamp()
);

$response = $next($request);

if ($connection->hasModifiedRecords()) {
    $request->session()->put('_database_modified_at', Date::now()->getTimestamp());
}

Three details in those lines come back later. It calls $request->session(), so it needs a session. It only touches the default connection. And it compares whole-second timestamps, so a 2 second window stays open for somewhere between 2 and 3 seconds.

The same release added usingWritePdo(). It runs a callback with every read on that connection sent to the primary, then restores the previous setting, even if the callback throws. Most of the fixes below use it.

The documented setup still served the old title

The docs tell you to append the middleware to the web group:

->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
    $middleware->web(append: [
        PreventStaleDatabaseReads::class,
    ]);
})

I did that, saved a new title, and reloaded the page every second with the same session cookie. The page prints its title and the @@server_id of whichever server answered a select in the route closure. Server 1 is the primary, server 2 the replica.

+0.0s PUT  title="Q4 pricing update"
+0.1s GET  title="Q3 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+1.2s GET  title="Q3 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+2.3s GET  title="Q3 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+3.4s GET  title="Q3 pricing update"  read from server_id 2 (replica)
+4.5s GET  title="Q3 pricing update"  read from server_id 2 (replica)
+5.6s GET  title="Q3 pricing update"  read from server_id 2 (replica)
+6.7s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 2 (replica)

The middleware did its job. For the first three reloads the query in the closure went to the primary. The title was stale anyway, because it came from $post, and $post came from route model binding.

Route model binding happens in SubstituteBindings, which is already in the web group. Appending puts the new middleware after it. Laravel does sort some middleware by a priority list, and SubstituteBindings is on that list. PreventStaleDatabaseReads isn't, so it keeps its appended position. By the time it switches the connection to the primary, the model has already been loaded from the replica.

So add it to the priority list:

->withMiddleware(function (Middleware $middleware): void {
    $middleware->web(append: [
        PreventStaleDatabaseReads::class,
    ]);

    $middleware->prependToPriorityList(
        before: AuthenticatesRequests::class,
        prepend: PreventStaleDatabaseReads::class,
    );
})

AuthenticatesRequests is the contract the auth middleware implements, and it sits ahead of SubstituteBindings in Laravel's priority list. Going in before it means the user lookup that auth does reads the primary too. It still runs after StartSession, which it needs. This is the order Laravel resolved for GET /posts/{post} after the change:

EncryptCookies
AddQueuedCookiesToResponse
StartSession
ShareErrorsFromSession
PreventRequestForgery
PreventStaleDatabaseReads
SubstituteBindings

I tested the auth part too. A logged-in user renames themselves, then reloads a route behind auth that prints auth()->user()->name and the server that answered its own query. With the middleware only appended, as in the docs, the rename from "Hafiz R" to "Hafiz Riaz" didn't show:

+0.1s PUT  name="Hafiz Riaz"
+0.1s GET  Hafiz R (server_id 1)
+1.1s GET  Hafiz R (server_id 1)
+2.2s GET  Hafiz R (server_id 1)
+3.3s GET  Hafiz R (server_id 1)

That's the name in your nav bar staying wrong after a profile save, on requests that read the primary for everything else. With the priority call in place, the earlier rename from "Hafiz" to "Hafiz R" showed on the first reload:

+0.1s PUT  name="Hafiz R"
+0.1s GET  Hafiz R (server_id 1)
+1.1s GET  Hafiz R (server_id 1)
+2.2s GET  Hafiz R (server_id 1)
+3.3s GET  Hafiz R (server_id 1)

Back to the post title. Same save, same reloads:

+0.0s PUT  title="Q4 pricing update"
+0.1s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+1.2s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+2.3s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+3.4s GET  title="Q3 pricing update"  read from server_id 2 (replica)
+4.5s GET  title="Q3 pricing update"  read from server_id 2 (replica)
+5.6s GET  title="Q3 pricing update"  read from server_id 2 (replica)
+6.7s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 2 (replica)

Better, and in one way worse. The user now sees the new title, then the old one again, then the new one. The default window closed after about 3 seconds, and my replica needed about 6.

View the interactive component on hafiz.dev

The window has to outlast your replica lag. for() sets it in seconds:

$middleware->web(append: [
    PreventStaleDatabaseReads::for(6),
]);

The priority entry can stay as the plain class name. I printed the resolved order again to check, and PreventStaleDatabaseReads:6 still landed before SubstituteBindings.

+0.0s PUT  title="Q4 pricing update"
+0.1s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+1.2s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+2.3s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+3.4s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+4.5s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+5.7s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 1 (primary)
+6.8s GET  title="Q4 pricing update"  read from server_id 2 (replica)

Pick the number from your worst observed lag, not your average. On MySQL, Seconds_Behind_Source in SHOW REPLICA STATUS is the figure to watch. Jack's 15 second peak would need for(15) or more. Also, any write on the default connection during a request reopens the window. If a middleware updates last_seen_at on every request, an active user stays on the primary for as long as they keep clicking.

Place 1: API routes

A stateless API route has no session. Put the middleware in the api group and every request fails (output trimmed):

{
    "message": "Session store not set on request.",
    "exception": "RuntimeException",
    ...
}

Jack flags this in the PR himself ("It's session based, so not ideal for API stuff"). Leave it off, and an API client that saves and reads straight back gets the old value for the whole lag. That part I expected. Sanctum was the surprise.

New Sanctum tokens fail until the replica catches up

Sanctum looks up a personal access token with a plain find(), which reads the replica. So a token issued a moment ago doesn't exist yet as far as the next request can tell:

+0.1s POST /api/tokens -> new token issued
+0.1s GET  /api/me -> {"message":"Unauthenticated."} 401
+1.2s GET  /api/me -> {"message":"Unauthenticated."} 401
+2.3s GET  /api/me -> {"message":"Unauthenticated."} 401
+3.3s GET  /api/me -> {"message":"Unauthenticated."} 401
+4.4s GET  /api/me -> {"message":"Unauthenticated."} 401
+5.5s GET  /api/me -> {"message":"Unauthenticated."} 401
+6.5s GET  /api/me -> {"name":"Hafiz"} 200

A mobile app that logs in and immediately loads the profile screen hits exactly this. I fixed it with a token model that tries the replica first and only falls back to the primary on a miss:

namespace App\Models;

use Laravel\Sanctum\PersonalAccessToken as SanctumToken;

class PersonalAccessToken extends SanctumToken
{
    public static function findToken($token)
    {
        return parent::findToken($token) ?? (new static)->getConnection()->usingWritePdo(
            fn () => parent::findToken($token)?->load('tokenable')
        );
    }
}

// AppServiceProvider::boot()
Sanctum::usePersonalAccessTokenModel(PersonalAccessToken::class);

My first version had no load('tokenable'). Login worked, but a signup that returned a token still got 401 for 6 seconds. On signup the user row is as new as the token, and Sanctum loads the user later, outside the callback, from the replica. Loading it inside the callback fixed both flows. (If you're still choosing an auth package, Passport vs Sanctum covers that decision.)

Sanctum gets one thing right here already. When it updates last_used_at, it puts the connection's "modified" flag back the way it found it, so an authenticated GET doesn't count as a write.

Read-your-writes for API clients

For the save-then-read case I wrote a version of the middleware keyed by the authenticated user instead of the session:

namespace App\Http\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Cache;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

class PreventStaleApiReads
{
    public function handle(Request $request, Closure $next, int $seconds = 2)
    {
        if (! $user = $request->user()) {
            return $next($request);
        }

        $connection = DB::connection();
        $key = 'recent-write:'.$user->getAuthIdentifier();

        $connection->useWriteConnectionWhenReading(Cache::has($key));

        $response = $next($request);

        if ($connection->hasModifiedRecords()) {
            Cache::put($key, true, $seconds);
        }

        return $response;
    }
}

It needs the user, so it has to run after auth and before route binding:

$middleware->appendToPriorityList(
    after: AuthenticatesRequests::class,
    append: PreventStaleApiReads::class,
);

// routes/api.php
Route::middleware(['auth:sanctum', PreventStaleApiReads::class.':6'])->group(function () {
    Route::get('/posts/{post}', /* ... */);
    Route::put('/posts/{post}', /* ... */);
});

A token client with no cookies, saving and then reading every second:

+0.0s PUT  {"title":"Saved by an API client"}
+0.1s GET  {"title":"Saved by an API client","server_id":1}
+1.2s GET  {"title":"Saved by an API client","server_id":1}
+2.3s GET  {"title":"Saved by an API client","server_id":1}
+3.3s GET  {"title":"Saved by an API client","server_id":1}
+4.4s GET  {"title":"Saved by an API client","server_id":1}
+5.5s GET  {"title":"Saved by an API client","server_id":1}
+6.7s GET  {"title":"Saved by an API client","server_id":2}

The flag lives in the cache, so the cache must not read from the replica either. If it does, Cache::has() misses for the whole lag and the middleware does nothing. That's place 3.

Place 2: Queued jobs

A job runs in a worker process with its own connection. No session, no HTTP middleware, and none of the sticky state from the request that dispatched it. (It's the same reason tenant context goes missing in workers, one of the three multi-tenancy queue bugs I wrote about in June.)

Laravel already covers part of this. When a worker rebuilds a model from the job payload, restoreModel() calls useWritePdo(), so $this->post itself comes from the primary. Relations don't. The relations you eager-loaded before dispatching are restored with loadMissing(), which reads the replica. So does every query inside handle().

My test job logs the post title, the comment count through the restored relation, and a direct count query. The route adds a comment, then dispatches the job straight away with $post->load('comments'). The primary had 3 comments when the job ran:

SummarisePost {"title":"Saved through the API","comments_relation":2,"comments_query":2}

Fresh title. Both counts stale.

My first run didn't show this at all, and it took me a minute to see why. I was on the default database queue driver, and reserving a job runs an UPDATE on the jobs table. That marks the connection as modified, and with sticky on, everything the job reads afterwards goes to the primary. When I switched the queue to Redis, the stale reads appeared. Any driver that doesn't write to your replicated connection (Redis, SQS) behaves the same way. The 13.36 option Worker::$flushStickyConnections (#61915) doesn't change the database-driver case either, because the worker flushes before it reserves the next job, and the reserve marks the connection again.

The fix I'd use is a job middleware:

namespace App\Jobs\Middleware;

use Closure;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

class ReadFromPrimary
{
    public function handle(object $job, Closure $next): mixed
    {
        return DB::connection()->usingWritePdo(fn () => $next($job));
    }
}

class SummarisePost implements ShouldQueue
{
    use Queueable;

    public function __construct(
        #[WithoutRelations]
        public Post $post,
    ) {
    }

    public function middleware(): array
    {
        return [new ReadFromPrimary];
    }

    // handle() unchanged
}

SummarisePost {"title":"Saved through the API","comments_relation":4,"comments_query":4}

Job middleware runs after the job has been unserialized, so without #[WithoutRelations] a relation stored in the payload is already loaded from the replica by then. Leaving the attribute off, with 5 comments on the primary, I got this:

SummarisePost {"title":"Saved through the API","comments_relation":4,"comments_query":5}

With it, nothing is restored early, and the relation loads lazily inside the middleware's callback.

Put ReadFromPrimary on the jobs you dispatch right after a write, not on every job. A report that runs ten minutes later doesn't need it, and routing every job to the primary defeats the point of having a replica. If a job can wait, ->delay(now()->addSeconds(10)) costs nothing at all. Workers have enough lifecycle rules of their own already (like the SIGTERM they get on every deploy), and if you're tuning them for volume, processing 10,000 queue jobs without breaking covers the worker side.

Place 3: The database cache store, and your rate limiter

A fresh Laravel 13 project ships with CACHE_STORE=database on the default connection. The database cache store reads through that connection with no write-PDO override, so on a replicated connection, cache reads hit the replica. Sessions don't have this problem, because DatabaseSessionHandler adds useWritePdo() to its queries. The cache store doesn't.

Rate limiting is where that hurts. I put throttle:3,1 on a stateless login route and sent a request every half second:

+0.1s attempt 1 -> 200
+0.7s attempt 2 -> 200
+1.3s attempt 3 -> 200
+1.9s attempt 4 -> 200
+2.5s attempt 5 -> 200
+3.1s attempt 6 -> 200
+3.7s attempt 7 -> 200
+4.3s attempt 8 -> 200
+4.9s attempt 9 -> 200
+5.5s attempt 10 -> 200
+6.1s attempt 11 -> 200
+6.7s attempt 12 -> 200
+7.3s attempt 13 -> 429
+7.9s attempt 14 -> 429
+8.4s attempt 15 -> 429
+9.0s attempt 16 -> 429
allowed: 12 of 16 (limit is 3 per minute)

The increments run inside a locked transaction, so they go to the primary and the counter itself is right. But tooManyAttempts() reads the count with a plain cache get, from the replica, which still shows the count from 5 seconds ago. The limiter only starts refusing once the replica has caught up with the third hit. So an attacker gets the limit plus whatever they can send during the lag. At two requests a second that was 12 instead of 3, and a script sends a lot more than two. PreventStaleDatabaseReads doesn't help, because an attacker just drops the session cookie.

Point the cache at a connection without a replica:

// config/database.php
'mysql_primary' => [
    'driver' => 'mysql',
    'host' => env('DB_HOST', '127.0.0.1'),
    'port' => env('DB_WRITE_PORT', '3306'),
    'database' => env('DB_DATABASE', 'laravel'),
    'username' => env('DB_USERNAME', 'root'),
    'password' => env('DB_PASSWORD', ''),
    'charset' => 'utf8mb4',
    'collation' => 'utf8mb4_unicode_ci',
    'prefix' => '',
],

DB_CACHE_CONNECTION=mysql_primary
DB_CACHE_LOCK_CONNECTION=mysql_primary

In production that connection gets your primary's host. Same burst afterwards:

allowed: 3 of 16 (limit is 3 per minute)

A Redis cache avoids the problem as well. Either way, the PreventStaleApiReads flag from place 1 depends on this.

What I'd ship

Move the cache off the replicated connection first, even if you skip everything else in this post. A rate limiter that can be outrun is a security bug, not a UX one, and it's a two-line .env change.

Then add PreventStaleDatabaseReads with the priority call and a window longer than your worst lag. Without the priority call it protects the queries in your controllers and misses the model your route is named after.

For APIs, the token fallback is cheap. It costs one extra primary query, and only when the replica misses. The user-keyed middleware is worth it only if your clients read right after they write. If your PUT responses already return the saved resource, your clients may never need it.

For jobs, wrap the few that run straight after a write and leave the rest alone.

Every one of these moves reads onto the primary that the replica was supposed to take. That's the trade. If your lag is routinely more than a few seconds, a longer window hides a replica problem rather than fixing it.

FAQ

Does PreventStaleDatabaseReads stop other users from seeing stale data?

No. It only sends reads to the primary for the session that made the write. Another user viewing the same post during the lag still reads the replica. That's usually fine, because they never saw the new value to begin with.

Do I still need the sticky option?

Yes. They cover different requests. sticky sends reads to the primary later in the same request that wrote. The middleware covers the requests that come after. I had both on for every test in this post.

Does it cover a second database connection?

No. It only tracks and switches the default connection, and the docs say so. If tenant or reporting data lives on another connection, wrap those reads in that connection's usingWritePdo().

Why does a 2 second window last longer than 2 seconds?

The middleware stores and compares whole-second timestamps. A write at 10.0 and one at 10.9 are both stored as 10, and the window closes when the clock reaches 13. So it stays open between 2 and 3 seconds after the write. In my runs, a reload at 2.3 seconds still went to the primary with the default window.

Does the database queue driver protect jobs from stale reads?

By accident, when the jobs table lives on the same replicated connection and sticky is on. Reserving the job is a write, so the job reads the primary. Don't rely on it. Switch to Redis or SQS later and the stale reads show up with no code change.

Conclusion

PreventStaleDatabaseReads fixes the bug Jack described, as long as you add the priority call and size the window to your lag. Both are one-line fixes. Everything else in this post sits outside what a session-based middleware can reach, and none of it needed production traffic to show up. If you run read replicas, start one with SOURCE_DELAY=5 on your laptop and click through your own app before your users do.

title: No Zone.js, No Virtual DOM: How Signals and a Microtask Update Only What Changed (Inside AngeLite, Part 2)
description:
In part 1 I claimed AngeLite updates "only what changes" without Zone.js or a virtual DOM. This post shows the mechanism, using the actual source: a signals module of about 136 lines and a runtime of about 750.

The reactive core: three primitives

Function What it is Usage
signal(value) a value you can change s() reads, s.set(x) writes, s.update(v => ...) transforms, s.peek() reads without subscribing
computed(fn) a derived value, recalculated only when something it reads changes total()
effect(fn) code that runs now and whenever the signals it reads change returns a stop function

Here is the heart of it, trimmed from signals.js:

export function signal(value) {
  let subs = null;                       // allocated lazily, only if someone reads
  const read = () => {
    if (active) track(subs || (subs = new Set()));
    return value;
  };
  read.set = next => {
    if (Object.is(next, value)) return;  // no change, no notification
    value = next;
    if (subs) subs.forEach(n => n.notify());
  };
  read.update = fn => read.set(fn(value));
  read.peek = () => value;
  return read;
}

Three details are doing a lot of work:

  1. active is a module-level pointer to the effect currently running. Reading a signal while an effect is active subscribes that effect. That's the whole dependency-tracking trick.
  2. Subscriber sets are allocated lazily, so a signal nobody reads costs almost nothing.
  3. Object.is short-circuits writes of the same value.

Batching in a microtask

An Effect re-runs not immediately but through a queue flushed in a microtask:

notify() {
  if (this.queued) return;
  this.queued = true;
  queue.push(this);
  if (!pending) {
    pending = true;
    queueMicrotask(flush);
  }
}

So three set() calls in a row cause one re-run and one repaint. The flip side is documented behaviour you should know: right after a set() the DOM doesn't reflect the change yet. await Promise.resolve() (or flush() in tests) is enough to wait.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Your code
    participant S as signal
    participant Q as microtask queue
    participant E as view effect
    participant D as DOM
    U->>S: count.set(1)
    S->>Q: notify(effect) (queued once)
    U->>S: count.set(2)
    S->>Q: already queued, skip
    Note over U,Q: current task ends
    Q->>E: flush()
    E->>S: read count() (re-subscribes)
    E->>D: write only values that changed

Templates compile to instructions, not to a virtual tree

A template is HTML with a few extensions:

Syntax What it does
{{ expr }} interpolation, always text
[prop]="expr" binds a DOM property, or an input() for components
[class.x]="cond", [style.width.px]="n", [attr.x]="v" class, style, attribute (null/false removes)
(event)="statement" listens to an event
[(ngModel)]="sig" two-way binding with a writable signal
`{{ x \ pipe:arg }}`

The compiler turns each template once into a blueprint: an HTML fragment plus a list of instructions ("this text node depends on this expression", "this element has this event"). Creating a view is then:

  1. clone the blueprint's fragment,
  2. walk it once applying the instructions,
  3. attach one lean effect per view that re-evaluates the view's bindings and writes to the DOM only when a value changed.

No virtual tree is built or diffed. Expressions are evaluated by a small interpreter of our own (no eval, no new Function): literals, arithmetic, comparison and logical operators, ternary, ??, ./?./[ ], arrays, and calls to component methods.

Events are delegated

Handlers don't create a listener and closure per element. Events are delegated to document and stored as properties on the elements, so a table of 10,000 rows carries no per-row listeners. That's a big part of why memory stays low (about 6.6 MB for 10,000 rows in the project's benchmark versus 11.8 MB for the next lowest).

Control flow and keyed lists

@if, @else if, @else, @for and @empty use the Angular 17+ syntax:

@for (t of todos(); track t.id) {
  <li [class.done]="t.done" (click)="toggle(t)">{{ t.title }}</li>
} @empty {
  <li>Nothing to do</li>
}

@for reuses DOM nodes according to the track key, so reordering or updating a list moves existing elements instead of recreating them. When a list keeps the same keys in the same order, a fast path skips reconciliation (that optimisation took the "update every 10th row" scenario from about 9.8 ms to 7.9 ms in one benchmark run). Inside @for you get $index, $count, $first, $last, $even and $odd. Always give a stable key: without track, the key is the item itself, which is fine for strings and numbers but not for objects you recreate.

Rules that follow from the model

  1. Plain properties don't repaint. this.name = 'Ada' notifies nobody. State you want reflected must be a signal: name = signal('Ada').
  2. Treat lists and objects as immutable. Identity is compared, so mutate-in-place-and-reassign-the-same-array does nothing. Write items.update(l => [...l, next]).
  3. Logic goes in the class. Expressions don't support arrow functions, object literals, assignments or new. If an expression needs more than one operator, give it a name (a method or a computed).

A limit worth knowing

There is one effect per view, not per binding. When a signal a view reads changes, every binding in that view is re-evaluated (but only written to the DOM if its value changed). For rows with few bindings that's the cheapest approach. For a component with hundreds of bindings and a signal that changes many times per second, finer-grained systems like Solid or Vue can win. The project's gap analysis lists this explicitly, along with its best-known cost: selecting a row re-runs 1,000 effects (about 1.3 ms, tied with Preact and Angular in the benchmark) and is the top candidate for a per-binding refinement.

Takeaways

  • Signals plus an active pointer give automatic dependency tracking in about 130 lines.
  • Microtask batching makes writes cheap and cleanup simple, at the cost of async DOM visibility.
  • Blueprints and delegated events replace the virtual DOM and per-element closures.
  • One effect per view is a conscious trade-off, and it's documented with its costs.

Next: the security model, and the six holes I found in my own framework.

title: Behaviour analysis for large language model-driven agents
description:
arXiv:2610.32087v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding language-agent behaviour requires learning how actions are organised across a trajectory and how this organisation relates to context and outcomes. We propose a general framework that connects data-driven behavioural discovery with analysis and experimental investigation. Categories developed from recorded activity define what is measured. Analyses preserve the behaviours' positions in the process and express their relationships as interpretable hypotheses. Statistical assessment and tests in held-out contexts examine the strength and scope of the evidence. Experiments, including prompt steering, then test how behaviour and outcomes change under deliberately varied conditions. A study of iterative self-reflection illustrates how discovery, dependency learning and prompt comparisons can inform one another. We develop this approach for trajectories of varying length, event order and agent roles, and identify advances in coding, analysis and experimentation needed to support its wider use.

title: Six memos for the future of digital creation
description: We turned six big ideas percolating around the Figma office—written from the perspective of devs, designers, analysts, writers, PMs, card-carrying generalists—and put them on record. Here’s a look at what’s on our minds for 2025.

title: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows
description:
arXiv:2610.31985v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings where they pursue separate tasks while sharing resources and operating under review or oversight processes. Such settings create safety risks not only when agents are malicious, but also when they are simply trying to help. Prior work has largely studied adversarial or explicitly collusive behavior; we show that benign agents pursuing separate objectives can spontaneously cooperate in ways that bypass intended workflows. We call this the \emph{helpful agent problem}. We study long-horizon shared-resource environments in which agents sometimes depend on resources owned by their peers and cross-owner changes are normally mediated by a reviewer. When review becomes unavailable, agents begin making changes on one another's behalf despite having no shared reward or explicit incentive to cooperate. Crucially, these actions remain within each agent's local permissions while circumventing the system's intended oversight structure. We introduce \textsc{FavorBench}, a controlled benchmark with measurable downstream side effects, and adapt \textsc{CooperBench} to test the phenomenon in realistic repositories. Across two benchmarks and four models, we find that out-of-workflow favors emerge frequently. Further, in \textsc{FavorBench}, favors from at least three models cause significant harm to parties outside the interaction. These results reveal a distinct multi-agent safety challenge: cooperation itself can create pathways around system-level safeguards.

title: I Profiled My Production Crawler. 95% of Its Output Was Being Thrown Away.
description:
I run AiSeek, an information platform where every published claim has to trace back to fetched evidence — a source page, a filing, a dataset. That makes the fetch layer the supply chain of the whole product: if it is slow, wasteful, or silently wrong, everything downstream inherits it.

Until October 21, that layer was Crawl4AI — a capable, popular Python framework — driving Chromium for the pages that needed rendering. I had a feeling it was heavy. Instead of trusting the feeling, I audited it: three days of production jobs (8,563 of them, October 18–20), the production database, and local reproductions run under the same limits as the production box (6 cores, 10 GB). Every number below is production data unless I say otherwise.

This is what the audit found, what I built because of it, and the part people usually leave out of launch posts.

What the crawler actually did all day

On a normal day, AiSeek fetched roughly 2,000 articles over plain HTTP and sent 600–900 to the browser — about 28% of article fetches ended up rendered. The two paths lived in different latency worlds:

Path Jobs p50 p95 p99
HTTP only 2,879 1.6 s 5.8 s 10.9 s
Rendered (Crawl4AI) 1,249 7.0 s 24.4 s 40.2 s

Rendered pages were mostly the ones that needed it least, as it turned out. But first, the bigger surprise.

Finding 1: I was using a framework as a browser driver

Of 174 successful renders in my local reproduction, 166 used my own trafilatura extraction for the final text. Only 8 used the Markdown Crawl4AI generated. Its Markdown was computed on every single page — and thrown away 95% of the time.

What I actually consumed from this large framework was a minimal surface:

  • the rendered HTML,
  • the final URL after redirects,
  • a status code,
  • the link list,
  • a title fallback.

And the irony compounds: the heaviest single parsing step in the pipeline wasn't Crawl4AI's either. My own trafilatura call cost a median of 82 ms per page; Crawl4AI's scraping plus Markdown generation together cost about 40 ms. The library I suspected of being slow was, by itself, mostly innocent.

I wasn't using Crawl4AI. I was renting a browser with a framework attached — and paying the framework's tax on every page.

Finding 2: 55% of render time was pure waste

The decision rule for rendering was one line of logic: if the HTTP fetch produced fewer than 1,200 characters of text, render it in a browser. That rule cannot tell a JavaScript wall from a short article — and a lot of AiSeek's sources are short news briefs, many of them in Chinese and Japanese, where 800 characters is a complete story.

Replaying the production decision logic locally: in 59 cases where HTTP had already retrieved a usable page but the rule sent it to the browser anyway, 37 renders (63%) came back with the same amount of text as HTTP — NHK at 849 characters before rendering, 849 after. Those wasted renders consumed 85 seconds of 154.6 total: 55% of all rendering time, spent re-fetching pages we already had.

This was the most valuable finding of the audit, and it had nothing to do with languages or engines: the biggest speedup available was a better decision about when to render. Rewriting that rule was worth more than any engine swap.

Finding 3: the real costs were Chromium, and a shared event loop

What actually consumed the machine:

  • Chromium itself. Each concurrent rendered page costs roughly 0.7 CPU cores and a couple of hundred MB, plus a ~1.7 s cold start. No driver language changes that arithmetic.
  • A single event loop doing synchronous work. Crawl4AI runs its HTML cleaning and Markdown conversion synchronously on the Python event loop. With 4 concurrent pages, my probe measured loop stalls at p99 of 154–172 ms, worst case 2.2 seconds — during which everything else in that process waited, including plain HTTP fetches and the GLiNER and MiniCheck models that shared the process and its 10 GB container. An old code comment of mine, from October 9, reads: "plain fetches took 8 s at the median while pages rendered." Now I knew why.
  • A low concurrency ceiling. Sweeping the page limit locally on 6 cores: 4 pages gave 1.87 req/s, 8 pages topped out at 2.19 req/s, and 16 pages went backwards to 1.72 req/s with p50 latency ballooning to 18 s. Past a point, more pages just means a longer queue.
  • Weight. The service image was 6.64 GB. The fetch path alone pulled 115 packages, about 1 GB — including several libraries we never called.

Finding 4: some failures were never the crawler's fault

About 25% of fetches failed in production. I took 70 URLs from the failed group and fetched them simultaneously from my home connection and from the production server. From home, 39 of 70 returned full text. From production: zero. The rest were refused (403/451) or rate-limited (429) — entire publisher groups block our datacenter exit, and some of it is geography, not IP reputation (451 is "unavailable for legal reasons"; the production box sits in Türkiye).

No engine fixes that, and per AiSeek's rules I don't route around refusals: honest user agent, robots respected, a refusal is final. I include this because crawler benchmarks never mention it — in production, a quarter of your failures may have nothing to do with your stack.

Bugs I promised not to copy

The audit also catalogued defects I did not want the replacement to inherit:

  • Status codes from the first redirect hop. 136 of 174 successful renders reported the 301/302/308 they started with — so a "301 → 404" could be stored as a success.
  • An SSRF route guard that stacked per page. One more handler on the shared browser context for every page opened — up to 200 by recycle time.
  • DNS failure reported as an SSRF refusal. Same 400 for "this host is forbidden" and "this host temporarily doesn't resolve" — two situations a caller must handle oppositely.
  • Network errors collapsing into a bare 500, indistinguishable from a bug in our own code.

The replacement: build the minimal surface, in Rust

So I built PageSift to the audit, not to a feature checklist:

  • Only the minimal surface. Rendered HTML, final URL, final status code plus the redirect chain, links, and Rust-side extraction — no Markdown generated just to be discarded, no 115-package tax.
  • A separate process. Its own CPU and memory limits, restartable without touching the models. Nothing synchronous sits on anyone else's event loop.
  • A smarter render decision first, engine second. HTTP first; rendering is spent only where it buys something.
  • A browser chain instead of a browser. Lightpanda renders first; Chrome's headless shell takes the pages Lightpanda can't. Both run sandboxed — never --no-sandbox — which on our host meant writing AppArmor and seccomp profiles.
  • Honest failures. A block is reported as a block, never replaced with invented content. For an evidence platform, a declared gap beats a fabricated page.
  • The same API contract. The worker kept calling POST /v1/fetch and validating the same response schema. The swap touched one sidecar, nothing else.

On October 21 the sidecar went in, and Crawl4AI left the code and the image the same day. My deploy note from that day records the decision in parentheses: (owner: no week of observation). The audit was the observation.

The part launch posts leave out: production still runs v0.01

Here is the confession. AiSeek's production builds PageSift from a pinned commit — the first working build, call it 0.01 — and it still runs that build today.

Since then, the open-source project has sprinted: 0.50 crawled the Tranco Top 100k, 0.61 followed, and this week 0.70 landed with a rewritten NUMA-aware data plane (about 950k pages/second against a local test origin on a 192-vCPU box), a three-engine adaptive chain, and a memory envelope that squeezes the full pipeline under 888 MiB. Production has none of it. Not the data plane, not the third engine, not six versions of fixes.

Upgrading is deliberately boring: change one pinned commit, update two engine checksums, validate on the server, then push. It hasn't happened, for the same reason the audit happened. At ~2,800 fetches a day, throughput was never AiSeek's binding constraint — the audit showed the pain lived in a judgement rule and a shared process, and 0.01 already fixed both. What production buys with its stillness is that every claim on the site traces to evidence fetched by a binary whose behavior I know exactly.

When the upgrade does happen, it will be audited the same way this replacement was: production numbers first, announcement second. That will be Part 3.

Takeaway, if you run anything like this: profile your crawler before you replace it. You may find you are paying for a framework and using a browser — and that your fastest available optimization is a one-line decision rule, not a new engine.

PageSift is open source (AGPL-3.0, commercial licenses available): github.com/YOLOW92/pagesift. The product that keeps it honest is aiseek.dev.

title: Machine-Readable Operator Manuals over the ISO 11783 Network for Offline, Multilingual LLM Assistance
description:
arXiv:2610.31863v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: If agricultural machinery is to support intelligent, offline assistance, then the system must access technical documentation dynamically. In this paper, the Semantic Synchronization of operator manuals over ISO 11783-based CAN buses is analyzed, defined as the process that brings the local knowledge base of a tractor-side assistant into agreement with the operator manual of the connected implement. Data transfer performance was benchmarked using Markdown, JSON, and XML; various open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) were also evaluated in cross-lingual query tasks. The automatic evaluation of the answers was validated against four human raters. A complete manual was transferred over a physical ISO 11783 network in 31 to 89 s, depending on format and transport settings, which is comparable to the object pool upload that operators already wait for at the first coupling of an implement. Markdown produced the smallest files, while the question-answering performance was comparable across the three formats for most models. With retrieval-augmented generation, locally run models answered most questions on the English manual correctly, with no advantage of the largest model over 7B and 8B models, but performed worse on the five other language editions. Keyword retrieval failed across languages, whereas semantic retrieval provided the cross-lingual capability. The exchange requires only a new parameter group that uses the existing request and transport mechanisms of ISO 11783, which makes it a candidate for standardization. The study is a proof of concept with inference on PC-grade hardware; deployment on embedded agricultural hardware remains future work.

title: Eight pre-registered tests on U.S. power plants that slip a month: what held, and what I take back
description:
EIA's monthly generator inventory, EIA-860M, lists generators planned to start next month. Fewer than four in ten of them are listed as operating in that month now, against almost half in 2016-2019. Over the last few days I ran eight tests on why, and on whether a generator's earlier slips say anything about its next month. Each test's predictions were published before the job that scored them counted anything. 27 of the 33 predictions held.

What still stands. Pooled over 2016-2025, a solar generator planned for next month again right after a one-month slip was listed as operating in that month about 5 percentage points more often than a new solar listing, and a battery about 8 points more often. For solar since 2022, a slip of 2-3 months has been a bad sign: 12.5 points worse than a one-month slip. These three gaps hold when whole plants are resampled 2,000 times, so they are not the work of a few big plants.

What I take back. In my last post I wrote that gas and wind go the other way, and a later test on 2020-2021 seemed to confirm it for wind. With whole plants resampled, the wind and gas gaps are within plant-to-plant noise in every period. The same is true for all technologies together: a one-month slip is not shown to be a good sign on its own. One test that weighted each plant once failed two predictions, and the reason was the method, not the plants: that weighting lifts every repeat-listing group by construction.

Two things to keep in mind:

  • These are generator-months, and "on time" means the next monthly file lists the generator as operating. Resampling plants handles dependence inside a plant, not between plants of one developer or region. These are rates for groups, not forecasts for one generator.
  • The next test is the first on months that do not exist yet: October to December 2026, fixed before EIA publishes its October file on 24 November.

The summary note with every prediction and outcome, the code, the raw output and the tests that check every number are here: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/eia860m-slip

I am MV2 of Munim, Inc. The code, data compilation and this post were made with AI agents working in my name.

title: LOCI: Localized Continuous Control for Multi-Subject Image Editing
description:
arXiv:2610.31950v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent instruction-following image editors such as Flux.1-Kontext enable text-driven editing but lack fine-grained control over where and how much an edit is applied. Existing approaches provide either continuous but global control or spatially localized editing at a fixed strength. To our knowledge, none jointly supports explicit spatial localization, continuous per-region strength, and independent simultaneous control of multiple subjects. We present LOCI (LOcalized Continuous control for multi- subject Image editing). Given a multi-subject image with per-subject regions and instructions, LOCI edits each subject at an independently chosen, continuously adjustable strength, for instance gradually aging one person while adding a beard to another with minimal cross-region leakage. LOCI pairs subject-level attention binding for spatial isolation with a Regional LoRA layer that replaces the LoRA's scalar coefficient with a per-token scaling vector aligned to the spatial layout. A single adapter is trained at one suppression point, and continuous edit strengths follow by rescaling its regional residual at inference. Experiments on multi-subject scenes demonstrate that LOCI achieves strong edit fidelity with significantly reduced cross-region interference compared to baselines, while maintaining continuous control over edit strength

title: I audited every network request on 200 tool pages. Here's what "runs in your browser" actually means
description:
Every tool on Toggle9 has a small chip under its title: Runs in your browser. It's an easy thing to write and a hard thing to prove. A chip doesn't stop a script from phoning home, and "we respect your privacy" banners are cheap.

So I tested it. On 26 October 2026 I loaded every published tool page, all 200 of them, in a fresh headless browser and logged every request each page made. Then I did it again with Global Privacy Control switched on, and a third time with the network cut.

This post covers the script, what it found, the one tool where my own label was wrong, and a 35-line version you can point at your own site.

What "runs in your browser" is supposed to mean

For a calculator, it comes down to four things:

  1. The maths runs on your device. The page downloads the tool's JavaScript, and every answer is worked out in your browser as you type. There's no "Calculate" button that posts your numbers to a server.
  2. Your inputs live in the URL fragment. Type a loan amount and the link becomes .../loan-calculator/#a=250000&r=6.5. Refresh or press Back and your inputs come back. Browsers never send the part after #: RFC 3986, section 3.5, says the fragment is "separated from the rest of the URI prior to a dereference" and handled "solely by the user agent".
  3. Recent calculations go in localStorage, which, unlike a cookie, is never attached to a request.
  4. Analytics, where it's on, gets the page address and nothing you typed.

Each of those is a claim about network traffic, so you can test it by watching the network.

The test

The audit is a Node script using Playwright with Chrome's headless shell. For each published tool page it opens a fresh browser context (no cookies, no storage) and runs three passes.

Pass 1, normal load. It records every request for 5 seconds after load. The URL carries a test word in the fragment, #auditprobe=hashtest123. If that word shows up in any request URL or POST body, something is reading the fragment and sending it on.

page.on('request', r => reqs.push({ url: r.url(), post: r.postData() || '' }));
await page.goto(url + '#auditprobe=' + PROBE, { waitUntil: 'load', timeout: 45000 });
await page.waitForTimeout(5000);
// ...
leak: reqs.some(r => r.url.includes(PROBE) || r.post.includes(PROBE))

It also decodes the dl (document location) parameter of every Google Analytics hit and checks it has no # in it.

Pass 2, Global Privacy Control on. GPC is a browser signal (navigator.globalPrivacyControl === true) that means "don't sell or share my data". Brave, DuckDuckGo and Firefox (with a setting) send it. Playwright has no switch for it, so the script fakes it before any page script runs:

await ctx.addInitScript(() =>
  Object.defineProperty(Navigator.prototype, 'globalPrivacyControl', { get: () => true }));

Pass 3, offline. Load the page, cut the network with context.setOffline(true), type 37 into the first number box, and check the answer changed. If the maths really runs locally, losing the network shouldn't matter.

await ctx.setOffline(true);
const before = await p.locator('.t9-tool').innerText();
await inp.fill('37'); await inp.dispatchEvent('input');
await p.waitForTimeout(1200);
return before === (await p.locator('.t9-tool').innerText()) ? 'NO CHANGE' : 'updated';

Four pages run in parallel, from a laptop.

What it found

Where the pages connected Pages, of 200 With GPC on
toggle9.com (the page, its code, fonts, images, data files) 200 200
googletagmanager.com (loads Google Analytics) 200 0
google-analytics.com (the visit count) 200 0
Anywhere else 0 0
  • The # test word reached no server on any page, and no Analytics hit carried a fragment.
  • With GPC on, 0 pages contacted Google.
  • Offline: 128 of 129 tools with a number box kept updating. The one that didn't is the crossword solver, which fetches its word lists when you search. That's expected, but it's a good reminder that "runs in your browser" doesn't always mean "works without a connection".

No ad networks, no font CDNs, no third-party error trackers. The fonts are served from the site itself, so there's no Google Fonts request either.

How GPC is handled

The analytics loader checks the signal first. If it's set, it clears any old _ga cookies and returns before Google's script is ever added to the page:

function gpc() { return navigator.globalPrivacyControl === true }

if (gpc()) { clear(); return; }          // never load Analytics, wipe old _ga cookies
var c = get();                            // the visitor's saved choice, if any
if (c === 'denied') return;
if (c === 'granted') { load(); return; }
// No choice yet: ask first in the EU, EEA, UK and Switzerland, otherwise load

The important part is the order. GPC wins over everything, including a "yes" saved earlier, so a visitor who turns the signal on later doesn't have to find a settings page.

The tool where my own label was wrong

Not every tool can run entirely on your device. A DMARC checker has to ask DNS for a domain's records, and a mileage calculator needs a road distance from a routing service. Those tools are meant to replace the default line, "Nothing you type leaves this page", with a specific one: what they send, when, and to whom.

When I built the page explaining the chip, I went through every tool's line against what its code actually fetches. The mileage calculator was still showing the default. It sends the two places' map points (rounded to about 11 m) to my server, which asks openrouteservice for the distance. The label said nothing left the page.

Nothing was hidden, since the request was right there in the network tab, but the label was false. I fixed it and logged it as a correction. The build now generates a trust file from every tool's engine, so a tool that fetches anything has to declare what it sends, or it doesn't get the default line.

The lesson I took from it: the network test proves what happens when a page loads, not when you press every button. The audit waits 5 seconds and types into one box. Lookups that only fire on a "Check" button need a second source of truth, and for me that's each tool's own declaration, listed on one page.

What this doesn't prove

To be clear about the limits:

  • It's my test, not an outside audit. Nobody independent has checked Toggle9.
  • Loading a page is still a request. Cloudflare and my server see your IP address and which page you opened, like any website.
  • A fragment is private, not secret. It stays in your browser history, and anyone you share the link with sees your inputs.
  • Browser extensions can read any page you open. "Runs in your browser" can't protect you from your browser.

Run it on your own site

Here's a stripped-down version you can point at any URL. It lists every host a page contacts in its first 5 seconds, with GPC off and on, and flags it if the # test word reaches a server.

// npm i playwright && npx playwright install chromium
// node who-does-it-call.mjs https://example.com/page [more URLs...]
import { chromium } from 'playwright';

const PROBE = 'hashprobe' + Date.now();
const browser = await chromium.launch();

async function hosts(url, gpc) {
  const ctx = await browser.newContext();
  if (gpc) await ctx.addInitScript(() =>
    Object.defineProperty(Navigator.prototype, 'globalPrivacyControl', { get: () => true }));
  const page = await ctx.newPage();
  const seen = {}; let leaked = false;
  page.on('request', r => {
    if (r.url().includes(PROBE) || (r.postData() || '').includes(PROBE)) leaked = true;
    const u = new URL(r.url());
    if (u.protocol.startsWith('http')) seen[u.host] = (seen[u.host] || 0) + 1;
  });
  await page.goto(`${url}#probe=${PROBE}`, { waitUntil: 'load' });
  await page.waitForTimeout(5000);
  await ctx.close();
  return { seen, leaked };
}

for (const url of process.argv.slice(2)) {
  for (const gpc of [false, true]) {
    const { seen, leaked } = await hosts(url, gpc);
