    console.log(`\n${url}  (GPC ${gpc ? 'on' : 'off'})${leaked ? '  ⚠ # word reached a server' : ''}`);
    for (const [h, n] of Object.entries(seen).sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1])) console.log(`  ${String(n).padStart(3)}  ${h}`);
  }
}
await browser.close();

On one of my pages it prints:

https://toggle9.com/compound-interest-calculator/  (GPC off)
   20  toggle9.com
    2  www.google-analytics.com
    1  www.googletagmanager.com

https://toggle9.com/compound-interest-calculator/  (GPC on)
   19  toggle9.com

Try it on a site you use every day. The list is often longer than you'd guess.

The full results for every tool, with each one's own line about what it sends, are on What "runs in your browser" means.

Have you ever run something like this on your own site? I'd like to know what turned up, especially anything you didn't expect to find.

title: Training an MoE LLM in MXFP4: How We Closed the Gap to BF16
description:
arXiv:2610.32229v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) in sub-8-bit arithmetic promises substantial gains in memory bandwidth and compute throughput, yet FP4 formats introduce quantization error severe enough to destabilize optimization if left unaddressed. We present ALTO, an open-source training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B, a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark under the MXFP4 microscaling format. The recipe combines established techniques from Abecassis, Felix et al. [arXiv:2509.25149] (hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, and stochastic rounding) with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme adapted from TetraJet-v2 [arXiv:2510.27527]. On C4 validation at global batch size 16, MXFP4 + RHT + SR + de-oscillation reaches a validation loss of 3.3350 at 16,128 steps, only 0.007 above the BF16 baseline (3.3283), closing roughly 50% of the gap left by MXFP4 without de-oscillation (3.3418). Measured by steps to reach the MLPerf quality target (validation loss 3.34), de-oscillation cuts the FP4 convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0%. We also report negative end-to-end results from differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling, despite each showing operator-level SNR gains. All experiments use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 hardware and wall-clock speed has not been optimized.

title: ACWM-RM: A Reference-Free Reward Model from Complementary Mismatch Preferences
description:
arXiv:2610.32222v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning has gained attention for improving action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), as it enables reward-driven optimization of visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF) beyond flow-matching optimization. Realizing this potential requires reward signals that reliably rank videos by both VQ and AF. However, existing rewards capture only one dimension: metric-based rewards assess VQ but require ground-truth videos and do not directly assess AF, while inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards assess AF without references but do not guarantee VQ. Moreover, IDMs, typically trained on real videos, may provide unreliable rewards for generated videos containing visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies. In this work, we introduce the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs that evaluate how reliably IDMs assess AF on real and generated videos. We then propose ACWM-RM, a reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF without ground-truth videos during reward computation. To train it, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs providing complementary supervision: action-mismatch pairs supervise AF, while video-mismatch pairs supervise VQ and expose the model to generated videos. We then pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on real videos to learn forward dynamics before jointly training it with a patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref to transfer these dynamics to AF assessment on generated videos. Evaluation on AVM-Eval reveals the limited reliability of IDMs on generated videos, while downstream RL experiments show that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in both criteria.

title: How to create this kind of hero animation using Codex—pure code, no video generation models needed.
description:
I recently built a homepage demo animation for Swayno, and the entire process was completed inside Codex.

My workflow: Find references → Generate a satisfactory image → Have Codex build the animation.

Here is the exact step-by-step breakdown.

  1. Find References & Lock in the Direction First, figure out what the hero animation needs to communicate.

For example, Swayno is an AI content marketing tool with a core workflow of: Input URL → AI generates content → Output short-form videos → Publish to social platforms.

An assembly-line style animation fits this concept well. I gathered several reference images of robotic arms, machines, and conveyor belts, and sent them to Codex for analysis.

  1. Generate the Base Image in Codex I wanted the scene to feature an AI generation machine where URL cards enter from the left, pass through the machine to turn into short-form videos, and are then distributed by a robotic arm to various social platforms.

At this stage, focus purely on the static look—don't rush into animation yet.

Iterate until you are happy with the visual, then have Codex build the animation based on that final approved image.

  1. Turn the Image into Code-Driven Animation with Codex
    Describe the complete motion sequence, such as: URL enters machine → Machine starts generating → Video cards emerge → Robotic arm distributes content → Reset to initial state.
    Have Codex build a previewable version first, then tweak it based on how it actually looks in motion.

  2. Export the Video & Embed on the Homepage
    Once the animation is locked in, ask Codex to export the video and a poster image.

I ended up using a 15-second, 1080p, 30fps silent MP4, set to autoplay on a loop on the homepage.
I initially tried 4K, but switched to a smaller 1080p file for faster web loading.

Finally, test how it renders on both desktop and mobile, and make sure the loop point feels seamless.

Appendix: My Animation Prompt for Codex
Using the approved reference image I uploaded as the visual baseline, write code to create a previewable, video-exportable looping homepage animation.

Maintain the composition, camera angle, materials, brand colors, and element proportions of the approved image. Use the original logo, platform icons, and content assets I provided.

First, analyze the elements that need independent motion, choose the appropriate technical implementation, and provide a complete runnable project with instructions on how to preview it.

Total animation duration: 15 seconds. Motion sequence:

0–3s: The left robotic arm grabs a URL card and places it onto the conveyor belt entrance. The conveyor belt carries the card into the generation machine.

3–5s: Soft green lighting glows inside the machine to indicate content generation in progress.

5–8s: Three vertical content cards emerge one by one from the machine's exit and move along the conveyor belt. The content area must strictly maintain a 9:16 aspect ratio.

8–13s: The right robotic arm picks up the content cards one after another and delivers them to the TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube receiving zones. Add a few floating heart reactions that drift upward and fade out.

13–15s: The robotic arms return to their home positions, transitioning seamlessly into the next production cycle.

Motion Requirements:
The robotic arm must approach, lower, clamp shut, and only then lift and move.

Once clamped, the card must follow the gripper's movement; release the gripper only after placing the card down.

Apply natural easing (acceleration and deceleration) to all movements.

Avoid clipping, sudden jumps, card teleportation, or aspect ratio distortion.

All state resets must happen off-screen or in hidden areas so the loop transitions without any flicker or jump.

Keep the camera locked, with the background and main machine body completely stable.

title: AudioLift: Audio-Driven Single Image to Full-Head Gaussian Avatar via Multi-view Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.31747v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing 3D talking avatar methods mainly rely on parametric face models including 3DMM or FLAME, whose compact motion representations limit their ability to synthesize extreme expressions and to model accessories such as headwear. We introduce AudioLift, a two-stage framework that uses generated multi-view videos as the intermediate representation for audio-driven avatar generation without parametric face models or per-instance optimization. Our framework combines a synchronized multi-view video generation stage with an inconsistency-robust Gaussian reconstruction stage to recover coherent full-head geometry from a single portrait image. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AudioLift produces 3D talking avatars capable of capturing more extreme facial expressions than existing methods, with improved geometric completeness and strong multi-view consistency across the full $360^\circ$ viewing range.

title: LazyFlash: Forward-Dense, Backward-Sparse Attention for Accelerated Long-Context Fine-Tuning
description:
arXiv:2610.31911v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long sequences, attention becomes a major computational bottleneck. Sparse attention mostly targets inference, yet many methods still train densely or cannot support sparse training, and their added complexity makes sparsity hard to turn into wall-clock speedups, leaving dense attention widely used in practice. This paper introduces LazyFlash, a forward-dense, backward-sparse attention method built on the observation that attention training is dominated by the backward pass. LazyFlash keeps the forward pass exactly dense, so the trained model remains a standard dense model that existing systems such as vLLM can serve without any change. For the backward pass, LazyFlash proposes a gradient-aware block sparsification design that ranks query blocks by their attention-output gradient norms and skips those contributing negligibly to parameter updates, turning the dense backward into a block-sparse one. A gradient-mass budget adapts the amount of skipped computation to each head and training step, while importance sampling preserves the dense gradient in expectation. These designs are implemented inside the tiled FlashAttention backward kernel, where skipped blocks are never loaded or computed, translating gradient sparsity into real wall-clock acceleration. Experiments on long-context text and speech LLMs show that LazyFlash maintains downstream performance while achieving up to 5.7x attention-backward speedup over FlashAttention and 1.7x end-to-end training speedup.

title: DIAL-S2ST: Learning Latency Control for Simultaneous Speech-to-Speech Translation
description:
arXiv:2610.32214v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose DIAL-S2ST, a post-training method for learning inference-time latency control in simultaneous speech-to-speech translation models. Our approach reuses pretrained translation capabilities through self-distillation from lookahead predictions, while limiting the influence of large text distillation losses to account for the imitation gap. This provides supervision for earlier emission without paired target data or reward computation. To make the learned timing adjustable at inference, we jointly train a single LoRA adapter across scales with matched lookahead guidance. Experiments on French-to-English translation with Hibiki demonstrate that only 10 hours of source speech enable this adaptation, providing flexible latency control with a favorable quality-latency trade-off.

title: Node.js Audio Transcription: Preserving Structured CRM Actions Through Retries
description:
A transcription worker should treat audio transcription as an unreliable boundary, not as the place where CRM writes happen. Put that boundary behind a durable job, persist the source and an idempotency key, validate the returned text, and let a separate action step produce and apply structured CRM changes. Retries then repeat a replaceable artifact instead of creating duplicate tasks, contacts, or follow-ups.

Short answer: in a Node.js service, call transcription through a small adapter, store the transcript with a content hash, and make every downstream CRM mutation conditional on a stable call ID. The endpoint is configuration; retry and commit rules belong to your system. This is the difference between transcribing a sales call and safely turning that call into CRM work.

What should happen when transcription times out?

Assume a worker receives call_8f2c, a recording identifier, and a tenant identifier. It creates one job key from the tenant and call ID, checks whether a completed transcript already exists, and only then calls the transcription service. A timeout moves the job to a retryable state. It does not authorize a second CRM update.

The state machine can stay small: queued -> transcribing -> transcript_ready -> actions_validated -> actions_committed. A terminal needs_review state is useful when the audio is accepted but the structured action result fails validation. That state is a controlled refusal to write uncertain data into the system the sales team uses as a source of truth.

No guessing.

Keep the original audio reference, the hash of the bytes or object, the transcript, the transcript version, and the action result separately. Reprocessing should be able to replace a transcript without silently replacing a manually edited CRM action. I initially treated the transcript as the durable output and the CRM record as a projection. That was too loose. A projection can be rebuilt; a sales task that has already sent a notification has an external effect.

A narrow Node.js boundary with a durable job

The Node.js part should be boring. Accept a job, load the recording, call an adapter, persist the result, and acknowledge the queue only after the durable write. Keep provider-specific headers, multipart details, and model configuration inside the adapter. The queue worker gets one observable contract, and a provider change remains a bounded code change.

Keep it boring.

The following Go example shows the adapter shape and retry decision. The same boundary can sit behind a Node.js worker; the point is the contract, not a copy-paste client for one service.

package transcription

import (
  "context"
  "encoding/json"
  "errors"
  "fmt"
  "io"
  "net/http"
)

type Result struct { Text string `json:"text"`; Model string `json:"model"` }

type Client struct { HTTP *http.Client; URL string; Token string }

func (c Client) Transcribe(ctx context.Context, audio []byte, callID string) (Result, error) {
  if len(audio) == 0 { return Result{}, errors.New("empty audio") }
  req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, c.URL, io.NopCloser(nil))
  if err != nil { return Result{}, err }
  req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.Token)
  req.Header.Set("X-Call-ID", callID)
  res, err := c.HTTP.Do(req)
  if err != nil { return Result{}, err }
  defer res.Body.Close()
  if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests || res.StatusCode >= 500 {
    return Result{}, fmt.Errorf("retryable transcription status: %s", res.Status)
  }
  if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
    return Result{}, fmt.Errorf("permanent transcription status: %s", res.Status)
  }
  var out Result
  if err := json.NewDecoder(res.Body).Decode(&out); err != nil { return Result{}, err }
  if out.Text == "" { return Result{}, errors.New("transcription response has no text") }
  return out, nil
}

The example deliberately leaves request encoding to the adapter implementation. A real integration may need multipart encoding, a content type based on the recording, or a service-specific request schema. Those details must be tested against the selected service. The invariant is stronger: a successful adapter call returns a complete, persisted artifact, and a retryable response cannot advance the CRM commit.

Use bounded exponential backoff with jitter. Cap attempts and record the attempt number. A queue that retries forever converts one bad recording into a growing blind spot; a queue that retries once turns a temporary 502 into a missed sales follow-up. The cap must be explicit and visible in the runbook.

How should a Node.js Whisper audio transcription API handle CRM retries?

Do not ask a transcript parser to write directly to a CRM. First produce a small action document with a strict schema, then validate it before any mutation. For a sales call, the document can contain the call ID, requested actions, due dates when stated, and an evidence span or timestamp for each action. Unknown values should be null or absent according to the schema, never guessed from a convenient default.

package actions

import (
  "fmt"
  "strings"
)

type Action struct { Kind string `json:"kind"`; Description string `json:"description"`; Evidence string `json:"evidence"` }
type Document struct { CallID string `json:"call_id"`; Items []Action `json:"items"` }

func (d Document) Validate(expectedCallID string) error {
  if d.CallID == "" || d.CallID != expectedCallID { return fmt.Errorf("call_id does not match job") }
  for i, item := range d.Items {
    if item.Kind == "" || strings.TrimSpace(item.Description) == "" { return fmt.Errorf("action %d is incomplete", i) }
    if strings.TrimSpace(item.Evidence) == "" { return fmt.Errorf("action %d has no evidence", i) }
  }
  return nil
}

Validation is necessary but not sufficient. Check tenant ownership, allowlisted action kinds, parseable dates, and a sane action limit. Schema validation catches malformed output. Domain validation catches a valid document that should not be committed.

The commit operation must be idempotent. Give each action a deterministic key such as tenant_id + call_id + action_digest, and enforce uniqueness at the persistence layer. The worker can safely retry after losing the CRM response. If the CRM has no idempotency mechanism, use an outbox and a reconciliation record so the worker can distinguish an unknown result from a clean failure.

There is a real tradeoff here. Holding action commits for review improves correctness when the transcript is ambiguous, but it adds human latency and an operational queue. This pattern is a poor fit for a workflow that needs immediate, low-risk notes and has no durable store; a simpler append-only transcript may be the more honest boundary. It is a good fit when a mistaken task or notification has a larger cost than a delayed one.

Verification before the pager rings

Test the boundary as a failure matrix: a truncated recording, a valid response with empty text, a timeout after request acceptance, a rate-limit response, malformed actions, two workers processing one call, and a commit response lost after the server applied the change. The last case exposes duplicate delivery.

For the timeout case, keep the job in transcribing until the lease expires, then let one eligible worker retry it. For an empty transcript, stop at needs_review rather than treating an empty string as a successful call. For a lost commit response, query the outbox key before creating anything else. Those distinctions make the next page actionable instead of merely loud.

Log a correlation ID, tenant ID, call ID, attempt, state transition, duration, response class, and transcript version. Do not log raw audio or unredacted transcript text by default. Metrics should distinguish transcription latency from queue latency and validation rejection from provider failure. One combined “job failed” counter is not useful.

Run a replay in a staging tenant with fixed recordings and expected action documents. Compare semantic fields and evidence references, not incidental JSON key order. Keep a small corpus for changes to decoding, chunking, schema rules, and retry policy. Replaying the same call should produce the same idempotency keys.

Rollback is a data decision. Stop new action commits before rolling back code. Pause the action consumer, leave transcription artifacts available, and mark affected jobs for review. If the defect is in the adapter, replay from stored audio or a known transcript version. If it is in action mapping, select a bounded window and compare proposed mutations before release. In 2026, keeping a 20 MiB response or transcript limit explicit in the adapter is also useful: it prevents an unexpectedly large payload from turning an ordinary retry into a memory incident.

A transcript is useful evidence, not permission. Choose the transcription boundary that you can retry, inspect, and replace without duplicating an external action. For a Node.js sales-call pipeline, the durable job, transcript artifact, schema-validated action document, and idempotent commit matter more than a clever single-request example.

That is the line.

References

  • https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch
  • https://github.com/openai/tiktoken
  • https://nodejs.org/api/http.html
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457
  • https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/observability-primer/

title: How to Package Shared Python Libraries with pyproject.toml
description:
You ship the job. It passes CI. Then, a colleague runs it in a notebook environment, and suddenly your shared utility library throws an ImportError because it pulled in a different version of pandas than the one used in your orchestration layer.

Many data teams still manage shared code by appending directory paths to sys.path or bundling messy setup.py scripts that haven't been updated since the mid-2010s. This is a fragile architecture that invites inconsistency. If you want a robust data platform, you should stop treating your internal tooling like an afterthought and start packaging it as a proper Python distribution using pyproject.toml.

Why the common approach falls short

The "copy-paste-folder" or "sys.path.append" strategy is an engineering debt bomb. When you rely on environment-level path hacks, you lose the ability to manage versioning, track dependencies, and enforce consistent execution environments across local development, CI/CD runners, and production compute clusters.

Legacy setup.py files are equally problematic. They rely on arbitrary code execution during the installation process, which is opaque, slow, and increasingly discouraged by the Python Packaging Authority (PyPA). If your build process requires a Python script to resolve its own environment, you’ve already lost control of your supply chain.

The transition to PEP 517 and PEP 621 standards, centered on the pyproject.toml file, moves configuration away from executable code into static metadata. This allows build tools to understand your project structure without running arbitrary code, leading to safer, more predictable builds.


Photo by Timelab on Unsplash

Standardizing with pyproject.toml

To build a modern shared library, you need to define your metadata and build backend in pyproject.toml. I recommend using hatchling or setuptools (>= 61.0.0). Here is a standard configuration that ensures your library is installable and its dependencies are tracked:

[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=61.0"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "data-utility-lib"
version = "0.1.0"
authors = [
  { name = "Data Platform Team", email = "platform@example.com" },
]
description = "Shared utilities for data pipelines"
requires-python = ">=3.9"
dependencies = [
    "pandas>=2.0.0",
    "pydantic>=2.0.0",
    "pyarrow>=12.0.0",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = [
    "pytest",
    "black",
    "ruff",
]

By defining these requirements in a static file, you enable tools like pip or uv to resolve the entire dependency graph before installation begins. This prevents the "dependency drift" that occurs when an environment installs one version of a library at the start of a pipeline and a conflicting version halfway through a dependency resolution chain.

Enforcing consistent environments

Once your library is packaged, you should treat it as a primary dependency in your project-specific environments. In your downstream data pipelines, you no longer rely on shared folders; you reference the library in your pyproject.toml or requirements.txt via a private package registry or a direct git URL.

When you install your library, you are pulling a defined artifact. If you need to upgrade a core dependency like pyarrow, you update the pyproject.toml in your library, bump the version, and propagate that change to your pipelines. This creates an auditable trail of who changed which dependency and when—a critical requirement for any regulated environment where data lineage and software provenance are non-negotiable.


Photo by Testalize.me on Unsplash

The objections (and my answers)

"But we have a small team, and packaging feels like overkill."

It feels like overkill until you spend four hours debugging why a UDF in a Spark job works locally but crashes on the cluster. Packaging your code forces you to define exactly what your code needs to run. If you can't state your dependencies explicitly in a pyproject.toml, you don't actually know what your code is doing.

"Won't this slow down our development velocity?"

Initially, yes. You have to learn how to version your internal library. However, the alternative is "dependency hell," where every engineer has a slightly different version of numpy or pandas in their local environment, leading to "works on my machine" syndromes that cost far more developer time than a formal packaging process ever will.

"What about internal package management?"

You don't need a complex Artifactory setup to start. You can install directly from a private Git repository using pip install git+https://github.com/org/repo@v0.1.0. Once your team matures, you can move to a simple private PyPI mirror, but the pyproject.toml format remains the constant that ensures your setup is compatible with modern ecosystem tooling.

Conclusion

Packaging your shared code is not just about "cleaner project structure"; it is about platform stability. By moving away from imperative setup.py scripts and loose file structures toward declarative pyproject.toml configurations, you transform your shared library from a liability into a reliable piece of infrastructure.

Stop appending to sys.path. Start building artifacts. Your pipelines—and your future self—will thank you when you can finally deploy with confidence.

Cover photo by Juanjo Jaramillo on Unsplash.

This article was drafted with AI assistance and is intended for technical review and fact-checking before publication.

title: Where's My Package? Three API Calls to Find Out
description:
A customer writes in: where's my package?

To answer, you start with their account. The account leads to their orders. One of those orders has an ID, and only with that ID can you ask the shipping service where the package is.

Three questions, asked in order, each one waiting on the answer before it. That's an API chain. None of it can run side by side, and if one answer comes back empty, the next question has nothing to go on.

What a chain actually needs

In API terms, that's three services: users, orders and shipping, each called with something the last one returned.

The hard part isn't making the calls. It's moving data between them. Somebody has to pick the right field out of one response, hand it to the next request, and decide what happens if the field isn't there. In most codebases that's hand-written glue, repeated for every new chain.

Passing data from step to step

In Unmeshed, each call is a step in a workflow, and a later step can reference the output of an earlier one using double curly brackets. So the order step can read a value from the user step's response, and the shipping step can read the order ID from the order step. You build the three calls as HTTP GET tasks, wire the references, and the platform runs them in order.

You never write the code that passes the values along. You also get a visual trace of the run, so you can open each step and see exactly what went in and what came back.

Three ways chains go wrong

  • A field is missing or shaped differently. The next call depends on it, so it fails or runs with an empty value. This is why every service in the chain should return JSON with consistent, predictable fields.
  • A step fails halfway. The earlier calls already happened. You need to know where it stopped, and you want to rerun from there, not from the beginning.
  • Environment details are baked in. Hard-coded URLs make a flow that works in testing and breaks in production. Keep the configuration separate from the logic so the same flow runs in more than one environment.

Keeping it reviewable

A flow that lives only in a visual editor is hard to review and hard to roll back. Unmeshed lets you export process definitions as JSON, so a chain can be versioned, reviewed and deployed with the rest of your code.

Chained calls are one of the most common integration patterns, and they're also the one most likely to turn into a pile of glue code nobody wants to touch. If you have a chain like this, try building it in Unmeshed and compare it with what you maintain today.

title: I estimated 500 RPS from the System Design book and measured 24. Here's what broke.
description:
There's a chapter everyone who prepared for a system design interview has read: "Back-of-the-envelope estimation" in Alex Xu's System Design Interview. Divide DAU by 86,400, double it for peak, multiply out the storage for a few years — and you get "1,160 writes per second, 11,600 reads, 36.5 TB". I could do that arithmetic too. Then I asked myself a simple question: "and will Postgres actually take it?" — and realised I didn't know. I knew how to compute the load. I had no idea what happens to the database when that load arrives.

So instead of guessing, I measured. I took the system from chapter 8 of the same book — the URL shortener — built it in Docker on my laptop, worked out from the book what it should sustain, and pointed a load generator at it. Below: the estimate, the stand, the numbers, and what I learned from them. Spoiler: the estimate missed the measurement not by a few percent but by three orders of magnitude, and that was the most useful thing that happened in all the time I spent with the book.

The estimate, by the book

The URL shortener from chapter 8. Xu's assumptions: 100 million new links per day, a 10:1 read-to-write ratio, 10 years of retention, about 100 bytes per record.

  • Writes: 100,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 1,160 per second.
  • Reads: ×10 ≈ 11,600 per second.
  • Records over 10 years: 100 M × 365 × 10 = 365 billion.
  • Storage: 365 billion × 100 bytes = 36.5 TB.

But 11,600 reads per second is company scale, not laptop scale. I needed a target I could check at home. I picked 500 read requests per second — roughly 4 million DAU at one click per user per day, with a peak factor of 2. A perfectly ordinary mid-sized service. And I wrote down my expectation: at that RPS, p95 latency should be around 20 ms — a key lookup in a table of a million rows, what could possibly take long.

This matters and I'll insist on it: write the expectation down before you run anything. Otherwise, after the measurement, your brain will helpfully tell you "yeah, that's about what I thought".

The stand

Docker Compose — three long-running containers plus k6, which only comes up for the duration of a run:

  • api — a Go service: POST /shorten takes a long URL and returns a short code (base62 of the id), GET /{code} looks it up and returns a 302. Database pool size: 10.
  • postgres — one table, urls(id, code, long_url, created_at).
  • redis — present but off (CACHE=off). It'll matter later.
  • k6 — the load generator, constant-arrival-rate scenario: exactly N requests per second regardless of whether the server keeps up.

I loaded a million rows with COPY — 11.7 seconds, 102 MB on disk. Picked 20 random codes out of them for k6 to hit with GETs.

One deliberate detail I'll state up front so it doesn't feel like a trick: there is no index on the code column. Only the primary key on id. Why will become clear from the result.

NAME                   SERVICE    STATUS
napkinlab-api-1        api        Up 24 minutes (healthy)
napkinlab-postgres-1   postgres   Up 56 minutes (healthy)
napkinlab-redis-1      redis      Up 56 minutes (healthy)

The measurement

Run: 500 requests per second, 60 seconds.

target_rps | actual RPS | p95, ms  | p99, ms  | error rate
500        | 24.17      | 22130.61 | 22808.33 | 0.00%

Read the second column again. I asked for 500 requests per second — the stand served 24. The rest didn't fail; they queued: p95 is 22 seconds. Not milliseconds. Seconds. I expected 20 ms and got 1,100× that.

A second run a couple of hours later, with fewer neighbours on the laptop, gave 72 RPS and a p95 of 7.5 seconds — this is what make report prints:

Stage 1 — estimate vs. measurement   (results/read_500rps_20261024T201101.json)

target_rps | actual RPS      | p95, ms    | p99, ms    | error rate
-----------+-----------------+------------+------------+------------
500        | 72.41           | 7477.01    | 7633.63    | 0.00%

Expected:  p95 ≤ 20 ms at 500 RPS — "will hold: simple query, only a million rows"
Dropped k6 iterations (ran out of VUs): 25162
Estimate vs. fact: p95 7477.0 ms against expected 20 ms (374× higher); actual RPS 72.4 below target 500
The estimate did not hold. Why — stages 2 and 3.

A 3× spread between runs is itself a lesson about measuring on a laptop. But the order of magnitude is the same: asked for 500, got dozens, waited seconds.

If this weren't a lab but production, it would look like this: users click a link, the page spins for twenty seconds, half of them close the tab. Meanwhile the logs show zero errors. Error-rate monitoring is silent. That's the second lesson: "0% errors" says nothing about whether the system is alive.

Where it broke

The arithmetic is simple, and it could have been done before the run if you knew where to look.

SELECT long_url FROM urls WHERE code = $1 without an index on code is a sequential pass over the whole table: Postgres reads a million rows to return one.

                                                     QUERY PLAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Gather  (cost=1000.00..16552.43 rows=1 width=31) (actual time=10.664..43.648 rows=1 loops=1)
   Workers Planned: 2
   Workers Launched: 2
   Buffers: shared hit=10344
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on urls  (cost=0.00..15552.33 rows=1 width=31) (actual time=26.482..35.769 rows=0 loops=3)
         Filter: (code = '3Gd3'::text)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 333333
         Buffers: shared hit=10344
 Planning:
   Buffers: shared hit=63
 Planning Time: 0.450 ms
 Execution Time: 43.693 ms
(12 rows)

Rows Removed by Filter: 333333 in each of three processes — that's the whole million, scanned for one row. Alone, on a warm cache, such a query takes 44 ms. But under load there are ten of them at once (pool size 10), each spawning two more parallel workers, all sharing the same cores: one query stretches to hundreds of milliseconds. Ten connections at 150–400 ms each is a ceiling of a few dozen requests per second. Everything above that waits for a free connection. At 500 incoming per second the queue grows by hundreds of requests every second, and after a minute p95 is queueing time, not query time.

I checked this with a separate run: load in steps of 10 → 25 → 50 → 100 requests per second, 20 seconds per step. At 10 and 25 the stand still answers in milliseconds; at 50, p95 crosses 200 ms; at 100 it's already 7 seconds. The limit is around 50 requests per second, and it doesn't depend on whether all requests hit 20 hot keys or are spread across a hundred thousand: without an index every request costs the same, and "hot keys" don't exist as far as Postgres is concerned.

Diagnostics confirm it: pg_stat_statements shows one query eating all the time; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) — a Seq Scan over a million rows; Postgres saturates every core it's given while the Go service sits at 30% CPU — it's just waiting. The pool queue peaks at 219 requests.

Now the main point. The book's estimate said: 500 requests per second is nothing, any database will handle it. And that's true — for a database with an index. The chapter 2 arithmetic gives you a number of requests. It does not and cannot give you the cost of one request, because that depends not on DAU but on the schema, the indexes, and whether the working set fits in memory. 500 RPS at 0.1 ms and 500 RPS at 300 ms are the same number in an estimate and two different universes in a measurement.

I knew that in theory. The gap between "knew" and "saw a 22-second p95 on my own laptop" turned out to be larger than I expected.

What to do about it

The obvious answer is to add the index, and it's the right one. With an index on code, the same stepped run found no limit up to 1,000 requests per second — I stopped there because the laptop couldn't honestly generate more. p95 at 100 RPS: 1 ms instead of 7 seconds. One CREATE INDEX — three orders of magnitude.

But I deliberately didn't stop there and tested the fix that comes to many people's minds first: a Redis cache. This is where it gets interesting. On the profile with 20 hot keys, the cache fixes things just as well as the index: limit above 1,000 RPS, p95 1.4 ms. On the profile with a hundred thousand uniformly spread keys it fixes almost nothing: limit around 100 RPS, p95 at that load 2.3 seconds. The cache rarely hits, and every miss is the same Seq Scan over a million rows. The index fixes both profiles; the cache fixes one — and which one you have in production, the chapter 2 estimate won't tell you.

Stage 5 — before / index / cache (steps 10 → 1000 RPS, 20 s each; limit = first step with p95 > 200 ms)

Profile hot
metric              | before       | index        | cache
--------------------+--------------+--------------+--------------
limit RPS           | ~50          | > 1000       | > 1000
p95 @100 RPS, ms    | 7252.25      | 0.96         | 1.38
p95 @500 RPS, ms *  | 9671.82      | 1.34         | 0.85
errors              | 0.00%        | 0.00%        | 0.00%

Profile uniform
metric              | before       | index        | cache
--------------------+--------------+--------------+--------------
limit RPS           | ~50          | > 1000       | ~100
p95 @100 RPS, ms    | 5155.77      | 1.5          | 2265.03
p95 @500 RPS, ms *  | 7828.10      | 1.28         | 7087.21
errors              | 0.00%        | 0.00%        | 0.00%

* there is no 500 step: the value is a linear interpolation between the 400 and 700 steps.

A caveat on the numbers: this is a laptop, other containers were running alongside, and measurements vary by 30–50% between runs. The orders of magnitude don't change, but if you get 40 RPS instead of 50, that's not a bug.

Takeaways, no moral

  1. A book estimate is a number of requests. What the system does with them, the estimate doesn't say. That's a different skill, and it's taught not by books but by measuring.
  2. Write your expectation down before you run. "That's about what I thought" is not knowledge.
  3. Zero errors is not a sign of health. Look at p95 and at the queue.
  4. "Hot keys" are a property of your traffic, not of your database. A cache helps exactly as much as your traffic repeats itself.

The whole stand is in an open repository: docker compose up, make seed, make stage1 — and ten minutes later you'll see the same table on your own laptop, with your own numbers. There's a chapter 2 worksheet in there too, so you can write your expectation down before you run. If you want to go through the rest by hand — find the limit, diagnose it from pg_stat_statements, write a prediction and test it with a measurement for the index, the cache, the pool and a 301 — those are stages 2–5, described in the README.

https://github.com/kamalov2000/napkinlab

If you have your own numbers from a similar stand — especially if they don't match mine — I'd like to hear them in the comments. Laptop measurements don't transfer to production, and the more different laptops, the more honest the picture.

title: Cline is now available in the AI SDK harness layer
description:
The AI SDK harness layer lets you run established coding-agent runtimes through one unified interface, so you can switch runtimes without changing your application code. Today we are adding Cline, which runs through the same HarnessAgent interface as other supported harness.

@ai-sdk/harness-cline is the official harness adapter for Cline, implemented in collaboration with the Cline team.

Cline runs fully in the host process and uses the sandbox as a remote filesystem and shell, so only its tools operate in the sandbox. No bridge process is installed inside the sandbox, similar to the existing Pi harness.

Read the Cline harness documentation to get started.

The full supported list of harnesses is now: Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Deep Agents, Grok Build, OpenCode, and Pi, with more coming soon.

title: Data Quality in RVL-CDIP: A Systematic Audit
description:
arXiv:2610.32126v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: RVL-CDIP is the de facto standard benchmark for document classification, and reported accuracy on it is now 98.8%. In this paper, we audit RVL-CDIP for data quality issues and find that approximately 10.5% of its 400,000 documents have erroneous labels and that 35.2% of the test set has a duplicate or near-duplicate in the training set. Identification codes on the pages are sufficient to classify at 69% accuracy, and a state-of-the-art model loses 11 points without them. Image-only models trained on RVL-CDIP lose 16 to 28 points on documents from other sources, and the choice of OCR engine changes accuracy by 4.1 to 8.3 points. We find that nearly 16,000 RVL-CDIP documents contain sensitive personal data, and produce de-identified versions of these documents. We re-benchmark 25 models, and with all defects remediated, the 13 that we retrain are 0.9 to 2.9 points more accurate than in the original condition; the most accurate of them, LayoutLMv3, is 96.5% accurate. We release the corrected corpus, the annotations and the out-of-distribution data.

title: I Built a Dashboard That Lights Up Your Java Beans in Real Time (Building Ligero, Part 5)
description:
Layered architectures have a visibility problem. You draw clean boxes on a whiteboard (controller, service, repository), but at runtime all you have is logs and a debugger. Which beans did this request touch? What went into the service layer, and what came out? How long did each layer take?

Ligero ships a development-time answer: ligero-devtools, a dashboard served at /ligero/dev where you run a request, watch it flow through your beans, and inspect the JSON going in and out of every layer, without a debugger, log statements, or Postman.

Think of it as "Swagger's try-it-out", plus a live dependency graph, plus a per-request tracer, in one self-contained page (no CDN assets) shipped inside your jar.

What you get

Without devtools With devtools
Fire requests from curl or Postman in another window Run any route straight from the dashboard
Read logs to guess which beans ran See the exact path light up in the graph
Add System.out.println to see a layer's args/result Click a node: arguments and return value shown as JSON
Wonder how long each layer took Every call carries its timing
Keep a mental model of your wiring The dependency graph is drawn for you, coloured by stereotype

Setup 

// development only
implementation 'com.ligeroframework:ligero-devtools:<version>'

Devtools devtools = Devtools.create();

Beans beans = Beans.builder()
    .bind(NameRepo.class,     b -> new JdbcNameRepo(b.get(DataSource.class)))
    .bind(GreetService.class, b -> new DefaultGreetService(b.get(NameRepo.class)))
    .instrument(devtools.recorder())   // spies interface-typed beans
    .start();

Ligero app = Ligero.create();
app.beans(beans);
devtools.install(app, beans);          // mounts /ligero/dev

Open http://localhost:8080/ligero/dev, pick a route, fill in path params, query and a JSON body, and send it.

How the spying works (no agents, no bytecode)

This is the part I like, because it's built on the design decisions from the previous posts rather than on tricks.

  1. The container exposes an instrumentation hook: Beans.Builder.instrument(BeanDecorator) can wrap every bean as it's created.
  2. devtools.recorder() is such a decorator. Beans bound as interfaces get wrapped in a JDK dynamic proxy: no bytecode generation, no Java agent.
  3. Beans bound as concrete classes can't be proxied by the JDK. They pass through untouched and the dashboard marks them "not traceable". Bind by interface if you want them traced (which is the architecture Ligero promotes anyway).
  4. A middleware opens one trace per request, recording the matched route, request inputs and response body, and keeps the last 100 traces.
  5. The dashboard's own endpoints are never traced. 
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser (dashboard)
    participant M as TraceMiddleware
    participant C as Controller (proxy)
    participant S as Service (proxy)
    participant R as Repository (proxy)
    B->>M: POST /api/orders (X-Ligero-Dev: trace-id)
    M->>C: handle
    C->>S: placeOrder(args)
    S->>R: save(args)
    R-->>S: result + timing
    S-->>C: result + timing
    C-->>M: response
    M-->>B: response + trace (SSE)

Each proxy records arguments, return value and elapsed time. A small, dependency-free reflective serializer (JsonValue) renders any layer's arguments and results as real JSON (records, beans, collections, maps) with depth and size caps and cycle guards.

Request correlation

When the dashboard fires a request it stamps an X-Ligero-Dev header. The trace middleware uses it as the trace id, so the browser can match the trace it receives over the live SSE stream to the request it sent. Outside the dashboard, the middleware reuses the request id when the request-id middleware is on. It's a good example of keeping a feature useful without adding a new protocol.

The graph is the real graph

The dependency graph isn't inferred from annotations or file layout. beans.graph() returns nodes tagged by stereotype and edges captured from the real resolution order at startup. Selecting a request highlights the transitive closure of beans it can reach (its dependency graph), and sending it overlays the actual execution path in the HTTP method's colour. Branches a run didn't take stay visible as dependencies but aren't part of the execution. Clicking a node shows each invocation with arguments, return value and timing.

The commerce-devtools example is a good stress test: an e-commerce backend with three modules (catalog, customers, orders) and around 15 beans with cross-module dependencies. Run it, pick POST /api/orders, and watch about 21 calls light up the path across services and repositories.

Endpoints

Endpoint What
GET /ligero/dev the dashboard (self-contained HTML)
GET /ligero/dev/api/routes registered routes
GET /ligero/dev/api/graph bean graph JSON (nodes, edges, unspied list)
GET /ligero/dev/api/requests last 100 traces, most recent first
GET /ligero/dev/api/stream SSE stream of completed traces

Never in production

Devtools exposes the arguments and return values of your beans. Two switches keep it out of production:

  1. Classpath (recommended): keep the dependency out of production builds. Zero overhead, because nothing is there. The CLI can scaffold a project without it (--devtools false).
  2. Environment: LIGERO_DEVTOOLS=false turns install() into a no-op without a code change.

Why this was cheap to build

Notice what devtools did not need: a classpath scanner, an agent, or annotation processing. Because wiring is explicit (post 3) and layers talk through interfaces (post 1), the framework already had the two things a tracer needs: a place to wrap objects and a graph of who depends on whom. Good architecture makes tooling cheap.

Takeaways

  • Instrumentation hooks in the container plus interface-typed beans let you trace every layer with plain JDK proxies.
  • Draw the real dependency graph from real resolution order, not from conventions.
  • Make dev tooling impossible to ship by accident: keep it off the production classpath.

Next: observability for production, where we trade the dashboard for health checks, route-pattern metrics, trace context and OpenTelemetry.

title: How we migrated the database behind every Vercel build
description:
Every build on Vercel starts in the build warm pool, which is a set of standby containers that let builds begin without waiting for new compute. The pool runs on state that tracks which containers are ready, the tokens each one uses to authenticate, and the mapping that ties every running build back to the deployment that gets billed for it. When we built the pool, we put all of that in Redis, which was fast and made sense at the time.

Over the years, though, that state turned into a liability. Tokens and container statuses can be rebuilt if they get lost, but the billing mappings can't, and all of it was sitting in a store that we ran as an ephemeral cache. That state needed to live somewhere durable, which is why we decided to migrate it to DynamoDB.

The problem is that the pool never stops. Containers are coming up, polling, picking up work, and expiring around the clock, which meant we couldn't pause the world, copy the data, and restart. The migration had to happen live, under production traffic, in phases, each one behind a flag with a rollback ready if we needed it.

Durable state in an ephemeral store

Redis was a good home for it at first. It was fast, familiar, and efficient for the access patterns the pool started with. But over time the state became more important than the store holding it. If Redis became unavailable or lost data, the pool could no longer reliably authenticate containers, track which of them were ready, or resolve the work in flight.

Lose a token and the pool rebuilds it within about ten minutes. Lose a mapping and the build is never billed, because nothing else records which deployment it belonged to.

We wanted it in durable storage and landed on DynamoDB. On-demand scaling fits bursty deployment traffic, TTL is native, and there are no connections to manage at high concurrency. But what it did not promise was Redis's latency.

What Redis made cheap

Inside Redis, the pool's state looked like this:

  • Tokens lived in a set so we could check membership, and in a sorted set so we could expire them

  • Each lifecycle status (pending, polling, building) had its own sorted set, which meant a status change was a removal from one set and an add to the next

  • A string tied each working container to its deployment

All of these operations were cheap, about a millisecond each, and the code grew to lean on that speed. A single run of the supply loop, which is the loop that refills each warm pool in turn, would make hundreds of count calls just to tally up the pending and polling containers.

That's how the warm pool grew, one easy write at a time, until data we needed to keep was sitting in structures built for speed. Untangling that layout was where the migration started.

Designing the schema from the access patterns

Most migration plans treat the database as the thing being replaced. You map the access patterns, copy the data, and verify that the two stores agree. We planned ours that way too, so before designing any schema, we listed everything the code actually asked of that state:

  • Verify a token when a container polls for work

  • Add a token when a new container comes up

  • Expire tokens past their deadline

  • Count tokens to size the pool

  • Move a container between lifecycle statuses

  • Count containers by status

  • Look up the deployment behind a container's callback

  • Remove expired containers

Almost every operation already knows which container it's touching, and only polling ever starts from a token. So we put the container at the center of the model. The container ID became the sort key, and the token became just a field on the record, stored as a hash so that reading the table never hands you a usable credential. Verifying a token now just means looking up its container and comparing the hashes.

Two of the access patterns couldn't be served by a key lookup alone. Status counts had to skip containers that were already past expiry, which takes a time-aware index. And the deployment lookups feed billing, so they needed consistent reads, and the mapping got a small table of its own.

Reading a container's state, moving its status, and clearing its token all became direct key lookups. Counting a status became a single read against the time-aware index, one query per status with expired containers already filtered out.

Where Redis had let the data structures imply what we needed, DynamoDB made us spell out keys, indexes, conditional writes, and TTL behavior. So instead of carrying the Redis structures forward, we modeled the container and added the indexes that its access patterns needed.

Shadow mode validated every write

The rollout ran as feature-flagged phases: Redis-only, then dual writes, shadow reads, DynamoDB-primary, and finally DynamoDB-only. Every phase kept a rollback open for as long as possible. The last step, which removed the Redis writes, was the only one without an easy rollback, but any lingering token expires within ten minutes anyway.

We started by baselining the existing Redis operations, their counts and their latencies, so that the dashboards had a normal to compare against. The new DynamoDB methods merged days before anything actually called them. Dual writes went out next, with Redis still the source of truth and DynamoDB failures logged instead of fatal. Then came shadow reads, which queried both stores and compared the results. And then primary reads flipped, with the Redis writes kept on until the new path had proven itself.

What the comparisons told us was whether the two stores agreed on the stored values, which is something tests alone couldn't. They said nothing about timing. We checked that every write landed in both stores, that expiration kept moving forward as containers changed status so stale state never piled up, that clearing a token left the rest of the container's record intact, and that the counts stayed close enough to steer the pool.

On top of the comparisons we built dashboards that watched match rates, write errors, per-query latency, and expiration counts while Redis was still serving production. That way any divergence surfaced while it was still cheap to investigate, instead of showing up as a cutover failure. Every mismatch got chased down to a real bug, a dual-write race, or an expected difference before we moved on. Those dashboards decided when each phase advanced, and every time the numbers held steady under production traffic, the next step felt safer.

Two failures along the way

In March, one region's builds went down, and the investigation pointed at our own comparison machinery, which was the added load of checking two stores against each other. The scenario had actually come up in review, and we had throttled the comparisons for exactly that reason, but the throttling wasn't enough. Four days later, a pull request citing the incident added the index that the status counts needed. Without it, every count was O(n) work, and the comparisons were counting constantly. With the index in place, the rollout continued.

Later that month, the Redis infrastructure that we were migrating off actually went down. The warm pool and its token handling stayed up, because both of them were already reading from DynamoDB as the source of truth. Builds still felt the outage, but through services further up the pipeline that hadn't moved yet. The failure we'd been migrating away from arrived before the migration was even finished, and the state that had already moved survived it.

The supply loop stalled on slower reads

In April, the supply loop began to stall. The shadow data had looked healthy when we advanced primary reads, and the per-query latency had looked acceptable on the dashboards. What failed was a behavior that neither one measured.

We drew the loop to see where the time was going.

At P95 on getWarmPoolTokenCount, that check measured 1.29ms on Redis and 5.13ms on DynamoDB. At the time we shorthanded it as two to three times slower per query, which turned out to be an underestimate.

A few extra milliseconds cost nothing when you only pay them once. But the loop was paying them before every container, hundreds of times per run, and that stretched runs out to minutes at their worst, which meant the pool couldn't stay ahead of demand. The loop was an N+1 query, and Redis had just simply been fast enough to hide it.

No one wrote "this loop requires millisecond reads" anywhere. But the assumption lived in the design, and at a millisecond per check, nothing had ever made us stop and look.

We rebuilt the loop around the new latency

DynamoDB was never going to match Redis's millisecond, so instead of chasing it, we designed the requirement out.

The first attempt was batching, which is the shape drawn at the bottom of the sketch. The size of the gap depends on which percentile you look at, and at P90, where it was widest, the gap was about 17x. So the batch design checked state once per 17 containers, with one read amortized across the whole batch, and that constant was lifted straight from the measurement. But the constant was also the reason we walked away from it. It hard-coded a latency ratio that would drift with load, which meant one more unwritten dependency on the store's speed. Concurrency didn't need a constant at all.

What shipped instead let the loop's supply calls run concurrently, so each warm pool was no longer waiting behind the one before it, and each call worked from the last state it saw. Overlapping the reads bought us the same thing that batching would have, which is that no run serialized on any single read. The worst case is a few extra containers created from a stale picture of the pool, and that went into the pull request as an accepted cost. The redesign meant we could keep the more durable store without compromising the thing users actually care about, which is builds starting quickly and reliably. The fixes landed the same way the rollout did, one measured step at a time. As one of us put it, "we have less risk on each iteration because we've corrected for a previous misestimation."

It turned out the loop had stalled under Redis too, sometimes for a minute or more, and we only learned that while we were diagnosing DynamoDB. The evidence had been in our telemetry the whole time, but because the pool sits ahead of demand rather than in any request path, nothing had ever forced us to go look until the migration did. And the redesign ended up removing a flaw that was older than the project itself.

Migrating the assumptions

The migration completed in April, with the Redis calls gone from the warm pool paths. Copying the data turned out to be the easy part. The real work was finding the assumptions that had been built on top of the store, and then redesigning the loop that had held them. The state that every build depends on now lives in a store that was built to keep it, and the loop that manages it no longer serializes on any single read.

The April retrospective put the lesson in one sentence. "Even a 1ms-to-15ms query time degradation on P90 could bring down our warm pool management logic." Nobody had written that sentence in February, when the migration started.

Read more

title: Disentangling Question, Response, and Verifier Languages in Multilingual P(True) Self-Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.32144v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a language model is asked whether its own answer is correct, three languages are involved: that of the question, that requested for the answer, and that of the verifier instruction asking for the judgment. Multilingual confidence evaluations seldom separate the three. We vary them independently in a six-language factorial design with ten open-weight models (3B-14B) on LSQA, MMMLU and TriviaQA, holding each answer fixed across verifier languages and measuring confidence with a first-token P(True) probe. The three languages move different parts of the evaluation: which of them governs accuracy depends on the benchmark, matching the response language to the question or verifier language sharpens discrimination but not calibration, and the verifier language alone shifts calibration error by up to 0.04 without changing accuracy. The scorer matters as well: an unvalidated judge would have shrunk the MMMLU English-Hindi accuracy gap from 0.198 to 0.038. Multilingual confidence results, model rankings included, are therefore comparable only when all three languages are reported and the scorer is validated.

title: Two Roads, One Plan View: Modeling Seattle's SR 99 Tunnel in 3D
description:
The first version of my SR 99 model looked fine from above and wrong from everywhere else. I traced the footprint from a map, extruded it, and called it done. Then I cut a section through the middle and found one road where there should have been two. The plan view had folded the upper and lower decks into a single line, and my model had believed it.
Then the project got interesting.

A plan view cannot hold a stack

Most map data describes the ground in two dimensions. A road is a line, a building is a polygon, a tunnel is a corridor. That works until the corridor carries traffic on two levels. Under downtown Seattle, both directions share the same coordinates and differ only in elevation. A flat file has nowhere to put that.
The fix is simple but deliberate. I treated the alignment as a spine with a station value, then attached a cross-section to each station. The map gave me the spine. The section gave me everything else.

What the map selection provides

I drew a polygon in GenAnywhere around the corridor, from the north portal near Seattle Center to the south portal in SODO, and included the blocks on both sides. The tool returned a massing model of the district with the tunnel represented as a buried volume.
That model was useful for context: portal mouths, surrounding buildings, the two ventilation structures, and the street grid above. It was not useful for the inside of the bore. A footprint model has no reason to know about a central slab.

The section carries the truth

The bored tunnel is roughly 57.5 feet in diameter. Inside that circle, a thick horizontal slab divides the space into an upper roadway and a lower roadway, each with two lanes. Southbound traffic runs on top; northbound runs below. Once I had that section, I could sweep it along the alignment and get a model that behaved correctly in every view.
I kept the section separate instead of baking it into the mesh. When the deck elevation changed, I edited one number and rebuilt the sweep. When a colleague wanted a section drawing, the same source worked.

Portals are where models usually drift

The north and south portals sit at different elevations and connect to different street grids. If the alignment is slightly off, the tunnel will appear to enter a building or float above the road. I checked both ends against the surface model before adding any interior detail.
The ventilation buildings deserve the same treatment. There are two, one at each end, and each connects to the bore through shafts and ducts. In the model I represented the buildings as simple volumes and the shafts as vertical connections. That was enough to test whether the stack of spaces made sense.

Three checks that caught real errors

The first check was deck separation. I measured the vertical gap between the two road surfaces at three stations and compared it with the section. My first sweep had the slab too low, which made the lower deck feel like a basement.
The second check was portal elevation. I compared the road surface at each end with the street surface above it. One portal was off by more than a meter because I had used the wrong ground sample.
The third check was shaft alignment. The ventilation shafts have to land inside the bore, not beside it. In plan view they looked correct; in section they were close to the lining. A ten-minute check saved a day of rework.

Where the model still fails

Two decks in the same footprint create z-fighting in a web viewer, and a cutaway can hide the very deck you want to show. I handled it with visibility rules: upper deck on, lower deck off, then the reverse.
The model is also not a survey product. It is a communication tool built from a map footprint and a published section. For construction, you would need as-built geometry, and for driving, you would need signs. The model is for understanding how the pieces fit.

What I would do next

I would add the emergency exits as explicit nodes rather than holes in the wall. Fifteen of them connect the bore to the surface. I would also separate the lining, the road structure, and the ventilation into layers that can be switched independently.
For now, the section sweep is enough. It turned a flat line on a map into two roads in a tube, which is what the tunnel actually is.

title: DriveMind: Mind-Evolving Belief Tracking for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving
description:
arXiv:2610.32069v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.

title: IFC-SSL-Bench: Benchmarking Self-Supervised Learning for Annotation-Efficient Multispectral Imaging Flow Cytometry
description:
arXiv:2610.31848v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Imaging Flow Cytometry (IFC) generates large multispectral datasets, yet the need for expert annotations bottlenecks the development of supervised deep learning models. While Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) offers a solution, its application to IFC remains fragmented and lacks systematic benchmarking. To address this, we present IFC-SSL-Bench, a modular framework for evaluating SSL in IFC. We benchmark six SSL approaches across four backbones on two heterogeneous datasets. By assessing downstream classification performance across annotation regimes of the training sets (1%-100%), we quantify annotation efficiency and identify optimal configurations for high-dimensional biological imaging. SSL matches the performance of fully supervised baselines trained on 100% of annotated data while using as little as 5% of annotations for morphological classification, with advantages in low-data regimes below 5%. Across both datasets, the contrastive approach MoCo-v2 paired with ConvNeXt backbones emerged as the top-performing configuration, with ConvNeXtV1-T best for immunological synapse classification and ConvNeXtV2-T for morphological classification. We identify a clear pattern in transfer dynamics: ImageNet initialization benefits morphological classification, consistent with its visual similarity to natural images, whereas random initialization better captures the more domain-specific immunological synapse classification. SSL elevates class-specific F1-scores by over 35 percentage points for structurally complex classes at 1% of annotated data. We synthesize these insights into a unified set of guidelines for deploying self-supervised workflows in high-throughput IFC, and release the benchmark as a resource for future work.
