title: Let's Encrypt Goes to 64-Day Certificates in February. Grep Your Server for 60, 80 and 83 First.
description:
Let's Encrypt posted a short note on October 7 that most small SaaS founders will scroll past. Starting February 10, 2027, every certificate it issues or renews will be valid for 64 days by default, not 90. Then on February 16, 2028, it drops again to 45 days.

The post also has one line I'd tape to the monitor:

Grep for common hardcoded numbers like 83, 80 or 60 in cron jobs, wrapper scripts and runbooks if you're not sure.

That's the whole risk in one sentence. If your HTTPS renewal was set up two years ago by "past you" and has worked silently since, there's a decent chance a 60 is hiding somewhere in it. On 90-day certs that 60 left you 30 days of slack. On 64-day certs it leaves 4. On 45-day certs it renews two weeks after the cert already died.

This post is the boring checklist I'd run on a tiny SaaS before February. Most of it takes an hour.

The dates, in one place

There are two separate things changing and people mix them up.

The industry rule. The CA/Browser Forum (the group whose rules every public CA follows) passed ballot SC-081 in 2025. Max certificate lifetime for certs issued:

  • from March 15, 2026: 200 days (it was 398)
  • from March 15, 2027: 100 days
  • from March 15, 2029: 47 days

Let's Encrypt's own schedule, which runs ahead of that:

  • now: 90 days by default
  • opt-in already: the shortlived profile issues ~6-day certs, and since May 13, 2026 the tlsserver profile issues 45-day ones
  • since October 14, 2026: the staging environment already issues 64-day certs, for testing
  • February 10, 2027: default goes to 64 days
  • around May 11, 2027: the last 90-day Let's Encrypt cert expires
  • February 16, 2028: default goes to 45 days

Nothing gets revoked. You just get the shorter cert at your next renewal after each date.

If you buy certs instead (from your registrar, or a "1 year SSL" upsell), you're already on the 200-day rule. A public example: as of late October 2026, dev.to itself serves a certificate issued in November 2025 that runs until December 12, 2026. That's 397 days, issued before the cutoff. Its replacement can't be longer than 200 days, and the one after March 2027 can't be longer than 100. If someone on your team installs a bought cert by hand once a year, that turns into at least twice a year now, about four times a year from 2027, and eight or more a year from 2029. Manual stops being a plan.

Why a tiny SaaS should care more than a big one

Big companies have a platform team and a cert inventory. At 30 customers, the cert inventory is "whatever certbot did in 2024."

Two things make it worse now:

  1. Nobody emails you anymore. Let's Encrypt stopped sending expiry reminder emails on June 4, 2025. If you set things up when those emails existed, your safety net was quietly removed. Certbot's own docs still have a line saying the CA will email you, which doesn't help.
  2. Webhooks fail before customers notice. Stripe needs a valid certificate on your webhook endpoint in live mode. If the cert expires, deliveries show a TLS error and Stripe retries for up to three days. After that you're replaying events by hand, and in the meantime renewals, cancellations and failed payments aren't reaching your app. Your marketing site might be on a host that handles certs for you while api.yourapp.com sits on a VPS that doesn't.

Step 1: find out what actually renews your certs

Before grepping anything, figure out which tool is in charge. On a typical small setup it's one of these:

  • A managed host or proxy (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, Render, Fly, a managed load balancer). They issue and renew for you. Mostly not your problem, but check any custom domains you added by hand.
  • Caddy. It handles renewal itself and has supported ACME Renewal Information (ARI) since 2.8, so it asks Let's Encrypt when to renew.
  • Certbot. Usually a systemd timer or a cron entry someone added.
  • acme.sh. A cron entry under your user.
  • Something homemade. A script, a Docker container that runs certbot once, a GitHub Action. These are the ones that bite.

On a Linux box, this finds most of them:

systemctl list-timers --all | grep -i -E 'certbot|acme'
sudo grep -rn -i -E 'certbot|acme|renew' /etc/crontab /etc/cron.d /var/spool/cron 2>/dev/null
crontab -l 2>/dev/null | grep -i -E 'certbot|acme|renew'
certbot --version 2>/dev/null
~/.acme.sh/acme.sh --version 2>/dev/null

Write down what you find. Seriously, one line in a notes file: "api box, certbot 2.x, systemd timer, nginx reload hook: no". You'll need it in step 3.

Step 2: grep for the hardcoded numbers

Here's what common renewal rules do on each lifetime. "Slack" is how many days are left on the old cert when renewal first tries.

Renewal rule 90-day cert 64-day cert 45-day cert
Ask the CA via ARI (about 2/3 of lifetime) ~day 60, ~30 left ~day 43, ~21 left ~day 30, ~15 left
Certbot 4.0+ default (1/3 lifetime left) day 60, 30 left ~day 43, ~21 left day 30, 15 left
Old certbot default (30 days left) day 60, 30 left day 34, 30 left day 15, 30 left
acme.sh 3.1.2 and older default (59 days after issue) 31 left 5 left expired 14 days earlier
Hand cron, --force-renewal every 60 days 30 left 4 left expired 15 days earlier
Runbook "renew at 80 / 83 days" 10 / 7 left expired expired

The "days left" rules are fine. The "days since issue" rules are the ones that break. That's what Let's Encrypt means by grepping for 60, 80 and 83.

Where to look:

# certbot: per-cert overrides (no output is good)
sudo grep -rn renew_before_expiry /etc/letsencrypt/renewal/

# acme.sh: older versions wrote Le_RenewalDays='60' into every cert's conf
grep -rn Le_RenewalDays ~/.acme.sh/
# (if you never passed --days, a 60 here is just the old default)

# anything homemade that forces renewal on a fixed schedule
sudo grep -rn -E 'force-renew|--days|renew.*(60|80|83)' /etc/cron* /var/spool/cron /etc/systemd/system ~/bin ~/scripts 2>/dev/null

A few things from the changelogs worth knowing:

  • Certbot 4.0.0 switched its default from a fixed 30 days to "renew when less than 1/3 of the lifetime is left". Certbot 4.1.0 added ARI support, and an early ARI answer wins over a later renew_before_expiry. So a recent certbot with the stock timer is basically fine. An old certbot pinned by your distro is the thing to check.
  • acme.sh changed its default from 60 days to 30 days and added ARI in 3.1.3 (April 2026). Before that, the default renewal was 60 days after issue, minus a day. If you installed it a while ago and turned off auto-upgrade, acme.sh --upgrade is step one. Then run acme.sh --info -d yourdomain.com and look at Le_NextRenewTimeStr to see when it actually plans to renew, instead of trusting what you remember.
  • If your "automation" is a cron line with --force-renewal on a fixed calendar, replace it with the plain certbot renew running twice a day. Certbot's docs recommend exactly that and say it's safe to run as often as you like, since it does nothing until a cert is due.

Step 3: renewal isn't deployment

This one gets people even with perfect timing. Certbot renews the file on disk. Nginx keeps serving the old cert from memory until it reloads. If nothing reloads it, the new cert sits there unused and the old one expires right on schedule.

With certbot, add a deploy hook. It only runs after a successful renewal:

sudo tee /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/reload-nginx.sh > /dev/null <<'HOOK'
#!/bin/sh
nginx -t && systemctl reload nginx
HOOK
sudo chmod +x /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/reload-nginx.sh

With acme.sh it's the --reloadcmd you pass when installing the cert. Their README flags it as IMPORTANT, and they're right.

Other places the new cert never reaches: a Docker image that copied the cert in at build time, a load balancer or CDN where you uploaded a cert by hand, a second server that gets the cert by rsync from the first one. On 90-day certs you might've caught that by accident. On 64-day certs, you get fewer accidents.

To test the renew-plus-hook path without touching real certs:

sudo certbot renew --dry-run --run-deploy-hooks

--dry-run talks to the staging server and doesn't save anything. Deploy hooks don't run during a dry run unless you add --run-deploy-hooks.

Step 4: check the certificate people actually get, from outside

Checking the file on disk tells you what certbot did. It doesn't tell you what browsers and Stripe see. I'd run something like this from a machine that isn't the server, once a day:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# check-certs.sh: fail if any cert you actually serve expires within DAYS days
DAYS=14
HOSTS="example.com www.example.com api.example.com status.example.com"

fail=0
for h in $HOSTS; do
  cert=$(echo | timeout 10 openssl s_client -connect "$h:443" -servername "$h" 2>/dev/null)
  end=$(echo "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -enddate 2>/dev/null | cut -d= -f2)
  if [ -z "$end" ]; then
    echo "FAIL $h: couldn't get a certificate"
    fail=1
  elif ! echo "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -checkend $((DAYS * 86400)) >/dev/null; then
    echo "FAIL $h: expires $end"
    fail=1
  else
    echo "ok   $h: expires $end"
  fi
done
exit $fail

-checkend takes seconds and exits 1 if the cert expires inside that window. -servername matters if more than one site lives on the same IP, otherwise you might be checking the wrong cert.

Pick the alert threshold for the new lifetimes. A lot of us have a "warn at 30 days left" rule from the 90-day era. On a 64-day cert renewed at about 2/3, a healthy cert hits 30 days left around day 34, roughly 9 days before renewal even tries. So the alert fires on every healthy cert, you mute it, and then it can't help you when it matters. I'd use 14 days for 64-day certs and something like 7 to 10 once you're on 45-day ones.

Where the alert goes matters as much as the check. The SideHunt guide on monitoring a side project when you can't watch it all day splits alerts into "interrupt me now" and "tonight is fine". A cert with 14 days left is a tonight one. A cert with 2 days left, or a FAIL on the webhook host, is a now one.

And the check script is itself a cron job that can die quietly. If it stops running, "no alerts" looks exactly like "everything's fine". I wrote about heartbeat checks for the jobs a tiny SaaS runs. Same idea here: ping on success so you hear about it when the check itself stops.

Step 5: find the certs you forgot about

The hostnames list in that script is only as good as your memory. Certificate Transparency logs remember better. Every public cert gets logged, so you can see every name anyone got a cert for on your domain:

curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=example.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u

crt.sh is free and kind of slow, and sometimes it just returns a 502. Retry in a minute. What usually turns up: an old staging. subdomain still pointing at a box, status. on some service you set up once, a mail. cert on the mail server, a customer's custom domain. Anything still live goes into HOSTS. Anything dead, delete the DNS record so it stops being a thing.

While you're thinking about expiry dates, the domain itself expires too, and a cert check won't catch that one. The IndieHunt guide on protecting a small SaaS from account lockouts covers registrar lock, auto-renew and the "renewal emails go to the domain that expired" trap.

Step 6: if anything still renews by hand, fix that now

Two cases I'd look for:

Manual DNS challenges. If you ran certbot certonly --manual with DNS and paste a TXT record each time, certbot's docs are clear that those certs won't renew automatically unless you add auth hook scripts. Today Let's Encrypt reuses a successful validation for 30 days. From February 2027 that's 10 days, and on the 45-day schedule in 2028 it's 7 hours. So basically every renewal will need a fresh challenge. Move to a DNS plugin for your DNS provider, or to HTTP validation if the box is reachable on port 80.

Bought certs. If you pay a registrar for a cert because "that's how we did it in 2019", see whether your host can do ACME instead. A lot of paid CAs support ACME too, if you need a paid one for some reason.

Step 7: try the short certs early, on something that doesn't matter

You don't have to wait for February to find out what breaks. Two options:

  • Staging is already on 64-day certs. Point a throwaway subdomain at a test box, issue with --staging, and watch it over a couple of weeks.
  • Or opt one low-stakes production name into 45-day certs now. In recent certbot that's --preferred-profile tlsserver, which falls back to the default profile if the profile ever disappears. --required-profile fails instead, which you probably don't want on a real site.

If your setup survives 45-day certs, February is a non-event.

The one-hour version

If you only do part of this:

  1. Find what renews each cert, and write it down.
  2. Grep for 60, 80, 83, --force-renewal and renew_before_expiry. Upgrade old certbot and acme.sh.
  3. Make sure a successful renewal reloads whatever serves the cert.
  4. Add the outside check on every hostname, including the webhook host, alerting at 14 days, with a heartbeat on the check.
  5. Run crt.sh once to find hostnames you forgot.

Most of the time nothing is wrong. But "the cert expired" outages are almost always on a box someone set up once and stopped thinking about, and February takes away a lot of the slack those boxes have been living on.

What renews the certs on your server right now, and do you actually know what day it fires? And if anyone has already moved a real site to the 45-day tlsserver profile, did anything break?

title: SyncVid: World-Equivariant Diffusion for Synchronized Video Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.31765v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating multiple videos of a dynamic scene from a single reference video requires synthesizing both observed and unobserved content consistently across viewpoints. Existing camera-control methods for video diffusion typically rely on architectural mechanisms, including camera embeddings, cross-view attention, and geometric conditioning. Although effective for static scene content, these approaches often struggle with the fine-grained, dynamic geometry that must remain coherent across views and over time. We synchronize the diffusion process itself by sampling the Gaussian noise prior in a canonical 3D space derived from the source video and rasterizing it into target cameras, rather than sampling independently in each 2D image plane. Our method, SyncVid, lifts a monocular video into a canonical 4D representation, associates noise with scene geometry and unseen space, and rasterizes the resulting structured noise into arbitrary views. Because rendering can introduce local correlations, we further propose a cross-view-consistent whitening procedure that decorrelates neighboring pixels while preserving correspondence across views. The structured noise serves as the diffusion prior for a LoRA-adapted pretrained video diffusion model, requiring no architectural modifications. By enforcing spatiotemporal and cross-view coherence at the source of stochasticity, SyncVid generates synchronized videos and improves both perceptual quality and cross-view consistency in our experiments. Project page: https://qualcomm-ai-research.github.io/SyncVid-Webpage.

title: WhatsApp Usernames Will Break Your Phone-Keyed Contacts: Migrating to Business-Scoped User IDs
description:
If your WhatsApp integration stores contacts by phone number, 2026 is the year that stops being safe. WhatsApp is rolling out usernames, and Meta now identifies every user with a business-scoped user ID (BSUID). For someone with a username, a webhook may arrive with no phone number at all. Here's what changed, the quiet failure it causes in a phone-keyed pipeline, and the identity model and TypeScript we'd use to migrate.

The snippets are small, self-contained versions of the pattern, and each was run against the cases shown.

What changed

From Meta's business-scoped user IDs page:

  • A BSUID "is a unique user identifier that can be used to message a WhatsApp user when you don't know their phone number". It looks like US.13491208655302741918: a two-letter country code, a dot, then the ID. Use it whole.
  • It's scoped to your business portfolio. The same person has a different BSUID with a different business, and it only works with phone numbers in your portfolio.
  • It changes when the user changes their phone number.
  • The timeline: BSUIDs began appearing in webhooks in April 2026. Businesses could reserve usernames from June 29, 2026. Sending to a BSUID has been supported since July 2026. Usernames reach WhatsApp users gradually through 2026.
  • It isn't optional. Meta's page says supporting BSUIDs "is required for all partners", and extends that to businesses integrated directly.

When the phone number disappears

For a user with a username, Meta includes their phone number in webhooks only if, for that business phone number, one of these is true:

  • you messaged or called their phone number in the last 30 days;
  • they messaged or called you from it in the last 30 days;
  • they're in your contact book (a Meta-hosted list built from your interactions).

Otherwise wa_id and from are simply left out. An inbound message can look like this:

{
  "contacts": [{ "profile": { "name": "Sam", "username": "sam.builds" }, "user_id": "US.13491208655302741918" }],
  "messages": [{ "from_user_id": "US.13491208655302741918", "id": "wamid.HBg...", "type": "text", "text": { "body": "Is the blue one in stock?" } }]
}

Status webhooks change the same way: recipient_user_id sits next to recipient_id, and the phone-based field can be missing.

The failure is silent

Trace what your code does with that message. A typical phone-keyed pipeline does something like this:

const phone = splitPhone(`+${message.from}`);          // "+undefined"
const contact = await Contact.findOrCreate({ where: { contact_no: phone.number } });

"+undefined" doesn't parse. If your helper falls back to the digits it can find, that's an empty string. findOrCreate finds or creates a contact whose number is "". Nothing throws. The next username-only customer matches the same empty number, and so does the one after that. Every customer without a visible phone number ends up in one shared contact and one conversation, and a reply to it goes to an invalid recipient.

No error, no log line, and it only starts once usernames reach your customers. Search your webhook handler for every read of from, wa_id and recipient_id, and check what happens when each is undefined.

Give contacts identities, not a phone number

The fix is to stop treating the phone number as the contact. A contact is your own row; phone numbers and BSUIDs are identifiers that point to it:

CREATE TABLE contact_identities (
  business_account_id VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,
  contact_id          VARCHAR(36) NOT NULL,
  kind                ENUM('phone', 'bsuid') NOT NULL,
  value               VARCHAR(160) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (business_account_id, kind, value)
);

Scope it by business account, because a BSUID only means something within one portfolio. Then resolve inbound senders by whatever Meta sent, and remember every identifier you see:

// identity.ts
// A contact is our own row. Phone numbers and BSUIDs are identifiers that point to it.
export type IdentityKind = "phone" | "bsuid";
export type Contact = { id: string; name?: string; username?: string };

export interface IdentityStore {
  findContact(kind: IdentityKind, value: string): Contact | undefined;
  link(contactId: string, kind: IdentityKind, value: string): void;
  unlink(kind: IdentityKind, value: string): void;
  createContact(fields: Omit<Contact, "id">): Contact;
}

type InboundContact = { wa_id?: string; user_id?: string; profile?: { name?: string; username?: string } };

// Match on whatever Meta sent, then remember every identifier we saw.
export const resolveInbound = (store: IdentityStore, sender: InboundContact): Contact => {
  const phone = sender.wa_id;
  const bsuid = sender.user_id;
  if (!phone && !bsuid) throw new Error("Inbound message with no sender identifier");

  const contact =
    (bsuid && store.findContact("bsuid", bsuid)) ||
    (phone && store.findContact("phone", phone)) ||
    store.createContact({ name: sender.profile?.name, username: sender.profile?.username });

  if (bsuid && !store.findContact("bsuid", bsuid)) store.link(contact.id, "bsuid", bsuid);
  if (phone && !store.findContact("phone", phone)) store.link(contact.id, "phone", phone);
  if (sender.profile?.username) contact.username = sender.profile.username;
  return contact;
};

What this gets you:

  • Existing contacts migrate themselves. A customer you've only known by phone sends a message that carries both wa_id and user_id; the BSUID is attached to their existing contact. No backfill job needed for active customers.
  • Username-only customers get their own contact, keyed by BSUID, instead of sharing a ghost.
  • A phone number that arrives later joins the same contact, rather than creating a duplicate.
  • A message with no identifier at all is an error you'll see, not a silent merge.
  • The username is display data. Store it for the agent's benefit; never key anything on it.

When the number (and the BSUID) changes

A user who changes their phone number gets a new BSUID. Meta tells you with a system message on the messages webhook, carrying both the new and the previous ID:

{ "type": "system", "system": { "type": "user_changed_number", "wa_id": "<NEW_PHONE>", "user_id": "<NEW_BSUID>", "previous_user_id": "<OLD_BSUID>" } }

There's also user_changed_user_id for a BSUID change without a phone number. Handle both, or the customer's next message creates a stranger:

// system-events.ts
import type { IdentityStore } from "./identity.ts";

type SystemMessage = {
  type: "user_changed_number" | "user_changed_user_id";
  wa_id?: string;
  user_id: string;
  previous_user_id: string;
};

// A new number means a new BSUID. Move both identifiers to the same contact
// instead of letting the next message create a stranger.
export const applySystemEvent = (store: IdentityStore, event: SystemMessage) => {
  const contact = store.findContact("bsuid", event.previous_user_id);
  if (!contact) return;
  store.unlink("bsuid", event.previous_user_id);
  store.link(contact.id, "bsuid", event.user_id);
  if (event.type === "user_changed_number" && event.wa_id) {
    if (!store.findContact("phone", event.wa_id)) store.link(contact.id, "phone", event.wa_id);
  }
};

Decide separately what to do with the old phone number. Numbers get recycled; keeping it linked forever means a future owner of that number lands in this customer's history.

Sending: to or recipient

Send requests now take either to (a phone number) or recipient (a BSUID). If you send both, to wins. Meta's Marketing Messages API docs recommend sending to phone numbers where you can, "primarily so you can continue to receive phone numbers in webhooks", and the same logic applies to ordinary sends. And some messages can't go to a BSUID: one-tap, zero-tap and copy-code authentication templates need a phone number (error 131062 otherwise).

// send-target.ts
export type Identifiers = { phone?: string; bsuid?: string };
export type MessageKind = "text" | "template" | "auth_otp_template";

export type SendTarget = { to: string } | { recipient: string };

// Prefer the phone number: sending to phones keeps phone numbers coming back
// in webhooks. One-tap, zero-tap and copy-code OTPs need one.
export const sendTarget = (ids: Identifiers, kind: MessageKind): SendTarget => {
  if (ids.phone) return { to: `+${ids.phone}` };
  if (kind === "auth_otp_template") throw new Error("This authentication template needs a phone number");
  if (ids.bsuid) return { recipient: ids.bsuid };
  throw new Error("Contact has no identifier we can send to");
};

Match delivery statuses by message ID (wamid), not by recipient. It's the one field that's always there.

Asking for the phone number

Sometimes you genuinely need the number: for delivery, for a CRM, for an OTP. Meta added a REQUEST_CONTACT_INFO button for utility and marketing templates and interactive messages. If the customer taps it, their number is shared in the chat, and your webhook receives a contacts message with "origin": "contact_request" and the phone number. Feed it through resolveInbound and it joins the existing contact.

Everything else that's keyed on a phone number

The contacts table is the obvious one. Audit these too:

  • Opt-outs. An opt-out stored against a phone number won't match a username-only customer. Store it on the contact.
  • Block lists. Meta's Block Users API accepts a BSUID (user_id) as well as a phone number.
  • Campaign audiences and imports. Imports still bring phone numbers; that's fine, they become phone identities. De-duplicate on identities, not a phone column.
  • CRM and other integrations that match customers by phone.
  • Analytics that count "unique customers" by phone number.
  • Calling, where call events carry the same BSUID fields.

Checklist

  • Find every read of from, wa_id and recipient_id, and make undefined an error you can see.
  • Move identity to a separate table: phone and BSUID, scoped by business account.
  • Resolve inbound senders by BSUID first, then phone, and link whatever is new.
  • Handle user_changed_number and user_changed_user_id.
  • Send with to when you have a phone number, recipient when you only have a BSUID; keep OTP templates on phone numbers.
  • Match statuses by message ID.
  • Re-key opt-outs, blocks, de-duplication and integrations on the contact, not the phone number.
  • Test with Meta's sample messages webhook from your app dashboard before your customers do it for you.

Usernames are good for users: people can talk to a business without handing over their number. Code that assumed a phone number would always be there has to catch up.

I work on WAPGROWAI, a WhatsApp Business platform built on the Cloud API. Earlier in this series: phone numbers, webhooks, WhatsApp Flows and build vs buy.

title: What are the best RunPod alternatives for AI training in 2026?
description:
If your training runs long enough that losing a machine hurts, Nodus is the strongest RunPod alternative. It restores your latest checkpoint on a new machine when capacity is reclaimed, so cheaper interruptible GPUs can finish long jobs, and its listed NVIDIA H100 rate is below RunPod's Secure Cloud rate. Modal suits short Python jobs, CoreWeave and Together AI suit clusters bought by the node, and AWS SageMaker or Google Vertex AI suit cloud credits; RunPod stays the pick for cheap interactive pods.

We build Nodus, so read this list with that in mind. Every competitor fact below links to that company's own pricing page or docs, and the cost math is written out so you can redo it with your own rates.

How do the main RunPod alternatives compare for training?

The short version: they differ less on the hourly price than on who restarts your run when a machine disappears.

Platform Best for How you pay H100 per GPU-hour (listed) When a machine is reclaimed
RunPod Interactive pods, cheap consumer GPUs Per second, prepaid balance $2.69 Community Cloud, $3.99 Secure Cloud (H100 SXM) On-demand pods are not displaced by other users
Nodus Long or interruptible training, fine-tuning, inference and agents on one platform Prepaid credits $2.60 (H100 SXM) Latest checkpoint restored on a replacement machine
Modal Short and medium Python jobs, serverless endpoints Per second $3.95 (H100 SXM5) Function restarts on the same input; you write the checkpointing
Together AI Preemptible clusters, hosted fine-tuning API Per GPU-hour $1.99 preemptible, $3.99 on demand (HGX H100) Preemptible tier listed; recovery not stated on the pricing page
CoreWeave Large multi-node runs bought by the node Per 8-GPU node-hour $6.16 on demand, about $2.46 spot (HGX H100) Spot rate listed; recovery not stated on the pricing page
AWS SageMaker Teams spending AWS credits By instance and time Varies by instance and region Managed spot copies checkpoints to and from Amazon S3
Google Vertex AI Teams spending Google Cloud credits By machine type and time Varies by machine type and region Job restarted up to six times; you write the checkpoints
Baseten Teams that already serve on Baseten Per minute $6.50 Not stated on the pricing page

Prices checked October 25, 2026 on each vendor's page: RunPod pricing and Pods docs, Nodus pricing, Modal pricing and preemption docs, Together AI pricing, CoreWeave pricing, SageMaker managed spot training, Vertex AI Spot VMs for training and Baseten pricing. Modal's $0.001097 per second and Baseten's $0.10833 per minute are multiplied out to hours. CoreWeave's 8-GPU node prices ($49.24 on demand, $19.71 spot) are divided by 8. The Nodus H100 SXM figure is listed at $2.60/hr on the Nodus pricing page.

A naming note: the company now styles itself Runpod, per its docs. Most people still search for RunPod, so we use that spelling here.

Why do teams look for a RunPod alternative?

Most reasons come straight from RunPod's own pricing docs, and they matter more for a 10-hour training run than for a notebook session.

The H100 price depends on which cloud you pick. RunPod lists an H100 SXM at $2.69/hr on Community Cloud and $3.99/hr on Secure Cloud. Its concepts page describes Secure Cloud as T3/T4 data centers and Community Cloud as individual compute providers connected through a vetted peer-to-peer system. Teams that need the data-center tier pay the higher rate.

An empty balance ends work hard. RunPod's Pods pricing docs say pods stop when the balance reaches $0, and pods without a network volume are terminated with data that cannot be recovered. Container disk is erased whenever a pod stops.

There is a default ceiling on spend. The same page sets a default limit of $80/hour across all resources. An 8 x H100 SXM pod on Secure Cloud is 8 x $3.99 = $31.92/hr, so two fit under the limit and a third does not until support raises it.

Discounts moved to sales. RunPod's savings plans are deprecated and can no longer be bought, so lower rates for steady use now go through its enterprise sales team.

Clusters have a stated size. Instant Clusters run 2 to 8 nodes, 16 to 64 GPUs, in one data center.

None of this is a claim about RunPod's uptime. It is what the docs say happens to your files and your bill.

What does one 80 GPU-hour training run cost on each?

On listed H100 rates, the same 8 x H100, 10-hour run ranges from about $159 on preemptible capacity to $520 on per-minute billing. We worked these from each vendor's published price, GPU compute only, with storage and egress left out.

Platform and capacity Rate used 8 x H100 for 10 hours
Together AI, preemptible $1.99/GPU-hr $159.20
CoreWeave, spot node $19.71/node-hr $197.10
Nodus $2.60/GPU-hr $208.00
RunPod, Community Cloud $2.69/GPU-hr $215.20
Modal $3.9492/GPU-hr $315.94
RunPod, Secure Cloud $3.99/GPU-hr $319.20
Together AI, on demand $3.99/GPU-hr $319.20
CoreWeave, on demand node $49.24/node-hr $492.40
Baseten Training $6.4998/GPU-hr $519.98

Each row is 80 GPU-hours times the rate, or 10 node-hours for CoreWeave. Against RunPod Secure Cloud, the Nodus figure is $111.20 lower for this run.

The cheapest rows are interruptible, and their real price depends on what a reclaim costs you. Say a reclaim lands at hour 6 and your last checkpoint was 25 minutes earlier.

A run that restores that checkpoint loses 25 / 60 x 8 = 3.3 GPU-hours. A run that restarts from zero loses 6 x 8 = 48 GPU-hours, more than half the job, plus the time someone spends noticing and relaunching it. That gap is why we rank recovery above the hourly rate.

Which RunPod alternative should you pick?

Start from the job, not the price list. This is the rule we use when people ask us.

If you need Pick
A long single-node run where the bill matters and your script can checkpoint Nodus
To keep your RunPod account and balance but add automatic recovery Nodus, with RunPod connected as a cloud account (Beta)
Training, fine-tuning, inference endpoints and agents billed in one place Nodus
Short Python jobs next to web endpoints Modal
A hosted fine-tuning API instead of your own training loop Together AI fine-tuning
More than 8 nodes on one fabric, bought by the node CoreWeave or Together AI
To spend AWS credits or commitments AWS SageMaker with managed spot training
To spend Google Cloud credits Google Vertex AI with Spot VMs
Training next to models you already serve on Baseten Baseten Training
A cheap consumer GPU with SSH for an afternoon Stay on RunPod Community Cloud

How does Nodus keep a preempted run going?

Nodus treats every run as a series of attempts, and a new attempt starts from your latest committed checkpoint. The attempts and recovery docs spell out the order. On a reclaim notice, Nodus asks your run for an urgent checkpoint and prepares a replacement machine at the same time. The replacement starts only once the old machine is provably gone, so two copies never write over each other.

A Checkpointed run loses at most the work since its last committed checkpoint, and a checkpoint taken during the reclaim notice still counts. Your program writes its weights, optimizer state and step to /nodus/state and reads them back on start. Nodus restores files, not process memory, and never adds resume flags to your command.

Interruptible capacity is a placement choice, not a separate product. Nodus docs describe interruptible: Allow as using interruptible capacity only when it is cheaper to finish. Money stops are graceful too: when credits run out, a checkpointed Job takes an urgent checkpoint, suspends, and resumes from it once funded.

The same account runs Jobs, Sandboxes, Functions, inference endpoints, durable agents and TrainingJobs (Beta). Coding agents can drive it through the Nodus MCP server. Creating a resource there requires an accepted dry run, and the agent works inside the person's own projects and spending limits. RunPod also offers an MCP server, so MCP alone is not the difference; the estimate-before-spend step is.

Can you keep your RunPod account and still use Nodus?

Yes, if your organization has the feature turned on. The cloud accounts docs list RunPod among the accounts you can connect with an API key and a credit limit (Beta, enabled per organization by Nodus support). Nodus then places your Jobs, Workspaces and other single-node work in that account first, up to the limit, and uses Nodus capacity when the account is full or out of credit. Sandboxes and multi-node runs use Nodus capacity.

This is the documented command. The key is read from standard input, never from the command line:

printf '%s' "$RUNPOD_API_KEY" | nodus cloud connect runpod my-runpod --credit-limit 200

The --burst flag decides what happens when that account is full: allow Nodus capacity (the default), ask for approval, or deny it.

Where is RunPod still the better choice?

RunPod wins for cheap, hands-on GPU time. Its pricing page lists an RTX 4090 at $0.34/hr on Community Cloud, pods bill by the second, and its docs state no fees for data ingress or egress. If you want SSH into a box, a Jupyter notebook and an hour of tinkering, that is hard to beat.

It also has a serverless product for inference, a template hub, and Instant Clusters with 3200 Gbps networking on H200 and B200 nodes. If your training already fits in one pod, saves its own checkpoints to a network volume, and someone is watching it, moving may not be worth the afternoon.

Modal stays ahead for short functions wired to web endpoints. CoreWeave and Together AI are built for very large clusters, where Nodus multi-node training is still in Beta.

How do you move a RunPod training job to Nodus?

Point your checkpoint writes at /nodus/state, then run the same command through the CLI. First install and sign in:

pip install nodus-compute
nodus login

Then dry-run the job to see the estimate before anything is billed. Every flag here is documented in the nodus run CLI reference; the torchrun part is your existing command:

nodus run --name ft-h100 --gpu H100:8 --image nodus/pytorch \
  --checkpoint /nodus/state --continuity Checkpointed --interruptible \
  --max-cost 250 --dry-run -- torchrun --nproc_per_node 8 train.py

Drop --dry-run to submit it. The --max-cost 250 cap sits just above the $208 worked out earlier, so a run that goes long stops at the cap instead of draining your balance. For a head-to-head with Modal, see Nodus vs Modal. If you are weighing Modal too, our Modal alternatives for training list covers the same ground from that side.

FAQ

Is Nodus cheaper than RunPod Community Cloud?

For an H100 SXM, slightly, at the rates checked for this post: $2.60/hr listed on the Nodus pricing page against $2.69/hr on RunPod Community Cloud. For consumer cards such as the RTX 4090 or RTX 3090, compare both pricing pages on the day, because the gap is small and changes.

Does Nodus run my work on RunPod?

Only if you connect your own RunPod account and your organization has that feature enabled. Otherwise your work runs on Nodus capacity.

What happens to a Nodus job if my credits run out mid-run?

A checkpointed Job takes an urgent checkpoint, suspends, and resumes automatically from that checkpoint once you add credit. Nothing runs past what you funded.

Do I need to rewrite my training script?

Usually not. You need it to save state to /nodus/state and load whatever is there on start, the same save-and-resume pattern you already need for any long run.

Is there a free tier?

Nodus gives a first organization $2.00 of starter credit after email and card verification, and adds another $28.00 after a paid top-up, both expiring 30 days after the grant. Modal's Starter plan includes $30 of compute per month.

Originally published on the Nodus blog.

title: React Charts with SciChart.js: Introducing scichart-react
description:
TLDR: In this blog post we introduce a brand new open source library called scichart-react (npm, GitHub). This makes it easy to create stunning high-performance charts and data visualizations in React.

SciChart-React has now been released and is on npm as scichart-react. Examples, samples, documentation & tutorials are coming soon.

The official SciChart / React package solves the problem of component lifecycle with SciChart.js and avoids common pitfalls when creating charts in React. Code examples are given below of how to create React Charts, as well as where to find further information about this new React chart component.

Why Choose React JS for Chart Creation?

React JS has become the preferred choice for enterprises seeking robust and efficient application development, largely due to its component-based architecture, high performance, and rich ecosystem. Unlike other frameworks like Angular, React stands out for its virtual DOM, which ensures faster rendering and smooth handling of complex, data-intensive visualizations. Its modular nature allows for the creation of reusable, maintainable chart components, streamlining development and scalability. Additionally, React's vast library of tools and strong community support offers a wealth of resources, making it more adaptable to various charting requirements. The combination of flexibility, efficient data handling, and cross-platform compatibility positions React as a dominant force in the realm of enterprise-level data visualization, outpacing competitors in terms of performance and versatility.

Why Choose SciChart.js for React Charts?

SciChart.js is an advanced react chart library for use in complex and advanced mission critical applications. SciChart's key features include extremely high performance for big-data sets, a wide set of chart types, deep features and customisability.

For a full run-down of SciChart.js' features and why you should consider it for enterprise apps with complex requirements, read the following post:

https://www.scichart.com/blog/the-best-javascript-chart-10-reasons/

Create React Charts easily with SciChart-React

Earlier in the year, we published an article titled How to create a re-usable react component for SciChart.js. This demonstrated how to create charts in React by applying a few criteria for creation of a React Chart component:

  • The component should be reusable for different chart configurations
  • It should be possible to safely create several instances of the component
  • It should be easy to add custom functionality to the component
  • When chart instantiation is an async function, this should be properly handled
  • When the chart requires a root <div> element in the DOM it should exist before chart instantiation
  • Finally, the chart should be properly disposed and memory deleted after the component is unmounted.

As background reading it's worth reading the article. Problems which occurred in the past when creating React Charts with SciChart.js included double re-render, and potential memory leaks if your code improperly disposed of a chart surface by failing to call .delete().

We've created a new library called scichart-react which is open sourced and available on Github and npm. This solves the problems above and ensures that you have good quality code managing your react components and provides a clean, neat way to instantiate charts in react using simple props.

Step-by-Step Guide: Building Your First Chart in React with SciChart.js

SciChartReact provides an easy solution for using the SciChart core library for charts in React.

In the next sections, we will demonstrate a basic usage of the component.

Basic React Chart Example

Follow the prerequisites and installation sections from https://www.npmjs.com/package/scichart-react.

And just with few lines of code, you can set up a chart in React.

Create a Chart with Config (Builder) API

The Builder API in SciChart allows you to create charts in JavaScript with JS objects or JSON. This can be translated into React using scichart-react as follows.

The example uses the config property which accepts a configuration object of the chart. You can also pass a string with serialized chart configuration.

import { SciChartReact } from "scichart-react";
import { ESeriesType, EThemeProviderType } from "scichart";

/**
 * The chart configuration object acceptable by the Builder API
 * @type {import("scichart").TSurfaceDefinition}
 */
const chartConfig = {
  surface: {
    theme: { type: EThemeProviderType.Dark },
    title: "Basic Chart via Config",
    titleStyle: {
      fontSize: 20,
    },
  },
  series: {
    type: ESeriesType.SplineMountainSeries,
    options: {
      strokeThickness: 4,
      stroke: "#216939",
      fillLinearGradient: {
        startPoint: { x: 0, y: 0 },
        endPoint: { x: 1, y: 1 },
        gradientStops: [
          { offset: 0.3, color: "#2d2169" },
          { offset: 1, color: "transparent" },
        ],
      },
    },
    xyData: { xValues: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4], yValues: [3, 6, 1, 5, 2] },
  },
};

export const BasicChart = () => (
  <SciChartReact style={{ width: 400, height: 300 }} config={chartConfig} />
);

Here's the output

**Note* SciChartReact extends properties of the HTMLDivElement and propagates them to the underlying div element.*

Create a React Chart with Programmatic API

Alternatively, SciChartReact accepts an initialization function. This allows the creation of a chart with the usual SciChart.js API. In this case the chartInitializationFunction below must be async and accepts the <div> rootElement created by scichart-react as a parameter. This can be passed straight to SciChartSurface.create().

import { SciChartReact } from "scichart-react";
import {
  EThemeProviderType,
  NumericAxis,
  SciChartSurface,
  SplineMountainRenderableSeries,
  XyDataSeries,
} from "scichart";
/**
 * A function executed within SciChartReact with provided chart root element,
 * creates a SciChartSurface instance and returns a reference to it.
 *
 * @param {string | HTMLDivElement} rootElement
 * @returns {Promise<{sciChartSurface: SciChartSurface}>}
 */
const chartInitializationFunction = async (rootElement) => {
  const { sciChartSurface, wasmContext } = await SciChartSurface.create(
    rootElement,
    {
      theme: { type: EThemeProviderType.Dark },
      title: "Basic Chart via Init Function",
      titleStyle: {
        fontSize: 20,
      },
    }
  );

  sciChartSurface.xAxes.add(new NumericAxis(wasmContext));
  sciChartSurface.yAxes.add(new NumericAxis(wasmContext));
  sciChartSurface.renderableSeries.add(
    new SplineMountainRenderableSeries(wasmContext, {
      dataSeries: new XyDataSeries(wasmContext, {
        xValues: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4],
        yValues: [3, 6, 1, 5, 2],
      }),
      strokeThickness: 4,
      stroke: "#216939",
      fillLinearGradient: {
        startPoint: { x: 0, y: 0 },
        endPoint: { x: 1, y: 1 },
        gradientStops: [
          { offset: 0.3, color: "#2d2169" },
          { offset: 1, color: "transparent" },
        ],
      },
    })
  );

  return { sciChartSurface };
};

export const BasicChartWithInitFunction = () => (
  <SciChartReact
    style={{ width: 400, height: 300 }}
    initChart={chartInitializationFunction}
  />
);

Additionally, it is possible to easily add more customizations and functionality by providing arguments to other props:

  • fallback - a JSX element to render while the chart initialization is in progress
  • onInit - a callback that is executed after the chart initialization has been completed
  • onDelete - a callback executed when a fully initialized chart is unmounted

Advanced React Chart example - Selection and Synchronization with a DataGrid

Let’s look at another more complex example:

  1. For this case, we will take a setup with a Scatter Chart that fetches data asynchronously.
  2. The points on the chart could be selected by click and drag action.
  3. Upon selection, the point info appears within a grid at the side of the chart

Step 1 - Fetching Data Asynchronously and loading the Chart

Considering that the data fetching as well as a chart initialization potentially can take a noticeable amount of time, let’s make sure to set a custom loading UI with fallback property.

/**
 * @param {string | HTMLDivElement} rootElement
 * @returns {Promise<{sciChartSurface: SciChartSurface}>}
 */
const chartInitializationFunction = async (rootElement) => {
  const createChart = async () => {
    // for demonstration purposes, here we have used Builder API explicitly
    const { sciChartSurface } = await chartBuilder.build2DChart(rootElement, {
      xAxes: {
        type: EAxisType.NumericAxis,
        options: {
          autoRange: EAutoRange.Once,
          growBy: new NumberRange(0.2, 0.2),
        },
      },
      yAxes: {
        type: EAxisType.NumericAxis,
        options: { autoRange: EAutoRange.Never },
      },
      surface: {
        theme: { type: EThemeProviderType.Dark },
        title: "Scatter Chart",
        titleStyle: {
          fontSize: 20,
        },
      },
    });

    return sciChartSurface;
  };

  // a function that simulates an async data fetching
  const getData = async () => {
    await new Promise((resolve) => {
      setTimeout(() => resolve({}), 1500);
    });

    return { xValues: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4], yValues: [3, 6, 1, 5, 2] };
  };

  const [sciChartSurface, data] = await Promise.all([createChart(), getData()]);

  const wasmContext = sciChartSurface.webAssemblyContext2D;

  sciChartSurface.renderableSeries.add(
    new XyScatterRenderableSeries(wasmContext, {
      dataSeries: new XyDataSeries(wasmContext, {
        ...data,
      }),
      strokeThickness: 4,
      stroke: "#216939",
    })
  );
  return { sciChartSurface };
};

// ...
// then in JSX
// ...

<SciChartReact
  style={{ width: "50%", height: 300 }}
  fallback={
    <div className="fallback">
      <div>Data fetching & Chart Initialization in progress</div>
    </div>
  }
  initChart={chartInitializationFunction}
/>

Step 2 - Adding in Selection Behavior to the Chart

To achieve this behavior we can use DataPointSelectionModifier, which is a built-in behaviour in SciChart to allow selection, and multi-selection of data-points on a chart.

  // ...

  /**  
   * @param {{sciChartSurface: SciChartSurface}} initResult 
   *    - a resolved object returned by the initialization function 
   */
  const onChartInitializationComplete = (initResult) => {
    const dataPointSelectionModifier = new DataPointSelectionModifier({
      allowClickSelect: true,
      allowDragSelect: true,
      selectionStroke: "lime",
      selectionFill: "#ff879f33",
      onSelectionChanged: (args) =>
        setSelectedPoints([...(args?.selectedDataPoints || [])]),
    });

    initResult.sciChartSurface.chartModifiers.add(dataPointSelectionModifier);
  };

  const onChartCleanup = () => setSelectedPoints([]);

  // ...

  <SciChartReact
    style={{ width: "50%", height: 300 }}
    fallback={
      <div className="fallback">
        <div>Data fetching & Chart Initialization in progress</div>
      </div>
    }
    initChart={chartInitializationFunction}
    onInit={onChartInitializationComplete}
    onDelete={onChartCleanup}
  />

Step 3 - Synchronising Selection Data from a Chart to a DataGrid

Now to bind the point selection to a grid, we are adding an appropriate callback to the DataPointSelectionModifier - onSelectionChanged.

It can be used to get the list of the selected points and then we should be able to easily put them into a grid.


// ...

<div className="flex-container">
  <SciChartReact
    style={{ width: "50%", height: 300 }}
    fallback={
      <div className="fallback">
      <div>Data fetching & Chart Initialization in progress</div>
      </div>
    }
    initChart={chartInitializationFunction}
    onInit={onChartInitializationComplete}
    onDelete={onChartCleanup}
  />

  <div className="data-grid">
    <div className="grid-cell grid-header">
      <div>Selected Points</div>
    </div>
    <div className="grid-cell column-header">
      <div>X Value</div>
    </div>
    <div className="grid-cell column-header">
      <div>Y Value</div>
    </div>

    {selectedPoints.map((point) => (
      <>
        <div key={`x-val-${point.index}`} className="grid-cell">
          <div>{point.xValue}</div>
        </div>
        <div key={`y-val-${point.index}`} className="grid-cell">
           <div>{point.yValue}</div>
        </div>
      </>
    ))}
  </div>
</div>

Further Examples of React Charts with scichart-react

The full source-code for all three examples in this blog post, showing how to create a Basic React Chart with config, a Basic Chart with programmatic API, as well as the DataGrid sync example are included in the Codesandbox here.

Additional resources can be found below.

  • Simple Examples: SciChart-react code examples - Github Pages
  • Source: SciChart-React source-code on Github
  • npm: SciChart-React package on npm
  • Advanced examples: we're working through the SciChart.js Demo to update all our examples to use scichart-react.

Conclusion

Integrating SciChart with React for Powerful Charting

It has always been possible to use SciChart's JavaScript Charts within React. We previously documented how to create a reusable react component talking about some of the issues such as correct component lifecycle and handling SciChart's async initialisation.

We've now wrapped this up into an open source library called scichart-react to make creating React Charts easy.

Try out SciChart-React!

We encourage you to try out scichart-react: our React Chart component and see if it helps you simplify the development of charts with SciChart.js.Internally we've handled a lot of the problems associated with React such as double-render, component unmount and proper deletion of SciChart charts, wrapping it all up neatly in a small package which adds only 3kb of JavaScript to your application.

We'll be talking about further examples and utilities in the future, so do watch our blog for further updates!

Also see

See our related posts comparing JavaScript chart libraries, plus a showcase of the best React Charts and Graphs

https://www.scichart.com/blog/showcase-of-the-best-react-charts-and-graphs/

https://www.scichart.com/blog/alternatives-to-chart-js/

title: ReLEAP: Upcycling Vision Datasets through Cross-Task Unification and Semi-Supervised Annotation
description:
arXiv:2610.32289v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Developing robust vision models requires large amounts of annotated data, especially for tasks involving fine-grained class distinctions under variable environmental conditions. Even in domains with numerous existing datasets, differences in annotation formats, label definitions and targeted learning tasks hinder data reuse and integration. To address this challenge, we introduce ReLEAP, a scalable Python framework for unifying heterogeneous image datasets through data-source abstraction, systematic reuse of annotations across learning tasks, and mapping of labels to a shared hierarchical taxonomy. We demonstrate its applicability in precision agriculture by integrating fifteen diverse datasets covering a broad range of plant species and annotation types. Beyond unification, ReLEAP enables systematic recycling of existing data and provides a robust foundation for learning-based annotation upcycling. Leveraging this foundation, we conduct extensive cross-dataset and fine-tuning experiments to investigate how domain-specific models trained on unified data and foundation models can be used to automatically generate higher-level annotations under unsupervised, weakly supervised and semi-supervised settings, and how dataset characteristics influence their effectiveness. Our results show that unified data access and annotation upcycling substantially expand the pool of reusable training data and annotations while improving data transparency, enabling more sustainable and resource-efficient use of existing datasets. We release the framework and trained models for academic use to support accessible and collaborative research, particularly in data-scarce and heterogeneous domains.

title: AI Agent Status Updates: Build Progress Users Can Trust Without Exposing Chain of Thought
description:
An agent that goes quiet for ten minutes does not feel autonomous. It feels broken. A spinner and a made-up “82% complete” label are not much better: they encourage users to trust a number your system cannot justify.

The fix is not to stream the model's hidden reasoning. It is to publish a small, evidence-backed account of the work: what phase the run is in, the last verified milestone, whether it needs a person, and what will happen next. This article shows how to build that contract for long-running, tool-using AI agents.

The progress problem is really a trust problem

Users ask three practical questions while an agent runs:

  1. Is it still alive?
  2. Did it make meaningful progress?
  3. Do I need to do anything?

A token stream answers none of these reliably. It can continue while a tool is stuck, and it can stop even though a durable workflow will resume later. Likewise, an LLM-generated status such as “almost finished” is a prediction, not evidence.

Treat status as a product contract. The user-facing timeline should be derived from workflow events your system can verify: a job was accepted, a connector returned records, validation passed, an approval is waiting, or a final artifact was stored. The model may suggest a label, but it should not be the source of truth for state.

This distinction also protects privacy. A useful update is “Checked 42 invoices; 3 need review,” not a transcript of the agent's scratch work, retrieved customer text, or chain of thought.

Start with a state machine, not a progress bar

Long-running agent work has more states than running and failed. Model the states explicitly and make transitions durable.

State Meaning to the user Required evidence Useful UI action
queued Work is accepted but has not started run record created Cancel
running A worker currently owns the run lease heartbeat Stop
waiting_on_tool The run is awaiting a bounded external call tool request ID and deadline Cancel
waiting_on_user A decision or missing input is required approval or question ID Review / answer
retry_scheduled The system will retry later retry time and error class Cancel / view details
succeeded The requested result was verified and saved output receipt Open result
failed The run cannot continue automatically failure class and last checkpoint Retry / contact support
cancelled Work was intentionally stopped cancellation receipt Restart

Avoid a vague paused state. If the workflow is paused because it needs an address, show waiting_on_user. If it is paused because a vendor rate-limited it, show retry_scheduled. Specific state names let a user decide what to do without reading logs.

Here is a compact TypeScript event shape. It is deliberately about observable work, not hidden reasoning.

type RunEvent = {
  runId: string;
  sequence: number;          // monotonic per run
  at: string;
  type: "phase_started" | "milestone" | "approval_needed" |
        "retry_scheduled" | "completed" | "failed";
  phase?: "preparing" | "collecting" | "verifying" | "delivering";
  message: string;           // reviewed, user-safe copy
  evidence?: {
    kind: "artifact" | "tool_receipt" | "checkpoint" | "approval";
    id: string;
  };
  action?: { label: string; url: string };
};

Persist these events in the same transaction that changes workflow state, or attach them to an outbox. A UI event that says “report ready” before the report is stored is worse than no event at all.

Publish milestones, not a narrated thought process

Choose milestones at boundaries where the system can prove something changed. Good milestones are stable across model versions and useful if a run resumes tomorrow.

For a document-analysis agent, the timeline might be:

  • Request accepted
  • Source file scanned and indexed
  • 42 records extracted
  • Policy checks completed
  • Three exceptions need a decision
  • Final report saved

Notice what is absent: “thinking about clause 7” or “I believe this source is probably relevant.” Those claims are neither a dependable progress signal nor an appropriate audit record.

Each milestone needs an owner. The workflow engine owns checkpoint messages; the connector owns data-fetch receipts; the policy service owns validation results. If no component can produce evidence for an update, leave it out.

That rule prevents a common failure mode: a chat interface keeps emitting cheerful prose while the actual job stopped moving. Your supervisor should detect stale progress independently of the agent. For example, mark a run stalled internally when its lease heartbeat is fresh but neither a checkpoint nor a tool receipt has advanced within the expected phase window. The user-facing text can then say, “Still working longer than expected; no action needed yet,” or escalate honestly to “This task needs attention.”

Design an honest progress model

Percent complete works only when units of work are known. A migration over 10,000 rows has a denominator. An open-ended research task generally does not.

Use one of these models instead:

Work shape Best indicator Example
Fixed batch completed / total 318 of 500 files checked
Known workflow completed phase Verifying findings (3 of 4 phases)
Open-ended work elapsed time plus latest verified event Last verified update: sources indexed
Approval flow blocked state and decision impact Needs approval before sending 3 emails
Retryable external work next retry and preserved checkpoint Retrying connector at 14:05; 18 items saved

Do not convert phase count into a false percentage. Four phases do not necessarily take equal time, and the model can loop inside one phase. If you show an estimate, label it as a range derived from similar completed runs, and hide it when the sample is weak.

function statusCopy(run: Run) {
  if (run.status === "waiting_on_user")
    return "Your decision is needed before this task can continue.";

  if (run.completedUnits != null && run.totalUnits != null)
    return `${run.completedUnits} of ${run.totalUnits} items verified`;

  return `Last verified update: ${run.latestMilestone.message}`;
}

The word verified matters. It teaches users what the timeline represents and sets a standard your team can test.

Make waiting visible and actionable

The most damaging silence is not a slow model call. It is an agent waiting for a person while the product looks busy.

An approval event should include the decision, the consequence, the safe default, and an expiry rule. Keep the payload concise and reviewable:

{
  "type": "approval_needed",
  "message": "Three customer records have conflicting addresses.",
  "question": "Which address should be used for the renewal notice?",
  "options": ["CRM record", "latest support ticket", "skip these records"],
  "default": "skip these records",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-26T15:00:00Z",
  "evidence": { "kind": "approval", "id": "apr_8f2" }
}

Never bury an approval in a scrolling chat. Surface it as a run state, send a notification only when action is required, and ensure a resumed run re-reads the approved decision from durable storage. This pairs well with approval gates, but it solves a different problem: making the wait understandable to the person who initiated the work.

Transport updates without building a fragile realtime system

Start with the simplest transport that fits your product.

  • Polling is enough for minute-scale background jobs. Return status, latest_event, and etag; back off when nothing changes.
  • Server-sent events work well for one-way timelines and reconnect cleanly with Last-Event-ID.
  • WebSockets fit collaborative workspaces where users can also approve, stop, or redirect a run live.
  • Notifications should be sparse: completion, failure, and waiting_on_user are normally worth interrupting someone; routine milestones are not.

Regardless of transport, the client must tolerate duplicate and out-of-order events. Use the sequence field, make the event stream append-only, and fetch the authoritative run snapshot after reconnecting. The UI is a projection; the workflow database remains the authority.

Build the API around a durable run record

A small API surface is easier to secure and test than a channel full of ad hoc text.

GET /runs/run_123

{
  "status": "waiting_on_user",
  "phase": "verifying",
  "latest_event_sequence": 17,
  "latest_event": {
    "message": "42 records verified; 3 need a decision",
    "at": "2026-10-26T12:04:12Z"
  },
  "actions": [{ "kind": "approve", "approval_id": "apr_8f2" }]
}

Keep sensitive tool arguments, raw documents, and internal exception stacks behind a permissioned diagnostics view. The default run page should disclose only the minimum a user needs to understand progress and take the next action.

Test the status contract like an API

Status is part of the user experience, so add tests beyond the happy path:

  1. A run cannot become succeeded without an output receipt.
  2. A waiting_on_user run always exposes a decision action and cannot spend tools until it resumes.
  3. Replayed events create the same final timeline.
  4. A reconnect receives no duplicate visible milestones.
  5. A cancelled run cannot later publish a success event.
  6. A stale worker lease produces an honest recovery state, not permanent “Working…” copy.
  7. User-safe messages contain no prompt, secret, customer text, or chain of thought. 
it("does not claim success before output exists", async () => {
  await workflow.emit({ type: "completed", evidence: undefined });
  expect(await runs.get("run_123")).toMatchObject({ status: "failed" });
});

This is also where observability earns its keep. Measure time to first verified milestone, time spent waiting for users, stale-run recovery rate, and the share of runs that finish with a useful artifact. Avoid treating the number of progress messages as a health metric; a noisy timeline can conceal a poor workflow.

A practical rollout plan

Do not retrofit every agent at once. Start with one workflow where users currently refresh a page or ask support whether a job is stuck.

  1. Define the state machine and ownership of each transition.
  2. Add durable run records and one evidence-backed milestone per phase.
  3. Replace generic spinners with the latest verified update.
  4. Promote approval waits to a clear, resumable state.
  5. Add stale-run detection and a recovery message.
  6. Instrument completion quality, not just elapsed time.

The result is deliberately less theatrical than a stream of simulated thinking. It is far more useful: people can leave a long-running agent alone, return with context, and intervene exactly when their judgment is needed.

Keep the language stable across releases

Treat visible status copy as part of your API. Changing waiting_on_user from “Needs your decision” to “Paused” may seem cosmetic, yet it can break notification rules, customer runbooks, and accessibility labels. Version the event schema, localize messages at the presentation layer, and keep a small compatibility test suite for every public state. That discipline pays off when new models, tools, and workflow engines arrive: the user still receives the same clear promise about what has happened and what they can do next.

FAQ

Should an AI agent show its chain of thought as progress?

No. Show concise, evidence-backed milestones instead. They are more reliable, safer for sensitive data, and easier for users to act on.

How often should an agent send status updates?

Update on meaningful state changes, verified milestones, and action-required moments. For long silent phases, add a bounded heartbeat that says the job is still owned, not a stream of filler messages.

Is a percentage complete useful for AI agents?

Only when the work has a known denominator, such as files processed or records checked. Otherwise show the phase, elapsed time, and most recent verified milestone.

What is the best state for an agent waiting on a person?

Use a specific waiting_on_user state with the exact question, a safe default, and a resumable approval ID. Do not leave the run labeled running.

Can polling work for long-running AI workflows?

Yes. Polling is simple and reliable for background tasks that update every few seconds or minutes. Use ETags and backoff, then move to SSE or WebSockets only when the interaction requires it.

How do you detect an AI agent that is stuck?

Track worker leases, tool deadlines, and the time since the last verified milestone. A supervisor outside the model should classify stale runs and surface a recovery state.

title: Building a Digital Abacus: React Native UI/UX Challenges for Kids' EdTech tags: reactnative, webdev, ui, edtech
description:
Translating a 2,000-year-old physical tool into a digital mobile experience is harder than it looks—especially when your primary users are between the ages of 4 and 15.

At the Orphosys Foundation, our goal is to modernize cognitive child development. We teach Meta-Skill Abacus and Vedic Math, traditionally relying on physical abacus frames where kids use their thumbs and index fingers to slide beads at lightning speed.

When we set out to build Orphosys Kids, our companion mobile app, we had to figure out how to make a glass screen feel as responsive and intuitive as a wooden bead. Here is how we tackled the UI/UX and gesture challenges using React Native.

  1. The "Fat Finger" Problem & Hitboxes

Children don’t tap screens with pinpoint accuracy. When sliding a digital bead up to the reckoning bar, they often drag their fingers outside the visual bounds of the bead.

If we strictly tied the touch area to the visual SVG of the bead, the app would drop the gesture mid-slide, frustrating the student. Our solution was to decouple the visual component from the touch component. We wrapped our SVGs in invisible, expanded containers with padded hitboxes, ensuring that even if a child's finger slipped slightly, the gesture was maintained.

  1. Snappy Physics with Gesture Handler

Mental math relies on speed. If a digital bead has a sluggish frame-rate or floating animation, it disrupts the child's calculation rhythm.

Using react-native-gesture-handler, we captured the vertical pan gestures but bypassed standard smooth spring animations. We engineered the state to immediately snap the bead to the active or inactive position once it crossed a specific Y-axis threshold. It feels rigid and mechanical—which is exactly how a real abacus behaves.

  1. A Unified EdTech Stack

We chose React Native because we are already heavily invested in the React ecosystem.

Our main Education Management System (used to manage our regional hubs and independent Abacus franchise centers) is built on Next.js and Supabase. By using React Native, we can share state-management logic and backend sync protocols across both web and mobile. When a student completes an offline arithmetic worksheet on the app, the moment they hit Wi-Fi, their accuracy scores sync seamlessly back to their teacher's web dashboard via Supabase.

What's Next?

Our next major milestone is integrating Python and C++ to handle camera-based, touchless DMIT (Brain Mapping) scans directly through the app.

If you're building in the EdTech space or wrangling complex gestures in React Native, let me know how you've handled similar UI challenges in the comments below!

title: "Not" is Not Lost in Translation: A Causal Analysis of Negation Representations in Multilingual LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.32281v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Negation occurs in every language, yet its surface realization differs drastically. Despite this, multilingual large language models (LLMs) translate negation robustly, raising the question of whether they share an underlying representation of negation across languages. We study this question in six open models across English, French, Vietnamese, and Chinese, using causal interventions on a synthetic contrastive dataset and a negation translation dataset derived from FLORES-200. Across models, we find strong evidence that negation representations are causally controllable and largely shared across languages. In particular, we show that a contrastive activation direction extracted from one language can induce or remove negation in the others, and directions extracted from different languages are substantially aligned. We further find that negation is represented in sparse features: a single sparse autoencoder (SAE) feature per model suffices to control polarity across languages, while responding selectively to negated inputs. Finally, both dense and sparse interventions generalize to four additional languages and FLORES-derived sentences. We release data and code to support future work: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/negation-translation/.
