title: Summarizing Large Marketplace Documents in Go: LLM API Batch or Streaming
description:
Go LLM Operations for Marketplace Knowledge Bases: Async Jobs Versus Live Output

Use asynchronous batch jobs for large or numerous private documents, and use streaming chat for a person waiting on one answer. The important implementation choice is the recovery contract: a lost response must be safe to replay, and a completed summary must be safe to write twice. For a marketplace knowledge base, I would keep that contract inside a Go adapter so changing the model provider does not change document ownership, revision tracking, or rollback.

The first operational rule is simple: assign a stable identity before sending work. Persist the document revision, chunk manifest, prompt revision, provider choice, and attempt state. Then a retry can refer to the same logical summary rather than creating a second one by accident.

For this adapter, Infrai is worth testing early because its public discovery surface is self-describing and needs no key, so request and response schemas can be checked before the provider is wired into the marketplace workflow. It is not the right choice when a direct vendor's model-specific controls or regional availability are the acceptance criteria.

What does the failure path need to preserve?

The dangerous event is not a visible error. It is ambiguity. A connection can disappear after the service accepted a request, a rate limit can arrive halfway through a traffic spike, or a worker can die after receiving results but before recording them. Treating each of these as “try again” is how duplicate summaries enter a private knowledge base.

Use a key such as marketplace-doc-8472-revision-19-summary-v3, derived from the document revision and summarization policy. Store it before submission. The result writer should compare that identity with the current accepted attempt and document revision; a late result must not replace a newer summary merely because it arrived last.

Rate limits deserve bounded waiting. Honor Retry-After when it is usable, otherwise apply exponential backoff with jitter and a deadline. A malformed request is a terminal 4xx and should surface its response body. A timeout or transient 5xx can be retried, but only while the job remains recoverable after the process exits.

This gives the platform team three useful SLOs: the share of summaries accepted before the freshness deadline, the age of the oldest pending job, and duplicate-write prevention events. Request latency alone is not enough. A fast API can still leave a marketplace search index stale for hours.

How should I summarize large documents with an LLM API?

For a large document, pre-check the token count before submission. If the input exceeds the selected model context, split it first, summarize each chunk, and then summarize the chunk summaries. Record the chunk manifest; otherwise a retry may silently use a different decomposition and produce a result that cannot be compared with the first attempt.

For many documents, submit asynchronously through the batch interface, poll the job status, and fetch the results when the job is ready. Keep polling state in the application, with a maximum age and an operator-visible stale state. If work must stop, use the documented cancellation operation and preserve any already-received output for reconciliation. Cancellation is a state transition, not proof that every downstream effect disappeared.

For one real-time request, chat streaming gives a buyer, seller, or support agent progressive output. Streaming is the better interaction for a person already looking at the screen. It is awkward as the ingestion mechanism for thousands of revised listings because every interrupted connection needs its own decision about partial output and replay.

The decision table is intentionally about waiting behavior, not provider fashion:

Workload Processing shape Recovery rule
One buyer-facing question Chat completion with streaming Treat partial text as provisional until the request finishes
A large document Token count, chunk, then summarize Persist chunk order and prompt revision
A nightly set of policy or catalog revisions Batch submit and poll Reuse the job identity and make the result write idempotent

That division also protects the portability boundary. The marketplace owns document identity, acceptance tests, and the summary ledger. The provider adapter owns request translation and asynchronous state mapping. A provider swap should change the adapter configuration, not the rule that revision 19 can have only one accepted summary.

That is the whole boundary.

In practice, the awkward case is a 19-revision document that is submitted just before a worker loses its connection. The next worker sees no response, finds the same revision still pending, and is tempted to submit again. If the identity was persisted first, the worker can retry with the same logical key, poll the existing state, and let the result writer reject a late output from an older attempt. If the identity was created after the network call, no amount of dashboard inspection can reliably distinguish “never accepted” from “accepted but not observed.”

The small Go probe below checks the public discovery surface before an adapter release. It has no provider secret because this endpoint is public; production calls to authenticated capabilities still use the platform's Bearer key.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func main() {
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))

    resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()

    body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("discovery failed: status=%d body=%s", resp.StatusCode, body))
    }
    fmt.Printf("discovery is available: %d bytes\\n", len(body))
}

Where does provider portability actually help?

OpenAI Batch is a sensible choice for a team already invested in OpenAI request formats and operational tooling. Anthropic Message Batches is a strong alternative when Claude-specific behavior is part of the quality bar. Google Gemini Batch API fits a team whose models, controls, and operations already center on Google Cloud. These are real alternatives, not interchangeable labels: model quality, regional controls, batch semantics, and provider-specific features still belong in the evaluation.

Infrai fits the adapter when the team values a stable REST contract while the capability behind that contract changes. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and available without a key, exposing request and response schemas plus runnable examples; that makes a capability check part of code review instead of an SDK archaeology exercise. One credential can cover the platform's capabilities and one bill can replace a collection of provider credentials and invoices, which reduces bookkeeping when the adapter is evaluating more than one backend. One platform-wide discovery model can reduce the glue around provider evaluation, but it does not decide whether a summary is factually complete.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the marketplace's provider adapter when one REST contract, one credential, and inspectable capability schemas matter more than a specialist's model-only controls. Keep OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google in the lead when their model behavior, region, or evaluation results are the acceptance criterion. Limitation: Infrai is a poor fit for a team that needs a vendor's proprietary batch controls or a model unavailable in its deployment region; choose that specialist and accept the tighter coupling. Portability is a design constraint, not a substitute for a corpus test.

How should the runbook verify and undo a release?

Before production traffic, run a fixed corpus containing short policies, long catalog descriptions, duplicate revisions, malformed documents, and inputs that require chunking. Exercise a lost response after submission, repeated 429s, a permanent 4xx, a cancelled batch, and a worker restart during result persistence. Check one property above all: each document revision has at most one accepted summary, while rejected or late results remain explainable.

For rollback, stop new submissions, let in-flight work reach a known state or cancel it, and serve the last accepted summary. Keep provider job identifiers and raw error bodies long enough to reconcile late output. Compare the document revision and accepted-attempt identity before every write. If either differs, retain the result for review rather than silently overwriting the newer version.

No silent overwrite.

The same runbook works after a provider change because the marketplace ledger does not depend on the provider's internal job naming. Only the adapter and its verification results change. That is the practical value of a portability contract: recovery remains an application property even when the backend moves.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai AI discovery surface and verify capability and model readiness for the deployment region before enabling traffic.

References

  • OpenAI Batch API
  • Anthropic Message Batches
  • Google Gemini Batch API
  • MDN: Server-sent events
  • Infrai AI discovery surface

title: Vercel Connect adds managed Stripe API keys
description:
Vercel Connect can now create a separate restricted Stripe API key for each agent or task. When you create a Stripe connector, you can now choose Managed API Key as the connection method.

Vercel creates the key in your Stripe account, limited to the permissions you pick. The existing MCP and bring-your-own API key methods are unchanged.

type: embedded-entry-inline id: 3rOuKp0F4Nk80dMYJ5QX6U

Most apps and agents run on Stripe’s default secret key, which has full access to the account. With per-agent keys, each agent gets only the access its job needs. For example, a daily revenue report agent can be limited to read-only access to charges, and an onboarding agent can be limited to write access to customers.

Vercel creates and stores the key, so there is no secret key to paste. You can rotate it from the connector's settings without redeploying, and the old key stays valid for up to 24 hours while you switch.

Add the Stripe connector

Create a Stripe connector from the connectors directory, choose Managed API Key, pick its permissions, and attach it to your project. You can also start from the CLI, which opens the browser to finish setup:

title: The Power of CSS Grid in Modern Web Design: Beyond Layout Limits
description:
Let’s be completely honest: structural layout tools have come a long way. During the early days of frontend development, creating complex interfaces meant hacking together messy floats, tables, or heavy inline configurations.

While Flexbox solved many mobile alignment problems, it is fundamentally a one-dimensional system. When you need to build intricate, clean, and highly adaptive multi-column web layouts, CSS Grid is the absolute industry standard.

Maquetación patterns have evolved, and mastering native grids is what separates basic coders from elite frontend developers. Here is why you should ditch heavy frameworks and use clean grid properties today.

1. True Two-Dimensional Control

Flexbox forces you to choose between aligning elements horizontally or vertically per container. If you want to build a dynamic portfolio grid with varying card heights and spans, you end up nesting dozens of redundant div wrappers.

CSS Grid gives you native control over columns and rows simultaneously from a single parent element.

.blog-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(300px, 1fr));
  gap: 2rem;
}

With just three lines of clean, native CSS, you create a responsive layout that automatically recalculates columns based on the reader’s screen size—no media queries required.

2. Drastic HTML Code Reduction

One of the biggest bottlenecks for technical SEO is a bloated DOM tree. When you use old layout methods or heavy UI frameworks, your HTML file becomes a deep maze of structural elements that slow down browser rendering engines.

Because CSS Grid handles the entire structural placement directly from your style sheet, your HTML stays semantic, clean, and readable. This slashes initial file sizes and boosts your loading speed scores on Google Lighthouse.

3. Seamless Visual Reordering

Design requirements change completely when shifting from a wide desktop monitor to a narrow mobile viewport. Sometimes, a sidebar or an action button needs to appear first on mobile, even if it sits at the bottom of the desktop layout.

Instead of writing complex JavaScript logic to detach and move elements in the DOM, CSS Grid handles this instantly with the grid-area and grid-template-areas properties. You rewrite the visual flow in your style sheet without touching a single line of markup.

Embracing native CSS Grid structures is the best way to ensure your applications remain clean, scalable, and lightning-fast. Stop hiding behind heavy grid frameworks and start writing pure, modern CSS.

title: 18 of 40 Home Pages Handed Me the Same Facebook Page: facebook.com/2008
description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them is the unglamorous workhorse of the set: you give it a list of domains, it gives you back one flat row per domain — what the site runs (CMS, e-commerce, analytics, pixels, payments, hosting, chat), plus the e-mails, phone numbers and social profiles printed on the page it already had to fetch.

The technology half gets all the attention. The contact half is where the embarrassing bugs live: a wrong contact is still a valid-looking string, and nobody notices until they mail it.

Here is the one I found this weekend, measured on 40 live home pages on 26 October 2026.

Eighteen companies, one Facebook page

I pulled 40 real sites: 21 from a published gallery of small-business Squarespace sites (a skin clinic, a bakery, a notary, a juice brand, a surf shop) and 19 bigger names from earlier runs — Stripe, Shopify, Notion, Canva, Allbirds, Figma, Hubspot, Gymshark and friends. Then I looked at the facebook field.

facebook field, 40 sites:
  a real page          17
  facebook.com/2008    18
  facebook.com/pages    1
  empty                 4

Eighteen unrelated companies, one answer. facebook.com/2008 is not a page; it is a 404 with a shrug. And it is not a parsing accident on a weird site — it is the single most reliable thing in the whole sample.

The cause is one attribute in the opening tag:

<html xmlns:fb="http://www.facebook.com/2008/fbml" lang="en-US">

That is the Facebook Open Graph XML namespace, and the Squarespace template emits it on every page it builds. So on narcisorodriguez.com the first occurrence of the string facebook.com sits at byte 91. The company's actual page, facebook.com/NarcisoRodriguezStudio, sits at byte 11,847, in the footer, where a human would look.

My extractor used a non-global regex and String.match, which returns the first hit:

const SOCIAL = {
    facebook: /facebook\.com\/(?!(tr|sharer|plugins))[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{2,}/i,
    // …
};
const m = html.match(re);
if (m) socials[k] = `https://${m[0].replace(/^https?:\/\//, '')}`;

The negative lookahead is there because facebook.com/tr?id= (the Meta Pixel endpoint) and facebook.com/sharer had already burned me. So I knew the failure mode — I just kept patching it one reserved word at a time, and 2008 was never going to make that list by guessing.

Of the 40 pages, 19 ran Squarespace and 18 of those carried the namespace (one newer template had dropped it). Zero non-Squarespace sites carried it. A platform-specific artefact in a platform-shaped sample — which is exactly what a prospect list of small businesses is.

First match wins is the bug, not the regex

The repair is not a longer blocklist. It is to stop treating the first match as the answer: capture the handle, read every occurrence, and take the first one that can plausibly be a profile.

facebook: /facebook\.com\/(pages\/[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{2,}\/\d+|[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{2,}(?![A-Za-z0-9_.-])(?!\/fbml))/gi,

Three things earn their keep in that line:

  • (?!\/fbml) drops the namespace URL by its shape, not by its year.
  • (?![A-Za-z0-9_.-]) stops the engine from backtracking to capture 200 just to satisfy the lookahead. Without it the fix returns facebook.com/200, which is worse than before, because it looks less obviously wrong.
  • The pages/Name/12345 alternative comes first, because my own cleanup broke uncommongoods.com: its only Facebook link is the legacy form facebook.com/pages/UncommonGoods/44340057816, and my new reserved-word list had just killed pages. One of the ten sites I "fixed" on the first pass got worse, which is the argument for running the before/after on the full sample rather than on the site that annoyed you.

Numeric handles get a rule of their own: facebook.com/803046 is a legitimate page address but a useless one in a CSV, so it is a fallback, used only if the page names no handle anywhere.

Before and after, same 40 pages, same HTML:

Old New
A named profile 17 26
A URL that is not a profile 19 0
Empty 4 14

Nineteen of 40 rows changed: 9 recovered the company's real page out of HTML that had been in hand all along, and 10 traded a dead URL for null. Those ten sites genuinely have no Facebook link on the home page. null is the correct answer and it is the more valuable of the two changes — a row that says nothing invites you to look elsewhere, while a row that says facebook.com/2008 invites you to paste it into a CRM.

The other five social fields — Instagram, LinkedIn, X, YouTube, TikTok — came out identical on all 40 pages. I rewrote them the same way anyway: the next template that ships a namespace will not ship it for Facebook.

The same mistake, in the filters

What makes this worth a post rather than a changelog line: the actor made the identical mistake somewhere else, where it costs money.

Two inputs exist to turn a scan into a prospect list — keep only sites that use X, drop sites that use Y — and they match technology names loosely on purpose, so that shopify finds Shopify Plus and hubspot finds HubSpot CMS. Loosely meant String.includes:

if (mustNot.length && mustNot.some((m) => names.some((n) => n.includes(m)))) { … }

Over the actor's 209 signature names there are exactly eight pairs where one name contains another. Seven are the same vendor and behave as intended: Shopify/Shopify Plus, HubSpot/HubSpot CMS, Klarna/Klarna Checkout, Trustpilot/Trustpilot Widget, Cloudflare/Cloudflare Turnstile, LocalMed, Square Appointments. The eighth is not:

square  →  square | square appointments | squarespace

Square is a payment processor. Squarespace is a website builder. They share six letters and nothing else. So the obvious prospecting input — "online stores that have not already bought Square" — silently deleted every Squarespace site in the list.

Measured on the live platform, same input, two builds:

mustNotUse: ["square"], domains: [narcisorodriguez.com (Squarespace), hintwater.com (Shopify)]

build 0.0.21:  1 row delivered — narcisorodriguez.com filtered out
build 0.0.22:  2 rows delivered

This is nastier than the Facebook field: a filtered-out site produces no row, and filtered rows are not billed, so it leaves no trace in the invoice either. You do not get a wrong answer you can spot — you get a shorter list, and nothing tells you it was shortened for a reason you never asked for.

The fix is one predicate — match on whole words instead of raw substrings:

const nameMatches = (name, query) =>
    new RegExp(`(^|[^a-z0-9])${escape(query)}([^a-z0-9]|$)`, 'i').test(name);

shopify still matches shopify plus (boundary is the space). localmed still matches dentrix / localmed. square no longer matches squarespace, because the character after the match is s. All seven intended loose matches survived; the one collision died. Both fixes are live for buyers as build 0.0.23 of Tech Stack Detector.

What a row looks like

Input:

{
  "domains": ["uncommongoods.com", "narcisorodriguez.com"],
  "includeContacts": true
}

Real output, from the verification run:

{
  "domain": "uncommongoods.com",
  "technologies": ["Google Tag Manager", "Google Analytics 4", "Amazon CloudFront", "OneTrust", "Afterpay"],
  "categories": ["analytics", "cdn", "consent", "payments", "tag_manager"],
  "payments": ["Afterpay"],
  "consent": ["OneTrust"],
  "technologiesDetailed": [
    { "name": "Google Analytics 4", "category": "analytics", "foundIn": "tag-manager" },
    { "name": "Amazon CloudFront", "category": "cdn", "foundIn": "header" },
    { "name": "Afterpay", "category": "payments", "foundIn": "tag-manager" }
  ],
  "tagManagerContainers": ["GTM-PQPMHZ"],
  "emails": ["help@uncommongoods.com"],
  "facebook": "https://facebook.com/pages/UncommonGoods/44340057816",
  "x": "https://x.com/uncommongoods",
  "server": "AmazonS3",
  "readVia": "direct"
}

foundIn is worth keeping in your own build of this: two of those five technologies were not in the HTML at all, they were in the site's public Tag Manager container. And from the API it is four lines:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("<YOUR_API_TOKEN>")
run = client.actor("lergassy/tech-stack-detector").call(run_input={
    "domains": ["uncommongoods.com", "narcisorodriguez.com"],
    "mustNotUse": ["square"],
})
for site in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
    print(site.get("domain"), site.get("technologies"), site.get("facebook"))

When this is the wrong tool

It reads one page per domain — the home page — plus the Tag Manager container it points at. That is deliberate and it is the whole cost model, but it sets a ceiling: on these 40 sites only 16 printed an e-mail address on the home page. If contacts are the actual deliverable, a tool that crawls to /contact and /about will beat it, and Website Contacts API is where I send people for that. It also will not tell you what a site runs behind a login, and it is not a page-speed or SEO audit.

And the portable lesson, which cost me nothing to learn twice in one codebase: if your extractor takes the first regex match, you are trusting document order to agree with intent. On machine-generated HTML it never does. The template's boilerplate is always at byte 91. The human's answer is 11,000 bytes further down.

title: NUViT: Vision Transformers for Fourier Space Data
description:
arXiv:2610.32041v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated strong performance in many computer vision tasks but do not naturally extend beyond the natural image domain. One important example is Fourier-space data, which is used to represent a rich and diverse set of modalities, including medical imaging and microscopy. Standard ViT tokenization partitions an image into square patches on a Cartesian grid, which poorly fit the frequency and phase structure of Fourier-space data. We introduce Non-Uniform ViT, a simple, general-purpose vision transformer that redesigns image tokenization, data representation, and positional encoding to respect this structure. Experiments on Fourier-domain image classification, 2D crystal lattice identification, MRI annotation, and cryo-EM protein heterogeneity analysis show that NUViT consistently captures the structure of Fourier data better than standard architectures.

title: Dependency Injection Without Reflection: Wiring 100 Beans in 65 ms (Building Ligero, Part 3)
description:
Most Java developers meet dependency injection through annotations: @Autowired, @Component, a classpath scan, and a container that wires everything reflectively at startup. It works, and it's productive. It also hides where objects come from, and moves a whole class of mistakes (a missing bean, a cycle) from compile time to runtime.

Ligero takes the other road. Its container, Beans, is about 170 lines in ligero-core, and it's built on one idea: your wiring is plain code the compiler checks.

The API 

Beans beans = Beans.builder()
    .bind(DataSource.class,        b -> pgDataSource())
    .bind(ProductRepository.class, b -> new JdbcProductRepository(b.get(DataSource.class)))
    .bind(ProductService.class,    b -> new ProductService(b.get(ProductRepository.class)))
    .start();          // instantiates and validates the WHOLE graph here

Ligero app = Ligero.create();
app.beans(beans);      // every bean available to handlers via ctx.get(...)

app.get("/products/{id}", ctx ->
    ctx.json(ctx.get(ProductService.class).find(ctx.pathParamAsInt("id"))));

Each binding is a memoized singleton: the factory lambda runs once and every later get() returns the same instance. bindInstance registers an existing object; buildLazy() defers creation to first use if you prefer.

Fail-fast, with readable errors

start() resolves the entire graph immediately, so a broken wiring can never reach a request:

No binding for interface com.acme.Mailer (needed by com.acme.SignupService)
Dependency cycle: SignupService -> Mailer -> SignupService

Compare where each failure surfaces:

Scanning + reflection Beans (lambdas)
Missing dependency runtime error, sometimes deep in a request compile error, or fail-fast at start()
Startup cost scan classpath, build metadata, reflective injection plain constructor calls
"Where does this come from?" search annotations across the codebase Ctrl+click the lambda
GraalVM native needs reachability metadata or build-time processors works as-is (no reflection)

What it costs

On the project's benchmark harness, wiring a chain of 100 beans in fresh JVMs (median of 5 runs):

Container Median wiring time Relative
Ligero Beans ~65 ms 1x
Guice 7 ~400 ms ~6x
Spring 6.2 (component scanning) ~555 ms ~8.5x

The honest reading: most of Ligero's ~65 ms is plain class loading; the container itself works in microseconds. That's the whole point. Explicit lambda bindings do no scanning and no reflective injection, so "wiring" is essentially running your constructors. (The usual caveat applies: these are one harness on one machine, and Spring and Guice give you far more than wiring. The comparison is about this specific cost.)

Stereotypes are metadata, never magic

Ligero does provide @Component, @Service, @Repository and @Controller, but they never drive injection. They exist so tools can classify beans:

@Repository
public class JdbcProductRepository implements ProductRepository { ... }

@Service
public class ProductService { ... }

beans.graph() returns the typed dependency graph, with nodes tagged by stereotype and edges captured from the real resolution order. The devtools dashboard (post 5) draws exactly that.

Modules: vertical slices that own their wiring

A large app is a set of features. A LigeroModule groups the controller, service, repository and routes of one feature, and declares its own bindings:

public final class ProductsModule implements LigeroModule {

    @Override
    public void beans(Beans.Builder builder) {
        builder.bind(ProductRepository.class, b -> new JdbcProductRepository(b.get(DataSource.class)));
        builder.bind(ProductService.class,    b -> new DefaultProductService(b.get(ProductRepository.class)));
        builder.bind(ProductController.class, b -> new ProductController(b.get(ProductService.class)));
    }

    @Override
    public void routes(Ligero app, Beans beans) {
        beans.get(ProductController.class).register(app);
    }
}

Application just lists modules, so the startup class never grows:

static LigeroModule[] modules() {
    return new LigeroModule[] { new ProductsModule(), new UsersModule() };
}

All modules contribute to one container, so cross-module dependencies resolve naturally (a shared DataSource from an infrastructure module, say). Binding the same type twice fails at startup.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Products
        PC[ProductController] --> PS[ProductService] --> PR[ProductRepository]
    end
    subgraph Orders
        OC[OrderController] --> OS[OrderService]
    end
    OS --> PS
    PR --> DS[(DataSource)]

Interfaces between layers

Each layer depends on the next through an interface. Three payoffs: swap implementations without touching callers (in-memory to JDBC), inject fakes in tests, and let tooling wrap interface-typed beans in spy proxies. That last one is the bridge to devtools.

Lifecycle and instrumentation

beans.close() closes AutoCloseable beans in reverse creation order. beans.all(HealthCheck.class) returns every bean assignable to a type. And Beans.Builder.instrument(BeanDecorator) lets a tool wrap every bean as it's created; in production no decorator exists, so beans are exactly the objects your lambdas returned.

Trade-offs, plainly

  • You write the bindings. The CLI generates and registers them for you (ligero generate service Invoice --module Billing), and an optional compile-time annotation processor (ligero-processor) can generate the bind(...) calls, still with no runtime reflection.
  • No scoped beans (request scope, prototype) out of the box. Singletons cover most service-style apps; if you need request-scoped state, that's what the Context is for.
  • It's deliberately not a Spring replacement. It's the smallest container that gives fail-fast wiring, modules and tracing hooks.

Takeaways

  • Wiring as lambdas turns missing beans and cycles into startup failures with readable messages.
  • No scanning and no reflective injection means wiring cost is basically your constructors.
  • Stereotypes are metadata; modules keep each feature's wiring next to its code.

Next: the benchmark that told me my fastest engine was my slowest, and the one-line reason why.

title: Shorter Is Not Cheaper: A Controlled Comparison of Declarative Animation Specifications and Free-Form Code for LLM-Generated Explanations
description:
arXiv:2610.32129v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chat assistants increasingly answer conceptual questions with interactive, animated explanations, generated either as free-form HTML/JavaScript or as declarative specifications that a fixed runtime plays. The declarative route is widely expected to be cheaper, faster and more reliable, because its outputs are shorter and constrained. We test this expectation in controlled comparisons whose hypotheses and analysis plans were frozen before the runs. We designed ExplainSpec, a time-indexed declarative animation format, and an observation contract that makes every generated explanation programmatically inspectable; validated, pacing-agnostic checkers score 20 explanation requests from five domains. Three Claude models (360 jobs) and, in a follow-up, the open-weight Qwen3-14B with thinking enabled and disabled (240 jobs) answered every request in both formats. For every model the specifications were 25-48% shorter in answer tokens (output excluding reasoning), yet with reasoning enabled total output fell significantly only for the largest Claude model and no model generated significantly faster. The reasons differed. The Claude models reasoned far more before writing specifications (exploratory; for the two larger models, from 15-20% to 85-88% of generations). Qwen3-14B reasoned about as much in both formats (a pre-registered test of this shift was not supported), and its shorter answers saved little against a reasoning trace more than twice as long. Nor were specifications more reliable: free-form pages were valid after one repair round in 95-100% of jobs for every model, whereas Qwen3-14B produced valid specifications in only 33% of jobs and passed all semantic tests in 17% (HTML/JavaScript: 62%). For reasoning models, a shorter format alone therefore does not make generation cheaper, faster or more reliable, and a format learned in context can cost reliability.

title: Guided Zero-Shot Anomaly Explanation for Anonymized Crowd Video Monitoring: Context, Categorization, and Spatial Localization
description:
arXiv:2610.32073v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Despite the promising development of deep learning for video anomaly detection (VAD), explainability (XAI) of these models remains a challenge. Explainable and privacy-protecting VAD builds transparency and trust that facilitates adoption of computer vision systems, including safety and security monitoring. However, anomaly explainability in privacy-preserving VAD systems is underexplored. In this study, we present the XAVAD approach, a unified descriptive anomaly XAI for an anonymized VAD, that integrates flexible zero-shot anonymization, anomaly type categorization, visual localization, and scene context description. We provide empirical and qualitative assessments of multifaceted explanations integrated with full-body visual anonymization for privacy protection. We adopt a multimodal CLIP embedding for videos, using improved LLM-assisted prompting and pool-scoring mechanisms for anomaly-type identification. We enhance Grad-ECLIP for spatial anomaly heatmap localization, leveraging computation and accuracy through our novel prompt-guided patching autofocus mechanism. We employ VLMs to generate context and reasoning descriptions of detected anomalies through curated prompt engineering. We have evaluated the accuracy and computational cost of XAVAD on several publicly available CCTV and video datasets. Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains of our XAVAD over state-of-the-art benchmark approaches and provide insights into privacy protection trade-offs in XAI for VAD. We further present ablation studies and assessments across diverse configurations and modeling alternatives to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods. Code: https://github.com/muleina/XAVAD}{https://github.com/muleina/XAVAD .

title: Multi-Tenant SaaS Database Architecture in 2026: Shared Schema vs. PostgreSQL RLS vs. Database-per-Tenant
description:
Every B2B SaaS architect faces a core database decision: should all customer organizations share a single PostgreSQL schema, use schema-per-tenant, or run on dedicated database instances? Provisioning dedicated RDS instances too early inflates cloud bills at 200+ tenants, while a naive shared schema without database-level enforcement means a single missing WHERE tenant_id = :id leaks customer data across tenants.

At Loop Origin, we design and scale multi-tenant B2B platforms, logistics ERPs, and financial SaaS applications for high-growth teams. Below is our production engineering framework comparing the three multi-tenant database architectures in 2026—complete with real PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) policies, PgBouncer transaction-pooling safeguards, composite indexing rules, and a 4-column cost and isolation comparison matrix.

Which Multi-Tenant Database Architecture Should You Choose for a B2B SaaS in 2026?

Direct Answer: For 90% of B2B SaaS platforms, a Shared Database with Shared Schema enforced by PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) is the optimal default—delivering low infrastructure cost, sub-minute schema migrations, and kernel-enforced tenant isolation. Reserve Database-per-Tenant (Silo Model) for high-ACV enterprise tiers ($25k+/yr) requiring contractual data residency, custom backup retention windows, or dedicated compute isolation.

As covered in my guides on composite indexes in PostgreSQL and MySQL and custom software vs. off-the-shelf SaaS 3-year TCO, multi-tenant data architecture is a trade-off across four engineering axes:

1.
2.
3.
4.

4-Column Comparison Matrix: Shared Schema vs. PostgreSQL RLS vs. Schema-per-Tenant vs. DB-per-Tenant

Bookmark this architectural decision matrix when designing a new custom web application:

Architectural Dimension 1. Shared Schema (App-Level WHERE Filter Only) 2. Shared Schema + PostgreSQL RLS (Recommended Default) 3. Schema-per-Tenant (tenant_104.orders) 4. Database-per-Tenant (Dedicated Instance / DB)
Tenant Isolation Mechanism Application ORM global scopes (WHERE tenant_id = ?) Database engine enforces USING (tenant_id = current_setting(...)) on every query Separate PostgreSQL namespace per customer inside one cluster Physically separate database or cloud RDS instance per customer
Cross-Tenant Data Leak Risk High (One raw SQL query or forgotten ORM scope leaks all tenants) Near-Zero (PostgreSQL kernel blocks any row not matching session variable) Low (Requires explicit search_path switching per request) Zero (Separate credentials, storage volumes & network policies)
Schema Migration Speed (1,000 Tenants) < 2 seconds (Single ALTER TABLE statement) < 2 seconds (Single ALTER TABLE statement) 15–45 minutes (Loops through 1,000 schemas sequentially) 30–90 minutes (Orchestrated fleet migration pipeline required)
PgBouncer Connection Pooling Excellent (transaction mode works out of the box) Excellent (SET LOCAL scopes variable strictly to current transaction) Poor (pg_catalog metadata bloat degrades buffer cache past ~500 schemas) Expensive (Requires separate connection pools per tenant database)
Point-in-Time Restore (Single Tenant) Requires restoring snapshot to staging & exporting WHERE tenant_id = X Requires restoring snapshot to staging & exporting WHERE tenant_id = X pg_dump --schema=tenant_X allows logical per-tenant restore Instant native snapshot restore without touching other tenants
Est. Monthly Cloud DB Cost (500 Tenants) $180 – $450/mo (Single HA Primary + Read Replica) $180 – $450/mo (Single HA Primary + Read Replica) $650 – $1,400/mo (High RAM needed for catalog metadata cache) $7,500 – $22,000+/mo ($15–$45/mo minimum per isolated DB)

Why Application-Only tenant_id Filtering Fails in Production

In frameworks like Laravel, NestJS, or Django, teams typically start by adding a global ORM scope that appends WHERE tenant_id = ? to Eloquent or Prisma models. That works until six months later when an engineer writes a raw reporting query, a background queue worker processes a job without initializing the HTTP request context, or a LEFT JOIN references a secondary table without repeating the tenant predicate.

When isolation lives exclusively in application code, every single query written by every developer forever is a potential SOC2 security incident. Moving enforcement down into PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) guarantees that even if application code runs SELECT * FROM invoices;, the database engine refuses to return or modify any row whose tenant_id does not match the current transaction's authenticated tenant context.

Side-by-Side Implementation: Vulnerable Shared Table vs. Hardened PostgreSQL RLS

1. Vulnerable Shared Table (Application-Only Filtering) 

-- Naive table: relies 100% on developers never forgetting WHERE tenant_id = $1
CREATE TABLE invoices (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    tenant_id UUID NOT NULL,
    invoice_number VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    total_cents BIGINT NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- If an engineer runs a raw reporting query and forgets the tenant predicate:
SELECT status, SUM(total_cents) FROM invoices GROUP BY status;
-- RESULT: Silently aggregates revenue across ALL customers in the database!

2. Production-Grade PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) Setup 

-- 1. Enable AND Force Row-Level Security on the table
ALTER TABLE invoices ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE invoices FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- 2. Create a strict tenant isolation policy covering SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation_policy ON invoices
    AS RESTRICTIVE
    FOR ALL
    TO app_runtime_user
    USING (tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true), '')::uuid)
    WITH CHECK (tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true), '')::uuid);

-- 3. Create a tenant-prefixed composite index so RLS checks never cause sequential scans
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_invoices_tenant_status_created
    ON invoices (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC);

Three critical safeguards in the SQL above:
1.
2.
3.

Avoiding the PgBouncer Connection-Pooling Trap with SET LOCAL

The #1 mistake teams make when deploying PostgreSQL RLS with PgBouncer (in transaction pooling mode) is setting the tenant context using a session-level SET command:

-- DANGEROUS IN PGBOUNCER TRANSACTION POOLING MODE:
SET app.current_tenant_id = '7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7';

In transaction pooling mode, PgBouncer returns backend connections to the shared pool immediately after COMMIT or ROLLBACK. A session-level SET app.current_tenant_id persists on that pooled connection and leaks tenant-A context to subsequent requests.

The Production Fix: Always wrap tenant-scoped requests in a transaction and use SET LOCAL (or set_config(..., true)), which PostgreSQL automatically resets to empty at the end of the current transaction:

// Production Laravel Middleware / Database Transaction Wrapper for PostgreSQL RLS
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\DB;

public function runInTenantContext(string $tenantUuid, callable $callback): mixed
{
    return DB::transaction(function () use ($tenantUuid, $callback) {
        // Third parameter `true` = is_local (strictly scoped to this transaction!)
        DB::statement("SELECT set_config('app.current_tenant_id', ?, true)", [$tenantUuid]);
        return $callback();
    });
}

Why tenant_id Must Lead Every Composite Index and Foreign Key

Because RLS appends tenant_id = ... to every query plan, always lead composite indexes with tenant_id—as detailed in my guide on composite indexes in PostgreSQL and MySQL.

ALTER TABLE products ADD CONSTRAINT uq_products_tenant_id UNIQUE (tenant_id, id);

ALTER TABLE order_items
    ADD CONSTRAINT fk_order_items_product_same_tenant
    FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, product_id)
    REFERENCES products (tenant_id, id)
    ON DELETE RESTRICT;

The Hybrid "Pod / Tiered Isolation" Architecture for Enterprise SaaS

You do not have to choose between a single shared database for everyone and 5,000 separate RDS instances. At Loop Origin, we implement a Tiered Pod Architecture that gives you the best unit economics at every price tier:

  • Tier 1 (Self-Serve & Mid-Market Tenants — $49 to $999/mo): Hosted on shared multi-tenant PostgreSQL clusters with strict RLS, composite (tenant_id, ...) indexing, and per-tenant Redis rate limiting (see our guide on running Laravel queues in production with Redis).
  • Tier 2 (Enterprise & Regulated Tenants — $2,500+/mo): A central lightweight routing table (tenants_routing) maps each tenant_id to a database_cluster_key (shared_us_east_1, shared_eu_central_1, or dedicated_enterprise_acme).

6-Step Multi-Tenant Database Architecture Checklist

  • [ ] Enable and FORCE Row-Level Security on Every Tenant Table: Write automated CI schema tests that fail the build if any new migration creates a table with tenant_id without enabling RLS.
  • [ ] Connect Application Workers as a Non-Superuser Role: Ensure your app's PostgreSQL user does not have SUPERUSER or BYPASSRLS privileges.
  • [ ] Use set_config('app.current_tenant_id', $id, true) Inside Transactions: Never use session-level SET when running behind PgBouncer in transaction mode.
  • [ ] Lead Every B-Tree Index with tenant_id: Structure indexes as (tenant_id, status, created_at) so tenant queries hit narrow index slices.
  • [ ] Enforce Composite Foreign Keys (tenant_id, parent_id): Make cross-tenant relational corruption mathematically impossible at the DDL layer.
  • [ ] Tag Background Queue Payloads with Explicit tenant_id: When dispatching async jobs, serialize tenant_id in the job payload and initialize the RLS transaction wrapper inside the queue worker before running queries.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

1. Does PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) slow down query performance?

When your policy uses a simple scalar expression like tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_tenant_id', true), '')::uuid and your tables have composite indexes starting with tenant_id, the overhead of RLS is under 1% to 2%—because PostgreSQL pushes the tenant_id equality check directly into the B-Tree Index Scan.

2. Why does the "Schema-per-Tenant" approach hit a wall around 500 to 1,000 tenants in PostgreSQL?

If your application has 80 tables and you create 1,000 tenant schemas inside one PostgreSQL database, your pg_class and pg_attribute system catalogs must track 80,000 tables and ratusan of thousands of indexes.

3. How do we run analytics or super-admin queries across all tenants when RLS is enabled?

Create a separate, read-only database role (for example, analytics_readonly_role) granted the BYPASSRLS attribute, and restrict that role exclusively to your internal BI replica or admin reporting service.

4. Does SOC 2 Type II or HIPAA require a separate physical database per customer?

No.

5. How do we prevent a single large tenant from exhausting database CPU or I/O ("Noisy Neighbor")?

Combine three guardrails: (1) enforce statement timeouts (SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '5000ms'), (2) route heavy CSV exports and analytical queries to a read replica via async background queues, and (3) apply per-tenant concurrency limits in Redis so one tenant cannot consume more than N simultaneous worker slots.

6. Can we migrate a large customer from a shared RLS cluster to a dedicated database later without downtime?

Yes. If you are architecting a new SaaS platform or scaling an existing database, explore our Custom Web Application Development services or talk with our engineering team at Loop Origin.

title: Building a High-Performance EVM Chain on Consumer Hardware: Inside the IONA Testnet
description:
As the founder of Ionablokchain, I often get asked about our architecture. Most Layer 1 projects make bold claims about speed and security, but they usually test those claims on expensive, enterprise-grade server clusters.

We wanted to prove that a well-optimized Rust codebase and a modern cryptographic stack can deliver enterprise-level performance on hardware you can buy at any local PC store.

Take a look at our recent local testnet run. The dashboard shows a 0.48-second block time, a peak of ~1,975 TPS (transactions per second) during a load test, 5 active validators, and a 99.01% transaction success rate.

Here is the twist: all of this was running on a single AMD Ryzen 5 4500 with 16GB of RAM.

Let’s break down the cryptography, the architecture, and why some of the numbers on that dashboard look the way they do.

*The Cryptographic Engine: A Hybrid Approach
To run a modern, EVM-compatible chain that is ready for the future, you can't rely on basic cryptography. We built a hybrid stack to balance speed, compatibility, and zero-knowledge readiness:

Signatures & EVM Compatibility: We use secp256k1 (k256) for native Ethereum compatibility, alongside ed25519 (dalek) for lightning-fast node signatures.

Hashing: We implemented blake3 on the EVM side. It is significantly faster than traditional SHA-256, reducing CPU overhead during heavy transaction loads.

Consensus & Privacy: We use BLS12-381 (blst). It’s the gold standard for aggregated signatures and threshold encryption, allowing validators to reach consensus securely.

Future-Proofing (ZK): We integrated KZG commitments on the BN254 curve (ark-bn254). This prepares our network for ZK-proofs and proto-danksharding (EIP-4844) without bloating the compute requirements.

*The Latency Paradox: Why 7 Seconds is a Feature, Not a Bug
If you look closely at the dashboard, you’ll notice that while blocks are produced in 0.48 seconds, the transaction confirmation latency is around 6 to 7 seconds.

For an untrained eye, that might look like a bottleneck. In reality, it’s a deliberate design choice driven by security.

IONA utilizes a Verifiable Delay Function (VDF). Specifically, a sequential VDF chain is applied to 8 blocks after every epoch. By definition, a VDF is intentionally slow and impossible to parallelize. It forces a time delay that guarantees absolute randomness and prevents grinding attacks. Add threshold encryption via BLS12-381 into the mix, and those 7 seconds of latency are simply the mathematical price of rock-solid security.

*Networking: Bank-Grade Security, Minimal Overhead
How do 5 validators communicate so smoothly on a single machine without bottlenecking? We use libp2p with a dual-layer security model:

Noise Protocol (x25519 + chacha20 + poly1305): For fast, encrypted peer-to-peer gossip.

TLS via rustls (AES-256-GCM): With keys derived through PBKDF2-SHA256 for secure, reliable channels.

Because Rust doesn't use a garbage collector, network stability remains high even when the CPU is being hammered by heavy elliptic curve math.

*Radical Transparency: Addressing the 4,400+ Warnings
Look at the validator table at the bottom of the dashboard. You’ll see roughly 4,400 "Warnings" per validator. I want to address this directly because transparency matters.

Those warnings are not fatal errors (we have 0 network penalties and only 1 minor error per node). They are the natural result of pushing a Ryzen 5 to its absolute limits. We are running 5 validators simultaneously on a single consumer CPU, forcing it to handle BLS12-381 math, BN254 KZG commitments, and sequential VDF calculations all at once. The warnings are simply the system's way of reporting minor timeouts during an extreme load test.
The Road Ahead for IONA
This testnet proves that IONA’s core engine is highly efficient. We’ve managed to pack an Ethereum 2.0-level cryptographic stack into a setup that runs flawlessly on consumer hardware.

If we can achieve ~2,000 TPS on a budget Ryzen 5, imagine what IONA will do when deployed across distributed, dedicated servers.

We are still in the testing phase, but the data speaks for itself.

GitHub: https://github.com/Ionablokchain/Iona-protocol

Stay tuned. The future of blockchain is fast, secure, and written in Rust.

title: Cutting AWS Cloud Waste by 68%: An Enterprise Serverless Architecture Case Study
description:
In modern enterprise computing, the single largest driver of unnecessary cloud spend is zombie idle capacity. Traditional architectures maintain clusters of virtual machines (EC2) or container pods (EKS/ECS) sized for peak traffic—even though peak load typically occurs for fewer than 4 hours per day.

For a mid-market financial services platform processing 12 million transactions monthly, this antipattern resulted in an average monthly AWS bill exceeding $14,800 USD. Over 62% of this spend was allocated to idle CPU cycles, unoptimized relational database instances running 24/7, and redundant provisioned IOPS.

The Three Core Antipatterns of Legacy Cloud

  1. Over-Provisioned VM Footprint: 8 m5.xlarge EC2 instances running constantly at 12% average CPU utilization.
  2. Database Connection Bottlenecks: Spikes in traffic caused thread starvation on Postgres instances, requiring expensive vertical resizing.
  3. No True Scale-to-Zero: Weekends and overnight hours consumed the exact same hourly budget as peak Monday morning traffic.

The Solution: Deterministic Event-Driven Serverless Topology

LumiLore Technologies engineered a complete architectural pivot from always-on virtual infrastructure to a deterministic, event-driven serverless topology built on:

  • AWS Lambda (ARM64 Graviton3)
  • Amazon DynamoDB Single-Table Design
  • Amazon API Gateway HTTP APIs
  • Amazon CloudFront Edge CDN 
// ARCHITECTURAL EVENT TOPOLOGY
[ CLIENT (Edge) ]
       │ (HTTPS / HTTP/3)
       ▼
[ Amazon CloudFront CDN ]
       │ (Sub-150ms Edge Routing)
       ▼
[ Amazon API Gateway (HTTP) ]
       │ (IAM / JWT Authentication)
       ▼
[ AWS Lambda (Graviton3 ARM64) ]
       │ (Zero-Idle Compute Billing)
       ▼
[ Amazon DynamoDB Single-Table ]
       ◀ Sub-10ms P99 Query Latency

By migrating to ARM64 Graviton3 Lambda functions, compute costs were immediately reduced by 34% per million invocations compared to standard x86 architectures. Pairing this with DynamoDB on-demand billing eliminated all idle database infrastructure costs, ensuring that zero requests equate to zero billing.

Production Verification & Benchmarks

Here are the verified production metrics measured over a 6-month evaluation period:

Metric Legacy EC2 + RDS Cluster LumiLore Serverless Architecture
Monthly AWS Cost $14,820 USD $4,742 USD (-68%)
P95 Edge Response Time 480ms 142ms
Idle Cost per Hour $20.58 / hr $0.00 / hr (True Zero)
Production Uptime SLA 99.9% 99.99%

Production Code: High-Throughput Serverless Handler

Here is the production-tested ES Module Lambda handler utilizing AWS SDK v3 with single-table DynamoDB persistence:

import { DynamoDBClient } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';
import { DynamoDBDocumentClient, PutCommand } from '@aws-sdk/lib-dynamodb';

const ddbClient = new DynamoDBClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION || 'ca-central-1' });
const docClient = DynamoDBDocumentClient.from(ddbClient, {
  marshallOptions: { removeUndefinedValues: true }
});

/**
 * High-Throughput Event-Driven Serverless Handler
 * Sustains sub-150ms P95 latency with zero idle cost footprint
 */
export const handler = async (event) => {
  const startTime = performance.now();

  try {
    const payload = JSON.parse(event.body || '{}');
    if (!payload.organizationId || !payload.transactionAmount) {
      return {
        statusCode: 400,
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Missing required architectural parameters' })
      };
    }

    const item = {
      PK: `ORG#${payload.organizationId}`,
      SK: `TX#${Date.now()}#${crypto.randomUUID()}`,
      amount: payload.transactionAmount,
      currency: payload.currency || 'CAD',
      status: 'SETTLED',
      processedAt: new Date().toISOString()
    };

    // Sub-10ms single-table mutation
    await docClient.send(new PutCommand({
      TableName: process.env.DYNAMODB_TABLE_NAME || 'LumiLore_Ledger',
      Item: item
    }));

    const durationMs = (performance.now() - startTime).toFixed(2);

    return {
      statusCode: 200,
      headers: {
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        'X-Compute-Latency-Ms': durationMs
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        success: true,
        transactionId: item.SK,
        latencyMs: Number(durationMs)
      })
    };
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('[Production Serverless Error]', err);
    return {
      statusCode: 500,
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Internal system fault', incidentId: crypto.randomUUID() })
    };
  }
};

Frequently Asked Questions

How does an event-driven serverless architecture reduce AWS monthly spend by 68%?

By replacing 24/7 over-provisioned virtual machine clusters (EC2) with on-demand AWS Lambda compute and DynamoDB single-table storage. Compute billing is metered to the exact millisecond of execution; when traffic drops to zero overnight or on weekends, operational compute costs drop to exactly $0.00.

What causes AWS Lambda cold starts and how do we achieve sub-25ms execution?

Cold starts occur when a new microservice container must be initialized. We eliminate cold start latency through three tiers: compiling lightweight ES module bundles under 5MB, utilizing AWS Graviton3 (ARM64) architecture, and enabling SnapStart on high-velocity API endpoints.

About the Author & Architecture Firm

This architectural teardown was engineered and authored by Saad Sayed, Principal Cloud & Systems Architect at LumiLore Technologies.

Organizations looking to audit their cloud bills or eliminate legacy server overhead can schedule a 48-Hour Bespoke Architecture Roadmap directly at lumilore.ca/contact.

title: RADIANT: Object-Centric Feed-Forward Global Illumination
description:
arXiv:2610.32075v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Feed-forward neural renderers synthesize global illumination across novel 3D scenes without per-scene optimization or runtime ray tracing. Existing transformer-based renderers tokenize individual triangles, so self-attention scales quadratically with mesh resolution. Yet macroscopic radiative transport is governed by the underlying surface geometry and object arrangements rather than a particular mesh discretization; finer tessellation can thus inflate token counts without changing the underlying transport physics, motivating a discretization-agnostic and object-centric representation. We introduce RADIANT (RADiance-based Inter-Actor Neural Transformer), an object-centric architecture for feed-forward global illumination from point inputs. By representing each object with a compact budget of 32 surface-patch tokens, RADIANT decouples attention sequence length from polygon counts. In a single network, an inter-object scene transformer models 3D radiative exchange and a view decoder renders images at target camera poses. To capture light transport without materializing O(N^2) bias matrices, invariant form-factor attention embeds geometric distances and surface orientations directly into query-key dot products as SE(3)-invariant inner products weighted by learned area and material gains. For primary visibility without mesh connectivity, camera rays cross-attend scene tokens guided by depth-tested point splats in a shared spherical frame. Across a 1.03M-scene benchmark under matched model capacity, RADIANT reaches 25 dB tone-mapped PSNR in 5x fewer training steps than RenderFormer, and achieves 32.2 dB at 600k steps (+3.3 dB over RenderFormer and +7.6 dB over RenderFormer-V2). We further demonstrate the scalability of RADIANT, which completes a 512x512 forward pass of a 500-object scene in 0.83 s, with computational cost scaling with the number of objects rather than polygons.

title: Multi modal perceived conversation success prediction for spontaneous autistic and non-autistic dyadic interactions
description:
arXiv:2610.31682v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Conversation success is important for communication, social bonds, and well-being and is often reduced in autistic-neurotypical conversations. Previous studies have predicted perceived conversation success using acoustic and lexical features in pediatric autism-enriched samples, or using nonverbal behavior in non-autistic group interactions. Other work has characterized prosodic, facial, motor, and turn-taking synchrony in autistic interactions, but has primarily targeted diagnostic classification or group differences. The present study instead predicts participant perceived conversation success from complementary articulatory, facial, acoustic-prosodic, and turn-taking measures across three spontaneous dyadic-interaction datasets including autistic and non autistic individuals. By leveraging multimodal features, we demonstrate that conversational success is inherently multidimensional and requires a multi-faceted analytical framework. Combining these complementary modalities offers the potential to improve prediction of perceived conversation success by capturing information unavailable from any single modality.

title: ทำไมการตรวจงานคือคอขวดของ AI agent และจะทำให้มันตรวจเองได้อย่างไร?
description:
โดย Nokka (นก-กา) | ตรวจข้อมูล 25 ต.ค. 2026 · ตอนที่ 4 จาก 6 ของชุด "หนึ่งคนกับทีม agent"

บทความนี้เขียนโดย AI (deepseek-v4.1-flash · ผู้ให้บริการโมเดล: ollama-cloud) ผ่าน Hermes Agent ภายใต้การควบคุมและตรวจสอบคุณภาพโดยมนุษย์ - Nokka (นก-กา)

ประโยคที่ผมคิดว่าสรุปทั้งตอนนี้ได้อยู่ในคู่มือ pstack บรรทัดเดียว

"It compiles" is not evidence.

คอมไพล์ผ่านไม่ใช่หลักฐานว่างานเสร็จ [1]

และถ้าคุณยังใช้ "ดูแล้วน่าจะโอเค" เป็นเกณฑ์ตัดสิน คุณจะไม่มีวันปล่อย agent ทำงานเองได้จริง

ทำไมการตรวจถึงช้ากว่าทุกขั้น

ขั้นที่รอคนตลอด

คู่มือ pstack เขียนตรง ๆ ว่า การตรวจคือขั้นที่ช้าที่สุดในงานของ agent เพราะเป็นขั้นที่มักรอคน [1]

ถ้า agent ตรวจเองได้ คุณจะพ้นจากตำแหน่งคอขวด แต่ถ้าข้ามขั้นนี้ไป การเพิ่มจำนวน agent จะได้แค่งานที่ยังไม่ได้ตรวจเพิ่มขึ้นตามไปด้วย [1]

ผมคิดว่านี่คือเหตุผลที่หลายทีมลอง agent แล้วถอยกลับ เพราะเพิ่มกำลังฝั่งผลิตไว้ แต่คอขวดฝั่งตรวจยังเท่าเดิม

ตัวอย่างร้านอาหารเช้าอีกครั้ง

ตอนที่ 2 ผมเล่าเปรียบเทียบเรื่องไข่สามนาทีไปแล้ว ตอนนี้ผมจะขยายว่ามันแปลว่าอะไรในทางปฏิบัติ

ถ้าการทำซ้ำบั๊กใช้เวลา 20 นาที และคุณเป็นคนเดียวที่ทำได้ การแก้โค้ดเร็วแค่ไหนก็ไม่ทำให้งานออกเร็วขึ้น เพราะคิวจะไปติดที่คุณ

ทางออกจึงไม่ใช่ซื้อ agent เพิ่ม แต่คือสอน agent ให้ทำขั้นที่คุณเคยทำ

ตั้งเกณฑ์เสร็จตั้งแต่ประโยคแรก

ตัวอย่างที่วัดได้

คู่มือแนะนำให้ใส่ความหมายของ "เสร็จ" ลงไปใน prompt แรกด้วยถ้อยคำที่ตรงกับงาน [1]

/poteto-mode เพิ่ม output แบบ json ให้คำสั่งนี้
ข้อความเดิมต้องเหมือนเดิมทุกไบต์ json ต้อง parse ผ่าน
ทั้งสองแบบต้องรันกับโปรเจกต์ตัวอย่างได้
ขอหลักฐานมาให้ดู

แบบนี้ agent มีสามเกณฑ์ที่รันตรวจได้ ไม่ใช่อารมณ์ที่ต้องเดาใจ [1]

ถ้ามีเกณฑ์ข้อไหนรันไม่ได้ คำตอบที่ดีควรบอกว่า "สรุปไม่ได้" ไม่ใช่รายงานว่าเสร็จ [1]

ผมชอบตรงนี้เพราะมันกลับด้านนิสัยของเครื่องมือส่วนใหญ่ ที่มักตอบเข้าข้างตัวเอง

จับคู่การตรวจกับชนิดงาน

คู่มือแยกให้ชัดว่าตรวจอะไรกับงานแบบไหน [1]

  • งาน CLI ให้รันคำสั่งจริง
  • งาน UI ให้เดิน flow ที่เปลี่ยนในแอปที่รันอยู่
  • งาน parser หรือ migration ให้เล่นซ้ำ input ที่บันทึกไว้
  • งาน perf ให้เทียบ profile ก่อนกับหลัง
  • งาน storage ให้อ่านค่าที่เขียนกลับมา

ถ้าต้องเทียบภาพระดับพิกเซล คู่มือแนะนำให้ใช้ playbook visual-parity เทียบกับ baseline ที่ตรึงไว้ ไม่ใช่ให้คนดูด้วยตา [1]

ตัวเลขที่วัดมาแล้ว ก็เชื่อไม่ได้ทันที

เจ็ดคำถามก่อนเชื่อคำว่าเร็วขึ้น

ปัญหาที่สกิล benchmark-checklist ถูกออกแบบมาจับคือตัวเลขก่อนกับหลัง ซึ่งเป็นหลักฐานที่ผิดพลาดง่ายที่สุด [1]

แคชที่ยังอุ่น build ที่ต่างกัน หรือโค้ดที่ไม่ได้รันในช่วงที่จับเวลา ก็ทำให้ได้ความเร็วปลอมได้ทั้งนั้น [1]

สกิล benchmark-checklist ถามเจ็ดข้อ [4] ตั้งแต่ อะไรเป็นตัวจำกัดตัวเลข ทำไมไม่เร็วเป็นสองเท่า ทุกฝั่งรันด้วยการตั้งค่าแบบเดียวกับของจริงหรือไม่ ผลลัพธ์เกินขีดจำกัดทางกายภาพอย่างแบนด์วิดท์ดิสก์หรือจำนวนคอร์หรือไม่ มีอะไร error หรือคืนค่าผิดหรือไม่ ทำซ้ำหลายรอบสลับกันแล้วได้ค่ากลางเท่าไร งานที่จับเวลาเกิดขึ้นจริงในช่วงนั้นหรือไม่ และผลนั้นสำคัญจริงในเส้นทาง end-to-end ที่ผู้ใช้ต้องรอหรือไม่ [1]

คำตอบต้องเป็น เร็วขึ้น ช้าลง ไม่ต่าง หรือสรุปไม่ได้ พร้อมจำนวนรอบและช่วงค่า ถ้าบอกตัวจำกัดไม่ได้ ก็ต้องตอบว่าสรุปไม่ได้ [1]

แบบที่คู่มือยกตัวอย่าง คือแคชยังอุ่นทำให้ตัวเลขดูดี และนั่นคือเหตุผลที่ผมเห็นด้วยกับกฎนี้

verification skill คือของจริงของทั้งระบบ

โครงที่ agent ตัวต่อไปอ่านรู้เรื่อง

สกิล create-verification-skill เขียนไฟล์ให้โปรเจกต์ โดยมีหัวข้อบังคับห้าส่วนคือ Launch, Doctor, Drive, Evidence และ Cleanup พร้อมส่วน Helpers เมื่อสกิลมีสคริปต์แนบ [3]

พร้อมกันนั้นมันสร้าง feature map ไว้ในโฟลเดอร์ features ซึ่งจัดเรียงว่าแอปทำอะไรได้ และผลลัพธ์แบบไหนที่พิสูจน์ว่าฟีเจอร์นั้นทำงาน [1]

ก่อนส่งมอบ มันต้องพิสูจน์ตัวเองหนึ่งรอบเต็ม ตั้งแต่เปิดแอป ตรวจความพร้อม ขับหนึ่งฟีเจอร์ เก็บหลักฐาน ล้าง environment แล้วยืนยันว่าหลักฐานยังอยู่หลังล้าง [1]

ถ้าการพิสูจน์นั้นล้มเหลว คู่มือบอกตรง ๆ ว่าอย่าใช้ผลลัพธ์ที่มันสร้าง [1]

ดูแลไม่ให้โกหก

แอปเปลี่ยนตลอด แผนที่ฟีเจอร์จึงเก่าได้ คู่มือแนะนำให้รัน maintain-verification-skill อย่างน้อยวันละครั้ง หรือตั้งเป็น automation [1]

ผลลัพธ์มีสามแบบคือ clean แปลว่าครบไม่มีอะไรต้องแก้ changed แปลว่ามี PR แก้เฉพาะโฟลเดอร์ของ skill นี้ และ blocked แปลว่าติดอะไรบางอย่างที่ต้องบอกคน [1]

สิ่งสำคัญคือมันห้ามแก้โค้ดผลิตภัณฑ์ และถ้าเจอ regression ของจริง มันต้องรายงาน ไม่ใช่กลบด้วยการแก้เอกสาร [1]

ผมคิดว่านี่คือมาตรฐานที่ทีมส่วนใหญ่ยังไม่มี และเป็นเหตุผลที่งาน agent จำนวนมากจบด้วยคำว่า "ทดสอบแล้ว" ที่ตรวจย้อนหลังไม่ได้

เมื่อการทดสอบปกติไปไม่ถึง

ตรวจคุณสมบัติด้วยเครื่องมือพิสูจน์

คู่มือระบุว่าบางบั๊กอยู่บนเส้นทางที่ไม่มีใครเดิน เช่น การ retry สองครั้งที่ซ้อนกัน ล็อกที่หมดอายุกลางการเขียน หรือเหตุการณ์ที่มาผิดลำดับ [1]

สำหรับโค้ดที่ความผิดพลาดแบบนี้แพง มีสกิล create-formal-verification-skill ที่เลือกเป้าหมายจากโค้ดเอง แล้วเลือกเครื่องมือตามคำถาม [1]

ถ้าคำถามคือ "เหตุการณ์สลับลำดับกันได้ไหม" เครื่องมือที่เหมาะคือ model checker อย่าง TLA+ [1]

และมันต้องแสดงให้เห็นว่าคุณสมบัตินั้นพังบนโค้ดเวอร์ชันที่จงใจทำเสีย เพราะการตรวจที่ไม่เคยเห็นความล้มเหลวไม่พิสูจน์อะไรเลย [1]

ตัวอย่างจากงานจริง

StyleX กับ PR สี่แสนบรรทัด

ตอนที่ 2 ผมเล่าตัวเลขนี้ไปแล้ว แต่ผมอยากกลับมาดูวิธีตรวจ

agent ของเธอสร้างสคริปต์ที่เทียบค่า computed style ระหว่าง SCSS เดิมกับ StyleX ใหม่ และเก็บภาพสถานะที่วัดมาเทียบกันได้ครบ [2]

เมื่อนำไปใช้จริงกับโค้ดทั้งระบบ ยังเจอบั๊ก z-index, คลาสที่ถูกใช้จากที่อื่น และศึก specificity ที่ซ่อนอยู่ [2]

เธอจึงเปลี่ยน automation ให้ย้ายทีละ leaf component เก็บภาพ hover, focus, active, disabled และสถานะเฉพาะของคอมโพเนนต์นั้น ครบทั้ง light, dark และ high contrast แล้วให้ agent อีกตัวตรวจสื่อที่เก็บมา [2]

ถ้า build ล้มหรือค่าไม่ตรง ให้หยุดทันที [2]

ผลคือได้ PR เล็ก ๆ ที่มีภาพและวิดีโอครบ แทนที่จะเป็น PR ยักษ์ที่ตามตรวจแทบไม่ไหว

สามอย่างที่เริ่มได้สัปดาห์นี้

ไม่ต้องรอมีทีม agent ก่อน

หนึ่ง เขียนเกณฑ์เสร็จให้เป็นตัวเลขหรือเงื่อนไข ถ้าคุณเขียนว่า "ทำให้เร็วขึ้น" agent จะเดาแทนคุณ [1]

สอง เก็บหลักฐานทุกครั้งที่สั่งงาน ขอภาพหน้าจอ วิดีโอ หรือ output ของคำสั่ง ไม่ใช่คำอธิบาย [2]

สาม ทำให้การตรวจเป็นสคริปต์ เริ่มจากคำสั่งเดียวที่เปิดแอปและเดินหนึ่งฟีเจอร์ให้ได้ก่อน แล้วค่อยขยาย [1]

ผมใช้สามข้อนี้กับงานเขียนของตัวเองด้วย คือกำหนดเกณฑ์ผ่านไว้ล่วงหน้าและเก็บหลักฐานการตรวจไว้ทุกครั้ง

สิ่งที่ตอนต่อไปจะตอบ

ตอนนี้เรารู้แล้วว่าจะตรวจอย่างไร แต่ยังเหลือคำถามที่ใหญ่กว่า คือถ้าอยากให้ agent ทำงานตอนเราไม่เฝ้า ต้องเตรียมอะไรบ้าง

ตอนที่ 5 ผมจะลงไปใน playbook ว่าด้วย autopilot, orchestrate และการรันข้ามคืน ว่ามันมีด่านไหนที่หยุดงานได้ และมีอะไรที่พลาดบ่อย

ผมจะเขียนทีละตอนและรายงานความคืบหน้าให้คุณดูเหมือนเดิม

title: Many Perturbations, Shared Failure Dynamics: Tracing Direction-Sensitive Perturbation Influence in Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.32309v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Why can a task-preserving rewrite turn a correct answer into a failure while a larger internal change leaves the answer intact? We develop a direction-sensitive, readout-relative account of semantic fragility: heterogeneous language changes can share geometric and readout relationships without sharing an input-independent failure direction. Clean decision reserve, representation transformation, and response alignment provide complementary descriptions of this process. An exact longitudinal-transverse decomposition identifies directional information discarded by scalar transmission. A compact reserve-and-transmission model predicts failures across held-out families and items in Qwen3-32B and Gemma 4 31B, with useful but parameterization-dependent transfer to ReClor. Matched interventions show that orientation carries causal information beyond scalar geometry. Among naturally failed rewrites, attention-component tests on disjoint original items and subsequent answer-order controls favor the natural paired direction over tested random and same-answer-letter donor directions. Yet failures rarely persist across option orders, and current-order corrections use recomputed clean references. Shared predictive regularity thus coexists with context-dependent directional effects. Numerical path integration reduces, but does not eliminate, finite-patch approximation error within a fixed context; a larger discrepancy from the natural rewrite effect remains. A complementary fixed-CoT cue study extends this account to influence unacknowledged in recorded reasoning: readout associations transfer across domains, although the positive-mean causal criterion fails and signed-effect prediction remains post hoc. Together, these results support shared relations among reserve, transformation, and response while distinguishing local causal sensitivity from a complete explanation of natural failure.

title: DELA: Learning Controllable Edits for Diffusion Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.32096v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support bidirectional denoising and iterative refinement, but generation remains largely controlled by token-level masking schedules. This leaves draft-level refinement implicit and limits explicit control over when to insert missing content, delete redundant spans, revisit uncertain regions, or stop editing. We introduce Diffusion Editing Language Adapter (DELA), a plug-in framework that enables controllable draft refinement with a frozen DLM. DELA operates on clean, variable-length drafts using four explicit editing actions: Insert, Delete, Remask, and Stop. The controller determines when and where to edit the draft, while the frozen DLM fills masked regions through denoising, separating high-level edit control from token-level generation. A naive single-phase editor would be computationally expensive because arbitrary interior edits can disrupt prefix stability and limit reliable KV-cache reuse. To address this, DELA uses a two-phase decoding procedure: a fast, append-only drafting phase that supports KV-cache reuse, followed by a global refinement phase that enables targeted non-monotonic edits to the full draft. We train the controller using a staged curriculum that begins with learning local edit priors from synthetic recovery tasks and mined actions that improve draft quality. Subsequent stages refine edit selection through rollout-based outcome preferences and alignment with downstream task feedback. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that DELA achieves gains of up to 5.5 percentage points over direct diffusion decoding while keeping the backbone frozen. DELA thus provides a modular approach to explicit draft-level control in diffusion language models.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
description:
Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic.

OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers.

At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI, a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers.

Long-lived static credentials are insecure

Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand.

Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production.

Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again.

Better solutions already exist

With OIDC, your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant.

A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it.

We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob, AI Gateway, and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies. But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on.

The rest of the web hasn’t followed

We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods.

But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption:

  • Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key.

  • Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path.

  • Weak incentives for vendors to offer and prioritize secure authentication.

Our goal is to make secure authentication the default on Vercel, while also using our Marketplace to help push more vendors to support it.

Our commitment to a more secure web

We have a responsibility to make this change practical across the services we run, the tools developers use, and the integrations we build with partners.

Make secure authentication easier to use

Using a secure token has to be easier than pasting a key, or developers will keep pasting keys. On Vercel, code retrieves an OIDC token with a function call, and a custom audience specifies the service intended to receive it.

With Vercel Connect, applications and agents use their deployment identity to request provider tokens at runtime, without having to store long-lived provider secrets in environment variables. Once the connector is configured and linked to the project and the user’s account is connected, code can request a token for that user with scopes the provider supports.

We’re also extending OIDC support across the Vercel API and CLI to remove the need for long-lived Vercel tokens in deployment workflows.

OIDC UI for API providers

OIDC UI is a shadcn/ui component registry with a trust-policy configurator and a server-side token verifier. It includes provider forms for Vercel, GitHub, GitLab, Google, Bitbucket, AWS, Azure, and custom OIDC issuers. A provider can let customers configure trust for a particular Vercel project’s production environment, then verify incoming tokens against that policy without building the configuration interface and verification code from scratch.

Reduce the performance cost of secure authentication

A static key in an environment variable is already available when a function runs, so reading it requires no network request. Fetching a token or exchanging it for provider credentials can add network latency, so reducing those calls is part of making secure authentication practical.

Vercel Functions receive a platform-issued token in the request header, which the SDK reads without fetching another. The platform reuses unexpired tokens, while Vercel Connect caches provider tokens in process and refreshes them near expiry. Custom-audience and provider exchanges require network calls.

For example, an application can use the Azure SDK to access Cosmos DB with temporary credentials instead of a database key. With Azure configured to trust the Vercel project and its default token audience, the callback supplies a Vercel OIDC token to ClientAssertionCredential, which exchanges it for the Azure access token used by CosmosClient.

Give providers an incentive to support secure authentication

The Vercel Marketplace offers access to third-party databases, content management systems, observability tools, and more. Our goal is for all of these vendors to support short-lived, identity-based authentication, whether they accept OIDC tokens directly or exchange them for temporary credentials. We’re working to make integrations configure that authentication automatically when developers connect a service, so it does not require a separate setup step.

HTTPS everywhere did not win on ergonomics alone. Chrome put a “Not secure” label on plain HTTP, and then it set deadlines. Now we are setting ours. By November 30, 2026, vendors who do not support OIDC auth from Vercel to their services and use long-lived secrets for authentication will have a similar “Not secure” message on their listing. By January 2027, vendors who do not offer secure auth will be delisted. We are holding the Vercel API and our own native integrations to the same bar.

From static to dynamic

Fifteen years ago, encrypting every request felt like overkill. Today, the padlock is so normal that we only notice when it's missing. Secure authentication between services should become just as routine, so developers can connect the systems they need without storing another long-lived secret. Going from static to dynamic has always been the Vercel mission. It started with pages, and now it’s credentials.

Additional resources

  • OIDC federation covers how deployments get short-lived identity tokens, with guides for AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own API.

  • Custom OIDC token audiences scopes each token to the one service meant to receive it.

  • Vercel Connect requests short-lived, scoped provider tokens at runtime, so code and agents never store credentials.

  • Vercel Connect guides walk through building agents this way, from Slack bots to GitHub agents.
