title: MisconceptDialogue: Evaluation Criteria Shape Measured Success in LLM Math Tutoring
description:
arXiv:2610.31679v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as math tutors, raising two questions: can a single LLM detect a student's error, diagnose the underlying misconception, and remediate it through multi-turn dialogue - and can we trust the numbers that report how well it does? We address both with MISCONCEPTDIALOGUE, a fully automated framework that runs the full pipeline on five open-weight LLM tutors (7B-14B) interacting with LLM-simulated students over 5,000+ dialogues - a deliberately simulated protocol (paired conditions, a wrong-diagnosis control unsafe with real learners, scale) whose results do not establish real-student learning. On measurement, our headline finding is uncomfortable for the field: benchmark-style exact-match scoring common in standard math NLP - a lower-bound stress test - reports 42.1% measured Remediation Success Rate on identical dialogues where a human-calibrated LLM-as-judge reports 81.3%, a 39.2 percentage-point spread larger than the combined effects of tutor model, teaching strategy, and supplied diagnostic information. This is not a single-judge artifact: four independent LLM judges and 200 human annotations converge to within a few points (kappa up to 0.91). On capability, the verdict is equally striking: the score barely changes whether we tell the tutor the student's actual misconception or a deliberately swapped one - under the tested diagnosis-presentation format, these tutors show little evidence of reliably conditioning on the diagnostic information they are handed. For LLM tutoring evaluation to mature, multi-criterion scoring with multi-judge convergence and human anchoring should become standard practice - and the measurement question deserves as much scrutiny as the capability question it claims to answer.

title: Production-Hardening a Java Framework: Resilience, JWT/JWKS, Native Image and an MCP Server (Building Ligero, Part 7)
description:
A framework core can stay tiny only if the things real services need live somewhere else. In Ligero that "somewhere else" is a set of small, optional, mostly dependency-free modules. This last post of the series tours the production-hardening ones: resilience, scheduling, events, authentication, native image, and a couple of newer experiments (an HTTP QUERY method and an MCP server).

As with the rest of the series: Ligero is pre-1.0. Check the changelog for what's released versus unreleased.

Resilience: ligero-resilience

Outbound calls fail. The module gives you three primitives with no dependencies:

  • Retry with fixed or exponential backoff,
  • Timeout, which runs the call on a virtual thread and abandons overruns,
  • CircuitBreaker with the usual closed, open, half-open states.

The virtual-thread timeout is a nice example of Java 21 paying off: you can run the work on a cheap thread, wait with a deadline, and walk away from a hung call without a bespoke thread-pool strategy.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Closed
    Closed --> Open: failures exceed threshold
    Open --> HalfOpen: after cool-down
    HalfOpen --> Closed: probe succeeds
    HalfOpen --> Open: probe fails

Scheduling and events

ligero-scheduler is a small scheduler for background work: fixedRate, fixedDelay, once and dailyAt. Timing runs on a small daemon pool, but each task runs on its own virtual thread, so a slow or throwing job never stalls the timer or cancels its own schedule.

In ligero-core, an in-process Events bus provides typed publish/subscribe (with supertype delivery and isolated handler failures), and Ligero.onStart(...) / onStop(...) hooks run when the server starts and stops. There's also a Cache<K,V> SPI with load-through helpers and TTLs, an in-process InMemoryCache, and a distributed RedisCache in ligero-redis.

Authentication and authorization: ligero-auth

JWT support is implemented with the JDK's own crypto (javax.crypto / java.security), so there are no external dependencies. Properties worth calling out:

  • alg=none and algorithm-confusion tokens are rejected;
  • signature comparison is constant-time;
  • exp and nbf are enforced;
  • RS256 and ES256 (sign and verify) sit alongside HS256, and Jwks.parse(json, mapper) turns an OIDC provider's JWKS into JDK public keys by kid, so a service can validate tokens issued by an external identity provider. The verifier pins the algorithm, which defends against alg-confusion. 
Jwt jwt = Jwt.hs256(secret, new JacksonBodyMapper());   // secret >= 32 bytes
String token = jwt.sign(Map.of("sub", "ada", "roles", List.of("admin")), Duration.ofHours(1));

app.use("/api", JwtAuthMiddleware.of(jwt));
app.get("/api/admin/stats", ctx -> {
    JwtAuthMiddleware.requireRole(ctx, "admin");        // 403 without the role
    String user = ctx.attribute(JwtAuthMiddleware.USER_ATTRIBUTE);
    ...
});

The module also covers stateless double-submit CSRF (XSRF-TOKEN cookie echoed in X-XSRF-TOKEN), HMAC-signed-cookie sessions with a pluggable SessionStore, and Basic auth. Scale-out is a module away: ligero-redis provides Redis-backed rate-limit and session stores shared across instances.

Data, your way

Three independent modules so you take only what you want: ligero-jdbc (SQL to records, transactions, no ORM, with optional HikariCP pooling via DataSources.pooled(...)), ligero-jpa (a thin Hibernate helper, bring your own provider), and ligero-migrations (Flyway at startup). Request validation is annotation-based (ligero-validation) and turns violations into automatic 400s.

Native image

GraalVM native-image does a closed-world analysis: anything reached by reflection, dynamic proxies or unregistered resources must be declared in metadata. Ligero's earlier design decisions pay off here:

  • Reflection-free core: routing, the middleware pipeline and Beans use no runtime reflection (an architecture test in the repo enforces this), so there is nothing to register.
  • Compile-time DI option: ligero-processor generates the bind(...) wiring at compile time.
  • ServiceLoader over scanning: engines, body mappers and template engines are discovered via META-INF/services, which ligero-core already registers for native.

Modules that are native-ready by construction include ligero-core, ligero-server-jdk, ligero-scheduler, ligero-resilience, ligero-auth and ligero-jdbc. The reflective adapters (Jackson, Hibernate) bring their own metadata needs, and the design note documents those boundaries rather than pretending they don't exist. The CLI itself ships as a native binary.

Two experiments worth watching

HTTP QUERY. app.query(path, handler) registers handlers for the IETF QUERY method: a safe, idempotent method like GET that carries a request body, for queries too large or structured for a URL. You read the body with ctx.body(...) as for POST. It's an early standard, so treat it as an experiment.

MCP servers: ligero-mcp. The Model Context Protocol lets an LLM call tools exposed by your app over JSON-RPC 2.0 (Streamable HTTP). With Ligero (illustrative sketch; see the docs for the exact schema type):

McpServer mcp = McpServer.create("orders", "1.0.0")
    .tool("find_order", "Look up an order by id", schema, args -> lookup(args));

app.use(mcp.http("/mcp"));

It implements the initialize handshake, ping, tools/list and tools/call, surfaces tool failures as MCP error results, and, like the rest of the framework, is dependency-free and reflection-free. If you were going to expose existing service capabilities to an AI agent anyway, doing it in the same process as your authenticated, observable HTTP stack is a pragmatic place to start.

OpenAPI

ligero-openapi generates an OpenAPI 3 document from your routes, with an opt-in Swagger UI. OpenApi.model(Class) generates components/schemas from your record types (scalars, enums, temporals, collections and nested records), using reflection only at document-build time, never on the request path.

The shape of the whole 

flowchart TB
    core["ligero-core (router, middleware, Beans, SPIs)"]
    core --> eng["engine: jdk | jetty"]
    core --> obs["observability: otel, micrometer"]
    core --> sec["auth, validation, redis"]
    core --> data["jdbc, jpa, migrations"]
    core --> ops["resilience, scheduler, cache, events"]
    core --> dev["devtools, openapi, mcp"]

Everything hangs off a small core through SPIs and middleware. That's the series in one picture.

What I'd say after building it

  • Small core, sharp edges removed. The things that hurt in production (startup, hidden wiring, missing defaults) are the ones the core addresses directly.
  • Honesty is a feature. Docs state boundaries (what's native-ready, what needs metadata, what the JDK engine can't do), and the benchmark harness is public.
  • It's an open project. If you want to try it, break it, or contribute, start at the repo, the docs and the examples.

Thanks for reading the series. If there's a part you want to see go deeper, tell me in the comments.

title: SlothChat
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

  • SlothChat Digest (TL;DR My Friends) is a 100% local, privacy-first group chat summarizer built for the "Slow and Steady" theme that turns 400+ chaotic overnight Discord or WhatsApp messages into a lazy morning briefing in seconds.
  • Who gets to be lazier: Anyone who wakes up to hundreds of unread notifications from chaotic friend groups, gaming servers, or student club chats and refuses to spend 20 minutes scrolling through 3 AM memes just to see if they missed something important.
  • What effort it saves: Instead of manually reading a wall of text, you drop in your chat log (or test with 3 built-in chaotic 3 AM presets) and let your local Sloth AI generate:
    • 🦥 2-Line Sloth Summary: The entire night's chaos condensed into two punchy sentences.
    • 🔔 Ping Radar: Detects whether anyone actually called your name or needs a response from you (spoiler: probably not).
    • 🔥 Drama Thermometer: Rates the chat's unhinged energy on a 0% to 100% scale.
    • 💬 Lazy Reply Generator: One-click copy-paste responses so you can fake active participation and go right back to sleep.
    • 📊 Laziness ROI: Gamified metrics tracking total messages skipped, reading time saved, calories conserved, and $0.00 cloud cost.

Demo

  • Live Walkthrough (demo.gif):

  • The "Sloth Morning Briefing" Dashboard:

  • Input Zone & Chaotic 3 AM Presets:

  • Try It Zero-Setup: Clone the repo and open index.html directly in any browser—thanks to the built-in Smart Fallback Engine, you can test all 3 chaotic preset logs in instant offline demo mode even before spinning up Ollama!

Code

KrishnaBharadwaj67 / Slothchat

🦥 SlothChat Digest: TL;DR My Friends

Stop reading 400 chaotic overnight messages. Let your local Sloth AI do it.


Watch the lazy morning briefing in action: load presets, simulate local AI, view drama radar, and copy replies in seconds.

🎯 What Is This?

SlothChat Digest is a 100% local, privacy-first group chat summarizer powered by open-weight models via Ollama. Instead of reading 400 chaotic overnight messages from your Discord server or WhatsApp group, you drop the chat log and get a lazy morning briefing in seconds.

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Theme: "Slow and Steady" — rewarding laziness with local AI.

✨ Key Features

  • 🦥 2-Line Sloth Summary — The entire night's chaos in two punchy sentences
  • 🔔 Ping Radar — Know if anyone actually needs you (spoiler: probably not)
  • 🔥 Drama Thermometer — 0% to 100% Unhinged scale
  • 💬 Lazy Reply Generator — One-click copy-paste…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

  • Local Open-Weight AI Core: Built around Ollama (POST http://localhost:11434/api/generate), powering inference locally with open-weight models including Gemma 2 (gemma2:2b), Llama 3.2 (llama3.2:latest), Qwen 2.5 (qwen2.5:3b), Mistral, and Phi-3.
  • Processing & Structured Parsing Pipeline:
    • Chat Parser & Sanitizer: Cleans raw timestamps, multi-line noise, and formatting quirks from pasted exports or .txt files.
    • Structured Prompt Builder: Instructs the local open-weight model to analyze group dynamics, extract direct mentions/tasks for the target user, score the drama level, and return strictly structured JSON.
    • Robust JSON Parser & Smart Fallback Engine: Validates LLM output so small parameter models (2B–3B) never break the UI, and automatically routes to a deterministic offline engine if Ollama isn't running.
  • Dual Interface (Zero-Build Web + Zero-Dependency CLI):
    • Web App (index.html, styles.css, app.js): Built with vanilla JavaScript, Tailwind CSS (CDN), Lucide Icons, and Space Grotesk + JetBrains Mono typography—requiring zero npm install or build steps.
    • Terminal Companion (sloth_cli.py): Built strictly with the Python 3 Standard Library (urllib) so terminal sloths can run python sloth_cli.py chat_export.txt --model gemma2:2b --target "@YourName" without installing a single pip package.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • Maximum Privacy for Personal Conversations: Group chats are full of inside jokes, late-night rants, personal drama, and private details. Sending 400 messages from your friends' private server to a closed commercial cloud API means handing over everyone's conversations to third-party servers without their consent.
  • What Open Weights Made Possible:
    • Zero Data Leakage: By running open-weight models like Gemma and Llama locally via Ollama, 0 bytes of chat history ever leave localhost.
    • $0.00 Forever Cost: Summarizing massive text logs every single morning would rack up API token costs over time. Local open-source inference makes daily summarization completely free forever.
    • No Lock-In or Black Boxes: The entire codebase is auditable, dependency-free, and immune to API key expirations, rate limits, or subscription paywalls.

The Lazy Payoff

  • Time & Effort Saved: Reading and mentally filtering 400 chaotic overnight messages from an active Discord server or group chat normally takes 15 to 20 minutes of groggy morning scrolling. SlothChat Digest cuts that down to 10 seconds.
  • Real-World Use This Week: Instead of dreading the unread badge on my Discord server (lahans dungeon) and college group chats after waking up or coming back from classes, I dumped the chat logs into SlothChat Digest:
    • Messages Skipped: ~350–400 messages per digest.
    • Actual Actionable Pings Found: Usually 0 or 1.
    • Participation Effort: 1 click to copy a context-aware lazy reply, paste it into chat, and get my morning back.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: SlothChat Digest supports Google's open-weight Gemma family (gemma2:2b / gemma3) running locally via Ollama to perform fast, low-memory structured JSON chat summarization, ping detection, drama scoring, and reply generation on everyday consumer hardware.

title: Do Halting Heads Really Save Compute in Looped Language Models?
description:
arXiv:2610.32246v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Looped language models run each token through the same layers several times, and each run is one iteration. To save compute, an extra layer, the halting head, gives after each iteration the probability that the token stops there, so that easy tokens can stop early. Pretraining models from scratch, up to 1.3B parameters, we find two problems. First, heads trained on a mix of all iterations predict that tokens need under half the iterations, yet under the standard stopping rule tokens run almost every iteration, because this training never scores the single iteration where a token stops. Scoring every iteration instead fixes this, but in our runs it works only with a strong penalty favoring early stops. Second, savings are commonly reported as an average number of iterations per token, but when sequences are generated in batches that run until their slowest token stops, a model without a head is almost as good at that cost. The reported average can therefore overstate the saving. We recommend reporting the iterations tokens actually run, with the stopping threshold and batch size, and give a test, run before training a head, that bounds its gain.

title: $\Psi$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
description:
arXiv:2610.32177v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.

title: 🦥 Fridge-to-Feast: Pure Veg Recipe Visualizer (Dual-Input Edition)
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Fridge-to-Feast is a zero-effort, local-first recipe visualizer specifically designed for exhausted, busy, or unapologetically lazy home cooks who adhere to a 100% pure vegetarian diet.

Instead of staring into an open fridge with decision fatigue—or giving up on home cooking because washing 5 greasy pots feels like a mountain of labor—Fridge-to-Feast turns random ingredients into an instant, satisfying feast with minimal physical effort:

  1. Dual-Input Fridge Intake: Snap and drop a quick shelf photo, or type scattered ingredients ("Potatoes, Tomatoes, Coriander"), or tap 1-click pantry staple chips.
  2. The Sloth Cooking Energy Slider: Select how much effort you can spare:
    • ⚡ Microwave Chef (3 mins): Zero pan watching, zero chopping, single mug or bowl.
    • 🍳 One-Pan Stir-Fry (15 mins): Quick sizzle, light dice, maximum flavor-to-effort ratio.
    • 🍲 Slow Simmer (30 mins): Low-heat stew or curry—walk away and take a nap while it simmers.
  3. "Minimize Dishes" 1-Vessel Lock: Automatically adapts every recipe to a single mug, skillet, or pot, eliminating cutting boards and prep bowls so cleanup takes 15 seconds.
  4. "Lazy Substitutions" (Zero-Store Swaps): Missing an ingredient? Don't leave your couch. Tap any pantry alternative (e.g., swapping Paneer with Tofu or Boiled Chickpeas, or Butter with Ghee + Salt). The cooking steps dynamically rephrase so instructions match how the swap actually behaves in the pan.
  5. 🦥 "Sloth Nap" Hands-Free Cooking Timer: Synced to your recipe duration with soothing Web Speech voice announcements ("Wake up, master... your feast is ready...") and real-time synthesized pentatonic chimes so you can rest your eyes without burning dinner.

Demo

  • Live Demo: Deployed on GitHub Pages
  • Local Preview: Simply open index.html in any modern browser—no build steps or package installations required!

Visual Walkthrough & Features:

  • Dual-Input Dropzone: Visual image scanning alongside quick-tag ingredient chips.
  • Strict Pure Veg Shield: Rejects meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, gelatin, and animal broths while intelligently preserving veg terms like eggplant and chickpeas.
  • Tactile Sloth Aesthetic: Warm cream (#faf6f0), roasted brown (#2b2420), and emerald green (#10b981) color palette with light and dark mode toggling.
  • Offline Sloth Mode: Fully functional with zero API key required through a built-in algorithmic culinary heuristic engine.

Code

The full source code is available in this repository:

  • Repository: Fridge-to-Feast on GitHub
  • License: MIT License

Clean Modular Architecture (Zero Heavyweight Framework Overhead): 

Week 3/
├── index.html                 # Semantic HTML5, Tailwind v4 theme, modal drawers & accessible UI
├── style.css                  # Custom tokens, tactile shadows, cross-browser scrollbars
├── favicon.svg                # Scalable vector sloth chef mascot with dark-mode awareness
├── package.json               # Lightweight development server scripts
├── .gitignore                 # Secrets, OS junk, logs, and build artifacts exclusion
├── .vscode/settings.json      # Workspace CSS & HTML linting configuration
└── js/
    ├── config.js              # Storage keys, pantry staples, cooking modes, pure veg regex rules
    ├── audio.js               # Web Audio API sound synthesizer (warm pentatonic pop & chime notes)
    ├── state.js               # Reactive state container, localStorage sync & canonical deduplication
    ├── timer.js               # Sloth Nap hands-free timer with Web Speech API voice synthesis
    ├── substitutions.js       # Pure veg zero-store pantry substitutions engine & AI rephraser
    ├── recipes-data.js        # Curated offline pure veg culinary database
    ├── recipe-engine.js       # Recipe synthesis engine & single-vessel constraint enforcer
    ├── gemini.js              # Google AI Studio dynamic model probe & API caller
    ├── scanner.js             # Client-side FileReader fridge photo dropzone & local visual analyzer
    ├── ui.js                  # DOM visual bindings, theme toggle, toasts & modals
    └── app.js                 # Application bootstrap & lifecycle orchestration

How I Built It

Fridge-to-Feast is built around a resilient hybrid AI and local-first architecture:

  1. Multimodal Vision & Recipe Synthesis (Google AI Studio / Gemini API):

    • Uses gemini-1.5-flash with dynamic fallback across Gemini models.
    • Inspects raw fridge photos to identify edible vegetarian produce and builds customized step-by-step recipes tailored to the user's chosen energy level.
    • When substituting ingredients, a dedicated AI rephrasing prompt rewrites instructions so cooking steps accurately reflect the culinary nature of the replacement item.

  2. The Offline Sloth Engine (Resilient Local Heuristic Inference):

    • When offline or when no API key is provided, the app seamlessly engages a local-first heuristic recipe engine.
    • Backed by OFFLINE_RECIPES_DATABASE and procedural single-vessel synthesis with canonical stem deduplication (using getCanonicalStem), ensuring ingredients and steps are never awkwardly repeated.

  3. Pure Vegetarian Guardrails:

    • A multi-tier regex and keyword sanitizer actively screens inputs to ensure 100% vegetarian compliance, preventing accidental non-veg contamination.

  4. Web Audio & Web Speech APIs:

    • Instead of loading heavy external MP3 audio assets, tactile clicks and soothing chimes are generated entirely in real-time via the browser's AudioContext.
    • The Sloth Nap Timer discovers system neural voices (such as Microsoft Aria/Jenny or macOS Samantha) to deliver unhurried, gentle wake-up announcements.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  1. Kitchen Privacy & Personal Sovereignty:
    Your personal fridge photos, dietary habits, and grocery inventory stay where they belong: inside your browser's localStorage. Closed commercial apps monetize user grocery data; open innovation guarantees user privacy by default.

  2. Resilience Across the Offline Gap:
    Cooking happens in real-world kitchens where Wi-Fi drops or data signals lag. By pairing open-source AI with local algorithmic heuristic engines, users can cook hot meals even when completely disconnected from the internet.

  3. Zero Paywalls for Daily Sustenance:
    Nobody should have to pay a recurring monthly subscription or hit API rate limits just to figure out what to cook with leftover potatoes and rice. Open-source keeps technology accessible to everyone.

  4. Community-Tailored Culinary Knowledge:
    Proprietary cooking apps frequently overlook global vegetarian traditions. An open-source codebase empowers developers worldwide to contribute regional pantry staples, spices, and authentic vegetarian substitution cheat sheets.

My Agent Session

This project was built pair-programming with the DeepMind Antigravity AI coding agent. Key milestones navigated during the session included:

  • Diagnosing and resolving subtle browser TextMate grammar traps (accept="image/*" comment collisions).
  • Modernizing Tailwind CSS v4 CSS-first token architectures with class-based .dark variants.
  • Eliminating compound substitution collisions (e.g. preventing "1 tbsp oil/butter" from duplicating into repeated terms).
  • Synthesizing tactile Web Audio API pentatonic soundscapes and crafting the custom scalable SVG sloth chef favicon.

The Lazy Payoff

  • Decision Fatigue Eliminated: Saves 25–35 minutes of scrolling through complex, ingredient-heavy recipes.
  • Dishes Avoided: Reduces kitchen sink pileup by 75–80%, locking meal prep to exactly 1 cooking vessel (0 prep plates, 0 cutting boards).
  • Zero Grocery Store Trips: The Lazy Substitutions engine spares you a 40-minute round trip to the supermarket just because you were missing one herb or dairy item.
  • Guilt-Free Rest: The Sloth Timer voice announcer lets you lie down on the sofa and nap peacefully while your one-pot stew or mug toss cooks safely.

Prize Categories

  • Primary Track: Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady
  • Partner Track: Google AI Studio / Gemini API (Multimodal Vision & Creative Recipe Synthesis)

Built with ❤️ and maximum kitchen laziness for Hacktoberfest 2026 🦥✨

Happy cooking, and even happier napping!

title: The Model Proposes, Rust Verifies: Triaging Job Postings with a Local Gemma
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

A job posting said it offered “a blend of remote flexibility and in-person collaboration.” My tool called it remote.
For someone applying from Nigeria, that isn't a small mistake. It can mean spending time on a role that isn't actually remote.
That wasn't the only problem I found while building JobKit. Some of the bugs were in my Rust rules. Others were in my reference labels—the answers I had prepared to judge whether the tool was correct.
I built JobKit to make the first read of a job posting faster. What I didn't expect was how much time I'd spend checking my own assumptions.
The model proposes, Rust verifies.

What I Built

Reading a job posting properly takes me about 17 minutes. Most of that goes on three boring questions: is it actually remote, what hours does it want, and how many years of experience does it ask for. I live at UTC+1, so those answers decide whether the posting is even for me.

JobKit is a Rust CLI that does that first read. Give it a posting and it tells me whether it's remote, what timezone and years it wants, which skills it names, and whether each skill looks required, optional or just mentioned. Every answer comes with the exact line it was found on, so I can check it in seconds.

A small local model, Gemma 3 4B, only names skills. Rust verifies and decides everything else. It runs on my laptop, and my job search never leaves it.

Demo

Code

Lymah123 / jobkit

A local, evidence-first triage tool for job postings, written in Rust.

JobKit

A local, evidence-first triage tool for job postings, written in Rust.

You give it a job posting and a short profile of yourself. It tells you whether the posting is remote, what timezone window and years of experience it asks for, which skills it names, and whether each skill looks required, optional or just mentioned. Every answer comes with the exact line of the posting it was found on, so you can check it in seconds.

A small local model (Gemma 3 4B through Ollama) only names skills Rust verifies and decides everything else. Nothing leaves your machine.

The model proposes, Rust verifies.

How it works

  1. Rules (no model). Plain regex rules read remote status, minimum years, UTC timezone windows and flag work-authorization or location sentences. Remote has three states: true, false (explicitly not remote, onsite, hybrid or in-person), or unknown.
  2. Model. Gemma lists the…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

Model: Gemma 3 4B (open weights), run locally through Ollama in WSL.

Language: Rust, with regex, serde ', andureq`.
Built with an AI assistant: I used Claude to help with debugging. I ran the code, collected and hand-labelled the postings, evaluated the results, and decided what to fix.

The model doesn't get the final say on whether a skill is real. Rust checks the posting itself:

If Rust finds no matching term in the posting, it rejects the proposed skill. If it finds one, it keeps the skill with a line of evidence for the user to inspect.

This is the core idea, simplified: the model proposes; deterministic code checks the evidence.

The rule: the model proposes, Rust verifies.

  1. The model names skills.
  2. Rust accepts a skill only if it appears in the posting as a whole term (aliases like Postgres and PostgreSQL allowed) and attaches the line it came from as evidence. A skill the posting never mentions is rejected as invented.
  3. Rust classifies each accepted skill from the headings and wording around it ("Nice to have", "preferred", "Good to have:").
  4. Plain rules read remote status, years and timezone windows, and flag work-authorization sentences. Anything uncertain becomes Review instead of a confident answer.

What went wrong (the interesting part)

  1. My first checker rejected 45 of 90 items, mostly for formatting. I had required the model to copy quotes exactly, and a 4B model can't do that reliably. Letting Rust find the evidence fixed it. On my first nine postings the model never named a skill that wasn't there (0 of 73). 2.** My rules started at 78% on remote**, 33% on years and 11% on timezone. The causes were a pattern that never matched "1 year", company history read as a requirement ("~2 years since we started"), and "no remote" counted as remote.
  2. My labels were wrong too. The harness checks that each labelled skill appears in its posting. It caught 8 that didn't, plus one marked required that sat under "Nice to Have".
  3. A section rule leaked. A "Good to have:" section ran into the stack list that followed it, because one unrecognised heading didn't end it. The heading "US citizenship/visa not required" also demoted real skills.
  4. The held-out set humbled me. It found a hybrid job ("a blend of remote flexibility and in-person collaboration") scored as remote, and "12-15+ years" read as 15. It also found "10+ years … including 2+ years in embedded roles" read as 2, a mistake I had made myself when triaging by hand.

Results

Metric 9-posting tuning set (includes 1 synthetic posting) 8 held-out postings
Remote classification 100% (up from 78%) 62%, then 75% after fixes
Minimum years of experience 100% (up from 33%) 75%, then 100% after fixes
Timezone classification 100% (up from 11%) 100%
Skills — loose mode (precision / recall) 0.51 / 0.88 0.32 / 0.37
Skills — strict mode (precision / recall) 0.59 / 0.45 0.33 / 0.27
Unsupported skill proposals caught by the checker 0 of 73 1 of 69

The held-out column is the honest one, and the "after fixes" numbers are no longer held-out, because I patched the rules after seeing those failures. Loose means a skill is required unless every mention is optional. Strict also needs requirement wording or a requirements heading, so stack lists like Backend: Go, Postgres count as mentioned. That trades recall for precision.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • My data stays mine. A job search involves my CV, my location, and which companies I'm looking at. With an open-weight model none of it leaves my machine.
  • I could see exactly how it failed. I turned each failure of the small model into a check: invented terms, malformed JSON, repeated keys. That's why no invented skills got through on the set I tuned on.
  • I could rerun it for free. I evaluated the whole set many times, and cached model output so re-scoring takes seconds and results are reproducible.
  • What I can't claim: I didn't compare against a hosted model, which would likely extract long skill lists better. My result is that a small local model is usable if you build verification around it.

The Lazy Payoff

  • By hand: 83 minutes for 5 postings, about 17 each.
  • JobKit's rules alone: 0.08 seconds per posting.
  • With the model: 43 to 143 seconds per posting, 96 on average over 8. It's slow, but it waits for me and I don't wait for it. Slow and steady.
  • My time with the tool: Approximately 2 minute to read and check the output for the same 5 postings.
  • Next step (an estimate): 3 of the 8 held-out postings were hard Skips from the rules alone. Skipping the model for those would save about 35% of the model time. I haven't built that yet.

Limits

  • 16 real postings plus one test case, all labelled by me, with mistakes I found along the way.
  • Gemma 4B under-extracts long skill lists.
  • The tool matches terms, not concepts like "distributed systems". "Mentioned in the posting" isn't "required".
  • Boilerplate can trip flags. A pay-transparency sentence raised a location flag.
  • I never measured whether the apply-or-skip verdict was right.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 3 runs locally as the extraction step, and the whole verification layer exists because of how a 4B Gemma fails.

What's Next

Three of the eight held-out postings were hard Skips under the rules-only evaluation. If JobKit can safely skip model inference for those cases, I estimate it could reduce model runtime by about 35%. That optimization isn't implemented yet.

I built JobKit because job hunting already takes enough time without repeatedly decoding postings that aren't a fit. The immediate goal is to make that first screening step faster and easier to verify—not to pretend a small model can make every application decision for me.

The model proposes, Rust verifies. The next step is making that process cheaper without making it less trustworthy.

title: PersonaScienceBench: Evaluating Scientific Agents with Diverse Simulated Researchers
description:
arXiv:2610.32106v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Scientific agents collaborate with researchers whose expertise and preferences differ, but benchmarks usually hold the collaborator fixed. We introduce PersonaScienceBench: 200 tasks from five benchmarks across four scientific domains. Simulated researchers provide context and feedback according to persona profiles, while task objectives and grading remain fixed. Agents encounter researcher preferences only through conversation. Across eighteen modelconfigurations, task performance, fact recovery, and self-repetition reveal different strengths. Detailed GPT 6 Astra analyses show distinct agent responses across researcher profiles; interaction traces illustrate targeted clar ification and workflow revision. These behaviors can differ even when final scores match. PersonaScienceBench therefore evaluates how agents collaborate with diverse researchers alongside whether they complete the task.

title: Kolibri: A Sovereign European Model on the Pareto Frontier
description:
arXiv:2610.31945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This report introduces Kolibri, an English-German mixture-of-experts transformer with 78.1B total parameters and 3.46B active parameters per token, released as open weights under the Apache 2.0 licence. We built Kolibri for sovereign and specialised deployment, with a particular focus on German and on regulated domains such as public administration, industry, and aerospace. To support these settings, we control the full model-development process, including data, architecture, training infrastructure, post-training, and evaluation.
  We train Kolibri on 24T tokens across pre-training, mid-training, and long-context extension, with German accounting for more than 20% of the data mix by bytes. To reach this share, we complement German datasets with more than 2T German tokens that we curate from the web with our own pipeline and generate synthetically. Post-training combines supervised fine-tuning on curated German and English data with reinforcement learning on more than 1.2M internally curated tasks, which cover reasoning, tool use, instruction following, code, and retrieval. The model activates 4.4% of its parameters per token, and among the open models evaluated in this report, it lies on the Pareto frontier of quality and serving cost in English and German.
  Kolibri builds on Kolibri Origin, an earlier iteration that validated our full pipeline at scale. Both models come from our Model Factory, which connects data, experimentation, training, evaluation, and deployment through version-controlled workflows.

title: Exa joins the Vercel AI Gateway and Agent Marketplace
description:
Exa is now available on the Vercel AI Gateway and Agent Marketplace as a native integration. Exa's neural search engine grounds models in current information.

  • Exa search is now a built-in tool on AI Gateway, which runs the search for you without an Exa account of your own.

  • You can also add Exa to a Vercel project from the Agent Marketplace to power search or a research agent, with a single API key that works across every Exa product and billing through your Vercel account.

Exa search on AI Gateway

Every model on AI Gateway can search with Exa through a built-in tool, with no Exa account or key of your own required. Pass gateway.tools.exaSearch() alongside your prompt and the gateway runs the search, hands the results back to the model, and keeps going until the model stops searching. You get one finished response with a synthesized answer rather than raw results to stream back yourself.

The tool takes the same controls as the Exa API, so you can set how many results come back, focus a search on a category such as news or research papers, restrict it to a country, and include or exclude domains.

Searches bill through AI Gateway next to your model usage at list price with no markup.

Exa on the Agent Marketplace

Install Exa from the Marketplace or deploy the Next.js Search template to integrate Exa's instant search, deep answers, and content extraction to your Vercel project.

About Exa: For developers building AI features on Vercel, Exa gives agents the web, organized for them. Whether you're answering questions, monitoring changes, or extracting structured data, Exa's one API for search, crawling, and research returns token-efficient highlights with grounded citations, so your agents get the context they need with fewer round trips, lower cost, and lower latency.

title: Modeling a Real Org Chart in Toronto: Group, Division, Department, Team
description:
A manufacturing group headquartered in Toronto, with a logistics division in Vancouver and a finance department that reports into both the division and a shared-services group at head office, is not an edge case. It is the normal shape of a mid-sized Canadian company. Most software tooling, though, still models access as a flat list of roles: admin, developer, viewer. That works for a ten-person startup. It falls apart the moment someone asks: who is allowed to approve a production release for the Vancouver warehouse system, and does that approval also need sign-off from the group's security lead in Toronto?

This is not a people-management question. It is an architecture question, and it belongs in the same conversation as authentication and data access, because an org chart that is wrong in software produces wrong approvals in production.

The org chart is a graph, not a tree

Group, division, department, team looks like strict nesting on a slide deck. In practice it rarely is. A QA lead might sit inside one department for reporting purposes but be the designated approver for releases across three teams. A plant manager in a Montreal facility might hold an operational role in the manufacturing division and a compliance role in a group-wide safety committee. Modeling this as a single-parent tree forces you to either duplicate the person across branches or flatten their permissions down to the lowest common denominator — usually the wrong one.

Corporate AI 365 treats the org chart as a real hierarchy with multi-hat roles: a person can hold distinct permission sets at different nodes simultaneously, and those permission sets are composable rather than bundled. There are 41 discrete permissions, not three role templates. That granularity exists specifically so that who can file a problem report, who can see the diagnosis, and who can approve the fix into production can be three different answers at three different nodes of the same hierarchy, without anyone being handed more access than their actual job requires.

Why the shape determines who can approve what

The product's delivery pipeline is Developer → QA → approval → production, implemented as real git branches and pull requests on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps. Each gate in that pipeline is a permission, and each transition is an audit record. The useful question in a security review is not whether that pipeline exists — most CI setups have something similar — but who is structurally allowed to sit at each gate, and whether that mapping survives the complexity of a real company.

Bind the approval gate to a department node and a national retailer's Toronto head office can require that only someone with release authority in that department — not just anyone with a developer badge — can push to production for a given system. Bind it to a division and you get regional autonomy: the Vancouver logistics team ships on its own cadence without waiting on Toronto, while the group retains visibility through the Manager console. This is the practical payoff of modeling the chart honestly: the governance gates mean something, because they're attached to the actual structure of who answers to whom, not to a generic role label.

Reporting problems without routing them through scarce senior engineers

Production downtime is expensive at any scale — industry estimates (ITIC) put the median cost for large enterprises at roughly US$9,000 per minute — and the usual bottleneck isn't willingness to fix things, it's finding someone senior enough to diagnose the root cause fast. That person is increasingly hard to find. Surveys across other markets report skills gaps as high as 90% of organizations in the Gulf and 57% of firms in Europe unable to find qualified developers; Canadian engineering leaders describe the same structural pressure anecdotally, even without a single national figure to cite. A lean IT team in Winnipeg or Halifax feels this as directly as one in Toronto.

This is where the org chart becomes operationally useful rather than administrative. The Employee support portal lets anyone in the company — a warehouse supervisor, an accounts clerk, a plant operator — file a problem report in plain language, no ticket taxonomy required. The hierarchy then routes that report to the right team automatically, because the system already knows which department owns which codebase. The AI reads the team's actual source code and scripted schema, proposes a root cause down to file, class, or line with a confidence score, and that diagnosis is cached against a hash of the issue text, the code snapshot, and the model — so a junior developer reviewing it a day later sees the same answer a senior one would have. That reproducibility is what lets a smaller team run production support without a bench of specialists standing by.

Worth stating plainly, because it matters in a review: none of this requires the AI to touch a live database. It reasons over source code and a scripted schema export you control. If the diagnosis genuinely needs live data, it writes a read-only query for your own developer to run — the result never comes back to us. The org hierarchy, the permissions, and the approval trail live entirely within your connected repository and your directory; verified domain join by DNS and SSO with Microsoft, Google, or GitHub mean the structure is yours, not something we infer or store independently.

title: Beyond Pattern Matching in 3D MLLMs: Part-Level Functional Reasoning for Generalizable Recognition
description:
arXiv:2610.32262v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: 3D MLLMs recognize objects via pattern matching, which fails when geometrically similar objects require functional reasoning to disambiguate (e.g., dresser vs. wardrobe). Our per-sample Geometric Confusion Score (GCS) exposes this failure: baseline accuracy is 33.7% on ModelNet40's most ambiguous 20% versus 84.0% on its least ambiguous 20%. We identify a function-as-annotation pattern, in which functional language decorates a known identity instead of supporting inference, and hypothesize that reversing this information flow should concentrate improvements on the most ambiguous samples. PFIR (Part-level Functional Inference for Recognition) reverses that flow. Built on PartNeXt part segmentation, its data pipeline produces 507K QA pairs with functional CoTs (geometry $\to$ function $\to$ identity), and its progressive curriculum culminates in dual-objective GRPO: strict functional reasoning and descriptive grounding for Objaverse's diverse distribution. The two RL objectives yield nearly orthogonal task vectors ($\cos = 0.056$), enabling composition via Task Arithmetic. Under a strict dual OOD protocol (Objaverse $\to$ ModelNet40; XYZRGB $\to$ XYZ-only), PFIR raises zero-shot accuracy from 60.5% to 66.7%, with gains concentrated $2.6\times$ more on geometrically ambiguous samples---supporting part-level functional reasoning as an effective route to more generalizable 3D recognition. Code: https://github.com/this233/pfir-3d.

title: Legacy ERP & Monolith Modernization: How to Execute a Strangler-Fig Migration Without Downtime or Data Loss
description:
When an established enterprise outgrows a 10-year-old legacy ERP or tightly coupled PHP/Java/.NET monolith, the default impulse is a "Big-Bang Rewrite": freeze features, rebuild from scratch for 14 months, and cut over on launch weekend. In practice, Big-Bang rewrites routinely stall or cause multi-day cutover outages when undocumented billing and inventory edge cases surface.

At Loop Origin, we rescue and modernize mission-critical legacy ERPs, dispatch platforms, and high-volume e-commerce systems without ever taking the business offline. Using the Strangler-Fig Migration Pattern, you place an intelligent routing proxy in front of your legacy monolith, extract one bounded domain at a time into a modern Laravel + Vue/Nuxt + PostgreSQL service, synchronize data via Change Data Capture (CDC) and Anti-Corruption Layers (ACL), and retire the legacy system incrementally with zero downtime.

How Do You Execute a Strangler-Fig Migration on a Legacy ERP Without Downtime?

Direct Answer: A zero-downtime Strangler-Fig migration places a reverse proxy or API Gateway (Nginx, Envoy, or Kong) in front of the legacy monolith, extracts one high-ROI business domain at a time behind an Anti-Corruption Layer, synchronizes state via Change Data Capture (CDC) or transactional outbox events, verifies parity through shadow reads, and shifts traffic incrementally (1% → 10% → 100%) with sub-second rollback.

As covered in my guides on preventing double-booking with database locks and holds and using Strategy and Factory patterns to decouple payment and courier integrations, legacy monoliths become brittle because presentation, business rules, third-party SOAP/REST calls, and raw SQL queries are tangled inside the same 3,000-line controller files—often sharing a single unindexed database where 40 tables mutate each other via hidden SQL triggers.

Trying to rewrite all 40 tables and 200 screens simultaneously guarantees failure.

1.
2.
3.
4.

Comparison Matrix: Big-Bang Rewrite vs. Database-First Refactor vs. Strangler-Fig Migration

Use this executive comparison table when evaluating modernization proposals with your board, COO, or engineering leadership:

Evaluation Dimension 1. Big-Bang Rewrite (Freeze & Rebuild From Scratch) 2. In-Place Database-First Refactor (Shared Legacy DB) 3. Strangler-Fig + CDC / Outbox Migration (Recommended)
Time to First Production Value 12 – 24 months (Zero business value delivered until final cutover day) 3 – 6 months 4 – 6 weeks (First extracted module goes live in production immediately)
Cutover Downtime & Blast Radius Extreme (All-or-nothing weekend switch; rollback after new writes is nearly impossible) High (Schema changes on live legacy tables risk locking legacy queries) Near-Zero (Per-route Nginx/gateway canary shift; instant <2s rollback)
Data Loss / Inconsistency Risk High (One-shot weekend ETL script often drops edge-case records) Moderate (New and old code fight over legacy table locks) Very Low (Continuous CDC sync + automated checksum reconciliation before cutover)
Impact on Ongoing Feature Velocity Freezes roadmap for 1+ year or requires building features twice Slowed by legacy schema constraints High (New features are built directly inside modernized vertical slices)
3-Year Engineering Cost Predictability Poor (65%+ of Big-Bang rewrites exceed budget by 2x or stall) Moderate High (Fixed-scope milestone sprints per module)

Step 1: Edge Route Interception with Nginx (Canary & Path-Based Strangling)

Before writing a single line of new application code, put an Nginx reverse proxy (or Cloudflare Enterprise / Envoy gateway) in front of the legacy monolith. This lets you carve out specific URL prefixes—such as /inventory, /dispatch, or /api/v2/pricing—and route them to your new Laravel + Nuxt application while every other route continues hitting the legacy server transparently:

# /etc/nginx/conf.d/strangler-gateway.conf
upstream legacy_erp_monolith {
    server 10.10.1.50:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    keepalive 32;
}

upstream modern_laravel_service {
    server 10.10.2.100:9000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    keepalive 64;
}

# Canary split: route 10% of read traffic to the new service, 90% to legacy
split_clients "${remote_addr}${request_uri}" $inventory_read_upstream {
    10%     modern_laravel_service;
    *       legacy_erp_monolith;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name erp.yourcompany.com;

    # 1. Fully migrated vertical slice: 100% handled by Modern Service
    location ^~ /api/v2/dispatch/ {
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_pass http://modern_laravel_service;
    }

    # 2. Canary-tested slice: percentage split controlled via split_clients
    location ^~ /api/v1/inventory/availability {
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_pass http://$inventory_read_upstream;
    }

    # 3. Default fallback: all remaining unmigrated routes go to Legacy ERP
    location / {
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_pass http://legacy_erp_monolith;
    }
}

If an unexpected edge case appears when you dial $inventory_read_upstream from 10% to 50%, reverting traffic back to the legacy monolith takes one Nginx reload (nginx -s reload) in under 500 milliseconds with zero dropped connections.

Step 2: Why Application Dual-Writes Corrupt Data (And How Transactional Outbox / CDC Fixes It)

Once both the legacy monolith and the new service are running side-by-side, how do you keep customer records, inventory counts, and invoices synchronized between the legacy database and the new PostgreSQL database?

The Anti-Pattern: Synchronous Application Dual-Writes

Many teams try to write to both databases inside their application controller:

// BROKEN DUAL-WRITE ANTI-PATTERN: Causes permanent data drift on partial failure!
public function updateStock(int $skuId, int $qty): void
{
    $this->legacyMysqlDb->table('tbl_inv_mst')->where('sku_id', $skuId)->update(['q_oh' => $qty]);
    // What if the network blips or the new DB times out right here?!
    $this->modernPostgresDb->table('inventory_items')->where('sku_id', $skuId)->update(['on_hand' => $qty]);
}

If the first write commits to the legacy database and the second write fails due to a transient timeout (or vice versa), your legacy ERP and modern platform now show different inventory balances—without distributed two-phase commit (2PC), synchronous dual-writes will inevitably diverge under production load.

The Production Pattern: Transactional Outbox + Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL)

Instead of dual-writing across network boundaries, commit state to a single source-of-truth database alongside an atomic outbox_events row inside the same local ACID transaction (or stream the database's binary log / WAL via Debezium Change Data Capture).

// Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) Translator: Legacy ERP Row -> Clean Modern Domain DTO
final readonly class LegacyOrderAclTranslator
{
    public static function fromLegacyRow(array $raw): ModernSalesOrderDto
    {
        return new ModernSalesOrderDto(
            externalLegacyId: (int) $raw['ORD_ID_PK'],
            customerUuid:     Uuid::fromString($raw['CUST_GUID']),
            totalCents:       (int) round(((float) $raw['TOT_AMT_DEC']) * 100),
            status:           match ((int) $raw['ORD_STAT_CD']) {
                0       => OrderStatus::Draft,
                1, 2    => OrderStatus::Confirmed,
                9       => OrderStatus::Dispatched,
                99      => OrderStatus::Cancelled,
                default => OrderStatus::PendingReview,
            },
            placedAtUtc:      CarbonImmutable::createFromFormat('YmdHis', $raw['CRT_DT_STR'], 'Asia/Karachi')->utc(),
        );
    }
}

The ACL quarantines legacy quirks—converting floating-point dollars (TOT_AMT_DEC), magic status integers (0, 1, 9, 99), and local date strings into clean PostgreSQL BIGINT cents, typed enums, and UTC TIMESTAMPTZ values.

Which Module Should You Strangle First? The First-Slice Selection Rule

Do not pick the most complex core general-ledger table as your first Strangler-Fig slice—and do not pick a trivial static settings page that proves nothing.

  1. High Operational Pain / High ROI: For example, a slow customer/dealer order portal, a warehouse barcode scanning workflow, or a courier dispatch module (like our Car Carrier Management System). 2. 3.

The 7-Point Zero-Downtime Legacy Modernization Checklist

  • [ ] Place an API Gateway / Nginx Proxy in Front of the Monolith First: Decouple public URLs and DNS from the legacy server IP on Day 1.
  • [ ] Unify Authentication via Shared SSO or Signed JWTs: Allow users to move seamlessly between legacy screens and newly modernized screens without logging in twice.
  • [ ] Build an Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) for Every Synced Entity: Never copy cryptic legacy table schemas (tbl_usr_01) into your new PostgreSQL database.
  • [ ] Use Transactional Outbox or CDC Instead of Application Dual-Writes: Eliminate split-brain data drift between old and new databases.
  • [ ] Run Automated Shadow-Read Parity Checks Before Cutover: Compare 48 hours of production read responses (legacy JSON vs.
  • [ ] Flip Write Ownership One Bounded Domain at a Time: Once a domain slice reaches 100% traffic on the new service, revoke write permissions (REVOKE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on the retired legacy table so dead code can never silently mutate old rows.
  • [ ] Containerize Both Legacy and Modern Services: Use lean multi-stage Dockerfiles and automated health checks (managed server infrastructure) throughout the transition.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

1. How do we prevent users from noticing they are moving between the legacy ERP and the new web app?

Use two unification techniques: (1) serve both the legacy application and the new Nuxt / Vue frontend under the exact same parent domain (erp.yourcompany.com) via Nginx path routing, and (2) share a single navigation shell and HttpOnly authentication cookie / JWT so clicking from an unmigrated Accounting tab to a modernized Inventory & Dispatch tab feels like a single cohesive product.

2. What if our legacy ERP database has no source code access or uses proprietary stored procedures?

Even when a legacy vendor locks application code inside compiled binaries or encrypted stored procedures, you still control the underlying SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, or PostgreSQL database.

3. How do we handle foreign keys when one table is in the new PostgreSQL DB and another is still in the legacy DB?

During the transition window, the new service stores a read-only local projection (replica cache) of the parent entity (legacy_customer_id, customer_name, credit_limit_cents) updated in real time by your CDC/Outbox worker.

4. How long does a full Strangler-Fig ERP modernization take compared to a rewrite?

While a full multi-module enterprise ERP replacement typically spans 4 to 8 months across all phases, the critical difference is that Phase 1 goes live in production in Week 6 to Week 8.

5. How do we verify zero data loss before shutting off a legacy module permanently?

We run an automated Reconciliation & Checksum Job that compares row counts, SUM(total_cents) financial aggregates, and SHA-256 field hashes across 100% of records in both databases.

6. Can we modernize a legacy WooCommerce or Magento store using this same Strangler-Fig pattern?

Yes. WooCommerce](https://looporigin.com/blog/custom-ecommerce-vs-shopify-plus-vs-woocommerce-2026?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=legacy-erp-monolith-modernization-strangler-fig-migration-zero-downtime), high-volume retail brands frequently strangle legacy stores by extracting the high-speed Nuxt 3 SSR product catalog and checkout first while syncing inventory and order fulfillment in parallel.
