title: Complementing DINO Features with Image Structure for Part Discovery
description:
arXiv:2610.32293v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs) like DINO encode rich semantics, enabling training-free segmentation of objects from the background and discovery of their parts via feature clustering. This paper focuses on part discovery: partitioning a foreground object into semantic parts. Existing approaches produce imprecise part boundaries. We trace this to the rigid ViT patch grid used in training DINO, where patches straddling boundaries contain pixels from multiple parts. While DINO's invariance-based training could absorb this pixel-level mixing into clean features, experiments with over 26K foreground patches show it does not: boundary-overlapping patches produce features with higher entropy and lower assignment confidence, blurring predicted part boundaries. Rather than make the massive effort of retraining DINO over geometrically coherent regions, an easier approach is to take boundaries directly from a boundary detector, which supplies the geometric information DINO's features lack. Motivated by this, we introduce Part-DINO, a training-free framework that combines boundaries from low-level image segmentation with DINO's semantic features. We use the boundaries to partition the image into regions, pool DINO features within each region, and group them to discover parts. Without any training, Part-DINO produces structurally coherent part assignments, outperforming training-free baselines across four standard benchmarks (CUB, CelebA, PartImageNet-OOD, PartImageNet-Seg) and remaining competitive with weakly-supervised and unsupervised methods.

title: Designing an Honest Loading State for AI UI Generation
description:
A model taking a while is a backend problem. Making the whole editor look frozen while it waits is a product problem too.

In Napkin, users describe a UI idea or upload a sketch and ask the app to generate a responsive HTML draft. When Gemini took close to two minutes, the existing draft stayed safe—but the feedback was a generic spinner over the editor. It obscured the workspace without showing where the result would appear.

Put the wait where the result will be

For the first generation, the empty preview canvas now changes into a small animated mockup: a header, a feature card, and text blocks draw in while a subtle sweep passes over the frame. The animation lives inside the “Your idea goes here” canvas, not across the editor. A brief status label explains what is happening, and the existing draft remains visible during regeneration.

The key idea is contextual feedback: make the loading state resemble the outcome, rather than covering the product with an unrelated spinner. The motion is CSS-based and the app already disables animation for users who prefer reduced motion.

Make the request bounded, not magical

I also tightened the Gemini prompt, capped output at 8,192 tokens, and shortened the request timeout to 45 seconds. These changes constrain work and make a stalled request fail sooner; they do not guarantee the model will return within that time. The client only replaces the current draft after a complete successful response, so a timeout does not erase work. This route still waits for the full response rather than streaming partial HTML.

The relevant request settings are intentionally small:

generationConfig: {
  temperature: 0.25,
  maxOutputTokens: 8192,
},
signal: AbortSignal.timeout(45_000),

A good loading state improves the wait, but it cannot make a slow provider fast. Keep the timeout message honest, preserve recoverable work, and measure actual provider latency separately from perceived responsiveness.

Further reading

  • ⚡ Better Loading States for AI Apps by @vectorchi argues that open-ended model waits need more useful feedback than a spinner.
  • ⏱️ The Cost of a Pause: Designing for the Doherty Threshold by @rverwey frames response feedback as part of the interaction, not merely a backend metric.

Napkin is open source: nonydev27/napkin.

title: What the Query Remembers: Query Abstraction Governs Lexical and Dense Retrieval of Classical Arabic Poetry
description:
arXiv:2610.31821v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How well a poetry archive can be searched depends on what the user still remembers, not only on what the model understands. We show this for Classical Arabic poetry, benchmarking nine dense encoders and BM25 over two corpora, three indexing modes and two evaluation protocols. Which retriever wins is governed by how much of a poem's wording the query still carries. On tip-of-the-tongue queries BM25 leads every dense encoder, including an 8B state-of-the-art model (0.746 vs. 0.717 Recall@5); on abstract queries it falls to eighth out of ten (0.392 vs. 0.748). Editing the wording of the same queries shows that this ranking largely reflects query composition: adding one remembered half-verse raises BM25 by 38 points, rewriting the quoted words by hand leaves BM25 level with the 8B encoder, and BM25's sensitivity to remembered wording is significantly steeper than that of the strongest dense encoder. The same axis controls explanation augmentation, whose effect swings from +37 to -39 points. The mechanism splits by system type: lexical containment predicts BM25's behaviour, while embedding proximity predicts dense encoders. Finally, the field's two standard protocols, known-item retrieval and thematic relevance, dissociate on the same systems, a result reproduced by two blind human annotators and by two open-weights judges, one of them under a rubric with no literal-match criterion. A benchmark that reports one protocol, or one query register, can give a materially wrong picture. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ellzo/what-the-query-remembers.

title: Rulewright: A Smarter Way to Categorize Transactions with AI
description:
Introducing Rulewright: A Smarter Way to Categorize Transactions

The Problem

Managing personal finances often means going through long lists of transactions from banks, UPI apps, and digital payment platforms. Categorizing every transaction manually can be repetitive and time-consuming.

I wanted to explore a simpler approach: what if transaction categorization could combine reusable rules with AI-powered suggestions while keeping the user in control?

That idea led me to build Rulewright.

What Is Rulewright?

Rulewright is a Python and Streamlit-based bookkeeping prototype that helps users categorize transaction records from CSV files.

The goal is to make transaction organization easier while allowing users to review suggestions before exporting their final ledger.

Key Features

1. CSV Transaction Import

Upload a CSV containing transaction descriptions and supported fields to get started. A fictional sample ledger is also available for testing.

2. Offline Categorization Rules

Create reusable merchant-based rules to categorize transactions without sending them to an AI service.

3. Gemini AI Suggestions

Rulewright can request category suggestions from the Google Gemini API. The suggested categories are drafts, not automatically approved financial records.

4. Human Review and Approval

Users can review and edit suggested categories, approve selected transactions, and inspect the final approved ledger before exporting it.

5. CSV and Rules Export

Download categorized transactions, approved records, and reusable rules for further work.

How It Works

The current workflow is straightforward:

  1. Upload a transaction CSV or load the fictional sample ledger.
  2. Define the categories you want to use.
  3. Generate offline rules or request AI suggestions.
  4. Review and edit the proposed categories.
  5. Approve the transactions you want to include.
  6. Download the resulting CSV.

Technology Stack

  • Python — application logic and transaction processing
  • Streamlit — interactive web interface
  • Pandas — CSV loading and tabular data processing
  • Google Gemini API — optional AI-powered category suggestions
  • Pytest — automated tests for core functionality

Privacy and Responsible AI

Financial transaction data can be sensitive. Rulewright includes a warning that transaction descriptions are sent to an external service when Gemini suggestions are requested.

For testing, I recommend using fictional data rather than real bank statements. Offline categorization is available without sending transaction descriptions to Gemini.

AI suggestions should always be reviewed before being treated as final financial records.

What I Learned

Building Rulewright helped me explore CSV processing, reusable categorization rules, API integration, data validation, approval workflows, and automated testing.

It also reinforced an important principle: AI can help make repetitive tasks easier, but users should remain in control of decisions involving their financial data.

Try Rulewright

  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/LaxmikanthJanardhan01/rulewright
  • Live demo: https://rulewright-vzkikduphnnvksu7vgzouu.streamlit.app

What's Next?

I plan to improve the dashboard design, make transaction review more intuitive, strengthen CSV handling, and continue testing the application with fictional transaction data.

Rulewright is a prototype, and there is still plenty of room to improve it.

I'd love to hear your feedback: What feature would make a transaction categorization tool more useful to you?

Thanks for reading!

title: Node.js Express Backend: Single Key for OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini Model Switching
description:
Decision rule: if a logistics application judges candidates against a rubric and structured output is the primary decision axis, put the model choice behind one Node.js contract. Change the model ID in configuration; do not create a new Express branch, credential path, or parser for OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini.

The contract is small: one base URL, one bearer key, one chat request shape, and a JSON schema for the score. The useful boundary is the response contract, not the brand behind it. A model directory should populate the allowed choices before an administrator can select one.

The failure is visible.

Keep it bounded.

This is also why I would keep the batch result and the PDF artifact on the same operational surface. The score is data; the rendered review packet is an artifact. If both use one key and one base URL, their cost metadata and request IDs can be audited together. That is a concrete architecture decision, not a claim that one provider is universally best.

How can a Node.js backend use a single key to switch OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini?

The invariant is the rubric envelope. A candidate record should enter the system with stable fields such as candidate_id, role, requirements, and evidence. The model may vary, but the application should still receive a JSON object containing the same score dimensions, a bounded recommendation, and evidence references. An invalid object is a failed decision, even if the prose sounds persuasive.

I would treat model selection as data, for example MODEL_ID in deployment configuration or a controlled admin dropdown populated from /v1/models. The startup refresh matters: hard-coding a vendor's catalog makes a model switch look like a code release and can leave an unavailable choice in production. The catalog is a guardrail, not an evaluation. Each selected model still needs representative rubric tests.

The unified REST option is a good first architecture for a junior developer shipping in US or EU markets because the Express or Next.js surface remains narrow. A single chat endpoint can also carry structured JSON extraction for later features. That reuse is valuable, but it does not remove the need to validate the schema, reject missing evidence, and retain the raw request ID for review.

A cost analyst's version of this rule is less romantic: every label increases cardinality, every log line is bytes stored, and every retained payload is a future query. I count 295 routes across 20 modules as platform breadth, not as 295 reasons to add telemetry. Record the model ID, outcome class, latency metadata supplied by the API, and request ID. Do not copy full candidate evidence into every retry log.

Which option fits a rubric-scoring backend?

The choice depends on where you want the failure boundary. Direct vendor clients expose vendor-native controls, while a unified layer makes replacement cheaper in code. Neither side is free.

Option Strength Boundary to test Fit for this workflow
OpenAI API and SDK Mature client conventions and documented function calling OpenAI-specific response and tool semantics Strong when OpenAI features are the product requirement
Anthropic Claude API Direct access to Claude models and their native request conventions A separate auth, client, and structured-output integration Strong when Claude-specific behavior is the evaluation target
Google Gemini API Direct Google model access and its own SDK/API surface A third request shape, credential set, and response adapter Strong when Google platform alignment matters
Unified OpenAI-compatible REST surface One key, one chat shape, and model IDs that can be switched in configuration Provider abstraction, catalog readiness, and schema conformance Strong for a portable first version with a stable application contract

The three direct options are real competitors, not interchangeable labels. OpenAI's function-calling documentation is a useful reference for tool and schema-oriented designs; Claude and Gemini each deserve their own adapter when their native capabilities are the reason for choosing them. A portability layer should not pretend that every model has identical behavior.

The trade-off is operational concentration. One unified provider means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. That is the honest cost of the simpler application boundary. A regulated or high-availability system may choose two direct integrations for redundancy, accepting more adapters and more telemetry dimensions.

How does the batch-to-PDF handoff preserve the decision trail?

The handoff is where a two-capability design earns its keep. Submit candidate scoring as a batch, collect its result, then pass the result to PDF generation for a review packet. Both calls use the same Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY header and the same INFRAI_BASE_URL value, set to the platform's versioned API base. The request bodies should be generated from the public discovery schemas for the two capabilities; that is safer than guessing field names from prose.

The critical path is deliberately boring:

curl --fail-with-body --request POST \\
  --url "${INFRAI_BASE_URL}/ai/batch/submit" \\
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \\
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \\
  --data-binary @batch-submit.json

curl --fail-with-body --request POST \\
  --url "${INFRAI_BASE_URL}/pdf/generate" \\
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \\
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \\
  --data-binary @pdf-generate.json

The files in that example are not arbitrary hand-written payloads. batch-submit.json and pdf-generate.json should be validated against the schemas returned by the public discovery surface, with the batch output mapped into the PDF input by the worker. This keeps the example honest about what is verified: the batch-submit and PDF-generate routes are real, but their complete request fields are schema-defined and should not be invented in an article.

The same-key handoff gives the audit trail a useful join key: batch request ID to generated artifact request ID. It also puts the work on one bill, while still requiring an application-level record that says which candidate rubric version produced the document. One wallet cannot tell you whether a score was semantically correct. Infrai is a reasonable fit for this narrow seam because its verified surface puts 295 routes across 20 modules behind one key, while discovery describes readiness instead of hiding it.

For comparison, an OpenAI Batch plus wkhtmltopdf stack would involve one OpenAI signup and one provider credential set, while the renderer would be separately installed and operated with no provider credential. You would write the batch polling, result normalization, HTML templating, process supervision, artifact retention, and cross-system cost correlation yourself. That stack is valid when HTML rendering control is the priority. It has two operational systems and two audit vocabularies.

Where should the abstraction stop?

Do not make the unified route a promise of feature parity. The model catalog is the source for available choices, and readiness can differ by capability. Speech transcription is not a safe fallback here: the ASR entry is present but available=false. Real-time voice sessions have pending key status and are limited to the western region. There is no dedicated moderation endpoint, so moderation must be treated as a chat-model JSON-schema task with an explicit review policy. Image upscaling is limited to Lanczos.

Those boundaries affect a logistics product. Candidate scoring can use a text chat contract; a scanned résumé may require a separate document or OCR decision; a voice interview cannot be quietly assumed to work because a route-shaped entry exists. The correct response to an unavailable capability is a product state such as unsupported, not a retry loop that produces noisy logs and a misleading success rate.

I would also make retries part of the contract. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After and use exponential backoff. For any write, send an idempotency key when the capability supports it, and make the consumer idempotent because batch and queue processing are not a license to assume exactly-once delivery. Retain only the fields needed to explain a rejected score. A 24-hour deduplication window is useful operational context, but it is not a substitute for a durable application key.

Decision

Choose the unified API when the product's durable asset is a stable structured score and the team values a small Node.js integration more than vendor-native surface area. Keep the model ID configurable, load choices from /v1/models, validate every response, and treat the batch-to-PDF handoff as one traceable workflow.

Choose direct OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini integrations when a provider-specific capability, regional requirement, or independent failover boundary justifies the extra adapters. The neutral test is simple: can the team name the exact behavior it needs that the contract cannot represent? If not, three SDKs buy complexity before they buy correctness.

The architecture succeeds when a model swap changes a configuration value and an evaluation result, not the shape of the logistics application.

References

  • OpenAI, Function calling guide: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/function-calling
  • OpenAI, Batch API guide: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/batch
  • Anthropic, API documentation: https://docs.anthropic.com/en/api/getting-started
  • Google, Gemini API documentation: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs
  • wkhtmltopdf project: https://github.com/wkhtmltopdf/wkhtmltopdf
  • pgvector, Postgres vector similarity extension: https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector

title: GBase Database Pre-Installation Checklist: 6 Linux System Checks Before Deploying GBase 8a
description:
Summary: Before installing GBase Database(GBase 8a), verify the Linux environment on every cluster node. These six pre-installation checks cover OS compatibility, disk capacity, network ports, kernel settings, dependencies, and Python runtime configuration.

A database installer can automate deployment, but it cannot guarantee that every server has the correct operating system configuration.

When deploying GBase Database(GBase 8a), a mismatch in the Python interpreter, a missing dependency, an occupied port, or an inconsistent kernel setting can delay installation or cause problems when cluster services start.

I use the following six checks before deployment. On a small three-node cluster, the initial inspection can take around ten minutes, depending on the environment.

The key rule is simple: run every check on every node, not just the first server.

1. Check the Operating System and Hostname

Start by confirming the OS release, kernel version, and hostname.

cat /etc/redhat-release
uname -r
hostname
hostname | wc -c

For virtual machines, check whether the CPU exposes the rdtscp instruction if it is required by your target GBase Database version:

grep -m1 -o rdtscp /proc/cpuinfo

Verify that all nodes use a supported and consistent OS and kernel configuration. The hostname should comply with the product's documented length restrictions; for the environment covered by this checklist, the target is fewer than 46 characters.

Do not assume that two machines running the same Linux distribution are identical. Minor-version differences, virtual CPU settings, and kernel configurations can affect deployment.

2. Check Disk Space, Inodes, and Swap

Insufficient disk space is easy to notice. Insufficient inodes can be less obvious, especially when a workload creates a large number of small files.

Inspect the filesystem containing the installation directory and review available memory and swap:

df -h /opt
df -i /opt
free -h

Check the target filesystem against the requirements of your specific GBase Database release.

For the environment described here, the planning baseline includes:

  • At least 1 GB of available installation space

  • Approximately 300 MB for metadata, plus additional operational headroom

  • Sufficient free inodes for the expected file workload

  • A filesystem type supported by the target OS and product version

The exact filesystem, free-space, inode, and swap requirements must be verified against the applicable installation manual. For example, older RHEL releases and newer releases may have different recommended filesystem configurations.

Why check inodes? A filesystem can have free storage capacity while running out of available inodes. When that happens, creating files may fail even though df -h appears healthy.

Correcting a filesystem layout after deployment can be much more disruptive than validating it beforehand.

3. Check Network Connectivity and Required Ports

GBase Database(GBase 8a) uses different ports for cluster components. Confirm the required port list during planning, before installation begins.

Commonly referenced ports include:

Component Port
GCluster 5258
GNode 5050
GCware 5918, 5919
syncServer 5288
GCRecover 6268

Confirm these values against the configuration and documentation for your release. Also check any additional ports required by the selected deployment topology.

To inspect TCP ports currently listening on a node:

ss -tlnp

To check whether the ports above appear in the local listening socket table:

for p in 5258 5050 5918 5919 5288 6268; do
  if ss -H -ltn "sport = :$p" | grep -q .; then
    echo "LISTENING $p"
  else
    echo "NOT LISTENING $p"
  fi
done

Important: NOT LISTENING does not prove that a port is available for installation. A service could bind to it later, and UDP sockets are not covered by this TCP check. Review existing services, configured port reservations, firewall rules, and connectivity between nodes as well.

4. Check Kernel Settings and Process Limits

System settings can affect database deployment and cluster service startup.

Start by inspecting the current configuration:

ulimit -v

cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled

cat /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler

systemctl show -p DefaultTasksMax

Check the following against the target GBase Database release:

  • Virtual memory limits for the installation and database users

  • Transparent Huge Pages (THP) configuration

  • I/O scheduler settings for the actual data devices

  • Systemd task limits

For environments requiring THP to be disabled, the expected output from the THP check typically marks never as the active setting in square brackets:

always madvise [never]

The scheduler command above uses /dev/sda as an example. If your data devices use different names, inspect the actual devices instead.

If your deployment guide requires DefaultTasksMax=infinity, configure it in the appropriate systemd configuration file:

DefaultTasksMax=infinity

Then apply the change using the procedure supported by your OS, for example:

systemctl daemon-reexec
systemctl show -p DefaultTasksMax

Recheck the effective value afterward.

Avoid applying settings blindly across different Linux distributions. The supported values and recommended configuration should come from the installation guide for your GBase Database version.

5. Verify Required Dependency Packages

Missing system packages can cause deployment scripts or service-management commands to fail.

For RPM-based systems, inspect the following dependencies:

rpm -q psmisc libcgroup python2

This command reports whether the packages are installed in the RPM database.

  • psmisc provides utilities such as killall.

  • libcgroup provides cgroup-related functionality where required by the product and OS.

  • python2 provides the Python 2 runtime where required by the installer.

A missing package should be resolved before deployment, but package availability and names differ across OS versions. Confirm the dependencies specified by your GBase Database installation package.

Do not assume that a package available on one Linux release is present under the same name on another.

6. Verify the Default Python Interpreter

Python runtime compatibility is one of the most important pre-installation checks for some GBase Database(GBase 8a) releases.

An installer written for Python 2 may fail if the default python command resolves to Python 3. Having Python 2 installed is not sufficient if the installation scripts invoke a different interpreter.

Check the command resolution:

which python
python --version

Run these commands under both the root account and the intended database installation account, such as gbase.

Compare the results and confirm that the installer will use the expected interpreter.

On CentOS 8 or RHEL 8 environments, Python 2 may need to be installed separately, depending on the OS image and available repositories. Package names and supported runtime options should be verified for the target platform.

Do not change the system-wide Python configuration without checking its impact on OS utilities and other applications. If the installer supports an explicit interpreter or a documented runtime setup, follow that procedure.

Run the Environment Configuration Script

After the six checks pass, use the environment configuration procedure documented for your GBase Database release.

For versions whose installation guide specifies this command, the syntax may look like:

cd gcinstall
python SetSysEnv.py --dbaUser=gbase --installPrefix=/opt/gbase

Confirm the script location, supported arguments, Python runtime, and installation prefix before executing it.

SetSysEnv.py helps apply a consistent environment configuration. It does not replace manual verification of the Python interpreter, dependency packages, node connectivity, or system prerequisites.

Do not treat a successful script run as proof that every node is ready.

Save the Results for Every Node

The final step is to retain evidence.

Run the checks on every machine and save the output with the corresponding node inventory. For example:

mkdir -p ~/gbase-precheck

{
  date
  hostname
  cat /etc/redhat-release
  uname -r
  python --version 2>&1
  rpm -q psmisc libcgroup python2
  df -h /opt
  df -i /opt
  free -h
  systemctl show -p DefaultTasksMax
} > ~/gbase-precheck/precheck-$(hostname).txt 2>&1

This sample captures a useful subset of the checks. Add the port, THP, scheduler, and connectivity results required by your deployment process.

The record gives the team a baseline for troubleshooting, expansion, and future upgrades. When a new node joins the cluster, engineers can compare its environment against the existing configuration instead of repeating the investigation from scratch.

Final Thoughts

Reliable GBase Database deployment starts before the installer runs.

Check the OS, disk and inode capacity, ports, kernel settings, dependencies, and Python interpreter on every node. Validate the exact thresholds against your product version, and retain the results so the checks can be repeated later.

Ten minutes of structured verification can prevent hours of avoidable troubleshooting. More importantly, it turns pre-installation checks from an individual engineer's habit into a repeatable deployment process.

How does your team validate Linux prerequisites before deploying GBase Database(GBase 8a)? Do you run a standard pre-check script on every node, or verify the environment manually during installation?

title: DeepSeek overtakes Google on volume, cost per token falls 13.6%
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — August 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from May, June, and July.

August 2026 Summary

The August index reports on AI Gateway data collected through July 2026.

  • The average price paid per token fell 13.6% in July, after rising almost 20% in May and holding steady in June. Token consumption grew so quickly that even with 37% growth in spend, cost per token saw a double-digit drop.

  • DeepSeek became the second-largest lab by token volume, now running more than twice Google's volume.

  • Anthropic collected 65% of gateway spending on 30% of token volume, at 4.4 times the average price of every other lab's tokens.

  • Both media leaderboards changed hands. Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image volume from OpenAI's GPT Image, and ByteDance's Seedance led video in both volume and dollars.

Kimi K3 launched into agent work

Moonshot released Kimi K3 on July 16. Like Z.ai's GLM 5.2 released in June, it is built for long-horizon agent work, so its usage was heavy from the start at about twelve times the tokens per request of its predecessor, K2.5.

It scaled quickly. K3's daily volume tripled between launch week and the final week of July, and by month end its requests were as heavy as Claude Opus 4.8's. On the last full day of July it ranked eighth on the gateway by token volume.

The demand was new rather than diverted. K3 processed nearly two-thirds of all Kimi tokens within two weeks and 82% by the final week, while the rest of the family's volume fell only slightly.

Open weight's share of gateway spend more than doubled in July to 8.6%. More than 90% of that growth is Moonshot and Z.ai. Moonshot's share of total gateway spend quadrupled, to 2.3%. Cheap open-weight models have been taking volume for months without taking revenue. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are the first to capture significant volume at more than eleven times DeepSeek's rate per token.

DeepSeek is now second by volume

In June, this report said DeepSeek had entered the fight for token volume. Last month, we said an open-weight lab would soon be second by volume. In July, DeepSeek surpassed Google to take that place.

Google ran nearly 40% of the gateway’s token volume in April, and DeepSeek less than 1%. By July, DeepSeek ran a quarter, more than twice Google’s 11%. DeepSeek V4 Flash, its cheapest model, ran more tokens alone than all of Google.

The reversal is concentrated in consumer-facing work. Google's share of personal-assistant tokens fell by more than half in a month while DeepSeek's more than tripled, and most of the token share Google gave up went to DeepSeek. DeepSeek's V4 Flash ran more tokens than any other model on the gateway in July, nearly a fifth of the total and 70% more than the next model.

Open-weight models previously owned the cheap end of the market. Their share of gateway token volume nearly tripled between April and June, from 11% to 29%, while share of spend stayed under four cents of every gateway dollar.

In July, volume continued its growth trend, increasing to 36%. Spend broke its trend, more than doubling to nearly nine cents of every dollar, the highest in the index's history.

The four largest frontier labs' combined share of token spend, which had not fallen below 93% in seven months, fell to 89%. Google accounted for most of the decline. Almost none of the spend it lost went to DeepSeek, whose share barely moved even as its volume grew. Z.ai and Moonshot's latest models account for the entire open-weight spend increase.

Buyers sort models by what the task requires, then choose inside that tier according to price. DeepSeek and Opus were never competing. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K3, both released in the last two months, are the first open-weight models running a meaningful share of the workloads historically owned by closed-weight labs.

Average price per token fell 13.6%

Companies bought more inference in July and ran more of it on cheap models. Volume grew 59%, spend grew 37%, and the average price paid per token fell 13.6%.

Holding June's mix of models constant, the average price would have held essentially flat instead of declining. OpenAI is one example: the average cost of an OpenAI token fell to 58% of its June level, because 85% of the volume it added went to GPT-5-Nano, the cheapest model in the GPT-5 family.

The entire decline in average price came from what companies chose to route. Among the thousands of teams that ran more than 10 million tokens in both months, three in four changed at least a tenth of their model mix. Three in five changed at least a quarter.

The median team's cost per token fell 2.9%, but only one team in six stayed within five percent of where it started.

A quarter pared cost by more than 30%, typically teams that entered the month paying well above the gateway average per token. Another quarter paid at least 20% more, typically teams that had been paying below the average. Concurrently, the expensive end shifted down and the cheap end migrated up.

81% of July’s tokens ran on models that were not on the gateway six months ago. Open-weight models crossed a third of all volume, at about a seventh of frontier rates. Google fell from 24.0% of gateway token volume to 10.7%. Anthropic slipped two points to 29.8%, and OpenAI’s share rose to 12.8%.

Gateway spend is up 74% since May and volume has doubled, with July's token growth running at nearly double June's pace. Spend on inference continues to increase even as each dollar buys more tokens than it did in the previous month.

Anthropic's premium widened as prices fell

Anthropic has held more than 60% of gateway spend in every month we have measured, through a period in which open weight tripled its share of volume. In July, it collected 65.1% of all spend on 30% of total volume.

The average price per Anthropic token ran 4.4 times the average across every other lab, up from 3.4 in June. Part of that rise was Claude Fable 5, which returned on July 1 after a three-week export-control suspension and quickly grew to 13.2% of all gateway spend, second only to Opus 4.8. In coding agents, the gateway's largest use case by tokens, Anthropic collected more than 80% of spend.

Anthropic has no model at the bottom of the market. Haiku 4.5, its least expensive, runs just over two-thirds of the gateway average price per token. OpenAI's GPT-5-Nano runs a sixth; DeepSeek's V4 Flash a sixteenth.

Customers cutting costs on OpenAI or Google can stay in the catalog. Cutting costs on Anthropic means leaving Anthropic, and in July it still took a majority of all spending. Anthropic’s premium is the gap between what the cheap tier can do and what its customers need done.

Switching models on the AI Gateway is a one-line change, so nothing locks a customer in. When Fable 5 came back, daily volume returned to the pre-ban level almost exactly, but nine in ten of the teams running it in July had not used it before. The work returned; the customers were different.

The rest of the market's tokens averaged less than a quarter of Anthropic's price, and Anthropic still took two of every three dollars spent on the gateway. Price competition is happening, but it's happening in the part of the market with the least money in it.

Google took images, ByteDance took video

In June, OpenAI's GPT Image generated most of the gateway's images. In July, Google's Nano Banana led, at 45% of images to GPT Image's 42%, with spend split almost evenly between them. Nearly all of Nano Banana's gain came from one model, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Image. Google took the image lead in the same month it fell to fourth by token volume.

ByteDance's Seedance led video on both counts, in videos generated and dollars spent. xAI's Grok Imagine, June's volume leader, fell to second. Chinese labs collected about seven of every ten dollars spent on video.

Also in July’s data

  • Within coding, the gateway's largest workload by tokens, DeepSeek ran nearly a third of the volume and Anthropic collected more than four of every five dollars.

  • Back-office agents remain the most expensive work per token, with a share of spending roughly two and a half times their share of volume.

About this report

This analysis is based on anonymized, aggregate routing data from the Vercel AI Gateway through July 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Volume counts all tokens routed through AI Gateway.

  • Spend values every request at the lab's published list price.

  • Price per token is calculated as total spend divided by total volume.

  • Open-weight volume and spend shares count the four open-weight labs serving their own models at scale (DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot, and Z.ai).

  • Image and video figures count media generated, not requests or tokens.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: Healthtech Trust Boundaries: Choose Image Generation Model DALL-E 3 vs SDXL
description:
Short answer: choose DALL-E 3 when a support illustration must follow a detailed brief and render legible text, SDXL when the triage interface needs many previews, and Flux when the team wants a faster result without taking the weakest visual compromise. In a healthtech support application, however, the model is not the first boundary to draw. Redact the ticket, decide which processor may receive the resulting brief, then select the model whose quality and latency fit that approved path.

An incoming ticket can combine a device description with a patient name, appointment date, diagnosis, and conversation history. An image worker needs the first item and perhaps a few visual constraints. Forwarding the whole ticket is a data-handling decision disguised as an API call.

What must cross the image-generation boundary?

Start with a small, versioned image brief. It should contain the subject, intended audience, visual exclusions, and generation version. It should not become a second copy of the health record. The original ticket remains under the application's retention policy; the generated asset gets its own policy; the audit entry records the ticket identifier, redaction decision, selected model, request identifier, and outcome.

Four questions decide if a provider belongs in the path: which region receives the prompt, how long the provider retains the prompt and output, how deletion is requested and verified, and which processor is authorized for that data class. An image runtime can route a request. It cannot replace a data-processing agreement, a healthcare review, or an internal deletion owner.

This is the operational rule I would put in the worker: send synthetic or redacted content to a general image service, and keep identifiable or clinically sensitive material behind the specialist provider and contractual controls approved for it. If the system cannot name the region, retention period, and deletion owner for a path, that path is not ready for real ticket content.

It is a boundary, not a slogan.

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the portable, redacted part of this design because one REST API and one credential can keep the application contract stable while the provider behind the capability changes. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and available without a key, so an integration can inspect declared capabilities before wiring a worker. That convenience does not establish healthcare residency or retention terms; those remain questions for the selected processor.

The recommendation is specific: try Infrai for a redacted image-generation worker when provider portability is the main requirement and the application wants one interface across its backend, while retaining a specialist direct provider for tickets whose region, deletion, or contractual healthcare controls are decisive. Choose the specialist directly when those guarantees are stronger or more important than changing providers without rewriting the triage path.

How do I choose an image generation model for DALL-E 3 or SDXL?

Once the trust boundary is approved, compare the whole support interaction rather than a single latency figure. A fast draft that an agent rejects twice is not fast for the workflow. A premium result for a disposable preview creates the opposite waste.

Model Best fit for ticket triage Approximate latency Main trade-off
DALL-E 3 A finished illustration with precise wording or labels 2–5 seconds Highest cost per image
SDXL High-volume previews and user-generated support content 0.5–2 seconds Less capable prompt interpretation than DALL-E 3
Flux dev/schnell A stronger visual result under an interactive budget 0.3–1 second for schnell Variant and quality target still require validation

DALL-E 3 is the fidelity choice. It is the safer selection when the brief has several constraints or when text inside the image must be readable, such as a device-preparation handout for an agent to review before sending. OpenAI is the relevant direct ecosystem for that option, but the organization still has to verify the account's region, retention, deletion, and healthcare terms.

SDXL is the volume choice. It suits a triage screen that generates a draft for many tickets or offers several candidates before an operator commits to one. Stability AI's SDXL ecosystem is relevant for teams prepared to tune a high-throughput route and accept a weaker interpretation of complex prompts in exchange for a quicker, more economical exploratory path.

Flux is the middle choice. Black Forest Labs' Flux family is relevant when an agent needs a useful visual result quickly and the product cannot tolerate a poor preview. The schnell range is an approximate inference figure, not a promise for the complete user experience; queueing, network time, review, and regeneration belong in the application's measurement plan.

These are real alternatives, but their provider boundaries are not interchangeable. OpenAI, Stability AI, and Black Forest Labs may differ in regional availability, retention language, deletion procedures, and healthcare commitments. OpenRouter and Together AI are additional routing alternatives to investigate when portability matters, although their current image support and healthcare terms must be verified for the intended account. A routing layer can preserve the application's image contract while the provider changes. It cannot make unlike contractual boundaries equivalent.

The October 24, 2026 discovery snapshot records 295 routes across 20 modules, but that breadth is not a substitute for a provider review. Treat the model catalog, account region, and processor terms as separate checks.

Can the worker call the portable boundary safely?

The following minimal Go worker keeps the model decision outside the source code. It uses the documented base URL, an environment-provided key, an application-derived idempotency key, explicit POST, and bounded backoff for HTTP 429. The response body is printed only after a successful status; a provider error remains an error.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type generationRequest struct {
    Model  string `json:"model"`
    Prompt string `json:"prompt"`
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    model := os.Getenv("IMAGE_MODEL")
    if key == "" || model == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY and IMAGE_MODEL are required")
    }

    body, err := json.Marshal(generationRequest{
        Model:  model,
        Prompt: "A clear, non-diagnostic support illustration of preparing a replacement device",
    })
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/images/generations", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "ticket-123-image-v1")

        res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }

        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            wait := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(res.Header.Get("Retry-After")); parseErr == nil {
                wait = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(wait)
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("image generation returned %s: %s", res.Status, data))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(data))
        return
    }

    panic("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

Does portability solve the trust problem?

No. It solves one part of the integration problem.

The triage UI can request an image brief, a policy service can approve it, and a worker can select DALL-E 3, SDXL, or Flux without every consumer importing a vendor-specific SDK. The application still owns redaction, approval, retention, deletion, and auditability. Those responsibilities should be explicit in the data flow rather than hidden inside a model selector.

Infrai's second useful property here is the breadth of a common interface: its verified discovery inventory covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For a support backend that adds operational or storage capabilities around the image worker, that shared boundary can reduce adapter and credential-reconciliation work. It does not grant permission to send every ticket field to every capability, and it does not turn a general image service into a specialist healthcare processor.

The same discipline applies to outputs. Keep filenames opaque, avoid public-sharing assumptions, and record the provider request identifier beside the policy decision. A returned asset URL is an implementation detail until the application decides where the asset is stored, who can retrieve it, and when it is deleted.

How should the worker roll out safely?

Begin with synthetic tickets, then use redacted briefs whose fields are enforced by schema rather than assembled from the full support transcript. Record the approved region, retention period, deletion owner, model, generation version, and request identifier in the policy record. Run SDXL for a quick preview, Flux when the screen needs a stronger quality-speed balance, and DALL-E 3 for a finished result whose wording carries more weight.

The worker should treat generation as an external side effect. Retries need a stable application-derived idempotency key, rate-limit responses need exponential backoff that honors Retry-After, and non-success responses must remain visible instead of becoming empty “successful” assets. The exact-once mindset belongs in the consumer even when the surrounding queue can deliver a job more than once.

For each model, measure queue time, network time, review time, rejection rate, regeneration rate, and deletion completion in the approved environment. Promote a path only after the evidence covers the entire interaction, not just the model's reported inference range. The selection rule then becomes maintainable: DALL-E 3 for fidelity, SDXL for volume, Flux for the middle ground, and a specialist provider whenever the data boundary requires it.

If that boundary fits the system, start with the Infrai documentation and verify the current capability and provider terms before sending any ticket-derived content.

Sources

References used for the model and operational comparison:

  • Infrai official documentation
  • OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
  • MDN: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
  • OpenAI image generation documentation
  • Stability AI developer documentation
  • Black Forest Labs documentation

title: Solvent: Long-Horizon Reasoning for Multi-Step Retrosynthesis
description:
arXiv:2610.32308v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-step retrosynthesis requires recursively transforming a target molecule through successive reaction steps into purchasable building blocks, and recent work has begun to draw on large language model (LLM) reasoning to tackle the task. In its latest evolution, LLM reasoning has entered the long-horizon regime: models pursue objectives across interdependent steps, interact with environments, and adapt to feedback. This shift has markedly advanced LLM capabilities, as illustrated by breakthroughs in AI-driven mathematical research. At this frontier, we introduce Solvent, an 8B LLM that successfully extends long-horizon reasoning to multi-step retrosynthesis. Through a two-round post-training curriculum, Solvent learns to interleave iterative synthesis planning, external availability verification, and adaptive route revision. Experiments show that, following a $2.1\times$ performance boost from RL, Solvent scores 61.86% across four benchmarks, surpassing mid-scale language models and prior search-based retrosynthesis systems, and rivaling frontier trillion-parameter LLMs.

title: Python: A Powerful, Friendly, and Everywhere Programming Language
description:
Python is a general-purpose, high-level programming language known for its simple syntax, huge ecosystem, and use in web development, automation, data science, AI, and more. It was created by Guido van Rossum, with its first public release in 1991 and Python 1.0 arriving in 1994.

Why Python Is Popular

Python is often described as:

  • Powerful and fast to develop with — you can build useful programs with less code.
  • Friendly and easy to learn — its syntax is close to plain English.
  • Open — Python is open-source and free to use.
  • Cross-platform — the same Python code can usually run on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
  • A team player — Python integrates well with databases, web services, C/C++ libraries, and other tools.

Python is a high-level language, meaning it hides many low-level computer details such as memory management and processor instructions. This makes development easier, though it may be slower than languages such as C or C++ for some performance-critical tasks.

Where Python Is Used

  • Python is not limited to one type of application. It is widely used for:
  • Desktop applications — GUI tools using Tkinter, PyQt, or Kivy.
  • Web applications — backend services using Django, Flask, and FastAPI.
  • Database applications — connecting to MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, MongoDB, and other databases.
  • Network programming and scripting — automation, APIs, system administration, and network tools.
  • Data science, AI, and ML — data analysis, machine learning, deep learning, and prompt engineering workflows.
  • Automation — file handling, Excel automation, web scraping, testing, and task scheduling.

Python and Other Languages
Python “plays well with others” because it can connect with many technologies.

Implementation Works with Main idea
CPython C The standard/reference Python implementation; compiles Python to bytecode and runs it on a virtual machine. wikipedia
Cython C A Python superset that can compile Python-like code to C for better performance. wikipedia+1
Jython Java Runs Python on the Java platform. wiki.python
IronPython C# / .NET Runs Python on the .NET Common Language Runtime. wiki.python
PyPy Python An alternative implementation focused on faster execution. wiki.python

So, when people say “Python with C,” they often mean Cython or C extensions. “Python with Java” usually means Jython, and “Python with C#” means IronPython.

High-Level vs Low-Level Languages

A high-level language is easier for humans to read and write. Python, Java, and JavaScript are high-level languages.

A low-level language is closer to the hardware. It gives more control but is harder to write and maintain.

Feature High-level language Low-level language
Readability Easy Difficult
Hardware control Limited Strong
Development speed Fast Slower
Examples Python, Java Assembly, machine code

What Is Assembly Language?

Assembly language is a low-level language that uses short human-readable instructions such as MOV, ADD, and JMP. Each assembly instruction usually corresponds closely to a machine instruction.

Computers ultimately execute binary — sequences of 0s and 1s. Assembly is a step above binary because it uses readable names instead of raw numeric machine code.

Microprocessor vs Microservices

These terms sound similar but are completely different.

Term Meaning
Microprocessor A hardware chip that acts as the CPU of a computer or device.
Microservices A software architecture where an application is split into small, independent services.

For example, an e-commerce app may have separate microservices for users, payments, orders, and notifications. Each service can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently.

Python 2 vs Python 3

Python 2 and Python 3 are different major versions of Python. Python 3.0 was released on December 3, 2008, and was intentionally not fully backward-compatible with Python 2.x.

Key differences include:

  • Python 3 uses print() as a function: print("Hello").
  • Python 3 handles Unicode text more naturally.
  • Integer division behaves differently: in Python 3, 5 / 2 gives 2.5.
  • Python 2 reached end of life on January 1, 2020

For any new project, use Python 3.

Python History and Major Releases

Version Release year Importance
Python 0.9.0 1991 First public release. developer.ibm
Python 1.0 1994 First major stable release. cvw.cac.cornell
Python 2.0 2000 Added major improvements such as list comprehensions and Unicode support. wikipedia
Python 3.0 2008 Major redesign; not fully compatible with Python 2. python
Python 2.7 2010 Final Python 2 release line; support ended in 2020. devguide.python

Python development began in December 1989, and the language has continued to evolve through regular Python 3 releases.

Interpreter and Compiler

Python is commonly called an interpreted language, but this is slightly simplified.

Compiler: Converts the entire source code into machine code or another lower-level form before execution.

Interpreter: Reads and executes code step by step.

CPython first compiles Python source code into bytecode, then executes that bytecode using the Python virtual machine. So Python uses both compilation and interpretation internally.

Backward Compatibility
Backward compatibility means that newer software can still run code written for an older version.

Python 3 was not fully backward-compatible with Python 2, which is why many older programs needed changes when moving from Python 2 to Python 3. However, within the Python 3.x series, most newer versions aim to remain compatible with earlier Python 3 code, with only occasional small changes.

Standalone and Task-Based Applications

A standalone application is a program that runs on a user’s device without needing a web browser. Python can create standalone desktop tools using GUI libraries and packaging tools such as PyInstaller.

A task-based application focuses on doing one specific job well, such as:

  • Automating Excel reports
  • Sending email notifications
  • Backing up files
  • Scraping product prices
  • Processing images
  • Running a machine-learning prediction

title: Node.js Commerce Watch Parties: Host Authority With Durable Notification Recovery
description:
A single authoritative host is the practical default for a Node.js commerce watch party. Let that host publish playback position and timed product-drop events; let viewers follow rather than vote. Peer consensus survives host loss more elegantly, but it adds election, split-brain, ordering, and reconciliation work to a feature whose honest promise is approximate synchronization.

Short answer: choose host authority, make departure a named state transition, and keep notifications for offline shoppers in a durable queue or outbox. The socket is delivery, not storage. Tell viewers that playback may drift instead of implying frame-perfect sync.

Infrai fits one specific part of this design: a small team can put the durable queue and realtime publish contract behind the same API key, then inspect both contracts through public discovery before writing the worker. It does not decide playback authority for the application.

This experiment is constrained by delivery guarantees at fan-out, not by the prettiest SDK. A product reveal sent to 8,000 viewers has two different obligations: connected viewers should see it quickly, while disconnected viewers must not lose it. Treating one transient publish as both obligations is the simple design that fails.

Two obligations. Two mechanisms.

Should a watch party use an authoritative host or peer consensus for playback?

Consensus sounds fair because no participant is special. It also forces the application to answer questions that host authority deletes: Which clock wins? How many peers form a quorum after a mobile network split? Can a late tab overturn a newer seek? What happens when two partitions each elect a leader? WebRTC defines browser real-time communication primitives; it does not supply the application-level consensus protocol for a watch party.

One source removes almost all of that machinery. The host emits a monotonically increasing event sequence with its media position and a server timestamp. A viewer applies only a newer sequence. Product notifications refer to that same sequence, so a "buy now" prompt cannot legitimately precede the scene that introduces it.

The trade-off is blunt. If the host disappears, authority disappears too. Handle that event explicitly: pause authoritative product-drop publication, appoint a replacement under a documented policy, then resume from the last accepted sequence. Do not quietly turn every viewer into an authority.

Perfect synchronization is unavailable. Say that in the interface. "Synced to host" and "Reconnecting" are defensible states; a promise that every display is on the same frame is not.

That wording matters.

The fan-out boundary decides the real operating bill

The useful cost model starts with workload shape: concurrent viewers, events per minute, reconnect frequency, offline duration, retained notifications, and duplicate-processing rate. Vendor unit prices are only one input. Engineering time spent joining identity, retry semantics, credentials, logs, and invoices belongs in the bill too. So does downstream damage from showing a product prompt twice or dropping it entirely.

Count the glue.

For online delivery, a realtime channel is enough. For an absent shopper, the notification must become a durable message before the live publish is attempted. A worker can later deliver it in order, and its consumer must be idempotent because standard queues are at-least-once. Use a stable event ID such as drop_1042, store the last applied playback sequence per viewer, and make duplicate receipt a no-op.

This is where Infrai is an interesting fit, rather than an automatic winner. Its public discovery surface describes each capability with request and response JSON Schema, billing information, and runnable examples, so evaluating a new operation is one discovery read instead of an SDK adoption. The same key covers realtime and queue capabilities; that can reduce credential and invoice glue around the online/offline handoff. The platform reports 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth is less important here than a consistent contract at this exact boundary.

I would try Infrai for a small team that needs realtime fan-out plus durable offline notification handling under one credential, because the self-describing contract reduces integration work at the boundary where messages are commonly lost. The supporting advantage is operational: one key and one bill replace separate credential rotation and reconciliation for these two capabilities. The cost is concentration. One vendor becomes one trust boundary, one bill, and one shared dependency.

A focused Node.js contract check

Do not guess a queue or publish payload from a product description. The discovery response supplies the method, path, full request JSON Schema, response schema, billing data, and runnable examples. This TypeScript program fetches that contract, selects the two capabilities at the handoff, and prints their actual paths and examples before any integration code is written.

type Capability = {
  id: string;
  module: string;
  method: string;
  path: string;
  available: boolean;
  idempotent?: boolean;
  params?: unknown;
  examples?: unknown;
};

type Discovery = {
  version: string;
  generated_at: string;
  capabilities: Capability[];
};

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;

if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

async function loadContracts(): Promise<void> {
  const response = await fetch("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", {
    method: "GET",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}`,
    },
  });

  if (response.status === 429) {
    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter) ? retryAfter * 1_000 : 1_000;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
    return loadContracts();
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    const reason = await response.text();
    throw new Error(`Discovery failed (${response.status}): ${reason}`);
  }

  const discovery = (await response.json()) as Discovery;
  const selected = discovery.capabilities.filter(
    (capability) =>
      capability.path === "/v1/realtime/publish" ||
      capability.module === "queue",
  );

  if (!selected.some((capability) => capability.path === "/v1/realtime/publish")) {
    throw new Error("Realtime publish contract was not discovered");
  }

  console.log(JSON.stringify(selected, null, 2));
}

await loadContracts();

Discovery is public and does not require a key; the sample still supplies the same INFRAI_API_KEY that the subsequent queue and publish calls use as Authorization: Bearer <key>. Write retries use a stable Idempotency-Key. Select paths from the returned path fields and start from the runnable TypeScript examples. That keeps the code tied to the live schema instead of a hand-written route guess.

The handoff itself has one invariant: durable acceptance happens before realtime publication. A production worker acknowledges its queue message only after publication succeeds, while each client records eventId and playbackSequence before rendering. Those checks cover different duplicates: redelivery at the worker and replay or reconnect at the viewer.

How do the real alternatives differ?

Pusher Channels is a focused hosted pub/sub choice. Pairing it with Amazon SQS gives a familiar division between online fan-out and durable work, but it requires two signups, two credential sets, two billing relationships, and glue that maps an SQS message to a Pusher event. That separation can be desirable when independent vendor boundaries matter more than integration overhead.

Ably also specializes in realtime messaging and documents channel behavior. It is a sound direction when the realtime layer needs a specialist and the team accepts a separate queue or outbox contract for offline business notifications. LiveKit is centered on realtime media and data in rooms; it deserves a close look when audio/video transport, participants, and room control dominate the project, though the application must still decide who controls playback and where absent-user notifications persist. Socket.IO is different again: it is a library and protocol you can operate within your Node.js system. It offers control and avoids handing the whole realtime tier to a hosted service, in exchange for owning deployment, scaling, presence behavior, and the durable-message connection yourself. These are meaningful differences, not logo choices: the first decision is whether the team wants an integrated API, a realtime specialist joined to a queue, a media-room platform, or infrastructure it operates directly.

Pick the ownership model first.

Stack Best fit Delivery boundary to own Operational trade-off
Infrai realtime plus queue capabilities Small team minimizing integration surfaces Idempotent worker-to-publish handoff One credential and contract; one shared vendor dependency
Pusher Channels plus Amazon SQS Teams preferring specialized services SQS consumer, Pusher publisher, and identity mapping Two signups, credential sets, bills, and explicit glue
Ably plus a durable queue Realtime behavior needs a specialist platform Queue retention and replay into channels Separate offline-message lifecycle
LiveKit plus an outbox Media rooms are the center of the product Room data versus durable commerce events Media-oriented system plus a persistence layer
Socket.IO plus a queue Teams that want infrastructure control Scaling, presence, replay, and persistence More operations owned by the application team

No row wins in the abstract. The smallest credible design depends on what failure you are willing to own. For an indie product, host authority plus an explicit durable handoff is usually tractable. For a team already operating AWS, the separate Pusher-and-SQS shape may justify its extra glue. For a media-heavy experience, LiveKit can be the better center of gravity. A team willing to run its own realtime infrastructure may prefer Socket.IO.

What should you measure before copying this design?

Measure the workload, not a demo. Record connected viewers per party, publish attempts per event, 429 retries, reconnects, duplicate deliveries rejected, queue age at successful fan-out, and the interval between host departure and restored authority. Track the percentage of product notifications that reach an online client and the percentage later recovered for an offline client as separate numbers. Mixing them hides the precise failure this architecture is meant to prevent.

Also test ugly state transitions: the host closes a laptop during a product drop; replacement authority starts while an older event is in flight; a viewer reconnects with a stale sequence; the worker stops after publish but before acknowledgement. Each test needs an observable expected state. None requires peer consensus if the authority rule and idempotency contract are explicit.

The nastiest sequence is longer. The queue accepts drop_1042; the worker publishes it; the host leaves before the worker acknowledges; a replacement resumes from playback sequence 381; then the worker receives the same queue item again. The correct result is still one visible prompt. The worker reuses the stable idempotency key, the viewer rejects an already-recorded event ID, and the replacement host cannot move playback backward because clients reject an older sequence. This is why delivery guarantees at fan-out need several small contracts rather than one vague claim of reliability.

Keep the promise modest. A watch party can coordinate playback and product prompts without claiming perfect sync. Host authority keeps the steady state understandable; durable notification storage protects the shopper who was absent; a deliberate succession policy covers the one failure authority introduces.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the discovery schema and runnable example for each capability before wiring it into the worker.

References

  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Amazon SQS developer guide
  • Ably documentation
  • LiveKit documentation
  • Socket.IO documentation
  • Infrai official documentation
