title: We cut our scanner binary by 68% — and removing packages one by one wasn't how
description:
Finding unmaintained dependencies is the easy part. Removing them is where it gets hard.

This is the story of how we slimmed down vuls, the open-source vulnerability scanner I created — what didn't work, what did, and the tooling we built after doing it all by hand.

The easy win: 15 minutes

mitchellh/go-homedir has been archived for years. Vuls used it in a couple of lines in two source files:

- import "github.com/mitchellh/go-homedir"
- dir, err := homedir.Dir()
+ dir, err := os.UserHomeDir()

Fifteen minutes, start to finish. The standard library has done this since Go 1.12.

Trivy used the same package, so we sent them a similar fix. The Trivy maintainers reviewed and merged it within three weeks.

We felt good. Let's keep going.

The part where almost nothing happened

We kept going. Over two weeks we replaced 9 direct dependencies with standard-library code or a few lines of our own. go.mod went from 60 direct dependencies to 51.

Then we looked at what had actually left the build. go.sum went from 1,220 lines to about 1,210. Only 5 modules disappeared completely. Most of the packages we had stopped calling were still required by other modules, so they stayed in the dependency list anyway.

Adding a dependency takes one line. Removing one can take real work and barely change what you ship.

Just like a real diet.

What worked: removing a whole layer

So we stopped picking off packages one by one and looked at which layer they came in through.

Vuls uses Trivy's parsers to read lockfiles (package-lock.json, go.mod, Cargo.lock, and so on). We called them through fanal, Trivy's analysis framework. fanal is built for everything Trivy scans — container images, disk images, filesystems, infrastructure-as-code. That breadth is exactly what Trivy needs. Our scanner only needed the part that reads lockfiles, but the way we had wired fanal in registered 25+ analyzers through blank imports, and with them the infrastructure-as-code and misconfiguration packages that Trivy needs and we never called.

We changed Vuls to call Trivy's lockfile parsers directly. Much less code compiled in, and — as we checked below — the same results on almost every project we tested. (Vuls still depends on Trivy — we use its parsers, just not through fanal.)

The result (vuls PR #2476):

Metric Before After Change
Scanner binary 106.6 MB 34.1 MB -68%
Scanner build time 7.8 s 3.2 s -59%

How we measured: scanner-only builds (-tags scanner) with our release build settings, CGO_ENABLED=0 GOEXPERIMENT=jsonv2 go build -a -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w". The build times are with a warm build cache.

To be precise about what shrank: this is the scanner binary. The full vuls binary, which also includes the vulnerability detection and reporting code, went from 139.1 MB to 138.5 MB after this change and a follow-up one. That code still uses Trivy's vulnerability database layer, so most of the weight stays.


Packages in the scanner build counted with go list -tags scanner -deps ./cmd/scanner before and after PR #2476.

Don't pick leaves one by one. Find the branch they hang from.

How we tested it

The change rewrote how the whole scanner package reads lockfiles. Here's how we checked it.

Layer 1: Golden tests. JSON output for 35 lockfile types, compared for an exact match.

Layer 2: A/B comparison on real projects. We collected real lockfiles from 129 open-source projects across 13 ecosystems. Then:

old code + lockfile → result A
new code + lockfile → result B
diff(A, B)

No mocks. No hand-written expected values. Just: "does the new code produce the same results as the old code?"

127 of 129 were identical. The other 2 differed only in the pnpm dev flag, which our old wrapper code had been losing along the way. Calling Trivy's pnpm parser directly gave us the parser's correct output.

Building the comparison set taught us something too. On the first pass, many fixtures produced zero packages — requirements.txt files with no pinned versions, a nearly empty yarn.lock, a root pom.xml with only <modules>. "Identical" on an empty result proves nothing, so we replaced those fixtures with ones that actually exercised the parsers.

This lives in vuls as make compare-lockfile. It didn't catch everything: code review and testing on Windows still found a case the comparison had missed (.exe files weren't detected as executables), which we fixed before merging.

The tool we built afterwards: uzomuzo diet

We did all of the above by hand, in March 2026. Looking back, the expensive part wasn't writing code. It was deciding where to start — and our first choice was wrong.

So in April we added a diet command to uzomuzo, our dependency lifecycle scanner. It ranks your direct dependencies as candidates for removal:

  1. Dependency graph — from a CycloneDX SBOM: what would disappear along with each direct dependency?
  2. Source coupling — tree-sitter reads your code: how many files import it, how many call sites?
  3. Health — maintenance status (Active, Stalled, Archived, ...), from the same signals uzomuzo scan uses
  4. Score — high impact, high risk, and easy to remove rises to the top

scan and diet are rule-based. No LLM is involved. Their results reflect the dependency and maintenance data available when you run them.

One caveat up front: diet is experimental. An audit against hand-checked expected values found cases where a dependency that is in use is reported as unused or trivial — for example when it's imported from a skipped directory or in an import style the analyzer doesn't recognize yet. The CLI prints a notice saying so after every run, and the Accuracy section of the docs lists what to check. Treat its output as a list of places to look, not a list of things to delete.

Here's an excerpt from a run on Terraform (commit 9ec49e0, October 13, 2026; SBOM generated with cyclonedx-gomod; run on October 26, 2026):

$ uzomuzo diet --sbom terraform-bom.json --source ./terraform

RANK  SCORE  EFFORT    PURL                          REMOVES  IMPORTS  CALLS  STATUS
3     0.13   trivial   github.com/mitchellh/gox            1        1      1  Archived
5     0.10   hard      github.com/mitchellh/colorstring    0       22     79  Archived
6     0.10   moderate  github.com/mitchellh/go-homedir     0        9     11  Archived
 ...
72    0.00   hard      github.com/hashicorp/hcl/v2         0      352   6764  Active

(Edited for width: four of the 77 direct dependencies, PURLs shortened to module paths, and the REMAINS column omitted. Ranks 1, 2 and 4 are not shown: 1 and 4 are Terraform's own nested internal/backend/remote-state/* modules, which the SBOM lists as direct dependencies, and 2 is an active OpenTelemetry package. The full run also reported zero "quick wins".)

The ranking is a starting point for investigation, not a verdict:

  • gox is archived and has one import and one call site, so it gets a trivial effort label. That's exactly the kind of label to verify: check that one call site, what it does, and what replaces it.
  • go-homedir is the same package we removed from vuls in 15 minutes. Here it's imported in 9 files, so it's rated moderate. Removing the direct use wouldn't drop it from Terraform's dependency list either — another module still requires it.
  • hcl/v2 is at rank 72: 352 importing files, 6,764 call sites, and actively maintained. Don't start here.

It works for Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Java.

The last mile: Claude Code skills

Ranking is automated. Actually removing a dependency — tracing what data flows through it, writing the replacement, getting the change accepted — still takes judgment. uzomuzo ships three Claude Code skills for that part:

/diet-assess-risk (how risky is it to keep?), /diet-evaluate-removal (is it worth the effort?), and /diet-remove (draft the change or the upstream report). They use an LLM, so review what they propose before you use it.

The rules in /diet-remove come from our own mistakes. When we found that Next.js still depended on @vercel/kv, which Vercel has deprecated on npm in favor of Upstash Redis, we tried three channels by hand:

  • PR → we closed it ourselves after CI failed. It's a large pnpm-workspaces monorepo, and we couldn't reproduce its CI locally.
  • Issue → the repository's bot closed it within seconds, pointing to the bug report template. The issue tracker is for bugs with a reproduction, and ours wasn't one.
  • Discussion → the channel the repository's templates point to. It's still open with no reply yet.

So the skill now defaults to drafting an issue rather than a PR for projects you don't own, checks whether the repository accepts blank issues, and falls back to a Discussion when it doesn't. Those rules are written from that manual experience; we haven't yet published an end-to-end run of the skill itself. And getting the channel right doesn't guarantee a response. Of our four upstream reports in April, two have been fixed and two are still waiting. Whether to fix something is the maintainers' call.

Start your diet 

go install github.com/future-architect/uzomuzo-oss/cmd/uzomuzo@latest
CGO_ENABLED=1 go install github.com/future-architect/uzomuzo-oss/cmd/uzomuzo-diet@latest   # needs a C compiler
export GITHUB_TOKEN=...   # read-only is enough; gives uzomuzo repository signals such as archived status

The output in this post was produced with v0.10.0.

  1. Run uzomuzo scan --file go.mod (or pipe in an SBOM for other ecosystems). See what's unmaintained.
  2. Generate a CycloneDX SBOM — for example trivy fs . --format cyclonedx -o bom.json, or for Go, cyclonedx-gomod mod -json -output bom.json — and run uzomuzo diet --sbom bom.json --source ..
  3. Pick a dependency whose use and replacement you understand. Remove it, then measure: binary size, dependency list, build time. If nothing moved, look for the layer it came in through.

And don't give up on your diet.

Earlier posts: "Your dependencies are 48% unmaintained — and SCA tools can't see it" and "Your CI runs other people's code. Is anyone still maintaining it?"

Source and docs: github.com/future-architect/uzomuzo-oss (Apache 2.0)

Kota Kanbe — Creator of vuls, an open-source vulnerability scanner.

title: RVG-Bench: A Benchmark for Reasoning-Driven Audio-Visual Temporal Grounding
description:
arXiv:2610.32268v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Existing temporal video grounding (TVG) benchmarks primarily focus on localizing target video segments according to descriptive text queries of the visual content. However, real-world queries are more diverse and often require the model to first understand the user's intent before localization, such as finding visual evidence, identifying the cause of an event, or recalling a remembered moment, yet such queries remain largely overlooked. To mitigate this gap, we introduce RVG-Bench, a benchmark for reasoning-driven audio-visual temporal grounding, where every query is constructed such that the target segment can only be identified through reasoning about the query's underlying intent. We carefully construct the benchmark and rigorously verify its data quality to ensure models truly comprehend the audio-visual content. RVG-Bench comprises 1,255 videos and 1,890 query-interval pairs across eight reasoning types. We evaluate 22 models and find that the strongest, Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash, achieves only 49.6 mIoU. Through a series of controlled analyses, including oracle-grounding probes and test-time scaling experiments, we systematically examine where and why current models struggle, providing insights for future model development.

title: Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
description: This post announces native PyTorch backends for vLLM and SGLang powered by TorchTPU, enabling developers to run and optimize serving workloads using familiar PyTorch tools. Built in collaboration with open-source project maintainers, these engines include optimized TPU kernel implementations, production-ready features like KV cache management with TPU Sync, and disaggregated serving. Public benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and industry-leading cost efficiency on Ironwood TPU across long-context and agentic workloads.

title: Exploring JEST React Testing Library: A Complete Overview
description:
Welcome to the comprehensive guide on mastering JEST React Testing Library! In this tutorial, we will explore the ins and outs of the JEST React Testing Library, a powerful tool for testing React components. Whether you are a beginner or an experienced developer looking to enhance your testing skills, this guide will equip you with the knowledge and techniques to write effective tests using JEST React Testing Library.

What is JEST?

JEST is a JavaScript testing framework that enables developers to write tests for JavaScript and React applications. It offers features like test runners, assertions, mocks, and code coverage analysis. JEST simplifies the process of writing and running tests, making it a popular choice for testing React applications.

Official Documentation:

  • JEST Official Documentation

  • JEST React Testing Library

Prerequisites:

Before exploring the JEST React Testing Library, ensure that you have the following prerequisites:

  1. Basic knowledge of React.
  2. Node.js and npm are installed on your machine.
  3. React project setup.

Now, let’s get started with JEST React Testing Library!

Getting Started:

Step 1. Install JEST and React Testing Library:

Open your terminal and navigate to the main directory of your project. Then, execute the following command:

npm install –save-dev jest

Step 2. Implementing the Button component:

Create a new file named “Button.js” in the src directory and paste the following code:

import React from "react";
const Button = ({ label }) => {
  return <button>{label}</button>;
};
export default Button;

The Button component is functional and renders a button with a provided label prop.

Step 3. Writing your first test:

Create a new file named “Button.test.js” in the src directory and paste the following code:

import React from "react";
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import Button from "./Button";
test("renders button correctly", () => {
  render(<Button label="Click me" />);
  const buttonElement = screen.getByText(/click me/i);
  expect(buttonElement).toBeInTheDocument();
});

In this example, we import and used the necessary functions from @testing-library/react to render our component and interact with the rendered output, so let’s explore the purpose of those functions:

  • Render: This function is provided by React Testing Library and is used to render React components for testing purposes.

  • Screen: The screen object provides utilities to access and interact with the rendered components. Functions like getByText, getByRole, and more can be used to search for specific elements within the rendered component.

  • Expect: This is an assertion function provided by JEST. It allows us to make assertions about the behavior of our code and the rendered components.

  • toBeInTheDocument: This is a matcher provided by JEST that checks if an element is present in the document.

  • Then we render the Button component with a specific label and use the screen.getByText method to find the button element by its text content.

Step 4. Running the test:

Open your terminal and navigate to the main directory of your project. Then, execute the following command:

npm test

JEST will run the tests, and you will observe the test results in the terminal.

Screenshot of successful test execution:

  • Understanding describe(), test() and it():

  1. describe(): describe() is used to group related test cases together. It creates a test suite or category of tests, allowing you to organize and structure your tests.

  2. test() and it(): Both test() and it() are used to define individual test cases. They take a description of what the test is doing and a function where you write the test logic.

These functions help organize and structure your tests, making them more readable and maintainable. They provide a way to group related tests and clearly define the purpose of each individual test case.

Search Variants and Types:

  1. Search Variants: Search Variants in JEST React Testing Library are methods to find elements in the rendered output based on specific.
  • getBy(): Finds a single element that matches the query. In case no element is found, it will raise an error. 
const buttonElement = <button>Click Me</button>;
test("To test getBy search variant", () => {
  render(buttonElement);
  const foundButton = screen.getByRole("button");
  expect(foundButton).toBeInTheDocument();
});
  • getAllBy(): Finds multiple elements that match the query. In case no element is found, it will raise an error. 
const linkElements = (
  <div>
    <a href="#">Link 1</a>
    <a href="#">Link 2</a>
    <a href="#">Link 3</a>
  </div>
);
test("To test getAllBy search variant", () => {
  render(linkElements);
  const foundLinks = screen.getAllByRole("link");
  expect(foundLinks.length).toBe(3);
});
  •  queryBy(): Finds a single element that matches the query. Returns **null** if no element is found. 
const headingElement = <h1>Hello, world!</h1>;
test("To test queryBy search variant", () => {
  render(headingElement);
  const foundHeading = screen.queryByText(/hello/i);
  expect(foundHeading).not.toBeNull();
});
  • queryAllBy(): Finds multiple elements that match the query. When no elements are found, it returns an empty array. 
const inputElements = (
  <div>
    <input type="text" />
    <input type="text" />
    <input type="text" />
  </div>
);
test("To test queryAllBy search variant", () => {
  render(inputElements);
  const foundInputs = screen.queryAllByRole("textbox");
  expect(foundInputs.length).not.toBe(0);
});
  •  findBy(): Finds a single element asynchronously that matches the query. Resolves the promise with the element when found. 
async function fetchData() {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    setTimeout(() => resolve(<div>Data Loaded</div>), 1000);
  });
}
const asyncElement = fetchData();
test("To test findBy search variant", async () => {
  render(await asyncElement);
  const foundElement = await screen.findByText(/data loaded/i);
  expect(foundElement).toBeInTheDocument();
});
  •  findAllBy(): Finds multiple elements asynchronously that match the query. Resolves the promise with an array of elements when found. 
async function fetchDatas() {
  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    setTimeout(
      () =>
        resolve(
          <ul>
            <li>Item 1</li>
            <li>Item 2</li>
            <li>Item 3</li>
          </ul>,
        ),
      1000,
    );
  });
}
const asyncElements = fetchDatas();
test("To test findAllBy search variant", async () => {
  render(await asyncElements);
  const foundElements = await screen.findAllByRole("listitem");
  expect(foundElements.length).toBe(3);
});
  1. Search Types: Search Types are used in conjunction with the search variants to target specific attributes of elements for querying.
  • ByRole: Matches elements by their role attribute, such as button, link, textbox, listitem, etc. 
const buttonElement1 = <button>Click Me</button>;
test("To test ByRole search type", () => {
  render(buttonElement1);
  const foundButton = screen.getByRole("button");
  expect(foundButton).toBeInTheDocument();
});
  • ByText: Matches elements based on their visible text content. 
const headingElement1 = <h1>Hello, world!</h1>;
test("To test ByText search type", () => {
  render(headingElement1);
  const foundHeading = screen.getByText(/hello/i);
  expect(foundHeading).not.toBeNull();
});
  • ByLabelText: Matches elements based on their associated label text. 
const usernameInput = (
 <div>
 <label htmlFor="username">Username</label>
 <input type="text" id="username" />
 </div>
);
test("To test ByLabelText search type", () => {
 render(usernameInput);
 const foundInput = screen.getByLabelText(/username/i);
 expect(foundInput).toBeInTheDocument();
});
  •  ByPlaceholderText: Matches elements based on their placeholder text. 
const searchInput = <input type="text" placeholder="Search" />;
test("To test ByPlaceholderText search type", () => {
 render(searchInput);
 const foundInput = screen.getByPlaceholderText(/search/i);
 expect(foundInput).toBeInTheDocument();
});
  •  ByDisplayValue: Matches form elements based on their displayed value. 
const checkboxElement = (
 <input type="checkbox" checked={true} value={"checked"} />
);
test("To test ByDisplayValue search type", () => {
 render(checkboxElement);
 const foundCheckbox = screen.getByDisplayValue("checked");
 expect(foundCheckbox).toBeInTheDocument();
});
  • ByAltText: Matches elements based on their alt attribute value. 
const imageElement = <img src="logo.png" alt="Logo" />;
test("To test ByAltText search type", () => {
 render(imageElement);
 const foundImage = screen.getByAltText("Logo");
  expect(foundImage).toBeInTheDocument();
});
  • ByTitle: Matches elements based on their title attribute value. 
const tooltipElement = <div title="Tooltip">Hover me</div>;
test("To test ByTitle search type", () => {
 render(tooltipElement);
 const foundElement = screen.getByTitle("Tooltip");
 expect(foundElement).toBeInTheDocument();
});
  • ByTestId: Matches elements based on their data-testid attribute value. 
const elementWithTestId = <div data-testid="my-element">Element</div>;
test("To test ByTestId search type", () => {
 render(elementWithTestId);
 const foundElement = screen.getByTestId("my-element");
 expect(foundElement).toBeInTheDocument();
});

These examples demonstrate how to use JEST React Testing Library search variants and types with both React components and test cases. These combinations allow you to precisely query elements and assert their presence or absence based on specific criteria.

  • JEST Debugging Functions and Methods: JEST React Testing Library offers debugging functions like screen.debug() and screen.logTestingPlaygroundURL() for effective troubleshooting and inspection of tests.
  1. screen.debug(): This function logs the current state of the rendered output to the console. It helps inspect the rendered HTML structure and component properties during test execution. 
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import DebuggingFunctions from "./DebuggingFunctions";
test("To debug the DebuggingFunctions component using debug() function", () => {
 render(<DebuggingFunctions />);
 screen.logTestingPlaygroundURL();
});

When you run this test case and call screen.debug(), it will output the rendered component structure and its attributes in the console:

  1. screen.logTestingPlaygroundURL(): This function logs a URL to the console that can be opened in a browser. It allows you to view and interact with the rendered output in the Testing Playground. 
import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import DebuggingFunctions from "./DebuggingFunctions";
test("To debug the DebuggingFunctions component using logTestingPlaygroundURL() function", () => {
 render(<DebuggingFunctions />);
 screen.logTestingPlaygroundURL();
});

Testing Playground:

The Testing Playground is a web-based tool that provides an interactive environment for debugging and exploring your React components. It allows you to inspect the component hierarchy, modify props, and test different scenarios. You can export logs and share the testing playground URL with others for collaborative debugging.

Conclusion:

This detailed guide has covered the fundamentals of the JEST React Testing Library. We learned how to write tests, simulate user interactions, and use various methods to find elements. Additionally, we explored debugging functions. Now, you have the knowledge to create solid and reliable tests for your React components.

title: TGR-EvoDAG: A DAG-based Multi-Agent Code Evolution Framework for Generative Recommendation on Tencent
description:
arXiv:2610.32326v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have enabled automated code evolution for algorithm discovery. However, current recursive self-improvement (RSI) research for sequential recommendation faces a dilemma: general-purpose frameworks lack domain-specific feedback, while recommender-specific frameworks rely on linear evolution. Crucially, naively integrating them fails when applied to Generative Recommendation (GR). Unlike end-to-end models, GR relies on a module-cascaded pipeline (tokenization, pre-training, and alignment). In this paradigm, existing evolution methods suffer from: i) cost blindness, squandering budgets by ignoring stage-asymmetric retraining overheads; and ii) short-sighted evaluation, discarding promising upstream innovations that temporarily regress metrics before downstream adaptation. To bridge these gaps, we propose TGR-EvoDAG, a multi-agent code evolution framework tailored for GR. TGR-EvoDAG models code evolution as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to maintain multiple evolution branches and merge complementary innovations, unifying advanced search with rich GR diagnostic feedback. We further introduce stage-aware cost planning to optimize GPU-hour budgets, and active downstream co-adaptation to navigate temporary regressions and unlock cross-stage gains. On public Amazon datasets, TGR-EvoDAG enables the first autonomous evolution of a complete GR pipeline, improving offline metrics by up to 37.4% and Agent4Rec simulated user satisfaction by 19.7% over the strongest baseline. Furthermore, in industrial deployment on Tencent's large-scale commercial media platform, the evolved GR achieves a 12.16% relative improvement in offline Hit@1 and a statistically significant 0.40% increase in online click-through rate (CTR).

title: TileShare: Training-Free Acceleration of Overlapping Tiled ViT Decoding
description:
arXiv:2610.32233v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fixed-window Vision Transformer (ViT) decoders run at deployment resolution as overlapping tiles: every token in an overlap band is processed by several full decoder instances. In the 2.4B-parameter MiniMax-H3 video decoder, about half of all per-token computation is duplicated. Removing the tiles fails because attention, global tokens and coordinates are bound to them. TileShare keeps each released tile's attention and computes every other operation once per token. The released computation changes at one kind of step only: an overlap token's per-tile results are blended into one shared state with the released weights. Interventions show that this blend costs quality where attention reads the shared states, mainly in the first few layers, which TileShare therefore keeps per tile. Without training, keeping six layers per tile decodes 1.38-1.51x faster than batched and compiled tiling on two GPU types (up to 1.96x with FP8) and is equivalent to the released decoder in PSNR, LPIPS and DISTS on DAVIS videos. On unseen UVG videos with the setting frozen beforehand, it matches PSNR and DISTS and improves LPIPS. TileShare carries over to two further decoders and is again confirmed on unseen data. It is equivalent in PSNR and DISTS on MAGI-1. On the ViTok-v2 image autoencoder at 2K-4K, it matches overlapping tiling in PSNR, improves LPIPS and DISTS and decodes 1.5-1.8x faster. How many layers stay per tile is measured once per model (for decoders, without labels); we report it for 14 decoders and encoders. Optionally, two GPU-hours of self-distillation let MiniMax-H3 share every layer without a loss in PSNR, and a coordinate field trained while the network stays frozen brings fully shared CLIP-based open-vocabulary segmentation to parity with sliding windows on seven benchmarks.

title: SWE-Shift: Evaluating Coding Agents in Evolving Workspaces
description:
arXiv:2610.32196v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Repository-level coding benchmarks largely assume that tasks and environments remain unchanged throughout execution. In software development, code, dependencies, runtime state, and requirements can change while an agent is still working. We introduce SWE-Shift, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under such mid-execution changes. From the same saved history and workspace, a Clean continuation proceeds without intervention, while a matched Shifted continuation receives a task-relevant update. Success requires completing the current task, preserving still-valid work, and satisfying the applicable state and evidence checks. The benchmark contains 120 scenarios across 12 change families, each evaluated at nine scheduled intervention positions. We evaluate 17 coding-agent systems, all of which have lower Shifted than Clean success. GPT-6 Astra drops from 67.35% to 24.79%, with 20.34% paired success. Tool/session changes and stale evidence yield zero paired success across all systems. Late-position paired success is lower for some systems and higher for others. These results show that success on the unchanged task can coexist with failures to preserve work, recover state, or refresh evidence after an update.

title: Step-Up Verification: OTP, Magic Link
description:
We already use Firebase Authentication for primary login—ID tokens on the client, verified on the backend with the Admin SDK. That answers who the user is. It does not always prove they still control the account at the moment they confirm a payment, change payout details, or export sensitive data. Step-up verification—email one-time passwords (OTP) or magic links—closes that gap.

Step-up does not replace Firebase. Users keep sending the same ID token; sensitive routes additionally require recent proof via email. Because Firebase is already in the stack, Firebase email-link sign-in was the obvious first idea. This post compares that shortcut with a custom OTP service layered on the same auth.

Primary login vs step-up

Layer Responsibility
Firebase (existing) Sign-in, session, ID token, firebaseUid → internal user
Step-up (new) Short-lived proof before payments, billing changes, exports, etc.

The backend pattern stays familiar: verify the Firebase token first, resolve the user, then—for protected actions—check a step-up credential or reject with 403 and prompt for verification.

When step-up matters

Typical triggers:

  • Confirming or changing payment methods and billing settings
  • Approving a transfer or purchase above a threshold
  • Exporting or deleting account-held data
  • Any action where a stolen session should not be enough

For those flows the API usually needs two answers:

  1. Is the caller authenticated (session or ID token)?
  2. Have they recently verified via a channel you control (email OTP or equivalent)?

The shortcut we tried first: trigger Firebase email-link sign-in, then read last sign-in time and sign_in_provider from the ID token or Admin SDK user record. If the provider indicated email link and sign-in fell within a window (for example 15 minutes), allow the action—no new OTP tables or send endpoints.

That only works—if the metadata matches what the user actually did.

Options considered

Firebase email-link step-up Custom OTP
Implementation Reuse Firebase send/link APIs + session metadata POST /otp/send, POST /otp/verify, DB, email
User steps Open email, tap link (device matters) Open email, type or paste code (any device)
Proof on backend Last login time + sign_in_provider OTP record + short-lived step-up token
Ops burden Low if metadata is trustworthy You own security, delivery, and abuse controls

Security concerns

Firebase email-link step-up

  • Weak backend proof — If you gate on sign_in_provider and last login, a normal password sign-in can look like step-up; policy mistakes can skip re-verification entirely.
  • Link as bearer secret — Anyone with the magic link can consume it; forwarded email or a shared inbox completes the flow.
  • Full sign-in side effects — Email link is real authentication, not a scoped step-up token—sessions refresh, audit trails mix login with “confirm payment,” and revocation semantics are coarser.
  • Device binding — Links opened on the wrong device can strand or confuse users; support pressure rises before security does.

Custom OTP

  • Your threat model — Brute force, credential stuffing on /otp/verify, and OTP spraying via /otp/send need rate limits, lockouts, and monitoring you implement and operate.
  • Storage and logs — Plaintext OTPs in the database or logs are a common failure mode; hash at rest and never log codes.
  • Email channel — Same mailbox risks as a magic link; a short numeric code can be easier to phish or shoulder-surf if UX is careless.
  • Step-up token lifecycle — Issue tight TTL, bind to user (and optionally device/session), and reject replay; otherwise a verified OTP window becomes a long-lived bypass.

Option 1: Firebase sign-in via email link

Firebase documents this flow as passwordless email-link authentication on the web—see Authenticate with Firebase Using Email Link.

Why it is attractive

  • Reuse existing Firebase auth — same project, Admin SDK, and email patterns as primary login.
  • No OTP product to build — Firebase generates and validates the link; you focus on when to require step-up.
  • Deep links — mobile clients can resume in-app after the user taps the link.
  • Continue URLs / query params — return the user to the payment or settings screen that triggered verification.

Where it breaks down

  • Cross-device UX — magic links often complete on the device that opened the email. Starting checkout on phone and opening mail on a laptop breaks the flow unless you invest in handoff.
  • Session edge cases — expired links, stale tabs, and multiple active sessions need explicit testing.
  • POC friction — a quick spike often surfaces integration details that are not obvious from the docs; Firebase handles sign-in, not necessarily your step-up policy.
  • The blocker: sign_in_provider — after email-link sign-in, Firebase reports sign_in_provider as password, not a distinct email-link provider. You cannot tell “just completed email link step-up” from “signed in with email/password” using provider alone. Last login time + provider is an unreliable gate before a payment or similar action.

Unless you add another durable signal (custom claims from a Cloud Function on link completion, a dedicated step-up flag, etc.), Option 1 does not give the backend clean, auditable step-up proof.

Option 2: Custom OTP

Firebase stays primary auth. Step-up is a narrow API beside it: send a code to the email on the Firebase user (or your internal profile), verify it, issue a short-lived step-up token (or a server-side “verified until” timestamp keyed by user id).

Pros

  • Explicit proof — the backend knows an OTP was sent, verified, consumed, and when.
  • UX control — codes work when email is read on another device; resend, cooldown, and validation UI are yours.
  • One pattern, many gates — the same flow can guard payments, billing changes, and exports.
  • No Firebase metadata quirks — step-up does not depend on sign_in_provider semantics.

Cons

  • Build and maintain — generation, hashing, expiry, single-use, templates, monitoring (see security notes above).

Flow 

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant C as Web / Mobile Client
    participant A as Backend API
    participant D as Database
    participant E as Email Service

    Note over U,E: Send OTP
    U->>C: Start protected action (e.g. confirm payment)
    C->>A: POST /otp/send (Firebase ID token)
    A->>A: Verify token, resolve user
    A->>A: Generate OTP, store hash + expiry
    A->>E: Send email with code
    E-->>U: Email delivered
    A-->>C: 200 OK

    Note over U,E: Verify OTP
    U->>C: Enter code
    C->>A: POST /otp/verify (code)
    A->>D: Load pending OTP for user
    alt Valid and not expired
        A->>D: Mark OTP used
        A->>A: Issue step-up token or session flag
        A-->>C: 200 OK
        C-->>U: Continue protected action
    else Invalid or expired
        A-->>C: 401 / 400
        C-->>U: Retry or resend
    end

In words:

  1. Send — Client calls /otp/send with the usual Firebase ID token. Backend verifies it, resolves the user, stores a hashed OTP with expiry, sends email. Never store plaintext codes.
  2. Verify — Client submits the code. Backend checks hash, expiry, and single-use, marks the OTP consumed, returns a step-up credential (JWT claim, cookie, or server-side “verified until”).
  3. Protected APIs — Require a fresh step-up credential within the policy window in addition to normal auth—for example before submitting a charge or updating a payout account.

Implementation notes (custom OTP)

  • Hash OTPs at rest; short TTL (for example 10–15 minutes); one active send per user with resend cooldown.
  • Rate limit send and verify; cap attempts per OTP before invalidation.
  • Email — state the action (“Confirm payment”, “Update billing”) so users know why they received a code.
  • Audit — log send/verify outcomes without logging the code.
  • Clients — one backend contract; web and mobile differ only in how they collect the code.

Takeaway

We wanted step-up without ripping out Firebase. Email-link step-up is the natural fit, but sign_in_provider reporting password breaks the simple “provider + last login” rule. Patching that with custom claims or Cloud Functions adds moving parts—and still blurs sign-in with step-up.

Custom OTP is more code, but it sits cleanly on top of existing Firebase auth: same ID token at the edge, plus an explicit step-up proof the API can enforce before payments and other sensitive work.

A practical rollout: ship a thin vertical slice (send + verify + one protected endpoint, such as payment confirmation) behind a feature flag, and load-test rate limits before widening coverage.

title: Make Handoffs Explainable Before You Make Them Automatic
description:
“Send this to a person” looks like a complete fallback until the person opens the queue.

They still need to discover why the item arrived, what the system already checked, which source is authoritative, and what action they are expected to take. If that reconstruction is missing from the design, the handoff transfers work without transferring enough context.

I have documented context-aware reception and human-reviewed commercial follow-up patterns in my portfolio. Those public pages describe design directions, with operational outcomes still listed as metrics to collect. This note develops the handoff contract; it does not report a new live automation or a measured productivity improvement.

Start with the decision the recipient owns

A reception workflow and a commercial follow-up workflow do not share every responsibility. A conversation about an unresolved service issue should not automatically become a sales reactivation opportunity.

The documented patterns therefore distinguish commercial context, follow-up lanes, operational limits, and human review. The handoff should preserve that distinction rather than route every uncertain item to a generic inbox.

The recipient needs an answerable request: inspect a conflicting source, decide whether a message can be sent, or redirect the matter to the appropriate team. “Low confidence” can explain part of the trigger, but it does not define the work.

Use a packet a person can challenge

Here is an entirely invented handoff example:

Reason: current request conflicts with earlier campaign context
Current interpretation: product clarification may be required
Evidence: latest message and approved response guidance
Unresolved: which product the person means
Action requested: choose the appropriate clarification
Ownership: reception reviewer
External action: pending human decision

This is an illustrative contract, not an export from a customer conversation.

The packet should distinguish observed facts from the system's interpretation. A reviewer can then reject the interpretation without losing the evidence. It should also show what remains unresolved, rather than presenting an AI summary as a completed investigation.

Evidence references must respect the recipient's access. A handoff is not a reason to copy every historical message into every queue. The useful context is the minimum needed for the assigned decision.

Model ownership after delivery

A route is not complete merely because an item appears in a queue. The design needs an owner, an accepted or pending state, and an escalation path if the receiving role cannot act.

A sales reviewer may be able to approve a follow-up but unable to resolve a policy exception. That should become an explicit transfer with a reason. Otherwise, the queue can look active while responsibility is still absent.

Similarly, a retry should not create several independent tasks for the same unresolved situation. Stable identity and explicit state transitions are important even when the final action remains human.

These are proposed engineering requirements for a dependable handoff. The portfolio pages do not establish that every requirement has been deployed or that every queue transition has been measured.

Keep the outcome in the quality loop

A reviewer may confirm the interpretation, correct it, request more context, or decline the proposed action. Those outcomes help explain which handoffs were useful and which merely moved ambiguity around.

I would measure unresolved ownership, missing evidence, repeated transfers, and corrected interpretations alongside response time. A fast transfer can still be a poor result if the next person cannot make the decision.

A practical handoff review asks:

  • Is the requested human decision named?
  • Are source facts separate from interpretation?
  • Is the trigger specific enough to investigate?
  • Does the recipient have the necessary authority and access?
  • What happens when ownership is rejected or unclear?
  • Can the system record the human outcome without inventing one?

The context-resolution case and commercial follow-up design provide the surrounding patterns. What would a colleague need to receive a handoff and act without rebuilding the entire conversation?

title: RxnExBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Structured Chemical Reaction Extraction from Scientific Literature
description:
arXiv:2610.32221v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Screen Tables and Substrate Scopes are information-dense figures widely used in synthetic chemistry literature, yet automated extraction of structured reaction data from them remains challenging. We introduce RxnExBench, a multimodal benchmark for fine-grained reaction-level evaluation. Built from high-impact chemistry journals, it contains 3,565 expert-annotated reactions and 2,361 molecular structures. The dataset adopts a unified schema with 15 reaction roles and 26 core fields, supporting downstream AI-for-Chemistry tasks such as retrosynthetic planning, yield prediction, and reaction condition recommendation. RxnExBench further provides a reasoning-driven difficulty taxonomy, a modular annotation pipeline, and the Oracle-MolRec protocol, which disentangles molecular recognition from higher-level reasoning. Evaluation of 9 state-of-the-art VLMs shows that performance degrades substantially as schema complexity and reasoning demands increase. Under the Oracle-MolRec setting, results further reveal that accurate molecular recognition alone is insufficient, with multimodal integration and chemistry-aware reasoning remaining the primary bottlenecks. We release all data and code to facilitate future research in chemistry-aware multimodal understanding and AI-for-Chemistry dataset construction. The dataset and code will be released at https://github.com/opendatalab/RxnExBench.

Google Cloud Contact Center as a Service

Announcement

Advanced reporting dashboards prerelease notes 6.16

Here are the pre-release notes for updates to the advanced reporting dashboards and other reporting in CCAI Platform. When we release these updates, we expect the new capabilities to be as shown here.

Important: The next version of the advanced reporting dashboards could be greater than 6.16.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where the Agent Performance tile on the Real-time Agent Monitoring dashboard executed redundant database queries during auto-refreshes.

  • Updated advanced reporting filter prompts so they behave consistently across all dashboards and display the complete list of configured values:

    • List-backed filters now open directly into a searchable list on the first click.

    • Dropdowns that previously returned empty or partial lists now display the full configured list, including Agent Name, Agent Email, Agent Custom ID, Agent Teams, Location, Language, Answered By, and Projection Result.

    • Disposition Codes and Disposition List filters now display the codes configured for your instance.

    • Agent Teams and Team Name filters now match agents in any of their assigned teams.

    • Configuration renames (Queue Group, Queue, Agent Team, Disposition Code, Location, Role, and Skill) now appear in filter dropdowns within 30 minutes instead of up to six hours.

    • The Projecting filter on the live Queued dashboards is now clearable, so you can reset it to show all queued interactions, and offers only Yes.

    • Fields without a predefined list of values (such as consumer phone numbers and ID fields) now display a plain text box with an operator so you can type a value directly.

    • Call Status and Deflection Type filters now display values that existed in the data but were previously missing from the list.

    • Channel now reports a value on the live Voice and Chat dashboards, and on historical Chat dashboards, for interaction types that previously appeared blank (including internal, API-initiated, campaign, UCaaS, callback, and extension calls).

    • On the Agent Audit dashboard, the Change Details table now displays its timestamp column and sorts it correctly.

Change

Because the node keeps its underlying VM, it also keeps its compute capacity during the upgrade. This lowers the risk that a node upgrade fails or stalls because resources aren't available.

To enable this type of upgrade, use surge upgrades with the maxUnavailable field set to a value greater than 0. For more details about when GKE reuses the same Compute Engine instance, including exceptions, see maxUnavailable: GKE makes an existing node unavailable to recreate it.

This change applies to all GKE versions. To opt out, contact Cloud Customer Care.

title: Observability in a Lightweight Java Framework: Health, Metrics, Traces and OpenTelemetry (Building Ligero, Part 6)
description:
Devtools (previous post) is for development. In production you need something different: signals you can alert on, correlate across services and export to whatever backend your team already runs.

Ligero's approach to observability is shaped by one rule: the framework defines vocabulary and SPIs; the client chooses the backend. This post walks through the four pillars (health, metrics, logs, traces) and the design decisions behind each.

1. Health checks 

app.use(HealthMiddleware.builder()
    .path("/health")
    .check("db", () -> dataSource.getConnection().isValid(1))
    .build());

GET /health returns 200 {"status":"UP","checks":{"db":"UP"}}, or 503 with the failing checks marked DOWN. Named checks matter operationally: the response tells the on-call engineer which dependency is down, and a 503 drives readiness in orchestrators.

2. Metrics: label by route pattern, not by path

MetricsMiddleware records method, matched route pattern, status and duration through the MetricsCollector SPI.

The key word is pattern: /users/{id}, not /users/48213. This is the single most important decision in HTTP metrics. Using raw paths as a label creates one time series per user id, which is unbounded cardinality, which is how you take down a metrics backend. The router already knows which pattern matched, so the middleware gets a bounded label for free.

// dependency-free; expose however you like
InMemoryMetricsCollector metrics = new InMemoryMetricsCollector();
app.use(new MetricsMiddleware(metrics));
app.get("/metrics", ctx -> ctx.json(metrics.snapshot()));

// or Micrometer (ligero-metrics-micrometer) for Prometheus/Datadog/...
MeterRegistry registry = new PrometheusMeterRegistry(PrometheusConfig.DEFAULT);
app.use(new MetricsMiddleware(new MicrometerMetricsCollector(registry)));

Two adapters, one SPI: the dependency-free in-memory collector for small services and tests, Micrometer for everything else.

3. Logs: structured, and joined to traces 

app.use(new RequestLoggingMiddleware());     // GET /users -> 200 (431 µs)
app.use(RequestLoggingMiddleware.json());    // {"method":"GET","path":"/users","status":200,...}

The JSON form includes the request id when RequestIdMiddleware runs first. Logs are only useful in an incident if you can pivot from a log line to the trace and back, so the next piece matters.

4. Traces: W3C context and a vendor-neutral SPI

RequestIdMiddleware handles X-Request-Id passthrough/generation and parses the W3C traceparent header. Even with no tracing backend installed, it exposes the traceId as a context attribute, so your logs are correlatable across services.

For real tracing, the core defines a Tracer SPI and a TracingMiddleware; the first adapter is ligero-otel (OpenTelemetry). Datadog, New Relic, Jaeger and friends work through the OTel SDK or agent exporters, or you can implement the SPI directly.

// With the OTel Java agent (or SDK autoconfigure), ServiceLoader finds the tracer:
app.use(TracingMiddleware.fromServiceLoader());

// Or wire an explicit SDK:
app.use(new TracingMiddleware(new OtelTracer(openTelemetrySdk)));

Per request you get a SERVER span that:

  • joins the incoming W3C traceparent, so traces continue across services;
  • is named by the matched route pattern (GET /users/{id}), again bounded cardinality;
  • carries http.request.method, url.path, http.route and http.response.status_code;
  • records exceptions and marks the span ERROR on failures;
  • exposes its trace id as the traceId context attribute for log correlation. 
flowchart LR
    A[Service A] -- traceparent --> L[Ligero service]
    L -- "SERVER span per route pattern" --> O[OTel SDK / agent]
    O --> V[(Backend of your choice)]
    L -- JSON access log + traceId --> G[(Log pipeline)]
    L -- route-pattern metrics --> P[(Metrics backend)]

Why SPIs instead of picking a vendor

Three reasons, all about who pays the cost of change:

  1. Teams already have a stack. Hard-wiring one vendor means every adopter either accepts it or forks.
  2. OpenTelemetry is the lingua franca. One adapter covers most backends, and the SPI covers the rest.
  3. The core stays dependency-free. ligero-core depends only on slf4j-api; tracing and metrics libraries arrive only if you add the module.

A practical checklist

If you operate services like this, a few habits pay off regardless of framework:

  • Bound every label. Route patterns, not raw paths; status classes if you need to reduce further.
  • Propagate context everywhere. traceparent in, traceparent out on every outbound call.
  • Log the trace id. Make "log line to trace" one click.
  • Separate liveness from readiness. A /health that checks the database tells an orchestrator to stop sending traffic, which is not always the same as restart me.
  • Alert on symptoms. Latency and error rate per route pattern beat host-level resource graphs.

Takeaways

  • Health, metrics, logs and traces are built into the middleware pipeline, not bolted on.
  • Route-pattern labels give bounded cardinality for both metrics and span names.
  • The framework owns the vocabulary (SPIs); you own the backend (OTel, Micrometer or your own).

Next: what "production-ready" means beyond observability, covering resilience, auth, scheduling, native image and an MCP server.

title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
description:
arXiv:2610.32285v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.

title: Pixel-Perfect HTML to WordPress: How to Convert a Design Without Changing a Pixel (and Prove It)
description:
Almost every HTML-to-WordPress service and plugin says “pixel-perfect.” Very few show you a measurement. And most people who have moved a hand-made or AI-made design into WordPress know the feeling: it looks nearly right. The hero is two pixels taller, the cards wrap one breakpoint too early, the menu lost its hover underline, the footer font fell back to Arial.

“Nearly” is the problem. A design is a set of decisions, and every small drift is a decision someone else made. This article is about getting an HTML design onto WordPress without any drift at all—and about how to prove it, with numbers, instead of squinting at two browser tabs.

What “Pixel-Perfect” Should Mean

A useful definition is a testable one: at the same viewport, with the same content, the WordPress page renders the same pixels as the original HTML page. Not “looks the same to me”—the same pixels. That gives you two things you can check:

  1. The pixels: screenshot both pages at the same size and subtract one from the other. Anything left over is a difference.
  2. The cause: every rule in your stylesheets should still match the elements it was written for. If a selector stops matching, some part of the page is no longer styled as designed—even if you haven’t spotted it yet.

On our sample design, Copperline Studio (an invented studio’s site, made as plain HTML), Kerf’s import gives 134 of 134 CSS selectors matched, and the two screenshots at 1440×900 subtract to black: 0 of 1,296,000 pixels differ. You can watch that subtraction run live on kerf.site. The rest of this article explains why most conversions can’t get there, and how to check your own.

Where HTML-to-WordPress Conversions Drift

Copying the stylesheet across is the easy part. The design breaks because the HTML around it changes, or because the CSS arrives in a different order. These are the usual culprits.

1. Wrapper elements

Page builders and generic block converters wrap your markup in their own containers: a section becomes a row inside a column inside a widget. Every extra element breaks selectors that depend on structure—.hero > h1, .cards > article:nth-child(3), .grid > *—and puts a new box in the layout that CSS Grid and Flexbox now treat as the item instead of your element.

2. Renamed or normalised markup

A <nav> replaced by wp_nav_menu() outputs WordPress’s own ul.menu > li.menu-item list, and every rule your designer wrote for the original menu stops matching. A table becomes <figure class="wp-block-table">. A <button> becomes a link styled by the theme. Each change is small; together they are why the page “almost” matches.

3. Cascade order and WordPress’s own CSS

CSS is order-sensitive. If your reset.css, style.css and animations.css load in a different order, or WordPress’s block-library stylesheet adds margins to every block, rules resolve differently. The result is spacing that is off by a few pixels everywhere—the hardest kind of drift to diagnose by eye.

4. Rewritten asset paths

A stylesheet that says url(../images/hero.jpg) or url(../fonts/inter.woff2) only works if the folder structure around it survives. Move the CSS into a theme folder and the pictures under /uploads/2026/10/, and backgrounds vanish and fonts silently fall back.

5. Scripts that no longer find their elements

Sliders, menus, scroll reveals and counters usually look for an ID or class. Change the markup, or load a script before the library it depends on, and the page renders—but stuck in its “before JavaScript” state.

How Kerf Keeps the Design Identical

Kerf is a WordPress theme built around one rule: don’t rewrite the design, make it editable. It imports a ZIP of HTML, CSS, scripts and pictures—from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Google Stitch or a designer—and answers each source of drift above:

  • No wrappers, same tags. Structural elements become Kerf blocks that output the exact tag they came from—<section>, <article>, <nav>, <table>, <button>—with the same classes. The DOM WordPress serves is the DOM your CSS was written for.
  • The menu keeps its markup. You rename, reorder and re-link the menu’s items in WordPress, and it still renders your design’s own <nav>.
  • Stylesheets and scripts in source order. Kerf registers them through WordPress’s dependency system in the order your HTML loaded them, and by default it strips the block-library layout margins that would otherwise fight your CSS on imported pages.
  • Folders kept as they were. Your css/, js/, fonts/ and images/ folders are staged with their hierarchy intact, so relative URLs inside stylesheets resolve without rewriting.
  • A check before, a report after. Before anything is written, Kerf counts the pages, stylesheets, scripts and pictures in your ZIP and flags files the HTML refers to that are missing. After the import, the fidelity report checks every selector in your stylesheets against the WordPress page.

The fidelity report on Copperline Studio: 134 of 134 CSS selectors still match after the import.

And because the words, pictures, links and menu become blocks, everything stays editable in WordPress’s block editor—with your real stylesheets loaded in the editor canvas, so what you edit looks like the live page.

Prove It Yourself: A Screenshot Diff in Ten Minutes

Don’t take any tool’s word for “pixel-perfect,” including ours. Here is how to measure any conversion.

1. Render both pages under identical conditions

  • Same viewport (for example 1440×900, then 390×844 for a phone).
  • Logged out, so WordPress’s admin bar isn’t drawn on top.
  • Fonts loaded before capturing (document.fonts.ready).
  • Motion settled: wait for scroll-reveal and entrance animations to finish on both pages.
  • Same content. Compare before you edit anything.

2. Capture with a headless browser

With Playwright (Node), for example:

import { chromium } from 'playwright';

const browser = await chromium.launch();
const page = await browser.newPage({ viewport: { width: 1440, height: 900 } });
for (const [name, url] of [['html', 'http://localhost:8080/index.html'], ['wp', 'https://your-site.test/']]) {
  await page.goto(url, { waitUntil: 'networkidle' });
  await page.evaluate(() => document.fonts.ready);
  await page.waitForTimeout(1500); // let entrance animations finish
  await page.screenshot({ path: name + '.png' });
}
await browser.close();

3. Subtract one from the other

ImageMagick counts the differing pixels and draws them for you:

magick compare -metric AE html.png wp.png diff.png
# prints how many pixels differ: 0 means identical

No ImageMagick? Put the two screenshots on top of each other in a page and set mix-blend-mode: difference on the top one. Identical pixels cancel to pure black; any drift glows. That is the subtraction kerf.site runs in your browser.

4. Audit the selectors

A screenshot only covers what is on screen at that size. To catch problems in states a single snapshot misses, check that the stylesheet selectors still match something on the converted page:

// Run in the browser console, on the original page and then on the WordPress page
const unmatched = [];
for (const sheet of document.styleSheets) {
  let rules; try { rules = sheet.cssRules; } catch { continue; } // skip cross-origin sheets
  for (const rule of rules) {
    if (!rule.selectorText) continue;
    const sel = rule.selectorText.replace(/::?(hover|focus-visible|focus-within|focus|active|visited|before|after)/g, '');
    try { if (sel.trim() && !document.querySelector(sel)) unmatched.push(rule.selectorText); } catch {}
  }
}
console.log(unmatched.length + ' selectors match nothing', unmatched);

The selectors that match on the original page and not on WordPress are your drift. Kerf’s fidelity report runs this kind of check for you at the end of every import.

A Pixel-Perfect Checklist for AI-Made Designs

  • Export real HTML. HTML, CSS and JavaScript files, or a ZIP of them. Apps that need a build step—typical React projects—must be exported as static HTML first; Kerf doesn’t import them yet.
  • Keep assets local and relative. images/, css/, fonts/ inside the ZIP, referenced with relative paths.
  • Keep shared styles in a stylesheet rather than repeated inline <style> blocks, so every page shares them.
  • Compare before you edit. Run the screenshot diff right after the import, while the content is still identical.
  • Check phone width too. Most drift shows up at breakpoints.

Try It With Your Own Design

Pixel-perfect is a claim you should be able to test in minutes, not after a purchase. Try Kerf free in your browser: it opens a private WordPress with Kerf installed—no sign-up, nothing to install. Drop in your ZIP, read the check and the fidelity report, then screenshot both pages and subtract them.

The short version: A conversion drifts when the markup, the cascade order or the asset paths change. Kerf keeps all three as written, makes the content editable around them, and reports any selector that stops matching. On Copperline Studio: 134 of 134 selectors, 0 of 1,296,000 pixels different. Read the docs →
