title: Database Deadlocks in Production: Detection, Lock Trees, and Prevention Strategies
description:
title: "Database Deadlocks in Production: Detection, Lock Trees, and Prevention Strategies"
published: true
published_at: "2027-02-28T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Database Deadlocks in Production: Detection, Lock Trees, and Prevention Strategies. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [postgres, sql, database, backend]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Database Deadlocks in Production: Detection, Lock Trees, and Prevention Strategies is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Database Deadlocks in Production: Detection, Lock Trees, and Prevention Strategies matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of postgresql architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Row-Level Locks Vs Table Locks: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Cyclic Lock Dependencies: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Pg_Locks Introspection: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Ordering Update Statements: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Database Deadlocks in Production: Detection, Lock Trees, and Prevention Strategies functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: PostgreSQL Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

-- Production-Ready Schema & Query Pattern: Database Deadlocks in Production: Detection, Lock Trees, and Prevention Strategies
-- Focus areas: Row-level locks vs table locks, cyclic lock dependencies, pg_locks introspection, ordering update statements, and NOWAIT clauses.

BEGIN;

-- 1. Create optimized table structure with strict constraints
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS system_records (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    entity_code VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    state VARCHAR(32) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
    metadata JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- 2. Covering partial index to maximize query speed and avoid sequential scans
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_records_tenant_state_active
ON system_records (tenant_id, created_at DESC)
INCLUDE (entity_code, metadata)
WHERE state IN ('PENDING', 'PROCESSING');

-- 3. Optimized query utilizing index-only scan
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, entity_code, metadata
FROM system_records
WHERE tenant_id = 'tenant_production_01'
  AND state = 'PENDING'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

COMMIT;

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: How to Build a Realtime Kitchen Order Status Board in Node.js — 2026 Kiosk Tokens
description:
Short answer: publish order state transitions to one room channel, let every kiosk subscribe read-only, and refetch the current board after reconnect. For a Node.js team that wants a self-describing REST API, Infrai is a reasonable fit for the publish and token-issuing parts; the decision should rest on delivery behavior and operator effort, not a price leaderboard.

At 3am, “realtime” is not a latency trophy. It is a question from the pager: which page fired, and can the next display prove what it missed? A kitchen order status board makes that concrete. Several kiosk displays need the same small update when an order moves from queued to cooking or ready, while nobody wants a display to write an order back into the system.

The design below treats the channel as a notification stream, not the database. The order service remains authoritative. A transition wakes displays up; a reconnect fetches truth again. It doesn't need a clever cache protocol, but it does need an explicit recovery rule and logs that let an on-call engineer follow one order from publish to paint.

Keep it boring.

What should a Node.js realtime API do for kitchen kiosk displays?

Start with the failure mode. A display can lose Wi-Fi during a transition, reboot after a power dip, or reconnect after the access token expires. If the event is a full board snapshot, every fan-out message grows with the number of active orders. If it is only a transition, the message stays small and the display can ask the order service for the latest state when its local sequence is uncertain.

Give each kiosk a token scoped to subscription on the room channel. Displays are subscribers, never publishers. The kitchen terminal or order service owns the publish credential. That single permission boundary prevents a compromised wall tablet from changing an order, and it makes an audit trail much easier to read.

I would name the channel after the workspace, such as kitchen-west-04, and put an order identifier, previous state, next state, and transition identifier in each event. Keep the transition identifier stable. It gives the display a way to ignore a duplicate after a retry without pretending the transport is exactly-once.

The useful rule is short: notify with a transition, recover with a read.

A minimal Go publisher with scoped kiosk tokens

The following Go program shows the two writes a small service needs: issue a subscriber token, then publish a transition. It reads the key from the environment, sets the method explicitly, checks response status, honors Retry-After on 429, and sends an idempotency key for the publish. The API discovery surface documents request schemas and runnable examples, so check the live schema before adding fields to your own event envelope.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func post(url string, payload any, idempotency string) ([]byte, error) {
    body, err := json.Marshal(payload)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if idempotency != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotency)
        }
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
            if s, e := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); e == nil && s > 0 {
                delay = time.Duration(s) * time.Second
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s: %s", resp.Status, string(data))
        }
        return data, nil
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limit persisted after retries")
}

func main() {
    if os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    channel := "kitchen-west-04"
    _, err := post("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/token/issue", map[string]any{
        "channel": channel,
        "permissions": []string{"subscribe"},
        "subject": "kiosk-17",
    }, "")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    _, err = post("https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", map[string]any{
        "channel": channel,
        "event": "order.transitioned",
        "data": map[string]string{
            "order_id": "A-1042",
            "from": "queued",
            "to": "cooking",
            "transition_id": "A-1042-queued-cooking-0007",
        },
    }, "A-1042-queued-cooking-0007")
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
}

That token call is deliberately separate from publishing. A kiosk process receives the scoped token through your enrollment flow, subscribes to the room, and has no credential that can call the publish route. Do not put the platform key in browser JavaScript.

How do reconnects, fan-out delivery, and order status recovery work?

The display should render the transition immediately, but it should also track the last transition it applied. On reconnect, fetch the authoritative order board and replace the local view; do not try to reconstruct a gap by guessing which messages arrived. This is the part teams skip when the demo is green. It is also the part that turns a flaky network into a bounded recovery step.

Use a monotonically increasing version from the order service if you have one. If the incoming transition is older than the displayed version, ignore it. If it is newer but not adjacent, mark the local view stale and refetch. Your mileage may vary if the order service uses timestamps instead of versions, so make the comparison rule explicit in the client and log the decision.

Before rollout, test the boring cases: five displays subscribing to one channel, a duplicate transition, a token with publish permission removed, and a reconnect during a state change. Record the transition identifier and request identifier in logs. A dashboard that only says “connected” is not evidence that every display is showing the right order.

Comparing practical options for a shared kitchen board

The transport choice changes the effective operating bill: integration time, permission modeling, replay behavior, and the work required at 3am all count. Here is a deliberately compact comparison of common options.

Option Strength for this board Cost or limitation to verify
Infrai realtime One REST surface with public discovery and runnable examples, useful when the same service already handles other backend capabilities You still own the authoritative order read and reconnect reconciliation; a specialist realtime provider may offer deeper presence and replay controls
Ably Mature pub/sub model and documented connection recovery patterns Adds another vendor surface and credential model if the rest of your stack lives elsewhere
Pusher Channels Straightforward hosted channel fan-out for browser and kiosk clients You need to model publisher versus subscriber authorization and keep a separate order API authoritative
Socket.IO Familiar application-level rooms when you want to operate the transport yourself You carry connection scaling, deployment, and incident response for the socket tier

Try Infrai when your team values a self-describing API and one key for a broader platform: its discovery can show the capability schema and runnable examples before you learn another SDK, while 295 routes across 20 modules can remove a second credential and integration review when the order service already needs storage or observability. Pick Ably when managed realtime semantics and replay are the primary requirement. Stick with Socket.IO when you already operate that tier and the operational ownership is intentional. The catch is that no option makes a missed transition impossible; the refetch-on-reconnect rule remains yours. Start by checking the realtime discovery documentation against your channel and token policy.

Verification, rollback, and the 3am decision rule

Ship the publisher behind a feature flag. First publish a non-destructive transition to a test channel, confirm every kiosk receives it once or safely ignores a duplicate, then enable the production channel. Keep the order service read path unchanged so rollback means disabling publication and letting displays refresh on their normal interval.

If a display shows an impossible state, inspect the transition log before restarting it. A missing event should produce a refetch, not a manual edit. If the token scope is wrong, revoke that token and issue a subscriber-only replacement; do not widen permissions to make a symptom disappear.

The decision rule is simple enough to put in the runbook: transitions for fan-out, scoped read-only tokens for displays, and a full refetch after reconnect. That combination gives the kitchen a current board without making the transport pretend to be the database.

References

  • https://docs.infrai.cc
  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.ably.com/docs
  • https://pusher.com/docs/channels/
  • https://socket.io/docs/v4/

title: Learning Nonlinear Waveform Fusion Across Scales for Integrated Sensing and Communication
description:
arXiv:2610.32099v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fixed source superposition and frequency partitioning constrain how communication content interacts with a probing reference in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). We learn nonlinear waveform fusion across scales for image transmission and localization of multiple targets in range and angle. Reception uses the information available at each end. Adaptive temporal feature weighting and spectral updates combine image features and a deterministic linearly frequency-modulated reference in a shared complex state, generating a waveform with fixed total energy over the array frame. At the user equipment (UE), the reference and channel state information condition a neural demixer for image reconstruction. At the base station, the realized transmit pulse defines a coherent dictionary for sequential localization with learned local correction, physical refinement, and residual updates. We compare the proposed waveforms with superposition in the time domain and learned spectral linear fusion on 512 independent test images, using a shared fixed UE receiver and a baseline sensing receiver using coherent peak search. Averaged across eleven task weights, the proposed waveforms reduce normalized localization error by 29.0\% and 27.0\%, respectively, while increasing mean peak signal-to-noise ratio by 1.40 and 0.82~dB. With the proposed waveforms fixed, learned local correction reduces mean normalized localization error by 12.2\% relative to the same sequential receiver without learned correction.

title: Hyperparameter-Free Boundary-Interior t-vMF Dice Loss for Medical Image Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.32266v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Class imbalance and errors near anatomical boundaries remain challenges in medical image segmentation, motivating loss functions that account for these difficulties. Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss adjusts the similarity function during training but requires hyperparameter tuning. We propose Self-Tuned Boundary-Aware t-vMF Dice Loss (STB-tvMF Dice), which adapts the function separately for boundary and interior regions without tuning shape-adaptation parameters. Each region's shape parameter of t-vMF function is determined from its mean prediction-target cosine similarity in the preceding epoch and remains fixed throughout the current epoch. This rule maximizes the slope of the similarity function at the observed mean similarity, providing a principled basis for adaptation without validation-based parameter selection. Experiments on three datasets and architectures demonstrated its effectiveness. On Synapse with U-Net, STB-tvMF Dice achieved a mean DSC of 70.75%, compared with 63.03% for Adaptive t-vMF Dice Loss. Our code will be available soon.

title: The LLENS Platform for On-Premises Large Language Model Agents in a Japanese University Hospital: Development and Evaluation Study
description:
arXiv:2610.32151v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model agents that use tools could take on part of the electronic health record and desk work that occupies physicians' time, but in many hospitals the medical information systems run inside closed networks, so the model and the agent harness must also sit inside. We designed, implemented, and deployed LLENS, a clinical support AI agent platform that runs inside the closed network of Hokkaido University Hospital on one host with 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the open-weight model Kimi K2.6 (~1 trillion parameters), and a web application rebuilt from Open WebUI. The harness has 10 components, including page image reading, full-text attachment input, a path-addressed document tree without a vector index, a network-isolated sandbox, artifact return, self-checking of generated output, subagents, and saved procedures. Kimi K2.6 was chosen from 3 open-weight candidates and scored 480/500 on the 2026 Japanese Medical Licensing Examination; it generated 119 tokens/s for one user and served 16 concurrent requests at 908 tokens/s in total. On 180 questions over hospital documents (3 seeds each), mean accuracy was 10.7% with no documents, 81.3% with fixed retrieval (top 10 chunks of one lexical search), and 97.2% with interactive access, in which the model reads with document tools and the sandbox (15.9 percentage points above fixed retrieval, 95% CI 10.9-21.3); the difference lay in filtering/counting questions (16.7% vs 87.8%). Five scenarios with synthetic data ran on combinations of the components: needlestick injury response, batch adverse event grading, scanned referral letter transcription, falls data aggregation and plotting, and investigation of 3 topics by subagents. The platform has run on the hospital network since September 14, 2026.

title: RAG Chunking Done Right: Split on Structure, Attach Metadata, and Measure Recall Before You Touch chunk_size
description:
When a RAG system gives a wrong answer, most people go straight for the model or the prompt. In my experience, the cause is often upstream: the right passage was never retrieved, because the chunk that held it was cut in the wrong place, was too big to rank well, or had lost the context that made it findable.

Chunking is the first step of almost every RAG pipeline, and it's the one people think about least. This post is the practical version: the trade-off you're actually tuning, what overlap does and doesn't buy you, why I split on document structure instead of fixed character counts, why every chunk should carry metadata, and how to measure recall before changing anything.

(Earlier posts covered hybrid search, lost in the middle, and long context vs RAG. This one sits one step before all of them: what goes into the index in the first place.)

1. Chunk size is a precision vs. context trade-off

There's no universally "right" chunk size, because two forces pull in opposite directions:

  • Small chunks are precise. Each embedding represents one idea, so a focused query matches it cleanly and you send fewer irrelevant tokens to the model. But a small chunk can lose the context it needs to make sense on its own.
  • Large chunks keep context together, but they dilute the embedding with unrelated content and fill your context window with tokens the model doesn't need.

Chroma's research team measured this directly in their report Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval. They evaluated retrieval at the token level (recall, precision and IoU) across five corpora and found that some chunking strategies outperformed others by up to 9% in recall. Some results worth knowing:

  • With text-embedding-3-large and 5 retrieved chunks, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter at 200 tokens with no overlap scored 88.1% recall and 7.0% precision. At 800 tokens with 400 overlap, recall was 85.4% and precision 1.5%.
  • They wrote that the heuristic recursive splitter at chunk size 200 with no overlap "performs well" and was consistently high across all their metrics.
  • They also noted that default settings of popular chunkers can perform relatively poorly. OpenAI's file search default (800-token chunks, 400-token overlap) gave slightly below-average recall and the lowest scores on their other metrics in that setup.

The speculation in that report matches what I see in practice: recall peaks somewhere in the middle. Too large and the relevant sentence is diluted; too small and the chunk doesn't carry enough context to be retrieved as one unit.

Know your defaults, because you're probably using one:

Tool Default / documented setting
OpenAI vector stores (file search) 800-token chunks, 400-token overlap; configurable from 100 to 4096 tokens, overlap at most half the chunk size (docs)
LlamaIndex SentenceSplitter Docs example uses chunk_size=1024, chunk_overlap=20 (docs)
LangChain RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter Measures size in characters by default, splits on ["\n\n", "\n", " ", ""] (docs)

Note that last one: a LangChain chunk_size=1000 is 1,000 characters, not 1,000 tokens, unless you pass a token-based length_function. I've seen teams compare "chunk sizes" across tools without noticing they were using different units.

2. Overlap is insurance, not a free upgrade

Overlap repeats the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so a sentence that falls on a boundary isn't cut in half. LangChain's docs describe it as helping "to mitigate loss of information when context is divided between chunks."

The cost is redundancy: the same tokens get stored, retrieved and sent to the model more than once. In Chroma's results, reducing overlap improved IoU because that metric penalizes repeated tokens. But overlap isn't useless: with the smaller all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding model, their best recall (82.4%) came from 250-token chunks with 125-token overlap, and it dropped to 77.1% with zero overlap.

My takeaway: overlap helps most when your boundaries are arbitrary. If you split on real structure (next section), you need much less of it.

3. Split on structure, not character counts

Fixed-size splitting ignores where ideas begin and end. A 500-character window will happily cut a table in half, or glue the last paragraph of "Refund policy" to the first paragraph of "Shipping."

Most real documents already tell you where the boundaries are: Markdown headings, HTML sections, PDF titles, code functions. Use them.

  • LangChain's MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter splits on the headers you specify and puts each header into the chunk's metadata (docs).
  • LlamaIndex has MarkdownNodeParser for Markdown and CodeSplitter for source code (which splits by language, with chunk_lines and max_chars limits).
  • LangChain's recursive splitter is already a mild version of this idea: it tries paragraphs first, then lines, then words.

The pattern I use is two-stage: split by section first, then apply a size limit inside each section only when a section is too long. LangChain's docs note that when you do this with split_documents, overlap is applied within a section and does not cross section boundaries, which is exactly what you want.

4. Attach metadata to every chunk

A chunk that says "The limit is 30 days" is nearly useless in isolation. Thirty days for what? In which product? Which version of the policy?

Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post describes this exact problem with an SEC-filing example: a chunk saying "The company's revenue grew by 3% over the previous quarter" doesn't say which company or which quarter. Their fix is to prepend a short, chunk-specific context (usually 50-100 tokens, generated by Claude) before embedding and before building the BM25 index. In their tests, contextual embeddings alone reduced the top-20 retrieval failure rate by 35% (5.7% â†’ 3.7%).

You can get a cheap version of this without an LLM call: store the document title and section path as metadata, and prepend them to the text you embed. Metadata also lets you filter (by product, version, tenant) before ranking, and it gives you citations for free.

5. Measure recall on real queries before changing chunk size

This is the step most teams skip. Changing chunk size changes every embedding in your index, so you should know whether it helped.

  1. Collect 50-100 real user questions (from logs, support tickets, or your team).
  2. For each, label the document section that actually answers it.
  3. Measure recall@k: the share of questions where a correct section appears in the top k results.
  4. Change one variable at a time (size, overlap, splitter), re-index, re-measure.

Anthropic's evaluation used exactly this kind of metric (1 minus recall@20). Chroma's report also showed you can generate an evaluation set from your own corpus with an LLM if you don't have labeled queries yet, though real queries are better.

Code: structure-aware chunks with metadata, plus a recall check 

from langchain_text_splitters import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

def chunk_markdown(doc_title: str, markdown: str):
    # Stage 1: split on real structure; headers go into metadata
    by_section = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(
        headers_to_split_on=[("#", "h1"), ("##", "h2"), ("###", "h3")]
    ).split_text(markdown)

    # Stage 2: cap size only inside long sections (chunk_size is in characters here)
    sized = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
        chunk_size=1200, chunk_overlap=100
    ).split_documents(by_section)

    for d in sized:
        section = " > ".join(d.metadata[k] for k in ("h1", "h2", "h3") if k in d.metadata)
        d.metadata.update({"doc_title": doc_title, "section": section})
        # Embed this text: title + section path + chunk body
        d.metadata["embed_text"] = f"{doc_title} | {section}\n{d.page_content}"
    return sized

def recall_at_k(eval_set, search, k=10):
    """eval_set: [(question, expected_section)], search(q, k) -> list of chunks."""
    hits = sum(
        any(c.metadata["section"] == expected for c in search(q, k))
        for q, expected in eval_set
    )
    return hits / len(eval_set)

The chunk_size=1200 and chunk_overlap=100 values are a hypothetical starting point, not a recommendation. Run recall_at_k with your current settings first, then change one value at a time.

A hypothetical example

Say an internal HR bot keeps answering "How many days do I have to submit expenses?" with the travel booking policy. The fixed 1,000-character chunk that holds the answer starts mid-sentence, and its only identifying text is "Submit within 30 days." After switching to section-based splitting with HR Handbook | Expenses > Deadlines prepended, the chunk carries the words the question uses. You would confirm that with recall@10 on your labeled questions, not by eyeballing one answer.

Takeaways

  • Chunk size trades precision for context. There's no universal best value; measure yours.
  • Know your tool's defaults and units (tokens vs. characters).
  • Overlap is insurance for arbitrary boundaries. Splitting on structure reduces the need for it.
  • Split on headings and sections first, then cap size within sections.
  • Put doc title and section path on every chunk, and embed them with the text.
  • Measure recall@k on real queries before and after every change.

References

  • Chroma Research, Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval (Smith & Troynikov, July 2024): https://research.trychroma.com/evaluating-chunking
  • Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval (Sep 2024): https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval
  • OpenAI, Retrieval guide (vector store chunking defaults and limits): https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/retrieval
  • LangChain, Recursive text splitter: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/splitters/recursive_text_splitter
  • LangChain, Markdown header text splitter: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/splitters/markdown_header_metadata_splitter
  • LlamaIndex, Node parser modules: https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/framework/module_guides/loading/node_parsers/modules/

title: Portable Knowledge-Base Summaries: A Node.js Retrieval Boundary for Embeddings and GPT
description:
Short answer: keep embeddings, context selection, and GPT summarization behind a small provider interface. Generate vectors for the source material, use them to select or refine the context, then send only that curated context to the summarizer. In a fintech knowledge base, this boundary matters more than the first model choice: it lets you change providers without rewriting retrieval, redaction, audit, and retry logic in the Node.js application.

The bill is usually made of tokens, not the vector lookup. If a corpus has 100,000 chunks and a summarization request sends 12,000 tokens every time, the repeated context dominates the spend and the latency. Embeddings help because they let the application retrieve a smaller, relevant slice before the GPT prompt. The change that moves the term is context selection, not adding a more elaborate prompt around the same oversized payload.

There is a cost to that decision. I deliberately stop keeping the full source text in the prompt path; when retrieval misses a relevant policy paragraph, the summary can be incomplete. That is a real operational trade-off, so the system should retain source references and let an operator inspect the selected passages. A short summary is not evidence.

How should a Node.js app summarize content with semantic embeddings and GPT?

Treat the provider as three operations with explicit inputs and outputs: embed a normalized chunk, retrieve candidates, and summarize a bounded context. The application should own chunk identifiers, source provenance, tenant boundaries, redaction rules, prompt templates, and the final citation map. A provider should not decide what a regulated tenant is allowed to see.

For a private fintech knowledge base, the request path can look like this:

  1. Pre-process large corpora: normalize whitespace, split documents into stable chunks, and attach document and version identifiers.
  2. Generate an embedding for each chunk and persist the vector beside its tenant and source metadata.
  3. Embed the question, rank candidate chunks, and apply authorization and freshness filters before prompting GPT.
  4. Ask for a summary of the selected context, while preserving the chunk IDs used for that answer.

The interface should return provider-neutral records such as chunk_id, score, text, and source_version. It should not leak a vendor response object into the rest of the codebase. That is the part that makes migration reversible. Swapping an SDK is easy; unpicking its types from controllers, queues, and audit events is not.

Infrai is a reasonable fit for the adapter when self-discovery is useful during integration. Its public discovery surface exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so wiring a capability can start with reading one endpoint rather than learning another bespoke SDK. The OpenAI-compatible surface also allows existing OpenAI client patterns to point at a different base URL and key, which reduces the amount of application code tied to one provider. Keep those details inside the adapter.

Infrai's one key and one bill cover both embedding and chat calls across its backend capabilities. For this workflow, that removes a small but persistent source of friction: secrets rotation and invoice reconciliation do not have to be designed separately for retrieval and summarization. It is an operational convenience, not a reason to skip provider-level evaluation.

My recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the embedding-and-chat adapter in a team that expects to test providers, because its self-describing contract and compatible surface reduce discovery and migration work. Do not make it the source of truth for authorization, retention, or evidence handling.

How do the real alternatives differ at the boundary?

Portability does not mean pretending that providers are identical. It means deciding which differences the application can tolerate and which ones must be represented in a local contract.

Provider Useful fit Portability concern
OpenAI A direct choice when the team already uses its embeddings and chat client conventions. Application code can become coupled to provider-specific response fields, model names, and operational defaults if the adapter is skipped.
Cohere A credible alternative for teams evaluating a separate embedding and retrieval-oriented stack. Embedding dimensions, ranking behavior, and request shapes still need to be normalized before they enter shared application code.
Google Vertex AI A fit when model access, identity, and deployment already live in a Google Cloud control plane. Cloud-specific authentication and regional configuration can make a later move to a different provider a broader infrastructure task.
Anthropic A sensible summarization option when the team already evaluates its models for long-form text. Embeddings still need a separate provider, so the application must keep the vector contract independent from the chat contract.
Google Gemini A sensible option when the team wants its summarization workflow close to existing Google tooling. Model naming, authentication, and response normalization remain provider concerns that should stop at the adapter.
Infrai A fit when one REST surface, public discovery, and an OpenAI-compatible chat surface are useful integration constraints. It is not a reason to erase provider metadata or assume every capability is ready in every region. Check discovery and readiness for the capability you need.

The comparison is intentionally boring. A retrieval score from one embedding model is not automatically comparable with a score from another model, even when both APIs accept text. Store the embedding model and preprocessing version with each vector. During a migration, dual-write a sample or rebuild the index; do not silently mix vectors and call the result a like-for-like comparison.

What should the Node.js service keep, and what should it discard?

The service should keep a compact audit record: tenant, document version, selected chunk IDs, embedding model identifier, summarization model identifier, prompt version, and request ID. It should not keep an unbounded copy of every intermediate prompt merely because storage is available. Retention has legal and operational consequences in a financial system, and a prompt can contain more sensitive material than the final answer.

The service should also make retries safe. Embedding generation can be retried for a stable chunk key; summarization should carry a request identity so a queue retry does not create two competing answer records. Rate limits deserve an explicit path: honor Retry-After when supplied, use exponential backoff for HTTP 429, and surface other 4xx responses instead of treating them as successful summaries.

A simple provider contract is enough:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Protocol


@dataclass
class RetrievedChunk:
    chunk_id: str
    text: str
    score: float
    source_version: str


class SummarizationProvider(Protocol):
    def embed(self, text: str, *, model: str) -> list[float]: ...

    def summarize(
        self,
        question: str,
        chunks: list[RetrievedChunk],
        *,
        model: str,
        request_id: str,
    ) -> str: ...

Here is the small, real request path behind that contract. The model IDs stay in environment variables because model availability changes independently of the application contract. The retry loop handles rate limits, while other HTTP errors remain visible to the caller.

import json
import os
import time
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


BASE_URL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
API_KEY = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]


def post(path: str, payload: dict) -> dict:
    body = json.dumps(payload).encode("utf-8")
    for attempt in range(4):
        request = Request(
            f"{BASE_URL}{path}",
            data=body,
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {API_KEY}",
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
            },
            method="POST",
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
                return json.load(response)
        except HTTPError as error:
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                detail = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
                raise RuntimeError(f"provider HTTP {error.code}: {detail}") from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
        except URLError as error:
            if attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"provider connection failed: {error}") from error
            time.sleep(2**attempt)


embedding = post(
    "/embeddings",
    {
        "model": os.environ["INFRAI_EMBEDDING_MODEL"],
        "input": "The account-opening policy requires identity verification.",
    },
)

summary = post(
    "/chat/completions",
    {
        "model": os.environ["INFRAI_CHAT_MODEL"],
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "system",
                "content": "Summarize only the supplied policy text and preserve exceptions.",
            },
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": "Policy text: The account-opening policy requires identity verification.",
            },
        ],
    },
)
print(json.dumps({"embedding": embedding, "summary": summary}))

The production implementation can use the OpenAI client idiom or an HTTP adapter, but the rest of the Node.js workflow should depend on this semantic contract, not on /v1/embeddings or /v1/chat/completions response details. The two routes are enough for the core operation; the surrounding code supplies preprocessing, authorization, ranking, and retention policy.

One practical trap is treating a large corpus as one embedding request. Chunk first, preserve stable IDs, and re-index when the chunking or embedding model changes. Another is using similarity as permission. Similarity ranks text. It does not grant access to text.

When is a direct provider the better choice?

Use OpenAI directly when its supported models, client behavior, and existing operational controls are already the requirement. Choose Cohere when its retrieval and reranking evaluation is materially better for the domain data. Choose Vertex AI when cloud identity, regional governance, and the surrounding Google platform outweigh the value of a neutral gateway.

Use a gateway when the main risk is provider change and the gateway exposes a contract you can inspect. Infrai's discovery response reports capability readiness and pending vendors, which is useful for checking that a planned route is actually available before deployment. It does not remove the need to test retrieval quality, redact inputs, or validate summaries against source passages.

That boundary is the point.

A portable system is not one that claims every model is interchangeable. It is one where the expensive decisions, such as chunking, access control, evaluation, and evidence retention, remain yours when the model changes. For a concrete migration test, run the same held-out questions through two providers, compare selected chunk IDs before comparing prose quality, and reject a move that improves wording while dropping source coverage.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the semantic search and rerank guide and verify the current capability contract before wiring production traffic.

Further reading

  • OpenAI embeddings guide
  • Cohere Embed documentation
  • Vertex AI text embeddings
  • MDN: Using Server-Sent Events
  • Infrai discovery schema

title: SyncPro: Synchronous Reasoning and Responding for Proactive Streaming Video Understanding
description:
arXiv:2610.32132v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires assistants to track unfolding events and respond when a user's requested condition is met. To make these decisions, assistants must accumulate relevant evidence and reassess response conditions as new observations arrive. Existing work offers complementary capabilities for this process: proactive video assistants learn when to respond, while streaming video reasoning methods generate scheduled intermediate text to organize observations and support subsequent answers. Together, these capabilities provide a foundation for proactive reasoning, but how to coordinate ongoing reasoning with timely responses remains underexplored. In a direct adaptation, fixed reasoning intervals can trigger updates when nothing relevant has changed or postpone useful updates until the next scheduled step. Sharing one generation path also couples two distinct requirements: preserving evidence for future decisions and producing only the response requested by the user. Moreover, responses generated after reasoning must wait for it to finish, even when sufficient evidence is already available. To address these challenges, we introduce SyncPro, a synchronous dual-stream framework with specialized generation paths for evidence tracking and user-facing responses. Its Inner and Response branches share causal history and activate independently, allowing relevant evidence changes to trigger internal updates and responses to proceed concurrently with ongoing reasoning. We construct 189K dual-stream examples and train SyncPro through supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. Experiments across three proactive benchmarks show improved response timing and more accurate answers to user requests.

title: BARC-Bench: Benign Asks, Risky Consequences
description:
arXiv:2610.32024v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Task instructions from users for agents are inherently underspecified, especially regarding safety boundaries--creating behavioral risks. To study these risks, we introduce BARC-Bench, a collection of 110 tasks across nine simulated workspace environments where benign requests leave openings for unsafe actions. In this benchmark, we evaluate agent behavior against safety boundaries established by workspace records, implicit environmental context, and unstated social norms. For example, an agent asked to schedule off-boarding discussions must arrange the meeting without prematurely revealing an employee's resignation through a shared calendar invitation. Evaluating four frontier model configurations across five attempts per task reveals that models are not consistently safe: the share of tasks completed safely on all five attempts ranges from 9.1% to 72.7%, with even the strongest configuration producing a safety violation on 27.3% of tasks. These results highlight an asymmetric operational risk: while models frequently complete complex workflows, their inability to consistently respect unstated boundaries presents a substantial barrier to safe autonomous delegation.

title: Lazy Notes: Let Local AI Do the Reading for You
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

Ever opened a long meeting transcript or a pile of lecture notes and wished someone would just tell you what matters?

That's why I built Lazy Notes — a lightweight AI-powered note summarizer that helps people spend less time reading and more time doing.

Users can paste their notes or upload a text file and generate:

  • Quick Summary: Understand the main idea without reading every line.
  • Key Takeaways: Get the important points in bullet form.
  • Action Items: Identify tasks and deadlines mentioned in the notes.
  • Two-Line Recap: Get the essential information at a glance.

The idea is simple: let AI handle the repetitive reading so you don't have to.

Demo

Code

💻 GitHub Repository:

ansh-rajpoot / lazy-noted

The project is built with Python and Streamlit, with Ollama powering local AI inference.

How I Built It

I used Python, Streamlit, and Ollama to build Lazy Notes.

Streamlit provides the user interface, while Ollama runs an open-weight language model locally to process the notes and generate structured summaries.

The workflow is straightforward:

  1. The user pastes notes or uploads a supported text file.
  2. The application sends the text to the locally running Ollama model.
  3. The model generates a summary, key takeaways, and action items.
  4. The results are displayed in a clean interface that is easy to read and use.

I kept the architecture simple and focused on building a useful tool rather than adding unnecessary complexity.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a tool that processes personal notes, meeting discussions, and study material, where the data goes matters.

Using a locally running open-weight model means Lazy Notes can process text without relying on a paid, third-party AI API.

This approach offers several advantages:

  • More control over data: Notes can remain on the user's machine when Ollama is configured locally and no other external services are used.
  • Model flexibility: Users can experiment with different compatible models instead of being locked into one hosted AI provider.
  • Lower ongoing costs: Local inference does not require paying a per-request AI API fee, although hardware and electricity still have costs.
  • More independence: The core summarization workflow can run without an internet connection once the required model is installed, provided the local setup is working.

Open innovation makes it possible to build a practical AI tool that users can run and control themselves.

The Lazy Payoff

The goal of Lazy Notes is to reduce the effort involved in reviewing long notes.

Instead of manually searching for the main ideas, users can start with a concise summary and review the details that matter to them.

I designed this project around one question:

What if getting the gist of your notes took less effort than reading them all?

title: VoIP, SIP Trunking & Custom WebRTC Contact Center Architecture: Reducing Call Latency, Jitter & Per-Seat SaaS Costs
description:
When a 50-to-200 seat sales or support operation scales on commercial CCaaS platforms (RingCentral, Genesys, Five9, Talkdesk), monthly bills hit $110–$180 per seat before carrier minute markups and storage fees. Meanwhile, distributed agents across the US, UK, GCC, and South Asia still experience robotic audio and 400ms+ talk-over lag because voice packets hairpin through a distant cloud region.

At Loop Origin, we engineer custom cloud PBX, SIP trunking, and browser-embedded WebRTC contact center platforms that integrate directly into our clients' CRMs and ERPs. Building on my earlier guide on planning a VoIP phone system for a small business with Asterisk and FreePBX, this deep dive breaks down the exact network and media-path architecture required to achieve under 120ms mouth-to-ear latency, Mean Opinion Score (MOS) > 4.2, and a 60% to 75% reduction in 3-year telecom TCO.

How Do You Reduce Call Latency and Per-Seat SaaS Costs in a Modern VoIP & WebRTC Contact Center?

Direct Answer: You eliminate both high voice latency and per-seat SaaS markups by decoupling SIP signaling from RTP/SRTP media anchoring. Using edge Kamailio + rtpengine media relays deployed near your agents and wholesale SIP trunks (Twilio Elastic SIP, Telnyx, or local tier-1 carriers) connected to Asterisk 20 LTS or FreeSWITCH, you keep voice packets on the shortest regional UDP path with zero per-agent licensing fees.

To understand why off-the-shelf browser dialers suffer from lag and jitter, look at the two distinct planes of any real-time voice call:

1.
2.

Reference Topology: Browser WebRTC to Carrier PSTN Without Media Hairpinning

Browser CRM dialers require WebRTC (WSS signaling, DTLS-SRTP media encryption, ICE/STUN/TURN NAT traversal, and Opus audio), whereas wholesale PSTN SIP trunks use standard SIP over TLS/UDP with G.711 (PCMU/PCMA) audio.

Instead of forcing your central Asterisk or FreeSWITCH server to transcode and relay every single packet from a single data center, a production architecture separates edge media anchoring from core queue logic:

[Agent Browser CRM (WebRTC: Opus + DTLS-SRTP over UDP)]
       │
       ▼  (Shortest Regional Hop: <35ms RTT)
[Regional Edge SBC: Kamailio (WSS Signaling) + rtpengine (DTLS-SRTP <-> RTP Bridge)]
       │
       ├──► Signaling Only (SIP) ──► [Core Asterisk 20 / FreeSWITCH Cluster + Laravel CRM ARI/ESL]
       │
       ▼  (Direct Regional Carrier RTP Path: G.711 / Opus)
[Tier-1 Wholesale SIP Trunk POP (Telnyx / Twilio Elastic SIP / Local PRI-SIP Gateway)]

In this architecture:

  • Kamailio terminates the browser's WSS WebSocket connection, authenticates ephemeral credentials, and forwards lightweight SIP signaling to Asterisk/FreeSWITCH.
  • rtpengine (running in Linux kernel-space forwarding via xt_RTPENGINE) anchors the browser's DTLS-SRTP stream at the closest regional edge POP and bridges it directly to the carrier's RTP stream without routing voice audio through your central application database server.

Codec Engineering Matrix: Opus vs. G.711 (ulaw/alaw) vs. G.722 vs. G.729

Choosing the wrong audio codec—or transcoding unnecessarily between codecs—destroys call clarity and inflates CPU load. Here is how the four primary VoIP codecs compare in production contact centers:

Audio Codec Sample Rate Bitrate (With IP/UDP/RTP Headers) Max Theoretical MOS Score Packet Loss Resilience (FEC / PLC) CPU Transcoding Cost Best Production Use Case
Opus (RFC 6716) 8 kHz – 48 kHz (Dynamic) 24 – 64 kbps (Adaptive) 4.50 (HD Wideband) Exceptional (Built-in In-Band FEC recovers up to 15% packet loss) Moderate Mandatory #1 choice for WebRTC browser agents and mobile softphones on variable Wi-Fi/LTE
G.711 (PCMU / PCMA) 8 kHz (Narrowband) 87.2 kbps (64 kbps payload) 4.41 (PSTN Toll Quality) Low (Relies on basic receiver PLC; struggles above 2% packet loss) Zero / Native Standard for PSTN SIP trunks and LAN-wired office IP desk phones
G.722 (Wideband) 16 kHz (Wideband) 87.2 kbps (64 kbps payload) 4.50 (HD Voice) Low-Moderate Very Low Internal extension-to-extension HD calls across office hardware phones
G.729 (Compressed) 8 kHz (Narrowband) 31.2 kbps (8 kbps payload) 3.92 (Compressed) Poor (1–2% packet loss causes audible metallic artifacts) High Legacy satellite/2G links only — avoid in modern 2026 deployments

Golden Rule of Codec Negotiation: Configure Opus (with useinbandfec=1; usedtx=0; maxaveragebitrate=32000) on the WebRTC leg between the agent's browser and your edge relay so last-mile home Wi-Fi jitter and 3–5% packet loss are absorbed cleanly by Opus Forward Error Correction (FEC). Negotiate G.711 (ulaw/alaw) on the fiber-backed datacenter leg to the PSTN SIP trunk.

Side-by-Side Configuration: Broken NAT/WebRTC Setup vs. Production pjsip.conf + QoS

1. Broken pjsip.conf Endpoint (Causes One-Way Audio & 30-Second Call Drops) 

; BROKEN CONFIG: Missing external media IP, symmetric RTP, and ICE/DTLS WebRTC settings
[agent-webrtc-broken]
type=endpoint
context=from-internal
disallow=all
allow=ulaw
aors=agent-webrtc-broken
; Result: SDP advertises private RFC1918 IP (10.0.1.14), causing complete one-way silence!

2. Hardened Production Asterisk 20 pjsip.conf for WebRTC + SIP Trunking 

; 1. Transport Layer with Explicit Public NAT Signaling & Media Addresses
[transport-wss]
type=transport
protocol=wss
bind=0.0.0.0:8089
external_signaling_address=pbx-edge.yourcompany.com
external_media_address=203.0.113.45
local_net=10.0.0.0/8

; 2. Hardened WebRTC Agent Endpoint Template (Opus + DTLS-SRTP + Symmetric RTP)
[webrtc-agent-template](!)
type=endpoint
context=agent-outbound
disallow=all
allow=opus,ulaw,alaw
webrtc=yes
dtls_auto_generate_cert=no
dtls_cert_file=/etc/letsencrypt/live/pbx-edge.yourcompany.com/fullchain.pem
dtls_private_key=/etc/letsencrypt/live/pbx-edge.yourcompany.com/privkey.pem
dtls_verify=fingerprint
dtls_setup=actpass
ice_support=yes
media_encryption=dtls
rtp_symmetric=yes
force_rport=yes
rewrite_contact=yes
direct_media=no
tos_audio=ef
cos_audio=5
timers=yes
timers_min_se=90
timers_sess_expires=1800

Key parameters in that template:

  • rtp_symmetric=yes & force_rport=yes: Sends return audio to the exact NAT source IP/port, curing 95% of one-way audio bugs.
  • direct_media=no: Disables peer-to-peer RTP reinvites across symmetric NATs.
  • tos_audio=ef (DSCP 46): Tags UDP voice packets with DiffServ Expedited Forwarding QoS priority.
  • timers=yes (1800s): Terminates hung ghost calls if a browser tab crashes.

3-Year TCO Comparison: Commercial CCaaS ($140/Seat) vs. Custom WebRTC + SIP PBX (100 Seats)

Below is an actual 3-year financial comparison for a 100-agent contact center logging 250,000 outbound/inbound minutes per month with CRM screen-pops and call recording:

Cost Category (100 Active Agents) Per-Seat Commercial CCaaS (RingCentral / Genesys / Five9) Custom WebRTC + Asterisk/FreeSWITCH + Wholesale SIP (Loop Origin Build)
Upfront Engineering & CRM Integration $12,000 – $25,000 (Implementation consultant fees) $24,000 – $42,000 (100% custom-engineered WebRTC dialer + PBX + CRM sync)
Annual Agent Seat Licenses (100 Seats) $168,000 / year ($140/seat/month) $0 / year (Unlimited agent extensions, supervisors & queues)
Wholesale SIP Minutes (250k mins/mo US/UK) $36,000 – $54,000/yr (Bundled overages & $0.015+/min markups) $18,000 – $24,000/yr (Direct wholesale carrier rates ~$0.006–$0.008/min)
Call Recording Storage (S3 Object Storage) $9,600 – $18,000/yr (Proprietary cloud storage add-on tiers) $720 / year (Automated Opus/MP3 compression to AWS S3 / Cloudflare R2)
Dedicated Cloud Servers & Managed SLA Included in seat tax $6,000 – $10,800/yr (Multi-region HA compute & 24/7 monitoring)
3-Year Cumulative Total Cost (TCO) $652,800 – $745,000 $98,160 – $146,400 (Saves $500,000+ over 3 years)

Beyond the $500,000+ 3-year savings, owning your contact center stack unlocks deep workflow automation: incoming calls trigger sub-100ms WebSocket screen-pops inside your custom Laravel + Vue CRM, dispositions update lead stages automatically without dual data entry, and post-call audio files flow directly into your own private transcription and QA scoring queue.

The 7-Point Production VoIP & WebRTC Hardening Checklist

  • [ ] Enforce Opus with In-Band FEC on Browser Legs: Set useinbandfec=1 so 2–5% Wi-Fi packet loss is reconstructed without audible clicks.
  • [ ] Deploy Regional coturn / rtpengine Relays: Anchor media in the same continent as your agent workforce (<40ms ping to relay).
  • [ ] Lock Down SIP Port 5060 Against Toll Fraud: Never expose UDP 5060 to 0.0.0.0/0.
  • [ ] Set Per-Destination Outbound Rate & Spend Caps: Configure carrier-level daily spend limits and block high-risk international premium prefixes (+882, +252, satellite ranges) in your dialplan.
  • [ ] Tag RTP Traffic with DSCP EF (tos_audio=ef): Prioritize UDP voice packets on office routers and VLANs.
  • [ ] Stream RTCP-XR Telemetry (MOS, Jitter, RTT): Log per-call packet loss and jitter metrics into PostgreSQL so supervisors can immediately tell whether bad audio came from an agent's ISP or a carrier trunk.
  • [ ] Automate Post-Call Recording Offload to S3/R2: Convert raw .wav recordings to 32kbps mono .mp3 or .opus via background workers after hangup, shrinking storage footprints by 88%.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

1. Should we build on Asterisk 20/22 LTS or FreeSWITCH for a custom contact center?

For contact centers under 300 to 500 concurrent calls per node, Asterisk 20/22 LTS with chan_pjsip and the Asterisk REST Interface (ARI) is exceptionally fast to build, maintain, and integrate with web backends.

2. Why do WebRTC browser calls sometimes fail to connect for agents on corporate VPNs or strict firewalls?

Corporate firewalls sometimes block arbitrary high UDP ports (10000–40000).

3. What causes "one-way audio" where the customer hears the agent, but the agent hears silence?

One-way audio is almost always a Session Description Protocol (SDP) NAT mismatch: the PBX or SIP gateway wrote its internal private IP (10.x.x.x or 172.16.x.x) into the SDP c= (connection) line instead of its public elastic IP, so the remote endpoint sends return RTP packets to an unroutable private address.

4. How much internet bandwidth does a 50-seat office need for simultaneous VoIP calls?

With G.711 (87.2 kbps per call with Ethernet/IP/UDP headers) or Opus (~45–60 kbps), 50 simultaneous active calls consume only 3.0 to 4.5 Mbps of symmetric upload/download bandwidth.

5. Can we keep our existing business phone numbers when migrating off RingCentral or a legacy PBX?

Yes.

6. How do we integrate a custom Asterisk/WebRTC dialer into our existing Laravel, React, or Vue CRM?

We embed a lightweight SIP.js or JsSIP WebRTC softphone component directly inside your web application's navigation bar and connect your backend to Asterisk's AMI/ARI event stream. title: Findings Are Rows, Not Paragraphs: Modelling Internal Audits, Independence Rules and Corrective Action Loops in a Food ERP
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

Most compliance software treats an audit as a document: a PDF report with a date, a score and a list of findings typed as paragraphs. That works until someone asks the questions that actually matter. Which findings from the March audit are still open? Which corrective actions were closed without anyone checking they worked? Which problem has been found in three audits in a row?

A report cannot answer those questions. A data model can. This post walks through how we think about modelling internal audits, findings and corrective action loops in an ERP for food and agro manufacturers in East Africa. The operational checklist behind it is in the original article.

What the domain rules say

The requirements read like a spec:

  • ISO 19011:2026 (published May 2026) defines an audit as a "systematic, independent and documented process for obtaining objective evidence and evaluating it objectively to determine the extent to which the audit criteria are fulfilled". Internal audits are "first-party" audits. Its listed principles include independence, an evidence-based approach and a risk-based approach. Source
  • Codex CXC 1-1969: verification "should be carried out by someone other than the person who is responsible for performing the monitoring and corrective actions"; root cause analysis "should be conducted where possible"; corrective actions should be reviewed periodically "to identify trends and to ensure corrective actions are effective". Source
  • 21 CFR 117.165: monitoring and corrective action records must be reviewed "within 7 working days after the records are created" (or a justified longer timeframe). Source
  • 21 CFR 117.170: the food safety plan must be reanalysed "at least once every 3 years", and sooner after significant changes or when a control is found ineffective. Source

Translated: an audit has a scope, criteria and auditors; auditors must not audit their own area; findings are discrete, graded, evidence-backed records; every finding needs a root cause and an owned, dated action; closure needs independent verification; and the system must be able to see repeats and trends over time.

The core entities 

AuditArea        (id, name, risk_level, owner_user_id, max_interval_days)
AuditProgramme   (id, year, approved_by, approved_at)
Audit            (id, programme_id, area_id, type, scope, criteria,
                  planned_for, performed_on, status)
AuditTeam        (audit_id, user_id, role)            -- lead, auditor, expert
Evidence         (id, audit_id, kind, ref, note)      -- record sample, observation, batch trace
Finding          (id, audit_id, area_id, clause_ref, grade,
                  requirement, observed, evidence_id, created_at)
CorrectiveAction (id, finding_id, root_cause, action, owner_user_id,
                  due_on, done_on, status)
Verification     (id, action_id, verified_by, verified_on, effective, note)

A few design choices matter more than the table names.

1. Findings are rows, not paragraphs

A finding with a grade, an area_id and a clause_ref can be counted, filtered, trended and escalated. A finding inside a free-text report cannot. Store the report as a rendering of the rows, never the other way round.

2. Independence is a constraint, not a policy

Codex and ISO both care about who audits. Make it impossible to break by accident:

-- reject an auditor who owns the audited area
CREATE FUNCTION check_auditor_independence() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
  IF EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM audit a JOIN audit_area ar ON ar.id = a.area_id
    WHERE a.id = NEW.audit_id AND ar.owner_user_id = NEW.user_id
      AND NEW.role IN ('lead','auditor')
  ) THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION 'Auditor owns the audited area';
  END IF;
  RETURN NEW;
END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

Small plants will need an override for the occasional exception. Make it explicit, reasoned and logged, so it shows up in review.

3. Corrective actions are a state machine 

open -> root_cause_found -> action_planned -> done -> verified_effective -> closed
                                               \-> verified_ineffective -> action_planned

Two rules carry most of the value:

  • action_planned requires a non-empty root_cause, an owner_user_id and a due_on. "Staff reminded" can be blocked by a short list of banned phrases, though a required "why" field does more.
  • closed requires a Verification row with effective = true and verified_by <> owner_user_id. The person who fixed it does not get to sign off that it is fixed.

4. Repeat findings are a query, not a memory

If findings carry area_id and clause_ref, a repeat is easy to detect:

SELECT f.area_id, f.clause_ref, COUNT(*) AS times_found,
       MIN(a.performed_on) AS first_seen, MAX(a.performed_on) AS last_seen
FROM finding f JOIN audit a ON a.id = f.audit_id
WHERE a.performed_on >= now() - interval '12 months'
GROUP BY f.area_id, f.clause_ref
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY times_found DESC;

Every row in that result is a corrective action that did not work. That is the trend review Codex asks for, in one statement.

5. Coverage is computed from the programme

Each AuditArea has a max_interval_days based on risk. Overdue areas fall out of a simple query:

SELECT ar.name, MAX(a.performed_on) AS last_audit,
       ar.max_interval_days
FROM audit_area ar
LEFT JOIN audit a ON a.area_id = ar.id AND a.status = 'completed'
GROUP BY ar.id
HAVING MAX(a.performed_on) IS NULL
    OR MAX(a.performed_on) < now() - (ar.max_interval_days || ' days')::interval;

6. Evidence links into operational data

The most useful audit step is tracing a real batch end to end. If Evidence.ref can point at a batch, a CCP record, a cleaning record or a QA hold in the same database, the auditor tests the live system rather than a printed copy, and the finding points straight at the record that failed.

7. Findings feed one corrective action system

Audit findings, customer complaints, supplier issues and process deviations all end in the same place: a non-conformance with a root cause and an action. Model one CorrectiveAction table with a source column rather than four separate trackers, so a manager sees one queue and trends across sources.

What this buys you

  • Open findings by grade, age and owner, with overdue actions on top.
  • Actions closed without independent verification (should be zero).
  • Areas overdue for audit against their risk-based interval.
  • Repeat findings in the last 12 months, by area and clause.

None of this is exotic. It is a handful of tables, a state machine and two or three constraints. The hard part is deciding that a finding is data, not prose.

FactoraERP is an ERP for food and agro manufacturers in East Africa, built by Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Full checklist: Food Safety Internal Audit Checklist.

title: Context or Knowledge: How LLMs Attribute Their Own Answers
description:
arXiv:2610.32109v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Language models can answer a question from a supplied document or from their parametric knowledge. When later asked where the answer came from, what determines their source report? We study this by intervening on the model's key-value (KV) cache after the answer is generated and before the source question is asked. On a controlled factual task with four models (7B-32B), changing or removing the document's cache never changes the report. In contrast, transplanting the question-and-answer (Q+A) cache between runs with identical question and answer tokens transfers it: every eligible report follows the donor, while the recipient's document is unchanged. On the two smaller models, steering Q+A values along directions fitted before any source question reverses 98.9-100% of reports across four document conditions at a fixed strength, while norm-matched random directions flip at most 1.1%. The components of keys and values along fitted directions carry the transplant effect: copying them alone nearly reproduces the report change; holding them fixed nearly prevents it. Applied during answer generation, the same value directions also change which source supplies the answer, though more weakly and depending on the prompt. Source reporting in this setting thus depends causally on cached state produced while answering. We do not establish general reporting accuracy or a complete interpretation of this state.

title: Understanding the Singleton Pattern: From Core Concept to Thread-Safe Java
description:
Imagine you are building an application with a settings screen. A user switches the app theme to "dark", and ten different screens across the app need to apply that choice.

If each screen instantiated its own settings object with new, one screen might read "dark" while another still holds "light". What you actually need is one single settings object that is initialized once, exists as a single unique instance, and is shared across your entire application.

That is the exact problem the Singleton design pattern was created to solve.

Defined by the Gang of Four (GoF) in Design Patterns, its intent comes down to two guarantees:

  1. Ensure a class has only one instance.
  2. Provide a global point of access to it.

A plain global variable gives you the second guarantee, but it never stops someone from calling new and creating another instance of that class. A Singleton gives you both—and it does so using three core pieces:

  • A private constructor: locks the front door so ordinary external code cannot instantiate the class with new.
  • A static access method (getInstance()): acts as the single reception desk that everyone must go through.
  • One cached instance: stored in a private static field and returned on every subsequent call.

The Textbook Java Implementation (and Why It Breaks)

If you write the classic lazy initialization version in Java—where the instance is created only when someone asks for it the first time—it looks like this:

public class AppConfig {
    private static AppConfig instance;        // the one and only instance
    private String theme = "dark";

    private AppConfig() { }                   // nobody else can call new

    public static AppConfig getInstance() {   // the global access point
        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new AppConfig();       // created on first request
        }
        return instance;
    }

    public String getTheme() { return theme; }
}

When you test this in a simple single-threaded main method, it works as expected:

AppConfig a = AppConfig.getInstance();
AppConfig b = AppConfig.getInstance();
System.out.println(a == b);   // true: both variables point to the same object

The Hidden Trap: Concurrency

This simple implementation has a critical flaw: it is only safe when one task runs at a time.

In a multithreaded application, picture what happens when Thread A and Thread B call getInstance() at the exact same moment:

  1. Thread A checks if (instance == null), sees that instance is null, and starts instantiating AppConfig.
  2. Before Thread A finishes creating and assigning the object, Thread B also calls getInstance(), sees that instance is still null, and enters the if block too.
  3. Both threads call new AppConfig(), leaving each thread holding a different instance.

It is just like two employees checking a cabinet, seeing there is no key yet, and each going off to have a new one made: individually, each person acted sensibly, but together they broke the "only one unique key" rule.

Fixing It in Java (Without Slowing Everything Down)

Developers have come up with several ways to make a Singleton thread-safe in Java, and each one trades something for something else:

  1. Eager initialization: create the instance right when the JVM loads the class—simple, but wasteful if the object is never used.
  2. synchronized method: put synchronized on getInstance()—thread-safe, but slow because threads must wait in line on every call.
  3. Double-checked locking: synchronize only on the first creation, using the volatile keyword so writes to instance are visible across threads and the JVM doesn't reorder the initialization steps inside new.
  4. The Bill Pugh Holder idiom: place the instance inside a nested static Holder class that isn't initialized until getInstance() is called: 
public class Logger {
    private Logger() { }

    private static class Holder {
        private static final Logger INSTANCE = new Logger();
    }

    public static Logger getInstance() {
        return Holder.INSTANCE;
    }

    public void log(String message) { System.out.println("LOG: " + message); }
}

Because the Java Language Specification (JLS) guarantees that the class initialization phase is sequential, the Holder idiom gives you lazy initialization and thread safety with no if, no synchronized, and no volatile.

  1. The enum Singleton: recommended as the preferred approach in a summary of Joshua Bloch's Effective Java, because it also guards against two sneaky ways a private constructor can be bypassed (Reflection and Serialization).

The Part We Need to Talk About: The Architectural Price

Even when you write a rock-solid, thread-safe Singleton, convenience comes with a real cost.

The very feature that makes Singleton so tempting—shared global access—is the same reason it:

  • Violates the Single Responsibility Principle (the class manages both its business logic and its own lifecycle/uniqueness)
  • Creates tight coupling across your codebase
  • Can mask bad design
  • Makes unit testing difficult due to shared global state

So before reaching for a Singleton, the most important question isn't just "how do I make it thread-safe?"—it's:

Does this component truly have to exist as a single unique instance, or am I using it just because it's handy?

Read the Full Deep Dive

I just published the full, fully cited article over on Leo's Station, where I walk through all of these pieces step by step, including:

  • A visual breakdown of how Singleton works vs. global variables
  • Detailed walkthroughs and summary cheat-sheet of all 5 Java approaches (Eager, synchronized, Double-checked locking, Holder idiom, and Enum)
  • How Reflection and Serialization (readResolve()) can break a Singleton's uniqueness
  • Where the standard Java library itself uses Singletons (Runtime.getRuntime(), Desktop.getDesktop())
  • A clear guide on when to use Singleton (loggers, config, caches, thread/DB pools) and when to think twice

Read the full article here:

Understanding the Singleton Pattern: From Core Concept to Thread-Safe Java — Leo's Station

Let's discuss!

When you need a single shared component in Java today, do you still write a Singleton (like the Holder idiom or an enum), or do you rely entirely on Dependency Injection / IoC containers? Share your thoughts below!

title: InstaBox: Free Cloud Sandboxes for AI Agents — Honest Notes After a Week of Testing
description:
InstaBox (instabox.sh), built by InsForge, is a cloud sandbox service made for AI agents — instead of running agent browser/automation work on your own machine, you spin up cloud machines and let the agent work there. It is currently an invite-based beta. I got in, activated the Free plan, and have been running two machines on it for about a week. Here is what is actually true about it.

What you get (Free plan)

  • Up to 5 machines; the agent-browser template is 4 vCPU / 8 GiB RAM / 20 GiB disk per machine
  • Files live on a persistent volume and survive pause, shutdown and reboot (only deleting the machine wipes them)
  • A real Chromium in the cloud your agent can drive, plus published HTTPS links / an SSH gateway to reach your services
  • Free plan is "never billed" in my account — the team describes the free tier as "free until we figure it out", so treat it as a generous beta, not a lifetime promise

What I used it for

  • A home base for browser automation that needs to stay logged in and reachable
  • Network experiments (Tailscale, exit routing) on a throwaway-but-persistent Linux box (Debian 13, systemd, sudo all work)

The honest limits (this is not a VPS replacement)

  • Machines auto-pause after ~30 minutes idle, and there is a max continuous run of ~8 hours — it is a workbench, not a 24/7 server
  • No public inbound IPv4 of your own; inbound is only via their HTTPS gateway links or SSH gateway
  • All machines share one NAT egress IP (a US AWS address, clean reputation but clearly a datacenter IP)

Verdict

As a free workbench for AI-agent experiments, I have not found anything else like it. If you are building agents that need a browser and a persistent Linux box, it is worth getting on the invite list at instabox.sh. Just do not plan your production hosting on a beta's free tier.
