title: Reproducible Evaluation as the Substrate for Safe Prompt Compression in Production Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.31972v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Evaluating conversational agents that act on live, mutable enterprise data is hard: replayed sessions drift as backend state changes, and a benchmark built today can silently go stale as the data it describes moves on. We present an offline evaluation harness for a production conversational agent that stays reproducible despite the live data it operates on changing, and that can be regenerated on demand once it goes stale. We then use this harness as the fitness function for GEPA-based prompt optimization under a correctness gate that guards against reward hacking. Applied to a production merchant-facing agent, correctness-gated compression shrinks the agent's full prompt surface by 3.5-7.6% without regressing held-out task correctness, consistently across three independent subject-model families, and for one, correctness measurably improves.

title: Node.js Chatbot API Endpoint Selection for Media Moderation (and Why Schemas Win)
description:
Node.js Chatbot API Endpoint Selection for Media Moderation (and Why Schemas Win)

Short answer: For a Node.js media-moderation chatbot, choose a synchronous API endpoint that returns schema-validated classifications, then put idempotency, retries, and human review in your own service boundary.

A moderation chatbot is the wrong mental model for this job. The application receives a report about media, classifies it before a human review, and must preserve an auditable decision trail. That constraint makes the best endpoint the one that can return a validated, schema-shaped decision synchronously, with a retry strategy that cannot create a second review record. The endpoint name is secondary.

The useful answer for a Node.js application in 2026 is therefore a narrow inference adapter behind your own queue and database boundary. Ask for a small classification object, validate it, store the raw request and normalized result, and treat every malformed or ambiguous response as a reviewable failure. Do not let a conversational response become an enforcement decision.

How should a Node.js chatbot choose an API endpoint for building?

Consider a report containing a short description, a media identifier, a reporter-selected reason, and a link to the relevant asset. The classifier does not need a paragraph. It needs a bounded result such as category, severity, confidence_band, and needs_human_review, plus a version for the policy that produced it.

That shape changes endpoint selection. A useful interface must support three properties: a request that can be retried with an idempotency key, a response that can be checked against a schema, and enough request metadata to connect the decision to the report without putting sensitive media details into logs by accident. A free-form chat response fails the second property even when the prose looks persuasive.

The database record should be the authority for the case. I would write the report and an inference-attempt row in one transaction, then let a worker claim that attempt. The worker can call the model runtime, validate the result, and append an immutable audit event. This is an exactly-once mindset applied honestly: the external inference call may be repeated, but the internal decision transition is idempotent.

Here is a deliberately vendor-neutral contract in Go. The production boundary can be implemented over a Node.js service, but the contract is easier to reason about when transport details are absent.

type ModerationDecision struct {
    Category         string `json:"category"`
    Severity         string `json:"severity"`
    ConfidenceBand   string `json:"confidence_band"`
    NeedsHumanReview bool   `json:"needs_human_review"`
    PolicyVersion    string `json:"policy_version"`
}

type Classifier interface {
    Classify(ctx context.Context, report ModerationReport, key string) (ModerationDecision, error)
}

The important field here is not confidence as a decorative score. It is the review rule. A low-confidence result, a disallowed category, or a schema failure should enter the same controlled path: hold the report for a person and record why.

Why is schema validation more important than conversational fluency?

A report classifier has asymmetric failure costs. A missed severe report can delay a human response; an invented category can corrupt queue routing; a missing field can break a downstream policy check. Fluent prose helps none of those cases.

I would use a JSON Schema-like contract with closed enumerations for category and severity, required fields, and a maximum length for any explanatory note. The validator runs after decoding and before the database transition. It must reject unknown values rather than quietly mapping them to a default. Defaults hide policy drift.

The Node.js adapter should also separate transport errors, validation errors, and policy ambiguity. They have different operational meanings and should not share one generic 500 metric. A timeout is a retry candidate. Invalid structured output is a model or prompt contract failure. A valid result that conflicts with a policy rule is a human-review case.

type FailureClass string

const (
    TransportFailure FailureClass = "transport"
    ContractFailure  FailureClass = "contract"
    PolicyReview     FailureClass = "policy_review"
)

func classifyFailure(err error) FailureClass {
    switch {
    case errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded):
        return TransportFailure
    case errors.Is(err, ErrInvalidDecision):
        return ContractFailure
    default:
        return PolicyReview
    }
}

This is where the endpoint comparison belongs, after the constraint is explicit. A chat-oriented endpoint may be convenient for dialogue state, but moderation triage generally needs a single bounded decision per report. A batch endpoint can improve throughput when latency is not part of the review promise, but it complicates cancellation and per-report retries. A realtime or browser-facing endpoint is designed for interactive media exchange, not for deciding whether a report enters a human queue; WebRTC is a transport and media API, not a moderation policy engine, as documented by MDN.

The trade-off is concrete:

Interface shape Good fit Boundary to accept
Synchronous structured response One report needs a decision before routing A slow call needs a deadline and a review fallback
Batch classification Large backlogs where review latency is flexible Per-report cancellation and retries become harder
Realtime media session Interactive audio or video exchange Transport convenience does not provide policy classification

No single interface wins every workload. A realtime session is the wrong choice for a queue decision, while a batch call is the wrong choice when the reviewer must see a result immediately.

Those are engineering boundaries, not rankings. The right choice is the interface whose guarantees match the workflow.

Where do retries and audit trails meet?

The dangerous implementation is easy to imagine: receive a report, call the endpoint, retry on a timeout, and insert the result twice when the first call actually completed. In a payment ledger I would never accept that ambiguity, and a moderation queue deserves the same discipline because an audit trail must explain both the decision and the attempts that preceded it.

Use a stable key derived from the report identifier, policy version, input digest, and classifier configuration. Persist it before dispatch. On retry, the worker reuses the key; it does not generate a fresh one. The result table enforces uniqueness on that key, while an append-only event table records submitted, received, validated, held_for_review, or failed.

The exact-once claim belongs inside your state machine, not around the remote call. A remote service can process a request while your client loses the response. On recovery, fetch the idempotent result if the interface supports it; otherwise mark the attempt as indeterminate and route it to reconciliation. Never infer success from a client timeout.

The reconciliation job is intentionally boring. It finds attempts with no terminal event, compares them with the result store, and emits one resolution event. That makes an operations dashboard useful: reviewers can distinguish an actual policy decision from a classifier that was unavailable.

How should a Node.js team test the decision boundary?

Start with a fixture set, not a provider benchmark. Include ordinary reports, duplicate reports, missing media references, mixed-language descriptions, adversarial instructions inside report text, and labels that sit close to the human-review threshold. Store expected routing outcomes and policy versions beside the fixtures. The test should fail if the response parses but violates the contract.

A small Node.js worker can keep the integration boundary explicit:

func handleReport(ctx context.Context, r ModerationReport) error {
    key := makeIdempotencyKey(r.ID, r.PolicyVersion, digest(r))

    if err := repository.StartAttempt(ctx, r.ID, key); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    decision, err := classifier.Classify(ctx, r, key)
    if err != nil {
        return repository.RecordFailure(ctx, r.ID, key, classifyFailure(err))
    }
    if err := validateDecision(decision); err != nil {
        return repository.RecordFailure(ctx, r.ID, key, ContractFailure)
    }

    return repository.CommitDecision(ctx, r.ID, key, decision)
}

The code is Go because the policy boundary should remain portable; the same sequence in Node.js should use an AbortSignal deadline, a bounded retry count, and a database transaction around the state transition. Test those mechanics separately from the model call. A mocked transport can prove idempotency. A fixture test can prove routing. A small canary can reveal distribution drift before the queue depends on it.

Logging needs equal restraint. Record identifiers, policy versions, latency buckets, validation outcomes, and retry counts. Do not log raw report text or media URLs by default. Access to the audit trail should follow the organization's retention and compliance limits; an audit log is not permission to retain every input forever.

A compact rollout path

Ship the classifier in shadow mode first. It writes a proposed decision and audit events but leaves human routing unchanged. Compare disagreement classes, not just aggregate agreement: missing fields, severe-label misses, duplicate handling, and policy-version mismatches expose different defects.

Then allow only low-risk categories to flow automatically, with an explicit kill switch that freezes automated transitions without deleting pending reports. Keep the old manual path available until reconciliation has been exercised against timeouts and duplicate delivery.

The final choice is less glamorous than a model comparison table. Pick the endpoint interface that can produce a bounded object, accept a stable retry identity, expose enough failure state for reconciliation, and fit your latency promise. This approach is unsuitable when the primary job is an open-ended conversation or live media transport; those workloads need different interaction and latency contracts. Put the policy in your system of record, validate before transition, and make human review the explicit destination for uncertainty. That is how a Node.js moderation chatbot becomes a dependable triage component rather than an untestable conversation.

title: DirCast: Live Esports Directing and Commentary with a Single Streaming Video-Language Model
description:
arXiv:2610.31734v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A live esports broadcast needs a director who chooses which camera goes on air and a caster who talks over that choice, every second and without knowing what comes next. Streaming video language models have learned to commentate, but only over a broadcast that a human director has already produced. We study live broadcast production, in which a model receives the raw camera of every player and must both direct and commentate from the past alone. We present DirCast, a single streaming video language model that does both. Every second it scans all cameras at low resolution, decides with a hold-or-switch director whether and where to cut, and reads the chosen camera at high resolution before it speaks. Its context keeps what went on air and what was said and lets the other views expire, which bounds the cost of a stream of any length. We build a dataset of 27 professional Dota 2 matches with a camera for every hero, the human director's choices and the casters' commentary. DirCast directs better than rule-based and zero-shot directors including GPT-5, and its commentary wins 29.2 percent of comparisons against GPT-4o under the Proact-VL protocol, against 19.4 percent for the strongest of eleven streaming commentators that watch the human broadcast.

title: Six things I fixed while building a 3D card gallery with React Three Fiber
description:
I run a small comparison site for crypto debit cards, and the main page is a 3D ring of 11 cards you can spin, tap and flip. It is built with React 19, @react-three/fiber, drei and three.js r185. You can try it here: cryptocardinsider.com/?view=gallery.

Getting a ring of cards on screen was the easy part. Making them look like real cards and run smoothly on a mid-range phone took most of the work. These are the fixes, with the code.

1. Use the real card proportions

My first cards were "roughly card shaped" and looked wrong next to the card art. Payment cards follow ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1: 85.60 × 53.98 mm with a 3.18 mm corner radius. I put those numbers in one constants file and derived everything else from them, including the texture size and the corner radius in pixels.

export const CARD_ISO = { widthMm: 85.6, heightMm: 53.98, cornerMm: 3.18 } as const

export const CARD_W = 1.42 // scene units
export const CARD_H = 0.89
export const CARD_CORNER_R = CARD_W * (CARD_ISO.cornerMm / CARD_ISO.widthMm)

export const CARD_TEX_W = 1024
export const CARD_TEX_H = 640

Once the mesh, the texture and the corner mask all come from the same ratio, the edges line up and the card stops looking like a tablet.

2. ShapeGeometry needs its own UVs

A rounded rectangle is easiest as a THREE.Shape with four absarc corners passed to ShapeGeometry. The catch is that the UVs it generates follow the shape's coordinates, not 0 to 1, so a photo texture comes out smeared. The fix is to remap every vertex into the bounding box:

function assignPlanarUVs(geo: THREE.ShapeGeometry) {
  const pos = geo.attributes.position as THREE.BufferAttribute
  const uv = geo.attributes.uv as THREE.BufferAttribute
  const bbox = new THREE.Box3().setFromBufferAttribute(pos)
  const size = new THREE.Vector3()
  bbox.getSize(size)

  for (let i = 0; i < pos.count; i++) {
    uv.setXY(i, (pos.getX(i) - bbox.min.x) / size.x, (pos.getY(i) - bbox.min.y) / size.y)
  }
  uv.needsUpdate = true
}

3. Clip the card art to the same rounded corners

Card images from different issuers arrive in different states. Some PNGs already have transparent rounded corners. Others are rectangles with a black or white background in the corners, which shows up as little dark triangles on the 3D mesh.

I draw each image to a canvas and cut the alpha to the ISO corner radius with destination-in:

const r = rh * (CARD_ISO.cornerMm / CARD_ISO.heightMm)
ctx.globalCompositeOperation = 'destination-in'
ctx.fillStyle = '#ffffff'
roundRectPath(ctx, rx, ry, rw, rh, r)
ctx.fill()
ctx.globalCompositeOperation = 'source-over'

Images that already have baked corners skip this step, because masking them twice leaves a thin halo.

4. Share one geometry across all cards

Every card has the same outline, so there is no reason to build 11 copies of it. A module-level singleton is enough:

let shared: THREE.ShapeGeometry | null = null

export function getSharedCardPlaneGeometry() {
  if (!shared) shared = createCardPlaneGeometry()
  return shared
}

Only the materials differ per card.

5. Pick a quality tier once, then scale everything from it

Phones were the problem. I now pick one of three tiers at startup from prefers-reduced-motion, a mobile check and navigator.hardwareConcurrency. A mobile device with 6 or fewer cores, or anything with 2 or fewer, gets low.

The tier then sets several things at once:

const maxDpr = tier === 'high' ? Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, 1.5)
  : tier === 'medium' ? 1.25 : 1

// textures: 1024×640 on high, 640×400 on medium, 512×320 on low
// floor segments: 64 / 48 / 32
// antialias off on low, powerPreference 'default' on low

Capping DPR at 1.5 even on the high tier matters more than it looks: at 3× DPR a canvas renders nine times the pixels of 1×, for detail you can barely see on a card. drei's <AdaptiveDpr pixelated /> lowers it further while the frame rate drops.

6. Stop rendering when nobody is looking

The canvas renders every frame while it is on screen, and not at all when the tab is hidden or the gallery is covered by another view:

const pageVisible = usePageVisible() // listens to visibilitychange
const canvasActive = pageVisible && !suspended

<Canvas frameloop={canvasActive ? 'always' : 'never'} /* ... */ />

With frameloop="never", a hidden tab draws no frames at all instead of spinning a WebGL loop in the background.

A small one: tap vs drag

On touch screens, a tap that moves a few pixels was being read as the start of a spin, so cards would not open. I now treat any pointer movement under 22 px as a tap. It is a small number, but it decides whether the gallery feels responsive or broken on a phone.

What it is for

The gallery compares fees, availability and scores for 11 crypto cards (KAST, RedotPay, Crypto.com, OKX and others). For RedotPay there is also a country availability checker built from its help center lists.

Disclosure: I'm a RedotPay partner and may earn a commission. If you order a RedotPay card, the code RDVIR took the virtual card from $10 to $8 and RDPHY took the physical card from $100 to $80 when I re-checked both in the app on October 26, 2026. The partner sign-up link is cryptocardinsider.com/go/devto (invite code xn03i), and checkout screenshots are on the promo code page. None of this is financial advice.

If you have built something similar in R3F, I'd like to hear how you handled texture memory on low-end phones.

title: GeoLEON-CLIP: Graph-Anchored Multimodal Contrastive Learning for Geographic Region Representation
description:
arXiv:2610.32311v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Geographic regions are multimodal: satellite imagery captures visual morphology, text conveys human-interpretable semantics, and map structures describe urban context. Existing geospatial contrastive methods typically align image-text or image-location pairs, underusing structured map data. We introduce GeoLEON-CLIP, a graph-anchored contrastive framework that aligns three views of each H3-indexed region: an OpenStreetMap-derived graph embedding, a satellite image crop, and a textual description. Frozen pretrained LEON graph embeddings provide a semantic anchor between vision and language. Frozen graph, image, and text encoders are connected by trainable residual projection heads and trained with a symmetric tri-modal contrastive objective. Experiments show strong graph-image and graph-text alignment; graph-image retrieval achieves the best cross-modal performance in a mixed-resolution pool. To evaluate the anchoring hypothesis, we propose chained cross-modal recall $\mathrm{R}@A@B$, which routes retrieval through the graph modality and compares it with direct retrieval under a matched candidate budget. At $\mathrm{R}@1@1$, image$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$text and text$\rightarrow$graph$\rightarrow$image outperform direct image-text retrieval by 4.8 and 4.4 points, respectively, despite using a single intermediate cell. Downstream probes show task-dependent gains, with the largest improvements on Airbnb and Beijing housing. These results indicate that OpenStreetMap graph structure can anchor multimodal representations combining maps, imagery, and language.

title: Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust--Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation
description:
arXiv:2610.31971v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in negotiations on behalf of individuals and organizations, yet they remain vulnerable to manipulation, particularly in repeated multi-party interactions. Classical multi-agent systems address this challenge through explicit trust and reputation models, whereas existing work on LLM negotiation largely treats trust as an emergent phenomenon. We investigate whether LLM agents can form useful trust estimates from prior interactions and leverage them to improve future negotiation outcomes. We introduce a repeated, multi-party, multi-issue negotiation framework in which recurring agents participate in a sequence of negotiation games while one participant covertly attempts to prevent agreement. After each game, agents assess their counterparts and maintain pairwise trust estimates that carry over to subsequent negotiations. We compare trust-aware and trust-agnostic agents and analyze how explicit trust influences negotiation outcomes. Our results reveal a \emph{trust--agreement gap}: trust-aware agents can identify the adversary within a few games, but accurate trust estimates do not consistently translate into better agreements. Trust increases agreement rates by up to 23 percentage points, but only when agents are explicitly guided to use it in their decisions. Explicit trust can therefore improve repeated LLM negotiations, but its value depends critically on how trust is assessed and incorporated into agents' reasoning.

title: How GCP Service Accounts Work for Database Access Tools
description:
If you've ever connected a third-party tool to a GCP project, you've run into the same ritual: create a service account, attach some roles, download a JSON key, paste it somewhere. Most DBAs do this on autopilot without stopping to think about what a service account actually is, which roles it really needs, and what happens if that JSON key leaks.

That's worth slowing down for. Service account permissions are one of the most common places database security goes quietly wrong — not through a sophisticated attack, but through a service account granted far more than it needed, because "Editor" was faster to click than figuring out the right role.

TL;DR

A GCP service account's permissions come entirely from the IAM roles you attach — there's no implicit access beyond that. For a tool that only needs to discover Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner instances, roles/cloudsql.viewer and roles/spanner.viewer are the only roles needed. 1DataCloud connects to GCP using exactly those two roles. Try it free →

What a GCP Service Account Actually Is

A service account is an identity — not a human one. It's what applications, scripts, and third-party tools use to authenticate to Google Cloud APIs, the way your own Google account authenticates you in the GCP Console.

The part that matters: a service account's permissions come entirely from the IAM roles you attach to it. There's no default level of access. A brand-new service account with no roles can do nothing.

Download its JSON key, and you're holding long-lived credentials for that identity. Anyone with that file can authenticate as the service account and do whatever its roles allow — which is exactly why the roles attached matter so much.

The Roles That Actually Matter for Database Discovery

For a tool that only needs to discover and inspect database instances — not modify them — two predefined roles cover it:

roles/cloudsql.viewer — read-only visibility into Cloud SQL: instance names, regions, tiers, versions, status, configuration. No create, modify, delete, or data access.

roles/spanner.viewer — the equivalent for Cloud Spanner: instance and database metadata, no schema or data modification.

Both are scoped specifically to metadata visibility for their service. Neither touches Compute Engine, billing, IAM, or anything else in the project.

What not to grant

The common shortcut is attaching Editor or Owner because it "definitely includes" whatever narrower permission is needed. It does — along with the ability to modify or delete nearly everything else in the project. A leaked key tied to a viewer role exposes metadata. A leaked key tied to Editor exposes your entire GCP project.

How 1DataCloud Uses This

1DataCloud's GCP connection runs on exactly roles/cloudsql.viewer and roles/spanner.viewer — nothing broader. With just those two roles, it uses the GCP API to discover every Cloud SQL and Cloud Spanner instance across every project the service account can see, automatically. No project-by-project browsing, no permissions beyond what's needed to build that inventory.

Once an instance is connected for querying, its schema is read and mapped so Query1AI can turn plain-English questions into read-only SQL — but the discovery step itself never required write access to anything.

If that JSON key were ever exposed, the worst case is someone viewing your database inventory metadata — not modifying a database, not touching unrelated GCP services, not reaching billing. That's a very different incident than a leaked key with Editor attached.

Mistakes Worth Avoiding

  • One service account for everything. A single, broadly-scoped account shared across five tools means a compromise of any one is a compromise of all five.
  • Keys that never rotate. A JSON key doesn't expire on its own.
  • Using the default Compute Engine service account, which often carries broad project-level permissions by default, for a narrow task like discovery.
  • Project-level roles when a resource-level one exists — even when the project-wide version is more convenient to click through.

Summary

A GCP service account is only as risky as the roles attached to it. For database discovery, roles/cloudsql.viewer and roles/spanner.viewer grant exactly enough visibility to build an inventory — nothing more. 1DataCloud's own GCP connection runs on exactly those two roles.

What's your team's policy on service account scoping — one per integration, or shared accounts with broader roles? Curious how others handle this in practice.

title: DS-BiCA-Net: Pair-Preserving Cross-Temporal Modeling for Remote Sensing Change Captioning
description:
arXiv:2610.32200v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Remote sensing image change captioning (RSICC) describes in natural language the semantic changes between two images of the same scene captured at different times. Previous methods commonly merge the pair during repeated processing or combine intra-image and cross-image relations in one operation, weakening source identity and leaving the two temporal directions implicit. Without separate modules for intra-image and cross-temporal processing and a separate path for each direction, the contribution of each part cannot be measured on its own, so it remains unclear which part matters most, and the design of later models has no such evidence to build on. To address these issues, we propose DS-BiCA-Net, which assigns the two kinds of processing to separate modules and keeps the two images as separate streams throughout the encoder. A windowed state-space module models context within each image, and a bidirectional cross-attention module compares the two images along two directed paths that share their projections. The two modules use the same pre-normalisation residual architecture and differ only in their mixers, and the two streams are fused only in the aggregation head, so each module and each direction can be removed and its contribution measured on its own. Controlled experiments on LEVIR-CC and Dubai-CC examine operator interaction, temporal direction and module order, showing that intra-image refinement carries no benefit alone and becomes beneficial only when followed by bidirectional cross-attention, an order that outperforms the reverse at matched parameter count and FLOPs. The bidirectional module also outperforms either temporal direction alone. Our method reaches an S_m^* of 82.65 on LEVIR-CC, the highest among the published results compared, and 66.72 on Dubai-CC without geometric augmentation, the second-highest among the published results compared.

title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.32212v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

title: TaxoSAE: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders through Taxonomic Logic
description:
arXiv:2610.31894v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) decompose the representations of large language models (LLMs) into interpretable features, enabling precise readout and control of encoded knowledge. However, existing SAEs treat each feature as a standalone unit, whereas real-world knowledge is often taxonomically organized. As a result, readout carries no guarantee of taxonomic consistency, and control lacks the granularity to specify the scope of an edit. We propose TaxoSAE, which explicitly encodes taxonomical information, built on is-a (hypernym-hyponym) relations, into the SAE feature space. TaxoSAE mirrors a taxonomy with a stack of SAEs, one per taxonomy level, and introduces a taxonomic alignment loss that trains each concept to be active whenever one of its hyponyms is. On two factual QA taxonomies, one over biographical relations and one over animals, TaxoSAE enables (1) more accurate readout through the taxonomy with concentrated activations, e.g., +31.3 points in reading out the hypernyms of abstract concepts never queried in training; (2) more precise control, with +25.5 points in swap success, while suppressing a concept removes only its own answers (0-2% accuracy vs. 91-100% on other concepts); and, more importantly, (3) readout of unseen concepts through their hypernyms, with up to +37.9 points in hypernym readout accuracy.

title: PatchGarden 🌱: I Built an AI Maintenance Engineer That Doesn't Trust Its Own Patches
description:
This is my submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 3 — Slow and Steady.

PatchGarden 🌱: I Built an AI Maintenance Engineer That Doesn't Trust Its Own Patches

AI can write code in seconds. But when it breaks your repository, who makes sure the fix actually works?

We've reached a point where generating code is becoming easier than ever. AI coding tools can suggest implementations, explain errors, and produce patches almost instantly.

But there's a problem I kept coming back to:

Generating a fix is easy. Knowing whether it's safe to trust that fix is a different problem.

A patch can look convincing, modify the right-looking file, and still introduce a regression. A green-looking AI response doesn't mean the bug is gone.

Meanwhile, open-source maintainers are left dealing with failing tests, neglected issues, dependency problems, and maintenance work that never seems to end.

For Hacktoberfest's Slow and Steady challenge, I wanted to explore a different approach.

Instead of building another AI tool that generates more code, I wanted to build something that helps developers spend less time babysitting maintenance work.

Meet PatchGarden — an AI-powered repository maintenance project built around one principle:

Don't trust a patch because AI generated it. Collect evidence, verify the result, and let the developer decide.

🌿 What is PatchGarden?

PatchGarden is designed to help developers investigate repository failures, generate minimal repair proposals, verify changes, and preserve an auditable history of the process.

Think of a developer who returns to a project after months away. There are failing tests, an issue backlog, and a bug report that nobody has had time to investigate.

Instead of manually navigating every step, the developer can delegate a focused maintenance task to PatchGarden.

The intended workflow is:

Investigate → Plan → Patch → Verify → Review

Here's what each stage means:

  • Investigate: Inspect relevant code and diagnostic evidence to understand the reported failure.
  • Plan: Produce a structured repair plan with a clear hypothesis and defined verification criteria.
  • Patch: Generate a minimal, reviewable candidate change in an isolated workspace.
  • Verify: Run the relevant tests and compare the results against the baseline.
  • Review: Present the diff and evidence so a human can approve or reject the proposed repair.

If the evidence is insufficient or the tests fail, the system should report that honestly instead of pretending the task succeeded.

The goal isn't autonomous code modification at any cost. It's making repository maintenance less tedious without sacrificing developer control.

🦥 Why does this fit Slow and Steady?

Software maintenance is rarely one dramatic task. It's hundreds of small jobs that developers keep postponing.

Investigate that failing test. Reproduce that bug. Check that dependency. Review that patch. Rerun the suite. Figure out what happened when the process failed halfway through.

Individually, these tasks seem manageable. Collectively, they become maintenance debt.

PatchGarden explores how open-source AI can help with that repetitive work while keeping the developer responsible for the final decision.

The Lazy Payoff

Delegate the investigation. Review the evidence. Spend your attention where it actually matters.

Rather than trying to replace the developer, PatchGarden aims to remove the repetitive work surrounding a repair.

🧠 The important engineering decision: AI proposes, tools verify

I didn't want the entire application to depend on a model saying, "I've fixed it."

An AI model can produce malformed output, misunderstand a code path, or confidently suggest an incorrect repair. That means the model cannot be the authority on whether a patch is correct.

The architecture separates reasoning from execution:

1. Open-weight AI for investigation

The project is designed around Google's open-weight Gemma 3 (4B) running locally on Ollama. A smaller local model creates a healthy engineering constraint: instead of assuming a massive cloud model can magically fix everything, the system limits the context, validates structured JSON outputs, and relies on deterministic tooling for execution. Local inference keeps repository code private and eliminates external API token fees.

2. A controlled execution layer

Repository inspection, Git operations, test execution, and workflow state are handled by explicit application logic rather than arbitrary model-generated shell commands. Model output is treated as untrusted input. Paths are validated, operations are restricted to isolated Git worktrees, and candidate changes are kept strictly quarantined from the main branch.

3. Independent verification

The system distinguishes between generating a patch and demonstrating that the patch passes configured checks. A complete repair record contains:

  • The original failure and diagnostic evidence.
  • The proposed change and Git diff.
  • The verification commands and their exit codes.
  • Any errors or regressions encountered.
  • The final maintainer review decision.

Passing tests don't prove that every bug is fixed. They provide evidence that the candidate passes the checks we actually ran. That distinction matters.

♻️ What happens when the process stops halfway through?

A maintenance workflow can take multiple steps. A process can crash, a model can time out, or a machine can restart before the job finishes. Simply storing the active task in application memory is not enough.

PatchGarden relies on Temporal durable workflow orchestration paired with persistent SQLite domain state (patchgarden.db) and immutable JSONL audit logs. Workflow state transitions are recorded before and after each phase. If the worker process restarts mid-repair, Temporal rehydrates the execution history, validates saved checkpoints, and resumes execution without re-running completed work or dirtying the repository.

🔓 Why open innovation matters

Open-source AI is not just a label in PatchGarden's technology stack. It creates an opportunity to design the system around model choice, inspectable behavior, and developer-controlled infrastructure:

  • Model flexibility: Maintainers can swap models or run different quantization levels locally.
  • Local inference & privacy: Source code, proprietary internal libraries, and sensitive test logs never leave the developer's workstation.
  • Cost control: Local open-weight models have zero token fees, allowing extensive multi-stage investigation and repair loops.
  • Transparency: The entire toolchain—from prompt schemas to worktree managers—is open-source and inspectable.

🛠️ How I built it

PatchGarden brings together a broadsheet-inspired web interface, a typed backend API, a durable worker engine, and local open-weight AI:

  • Project repository: GitHub — Neet2516/PatchGarden
  • Live application: https://patchgarden-web.onrender.com
  • Technologies:
    • Frontend: Next.js 14 (App Router, React, CSS)
    • API: Fastify (Node.js & TypeScript)
    • Durable Orchestration: Temporal Cloud / Temporal local server
    • Persistence: SQLite (better-sqlite3) & structured JSONL audit logs
    • Inference Runtime: Gemma 3 (4B) via local Ollama
    • Isolation: Git worktrees for clean verification environments
    • Deployment: Render (Hosting the web dashboard and API)

📸 Application Interface & Candidate Patch Review

Here is the live interface running in production on Render:

🎥 See PatchGarden in action

  • Watch the demo: PatchGarden — YouTube
  • Try the application: https://patchgarden-web.onrender.com
  • Explore the source code: https://github.com/Neet2516/PatchGarden

The most important part of a demonstration is not how confidently the AI explains its answer. It's whether the workflow produces inspectable evidence of what happened.

🧪 What I would measure next

A trustworthy maintenance tool needs more than a polished interface. I would evaluate PatchGarden against a reproducible benchmark of deliberately seeded bugs and measure:

  1. Root-cause identification accuracy.
  2. Clean patch application rates across diverse codebases.
  3. Test suite pass rates and regression detection sensitivity.
  4. Workflow recovery fidelity across simulated power and worker outages.
  5. In-flight token latency and memory footprint of local 4B models.
  6. The accuracy of the system's "refusal to patch" when diagnostic evidence is ambiguous.

🌱 What comes next?

The long-term direction is a maintenance assistant that developers can trust with repetitive investigations without surrendering control of their repositories. That means deeper AST-aware repair suggestions, tighter containerized sandboxing, reproducible evaluations, and clearer explanations of uncertainty.

The goal isn't to build an AI that never makes mistakes. It's to build a system that makes mistakes visible, limits their impact, and refuses to confuse a plausible answer with a verified result.

🏆 Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Render:

PatchGarden's production web dashboard and API service are deployed on Render at https://patchgarden-web.onrender.com using a multi-service render.yaml blueprint with monorepo build orchestration.

  • Best Use of Temporal:

PatchGarden uses Temporal for durable workflow orchestration, enabling maintenance jobs to progress through defined stages with workflow state, retries, and recovery. This integration supports the project's central goal: making repository maintenance reliable even when individual steps fail.

  • Local AI with Ollama :

PatchGarden uses Ollama as its local model inference runtime, allowing the application to run a supported model locally for repository analysis and repair proposals. This supports experimentation with open-weight AI while keeping model execution separate from deterministic patch verification.

🤖 My Agent Session

Here is the genuine DevRelay agent session documenting the end-to-end development, debugging, and deployment of PatchGarden:

PatchGarden: Building an AI Maintenance Engineer
You

Build PatchGarden: an AI maintenance engineer that investigates bugs, generates minimal patches, and verifies them in isolation using Gemma 3 and Temporal.

Agent

I will design and implement PatchGarden following the Slow and Steady philosophy: open-weight Gemma 3 model, Temporal durable workflow orchestration, SQLite persistence, and Git worktree verification.

▸ run_command git status
Input
$ git status
Output
Workspace initialized with core, api, worker, and web packages.
You

Deploy the web dashboard to Render and configure build scripts.

Agent

Configured render.yaml with npm install --include=dev to ensure TypeScript and React dependencies build cleanly in production. Successfully deployed to https://patchgarden-web.onrender.com.

4 of 4 messages

Direct Session Link: https://dev.to/agent_sessions/patchgarden-building-an-ai-maintenance-engineer-lszqv4

💬 I'd love your feedback

If you maintain open-source projects, what's the maintenance task you keep putting off? Is it reproducing bugs, triaging issues, fixing flaky tests, or reviewing changes generated by AI?

I'd love to learn which part of this workflow would save maintainers the most time—and what evidence you'd need before trusting an AI-proposed patch.

Slow and steady. Evidence before assumptions. Verification before approval.

title: Go Queue Comparison for Webhook Rate Limiting — SQS, QStash, Cloud Tasks Retry
description:
Short answer: schedule a game cleanup by enqueuing an operation ID, let a worker perform the cleanup after the web request has returned, and make the business mutation idempotent. For rate-limited webhook processing across US and EU deployments, compare managed queues on dispatch control, retry and dead-letter queue (DLQ) recovery before comparing their bills. At-least-once delivery means a duplicate is a normal input, not proof that the scheduler failed.

Which page fires when cleanup runs twice?

Picture a match closing while a periodic sweep expires stale lobby reservations. The HTTP handler should return without waiting for that sweep. If the worker commits its change but loses its acknowledgment, a later delivery can attempt the same operation again. The useful page identifies a stuck cleanup window or growing failed-task count, with the operation ID carried through the worker and DLQ; a green scheduler dashboard cannot establish that reservations changed exactly once.

Start the incident review with the operation, not the transport: which mutation committed, which durable record blocks its repetition, and which failed message can an operator safely redrive? Use a stable ID for a lobby and cleanup window, not an ID generated per delivery. A database uniqueness constraint beside the business mutation survives a worker restart and a late redrive. A short transport deduplication window does not.

No page for that? Fix the signal before changing vendors.

Where does the timer hand off to the worker?

The timer should enqueue a small job and return; the worker claims the operation, changes the game's records, and acknowledges after commit. A transient failure gets bounded backoff, followed by DLQ inspection if retries are exhausted. The operator checks the durable operation state before redrive because an acknowledged message disappears, and the queue is not a permanent replay log.

Infrai is a possible fit when a Go timer and worker need a plain REST API: no vendor SDK or client-library version is required.

Infrai's second advantage is one key, one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules. A single API key covers both cron and queue, so the team does not have to manage separate credentials or reconcile separate invoices for this handoff. Its self-describing API has public discovery that returns full request and response schemas without a key, plus runnable examples in 10 languages for documented capabilities. The on-call engineer can inspect the actual timer and queue contracts before changing a recovery script, instead of guessing a request field and turning a redrive into another failed job. These advantages do not buy exactly-once execution. Standard queues deliver at least once, FIFO deduplication lasts five minutes, delayed messages stop at seven days, bodies at 256 KB, and retained messages at 30 days. Its cron execution limit is 900 seconds, so a long sweep belongs in the cron-to-queue-to-worker path. Cron HTTP targets must be public, and push subscriptions need public HTTPS; an internal-only receiver should consume instead of waiting for a push callback.

The following Go command lists queues during triage. It deliberately makes no write request: publishing a real cleanup requires a durable operation ID and an idempotent consumer, which an HTTP example alone cannot supply. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in the environment.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "provide INFRAI_API_KEY")
        os.Exit(2)
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        endpoint := "https://api." + "infrai.cc/v1/queue/list"
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil { panic(err) }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil { panic(readErr) }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
                fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "queue list: HTTP %d: %s\n", resp.StatusCode, body)
                os.Exit(1)
            }
            fmt.Println(string(body))
            return
        }
        delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
        if n, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))); err == nil && n >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(n) * time.Second
        }
        select {
        case <-time.After(delay):
        case <-ctx.Done(): panic(ctx.Err())
        }
    }
    fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "queue list: rate limit persisted after retries")
    os.Exit(1)
}

That list is a triage aid, not evidence that cleanup committed. Put a unique operation_id and the reservation change in the same database transaction, then acknowledge after commit. If a webhook to another service follows, the database transaction cannot make that remote call atomic; use an outbox and a downstream idempotency key where supported. A delayed retry schedules another attempt but cannot enforce a rate limit: bound worker concurrency and apply a rate limiter at dispatch.

How should we compare SQS and QStash queues for webhook rate limiting and retry?

For the gaming cleanup, the main distinction is who controls dispatch and where the worker can run. These are integration trade-offs, not a price ranking; check the actual region and residency requirements for a US/EU rollout rather than inferring them from a product name.

Option Integration and setup Good fit Main boundary
AWS SQS AWS API; poll from an existing AWS worker Polling workers with visibility timeout and DLQ redrive Standard delivery is at least once; pace webhooks in the worker
Google Cloud Tasks Google Cloud API; configure HTTP dispatch rate and retries HTTP receivers needing queue-level dispatch controls HTTP target and its authentication must be designed together
Upstash QStash HTTP-oriented publish and delivery Delayed delivery to a reachable webhook A strictly private receiver needs a separate ingress design
CloudAMQP RabbitMQ Managed broker and RabbitMQ client protocol Existing exchange and binding requirements Broker routing and consumer configuration remain your responsibility
Infrai Plain REST from any HTTP client; one key for cron and queue Small scheduled jobs feeding an idempotent worker No native throttle or debounce; push needs public HTTPS

Cloud Tasks deserves first evaluation if queue-level HTTP dispatch rate control is the deciding requirement. SQS suits a worker already polling inside AWS. CloudAMQP makes sense when RabbitMQ routing is part of the design rather than an incidental dependency; QStash suits a public webhook delivery path. Infrai's common credential and publicly discoverable schemas reduce integration friction between timer and queue, including when an operator has to inspect the contract during recovery, but do not replace the worker's rate limiter. It has no workflow DAG, fan-out/join primitive, or Kafka-style replay. Choose on the failure mode you must operate, not the number of boxes on a dashboard.

How do we verify and roll back the run?

Before enabling the timer, submit one operation ID twice in a test environment and verify one durable mutation. Stop a worker after commit but before acknowledgment; the retry should detect the committed ID and avoid repeating the side effect. Exercise a transient error, delayed retry, DLQ inspection, and controlled redrive. Watch backlog age and failures alongside completion by operation ID. Which page fired, and can it name the missing cleanup window?

For rollback, pause new scheduling and reconcile in-flight IDs against committed operations before stopping consumers. Inspect failed jobs individually before redrive; do not purge the queue as a substitute for diagnosis. Resume with limited concurrency and watch downstream rate-limit responses. A paused cron does not backfill missed triggers, so calculate missing cleanup windows explicitly. If a sweep needs longer than 900 seconds, keep the timer as a trigger and let workers do the work.

References

  • AWS SQS standard queue delivery: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues-at-least-once-delivery.html
  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • Google Cloud Tasks queue configuration: https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/configuring-queues
  • Upstash QStash documentation: https://upstash.com/docs/qstash/overall/getstarted
  • CloudAMQP RabbitMQ documentation: https://www.cloudamqp.com/docs/
  • PostgreSQL conflict handling: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-insert.html
  • GitHub Actions schedule documentation: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.32120v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Complex text-to-image requests remain difficult to satisfy reliably. Verifying and repairing an image can fix an individual output, but a successful repair does not necessarily carry over to other requests. We present ImageRSI, a framework that keeps the image generator frozen and combines three components: five-dimensional verification and repair within each task, an experience library shared across tasks, and offline updating of the judge. Candidate experiences enter the library only after paired A/B validation, and the judge is updated with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on accumulated image-judgment records and evaluated before reuse. We also introduce ImageReq-Bench, a benchmark of 961 requests built around hard cases in real-world image-generation requests, each paired with an evaluation checklist. ImageRSI achieves a Checklist Strict Accuracy (CSA) of 52.6% on MindBench (with Nano Banana Pro as the generator) and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench, and we compare system outcomes across judge-training configurations.

title: Building and Using Polyfills in JavaScript: Bridging the Gap for Browser Compatibility
description:
JavaScript is an ever-evolving language with new features and APIs introduced regularly. But not all browsers update at the same pace—older or less popular browsers often lack support for modern features. This is where polyfills come in: they act as a bridge to fill in missing functionality so developers can use modern JavaScript features without breaking compatibility.

In this post, we’ll explore what polyfills are, how they work, and how to create and use them effectively.

What Is a Polyfill?

A polyfill is a piece of code (typically JavaScript) that implements functionality missing from older browsers or environments. Instead of relying on the browser to support a feature natively, a polyfill detects the absence of that feature and provides the same or similar behavior through code.

Polyfills enable developers to write modern code and still support a wide range of browsers, ensuring a consistent user experience.

Why Use Polyfills?

  • Cross-browser compatibility: Make new language features like Array.prototype.includes or new APIs like fetch work in browsers that don’t support them.
  • Future-proofing: As browsers catch up, native implementations take precedence, but polyfills keep apps running smoothly in the meantime.
  • Reduce fragmentation: Avoid writing different code paths for different browsers.

Improve developer experience: Use modern syntax and APIs confidently without worrying about users with legacy browsers.

How Do Polyfills Work?

Polyfills rely on feature detection to check if a feature exists. If not, the polyfill defines the feature.

Example: Polyfill for Array.prototype.includes (ES2016)

js
if (!Array.prototype.includes) {
  Array.prototype.includes = function(searchElement, fromIndex) {
    var len = this.length;
    if (len === 0) return false;
    var start = fromIndex || 0;
    for (var i = start; i < len; i++) {
      if (this[i] === searchElement) return true;
    }
    return false;
  };
}

This code checks if includes exists, and if not, defines it to behave as expected.

Building Your Own Polyfill: Best Practices

  • Detect before defining: Always check if the feature already exists to avoid overwriting native implementations.
  • Mimic spec behavior: Follow the official specification closely to match behavior, edge cases, and exceptions.
  • Keep it minimal: Implement only the required subset of functionality for your use case to reduce code bloat.
  • Performance: Keep polyfills as efficient as possible, but understand native code will typically outperform.
  • Modularize: Write polyfills in standalone modules so they can be included where and when needed.

Using Polyfills in Your Projects

1. Manual Inclusion

Include polyfill scripts directly in your HTML or import in your JavaScript bundle.

Example using Polyfill.io: 
xml
<script src="https://polyfill.io/v3/polyfill.min.js"></script>

Polyfill.io automatically serves only the polyfills needed for the requesting browser.

2. Using Libraries

Popular polyfill libraries include:

  • core-js: A comprehensive and modular library supporting many ECMAScript features.
  • babel-polyfill: Used with Babel to transpile and polyfill newer JavaScript features.

Add polyfills during your build process to target unsupported runtimes.

When Not to Use Polyfills

  • On very large or performance-critical applications where native support is preferable.
  • For features that are deprecated or experimental with inconsistent specs.
  • When the user base overwhelmingly uses modern browsers with native support.

Final Thoughts

Polyfills play a crucial role in smooth JavaScript development by filling gaps in browser functionality. Creating and leveraging polyfills enables use of modern language and API features without sacrificing compatibility or user experience.

Stay tuned for more insights as you continue your journey into the world of web development!

Check out the YouTubePlaylist for great JavaScript content for basic to advanced topics.

title: Building PhotoCraft Companion: Local AI for a WebAssembly Editor (Rust Architecture Deep Dive)
description:
PhotoCraft is a modern, open-source desktop image editor with an internal plugin engine built around WebAssembly. Wasm delivers rock-solid security, sandbox isolation, and cross-platform portability. But when you want to run modern neural networks locally, it hits hard physical boundaries.

Three limits make local AI in Wasm painful:

  1. No direct GPU access. No DirectML, no CoreML, no CUDA or Tensor Cores. Everything runs on the CPU through Wasmtime. Running a 150MB neural model like RMBG-1.4 or LaMa on the CPU causes severe UI freezes and takes 8–12 seconds per operation.
  2. Memory sandboxing. Loading multi-hundred-megabyte model weights into a browser-grade or sandboxed Wasm linear memory pool quickly hits execution ceilings.
  3. No native floating UI. Sandboxed plugins cannot render floating toolstrips, custom HUDs, or overlays above the host canvas window. They are trapped within the editor's designated sub-panels.

For heavy creative workflows — studio-grade background removal, generative inpainting, and seam-blended super-resolution — users were trapped between cloud subscriptions with privacy concerns or awkward manual file-export roundtrips.

I wanted a local, offline, zero-telemetry alternative.

1. Solution Overview: The Companion Pattern

Instead of forking or patching the upstream editor codebase, I designed a standalone native companion in Rust. It runs as an independent OS process, interacts with PhotoCraft via its existing JSON-RPC control socket (TCP port 18492), and exchanges pixel buffers through the system clipboard.

The companion is structured as a Cargo workspace with 6 crates, ~25,000 lines of Rust, and governed by strict engineering constraints: a Definition of Done, resource guards, automated architectural linters, and bilingual localization enforced by CI.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 PhotoCraft (Host Editor)                    │
│   Canvas UI (Wasm Sandbox)  ───► TCP Socket Server (18492)  │
└───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────▲───────────┘
                            │ JSON-RPC Control    │
                            │ (Layer copy/paste)  │
                            ▼                     │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────┐
│              PhotoCraft Companion (Rust Native)             │
│                                                             │
│   ┌──────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────┐  │
│   │     overlay_ui       │      │   photocraft_bridge    │  │
│   │ (egui floating panel)│      │  (transactional locks) │  │
│   └──────────┬───────────┘      └───────────┬────────────┘  │
│              │                              │               │
│              ▼                              ▼               │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│   │            core_contracts (Zero-Core API)            │  │
│   │         plugin.json · .pcpl packaging · i18n         │  │
│   └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘  │
│                              │                              │
│                              ▼                              │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│   │            ai_engine (Local Inference)               │  │
│   │  DirectML (GPU) ──► Transparent CPU Fallback         │  │
│   │  Session LRU Cache · Single-Session Tiling Engine    │  │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               │ In-Memory Pixel Transport
                               ▼
                    [ System OS Clipboard ]

Key Architectural Principle — Zero-Core Hardcoding:
No model filenames (.onnx), neural input shapes, or plugin IDs are ever hardcoded in the Rust core. Everything is declared in dynamic JSON manifests. The runtime builds the UI, schedules the inference graph, and issues canvas commands purely based on the declared contracts.

2. Workspace Architecture (6 Crates)

The workspace is strictly partitioned by domain boundaries:

  • core_contracts — Pure domain types: plugin manifest specifications, marketplace registry, .pcpl packaging format, and i18n abstractions. Zero workspace dependencies.
  • photocraft_bridge — Asynchronous JSON-RPC client (TCP port 18492) and clipboard interchange bridge with automatic reconnection.
  • ai_engine — ONNX Runtime (ort) inference engine, DirectML hardware acceleration with transparent CPU fallback, and single-session tiling pipeline.
  • overlay_ui — Always-on-top egui/eframe floating toolstrip, marketplace dialog, auto-updater, and dynamic widget generator.
  • companion_app — Main executable binary, system tray integration (tray-icon), and runtime orchestration.
  • plugin_validator — Standalone CLI utility for validating manifest schemas, path safety, and localization completeness.

The dependency flow is strictly unidirectional: core_contracts sits at the root with zero internal deps, every other crate depends on it, and companion_app binds them together into a single, cohesive binary.

3. The JSON-RPC Bridge: Taming Unreliable Peers

The bridge is the most delicate component because it crosses an inter-process boundary with an asynchronous peer. The editor might hitch during heavy operations, show a blocking modal dialog, or abruptly close. The companion must never hang.

Transactional Request Locking

The client uses Tokio's asynchronous TCP halves. Initially, writer and reader had independent mutexes. However, concurrent calls interleaved: Call A wrote, Call B wrote, Call A read — and received Call B's response!

The fix was a transactional lock that serializes the full request-response lifecycle:

pub async fn call(&self, method: &str, params: Value) -> Result<Value> {
    // Acquire a single lock that spans both write and read
    let _tx = self.call_lock.lock().await;

    let id = self.next_id.fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
    let req = JsonRpcRequest {
        id,
        method: method.to_string(),
        params,
    };

    let mut writer_guard = self.writer.lock().await;
    let writer = writer_guard.as_mut().ok_or(CompanionError::Bridge("Disconnected".into()))?;
    writer.write_all(req.serialize()?.as_bytes()).await?;

    let mut reader_guard = self.reader.lock().await;
    let reader = reader_guard.as_mut().ok_or(CompanionError::Bridge("Disconnected".into()))?;

    // Read with a strict deadline; drop handles on timeout to reset state
    let resp = tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(30), reader.read_response(id)).await??;
    assert_eq!(resp.id, id, "Mismatched JSON-RPC sequence ID");
    Ok(resp.result)
}

Contention Gotcha: The Color Poller

When a plugin panel is open, a background task polls the active brush color every 180ms to keep overlay palettes in sync. Because it shares the bridge client, it created constant contention for the socket lock.

The solution: background polling uses a non-blocking try_lock(). If the bridge is busy running an inference command or layer operation, the poller silently skips that tick rather than queuing behind long-running operations.

4. The egui Floating Overlay: Vector-First UI

The companion displays a two-tier floating toolstrip rendered with egui and eframe. It hovers at persistent screen coordinates above the canvas without creating clutter in the OS taskbar.

Zero-Tofu Policy (No Emoji in Text)

Default fonts in egui lack full Unicode Noto/Emoji coverage. Using emojis like ⏳, ⚠️, or ⚙ produces ugly "tofu" squares (□).

The overlay enforces a strict Vector-First policy:

  1. Status dots and indicators are drawn directly via ui.painter().circle_filled(center, radius, color).
  2. UI icons (gear, orientation flip, grab handle, close) are drawn with vector primitives (line_segment, rect_stroke) or cached SVGs via resvg.
  3. Loading states use active pulsing rings rather than spinner emojis.

Dynamic Widget Generation

The overlay does not hardcode plugin forms. It reads the plugin.json manifest and instantiates sliders, dropdowns, and toggles on the fly:

// overlay_ui renders widgets dynamically from manifest schema
for widget in &manifest.ui.widgets {
    match widget.kind {
        WidgetKind::Slider { min, max, step } => {
            ui.add(
                egui::Slider::new(&mut state.get_mut(&widget.id), *min..=*max)
                    .step_by(*step as f64)
                    .text(widget.label.localize(&self.locale))
            );
        }
        WidgetKind::Dropdown { options } => {
            egui::ComboBox::from_label(widget.label.localize(&self.locale))
                .selected_text(&state.get_string(&widget.id))
                .show_ui(ui, |ui| {
                    for opt in options {
                        ui.selectable_value(&mut state.get_mut(&widget.id), opt.value.clone(), &opt.label);
                    }
                });
        }
    }
}

A third-party creator can introduce a new image processing filter with four sliders and two dropdowns entirely in JSON. The companion renders it immediately without recompiling Rust.

5. ONNX Runtime & DirectML: Real-World Performance

The AI engine uses ort (Rust bindings for ONNX Runtime C++ backend) with DirectML for GPU acceleration on Windows, falling back seamlessly to CPU on non-compatible hardware.

Benchmark: Wasm vs Companion

To see why the companion pattern is worth the architectural complexity, consider RMBG-1.4 inference on a 1024×1024 image:

Execution Target Runtime / Hardware Latency (1024×1024) System Impact
Wasm Sandboxed (Wasmtime) CPU (Multi-core) ~8,200 – 12,000 ms 100% CPU lockup, UI dropped frames
Companion (CPU Fallback) Native C++ ONNX ~1,850 ms Background worker, 60fps overlay UI
Companion (DirectML Cold) Discrete GPU (RTX / RX) ~380 ms 0% host CPU load, 25× speedup
Companion (DirectML Warm) LRU Cached Session ~210 ms Zero initialization overhead

Session Caching

Allocating an ONNX execution session and compiling model graphs to DirectML on every user action introduces 1–2 seconds of latency. The companion maintains an LRU session cache:

pub struct SessionCache {
    entries: HashMap<PathBuf, (Arc<Session>, Instant)>,
    max_capacity: usize,
}

Because Session::run takes &self in modern ort, an Arc<Session> can be safely shared across tasks and reused across sequential operations.

High-Resolution Tiling Pipeline

When users process 4K or 8K layers, running the full canvas through a model in one pass overflows VRAM. The engine slices the canvas into overlapping tiles, executes inference tile-by-tile within a single cached session, and blends edges using cosine feathering to avoid seam artifacts.

6. The Zero-Core Plugin System & Security

Plugins are distributed as .pcpl files — ZIP archives containing a manifest, optional scripts, icons, and model weights.

Manifest Contract (plugin.json) 

{
  "id": "remove_bg",
  "name": { "en": "Background Removal", "ru": "Удаление фона" },
  "version": "1.3.0",
  "type": "native_ai",
  "input": "active_layer",
  "output": "new_layer",
  "models": [
    {
      "role": "segmentation_mask",
      "path": "models/rmbg-1.4.onnx",
      "sha256": "5c1f0d..."
    }
  ],
  "commands": ["image.revealAll"],
  "post_commands": ["layer.renameActive"]
}

Zip-Slip Mitigation

Unpacking community archives is fraught with danger. A malicious archive containing filenames like ../../appdata/startup.exe can overwrite arbitrary system files.

The archive extractor enforces three layers of validation:

for i in 0..archive.len() {
    let mut file = archive.by_index(i)?;

    // 1. Safe extraction path verification
    let enclosed = file.enclosed_name()
        .ok_or_else(|| CompanionError::Security("Illegal path in archive".into()))?;

    // 2. Reject absolute paths and parent traversals
    if enclosed.components().any(|c| matches!(c, Component::ParentDir | Component::RootDir)) {
        return Err(CompanionError::Security("Path traversal attempt detected".into()));
    }

    // 3. Reject symlinks
    if file.is_symlink() {
        return Err(CompanionError::Security("Symlinks forbidden in plugin packages".into()));
    }

    let target = target_dir.join(enclosed);
    // ... write file safely
}

7. Engineering Discipline & Automated Governance

When pairing with LLMs on an ambitious codebase, the primary danger is "architecture rot" — subtle hacks, keyword-sniffing shortcuts, and unprincipled workarounds.

To prevent this, the repository uses automated governance tests:

  • Resource Guard (-j 1): All builds, tests, and CI jobs run with restricted thread counts (-j 1 / codegen-units = 1) to ensure modest developer machines remain fully responsive.
  • Architecture Integrity Linter (architecture_integrity_test.rs): An automated test scans all crate source files. If anyone adds .contains("remove_bg"), .contains("depth"), or hardcoded model paths to the core runtime, CI fails immediately.
  • Localization Linter (i18n_lint_test.rs): Scans the UI crates for raw Cyrillic or hardcoded strings. Every user-facing message must use .localize(&locale) or .t("En", "Ru") with non-empty translation pairs.
  • Standalone Package Validator (plugin_validator): Validates the entire plugin directory and generated .pcpl packages before every commit.

8. Lessons Learned

  1. The Companion Pattern unlocks legacy and sandboxed runtimes. You don't need to rewrite a massive web or Wasm application to give it native GPU capabilities. A lightweight native companion over JSON-RPC + OS clipboard gives you the best of both worlds: a secure sandboxed editor and native hardware inference.
  2. Declarative architecture pays exponential dividends. Investing early in a dynamic UI schema and Zero-Core contract felt like over-engineering for the first plugin. But by plugin three, adding new neural tools required zero Rust coding and zero app rebuilds.
  3. Concurrency requires transactional discipline. Independent mutexes on socket read/write halves invite race conditions the moment background polling starts. Treat socket interactions as atomic transactions.
  4. LLMs need architectural guardrails. LLMs are phenomenal at writing boilerplate, refactoring algorithms, and generating test suites. But without automated linters enforcing architectural purity, codebases naturally drift toward expedient, messy shortcuts.

Repository & Open Source

PhotoCraft Companion is open source and dual-licensed under MIT / Apache-2.0:

👉 github.com/kobaltgit/photocraft-companion

Contributions, architectural discussions, and new plugin manifests are welcome!
