description:
arXiv:2610.31797v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Estimating a camera pose from 3D-2D correspondences - Perspective-n-Point - is one of the most fundamental problems in computer vision. Existing methods either solve a minimal problem or replace the objective with an easier one. Surprisingly, no scalable certifiable solver for the actual Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) exists. We propose PnP*, the first practical solver that guarantees efficient computation and returns a certifiable globally optimal solution. We prove that the underlying convex relaxation is exact under moderate noise, which to our knowledge is the first stability guarantee for any relaxation for the MLE of PnP. Furthermore, we reduce the relaxation by exploiting chordal sparsity pattern and quotient ring reduction such that the relaxation is tractable and scalable. The stability and scalability results are verified numerically, as PnP* returns a provably correct camera pose at over 10 Hz.

title: Node.js Property Imports Explained: Custom SaaS App Metrics Dashboard API Counters
description:
A Node.js SaaS app needs one boring guarantee from its metrics dashboard API: if a scheduled property import stops producing usable results, the on-call engineer hears about it before tenants do. The least complex option is a custom success counter plus a last-success age gauge, emitted by the worker and evaluated outside that worker.

TL;DR: choose the signal path that survives an application rollback. Keep product events separate from operational metrics, bound every label, and alert on the age of the last completed import rather than on errors alone.

Choice Detects silent stalls Rollback exposure Setup surface Best fit
Success counter only Indirectly Low Small Stable, frequent schedules
Last-success age gauge plus counter Yes Low Small Default for scheduled imports
Product-event pipeline as monitor Sometimes Higher Medium Cohort analysis, not primary paging

Recommendation: use the age gauge plus the counter. The runner-up is the counter alone when every import runs frequently enough that a rate window cannot hide a missed schedule. This choice is deliberately dull. It is also easy to remove during rollback and easy to test without a dashboard.

What should a Node.js SaaS app metrics dashboard API detect?

An error counter records an attempted operation that failed. A scheduler that never fires attempts nothing. A worker that loses its lease, waits forever on an upstream response, or exits before registering the job can leave the error count perfectly flat. Green charts can describe a dead pipeline.

Property data makes the distinction concrete. Suppose each management company expects a nightly unit-status import. The operational question is not “How many exceptions occurred?” It is “How old is the newest completed, usable result for this schedule?” That is a liveness question.

Track at least two signals: completed imports as a counter and seconds since the most recent successful completion as a gauge. The counter supports rates and longer-term capacity analysis. The gauge maps directly to the paging condition. Error counts and duration distributions still matter, but neither proves fresh output exists.

Do not put property_id, file name, lease ID, or raw error text in metric labels. Those values can grow without a known limit, which turns a tiny instrumentation patch into a storage and query problem. Use bounded dimensions such as import_kind, region, and result. Prometheus naming guidance also recommends a common application prefix, base units, and names whose sum or average remains logically meaningful.

That sounds fussy. It saves cleanup later.

No metric makes this free. The limitation of the age-gauge approach is that every schedule needs a trustworthy identity and freshness budget; it is a poor fit for ad hoc jobs with no promised cadence. In that case, a queue-depth signal or an explicit job deadline may describe the contract better. The trade-off is extra schedule metadata in exchange for a rule an operator can read at 03:00.

Rollback safety is a data-contract problem

A safe rollback does not require the old release to understand a new dashboard. It requires the telemetry contract to remain readable while old and new workers overlap. During a rolling deployment, both versions may emit for the same schedule. Counters must tolerate duplicate processes, while the last-success timestamp must move only after the imported result is committed and available to readers.

The ordering matters. Emit success before the database commit and a crash can produce a fresh-looking signal for data that never became visible. Emit it after commit and the monitor reflects the user-facing outcome. Keep the instrumentation non-blocking from the job's point of view: failure to publish telemetry should be visible in logs, but it should not undo a valid property import.

I would make the release decision with three checks:

  1. Can the previous worker version run while the new metric exists?
  2. Can a duplicate execution increase the counter without falsely advancing last success?
  3. Can the alert rule remain valid if the new release is rolled back immediately?

The third check kills clever schemas. Picture two releases overlapping for ten minutes: version A knows units and leases; version B adds a new result label; then the deployment rolls back while one slow import is still committing. If the alert depends on the new label, silence may mean “healthy,” “old worker,” or “query no longer matches.” Those are three different states hidden behind one empty graph. Add signals first, observe them across both releases, then switch the alert in a later change. A renamed label, a changed unit, or a status value bundled into the alert deployment makes recovery harder to reason about. Small diffs win.

Logs play a supporting role. RFC 5424 defines ordered severity levels from Emergency through Debug, but a severity label is not a liveness detector. Log the schedule identifier, bounded import kind, result, and duration as structured fields. Use an error severity for a failed attempt. Use the metric age for absence.

A minimal TypeScript boundary

The worker should depend on a tiny interface, not on a dashboard SDK spread through business logic. This keeps time-to-first-call short and makes rollback behavior testable with an in-memory recorder.

type ImportLabels = {
  importKind: "units" | "leases";
  region: "eu" | "us";
};

interface ImportSignals {
  completed(labels: ImportLabels, durationSeconds: number): void;
  failed(labels: ImportLabels, reason: "fetch" | "parse" | "commit"): void;
  lastSuccess(labels: ImportLabels, unixSeconds: number): void;
}

async function runScheduledImport(
  labels: ImportLabels,
  signals: ImportSignals,
  importAndCommit: () => Promise<void>,
  now: () => number = Date.now,
): Promise<void> {
  const startedAt = now();

  try {
    await importAndCommit();
    const completedAt = now();
    signals.completed(labels, (completedAt - startedAt) / 1_000);
    signals.lastSuccess(labels, Math.floor(completedAt / 1_000));
  } catch (error) {
    signals.failed(labels, classifyFailure(error));
    throw error;
  }
}

function classifyFailure(error: unknown): "fetch" | "parse" | "commit" {
  if (error instanceof SyntaxError) return "parse";
  return "commit";
}

The example has no network endpoint and no dashboard configuration. Good. The adapter can expose these calls through the metrics system already used by the service. The business boundary stays stable if that adapter changes.

There is one intentional constraint: classifyFailure returns a closed set. Passing error.message would create an unbounded dimension and leak implementation detail into queries. In production, classification should follow typed errors from the fetch, parse, and commit boundaries; the short fallback above only demonstrates the metric contract.

Test the outcome, not the chart. Use a fake clock and recorder to verify that a successful commit emits one completion and one timestamp, a rejected commit emits failure without advancing the timestamp, and telemetry exceptions do not change the persistence result. Then exercise the alert with missing samples and a stale timestamp. Missing data and old data are different states, even if both eventually page.

The two criteria worth benchmarking

First, benchmark detection delay against the schedule, not HTTP request latency. For a nightly import, a five-minute evaluation interval is noise; for a job expected every minute, it is material. Pick a freshness threshold from the schedule interval, normal completion variance, and the time operators need to act before stale property data affects downstream work. No universal number is honest here. I would benchmark two releases, one forced rollback, one missing run, and one delayed commit before accepting the rule; that is a small test matrix, but it exposes the ambiguous empty-series case quickly.

Second, measure integration drag. Count the configuration files, runtime dependencies, required environment variables, and lines crossing into domain code. I care more about those numbers than a polished default screen. Every extra coupling point expands the rollback checklist.

Also verify where telemetry is processed and retained if the service operates in EU and US regions. Region placement, access control, retention, and deletion are deployment requirements, not logo comparisons. Confirm them against the current contract and architecture of whichever system is under evaluation. They change.

For a self-serve comparison of PostHog, Grafana Cloud, and Better Stack, run the same acceptance test instead of scoring screenshots: emit the bounded counter and timestamp through a disposable adapter, remove one scheduled run, overlap two worker versions, then roll back. Record time-to-first-call, configuration count, alert behavior on absent data, and the steps needed to delete the adapter. This is not a ranking, and those product names are only candidates from the search question. Current deployment regions and service boundaries must be verified in their own documentation before selection.

The dashboard itself needs only a small operational view: current last-success age by bounded schedule group, completion rate, error counters by closed reason, and a latency distribution. Product analytics can answer different questions, such as how imported inventory changes tenant behavior. Do not make that event pipeline the only pager path. Its batching and transformation stages add failure modes between the worker and the alert.

Cheap ingestion is not the primary decision rule. A low bill cannot rescue an alert that lies during rollback.

When the runner-up is enough

A completion counter alone is reasonable when schedules are frequent, execution is uniform, and the query engine can reliably alert on an absent or zero rate. It has less state at the emitter and one fewer metric to maintain.

It becomes awkward for sparse schedules. Query windows must be wide enough to include expected runs, calendar behavior complicates evaluation, and “no series exists” may behave differently from “the series has value zero.” A last-success timestamp makes the rule legible: current time minus timestamp exceeds the agreed freshness budget.

Choose product events as the secondary path when analysts need tenant funnels, cohorts, or import-volume segmentation. Choose logs for diagnosis and audit context. Neither is a substitute for the low-cardinality operational signal that pages on silent absence.

The final decision is plain: prefer the smallest metrics boundary that remains truthful through commit, overlapping releases, and rollback. Alert on stale successful output. Everything else is context.

Further reading

  • Prometheus, “Metric and label naming”: https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/
  • IETF RFC 5424, “The Syslog Protocol”: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5424

title: How a CI Performance Budget Keeps a 6 KB Framework From Growing (Inside AngeLite, Part 4)
description:
Every framework starts fast and gets slower. Features accumulate, each justified on its own, and one day the "lightweight" library isn't. AngeLite's defence is a rule: no feature lands if it makes the core slower, bigger or hungrier for memory, and the rule is enforced by CI, not by good intentions.

This post explains the four layers of that enforcement and why they're arranged from cheapest and exact to expensive and noisy.

The problem with measuring time in CI

The obvious approach is "run the benchmark on every PR and fail if it got slower". It doesn't work. On a shared CI runner, time varies 10-20% from run to run, so a threshold tight enough to catch regressions is loose enough to flake constantly.

What is exact: how much work the code does (DOM calls, effect runs) and how many bytes it ships. So the budget leans on exact measurements first and uses noisy ones only as a backstop.

The four layers

Layer What it measures Where it runs Noise
1. Size gzip bytes of every bundle, and of what a user really downloads (the table app built with esbuild) CI, every PR none
2. Work DOM calls and effect runs per scenario (1,000 rows) against a stored budget CI (npm test), every PR none: deterministic
3. Relative time AngeLite vs Preact in the same run; ratio compared with a baseline on demand, weekly, and PRs touching the core; doesn't block medium
4. Full benchmark five frameworks, 12 measurements, memory and startup by hand before publishing high 
flowchart TB
    PR[Pull request] --> L1["Layer 1: bundle size (exact)"]
    PR --> L2["Layer 2: work budget (exact)"]
    L1 --> Gate{"Within budget?"}
    L2 --> Gate
    Gate -- no --> Fail["CI fails and names the figure"]
    Gate -- yes --> Merge[Mergeable]
    PR -. "touches core" .-> L3["Layer 3: relative time vs Preact (noisy, non-blocking)"]
    Release[Before publishing] --> L4["Layer 4: full 5-framework benchmark (by hand)"]

Layer 2 in detail: count the work, not the time

tests/perf-budget.test.mjs mounts the table app with every optional module loaded (portal, @defer, animations...) and counts, per scenario, calls to createElement, cloneNode, appendChild, insertBefore, remove, setAttribute, classList.toggle, textContent =, addEventListener and so on, plus Effect.run executions. It also asserts that the in-browser compiler and the precompiled template do exactly the same work. Today, for 1,000 rows:

Scenario DOM calls Effects
create 1,000 5,002 1,001
replace 1,000 5,004 1,001
update every 10th 100 101
select a row 1 1,000
swap 2 rows 2 1
remove a row 1 1
append 1,000 5,000 1,001
clear 4 1

If a change raises any figure, the test fails and says which one. If it's intentional, you explain it in the PR and run UPDATE_PERF=1 npm test, which rewrites the budget in the same commit, so the change is visible in review. And if a figure drops, the test says so too, so the improvement gets locked in.

This catches things time can't: a feature that adds one DOM call per row won't move a noisy millisecond number, but it changes a count of 5,002 to 6,002 and fails immediately.

Layer 3: relative time, because absolute time lies

Comparing AngeLite against Preact within the same run cancels most machine noise. A single operation fails if its ratio gets worse by more than 35%, or the geometric mean of all operations by more than 10%. It doesn't block merges because it's still statistical, but it catches what the exact layers miss, such as a new property access in a hot loop.

Design rules that keep the budget achievable

  1. Optional module by default. A feature not every app needs goes in its own file and hooks in through the ops registry or a module imported only when used. Apps that don't import it don't pay in bytes or in time.
  2. Don't touch the hot paths without measuring. They are instantiate, runView, ForState.reconcile and removeView. A new property on every row gets multiplied by thousands.
  3. Pay per component or template, not per row. Compile-time work in the AOT is nearly free; per-row work isn't.
  4. Mind object shapes. Adding fields to View, to the context or to elements changes their shape and can slow everything that touches them. Optional fields are created only when used (DI providers do this: the map is created on the first inject).
  5. Dev warnings don't live in the core. enableDevWarnings() wraps internals from the outside; the production build includes none of it.
  6. Every byte of the core is debated. Size budgets live in scripts and only go up in a commit that explains why.

What a budget buys you: an audit trail

Because budgets are data in the repo, the cost of every core feature is public. Before the "wave 1" feature work the precompiled table app was 5,968 bytes gzip; today it's 6,223 (+255 B, +4%). Post 5 breaks down where those bytes went.

Pending improvements, with data

The budget also acts as a to-do list, ordered by what the numbers already show:

  • Selecting a row runs 1,000 effects (every row reads selected() and is re-evaluated to change a class on two rows). About 1.3 ms and tied with Preact and Angular, but it's the best candidate for per-binding effects.
  • create1k does 5 DOM calls per row, two of which (a text write of the initial value and a classList.toggle to false) can be skipped.
  • remove/swap hover around a tie with Preact. A Chromium trace profile is still missing to separate noise from real cost before touching anything.

Takeaways

  • Measure exact things (bytes, DOM calls, effect runs) on every PR; use noisy time only as a ratio and only as a backstop.
  • Make budgets data in the repo, with an explicit update command, so every change is reviewed.
  • A performance rule you can't break by accident is worth ten you remember to follow.

Next: the module system that makes "optional" real, and what each core feature costs.

title: Internationalization (I18n) Implementation in React
description:
Internationalization (I18n) is a crucial aspect of building web applications that cater to a global audience. It involves adapting your application to different languages and regions seamlessly. In this blog, we will explore the implementation of I18n in a React app, ensuring a smooth user experience for diverse audiences.

Why Internationalization?

Before delving into the implementation details, let's understand why I18n is essential. Your app has the potential to reach users from different parts of the world. I18n helps you break language barriers, making your React app more inclusive and appealing to a diverse audience.

Setting Up Your React Project

Firstly, make sure you have a React app up and running. If not, you can create one using the Create React App or any other preferred method.

npx create-react-app i18n-react-app

cd i18n-react-app

Choosing an I18n Library

Several libraries can assist with I18n in React. One popular choice is 'react-i18next'.

Install it using:

npm install i18next react-i18next

Configuring I18n

Create a file named i18n.js to set up I18n:

import i18n from "i18next";
import { initReactI18next } from "react-i18next";
import translationEN from "./translations/en.json"; // Import JSON file for English Language
import translationES from "./translations/es.json"; // Import JSON file for Spanish Language
const resources = {
  en: {
    translation: translationEN,
  },
  es: {
    translation: translationES,
  },
  // Add translations for other languages here
};

i18n.use(initReactI18next).init({
  resources,
  lng: "en", // Default language
  interpolation: {
    escapeValue: false,
  },
});
export default i18n;

Managing Translations with a JSON File

Create a folder named 'translations' in your project root and add a file named 'en.json' (for English) and 'es.json' (for Spanish) with your translations:

en.json 

{
  "welcome": "Bienvenido a nuestra aplicación React!"
  // Add more key-value pairs as needed
}

es.json 

{
  "welcome": "Welcome to our React App!",
  // Add more key-value pairs as needed
}

Using I18n in Components

Now, let's put these translations to work in a React component. Consider a 'WelcomeMessage' component:

import React from "react";
import { useTranslation } from "react-i18next";
const WelcomeMessage = () => {
  const { t } = useTranslation();
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>{t("welcome")}</h1>
    </div>
  );
};
export default WelcomeMessage;

Language Switcher Component

Modify the 'LanguageSwitcher' component to include buttons for switching between English and Spanish.

import React from "react";
import i18n from "./i18n";
const LanguageSwitcher = () => {
  const handleChangeLanguage = (lng) => {
    i18n.changeLanguage(lng);
  };
  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => handleChangeLanguage("en")}>English</button>
      <button onClick={() => handleChangeLanguage("es")}>Español</button>
      {/* Add buttons for other languages as needed */}
    </div>
  );
};
export default LanguageSwitcher;

Bringing It All Together

Finally, integrate these components into your main app:

App.js 

import React from "react";
import WelcomeMessage from "./WelcomeMessage";
import LanguageSwitcher from "./LanguageSwitcher";
const App = () => {
  return (
    <div>
      <LanguageSwitcher />
      <WelcomeMessage />
      {/* Add more components as needed */}
    </div>
  );
};
export default App;

Output:

Conclusion
In this blog, we covered the importance of Internationalization in a React app and demonstrated how to implement it using the 'react-i18next' library. With proper translations and language-switching capabilities, your React app is now equipped to reach a broader, more diverse audience.

By following these steps, you can create a user-friendly, internationally accessible React application that resonates with users worldwide. Happy coding!

title: What Microduck's Latest Release Reveals About Its Unique Robotics Approach
description:
Objective Technical Assessment

Microduck is designed to tackle the challenges of creating a compact, agile bipedal robot that can perform various tasks through reinforcement learning policies. The repository serves as the brain of the robot, leveraging a control loop that operates at 50 Hz to manage the movement of fifteen servos using neural policies. This design allows the robot to adapt its behavior based on environmental feedback, showcasing an effective application of AI in robotics.

Architectural Strengths & Highlights

Microduck's architecture is built on a Rust workspace that encompasses multiple modules, each responsible for different functionalities:

  • robotd: Manages the control loop and motor bus.
  • updaterd: Handles the installation of signed releases and can roll back updates if the robot does not boot healthily.
  • configd: Manages WiFi connectivity and identity.
  • btd: Facilitates Bluetooth communication with devices.
  • mediad: Streams video from the robot's camera using WebRTC.

The recent update, daemon-v0.17.8, adds functionality for the robot to quack in response to commands, enhancing its interactivity. This release illustrates the project’s commitment to integrating user feedback and improving interaction capabilities.

Real-world Limitations & Pain Points

Despite its advanced capabilities, Microduck has some limitations. The reliance on a specific hardware platform, the Rockchip RK3566, may restrict its adaptability to other systems. Additionally, developers looking to modify or extend the robot's capabilities will need familiarity with Rust and the intricacies of the existing architecture, which may present a learning curve for newcomers.

Adoption Recommendation: Who is it for?

Microduck is ideal for robotics enthusiasts, researchers, and developers interested in exploring reinforcement learning in a physical robot context. Its modular design allows for experimentation and further development, making it suitable for academic projects or hobbyist applications.
Conversely, those seeking a plug-and-play robotic solution without the need for extensive programming or hardware customization may find it less suitable. The specific hardware requirements and the necessity for coding skills to adapt the robot could be a barrier for some users.

Our Call

Microduck presents an exciting opportunity in the realm of robotics, merging AI with physical interaction. Its latest release enhances its capabilities, but potential users should assess their technical proficiency and hardware compatibility before diving in.

Originally published on GitTrending — Explore daily architectural deep-dives and quality scores for trending open-source GitHub projects.

title: Benchmarking Data-Free Continual Model Merging for Whole-Slide Image Survival Analysis
description:
arXiv:2610.32207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Continual survival analysis on whole-slide images (WSIs) requires models to integrate knowledge from sequentially arriving cancer cohorts while preserving previously learned information. Model merging offers a data-free alternative by combining independently fine-tuned task experts without retaining previous training data. However, the relative behavior of different merging strategies for WSI-based survival prediction remains insufficiently understood. In this work, we establish an end-to-end benchmark for data-free continual model merging, covering task-specific fine-tuning, sequential merging, and inference under both TASK-IL and CLASS-IL settings. We systematically evaluate six representative merging strategies across four TCGA cancer cohorts and three task orders using C-index, IPCW C-index, Forgetting, and Backward Transfer under a controlled protocol. Results show that no merging strategy consistently dominates across all evaluation criteria, while censoring-aware evaluation can substantially alter the relative ranking of the compared methods. This benchmark provides a unified foundation for developing and evaluating more effective continual model merging methods for WSI-based survival analysis.

title: QApybara: Autonomous Open-Source AI QA Engineer for Web & Real Android Devices — Channeling Sloth Energy to Never Test a PR Manually Again
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

AI coding assistants have made developers write twice as much code in half the time. But nobody doubled the size of testing teams. Over 60% of startups ship without dedicated QA. Review bots like CodeRabbit and Greptile read your pull request diffs, but research shows that only around 15% of review comments catch real defects. The bugs that actually ruin a user's day — a dead checkout button, a broken dropdown, an Android ANR ("Application Not Responding"), or a silent 500 error — only reveal themselves when someone actually runs and interacts with the app.

Manually clicking through staging apps, filling out test forms, and inspecting devtools on every PR is tedious, dread-inducing work.

This week’s theme celebrates International Sloth Day: channeling your inner sloth, moving at a relaxed pace, and letting open-source AI do the work so you don't have to.

Enter QApybara (inspired by the capybara, the calmest, most unbothered creature in nature).

QApybara is an autonomous, open-source AI QA Engineer that doesn't just read your code — it runs it on a real Chromium browser and a physical Android phone plugged in over USB.

Instead of doing manual regression testing, you embrace pure sloth mode:

Push your code.
Slap a qa label (or comment /qa) on the GitHub pull request.
Sit back, relax, and take a nap.
QApybara spins up the app or installs the build APK on a physical phone, maps user journeys, exercises the app like a human user, catches crashes and console errors, captures screenshots and screen recordings, and posts an evidence-backed verdict directly back to your PR and team Slack thread.

Demo

qapybara-dashboard.vercel.app

Code

parth-lightning / QApybara

QApybara 🦥

Review bots read your code. QApybara runs it — on a real browser and a physical Android phone — and shows proof.

QApybara is an autonomous, open-source AI QA Engineer that tests pull requests by actually running and interacting with the application like a human user. When a developer labels a PR with qa or comments /qa, QApybara spins up the web preview or installs the APK on a USB-connected Android phone, maps user journeys, exercises the app, detects runtime errors, captures video and screenshot proof, and exports passing journeys as reusable Playwright or Maestro regression tests.

Built with open-weight models, the Eve agent framework, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP).

🌟 Key Highlights

  • Runs, Doesn't Just Read: Code review bots analyze syntax and style; QApybara boots your app, clicks buttons, fills out forms, tests edge cases, and verifies real runtime behavior.
  • Web & Real…
View on GitHub

parth-lightning / qapybara-store-app

Mobile e-commerce store (Stillform) for QApybara - contains all source files, assets, and build configurations to generate the Android .apk

Stillform mobile

An offline Expo shopping app for sneakers and clothes. Accounts, sessions, per-user bags, orders and appearance are saved locally with AsyncStorage. All photography and fonts are bundled; no backend or network is required. Payments and fulfillment are simulated.

Run

Node.js 22+, npm. Run npm ci, then npm start. Expo SDK 58, Expo Router, React Native 0.88, React 19.3 and TypeScript. Use a native development or release build for native modules.

Existing test login remains demo@qapybara.dev / Demo1234!. You can also create and sign into local accounts. Passwords are stored as salted SHA-256 digests; this local implementation does not provide server authentication or cross-device sync.

Website parity

Source: /home/shahid/codes/hackathons/qapybara-store-web, commits 7d6379a and 8e86a75.

  • lib/catalog.ts, lib/pricing.ts, lib/schema.ts and design/tokens.ts are byte-identical copies.
  • All 38 public/images/*.webp files are copied unchanged into assets/products. lib/images.ts maps their website paths to bundled native modules. Login uses…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

  1. Dynamic Agent Teams on the Eve Framework Many agent workflows use rigid, hardcoded pipelines (Explorer ➔ Tester ➔ Reporter). QApybara is built on the open-source Eve agent harness and decides its team dynamically:

For a small one-line PR, the main agent handles the check alone.
For a multi-component feature touching database schemas, APIs, and UIs, the main agent spawns an Explorer to map touched routes, spins up multiple Testers in parallel (one per critical journey), and terminates with a Reporter to synthesize the report.

  1. Real Android Automation & 3.2x Batch Tool Calling
    Most AI testing agents stop at the browser. QApybara drives real Android phones connected via USB. Rather than making a slow roundtrip to the model for every single tap or swipe, QApybara implements programmatic batch tool calling through MCP. The model generates batch sequences that execute in one go on the phone, speeding up Artemis execution by over 3.2x.

  2. Proof, Not Vibes (The Deterministic Proof Gate)
    An LLM claiming "Everything looks good!" is useless if it missed a broken submit button. In QApybara, code — not the AI — enforces the verdict:

No screenshot or video trace? No pass.
Unaddressed console errors or HTTP 500s? No pass.
Critical configured flow skipped? Run marked as "QA Incomplete".
Passing journeys are compiled into reusable Playwright (.spec.ts) and Maestro (.yaml) test scripts, ensuring you gain permanent automated regression tests without writing boilerplate.

  1. Rewarding Laziness: Zero-Dashboard Setup Even setting up QA should be effortless. Running npx qapybara init wires the QApybara MCP server and setup skills directly into your local coding agent (Claude Code or Codex). You simply say: "Set this repo up for QApybara". Your coding agent inspects your repository, configures build and start commands, pushes encrypted env variables, and executes a dry-run test on the QA host until it passes.

Where Open Source AI Fits In?

QApybara is built around open-weight models and open protocols:

Open-Weight Model Backbone: Powered through any OpenAI-compatible runner (such as Moonshot Kimi, Qwen 2.5, or Llama 3 via vLLM/Ollama/OpenRouter). Swapping models or providers is a simple environment variable toggle (QA_MODEL_ID), requiring zero code changes.
Role-Based Model Specialization: You can route different roles to different open-weight models:
Deep reasoning open models for the Explorer to map subtle test cases.
Fast, low-latency open models for the parallel Testers executing UI actions.
Local Simulation Mode (QA_MODEL=sim): For complete offline testing, local CI, and testing the agent tree without an internet connection or API keys, QApybara includes a fully deterministic scripted simulation harness.
Model Context Protocol (MCP): Built on Anthropic's open MCP specification, enabling standardized communication between the QA host, coding agents, and the interactive embedded MCP App report viewer (ui://qapybara/qa-run.html).

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Testing real applications involves pre-release code, sensitive staging environment credentials, internal databases, unreleased Android APKs, and proprietary business logic.

Here is why an open approach beats closed proprietary QA services:

Data Privacy & Zero Cloud Leakage: Proprietary cloud QA services require handing over full repository write tokens, internal staging URLs, database credentials, and APK binaries to third-party servers. With QApybara, open-weight models and self-hosted agents can run entirely on a local machine or a dedicated office laptop (like an old ThinkPad with an Android phone plugged in). Secrets are encrypted with local keys, and unreleased APKs never touch a third-party cloud.
Zero SaaS Tax / Costs Nothing to Run: Closed QA platforms charge steep per-seat monthly fees or price-gouge per browser minute. By running open-weight models on your own hardware or through cost-effective open endpoints, continuous PR testing costs virtually nothing.
Model Freedom & Future-Proofing: Closed platforms lock you into their specific model version and pricing whims. With an open architecture, you can swap models, run quantized models locally on an edge workstation, or fine-tune an open-weight model specifically on your application's design system and terminology.

The Lazy Payoff

Before QApybara, manually verifying a non-trivial pull request was a 45-minute chore nobody wanted to do:

Pulling the branch and starting the dev server or downloading and adb install-ing the latest APK build on a phone.
Manually clicking through 8 different user journeys (signing up, typing credentials, testing search cases, adding items to the cart, applying coupons, checking order history).
Keeping devtools open to watch for silent 4xx/5xx network errors and scanning adb logcat for hidden Android ANRs.
Typing out a bug report by hand with screenshots when something inevitably broke.
Writing end-to-end Playwright or Maestro test scripts from scratch so the bug doesn't happen again.
With QApybara, the "lazy payoff" is real:

~3 Hours Saved Per PR: Instead of context-switching away from coding to babysit staging deployments and manual test clicks, we just label the PR qa and walk away.
Zero Test-Writing Effort: Because QApybara automatically converts passing runs into deterministic Playwright (.spec.ts) and Maestro (.yaml) test scripts, our regression test suite grows without us writing a single line of test code by hand.
Used Live This Week: We ran QApybara against our benchmark store with 10 tricky planted bugs (like coupon double-application and silent signup errors). While we grabbed coffee, QApybara's autonomous agent team ran in parallel, caught all 10 bugs, recorded every screen video, captured the HTTP 500 traces, and posted clean reproduction steps back to our PR thread.
Total developer effort required: typing qa. That's true sloth-level productivity.

title: Distributional Alignment of LLMs and Its Generalization Properties
description:
arXiv:2610.31687v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate and probe human behavior, e.g., for surveys. For these applications, a key property is that outputs satisfy distributional alignment: to match its output distribution with some reference (in this case, human) distribution. An obstacle in achieving distributional alignment is generalizing from small training data. In this work, we study (1) how to distributionally align LLMs; and (2) how aligned LLMs might generalize to unseen samples and unrelated topics and tasks. Using two large-scale benchmarks, we find that LLMs can indeed achieve distributional alignment and generalize to unseen questions of the same domain. Cross-topic generalization depends on the relationship between topics (e.g., questions about politics are related to trust in institutions). However, aligned LLMs can degrade in surprising ways (e.g., lose their creative ability), suggesting that its generalization properties are inherently unpredictable and unstable.

title: Permission to Retry: A Study of Authorization and Recovery in AI Agent Workflows
description:
arXiv:2610.31916v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A durable agent can resume a consequential action while its authority changes and the action's external outcome remains uncertain. We study execution-time reliability of tool-using AI agents, isolating recovery decisions from language-model behavior. Checkpoint state, permission to dispatch, evidence of an external effect and permission to reconcile are distinct obligations. We present a finite conformance study that checks these obligations through histories scored against a provider effect ledger hidden from the recovering application. A prospectively frozen campaign executes 336 histories on native LangGraph and Temporal hosts, crossing 14 schedules, three provider contracts and four matched application policies. All 168 paired host cells have identical checked outcomes. Per host, retained-ledger reconciliation passes all 42 histories: 21 checked completions, 15 denials and six unknown outcomes with reservations retained. Cached retry, revalidation before retry and stable-key retry pass 30, 36 and 31 histories respectively. A separate 16-case component study of InfinityOS, an enterprise AI platform developed by Arya.ai, exercises exported authority, worker, recovery and settlement code over repository fakes. The results isolate the roles of current authority, provider contracts and retained observations in recovery, with safety, completion and unresolved obligations reported separately for the declared application profile.

title: Deploy FastAPI and React with Docker Compose
description:
Docker Compose gives you the same setup on your laptop and your server: one command builds and starts the API and the frontend. This guide covers both Dockerfiles, the one setting people get wrong (build-time variables for the frontend), and going to production.

The backend image

With uv, the image is small and the install is reproducible from the lockfile:

FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:latest /uv /bin/uv

WORKDIR /app
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN uv sync --frozen --no-dev
COPY app ./app

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["/app/.venv/bin/fastapi", "run", "app/main.py", "--port", "8000"]

Copying pyproject.toml and uv.lock before the code means dependency layers are cached until the dependencies change. Pin the uv image to a version in production instead of latest.

The frontend image

A React build is static files, so build with Node and serve with nginx:

FROM node:24-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
ARG API_URL SITE_URL
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:alpine
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

With an nginx.conf that falls back to the app for client-side routes:

server {
  listen 80;
  root /usr/share/nginx/html;
  location / { try_files $uri $uri/index.html /index.html; }
}

Build-time vs run-time settings

This trips everyone up once. The frontend's settings (the API URL, public keys, analytics ids) are baked into the JavaScript at build time. Setting them as container environment variables does nothing; they must be build args , and you rebuild when they change. The backend reads its settings at run time from the environment.

compose.yml 

services:
  backend:
    build: ./backend
    env_file: .env
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"

  frontend:
    build:
      context: ./frontend
      args:
        API_URL: ${API_URL:-http://localhost:8000}
        SITE_URL: ${SITE_URL:-http://localhost:5173}
    ports:
      - "5173:80"

Compose reads ${API_URL} from your .env file next to compose.yml, so one file feeds both.

docker compose up --build -d
docker compose logs -f backend

Production

  1. Set public URLs in .env: API_URL=https://api.example.com, SITE_URL=https://example.com, then rebuild (docker compose up --build -d).
  2. Put HTTPS in front. Bind the ports to localhost ("127.0.0.1:8000:8000") and use a reverse proxy on the host: nginx with certbot, Caddy, or Cloudflare Tunnel with no open ports at all.
  3. Real client IPs. If the proxy reaches the API over Docker's network, the API sees the proxy's container address. Set uvicorn's FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS to that address (for example the bridge gateway 172.18.0.1) so X-Forwarded-For is trusted.
  4. Restart policy. Add restart: unless-stopped to both services.
  5. Updates: git pull && docker compose up --build -d, then check the health endpoint.

Using it with FastAPI Supabase Starter

The starter ships both Dockerfiles and a compose.yml with every build arg listed (SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY, API_URL, SITE_URL, OAUTH_PROVIDERS, TURNSTILE_SITE_KEY, SENTRY_DSN, GA_MEASUREMENT_ID). Fill in .env and run docker compose up --build: the app is on port 5173 and the API on 8000. There's no database container, because Supabase hosts Postgres. See the quick start and Deploy to production.

title: Semantically Rich, Metrically Affect-Blind: A Geometric Blind Spot in Modern Text Embedders
description:
arXiv:2610.32122v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We report a systematic dissociation in modern text embedders: sentiment is almost perfectly decodable from their embeddings, yet almost entirely absent from their metric. Across eleven frozen encoders spanning 2021 to 2026, including 2026-generation models and the 4B-parameter LLM embedder Qwen3-Embedding-4B, a linear probe recovers sentence polarity at up to 91.3% accuracy while cosine similarity separates polarity by a margin of only 0.003-0.064. Qwen3-Embedding-4B, the strongest probe in the panel, reaches 91.3% probe accuracy but only 64.3 retrieval MAP. Because retrieval, clustering, deduplication, and retrieval-augmented generation operate on the metric rather than on a trained probe, these systems are effectively blind to information their encoder demonstrably contains. A task-conditioning control suggests this reflects the pretraining objective rather than a prompting artifact: conditioning Jina-v5 on its classification task rather than its retrieval task recovers only about half of the MAP gain that injection achieves on the same weights (63.2 to 73.8, versus 85.1), and leaves the alignment gap essentially unchanged. Sentiment-Injected Sentence Embeddings (SISE) train a small (0.13M-0.69M-parameter) supervised-contrastive head on a frozen encoder in seconds on a CPU, using the labelled training set. The head improves every encoder released since 2022 on full-data probe accuracy (up to +5.8 points), retrieval MAP (up to +26.0) and polarity margin (7-61x). This is a specialization, not a free gain: the compact 128-d head loses 38-41 Spearman points on STS-B, while a fused variant that concatenates it with the base embedding loses 2.4-12.0. With the head, a 0.6B encoder at 128 dimensions matches a 4B encoder given the same head (91.8 vs. 90.3 MAP). We release a CPU-reproducible pipeline and a reusable diagnostic, the Attribute Alignment Gap.

title: Patronizing and Condescending Language Detection in English and Mandarin
description:
arXiv:2610.31808v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Patronizing and condescending language (PCL) is a form of harmful language that belittles and assumes pity for vulnerable groups, reinforcing negative societal stereotypes. However, unlike overt hate speech, it is often difficult to detect, even for human judges. This paper proposes a system for the automated detection of PCL. Our first approach uses static word embeddings and a convolutional neural network for classification, while our second approach uses pre-trained BERT embeddings fine-tuned for the PCL task. Our second approach was considerably more successful, and achieved an F1 score of 0.528 over the development set.

title: When a MIDI Note Ends One Sixteenth Early
description:
MIDI gives us timed note events, not a finished score. When Pianory imports a MIDI file into its score player, it has to choose a readable written duration. A tiny release gap near the next note can be meaningful, or it can make notation look more staccato than the phrase suggests.

Our converter snaps starts and durations to a sixteenth-note grid: four grid units equal one quarter note. It builds one voice per hand, groups simultaneous starts into a chord, and caps that chord at the hand's next onset. For a held note released just before that onset, it fills a gap only when the gap is at most one grid unit and no more than a quarter of the note length. Otherwise it leaves the gap.

The focused test is concrete. A C5 note starts at quarter 0 and lasts 3.75 quarters; the next D5 starts at quarter 4. The first note spans 15 sixteenth units, followed by a one-unit gap. In a 4/4 bar of 16 units, that gap passes the rule, so the MusicXML contains a whole-note type and no ordinary rest. The test asserts that output.

This is a notation heuristic, not a claim that every MIDI performance is represented exactly. Triplets and swing are approximate on this grid, and a larger gap should remain a rest. The useful design choice is to make the threshold explicit and test a boundary case instead of letting a seemingly harmless release create an unwanted sliver of silence on the page. I make Pianory, the piano-learning app behind this converter. AI helped draft this article; I checked the claims against src/lib/music/midi.ts and the focused test. On 26 October, pnpm exec vitest run src/lib/music/midi.spec.ts passed all 16 tests.
