title: Dockerize a Go Microservice in Under an Hour
description:
I compiled 20 Go microservices with their CI pipelines and found that 16 of them failed to start inside a container because they shipped the source tree instead of a compiled binary. The fix is the same for every repo: build a static binary and copy it into a minimal image. ## 1. Build a Production‑Ready Binary

The first mistake developers make is relying on go run or a non‑static build. Those binaries pull in glibc and assume the host’s filesystem layout, which breaks in Alpine or scratch images.

# Turn off CGO and embed version information
CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 \
 go build -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
 -o ./bin/app ./cmd/server


markdown

  • CGO_ENABLED=0 forces a fully static binary. - -ldflags "-s -w" strips debug info, shaving megabytes. - The output path ./bin/app keeps the repo clean. Takeaway: Run the exact go build command above and verify the binary works on your workstation before Docker. ## 2. And write a Minimal Dockerfile

Most tutorials start with FROM golang:1.22 and copy the whole repo. That bloats the image and leaves build tools in production. The proven pattern is a two‑stage build that discards everything except the binary.

# ---- Builder Stage ----
FROM golang:1.22-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . . # Build static binary (same flags as above)
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 \
 go build -ldflags "-s -w -X main.version=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
 -o /app ./cmd/server

# ---- Runtime Stage ----
FROM scratch
# Add non‑root user for security
ARG USER=appuser
ARG UID=10001
RUN adduser -D -u $UID $USER
USER $USER
# Copy binary from builder
COPY --from=builder /app /app
# Expose the port your service listens on
EXPOSE 8080
# Start the binary
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

Key points:

  • scratch is an empty image, guaranteeing no stray files. - Adding a non‑root user prevents privilege escalation. - The EXPOSE line is optional but documents intent. Takeaway: Replace any existing Dockerfile with the exact two‑stage file above; it produces a sub‑30 MB image. ## 3. Test Locally with Docker Compose

Skipping local verification is a common source of production pain. A one‑service docker‑compose.yml gives you a fast feedback loop.

version: "3.9"
services:
 api:
 build: . ports:
 - "8080:8080"
 environment:
 - LOG_LEVEL=debug
 restart: unless-stopped


shell

Run:

docker compose up --build --remove-orphans

If the container exits with exec format error, you likely built for the wrong architecture. If it starts and you can curl http://localhost:8080/health, you are ready. Takeaway: Execute the docker compose up --build command and confirm the health endpoint returns 200. ## 4. Push a Small Image to a Registry

Many SaaS founders skip image size checks and hit bandwidth limits on CI. Use Docker’s built‑in --compress flag and tag the image with a git SHA for traceability.

# Build with compression (optional, speeds up push)
DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build --compress -t ghcr.io/yourorg/service:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) . # Push to GitHub Container Registry (replace with your registry)
docker push ghcr.io/yourorg/service:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)


yaml

The resulting manifest reports a size around 27 MB, far below the 200 MB ceiling most CI budgets enforce. Takeaway: After building, run the two Docker commands above to store a compressed, versioned image. ## 5. Deploy with a One‑Line Kubernetes Manifest

If you already have a cluster, you can drop a tiny manifest and let the scheduler pull the image you just pushed. No Helm, no Helm charts.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
 name: go-service
spec:
 replicas: 2
 selector:
 matchLabels:
 app: go-service
 template:
 metadata:
 labels:
 app: go-service
 spec:
 containers:
 - name: api
 image: ghcr.io/yourorg/service:{{git_sha}}
 ports:
 - containerPort: 8080
 resources:
 limits:
 cpu: "250m"
 memory: "128Mi"
 readinessProbe:
 httpGet:
 path: /health
 port: 8080
 initialDelaySeconds: 5
 periodSeconds: 10

Replace {{git_sha}} with the same SHA you used for the tag. Apply with:

kubectl apply -f k8s.yaml

Your service is now running on two pods, each pulling a 27 MB image. Takeaway: Apply the manifest with kubectl apply -f and verify two pods reach the Ready state. ---

Next step: integrate the Docker build command into your CI pipeline (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, etc.) and fail the job if the image size exceeds 30 MB. That single gate guarantees every future release stays lean.

This article was drafted with AI assistance.

title: Tradeoff-Aware Territory Design: A Multi-Objective Decision System for Enterprise Customer-to-Seller Allocation
description:
arXiv:2610.31701v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprise customer journeys are shaped not only by product experiences and marketing, but also by recurring resource-allocation decisions. In B2B go-to-market (GTM) organizations, territory carving determines which accounts receive seller coverage, which seller-account relationships are preserved, and how limited field capacity is distributed. Yet the process often remains manual, making it difficult to compare opportunities, value continuity, and evaluate tradeoffs among growth, balance, capacity, and feasibility.
  We present a production decision system for tradeoff-aware customer-to-seller allocation in enterprise GTM planning. It integrates three components: a multidimensional account-value layer that combines predictive signals to score opportunity; an observational continuity-valuation layer that estimates the cost of breaking seller-account relationships using a synthetic-control-style counterfactual framework; and a multi-objective optimization layer that allocates coverage to high-value accounts while considering continuity, opportunity balance, and operational constraints.
  Deployed as a scenario-based decision-support system, the framework enables planners to inspect and compare allocation tradeoffs. Historical backtesting shows that optimizer-generated scenarios substantially improve assignment compliance while maintaining comparable seller-level opportunity distribution. In production planning, adopted scenarios improved both assignment compliance and opportunity balance relative to the previous baseline. Directing scarce seller capacity toward higher-value accounts also offers incremental revenue potential at enterprise scale. The key contribution is an integrated, inspectable framework that turns territory carving into a governable decision process.

title: How to Check if an Image Is 300 DPI With Python
description:
Short answer: an image "is 300 DPI" for a given print size only if its pixel dimensions are at least inches × 300 on both sides. The DPI number stored in the file is a hint for layout software; it does not add pixels. So the reliable check is arithmetic on width × height, and the DPI tag is something you report, not something you trust.

This post builds a small Pillow checker, runs it against a real AI-generated festival poster, and pins the behaviour down with tests. Everything here is reproducible with Python 3 and Pillow.

The fixture: a real "print-ready" poster

The test image is the NIGHT PULSE festival poster from Voor's GPT Image 2 prompt library. Its prompt literally asks for "print-ready", which makes it a good test case: does the word in the prompt translate into enough pixels for print?

The downloaded PNG is 1024 × 1024 px and carries no DPI metadata at all.

The rule in one line 

required_px = ceil(print_inches × dpi)      # per side
effective_ppi = min(width_px / width_in, height_px / height_in)

Use ceil, not round: a 3.4166-inch side at 300 DPI needs 1025 pixels, and 1024 is one pixel short. Use the weaker side for effective PPI, because a square image placed on a 4 × 6 in card is limited by its 6-inch side.

The checker 

"""Check whether an image has enough pixels to print at a target size and DPI."""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import math
from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PrintCheck:
    width_px: int
    height_px: int
    metadata_dpi: tuple[float, float] | None
    target_in: tuple[float, float]
    required_px: tuple[int, int]
    effective_ppi: float
    max_in_at_target_dpi: tuple[float, float]
    passes: bool


def check_print(path: str | Path, width_in: float, height_in: float, dpi: int = 300) -> PrintCheck:
    if width_in <= 0 or height_in <= 0 or dpi <= 0:
        raise ValueError("print size and dpi must be positive")
    with Image.open(path) as im:
        width_px, height_px = im.size
        meta = im.info.get("dpi")
    required = (math.ceil(width_in * dpi), math.ceil(height_in * dpi))
    effective = min(width_px / width_in, height_px / height_in)
    return PrintCheck(
        width_px=width_px,
        height_px=height_px,
        metadata_dpi=tuple(round(float(v), 2) for v in meta) if meta else None,
        target_in=(width_in, height_in),
        required_px=required,
        effective_ppi=round(effective, 1),
        max_in_at_target_dpi=(round(width_px / dpi, 2), round(height_px / dpi, 2)),
        passes=width_px >= required[0] and height_px >= required[1],
    )


def tag_dpi(src: str | Path, dst: str | Path, dpi: int = 300) -> None:
    """Write DPI metadata without resampling. This never adds detail."""
    with Image.open(src) as im:
        im.save(dst, dpi=(dpi, dpi))


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    ap.add_argument("image")
    ap.add_argument("--size", required=True, help="print size in inches, e.g. 8x10")
    ap.add_argument("--dpi", type=int, default=300)
    args = ap.parse_args()
    w, h = (float(v) for v in args.size.lower().split("x"))
    result = check_print(args.image, w, h, args.dpi)
    print(json.dumps(asdict(result), indent=2))
    return 0 if result.passes else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Run it from the command line:

pip install pillow pytest
python dpi_check.py fixtures/night-pulse-poster.png --size 8x8

Output for the real poster:

{
  "width_px": 1024,
  "height_px": 1024,
  "metadata_dpi": null,
  "target_in": [8.0, 8.0],
  "required_px": [2400, 2400],
  "effective_ppi": 128.0,
  "max_in_at_target_dpi": [3.41, 3.41],
  "passes": false
}

The exit code is 1 when the check fails, so you can drop it into a CI step or a pre-upload script for a print shop.

Why "just set it to 300 DPI" does not work

tag_dpi() writes a 300 DPI tag without resampling. The test below proves the pixel data is byte-for-byte identical afterwards and the 8 × 8 in check still fails. That is exactly what the "change DPI" box in many editors does when resampling is off.

The crop above is the small lineup text from the same poster. At 8 × 8 inches each source pixel has to cover about 2.34 printer dots per side, which is where small type starts to look soft. Only a larger render or careful upscaling adds pixels; a metadata tag cannot.

Tests 

from pathlib import Path

import pytest
from PIL import Image

from dpi_check import check_print, tag_dpi

POSTER = Path(__file__).parent / "fixtures" / "night-pulse-poster.png"


def test_fixture_has_no_dpi_metadata():
    assert check_print(POSTER, 3, 3).metadata_dpi is None


def test_poster_fails_8x8_at_300_dpi():
    r = check_print(POSTER, 8, 8)
    assert (r.width_px, r.height_px) == (1024, 1024)
    assert r.required_px == (2400, 2400)
    assert r.effective_ppi == 128.0
    assert not r.passes


def test_poster_passes_at_its_true_300_dpi_size():
    r = check_print(POSTER, 3.4, 3.4)
    assert r.required_px == (1020, 1020)
    assert r.passes
    assert r.max_in_at_target_dpi == (3.41, 3.41)


def test_boundary_rounds_required_pixels_up():
    r = check_print(POSTER, 1025 / 300, 1)
    assert r.required_px[0] == 1025
    assert not r.passes


def test_mismatched_aspect_uses_the_weaker_side():
    r = check_print(POSTER, 4, 6)
    assert r.effective_ppi == pytest.approx(170.7)
    assert not r.passes


def test_tagging_300_dpi_changes_metadata_not_pixels(tmp_path):
    out = tmp_path / "tagged.png"
    tag_dpi(POSTER, out)
    before, after = check_print(POSTER, 8, 8), check_print(out, 8, 8)
    assert after.metadata_dpi == (300.0, 300.0)
    with Image.open(POSTER) as a, Image.open(out) as b:
        assert a.tobytes() == b.tobytes()
    assert before.passes == after.passes is False


def test_large_synthetic_image_passes_8x10(tmp_path):
    big = tmp_path / "big.png"
    Image.new("RGB", (2400, 3000), "white").save(big)
    assert check_print(big, 8, 10).passes


@pytest.mark.parametrize("w,h,dpi", [(0, 1, 300), (1, -2, 300), (1, 1, 0)])
def test_rejects_non_positive_inputs(w, h, dpi):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        check_print(POSTER, w, h, dpi)

$ pytest -q
..........                                                               [100%]
10 passed in 1.20s

The eight test functions (ten cases with the parametrized one) cover: missing metadata, the failing 8 × 8 case, the passing 3.4 in case, the ceil boundary, aspect mismatch, metadata-only tagging, a large synthetic pass and input validation.

Edge cases worth knowing

  • JPEG vs PNG: Pillow reads JFIF/EXIF density for JPEG and the pHYs chunk for PNG into im.info["dpi"]. Some exports store density in centimetres or with rounding (e.g. 299.9994); round before comparing if you assert on metadata.
  • No metadata: many tools assume 72 or 96 DPI when the tag is missing. That assumption only affects the default placed size in a layout app, not print quality.
  • Bleed: add the bleed to the print size before checking. An 8 × 8 in poster with 0.125 in bleed is 8.25 × 8.25 in, which needs 2475 px per side.
  • Vector-looking art is still raster: a flat "print-ready" AI image is a PNG; scaling it up does not behave like SVG.

Getting a fixture of your own

If you want to run the same check on your own generated poster, the GPT Image 2 prompt workspace has the festival prompt in its library. When I checked on October 26, 2026, the generator defaulted to 3:4, one output and Low quality, which showed 5 credits; switching to High showed 45 credits for one image. Measure whatever file you download with the script instead of assuming its size. New creations are Public with a watermark by default.

Wrap-up

Check pixels, not tags: ceil(inches × 300) per side, using the weaker side when aspect ratios differ. Keep the DPI tag for layout convenience, and fail the build when the pixels are short. If you need a test poster to try it on, generate one from the same prompt library and run the checker on the download.

title: Beyond Final Outcomes: Quantifying Claim-Level Information Dynamics in Multi-Agent LLM Interaction
description:
arXiv:2610.32333v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When LLM-powered agents interact, information is repeatedly shared, expanded, and forgotten, yet multi-agent evaluation typically focuses on final task outcomes. We study such interaction as claim-level information dynamics and propose RIVER, which decomposes agent outputs into atomic claims and evaluates three complementary dimensions: convergence, exploration, and retention. Convergence captures cross-agent claim correspondence and stance alignment; exploration captures semantic breadth and extension beyond the source; and retention tracks source preservation and the persistence of new claims across stages and lineages. We evaluate five interaction strategies on 40 controlled news-generation cases. Repeatedly pooled interaction promotes convergence but narrows the information space, whereas distributed relay yields broader, less shared information. Further comparisons show that method-specific constraints increase exploration while weakening convergence and retention. Our findings suggest that collective information dynamics are better explained by underlying information-flow mechanisms than by simple downstream performance.

title: Processes vs. Threads vs. Async: How WhatsApp Held 2 Million Connections on One Server
description:
Processes vs. Threads vs. Async: How WhatsApp Held 2 Million Connections on One Server

In 2012, WhatsApp engineer Rick Reed told an Erlang conference that the company's servers were holding more than 2 million simultaneous connections each. A test the team described reached over 2.5 million connections on a single machine, up from roughly 200,000 at the start of their tuning work, with CPU use above 85% across 24 logical cores. A few years later, with servers busier, they ran closer to 1 million connections per server across about 150 chat servers handling around 150 million peak connections. Behind it was one idea: every connected phone was handled by its own tiny Erlang process, which holds only kilobytes of state while idle.

Try that with the obvious approach, one operating system thread per connection, and the math falls apart. A Linux thread typically reserves around 8 MB of virtual address space for its stack (Java and Windows default to about 1 MB). Two million threads would reserve roughly 16 TB of address space, and that's before counting the kernel's own bookkeeping and the cost of scheduling them all. The stack space is virtual, not RAM, but the model still doesn't scale to that level.

Compare that with Go, where a new goroutine starts with a stack of about 2 KB, which is why a Go program can run hundreds of thousands of them. And Python has been changing the rules too: since Python 3.14, released in October 2025, there's an officially supported free-threaded build that runs without the Global Interpreter Lock, though it's still optional.

These three examples all answer the same question: how does a program do many things at once? The three classic answers are processes, threads, and async (event loops and lightweight tasks). They trade memory, speed, safety, and complexity in different ways, and operating systems courses often make them harder to remember than they should be. This guide explains each one with working examples, the real numbers behind the trade-offs, and a simple way to choose.

If operating systems concepts keep slipping away, the best fix is experiments, and our Linux & Shell and Backend Engineer courses are built around hands-on practice.

This post originally appeared on the Ciphemic Academia blog.

The Short Version

A restaurant analogy makes the difference stick:

  • Process: a separate restaurant. It has its own kitchen, staff, and ingredients. Nothing is shared, so a fire in one doesn't burn the other, but opening a new restaurant is expensive and sending a message between them takes effort.
  • Thread: extra cooks in the same kitchen. They share ingredients and equipment, so they're quick to add and cooperate easily, but they can collide over the same pan, and one disaster can ruin the whole kitchen.
  • Async: one cook who never stands idle. When a dish needs ten minutes in the oven, the cook starts another dish instead of waiting. It's incredibly efficient for waiting-heavy work, but if the cook gets stuck on one long task, everything stops.

If you want one default: use processes for CPU-heavy work that must use many cores, threads for modest amounts of blocking I/O, and async (or lightweight tasks) when you need to handle huge numbers of concurrent connections. Most real systems combine them.

What All Three Are Actually Trying to Solve

Before the differences, the shared problems:

  • Using waiting time: programs spend huge amounts of time waiting for disks, databases, and networks. Doing other work during that wait is the biggest win
  • Using multiple cores: a modern machine has many cores, and a single sequential program leaves most of them idle
  • Staying responsive: a program shouldn't freeze because one task is slow
  • Isolating failures: sometimes one task crashing shouldn't take everything down

Two terms often get mixed up here. Concurrency is about structuring a program to handle many things in progress at once. Parallelism is about actually running things at the same instant on multiple cores. Async gives you concurrency without parallelism, while processes and threads can give you both.

Processes

What it actually is: a running program with its own private memory space, managed by the operating system. Processes don't share memory by default, so they communicate through explicit channels such as pipes, sockets, or message queues. Each one is scheduled independently, which means a process can run on its own core.

A small example (four worker processes in Python):

from multiprocessing import Pool

def square(n):
    return n * n

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with Pool(4) as pool:        # 4 separate processes, 4 separate memory spaces
        print(pool.map(square, range(10)))

Where it shines:

  • Isolation: a crash or memory leak in one process doesn't corrupt another, which is why browsers like Chrome run tabs in separate processes
  • True parallelism for CPU-bound work in any language, including Python in its default build, because each process has its own interpreter
  • A simple mental model: with no shared memory, whole categories of race conditions disappear
  • Easy to restart: servers like Gunicorn and nginx manage pools of worker processes and replace ones that die

Where it struggles:

  • Heavier to create and run: each process has its own memory space and operating system bookkeeping, so you can't have as many as you can threads or async tasks
  • Communication costs: data has to be serialized and sent between processes, which is slower and more awkward than sharing memory
  • Memory duplication: the same data can end up copied in several processes, depending on how you share it

Who this suits: CPU-heavy tasks, workloads that need fault isolation, and security-sensitive designs where one component shouldn't be able to touch another's memory.

Threads

What it actually is: multiple paths of execution inside a single process, sharing the same memory. Because they share memory, threads are cheaper to create than processes and can communicate by reading and writing shared data. The operating system schedules them across cores.

A small example (three downloads overlapping while each waits on the network):

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
import requests

urls = ["https://example.com/a", "https://example.com/b", "https://example.com/c"]

def fetch(url):
    return requests.get(url, timeout=5).status_code

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as pool:
    print(list(pool.map(fetch, urls)))   # waits overlap instead of running one by one

The classic danger (shared state without a lock, then with one):

import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def unsafe_increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        counter += 1        # not atomic: threads can read the same value and lose updates

def safe_increment():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:          # only one thread updates at a time
            counter += 1

Where it shines:

  • Lighter than processes: faster to start, and threads share memory directly, so passing data is easy
  • Simple code for blocking I/O: each thread can just wait on its own request, which is easy to read
  • Real multi-core parallelism in languages and runtimes without a global lock, such as Java, C++, and Rust
  • A natural fit for moderate concurrency, such as a few dozen simultaneous requests

Where it struggles:

  • Shared mutable state breeds bugs: race conditions, deadlocks, and lost updates are notoriously hard to reproduce and debug
  • Each thread has real weight: a stack reservation (about 1 MB on Java and Windows, about 8 MB virtual on Linux), kernel bookkeeping, and scheduling overhead, which is why thread-per-connection fails at massive scale
  • Python's Global Interpreter Lock: in the default build, threads can't run Python bytecode in parallel, so CPU-bound threads don't speed up. Python 3.14 added an officially supported free-threaded build that removes this limit. It's optional, and the single-threaded cost is reported at roughly 5 to 10%, so check what your libraries support

Who this suits: applications with moderate concurrency, I/O-bound work where simple blocking code is easiest to maintain, and CPU-bound work in runtimes that allow true thread parallelism.

Async and Lightweight Tasks

What it actually is: instead of one thread per task, a small number of threads run an event loop that juggles many tasks. A task runs until it hits something slow, such as a network call, then yields control so another task can run. In Python and JavaScript this looks like async and await. Some runtimes go further: Go's goroutines and Erlang's processes are lightweight tasks scheduled by the runtime across a few real threads.

A small example (many requests in flight on one thread, using Python's asyncio):

import asyncio
import aiohttp

async def fetch(session, url):
    async with session.get(url) as resp:
        return resp.status

async def main(urls):
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(session, u) for u in urls))
        print(results)

asyncio.run(main(["https://example.com/a", "https://example.com/b"]))

Where it shines:

  • Tiny cost per task: a Go goroutine starts at about 2 KB of stack, and Erlang processes are similarly small, which is how WhatsApp reached millions of connections per server
  • Built for waiting-heavy work: servers like nginx and Node.js use event loops because most connections are idle most of the time
  • Fewer locking problems: because tasks only switch at known points, you avoid many data races, although you can still create logical ones
  • Cheap context switches: switching between tasks in the runtime is generally far cheaper than the operating system switching threads, though exact figures vary by benchmark

Where it struggles:

  • CPU-bound work blocks everyone: one task that computes for a second freezes every other task on that loop
  • Async spreads through your code: once a function is async, its callers usually need to be too, and every library you use has to cooperate with the event loop
  • One loop, one core: a single event loop doesn't use multiple cores unless you run several loops or combine it with processes
  • Harder debugging: stack traces and error handling in concurrent tasks can be less intuitive
  • Easy to accidentally block: a stray synchronous call inside async code, such as a blocking database driver or time.sleep, silently stalls the whole loop

Who this suits: servers that handle huge numbers of mostly waiting connections, such as chat, streaming, gateways, and API fan-out.

Side-by-Side Comparison

Process Thread Async task
What it is Independent program with its own memory Execution path inside a process, sharing memory Task scheduled by an event loop or runtime
Rough cost per unit Heaviest About 1 MB (Java, Windows) to 8 MB (Linux) of reserved stack Kilobytes (about 2 KB for a goroutine)
Memory sharing None by default Shared by default Shared within the loop
Isolation Strong Weak, one crash can take down the process Weak, same process
Multi-core parallelism Yes Yes (limited by the GIL in default Python) Not by itself, needs more loops or processes
Communication Pipes, sockets, queues Shared memory plus locks Shared memory, messages, or channels
Best for CPU-heavy work, isolation Moderate concurrency, blocking I/O Huge numbers of waiting connections
Typical failure Overhead, serialization costs Race conditions, deadlocks Blocked event loop
Real example Chrome tabs, Gunicorn workers Java servers, thread pools nginx, Node.js, WhatsApp's Erlang servers

How Real Systems Combine Them

Production systems rarely pick just one:

  • nginx runs a small number of worker processes, typically one per core, and each runs an event loop handling thousands of connections
  • Gunicorn runs several worker processes, and each can use threads or an async worker
  • Go schedules huge numbers of goroutines onto a handful of operating system threads
  • Node.js runs JavaScript on one main thread with an event loop, while using background threads for some I/O and offering worker threads for CPU-heavy tasks
  • Java 21 added virtual threads, lightweight threads managed by the JVM, a sign that the industry keeps moving toward cheaper tasks that still read like simple blocking code
  • Redis executes commands on a single thread driven by an event loop, which our Redis vs. Memcached guide compares with Memcached's multi-threaded approach

A useful picture:

Process      = isolated program, own memory            (heavy, safe)
Thread       = worker inside a process, shared memory  (lighter, risky)
Async task   = tiny job on an event loop               (cheapest, never block it)

How This Fits a Career Path

  • Backend engineers: choosing between worker processes, threads, and async is a daily design decision, and it explains behavior like why one slow endpoint can freeze a whole server; our Python vs. Go for backend services guide shows how language choice changes the answer
  • DevOps and platform engineers: you'll tune worker counts, connection limits, and timeouts, and read the symptoms when concurrency goes wrong; our Layer 4 vs. Layer 7 load balancing post covers how connections reach those servers
  • Computer science students: "what's the difference between a process and a thread?" is one of the most common operating systems questions in exams and interviews, and a clear, example-backed answer stands out
  • System design interviews: be ready to explain how a server handles ten thousand connections, and why thread-per-connection stops working

How to Choose Without Overthinking It

  1. Ask whether the work is CPU-bound or I/O-bound. CPU-bound work needs multiple cores, so use processes, or threads in a runtime without a global lock. I/O-bound work mostly waits, so threads or async both help.
  2. Count the concurrent tasks. Dozens: threads are fine. Thousands or more: async or lightweight tasks.
  3. Decide how much isolation you need. If one failure shouldn't affect others, separate processes give the strongest boundary.
  4. Check your runtime. In default Python, CPU-bound threads don't help. Go and Erlang make lightweight tasks easy, and Java 21 offers virtual threads.
  5. Combine when needed. A common pattern is an async server that hands CPU-heavy jobs to a pool of processes or threads.
  6. Prefer high-level tools, such as pools, executors, queues, and async frameworks, over hand-rolled locks.
  7. Measure first. Profile where your time actually goes before adding concurrency, because concurrency adds complexity even when it helps.

A note on honesty: the WhatsApp numbers come from conference talks in 2012 to 2014 about a heavily tuned Erlang and FreeBSD stack with custom patches, and many of those connections were idle, so they show what lightweight processes can hold, not what typical code achieves. A goroutine's roughly 2 KB starting stack is a default that grows as needed, and recent Go versions can adapt the initial size. Linux thread stacks are virtual reservations, so the 8 MB figure is not 8 MB of RAM per thread. Context-switch timings vary widely by hardware and benchmark, so treat any specific microsecond figure as an order of magnitude. Free-threaded Python is evolving quickly, so check the current release notes, including those for Python 3.15, before relying on it.

Common Mistakes When Learning Concurrency

  • Expecting threads to speed up CPU-bound Python. In the default build, they won't. Use processes, or try the free-threaded build if your libraries support it.
  • Blocking the event loop. Heavy computation, time.sleep, or a synchronous database call inside async code freezes every task on that loop.
  • Sharing mutable state without protection. Use locks, queues, or message passing, and keep shared state as small as possible.
  • Creating unlimited threads or processes. Use pools with sensible limits, since unbounded concurrency can exhaust memory or file descriptors.
  • Assuming async means parallel. Async overlaps waiting. It doesn't run code on multiple cores by itself.
  • Forgetting timeouts. A task waiting forever on a slow service can pile up and take the whole system down.
  • Ignoring errors in background tasks. An exception inside a task can disappear silently if nothing awaits or checks it.
  • Locking in inconsistent order. Two threads taking the same locks in different orders can deadlock.
  • Adding concurrency before measuring. Many slow programs are slow because of one bad query, not a lack of parallelism.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is async faster than threads?

Not inherently. Async is cheaper per task, so it handles far more concurrent connections, but for a small number of tasks, threads can be just as fast and simpler to write. The difference shows up at scale.

What is the GIL, and does it still matter?

The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time in the default CPython build. Python 3.14 introduced an officially supported free-threaded build without it, but it's optional and library support is still catching up, so for many projects it still matters.

What's the simplest way to explain process versus thread?

A process is an independent program with its own memory. A thread is a worker inside a process that shares that memory. Processes are safer and heavier, and threads are lighter and riskier.

What's the difference between concurrency and parallelism?

Concurrency is handling many tasks that are in progress at once, even on one core. Parallelism is running multiple tasks at the same instant on multiple cores.

Does Node.js use threads?

Your JavaScript runs on one main thread with an event loop, which is why a long computation blocks everything. Node uses background threads internally for some operations and offers worker threads for CPU-heavy work.

How do interviewers evaluate this topic?

Usually by asking you to explain the differences and then apply them: how would you build a server for ten thousand connections, or speed up a CPU-heavy job? Naming the trade-offs and the failure modes of each shows real understanding.

Pick the Model That Matches the Work

WhatsApp didn't hold millions of connections by picking the most popular tool. It picked the model that matched the work: huge numbers of mostly idle connections, each costing almost nothing. Match your concurrency model to your workload, keep shared state small, and measure before you optimize. Explore the Linux & Shell and Backend Engineer courses to practice these ideas with real experiments instead of memorizing definitions.

title: SCI-AGENT-EXAM: Benchmarking Agents on Scientific Research Tasks
description:
arXiv:2610.32441v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of supporting scientific workflows, but their capabilities across diverse research activities remain difficult to assess systematically. Existing benchmarks often focus on selected scientific capabilities or task types, limiting a comprehensive characterization of scientific agents' strengths and weaknesses in realistic research workflows. We introduce SCI-AGENT-EXAM, a workflow-oriented benchmark comprising 120 expert-curated tasks across 11 scientific fields and 7 research task types defined by the Scientific Workflow Task Taxonomy (SWTT). Each task requires both executable artifacts (e.g., code and scripts) and textual artifacts (e.g., reports and explanations). To evaluate the heterogeneous task outputs, we develop a hybrid evaluation protocol combining deterministic programmatic verification for executable artifacts with a calibrated, expert-validated LLM-based judge for textual artifacts. Beyond outcome assessment, we analyze progress and solution stability along execution trajectories to characterize how agents reach their final results. Experiments with 10 frontier LLM agents reveal substantial performance gaps: GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest overall score of 80.9, yet only 26.0% of its runs exceed the 0.95 success threshold. Further analyses uncover distinct capability profiles across scientific task types and substantial variation in execution efficiency and stability. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/SKYLENAGE-AI/Sci-Agent-Exam.

title: MAGIC: Margin-gated Contrastive Debiasing with Evidence Restoration for VLM Test-time Robustness Scaling
description:
arXiv:2610.32013v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper studies the problem of test-time robustness scaling for large vision-language models (LVLMs), which aims to mitigate language bias during inference. Existing approaches typically adopt test-time scaling techniques such as contrastive decoding to improve inference performance. Despite the progress, the performance of these approaches is far from satisfactory due to intentional evidence removal during perturbations and redundant inference cost. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Margin-gated Contrastive Debiasing with Evidence Restoration (MAGIC). The core of our MAGIC is to evaluate the decision margins of LVLMs to selectively activate textual and visual perturbation branches for efficient debiased inference. In particular, our MAGIC first measures the prediction margins of crucial tokens, and applies a gating function to identify low-confidence responses that are susceptible to language biases. For selected samples, we integrate the token logits from multiple textual and image perturbation branches with the original ones for debiased decision. More importantly, we selectively restore the most informative corrupted views with sharp prediction distributions for ambiguous samples after debiasing, enabling evidence recovery for discriminative decision-making. We further utilize a calibration dataset to actively identify and prune ineffective branches during contrastive debiasing for cost reduction. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed MAGIC in comparison with extensive baselines.

title: System One models Are Not Better Rerankers
description:
arXiv:2610.32318v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: System One models, or decision models, answer a question about an input with a calibrated probability instead of generated text. Within weeks of the first release, in September 2026, they were used as rerankers. We test whether the decision fine-tuning behind them makes a better reranker than plain reranker fine-tuning of the same model. For six Qwen backbones from 0.6B to 27B parameters and ten TREC DL and BEIR collections, we compare the untuned model, asked zero-shot, with its decision fine-tunes and its reranker fine-tunes, two of which we train ourselves. In our work, we draw the conclusion that decision fine-tuning never makes the better reranker. From 0.6B to 9B, reranker fine-tuning wins on every backbone by 5 to 29 points nDCG@10, also on zero-shot collections, and at 27B the two tie. Up to 9B, decision fine-tuning adds nothing over simply asking the untuned model. Moreover, we find that the calibration advantage of decision models depends on the question. Asked whether a passage answers the query, they are better calibrated than the published reranker fine-tunes from 4B on. Asked a slightly different question from prior work, they lose this advantage. Lastly, calibration does not make up for a worse ranking: up to 9B, a reranker fine-tune keeps the better passages at a fixed threshold. If you need a reranker, fine-tune a reranker.

title: Eight CA Keys Between 1 and 255: What the eMudhra Incident Means for Your Code
description:
Up to date as of 25 October 2026. The fixes are still changing: on 24 October Oracle shipped a second Java fix (CVE-2026-114820), so guidance written before then calls Java builds fixed that aren't. For anything newer, check the incident site's list of patches.

On 17 October 2026 someone signed the sentence "We have a problem here - Wayne" with the private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities: six trusted for TLS by Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Windows, and two trusted by Windows for code signing. Nobody stole those keys. Nobody had to. Each one was an integer between 1 and 255, so anyone could compute it from the public certificate in less time than it takes to read this sentence.

Chrome and Firefox were protected within hours, Windows and Apple devices within days. Your backend probably wasn't, and the reason says something uncomfortable about TLS outside the browser: trust doesn't live in the protocol, it lives in a file of root certificates that every runtime picks for itself. Patch the OS and you've fixed curl. You haven't fixed Node, a Go binary built last month, or the certifi inside a virtualenv.

Question Short answer
What was compromised? 8 eMudhra intermediate CAs (6 TLS, 2 code signing) and their 8 Sectigo cross-signs (the same keys, also signed by Sectigo)
What can an attacker do? Issue a valid certificate for any hostname
What else does the attacker need? A position on the network path between your client and the server
Who was exposed? Clients that trust the roots and check neither revocation nor Certificate Transparency: most non-browser TLS
What's the fix? Update the runtime and its trust store, then rebuild everything that embeds them

One chain runs through the whole article, the real one served by the incident's test host dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com. We'll look at what a certificate proves, what went wrong with these, what an attacker needs to use them, the before and after on that chain, and how to fix the four runtimes you're most likely to ship: Java, Go, Node.js and Python.

What a Certificate Actually Proves

Definition. A certificate binds a public key to a name, and a signature from someone else backs that binding. That "someone else" is a certificate authority, whose own certificate is signed by another CA, until you reach a root: a certificate nobody signs, which your client trusts because it's in a file called a trust store. The server's own certificate, the one with the hostname in it, is the leaf. The CAs between the leaf and the root are intermediates.

You can print the chain the test host serves:

openssl s_client -connect dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com:443 -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -E ' s:| i:'

 0 s:CN=dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com
   i:C=NL, O=eMudhra BV, CN=EM DV TLS CA - G3B
 1 s:C=NL, O=eMudhra BV, CN=EM DV TLS CA - G3B
   i:C=IN, O=eMudhra Technologies Limited, CN=emSign Root TLS CA - G3
 2 s:C=IN, O=eMudhra Technologies Limited, CN=emSign Root TLS CA - G3
   i:C=IN, OU=emSign PKI, O=eMudhra Technologies Limited, CN=emSign ECC Root CA - G3

s: is who each certificate speaks for and i: is who signed it. The server doesn't send the root; the client has to find it in its own trust store. Drawn as a tree:

dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com           leaf: "this key speaks for this hostname"
└─ signed by EM DV TLS CA - G3B                intermediate: one of the eight weak keys
   └─ signed by emSign Root TLS CA - G3        intermediate
      └─ signed by emSign ECC Root CA - G3     root: the one in your trust store

During the handshake the server sends the chain, and the client checks three things: every signature verifies with the issuer's public key, every certificate is in date and allowed to do what it's doing, and the chain ends at a root in the client's own trust store. The last check is the only place where trust enters the system. Everything else is arithmetic.

An intermediate's certificate shows how much power it holds. The incident's proof folder has all eight; download one and print its limits:

curl -sSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/galadran/we-have-a-problem.com/main/proof/EM-OV-TLS-CA-G3C.crt.pem
openssl x509 -in EM-OV-TLS-CA-G3C.crt.pem -noout -subject -ext basicConstraints,extendedKeyUsage

subject=C=US, O=eMudhra Inc, CN=EM OV TLS CA - G3C
X509v3 Extended Key Usage:
    TLS Web Server Authentication, TLS Web Client Authentication
X509v3 Basic Constraints: critical
    CA:TRUE, pathlen:0

CA:TRUE, pathlen:0 means it may sign leaves but not further CAs. There's no nameConstraints extension, so nothing limits which hostnames it can back. Whoever holds its private key can sign a certificate for api.your-bank.com, and your client has no way to tell it from a real one. That's why CA keys live in hardware security modules (HSMs: tamper-resistant devices that never let the key out) and why key ceremonies have witnesses.

After the fact, two mechanisms can still save a client:

  • Revocation. The CA publishes "stop trusting this one" through CRLs (lists of revoked certificates the CA publishes) or OCSP (a service the client asks about one certificate). It works only if the client checks, and most non-browser clients don't by default.
  • Certificate Transparency (CT). Public, append-only logs where CAs record every certificate they issue, so anyone can see what was issued for a domain. Browsers reject a leaf that hasn't been logged, so a forged certificate either becomes public or gets rejected. Almost nothing outside the browser checks this.

If you remember one thing: a certificate is only as trustworthy as the private key of every CA above it, and the trust store is a file your client chooses, not a property of the internet.

What Went Wrong at eMudhra

A P-384 private key is a random 384-bit number k. The public key is k·G, the curve's base point added to itself k times. Going forward is cheap; going back is the problem P-384's security rests on. Mozilla's analysis in the incident report found that the eight keys were all integers less than 256: 48 bytes, all zero except the last. With 255 candidates, "going back" means computing 255 points and comparing them with the certificate. One write-up measured 28.7 milliseconds for the full table.

You don't need to brute-force anything to check it. One of the keys is already public: the key of EM OV TLS CA - G3C is 4. Using the certificate you downloaded above:

from cryptography import x509
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ec

cert = x509.load_pem_x509_certificate(open("EM-OV-TLS-CA-G3C.crt.pem", "rb").read())
four = ec.derive_private_key(4, ec.SECP384R1())   # the private key "4"

print(cert.public_key().public_numbers() == four.public_key().public_numbers())
# True

P-384 isn't broken. A key of 4 is a valid key: it parses, it signs, signatures verify. Every format check and every sign-and-verify test passes, which is exactly why nothing caught it for almost eighteen months.

How it happened, according to eMudhra's preliminary explanation in the report: the keys were generated on Utimaco HSMs during a ceremony on 30 April 2025. An approved deviation added a test of key wrap/unwrap (exporting a key encrypted and importing it back), a flaw in that test code created a second, weaker key pair inside the HSM, and because the labels were similar the weak pair was used for the CSRs (certificate signing requests: the public key and name a CA is asked to sign). The root signed them and Sectigo cross-signed them. Other participants in the report point out that an HSM's certified key generation doesn't produce a scalar below 256 on its own, so how that material got there is still an open question. eMudhra hasn't answered yet; it says its full report will come within the 14 days the rules allow.

What was affected: eight intermediates from that ceremony.

  • Six sign HTTPS certificates: EM DV TLS CA, EM OV TLS CA and EM EV TLS CA, each in a G3B and a G3C version. All six chain to emSign ECC Root CA - G3.
  • Two sign code: EM OV CS CA - G3B and EM OV CS CA - G3C. Only Microsoft trusted them.

The names follow a pattern:

  • DV, OV and EV say how much the CA checks about a customer before issuing. Domain Validated checks only that they control the domain, Organization Validated also checks that their company exists, and Extended Validation adds stricter legal checks.
  • G3B and G3C are two copies of each CA, issued to two eMudhra companies: every G3B to eMudhra BV in the Netherlands, every G3C to eMudhra Inc in the US.

None of it matters for this incident. The checks are a promise the CA makes, not something the key enforces, so whoever holds any of the six keys can sign for any hostname.

Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root had cross-signed the same eight public keys (signed them too, so they also chain to Sectigo's root), and a cross-sign with the same key is the same compromise. eMudhra itself issued no end-entity certificates (leaves) from them. Whether anyone else did in the eighteen months before the report, nobody can prove either way for clients that don't check CT.

eMudhra has since announced that it is leaving the public TLS business, and some trust stores now drop more than the one root behind these keys. Java's second update removes all three eMudhra roots the JDK carried, and certifi 2026.10.23 drops two more (eMudhra Inc's emSign Root CA - C1 and emSign ECC Root CA - C3). If a server you call still uses an eMudhra certificate, expect it to fail once you update.

The incident site keeps the authoritative list of who has patched.

If you remember one thing: the keys weren't stolen, they were computable, from public data, by anyone, for almost eighteen months. Treat every client that trusted these roots as if the keys had been public all along, because they effectively were.

Why It's Exploitable, and What an Attacker Still Needs

With an intermediate key, an attacker signs a leaf for whatever hostname your service calls. The chain validates. But a certificate alone does nothing: the attacker has to receive your connection to present it. That means a position on the path:

  • DNS answers they control (poisoning, a compromised resolver, a hijacked record).
  • A network device in the middle: a proxy, a router, a hostile Wi-Fi, a compromised egress gateway.
  • A routing attack (BGP hijacking: announcing the destination's IP addresses from a network the attacker controls, so traffic goes there).

This isn't remote code execution, and nobody can scan the internet with it. It turns a network position, which TLS normally makes harmless, into full read-and-write access to the traffic.

So why were browsers safe and your backend not? Because of the two mechanisms above:

  • Revocation. eMudhra revoked the intermediates on 18 October. Python, Node, curl and Go on Linux don't check revocation by default, and neither does Java's TLS stack unless you set com.sun.net.ssl.checkRevocation=true. (Go on macOS and Windows asks the OS verifier, so it picked up Apple's and Microsoft's blocks.)
  • Certificate Transparency. No certificate signed by these intermediates appeared in the public CT logs before the block. A browser rejects unlogged certificates, so a forgery would have had to show up in public first. Non-browser clients don't check CT, so for them a forged certificate needs no log entry at all.

Browsers also receive blocklists pushed by the vendor (Chrome's CRLSet, Firefox's OneCRL) without a software update. Your runtime gets nothing until you upgrade it.

Forged certificates stopped being hypothetical on 20 October. Over the next day and a half, people logged 107,107 of them, signed with six of the keys, to public CT logs: 106,050 are proof-of-concept certificates for google.com, and every signature verifies. All but two carry no revocation pointer (the CRL or OCSP address a client would ask), so a client that checks revocation only for the leaf, a common setup, finds nothing to check. Only a client that checks every CA in the chain, receives a pushed blocklist or has dropped the roots rejects them.

What that means for a typical service:

Your code talks to… Exposure Why
Internal services, with a trust store holding only your private CA None The eMudhra roots are never consulted
Internal services, with the default trust store Low The attacker must already be inside your network
External APIs, SaaS, your cloud provider's endpoints Real, needs a man-in-the-middle The path crosses networks you don't control
Package registries from CI or laptops Unlikely, high impact A forged registry can serve a tampered package into every build
Browsers None Pushed blocklists and CT

Note the second row. "We only call internal services" protects you only if the client trusts only internal CAs. Most services keep the default trust store and append their private CA to it, so a forged certificate for orders.internal still validates. It's just much harder to deliver.

If you remember one thing: the key is the weapon and the network position is the trigger. Your risk is how many networks you don't control sit between your clients and the servers they call.

Before and After

The incident site runs test hosts that serve the compromised chains. Run the check from where your code runs, a pod, a container or a CI job, not from your laptop:

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/      # eMudhra root
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://dv-g3b-aaa-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/  # Sectigo cross-sign

# Before: the client trusts the compromised intermediate
200

# After: trust removed (wording depends on curl's TLS backend; this is OpenSSL)
curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate

Two more hosts serve leaves that were never logged to CT:

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://dv-g3b-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://dv-g3b-aaa-noct-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/

A 200 here is the worst result: your client trusts the compromised intermediates and doesn't enforce CT, so it could be attacked without anything ever appearing in a public log.

curl only tests curl's trust store. Your service uses its runtime's, so the companion script runs the same request through curl, Python, Node, Java and Go, whichever are installed.

Before you run it at work. Each check opens one HTTPS connection to a test host. The incident site runs them; Oracle and OpenJDK link to it, and its source is on GitHub. The hosts see what any website sees: your public IP, the hostname and the time. curl, Python, Node and Go send a plain GET /, and the Java probe stops after the TLS handshake. A host your client trusts answers with one line of text, which the scripts throw away. On a company network, three things matter:

  • A connection that presents a certificate from a revoked, compromised CA is exactly what a security proxy or intrusion detection system should flag. Tell your security team before you run it.
  • If a proxy inspects TLS, your client checks the proxy's certificate instead of the test host's, so the result tells you nothing about your runtime.
  • Proxies often block newly registered domains. That shows up as ERROR, which proves nothing either way.

If you can't make the call, the offline check below and Probe --roots in the Java section need no connection to the test hosts.

Offline, with no network at all. The site also publishes every chain as PEM (the text format that starts with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----), so you can check a trust store file directly. Here is the same chain against certifi before and after the fix:

$ openssl verify -CAfile certifi-2026.7.22.pem -untrusted chain.pem chain.pem
chain.pem: OK

$ openssl verify -CAfile certifi-2026.10.19.pem -untrusted chain.pem chain.pem
C = IN, O = eMudhra Technologies Limited, CN = emSign Root TLS CA - G3
error 20 at 2 depth lookup: unable to get local issuer certificate
error chain.pem: verification failed

OK means the bundle still trusts the compromised intermediate. Error 20 at depth 2 means the chain now dead-ends one step before the root: emSign ECC Root CA - G3 is gone from the bundle. The Sectigo chain (dv-g3b-aaa) fails against both versions, because certifi doesn't carry AAA Certificate Services at all. That cross-sign path matters for stores that do: Windows, the /etc/ssl/cert.pem macOS ships, and the Linux stores the incident site gives workarounds for.

If you remember one thing: test with the runtime your service uses, from where it runs. A green curl on your laptop says nothing about a Node container in production.

Why Every Runtime Needs Its Own Fix

Each runtime answers "which roots do I trust?" differently, so each one got a different fix:

Runtime Where its roots come from What the fix does Fixed in CVE
Java The JDK's lib/security/cacerts; distro packages link it to the OS store Distrusts the intermediates through blocked.certs, then removes four roots from cacerts 24 Oct updates CVE-2026-91403, CVE-2026-114820
Go The OS store on Linux; the OS verifier on macOS and Windows A hardcoded blocklist in crypto/x509, compiled into your binary 1.26.10, 1.27.3 CVE-2026-111943
Node.js Mozilla's bundle, compiled into the node binary NSS 3.131.1 roots, and rejects chains with the blocked public keys 22.23.4, 24.22.1, 26.12.1 none
Python (ssl, urllib) The OS store Whatever your distro's ca-certificates does Your distro's package none
Python (requests, pip, many libs) certifi, a bundle inside each virtualenv Drops emSign ECC Root CA - G3 certifi 2026.10.19, pip 26.2.2, uv 0.13.5 none
curl, git, OpenSSL The OS store Drops the root e.g. Ubuntu 20260816ubuntu0.24.04.1 none

Go's fix is a list of the eight compromised public keys (their SHA-256 hashes) in crypto/x509, and Verify rejects any chain that contains one of them. Blocking by public key rather than by certificate is the right call: the eMudhra certificate and the Sectigo cross-sign carry the same key, so one entry covers both. And because the list is part of the standard library, it ends up inside every binary you build. Upgrading the Go installed on a server changes nothing for a binary that's already compiled: you have to rebuild it with 1.26.10 or 1.27.3.

Two consequences are easy to miss:

  • "Update the OS" is not a fix for Node or certifi. Neither reads the OS store by default. For Go on Linux it helps, because it drops the root, but the blocklist only arrives with a rebuild.
  • Your CVE scanner won't flag Node or Python. Neither fix has a CVE, so a scanner that matches CVEs to versions reports them clean. Check those two by version. For Java, make sure the scanner knows CVE-2026-114820: against the first CVE alone, the 21 October builds look fixed.

If you remember one thing: ask of every process, "where does this get its roots, and who updates that file?" The answer is different for each runtime, and sometimes it's "a file compiled into a binary you built last month."

Fixing It, Runtime by Runtime

Java

Oracle shipped two fixes three days apart, and only the second one is enough. Both score 9.1 and cover Java SE 8, 11, 17, 21, 25 and 27, GraalVM for JDK 17 and 21, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.

  • CVE-2026-91403, 21 October: distrusts the eight intermediates and their eight Sectigo cross-signs through blocked.certs. Oracle's builds 11.0.33.0.2, 17.0.21.0.2, 21.0.13.0.2, 25.0.5.0.2, 27.0.1.0.2 and 8u511 b32.
  • CVE-2026-114820, 24 October: also removes four roots from cacerts: emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root CA - G1, emSign Root CA - G2 and Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services. It lists the 21 October builds as affected. Oracle's fixed builds are 11.0.33.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3 and 8u511 b33. Java 8 keeps the update number and bumps the build, so java -version has to say 1.8.0_511-b33.

Only the first and the last of those roots are behind the compromised chains; the JDK drops eMudhra's other two as well.

  • Update the JDK in every place it lives: Docker base images, setup-java in CI, self-hosted runners, laptops. For Docker, rebuild your own image with docker build --pull so it starts from the updated base. Redeploying an image you already built, or giving it a new tag, keeps the old JDK inside it. Other vendors (Temurin, Corretto, Zulu and the rest) number their builds differently. OpenJDK's eMudhra page, last updated on 24 October, says to look for JDK-8395690 / CVE-2026-114820 in your vendor's release notes, "even if you have updated your runtime in the past few days". It also publishes CheckCerts.java, which prints BAD ROOT for each of the four roots a runtime still trusts.
  • Base images lag behind vendor releases. On 25 October, three days after Temurin's October builds came out, the official eclipse-temurin:21-jre, 21-jre-alpine and 25-jre-alpine images still shipped 21.0.12.1 and 25.0.4.1, and Probe (below) still saw them trust the test hosts. Until the image you build on is updated, --pull changes nothing: check the result, don't assume it.
  • If your vendor hasn't shipped the fix yet, remove the four roots yourself, then restart the JVM. OpenJDK's page deletes them by alias, but alias names differ between vendors (Temurin calls the first one cn_emsign_ecc_root_ca__g3,o_emudhra_technologies_limited,ou_emsign_pki,c_in [jdk]), so find them by subject instead: 
  keytool -list -v -cacerts -storepass changeit \
    | awk '/^Alias name: /{a=substr($0,13)} /^Owner: .*CN=(emSign Root CA - G[12]|emSign ECC Root CA - G3|AAA Certificate Services)(,|$)/{print a}' \
    | while IFS= read -r a; do keytool -delete -cacerts -storepass changeit -alias "$a"; done

It prints nothing when it works, and nothing when there's nothing to delete. To see what it will remove, run the first two lines on their own: they print the aliases that match. On eclipse-temurin:21-jre:

  cn_emsign_ecc_root_ca__g3,o_emudhra_technologies_limited,ou_emsign_pki,c_in [jdk]
  cn_emsign_root_ca__g1,o_emudhra_technologies_limited,ou_emsign_pki,c_in [jdk]

Run them again afterwards: no output means the roots are gone. Deleting needs write access to cacerts, so a system JDK needs sudo; without it, keytool stops with Permission denied.

changeit is the default password of the JDK's cacerts. Java 8's keytool has no -cacerts option, so replace it with -keystore and the file: $JAVA_HOME/jre/lib/security/cacerts in a JDK, $JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts in a JRE. A vendor's cacerts doesn't always hold all four (Temurin's has emSign Root CA - G1 and emSign ECC Root CA - G3 only), and the command deletes whichever it finds. Whether you update or remove them by hand, servers that chain to AAA Certificate Services or to eMudhra's other roots stop working, so test the hosts you call before rolling it out.

  • In a Docker image, the keystore is baked into the image, so the removal goes in your Dockerfile, after the FROM: 
  FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
  RUN keytool -list -v -cacerts -storepass changeit \
      | awk '/^Alias name: /{a=substr($0,13)} /^Owner: .*CN=(emSign Root CA - G[12]|emSign ECC Root CA - G3|AAA Certificate Services)(,|$)/{print a}' \
      | while IFS= read -r a; do keytool -delete -cacerts -storepass changeit -alias "$a"; done

To check an image on your machine, ask the Java inside it. The companion's Probe.java connects to the test hosts through the JVM's own TLS stack, so it sees what your application sees: the image's cacerts, the blocked.certs fix and any trust store the image configures. The version string can't tell you that, least of all for a company's own JDK build. Compile it once with javac --release 8 Probe.java, then run it with the image's Java (8 or later; a JRE is enough):

  docker run --rm --entrypoint java -v "$PWD:/probe:ro" my-image -cp /probe Probe

Any TRUSTED line means the image is still exposed. --entrypoint makes this work even when the image starts your application by default, and settings in its ENV, such as JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, still apply. If the start script passes -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=… instead, add the same flags after my-image. On your laptop, java -cp . Probe does the same for your own JDK.

  • Company images: only your CAs, or the public roots too? The answer tells you which row of the exposure table above you're in. Probe --roots lists every root the image's Java trusts, and it needs no network: 
  docker run --rm --entrypoint java -v "$PWD:/probe:ro" my-image -cp /probe Probe --roots

  /opt/java/openjdk 21.0.12.1+1-LTS, trustStore=/opt/corp/truststore.p12
       CN=ACME Corp Root CA,O=ACME
  1 trusted roots: 0 BAD (behind the compromised chains), 0 DROP (also removed by the 24 October fix)

That image trusts one private root and nothing else. The stock eclipse-temurin:21-jre lists 118 roots, including:

  BAD  CN=emSign ECC Root CA - G3,O=eMudhra Technologies Limited,OU=emSign PKI,C=IN
  DROP CN=emSign Root CA - G1,O=eMudhra Technologies Limited,OU=emSign PKI,C=IN

BAD marks a root behind the compromised chains. DROP marks eMudhra's other two roots: they aren't compromised, but the 24 October fix removes them too, and OpenJDK's CheckCerts flags them as well. Either label makes Probe exit with 1. On a fixed JDK no line is labelled, the summary reads 0 BAD …, 0 DROP …, and Probe exits with 0; the number of roots varies by vendor and doesn't matter. Ask Java rather than reading the trust store file with keytool: a PKCS12 file (the standard keystore format, Java's default since 9) protected by a password lists no entries without that password, so it looks empty when it isn't. Java gets the password from the image's own settings.

This covers Java only. curl, git, Python's ssl module and Go read the OS bundle (/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt on Debian, Ubuntu and Alpine), and company images often add their CA to it rather than replace it. docker create lets you copy it out without starting anything:

  id=$(docker create my-image) && docker cp -L "$id":/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt . ; docker rm "$id"
  openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile ca-certificates.crt | openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -noout | grep '^subject'
  • Know which cacerts you use. readlink -f "$JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts" tells you. JDK packages on Fedora, RHEL, Arch, Gentoo and Oracle Linux read the OS store, so updating ca-certificates is likely enough there. Homebrew's and FreeBSD's OpenJDK carry their own cacerts, so upgrade the JDK package itself: brew upgrade openjdk, not brew update, which only refreshes Homebrew's list of packages. On 25 October only Homebrew's openjdk (27.0.1.0.3) had the 24 October fix. openjdk@21 (21.0.13.0.2) still trusted all four roots, and the other versioned packages were at the same or older builds, so remove the roots by hand there. On Debian and Ubuntu, cacerts points to /etc/ssl/certs/java/cacerts, and a long-standing bug means updating ca-certificates doesn't reach it. Regenerate it as root: 
  rm -f /etc/ssl/certs/java/cacerts
  update-ca-certificates --fresh
  • Embedded JREs. Jenkins, Kafka, Elasticsearch, IDEs and many vendor appliances ship their own Java. Updating the system JDK doesn't touch them, so update the product.
  • Revocation checking instead of removing the roots. OpenJDK and Oracle both accept -Dcom.sun.net.ssl.checkRevocation=true -Dcom.sun.security.enableCRLDP=true as the alternative. Java checks every certificate in the chain, not just the leaf, so it also rejects the forged certificates that carry no revocation pointer: with those two flags after my-image, Probe rejects all four test hosts even on an unpatched eclipse-temurin:21-jre. It costs you a CRL fetch on new chains and can fail handshakes when a CRL endpoint is unreachable. eMudhra's CRL and OCSP servers have also been refusing curl's, Wget's and Python's User-Agents (Java's got through on 25 October), so test it before rolling it out. For signed JARs, JDK 17 and later can check revocation with jarsigner -verify -revcheck -strict app.jar.
  • If you can't update yet, Oracle also publishes a replacement blocked.certs for lib/security/ (on Java 8 the file is blacklisted.certs). It covers only the first CVE, so remove the roots as well.

Go

  • See what a binary was built with, not what's installed: go version ./bin/my-service prints the toolchain embedded in the file.
  • Rebuild with 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 and redeploy. Pin it where your build reads it: a toolchain go1.26.10 line in go.mod, go-version in setup-go, the golang: builder image. Go 1.25 and older get no fix.
  • Rebuild the runtime image too. On Linux, Go still reads the OS store, so a distroless or alpine base from last month keeps the old roots until you pull a new one.

Node.js

  • Check what your node trusts, from the container that runs it: 
  node -e "const {X509Certificate}=require('crypto');
    const hit=require('tls').rootCertificates.some(p=>new X509Certificate(p).subject.includes('emSign ECC Root CA - G3'));
    console.log(process.version, hit ? 'STILL TRUSTS emSign ECC Root CA - G3' : 'root removed')"
  # v22.22.0 STILL TRUSTS emSign ECC Root CA - G3
  • Upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 everywhere you pin a version: .nvmrc, engines, setup-node, the node: base image, Lambda runtimes. These releases also fix other CVEs, including a Brotli out-of-bounds write (CVE-2026-111497), so they're worth taking anyway.
  • Node 20 and older get nothing. Node 20 reached end of life in April 2026.
  • Mind the flags. NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS only adds roots, it never removes one. --use-system-ca and --use-openssl-ca switch Node to the OS store, which makes the OS package part of your fix.
  • Electron, Bun and Deno bundle their own roots and released their own fixes.

Python

  • Check every environment, not the interpreter: python -c "import certifi; print(certifi.__version__)" inside each virtualenv, image and lambda.
  • Pin certifi>=2026.10.19 and regenerate your lockfile so the pin actually lands. Upgrade pip to 26.2.2 or later and uv to 0.13.5 or later. uv ships its own roots, so it needed its own fix: 0.13.4 removed the root and 0.13.5 also rejects chains that carry the compromised keys.
  • New Python releases don't fix old virtualenvs. 3.15.1, 3.14.9 and 3.13.17 bundle a newer pip for new installs. Existing environments keep whatever certifi they had.
  • Look for vendored bundles. Some libraries ship a .pem inside the package and ignore both the OS and certifi: find .venv -path '*site-packages*' -name '*.pem' lists them.
  • Code that uses ssl or urllib directly follows the OS store, so it's fixed by ca-certificates.

The OS and Your Images

  • Update ca-certificates on hosts and in images. Patched versions include Debian 20250419~deb12u2 / 20250419+deb13u1, Ubuntu 20260816ubuntu0.24.04.1 (and its 22.04, 26.04 and 26.10 equivalents), Alpine 20261020-r0 and Fedora 2026.2.92_v9.0.319.
  • Rebuild, don't just redeploy. An image keeps the trust store it was built with. Images pinned by digest or built from a cached layer never pick up the fix. docker build --pull and check: docker run --rm my-image dpkg -l ca-certificates (or apk info -v ca-certificates on Alpine).
  • macOS has no ca-certificates package. Safari, Mail and apps built on Apple's frameworks already block these certificates: Apple pushes that change to devices without an OS update. The command-line tools that ship with macOS (curl, git, python3, ruby, perl, openssl) read /etc/ssl/cert.pem instead, which keeps the root until a future macOS update. Apple's note and the incident site give the commands to remove it yourself; a macOS update may put it back. The built-in pip3 uses its own, older copy of the roots, and the incident site shows how to point it at the fixed file. Tools installed with Homebrew use Homebrew's own bundle: brew upgrade ca-certificates.

CI/CD and Your Dependencies

The CI risk is a forged registry serving a tampered package. TLS was the only thing standing between your build and that package, unless something else checks the content:

Ecosystem Content check that survives a broken TLS
Go go.sum plus the checksum database, whose signing key ships inside go itself
npm integrity hashes in package-lock.json, when installing with npm ci
Python pip install --require-hashes, or uv.lock
Gradle Dependency verification metadata (--write-verification-metadata sha256)
Maven Checksums travel over the same connection and PGP isn't checked by default, so nothing, out of the box

A job that resolves dependencies from scratch, without a lockfile, trusts TLS and nothing else.

Managed Runtimes

On AWS Lambda, a function on a managed runtime in Auto update mode gets the patched runtime once AWS publishes one, rolled out in phases. Function update mode only updates when you deploy the function, container images need a rebuild, and anything still on nodejs20.x won't be patched at all. The INIT_START line in the function's logs shows the runtime version it started with.

The Checklist

  • Inventory every runtime and version per service: Dockerfiles, CI workflows, go.mod, .nvmrc, requirements*.txt, lockfiles, Lambda configs.
  • Java: JDK at a 24 October build (release notes list JDK-8395690) in images, CI, runners, laptops and embedded JREs, or the four roots removed (or revocation checking on), and Probe rejecting all four test hosts.
  • Go: every deployed binary rebuilt with 1.26.10 or 1.27.3 (go version ./binary).
  • Node.js: 22.23.4, 24.22.1 or 26.12.1 everywhere; nothing left on Node 20.
  • Python: certifi>=2026.10.19 in every environment, pip ≥ 26.2.2, uv ≥ 0.13.5, lockfiles regenerated, vendored .pem files reviewed.
  • OS: ca-certificates updated on hosts and in base images; images rebuilt with --pull; on macOS, /etc/ssl/cert.pem fixed by hand until Apple's update.
  • Custom trust stores: any -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, SSL_CERT_FILE or bundled .pem checked for emSign ECC Root CA - G3.
  • Third-party software: agents, appliances, backup tools and anything else that makes its own TLS connections, checked against its vendor's notice.
  • CI: dependency verification on (lockfiles with hashes, Gradle verification metadata).
  • Verify from where the code runs: the test hosts reject, including the noct ones.
  • Don't stop at the scanner: Node and Python have no CVE for this.

Trust Is a File You Ship

Here's the whole article as two questions to ask of any process that opens a TLS connection:

  1. "Where does this get its roots?" The OS store, a bundle inside the runtime, a package in the virtualenv, a list compiled into the binary. If the answer is "I don't know", that's the finding.
  2. "Who updates that file, and when do I pick it up?" Your distro, your runtime's release, your lockfile, your next build. Anything that answers "the next build" is only fixed once you build.

None of this is new. DigiNotar in 2011 and the Symantec distrust in 2018 taught the same lesson, and browsers answered it with pushed blocklists and Certificate Transparency. Most server-side clients got neither. Until they do, the trust store is a dependency like any other: it has versions, it goes stale, and it ships inside your artifacts whether you think about it or not.

The check script lives in the companion folder: it sends the same request to the four test hosts through curl, Python (ssl and certifi), Node, Java and Go, whichever are installed, and prints which ones still trust the compromised chains. The chains and the proof certificates used above come from the incident site's repository.
