title: Cloud Storage Providers: How to Choose Scalable Go App Data Backups
description:
For scalable app-data backups with strong developer documentation, start with AWS S3 or Google Cloud Storage. Both have well-documented SDKs for major programming languages, which matters when a backup worker must upload, inspect, and delete objects without turning storage calls into a second application. Azure Blob Storage is a sound choice when the rest of the platform already lives in Azure. A REST storage adapter can be attractive for a mixed-runtime team, but only after its retention and deletion controls have been checked against the actual requirement.

Short answer: keep signed documents private, record the retention deadline and approval state outside the object store, and make deletion an explicit state transition. A bucket is not an audit log. The provider decision should follow the deletion contract and the regions where the application and its users operate, not a feature-count contest.

What should the on-call see when a document outlives its deadline?

The useful alert is small and specific: signed-document/retention-worker has found a document whose retain_until timestamp passed, but its status is still stored. The on-call should see the document ID, tenant ID, object key, deadline, and the age of the pending decision. They should not see a public download link, and the worker should not delete the object merely because a clock crossed midnight.

Work backwards from that page. The signal was a retention record whose deadline passed without an approval transition. The instrumentation change is to emit a counter for retention_review_due, a counter for successful and rejected deletion transitions, and an age metric for the oldest due record. Set the SLO around the review workflow, for example, “99% of due records become reviewed within the team’s stated review window,” rather than pretending object storage latency measures compliance.

The threshold has a cost on both sides. Too low, and an ordinary queue delay pages the team; too high, and the system silently accumulates documents past their declared deadline. I would begin with a review threshold that reflects the operational window, then tune it from the age distribution, not from a convenient round number. In practice, the page should carry enough context to distinguish a storage rejection from a missing approval, because those incidents have different owners and different clocks. A retry can repair the first. It should not silently approve the second.

The distinction matters.

Which cloud storage provider fits a scalable Go app's data backups?

Option Good fit Retention and deletion boundary
AWS S3 A team wants mature object storage and well-documented SDKs for major languages. Keep approval and retention state in the application; verify the S3 controls needed for immutable or replicated archives.
Google Cloud Storage Workers, users, and regional data requirements already align with Google Cloud. Use the documented SDK and keep the deletion decision independent from the object name.
Azure Blob Storage Identity, deployment, and operations already center on Microsoft services. Its strongest fit is an Azure-shaped platform estate; the application still owns the approval record.
A REST storage adapter Several runtimes need a small HTTP contract and discovery matters more than a vendor SDK. A uniform API does not automatically provide versioning, object lock, replication, or browser CORS configuration.

AWS S3 and Google Cloud Storage are the default recommendations for the stated question because their SDK documentation supports custom backup applications across major languages. Azure deserves the same respect in an Azure-centered estate. Infrai is a narrower option: its public discovery surface describes capabilities without a key, and documented capabilities include runnable examples in 10 languages, which can shorten the path from a new worker to a reviewed request. That discovery advantage is useful when the team prefers plain REST and has several backend capabilities to wire together; it is not a substitute for an archive control the storage layer does not expose.

There is a second, different trade-off. Infrai exposes 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, so a document-retention worker and adjacent backend jobs can share one credential and one interface instead of accumulating separate client libraries and credentials for each capability. That can reduce operational coordination for a small platform team. It also concentrates responsibility: the team must inspect each capability’s readiness, region availability, and storage semantics before treating the common interface as a common guarantee.

Step 1: Make the retention record the source of truth

A signed document is a file plus a decision trail. Store the stable document ID, tenant ID, object key, content type, digest, capture time, retention deadline, and lifecycle state in a database or durable audit record. Use states such as stored, eligible_for_review, delete_approved, and deleted. Listing objects by prefix cannot answer who approved deletion or why the deadline changed.

The key should be stable and boring. Do not put an access decision in a filename that another service has to parse. Here is a small Go policy layer; it deliberately makes expiry an eligibility decision rather than an automatic delete.

package retention

import "time"

type Document struct {
    ID          string
    TenantID    string
    ObjectKey   string
    CapturedAt  time.Time
    RetainUntil time.Time
    Status      string
}

func ReviewState(document Document, now time.Time) string {
    if document.Status != "stored" {
        return "keep"
    }
    if now.Before(document.RetainUntil) {
        return "keep"
    }
    return "eligible_for_review"
}

func DeletionAllowed(document Document, approvedBy string) bool {
    return document.Status == "delete_approved" && approvedBy != ""
}

The judgment is intentional. A legal hold, an unresolved signing dispute, or a failed downstream export can extend retention, but each exception belongs in the application record with an owner and timestamp. The storage provider should hold bytes; it should not become the only place where policy exists.

Step 2: Put a narrow Go adapter between policy and storage

The adapter needs only the operations this workflow uses: put, get, head, list, and delete. AWS, Google, and Azure SDK calls stay behind that boundary, while the retention worker deals with document IDs and state transitions. A plain REST implementation can use the same boundary from Go, JavaScript, or another runtime without installing a vendor SDK. The interface should stay intentionally narrow even if the provider exposes dozens of extra operations, because every extra operation becomes another policy surface for the platform team to review and support.

This is where a self-describing API can earn its place. A discovery response can show the request schema and runnable examples before the worker is wired, while examples in 10 languages help a mixed-runtime team compare equivalent calls. The right review question is still concrete: does the discovered storage capability support private writes and the signed-only read flow this document system needs?

package main

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type Object struct {
    Bucket      string
    Key         string
    ContentType string
    Body        []byte
    ACL         string
}

type ObjectStore interface {
    Put(context.Context, Object) error
    Delete(context.Context, string, string) error
}

func PutPrivateDocument(ctx context.Context, store ObjectStore, object Object) error {
    if object.Bucket == "" || object.Key == "" || len(object.Body) == 0 {
        return errors.New("bucket, key, and document body are required")
    }
    object.ACL = "private"

    // The application supplies a stable key so a retried write targets one object.
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        if err := store.Put(ctx, object); err == nil {
            return nil
        } else if attempt == 3 {
            return fmt.Errorf("private document write failed: %w", err)
        }
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            return ctx.Err()
        case <-time.After(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond):
        }
    }
    return errors.New("private document write failed")
}

func main() {
    if os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY") == "" {
        fmt.Println("set INFRAI_API_KEY only in the adapter implementation")
    }
}

The example keeps the object private and never treats a public URL as a document-access mechanism. In a provider integration, use a presigned URL for a temporary read or upload and do not send the storage service’s Authorization: Bearer header to that returned URL. Keep credentials in a secret manager; do not place them in source, logs, or object metadata.

Retries need two properties. The backoff must respect the provider’s rate-limit response rather than hammering the service, and the object key must be stable so a retry cannot create a second logical document. If the provider’s write primitive lacks an explicit conditional write, coordinate strict concurrent updates in a queue or database.

Step 3: Instrument approval, then delete

The deletion worker should consume a record that has already reached delete_approved. A standard queue is at-least-once, so the consumer must tolerate the same document arriving twice. The first successful deletion changes the state to deleted; a later delivery records a no-op after checking that state.

Keep the approval identity, approval time, reason, document ID, object key, and deletion result after the object disappears. This is the evidence the retention SLO can inspect. It also makes a failed delete actionable instead of turning a missing object into an ambiguous audit entry.

Regional API availability belongs in this review too. An API region should align with the app’s users and workers, but regional alignment does not prove immutability or deletion correctness. Test the workflow in the regions the application will actually use, then record the provider-specific controls in the runbook.

Where does this design stop being enough?

The REST option above has clear boundaries. It does not provide public or public-read ACLs, so it is not a fit for static website hosting, permanent public links, or an image host. It does not provide object versioning or object lock, so accidental overwrites are not recoverable through those mechanisms and financial-grade WORM retention needs an external solution. There is no If-Match conditional write, so strict concurrent mutation needs queue or database coordination.

It also lacks automatic cross-region replication and cross-cloud bulk migration tooling. Its lifecycle minimum is 1 day rather than an hour-level expiry, multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix filtering. Browser-direct upload needs extra care because there is no independently exposed CORS configuration route. A trial balance cannot pay for persistent writes.

Those limits are selection criteria, not footnotes. Choose S3 or Google Cloud Storage when immutable archive controls, mature replication options, or broad SDK support are non-negotiable. Choose Azure when Microsoft identity and regional alignment dominate the decision. Consider a REST adapter when a discoverable, consistent HTTP contract reduces integration work and the missing storage controls are acceptable.

The decision rule is narrow: define the signed-document retention state first, compare the provider’s deletion and archive semantics against it, and then choose the SDK or adapter that the on-call team can operate. Keep the original private. Keep the decision record longer than the object when the audit requires it.

Further reading

References:

  • AWS S3 documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • Google Cloud Storage documentation: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • Azure Blob Storage documentation: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/storage-blobs-introduction
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

title: MedCaseAgent: From Multimodal Clinical Evidence to Rare Disease Case Reports
description:
arXiv:2610.32258v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential in clinical documentation, generating the rigorous, evidence-based reasoning required for unprecedented, atypical, and rare disease case reports remains a significant challenge. We present MedCaseAgent, an end-to-end agentic reasoning paradigm that bridges this gap by synthesizing publication-quality reports from unstructured clinical notes. MedCaseAgent leverages a hierarchical structure, integrating patient-level data mining with iterative, tool-integrated reasoning. By dynamically querying medical literature and knowledge bases, the agent maintains high clinical fidelity and assesses case novelty. The framework is inherently modular, supporting various backbone LLMs in a plug-and-play fashion. To facilitate this research, we release MedCase-150K, a large-scale multimodal clinical case-report corpus, and MedCase-Bench, a robust temporally held-out evaluation suite. We also introduce an open-source model post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B and optimized specifically for this task. Under both LLM-judged and rule-based evaluation, MedCaseAgent outperforms existing general-purpose and specialized medical LLMs and agents. Blinded expert reviews and ablations further support the system's clinical relevance and evidence grounding.

title: The most expensive phrase in cloud: we'll clean it up later
description:
The most expensive phrase in cloud infrastructure is "we'll clean it up later"

I've heard it in every account I've worked with

A dev environment gets created for a sprint. We'll clean it up later

A service gets deployed with debug logging enabled. We'll turn that down later

A database gets provisioned at a size that's too large for current needs because the cost of under-provisioning feels riskier than the cost of over-provisioning. We'll rightsize it later

Later never comes. Not because the team is irresponsible. Because later becomes now and now is always full

The sprint ends and the next sprint starts. The debug logging produces useful information once and now removing it feels risky. The database has been running for three months and suddenly changing it requires coordination and a maintenance window and it's never the right week

The resource just keeps running

I've found dev environments running for 18 months that were created for a feature that shipped in week two

The cost isn't just the money. It's the compounding weight of things you meant to do that you didn't do. Every resource you know should be removed but haven't removed adds cognitive overhead. Every time someone looks at the account they have to decide again whether this thing is safe to touch. That decision cost happens over and over

The pattern that actually works is not doing the cleanup later

It's building cleanup into the creation

When you spin up a dev environment, set a termination date in the tags. Schedule a reminder. Make the cleanup part of the task, not an afterthought

When you enable verbose logging, create a ticket immediately to reduce log level before the service goes to production. That ticket sits in the backlog as a concrete reminder instead of a vague intention

When you provision infrastructure you might need to rightsize, set a calendar reminder for 30 days later to check utilization

The discipline is not the cleanup

The discipline is treating the cleanup as part of the work when the work happens

Later is a cost you pay monthly until you do

title: $1 million hacker challenge for Vercel Sandbox
description:
Agents need to run untrusted code, and the microVM has become the standard way to do it: a dedicated guest kernel per workload, isolated from the host and from every other workload on the same machine.

But recent security research and real-world incidents have revealed that agents running untrusted code do not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment; they only need one network path the security model failed to account for, which we explained in our post A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox.

Isolation only holds if both sides of it hold: the Firecracker microVM and the host-side network controls. Recently our CTO pointed an open-weight model with no safeguards at Vercel Sandbox. It did not escape, but it mapped the guest kernel, built a VM to reproduce its ideas, and wrote a fuzzer.

Defenders have first-mover advantage, but it won't last forever, and the choice is when to test the boundaries (we strongly encourage building a scanning program, which you can do on any budget with an open-source tool like deepsec and AI Gateway).

We are proactively choosing to test Vercel Sandbox on our own schedule, not an attacker's, and we are doing it in the open, with the best researchers in the world.

So for two weeks, we are paying up to $1,000,000 USD to the researchers who can escape a Vercel Sandbox.

The challenge

Starting today, Vercel is running a two-week public HackerOne program focused on Vercel Sandbox isolation.

  • Program: Public HackerOne program, open to all eligible researchers

  • Window: Tuesday, August 18 to Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the reward pool is exhausted

  • Max per report: $50,000 USD, for a vulnerability that lets a threat actor read or modify another Vercel tenant's data

  • Total pool: Up to $1,000,000 USD in total payouts

Bounties are paid per report, scoped to a single root cause, and assigned by Vercel triage based on the maximum demonstrable impact. The full bounty table, detailed scope, and the list of known-duplicate classes are on the HackerOne program page.

How Vercel Sandbox is built

Vercel Sandbox runs on bare-metal EC2 hosts. Each sandbox gets its own Firecracker microVM with a dedicated guest kernel, and inside that microVM a Linux container runs the operator's code. The microVM, not the container, is the security boundary, so operator-supplied code runs two layers removed from the host. We assume that code is fully hostile: root inside the container, full kernel access inside the microVM, and motivated to reach the host or another tenant.

The network side of the boundary is enforced on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it. The sandbox firewall intercepts outbound TCP and DNS, checks each connection against the operator's domain and CIDR policies, and can inject credentials at the boundary so they never enter the microVM.

What we're looking for

In short: anything that breaks the sandbox boundary.

  • Compute boundary: Escaping the Firecracker microVM to the EC2 host, or reaching another tenant's sandbox through the compute layer (reading, modifying, or executing code in it), or crashing another tenant's sandbox from within another sandbox

  • Network boundary: Defeating the sandbox firewall without crossing the microVM: reaching destinations the operator did not authorize, exfiltrating data, or retrieving brokered credentials

Container namespace escapes that only reach the Firecracker guest OS are not in scope. Namespaces are a developer-experience feature, not the security boundary.

Bounties

Severity

Bounty

Critical

$25,000 – $50,000

High

$10,000 – $25,000

Medium

$5,000 – $10,000

Low

$1,000 – $5,000

The full bounty table, with example vulnerability classes for each tier, is on the HackerOne program page.

How to participate

The program is open now and closes on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, or earlier if the $1,000,000 USD reward pool is exhausted. Reports go through the HackerOne program page.

To reproduce a finding, boot a sandbox with the @vercel/sandbox SDK and demonstrate the impact with a live proof of concept. The default sandbox OS is enough for most reports; bring a custom image from the Vercel Container Registry only if your PoC needs extra tooling. We will not reward static-analysis-only findings; to issue a payout, we need to see the boundary break.

Full rules, eligibility, the complete scope and bounty table, and the submission process are on the HackerOne program page.

Results and payouts

We will triage reports from the day the program opens through one month after it closes. As findings are confirmed, we will pay bounties, ship fixes, and credit every researcher whose report holds up. The techniques discovered during this program will become permanent additions to the sandbox boundary, protecting every workload on Vercel long after the challenge ends. After the program closes, we will publish a follow-up writeup of the techniques and the fixes we shipped.

Thanks to HackerOne for standing up the program, and to the researchers who will spend the next two weeks trying to break what we built.

title: Polyp-VSSD: A Pre-trained Transformer with Local-Global Joint VSSD Decoding for Polyp Segmentation
description:
arXiv:2610.32282v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Early detection of colorectal polyps is essential for preventing colorectal cancer, making accurate polyp segmentation a key component in computer-aided diagnosis systems. However, existing endoscopic segmentation methods often exhibit limited representational capacity and insufficient integration of global and local contextual information. To address these limitations, we propose Polyp-VSSD, a novel local-global joint decoding framework built upon a pre-trained Transformer backbone for high-precision polyp segmentation. Polyp-VSSD leverages the strong feature expressiveness of large-scale visual pre-training and unifies global semantic modeling with local fine-grained reconstruction to enhance segmentation fidelity. Extensive experiments on multiple public endoscopic datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both Dice and IoU. On the EndoScene dataset, Polyp-VSSD achieves mIoU and mDice scores of 0.903 and 0.946, respectively, highlighting its robustness and strong generalization capability. This work presents an effective and scalable solution for intelligent endoscopic image analysis.

title: Synthetic-to-Real Text-Based Person Anomaly Search via Multi-Model Retrieval Fusion and Cross-Encoder Reranking
description:
arXiv:2610.31930v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Text-based person anomaly search requires a model to retrieve individuals from a large image gallery using natural-language descriptions of both appearance and behavior. This task is challenging because model training relies on synthetic image-text pairs, whereas evaluation is performed on real surveillance images containing domain differences, near-duplicate frames, and many visually similar distractors. We present a multi-model retrieval and reranking framework designed to improve synthetic-to-real transfer. The framework first adapts Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B to synthetic person descriptions using bidirectional contrastive learning, explicit negative sampling, false-negative masking, and domain randomization. It then combines the normalized scores of six complementary Qwen3-VL checkpoints with those of a frozen SigLIP2 model using four-view gallery encoding. The fused retrieval scores identify the strongest candidates, which are jointly evaluated with the query using Qwen3-VL-Reranker-8B. The cross-encoder and retrieval scores are subsequently blended to produce the final ranking. We also construct a distractor-matched validation protocol entirely from synthetic data to select checkpoint weights, fusion coefficients, candidate depths, and reranking parameters without accessing the official test images. The final system achieves 94.7815% mAP and 90.8493% R@1 under the official AI City Challenge 2026 Track 4 test setting, with a reported eighth-place finish on the public leaderboard.

title: Tev plays Dino
description:
I had, in a moment I can only call optimism, installed a small “decision model” called tev1 via Ollama. Tev1 is a family of open-weight, Jev-inspired decision and text-classification models released by Together AI and available in 4B and 0.8B parameter sizes fine-tuned from Qwen3.5.

If you are hearing about Jev for the first time - it is a chat-less, pick-more kinda LLM model. “Unlike standard conversational language models that output free-form text, Tev1 takes a structured input state, a question, and 2 to 24 labeled options, returning a specific option choice and probability distribution”. And it picks one, like a man at a buffet who has already decided on the fish.

Naturally I pointed it at the Chrome dino game. Its only natural because my official laptop’s official game-allowances only allow for a Chrome browser. The dino, you’ll recall, has one job: jump, duck, or stand there like a chump. A 4B model seemed exactly qualified for a job with three possible wrong answers.

Next, Claude rigged Playwright to drive the actual game and feed tev1 the details each time trouble approached: a cactus here, a pterodactyl there, going this fast. Whatever it said, jump or duck or nothing, the dino did. If it ducked a cactus, it ducked the cactus, and paid for it in full.

Results were mixed - it once ducked a pterodactyl skimming along at ground level, the exact sort you’re meant to leap over, with the confidence of a man backing his car with confidence after a few too many beer. The dino hasn’t, to date, broken the 2000 points ceiling. It has, however, broken several personal records for dying in novel ways. Improvement to its reaction-time will follow soon and code is here.

Originally published at visualist.in.

title: Filling a PDF form on a laptop, and why I flatten the copy I send
description:
A lot of forms still arrive as PDFs with a note that says "print, fill, scan, and send back". Most of the time you don't need the printer. Here's how to tell what kind of form you have, fill it with free tools, and decide whether the copy you send should still be editable.

Three things that look like a form

  1. An AcroForm. The PDF stores a list of named fields (text boxes, checkboxes, radio groups, dropdowns), and each one has a widget on the page that draws its value. This is the kind almost every viewer can fill.
  2. An XFA form. An older Adobe format where the form is described in XML inside the PDF. Most viewers outside Adobe's own apps can't render it.
  3. A flat scan or export. Boxes and lines drawn on the page, with no fields at all. It only looks like a form.

pdfinfo (from poppler-utils) tells you which one you have on its Form: line:

$ pdfinfo form.pdf | grep Form
Form:            AcroForm

It prints AcroForm, XFA, or none.

The XFA gotcha

If you open a PDF and see only a page that starts with "Please wait... If this message is not eventually replaced by the proper contents of the document, your PDF viewer may not be able to display this type of document", that's an XFA form. Waiting won't help. Browsers and most free viewers show that placeholder page instead of the form. The realistic options are Adobe Acrobat Reader, which still fills XFA, or asking the sender for an AcroForm or Word version.

Filling an AcroForm without extra software

Chrome, Edge, Firefox and macOS Preview all fill AcroForm fields: open the file, click into a field, type, tick, and save. The saved file is still a form. Your answers sit in the fields, and anyone who opens it can change them.

If you get none, there's nothing to fill. You can still type on top using a viewer's text or annotation tool, but that's adding text to the page, not filling fields.

Filling from a script

For a form you fill often, a short pypdf script is handy. First list the field names, because they're whatever the form's author called them, not the labels you see:

import sys
from pypdf import PdfReader

for name, field in (PdfReader(sys.argv[1]).get_fields() or {}).items():
    print(name, field.get("/FT"), field.get("/_States_", ""))

On my test form:

full_name /Tx
agree /Btn ['/Off', '/Yes']

/Tx is a text field and /Btn is a checkbox or radio. The states in brackets are the exact values a checkbox accepts. Here it's /Yes, but some forms use /On or /1, so read them instead of guessing.

Then fill:

import sys
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

src, out = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
flatten = "--flatten" in sys.argv

reader = PdfReader(src)
writer = PdfWriter()
writer.append(reader)

values = {"full_name": "Test Person", "agree": "/Yes"}
for page in writer.pages:
    writer.update_page_form_field_values(page, values, auto_regenerate=False, flatten=flatten)

if flatten:
    writer.remove_annotations(subtypes="/Widget")
    del writer.root_object["/AcroForm"]

writer.write(out)

I tested this with pypdf 6.21. Without --flatten, the output is still a form with the values in the fields.

Why I flatten the copy I send

Flattening draws each field's appearance into the page content and removes the fields. The answers still show, but they're page content now, not a form someone can edit by accident (or on purpose) and send on.

With --flatten, my test file went from Form: AcroForm to Form: none, the field list came back empty, and pdftotext still printed "Test Person". Rendering the page with pdftoppm showed the name and the ticked box.

qpdf can flatten a file you already filled in a viewer:

qpdf --generate-appearances --flatten-annotations=all filled.pdf flat.pdf

--generate-appearances makes qpdf draw fields whose viewer didn't save an appearance, and --flatten-annotations=all burns them into the page. On my filled test file this gave the same result: Form: none and the values visible on the page. Note that all also flattens comments and other annotations, which is usually what you want for a final copy.

Two cautions. Keep an unflattened copy if you might need to change an answer, because flattening is one-way. And don't flatten a form the receiver asked for as a fillable file, since some offices read the field data straight out of it.

Signature fields

A signature field is a placeholder for a digital signature, not a text box. None of the methods above signs anything. If the form wants a drawn signature, add an image on the page; if it wants a real digital signature, that's a separate step with a certificate.

A browser option

I built ToolOcean, and it has a page that lists a PDF's AcroForm fields, lets you fill them, and downloads the result with flattening off by default. It runs in the browser without uploading the file, skips signature fields, and doesn't fill XFA forms: toolocean.co/pdf-form-fill.

Drafted with AI help, tested and checked by me.

title: Not All Information Is Worth Asking For: Decision-Informed Information Seeking with LLMs
description:
arXiv:2610.32181v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support decisions under incomplete information, where deciding what to look up and when to stop matters as much as the final answer. However, LLMs fall into an information trap: They pay for checks, i.e., costly pieces of evidence, that cannot change their decision or are not worth their cost, and they keep asking when the evidence is already sufficient. To this end, we propose Decision-Informed Value-of-information Acquisition (DIVA), a simple yet effective procedure for LLM information seeking based on the decision value of evidence. DIVA 1) lets the LLM specify a small decision model, i.e., how likely a bad outcome is and how each check would shift this probability, through short numeric questions and 2) values each candidate check by how much its imagined outcomes improve the decision net of its cost, stopping when no check is worth its cost. Its variant, DIVA-U, further accounts for the LLM's uncertain estimates of how strongly each check shifts this probability. DIVA is training-free and applies to any LLM. Across four domains and 20 LLMs, DIVA-U has lower regret, i.e., value lost relative to the best possible decision, than every LLM baseline on real-world data, mainly by stopping once evidence suffices, and DIVA cuts the regret of the best LLM baseline by 75% in synthetic scenarios where every check's reliability is given. Code: github.com/seunghan96/diva.

title: Understanding Communication Failures in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
description:
arXiv:2610.32060v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems aim to improve reasoning through debate, evidence sharing, and mutual correction, but interaction can also introduce failures that final accuracy alone cannot explain. Agents may converge too early, ignore dissent, suppress correct minority answers, or preserve a wrong framing across rounds. We present a corpus-grounded taxonomy of communication failures, built from 3,211 failed multi-round trajectories across medical QA, coding, finance, multi-hop reasoning, ethics, and embodied text tasks. Using this taxonomy, we analyze failure distributions across datasets and system designs, round-level error dynamics, recovery hardness, majority transitions, minority-signal suppression, and self-reported confidence. We find that failures are dominated by recovery/correction and consensus/decision problems rather than isolated first-round mistakes, with many emerging after agents first observe peer responses. Based on these findings, we recommend stronger disagreement handling, evidence verification, minority-signal preservation, and recovery checks before finalization.

title: Your Form Says “Invalid.” Your User Says “Now What?”
description:
You spend twenty minutes polishing a button.

Then the form tells someone: “Invalid input.”

Invalid what? The date? The phone number? The file?

A neat interface still needs to explain what to do next.

Change the message, not just its color

Imagine a profile form that accepts JPG and PNG images up to 5 MB. Someone selects a larger file.

“Upload failed” only reports the failure.

“Your image is over 5 MB. Choose a smaller JPG or PNG” gives the person a next step.

The wording must match the real rule. If the upload failed because the connection dropped, asking for a smaller image would be misleading.

The same idea works elsewhere:

  • “Invalid date” → “Enter the date as DD/MM/YYYY.”
  • “Required” → “Enter an email address so we can send your receipt.”
  • “Something went wrong” → explain the known problem, or say that you could not identify it. Do not invent a cause.

Put the help where the problem is

Show the message near the field. Keep the person's other entries. A red outline alone does not explain the fix.

W3C's form notification guidance recommends clear error descriptions and simple correction instructions. For developers, it also describes linking fields and messages with aria-describedby so that assistive technology can connect them.

A quick review: deliberately submit the wrong value. Read only the message. Does it tell you which field needs attention and how to continue?

If you have to ask the developer what the message means, the wording needs another pass.

Which error message in your product would you rewrite first?

title: PixGR: Pixel-Space Generative Decoding for Fast Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction
description:
arXiv:2610.31908v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present PixGR, an efficient framework that integrates lightweight pixel-space generative modeling into feed-forward 3D Gaussian reconstruction to model scene uncertainty. Context observations are encoded once into a scene latent representation, which conditions generative decoding from noisy target views to produce a shared 3D Gaussian representation. We formulate this process using pixel-space flow matching, enabling end-to-end optimization of 3D reconstruction with direct pixel-space generative supervision through differentiable rendering. This avoids VAE-based latent compression and error propagation inherent in previous two-stage pipelines. To preserve feed-forward efficiency, PixGR caches the scene representation and performs iterative inference using a lightweight DiT decoder. Experiments demonstrate that PixGR outperforms regression-based approaches in challenging sparse-view settings, particularly with widely spaced observations and view extrapolation. Meanwhile, it maintains sub-second inference and remains competitive with substantially heavier pretrained generative models. Our project page is available at https://ranrhuang.github.io/pixgr/.

title: Why I Stopped Paying for ElevenLabs in 2026: The Hidden Limitations for Commercial Video Workflows
description:
A transparent look at character caps, overage pricing shocks, and why deterministic neural engines took over my daily production.

Let me state this upfront: ElevenLabs is technically brilliant.

Their generative voice cloning models set the industry standard for short-form realism, dramatic range, and conversational warmth. If you are producing 30-second character skits or indie video game dialogue, their technology is unmatched.

However, after 10 months of running an active commercial video production pipeline—producing YouTube explainer series, technical tutorials, and long-form narrations—I recently cancelled my paid subscription.

It wasn't because the audio sounded robotic. It was because the platform’s business model and architecture create severe friction the moment you scale past hobbyist clips.

Here is the honest production reality behind why generative voice subscriptions break down for high-volume video workflows, and what I switched to instead.

1. The "Overage Tax" and Failed Render Burn

ElevenLabs charges on a monthly character quota (e.g., ~100,000 characters on the Creator tier).

On paper, 100,000 characters sounds generous (roughly 1.5 to 2 hours of audio). In a real production environment, you never render text once:

  • You adjust a sentence for better pacing → quota burned twice.
  • The generative model hallucinates a whisper or slurs a proper noun at minute four → full paragraph re-rendered, quota burned again.
  • You revise your video script based on client feedback → quota burned a third time.

In practice, rendering a clean 20-minute video master track typically consumes 3x the character count of the actual script.

Once you exceed your monthly quota, automatic overage fees kick in. I frequently found myself burning through a $22 tier within the first 10 days of the month, turning monthly audio expenses into an unpredictable $60–$90 variable cost.

2. Acoustic Inconsistency Across Long Scripts

Generative autoregressive models predict audio token by token. This produces wonderful emotional nuance, but it has a dark side: non-determinism.

If you render a 3,000-word narration in sections:

  • Section 1 sounds energetic and forward;
  • Section 2 sounds intimate and slightly hushed;
  • Section 3 introduces subtle vocal frying.

When spliced together on an editing timeline, the tonal shifts become jarringly obvious through studio headphones. To get a cohesive take, creators spend hours manually cherry-picking seeds—completely defeating the point of automated voice generation.

3. The Reverse Subtitle Dilemma

When producing video content, audio is only 50% of the deliverable. You must have synchronized subtitles (.srt).

Because black-box generative APIs output a flat .mp3 with zero word-boundary telemetry, you are forced to pipe that rendered audio back into an AI transcription engine (like Whisper) just to recover the timestamps you already owned in your source manuscript.

It adds extra render steps, introduces Whisper transcription hallucinations on quiet breaths, and doubles your processing latency.

The Pivot to Deterministic Neural Workbenches

For serious video creators and instructional designers, raw "vocal flair" matters far less than consistency, predictability, and friction-free editing.

Over the last few months, my daily production has transitioned almost entirely to browser-level workbenches built on Microsoft Azure’s Speech Core (such as the free VoiceIndex Studio):

Production Factor Generative Subscriptions (ElevenLabs) Deterministic Workbenches (Azure / VoiceIndex)
Pricing Model $22+/mo with hard character caps Free / Transparent Pay-per-use
Long-Form Consistency Tonal drift between takes 100% Deterministic & Fatigue-Free
Setup Friction Mandatory account & credit card Zero-signup instant browser export
Subtitle Synchronization Post-process Whisper pass required Native millisecond .srt output
Pacing Control Sliders with random seeds Precision W3C SSML breaks & prosody

Voices like en-US-RyanNeural, en-US-JennyNeural, and zh-CN-XiaoxiaoNeural may not sound like Shakespearean actors, but they deliver crisp, professional, fatigue-free audio that never drifts in tone, never charges surprise overages, and exports synchronized subtitles instantly.

Summary: Matching the Tool to the Job

  • Stick with ElevenLabs if: You produce short fiction, voice acting, gaming characters, or require high-stakes zero-shot voice cloning.
  • Switch to Deterministic Neural Tools if: You produce high-volume commercial video essays, tutorials, audiobooks, or documentation where predictable costs, zero setup friction, and instant subtitle synchronization determine your profit margins.

Are you currently using generative voice platforms or deterministic neural tools for your long-form video projects? Have you run into character quota burn during revisions? Share your workflow in the responses.

title: Your loop yields every 500 items. It still freezes. Here's why (and a fix)
description:
Every JavaScript developer eventually writes this loop:

for (const [index, row] of rows.entries()) {
  processRow(row);
  if (index % 500 === 0) await new Promise(resolve => setImmediate(resolve));
}

It's the textbook fix for a long loop that freezes the UI or stalls a server: do some work, give the event loop a turn, repeat.

It works in testing. It works in staging. Then production sends you a run of slow rows, and the app freezes anyway.

I hit exactly this, so I built a tiny library to fix it: time-sliced. This post is about why the usual fix breaks, what I did instead, and — most importantly — I'd like your feedback on it.

Why we built it

Picture a loop over a big array of records: building a search index, transforming API results, validating a CSV import, parsing JSON payloads. Most items are tiny and take microseconds. A few are heavy: a deeply nested object, a huge text field, a row that takes a slow code path.

We had the "yield every 500" pattern in place. It looked fine in testing, because test data is uniform. But real data isn't. When a cluster of heavy items showed up together, one chunk of 500 suddenly took a few hundred milliseconds. During that time:

  • the app beachballed,
  • timers fired late,
  • other requests waited, and some timed out.

The loop was yielding. It just wasn't yielding often enough when it mattered.

The root problem: "every N items" assumes every item costs the same. Real data doesn't work that way.

The idea: yield on time, not on count

Instead of counting items, measure time. Do work until a budget is spent (8 ms by default), then yield. Start a new slice and continue.

  • When items are cheap, you yield rarely, so overhead stays low.
  • When items are slow, you yield often, so nothing freezes. 
import {timeSlicedForEach} from 'time-sliced';

await timeSlicedForEach(rows, processRow);

That's the whole API for the common case.

The numbers

One job, run with each common "keep Node responsive" strategy: 20,000 rows at 0.02 ms each, with a run of 1,000 heavy rows at 0.5 ms in the middle. A 1 ms heartbeat timer measures the longest event-loop freeze. Median of 3 runs, Node.js 24.

Strategy Total time Longest freeze Result
Plain loop 897 ms 897 ms freezes
await every row 887 ms 887 ms freezes
async.eachSeries 882 ms 882 ms freezes
setTimeout(0) every row 24.6 s 16 ms responsive, 27x slower
setImmediate every row 1286 ms 6 ms responsive, 1.4x slower
setImmediate every 500 rows 908 ms 254 ms freezes
time-sliced 921 ms 11 ms responsive and fast

A few things surprised people when I showed them this:

  1. await doesn't help. Awaiting an already-resolved promise only runs microtasks. Timers, I/O and rendering still wait for the whole loop.
  2. Yielding every row works, but you pay per yield. setImmediate adds ~40% here. setTimeout(0) is clamped to 1 ms in Node (4 ms in nested browser timers), so the job takes 27x longer.
  3. Every-N is fast until the rows get slow. 500 cheap rows = 10 ms. 500 heavy rows = 250 ms. That's the freeze users see.

time-sliced finishes in about the same time as the plain loop, and the event loop never freezes much longer than the budget.

Real-world usage

Keep a server answering during an import 

app.post('/import', async (request, response) => {
  const rows = parseCsv(request.body);
  const records = await timeSlicedMap(rows, row => toRecord(row), {budgetMs: 25});
  await database.insertMany(records);
  response.json({imported: records.length});
});

Health checks and other API calls keep getting answered during a 50,000-row import. On a server, nothing needs 60 fps, so a bigger budget (25 ms) means fewer yields.

Your own loops: nested, while, recursive

When the work doesn't fit a map, use a slicer:

import {createTimeSlicer} from 'time-sliced';

const slicer = createTimeSlicer();

for (const category of categories) {
  for (const product of category.products) {
    updateSearchIndex(product);
    if (slicer.isSpent()) await slicer.yield();
  }
}

Cancel with AbortController

Great for search-as-you-type: abort the previous search, and it stops at its next yield instead of finishing work nobody will see.

const controller = new AbortController();
cancelButton.onclick = () => controller.abort();

await timeSlicedForEach(rows, processRow, {signal: controller.signal});

Test it without real timers

Inject a fake clock and yield function to assert how often your code yields:

let nowMs = 0;
let yields = 0;

await timeSlicedForEach(rows, () => {
  nowMs += 2; // each row "takes" 2 ms
}, {
  now: () => nowMs,
  yieldToEventLoop: async () => { yields += 1; },
});

How it yields

yieldToEventLoop() picks the best primitive for the runtime:

  • scheduler.yield() in Chromium
  • setImmediate in Node.js and Bun
  • MessageChannel elsewhere (avoids the 4 ms nested setTimeout clamp)
  • setTimeout(0) as a last resort

What it does not do

Being honest about the limits:

  • One item longer than the budget still blocks for that long. If a single item takes 200 ms, move it to a worker thread or split it.
  • It doesn't make work faster. It lets everything else run in between. Total time stays about the same.
  • Overhead is ~30 ns per item (one performance.now() call). For millions of trivial items, batch a few per callback.

Try it 

npm install time-sliced
  • Zero dependencies
  • Node.js 22+, Bun, Deno, browsers, Electron (main and renderer)
  • ESM + CommonJS, TypeScript types included
  • MIT licensed

📦 npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/time-sliced
💻 GitHub: https://github.com/RagedPanda/time-sliced

I'd love your feedback

This is an early release (v0.1), and I want to hear from people who've fought the event loop:

  • Is 8 ms the right default budget? What do you use on servers?
  • Have you hit cases where time-based yielding behaved worse than count-based?
  • Which runtime or environment should I test next?
  • Is the API (timeSlicedMap, timeSlicedForEach, createTimeSlicer) clear, or would you name things differently?

Drop a comment, open an issue, or run npm run bench on your machine and share your numbers. Stars on GitHub help others find it too. Thanks for reading!

title: Validating the Comparison, Not Just the Scorer: Why Overall Accuracy Can Mislead in Interactive LLM Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2610.31678v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many LLM studies compare how models respond to different follow-up prompts. For example, one prompt may neutrally ask a model to reconsider, while another insists that an invented film really exists. The difference is used to measure the effect of conversational pressure. An automatic scorer then labels whether each response makes an unsupported factual claim. Researchers commonly validate the scorer with one overall accuracy or $F_1$ score. However, high overall performance can hide prompt-specific mistakes: if the scorer makes more errors after one prompt, the measured difference can be too large, too small, or point in the wrong direction. An audit containing mostly difficult responses can also misrepresent performance in the full study. We derive how such errors alter a prompt comparison and examine the problem using six models, 180 invented-entity questions, and six prompt conditions. In a balanced audit of 288 responses, overall $F_1$ was $.916$. Yet, depending on the prompt, the scorer flagged 2.6%-33.3% of responses that the primary LLM rater judged not to contain an unsupported claim; these prompt-specific estimates were uncertain. In a second audit, the scorer and two separate LLM raters evaluated the same 300 model-question cases under each prompt. An apparent 9.3-point increase from asserting certainty rather than neutrally asking the model to reconsider fell to 2.3 points under both raters. The primary-rater interval included zero, so it did not establish an increase. Two other prompt comparisons kept their direction under both raters, while an attempted prompt-specific correction remained too uncertain for a firm conclusion. Researchers should therefore validate the exact difference they plan to report, not just the scorer as a whole: audit both prompts on matching cases and include scorer and rater uncertainty in the final result.

title: Redox OS September 2026 Update: Technical Improvements and New Features Released, Lacks Clear Problem Statement
description:
Introduction: The State of Redox OS in September 2026

Redox OS, an open-source operating system known for its microkernel architecture and Rust-based codebase, continues to evolve with its September 2026 update. This release, like many before it, showcases a flurry of technical advancements—from JIT compiler optimizations to external display hot-plugging support. Mechanically, these improvements stem from incremental code updates and kernel modifications, such as enhanced page fault handling, which directly address runtime inefficiencies by allowing the kernel to manage memory access violations more gracefully. However, the update’s narrative remains fragmented, lacking a central problem statement that ties these features to a broader vision.

The absence of a clear problem statement is not merely a communication oversight; it reflects deeper environmental constraints. Redox OS operates within a resource-limited ecosystem, where developer prioritization is driven by community feedback and technological dependencies. For instance, the integration of uutils 0.11 and SDL2 relies on external projects, introducing potential delays and compatibility risks. The Clang port, while strategically aimed at broadening contributor appeal, requires significant effort to align with Redox’s unique architecture, highlighting the trade-offs between feature additions and system stability.

From an analytical standpoint, the update’s reactive nature—driven by community requests and technological advancements—raises questions about its long-term sustainability. For example, rlimit support, while critical for resource management in multi-user environments, lacks context on how it addresses specific user pain points. Similarly, i586 dynamic linking, though beneficial for legacy hardware compatibility, constrains architectural evolution by necessitating backward compatibility. Without a unifying problem statement, these features risk being perceived as isolated improvements rather than steps toward a cohesive vision.

The stakes are high. Without a clear narrative, Redox OS risks being overshadowed by competitors with more focused value propositions. Effective communication of its goals is crucial for attracting developers, users, and stakeholders, ensuring its relevance in an increasingly competitive OS landscape. As Redox OS matures, the challenge lies not just in technical execution but in articulating why these advancements matter—a gap that, if unaddressed, could hinder its adoption and community growth.

Technical Deep Dive: Key Improvements and Features

Performance Enhancements: JIT Compiler and Beyond

The September 2026 update introduces significant JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler optimizations, a move that directly addresses the growing demand for efficient runtime performance in modern, resource-intensive workloads. By compiling code on-the-fly, the JIT mechanism reduces the overhead of interpretation, allowing applications to execute faster. This is particularly impactful for tasks like web rendering and game development, where every millisecond counts. However, the trade-off lies in increased memory usage during compilation, which could lead to performance bottlenecks in memory-constrained environments. The risk here is twofold: memory fragmentation and increased context switching, both of which can degrade overall system responsiveness. To mitigate this, developers must carefully balance JIT aggressiveness with memory management strategies.

Hardware Flexibility: External Display Hot-Plugging and i586 Dynamic Linking

The addition of external display hot-plugging support enhances hardware flexibility, enabling users to connect and disconnect displays without rebooting. This feature relies on kernel modifications that dynamically update the display driver’s state, ensuring seamless transitions. However, this introduces a risk of incompatibility issues with specific hardware configurations, particularly older GPUs that lack standardized plug-and-play protocols. The causal chain here is clear: driver miscommunication leads to signal corruption, resulting in display artifacts or complete failure. To address this, Redox OS must maintain a robust database of supported hardware and implement fallback mechanisms for unsupported devices.

Meanwhile, i586 dynamic linking ensures compatibility with legacy hardware but constrains architectural evolution. Dynamic linking allows applications to load shared libraries at runtime, reducing binary size and memory usage. However, this mechanism relies on backward-compatible ABI (Application Binary Interface), which limits the adoption of modern CPU features like SIMD instructions. The trade-off is stark: supporting legacy hardware preserves the user base but stifles performance gains on newer architectures. The optimal solution here is a phased approach, gradually deprecating i586 support while providing clear migration paths for affected users.

Developer Experience: Clang Port and Debugging Improvements

The Clang port represents a strategic shift to a more widely supported compiler toolchain, potentially attracting contributors familiar with LLVM-based ecosystems. Clang’s modular architecture and robust error reporting improve debugging workflows, but the porting process requires significant architectural alignment. The risk lies in compatibility breaks with existing Redox OS code, particularly in areas like system call interfaces and memory management. The causal mechanism is straightforward: mismatches between Clang’s expectations and Redox OS’s implementation lead to compilation errors or runtime crashes. To navigate this, developers must prioritize incremental porting, focusing on core components first and addressing edge cases iteratively.

Improvements to the terminal and debugging tools further enhance developer productivity. These enhancements include better error messages, integrated debugging commands, and improved logging mechanisms. However, the absence of a unified debugging framework risks fragmentation, with developers relying on disparate tools for different tasks. The optimal solution is to consolidate debugging features into a single, extensible interface, ensuring consistency and reducing the learning curve for new contributors.

System Stability: Page Fault Handling and rlimit Support

Enhanced page fault handling in the kernel reduces memory access violations, a critical improvement for system stability. By intercepting invalid memory accesses and either resolving them or terminating the offending process, this mechanism prevents data corruption and system crashes. However, aggressive page fault handling can introduce latency, particularly in applications with high memory turnover. The causal chain is clear: increased context switching between user and kernel space leads to pipeline stalls, degrading performance. To balance stability and performance, Redox OS must implement adaptive fault handling policies, prioritizing critical processes while allowing non-critical ones to fail gracefully.

The introduction of rlimit support enables resource management in multi-user environments, a key feature for server deployments. By enforcing limits on CPU, memory, and file descriptors, rlimit prevents resource exhaustion and ensures fair allocation. However, this mechanism relies on kernel-level accounting, which can introduce overhead. The risk lies in misconfigured limits, leading to unintended process termination or performance degradation. The optimal solution is to provide default configurations tailored to common use cases while allowing administrators to fine-tune limits as needed.

Conclusion: Incremental Progress with Lingering Questions

The September 2026 update demonstrates Redox OS’s ongoing commitment to technical excellence, with improvements spanning performance, hardware compatibility, and developer experience. However, the absence of a clear problem statement or unifying vision risks fragmenting these efforts, making it difficult to communicate the OS’s unique value proposition. To address this, the development team must articulate a cohesive narrative that ties these improvements to specific user pain points or long-term goals. Without such a narrative, Redox OS risks being perceived as a collection of isolated features rather than a holistic operating system solution.

The Missing Narrative: Identifying the Underlying Issues

Redox OS’s September 2026 update is a technical tour de force, packed with improvements like JIT compiler optimizations, external display hot-plugging, and rlimit support. Yet, the absence of a clear problem statement or unifying vision leaves the update feeling fragmented. This isn’t just a communication oversight—it’s a symptom of deeper systemic issues in the project’s development approach.

Reactive Development: The Root of Fragmentation

The update’s structure—a laundry list of features—suggests a reactive development model. Improvements like i586 dynamic linking and Clang porting are driven by community feedback and technological dependencies rather than a proactive vision. For instance, the JIT compiler optimizations address runtime inefficiencies, but their implementation is piecemeal, lacking alignment with a broader performance strategy. This reactivity risks creating a system where features are added without clear justification, leading to technical debt and architectural constraints.

Trade-Offs Without Context: The Cost of Missing Vision

Many updates involve significant trade-offs, but without a problem statement, their rationale remains opaque. Take i586 dynamic linking: it ensures legacy hardware compatibility but limits adoption of modern CPU features like SIMD. Similarly, the Clang port improves debugging workflows but requires architectural alignment, risking compatibility breaks. Without a clear narrative, these trade-offs appear arbitrary, undermining trust in the project’s direction.

Mechanisms of Risk Formation: Fragmentation and Sustainability

The lack of a unifying problem statement creates fragmentation risks. For example, page fault handling improvements reduce memory access violations but increase context switching latency due to aggressive fault interception. Without a clear vision, such optimizations may not align with user pain points, leading to perceived irrelevance. Similarly, rlimit support addresses resource management in multi-user environments but introduces kernel-level accounting overhead, a risk exacerbated by reactive development.

Optimal Solution: Articulate a Cohesive Narrative

To address these issues, Redox OS must articulate a cohesive narrative tying updates to user pain points or long-term goals. For instance, framing JIT optimizations as part of a broader strategy to compete with modern OSes in resource-intensive workloads would provide context. Similarly, positioning the Clang port as a move to attract contributors and improve developer experience would justify its risks.

Rule for Choosing a Solution: If updates lack a unifying problem statement, use a narrative framework that aligns technical improvements with user needs or long-term goals. This ensures clarity, engagement, and sustainability.

Typical Choice Errors and Their Mechanism

  • Error: Prioritizing technical novelty over user impact. Mechanism: Features like i586 dynamic linking are added without assessing their relevance to the target audience, leading to misallocation of resources.
  • Error: Ignoring trade-offs in favor of incremental progress. Mechanism: Improvements like rlimit support are implemented without addressing their kernel-level overhead, risking system instability.

Conclusion: Vision as a Catalyst for Growth

Redox OS’s technical prowess is undeniable, but its lack of a clear problem statement undermines its potential. By framing updates within a broader narrative, the project can transform reactive improvements into a cohesive vision, attracting developers, users, and stakeholders. Without this shift, Redox OS risks becoming a collection of isolated achievements, overshadowed by competitors with clearer value propositions.

Community and Developer Perspectives

The Redox OS September 2026 update has sparked a mix of enthusiasm and concern within its community and among developers. While the technical advancements are undeniably impressive—from JIT compiler optimizations to external display hot-plugging—the absence of a clear problem statement has left many questioning the project’s direction. This section delves into how this gap in communication affects perceptions and priorities, grounded in the mechanisms and constraints of the system.

Developer Reactions: Enthusiasm Meets Ambiguity

Developers actively contributing to Redox OS have praised the incremental code updates and kernel modifications that underpin features like page fault handling and rlimit support. For instance, the integration of uutils 0.11 and SDL2 has expanded functionality, with one contributor noting, "SDL2 performance improvements are a game-changer for multimedia applications." However, the lack of a unifying narrative has led to confusion. As one developer put it, "We’re building great tools, but what’s the endgame? Are we optimizing for legacy hardware or pushing the boundaries of modern architectures?"

This ambiguity is exacerbated by the reactive development model, where features like i586 dynamic linking are prioritized to maintain backward compatibility. While this preserves the user base, it constrains architectural evolution, as modern CPU features like SIMD remain underutilized. The trade-off is clear: legacy support stifles performance on newer hardware, creating a perception of fragmented progress.

Community Feedback: A Double-Edged Sword

Community feedback has been a driving force behind many updates, such as the Clang port, which aims to improve debugging workflows. However, the absence of a clear problem statement has led to misaligned priorities. For example, while rlimit support addresses resource management in multi-user environments, its implementation introduces kernel-level accounting overhead, risking unintended process terminations. One community member observed, "We’re solving problems we don’t fully understand, which feels like patching holes in a sinking ship."

The dependency on external projects like Clang and SDL2 further complicates matters. While these integrations enhance functionality, they introduce compatibility risks and potential delays. title: PPO vs. SAC: A Comparative Study for Cooperative Motion Control of Dual-Arm Space Robots
description:
arXiv:2610.32034v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing population of orbital debris has intensified interest in active debris removal and on-orbit servicing, for which dual-arm space manipulators offer improved grasping stability and load distribution relative to single-arm systems. However, coordinating two manipulators under inter-arm collision avoidance, orientation alignment, and sensing uncertainty remains challenging. This paper develops a coordinated reinforcement learning framework for cooperative motion planning of a dual-arm space manipulator in a target-reaching task with inter-arm collision-avoidance constraints. A centralized state representation combines joint-space, end-effector, and target-relative information, while a multi-objective reward function promotes target-reaching accuracy, orientation alignment, motion smoothness, synchronized task completion, and collision avoidance. Within this framework, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) are compared as representative on-policy and off-policy algorithms, and the learned policies are further evaluated for generalization to previously unseen target configurations. Across five random seeds, SAC substantially outperforms PPO within the considered fixed-base simulation scenarios: it reaches an 80% success threshold in every seed (median 1.6M environment steps) whereas PPO does not reach it within a 4M-step budget, and it attains a higher mean success rate (78.6% versus 7.4%) with lower position and orientation errors and tighter bimanual synchronization. Both algorithms degrade on unseen boundary targets, but SAC retains most of its performance while PPO's collapses. The results also expose a failure mode of PPO: under the two-phase shaped reward, it tends to converge to a reward-loitering local optimum rather than committing to the precision task. This behavior highlights the sensitivity of on-policy learning to reward shaping.

title: TACS-RF: Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave Modules
description:
arXiv:2610.31882v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present the framework of TACS-RF - a Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave modules. In this framework, a large-language-model (LLM) coding agent (Claude Opus 4.8) directly drives industry-standard electronic-design-automation (EDA) tools such as Cadence Virtuoso/Spectre, Calibre, Cadence EMX, and Ansys HFSS to design RF and mmWave modules. We validate the framework through the agentic design of a 240-251 GHz sub-THz transmitter in a 90 nm SiGe BiCMOS process. The agent semi-autonomously designed the sub-blocks including a 60 GHz push-push Colpitts VCO with second-harmonic extraction, multistage differential cascode power drivers, a push-push frequency doubler, a differential bowtie antenna, and all the interstage matching networks. The transmitter chain with parasitic-extracted devices and EM-verified passives delivers +5.1 to +6.3 dBm across an 11 GHz varactor-only tuning range, phase noise of -80 to -88 dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset while consuming a DC power of 361 mW. We describe the agent-driven design flow and the resulting division of labor between human and agent, taking a step toward a "text-to-ASIC" future for designing RF/mmWave hardware.

title: Financial Context-Rich Strategy for Actor-Critic based Agents: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Stock Trading
description:
arXiv:2610.32237v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In modern financial markets, more than 3/4th of the large volume trade is executed by algorithmic trading based on advanced trading strategies to attain higher precision and speed than traditional human traders. The conventional strategies focused on price-based indicators are inadequate in capturing the market dynamism arising from real-world events such as social sentiments, political instability, or sudden economic shifts. With the rise of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and data availability, there is a requirement for more efficient algorithms that can incorporate these external factors in trading strategies. DRL has shown potential in simulating real-world scenarios and in simplifying complex decision-making since DRL agents can automate the trading process i.e. executing trades in a manner comparable to human traders. They have shown reliable performance since they can update their policies based on risk and quantitative factors. In this paper, we propose a DRL approach based on partial and deep-infusion of sentimental analysis. It features distinct policy designs of actor-critic-based agents: only policy optimization (A2C & PPO) and policy optimization along with Q-learning principles (DDPG, TD3 & SAC). Our findings reveal, that the agents based on policy optimization combined with Q-learning, significantly and consistently demonstrate improved performance upon sentiment deep-infusion in profit maximization as well as risk-averse trading.

title: Correct Answers, Closed Gates: SolveBind for GUI Agents at the Verification Barrier
description:
arXiv:2610.32223v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Websites and applications deploy CAPTCHAs and anti-automation mechanisms that use behavioral signals such as interaction trajectories and timing, not outcomes alone, to distinguish humans from automated agents. We call these protected GUI environments, where correctly solving a verification task is insufficient for end-to-end task completion. Agents must turn solver outputs into accepted interactions and adapt execution to runtime feedback under time constraints. We introduce SolveBind, a GUI-agent framework combining hierarchical solving with runtime supervision. A hierarchical solving tree decomposes verification into interdependent Perceive, Ground, Solve, Act, and Verify capabilities. A runtime supervisor grounds action commitments in tool-derived evidence, revises them as evidence arrives, and mediates execution under explicit recovery budgets. Across nine CAPTCHA task families and nine backbone models, SolveBind achieves the highest success rate on eight backbones, outperforming the strongest baseline by 13.3-34.5 percentage points. It achieves the highest success rate on all six AndroidWorld backbones. In a paired GPT-5.5 analysis, MobileAgent produces correct answers but fails dynamic verification on 13 of 90 tasks; SolveBind succeeds on seven of these tasks. With automatic submission, removing binding reduces success from 82.22% to 71.56% and increases latency and token usage. Recovery caps reduce execution cost with a small observed success trade-off: removing them raises success from 82.22% to 83.56%, while increasing latency and token usage to 3.7x and 2.4x their full-supervision values, respectively. These results support evidence-grounded execution control while identifying a success-cost trade-off in recovery and failure boundaries of heuristic submission rules.

title: Introducing Vercel for Slack
description:
Vercel Agent now works in Slack. Mention it the way you'd pull a teammate into a thread, and it reads the discussion, answers with the context of the platform running your app, and turns the team's decisions into changes you approve. Vercel for Slack is available today in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams.

Work starts in conversation. An alert gets noticed in a channel, a fix gets agreed on in a thread, and then someone leaves Slack to do the work. With Vercel Agent, you can tag it in for answers about your infrastructure or hand it the work, all without leaving the conversation.

What is Vercel Agent?

When we introduced Vercel Agent, we called it an AI teammate for your development workflow. Today it's the first responder for your production apps. When something changes, it investigates your logs, metrics, and deployments, finds the root cause, and proposes a fix, often before anyone's opened a laptop. Give it a PR and it flags the regressions and risky changes that a passing CI run won't show.

In Slack, that agent joins the conversation itself. It is a core part of Vercel, so your deployments, build statuses, logs, metrics, code reviews, and PRs are in front of it before you've typed anything. Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM, and it answers like a teammate with every tab already open. And answering is only half of it, because once you know what's wrong, the agent can go fix it:

  • Diagnose issues: Investigate incidents, trace errors to the deploy that caused them, explain a cost spike, and answer questions about your codebase.

  • Code alongside your team: Fix failing builds and CI, review PRs with knowledge of how the code runs in production, and turn a thread's decision into a tested pull request.

  • Operate your projects: Roll back deployments, update configuration, manage feature flags, and resolve unusual usage before it becomes a bill.

The agent is read-only by default, and anything that changes code or configuration goes through a plan that you approve. Vercel for Slack brings that whole loop into the threads where you and your team are already discussing work.

Accelerating development with a conversation

Teams form decisions through collaboration. Incidents get triaged in a channel, code reviews are hashed out in threads, and features get scoped between standups. But once a thread settles on what needs to be done, the actions still need to be translated into tickets, terminal commands, and PR descriptions. Every handoff drops context, and the conversation that held the full picture becomes the thing everyone summarizes from memory. Vercel for Slack gives the agent the full context of the original conversation for every turn.

Answers in one place speed up the whole team

A deployment goes out at 1:42pm. By 1:51, checkout error rates are climbing and an alert lands in the platform engineering channel.

What used to happen next was a scatter. One responder opens logs to see how bad it is, another asks their coding agent to line up the anomaly up against the deploy timeline, a third starts reading the diff of the suspect PR. Each person investigates alone, in their own view of the same system, and the thread is where they reconcile by pasting screenshots, summarizing agent findings, and correcting each other as they establish the actual state of the situation. The minutes that matter get spent assembling the picture before anyone can act on it.

With Vercel for Slack, the first question goes to the agent, right in the thread.

"@Vercel, checkout errors spiked after the 1:42 deploy. What's going on?"

It sizes the blast radius, correlates the spike with the deployment, identifies the PR that shipped in it, and explains which change, in which file, caused which behavior. The answer arrives in the channel, where the whole team reads the same diagnosis at the same time.

Nobody has to re-run a teammate's investigation or wait for the recap, because everyone is looking at the same report. The engineer who knows the checkout code speaks to the change itself, the on-call weighs how many users are hit against how long a fix would take, and what's left for the thread is the decision, whether to roll back or fix forward.

Vercel Agent understands how your team already talks

The thread, channel, or DM is the beginning of the prompt itself. You don't have to re-explain anything that was already said, or pass in any context from your app or codebase. Bring it into a conversation like any other team member and it reads the room, picks up what the team has been discussing, and can act on it when asked.

One example of this was our iteration on Vercel Agent's plan card, the message it posts in Slack to request approval for the work it wants to do. The first version we tested internally was a wall of text, but when one of our engineers noticed that people were often approving actions without reading all of the details, we had a redesign thread that ran 47 replies deep on what a person needs to see before confirming an action on the group's behalf. Tagging Vercel Agent in at the end of that thread is what resulted in the card you see today.

By the time a PR from a conversation like this lands in a thread, the tests have already run and the preview deployment is live, so the team can start reviewing it in the conversation that kicked off the feature in the first place.

Vercel Agent reviews pull requests in the thread

Ask Vercel Agent for a review in the thread where the PR is being discussed, and the conversation is passed along with the request. What your team has been raising becomes context for what Vercel Agent checks, and its findings land back in the same thread, so discussing them, deciding, and fixing them is one loop instead of a trip to another tool.

One example from one of our own PR discussions was a review someone requested mid-thread. The agent came back with a bug sitting just outside the diff, the same title rendered twice in the UI.

A finding doesn't have to end as a comment. If the team agrees it should be fixed, the agent can patch the PR itself, and that change arrives the same way everything else does, as a proposal waiting on an approval.

Changes always go through a plan your team approves

When a thread lands on a change, Vercel Agent replies with a plan that says what will happen, in which project, and at what scope. Decisions in a channel form in fragments, across people and hours, and nobody types "DECISION:", so the plan is where all of that becomes one explicit thing to say yes to. Once approved, the agent does the work under its own identity, and the audit trail shows who asked, who approved, and what ran.

One example from our own threads was a cached page showing stale data after we shipped an update. Someone called for a cache purge scoped to just the specific pages, since it was peak hours, and asked the agent to set it up. The plan that came back matched the ask exactly, a purge of the specific path and its sub-paths with the rest of the site's cache left warm, and nothing ran until someone approved it.

Whether a thread ends in a diagnosis, a pull request, or a cache purge, the last step belongs to a person.

Getting started

The easiest way to get started is to simply ask Vercel Agent questions. Ask about the error you're chasing or the build that just failed, see what comes back, and let your team decide over time how much of the work the agent takes on. Until someone approves a plan, it's only ever reading.

Vercel for Slack is available in Public Beta for Pro and Enterprise teams. To start using Vercel Agent in Slack:

  • Open the Slack app in the Vercel Marketplace and click Connect Account.

  • Choose the Slack workspace to connect, then click Allow.

  • Mention @Vercel in a channel, a thread, or a DM.

  • Sign in to your Vercel account when it prompts you the first time.

See the Vercel for Slack docs for setup and permissions.
