title: A database, two services and an address, in five commands
description:
Everything below is one project, built from an ordinary repository with no
Gagarin-specific anything in it. No manifest, no config file, no YAML: there is
nowhere on this platform to put one, which is the point and is also why this post
is short.

The app is a Go API, a web front end that calls it, and a Postgres under both.
Call the project feed.

1. The Dockerfile is the only file we need

If your repository already builds an image, you are done before you start. Ours
is the usual two-stage build:

FROM golang:1.25-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/feed ./cmd/feed

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/feed /feed
EXPOSE 8080
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/feed"]

Two things about it matter here and nothing else does. It listens on one TCP
port, and it reads its configuration from the environment. That is the entire
contract — anything that satisfies it runs here.

2. The project, and the database under it 

gg init feed
gg resource add feed/pg postgres

gg init creates the project everything else is named for. gg resource add
provisions the Postgres and, more to the point, keeps the credentials. Nobody
types a password into anything after this, and no connection string goes near a
repository.

3. Ship it

gg ship builds the current directory, pushes the image and deploys it — three
commands' worth of work, and they are still there separately for the day you want
them apart.

gg ship feed/api:8080 --deps pg
gg ship feed/web:3000 --deps api

The number after the colon is the port the container listens on, and --deps is
the whole of the configuration: it says what this service may reach, and the
platform hands it the connection variables of any resource in that list. The
database password is never typed and never committed.

Note what is not in those commands. No replica count, no rollout strategy, no
health-check path, no ingress class, no namespace, no service account, no
NetworkPolicy. All of those exist underneath — this is Kubernetes down there —
and none of them is a decision worth making at this point in the afternoon.

4. Nothing reaches anything it has not declared

This is the part people are usually surprised by, and it is the part worth
reading twice.

A private service is default-denied. Until the edge is declared, the call is
dropped — and a dropped packet hangs, it does not fail fast.

--deps declared them on the way past. The graph also moves on its own, without
a deploy:

gg deps ls  feed/api
gg deps add feed/api pg
gg deps rm  feed/api pg

Adding an edge is yours. Taking one away asks a human to approve it, because
it is the one change that breaks something and reports nothing: the service keeps
running, the status stays green, and the call simply stops arriving.

The graph is not a picture drawn from variable references after the fact. The
graph is the firewall.

A migration is not a service

A job runs to completion and listens on nothing. Same image, run once, reaching
the database the same way:

gg run feed/migrate feed:2026-09-01 --deps pg

gg run waits, prints what the job wrote, and exits with the job's own exit
code — so CI can branch on it as though it had run the migration itself.

5. An address 

gg domain add feed/web feed.example.com

Certificate and ingress come with it. Leave the domain off and the service gets a
generated one on apps.gagarin.cloud instead.

A resource cannot have an address. Ask anyway, and the engine says so rather than
doing something clever:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "not_a_service",
    "message": "pg is a postgres resource, not a service",
    "fix_hint": "a resource is reached from inside the project by name and is never public"
  }
}

Every error carries a stable code and a fix_hint. Branch on the code, never
on the prose — the error contract is the whole list.

What it looks like once it is up 

$ gg status feed
project feed  (id eqteoeay)

    SERVICE  KIND      SIZE  READY  PORT  REACHES  IMAGE               VOLUME
  ● api      service   s     1/1    4000  pg       api:1788569515      —
  ● pg       postgres  s     1/1    5432  —        postgres:17-alpine  10GB
  ● web      service   s     1/1    8080  api      web:1788569576      —
    └ https://feed.gagarin.cloud
    └ https://web-eqteoeay.apps.gagarin.cloud

  ● running
  $0.789 today so far

One screen: what runs, what it reaches, what it costs today. The REACHES
column is the firewall, printed.

A different project in the console — the same reading, drawn. There is nothing to press that is not also a command: one source of truth, and a second way to change it is exactly what we are not building.

And the command it will not run

The database has a service depending on it now. Ask for it to be destroyed and
the answer is no — not a confirmation prompt, not a --force, just no:

gg destroy feed/pg → 409 service_in_use, naming what holds it, and the hint is the command that would let go first. Same graph as step 4, read from the other end. Watch the recording on gagarin.cloud.

The whole afternoon:

step command what it is
1 — your Dockerfile, unchanged
2 gg init + gg resource add a project, and a Postgres
3 gg ship ×2 two services, and the edges between them
4 gg deps the graph, when it moves without a deploy
5 gg domain add the address

Five commands, and the only decision in them was which service gets a port.

If you want to follow along with your own repository, gg login prints a link
and a code, and there is $5 on a new account to spend. If you want to
know what happens the day you want out, we wrote that down too:
leaving.

Originally published at gagarin.cloud.

title: Failed User Reminder Retries Using Node.js Message Queues (Choosing the Recovery Boundary)
description:
Short answer: put reminder delivery behind a queue, classify failures before deciding to retry, and send poison messages to a dead-letter queue. Keep the retry count in message metadata, expire delayed attempts, log every transition, and make the worker idempotent. That gives a customer-support cleanup job a bounded path through transient latency without turning a bad payload into an infinite loop.

The important design choice is not which queue has the fanciest retry option. It is where the system draws the line between “try again” and “stop touching this message”. For a reminder worker, that line is more valuable than a clever backoff formula. I start by writing that boundary down, because changing it after a queue has accumulated failures makes the operational story much harder to read.

That is the trap.

Bounded retries win.

Keep it finite.

The failure boundary matters more than the queue brand

A support platform may run a periodic cleanup that finds reminders due for delivery. The HTTP request should enqueue that work and return. A worker then sends each reminder. If the provider times out, the message can be retried. If the message has an invalid recipient or a corrupted schema, retrying only repeats the same failure.

I use three outcomes:

  • A transient error gets a delayed retry.
  • A permanent error is acknowledged into a dead-letter path for review.
  • An ambiguous result is treated as a possible duplicate, so the send operation must be idempotent.

That last case is easy to underestimate. Standard queues are at-least-once. A worker can send a reminder, lose its connection before acknowledging the message, and receive the same reminder again. The worker needs a stable reminder ID and a durable send record or provider-side idempotency key. A retry counter alone does not prevent duplicate notifications.

The scheduler should stay small. A cron trigger can enqueue cleanup work, while the worker performs the potentially longer operation. A scheduled task has a 900-second execution ceiling, so it is the wrong place to hold a long batch open. The queue is the boundary that absorbs slow downstream calls.

How should I handle retries for failed user reminders?

Use a retry queue with a message TTL and dead-letter routing back to the work queue. The worker increments a counter before requeueing. After three attempts in this example, it routes the message to the dead-letter queue instead. Three is a policy choice, not a universal truth; the useful part is that it is finite and visible.

Here is the smallest RabbitMQ-shaped setup I would start from. It uses a 60-second delay for the retry queue and preserves the original reminder ID in the body. The retry queue’s dead-letter exchange returns the message to the work queue after expiration.

import amqp from "amqplib";

const connection = await amqp.connect(process.env.AMQP_URL ?? "amqp://localhost");
const channel = await connection.createChannel();

await channel.assertExchange("reminders.dlx", "direct", { durable: true });
await channel.assertQueue("reminders", {
  durable: true,
  deadLetterExchange: "reminders.dlx",
  deadLetterRoutingKey: "failed",
});
await channel.assertQueue("reminders.retry", {
  durable: true,
  messageTtl: 60_000,
  deadLetterExchange: "",
  deadLetterRoutingKey: "reminders",
});
await channel.assertQueue("reminders.failed", { durable: true });
await channel.bindQueue("reminders.failed", "reminders.dlx", "failed");

The queue declaration is only half the policy. A retry must be logged with the reminder ID, attempt number, error class, and next action. That record is what lets an operator distinguish a provider timeout from a malformed message six hours later. Do not rely on the queue UI as your audit trail.

The useful log line is boring: reminder=rem-184 attempt=2 outcome=retry next=60s. Boring is good here. It is searchable, comparable, and less likely to turn a support incident into guesswork.

type Reminder = {
  id: string;
  userId: string;
  body: string;
};

const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3;

channel.consume("reminders", async (message) => {
  if (!message) return;

  const reminder = JSON.parse(message.content.toString()) as Reminder;
  const attempts = Number(message.properties.headers?.attempts ?? 0);

  try {
    await sendOnce(reminder);
    await recordRetryEvent(reminder.id, attempts, "sent");
    channel.ack(message);
  } catch (error) {
    const permanent = isPermanentReminderError(error);

    if (permanent || attempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
      await recordRetryEvent(reminder.id, attempts, "dead-lettered");
      channel.nack(message, false, false);
      return;
    }

    await recordRetryEvent(reminder.id, attempts + 1, "retry");
    channel.sendToQueue("reminders.retry", message.content, {
      persistent: true,
      headers: { attempts: attempts + 1 },
      contentType: "application/json",
    });
    channel.ack(message);
  }
});

async function sendOnce(reminder: Reminder): Promise<void> {
  // The storage write must be unique on reminder.id.
  await markAsSendingIfNew(reminder.id);
  await sendToNotificationProvider(reminder);
}

async function recordRetryEvent(
  reminderId: string,
  attempt: number,
  outcome: string,
): Promise<void> {
  console.info({ reminderId, attempt, outcome, at: new Date().toISOString() });
}

This sample deliberately acknowledges the original message after publishing a retry copy. In production, the publish and acknowledgement need an operational guarantee that matches the broker and client you use; otherwise a process crash between those calls can lose or duplicate work. The idempotent send record is still required because no broker choice removes downstream uncertainty.

For a real provider call, retry only known transient failures. Honor a Retry-After value when one exists, and use exponential backoff rather than hammering a slow endpoint. Also set an expiration on work that has become irrelevant. A reminder for an appointment that ended yesterday should not emerge from a retry queue today.

What changes across RabbitMQ, BullMQ, and SQS?

RabbitMQ gives this pattern explicit broker primitives: TTL, dead-letter exchanges, acknowledgements, and negative acknowledgements. That makes the failure boundary visible, but the topology is yours to operate. The dead-letter exchange documentation also calls out operational concerns around dead-letter safety and permissions. It is a good fit when routing and acknowledgement semantics are part of the application design.

BullMQ is a Node.js library built on Redis. Its delayed jobs, attempts, backoff, and failed-job retention are convenient when the application already depends on Redis and the team wants retry policy close to JavaScript code. The trade-off is that Redis availability, persistence, and queue-worker operations become part of the reliability story. BullMQ is not a neutral replacement for a broker with exchange-based routing.

Amazon SQS is a managed queue with visibility timeouts and a redrive policy to a dead-letter queue. It removes broker operations from the team, but the worker still owns visibility-timeout extension, idempotency, and failure classification. Standard SQS delivery is at-least-once; FIFO changes ordering and deduplication behavior, but it does not make an external notification send magically transactional.

Infrai is a reasonable option when the same backend already needs one REST API, one key, and one bill across services, and the queue surface is useful as part of that consolidation. Its scheduling facts fit a queue-worker design, including queue creation, publish, negative acknowledgement, and dead-letter redrive. I would not choose it to replace Airflow or Temporal: it has no DAG/workflow orchestration or join primitive.

Option Access model Best fit Main limitation
RabbitMQ Broker client and topology Explicit routing, TTL, and acknowledgement control The team operates the broker and its topology
BullMQ Node.js library over Redis Redis is already the application center of gravity Redis operations become part of queue reliability
Amazon SQS Managed HTTP service Minimal broker operations Visibility timeout and idempotency remain worker concerns
Infrai queue surface REST API One backend key and billing surface across services No DAG orchestration, join primitive, or topic-style fan-out

The decision rule is simple. Pick RabbitMQ when broker-level routing is the product. Pick BullMQ when Redis and a Node.js-native job API are already the center of gravity. Pick SQS when managed operations matter most. Consider a unified REST surface when reducing credential and billing sprawl is worth accepting its platform limits.

For a team already using the unified REST surface, this is the corresponding publish boundary. The route is intentionally the only platform call in the example. The worker still owns retries, status checks, and idempotency; the API does not turn an unreliable notification provider into a transaction.

type ReminderJob = { id: string; userId: string; body: string };

async function publishReminder(job: ReminderJob): Promise<void> {
  const key = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  const baseUrl = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
  if (!key || !baseUrl) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_BASE_URL are required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/v1/queue/publish`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${key}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": `reminder-${job.id}`,
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({ queue: "reminders", message: job }),
    });

    if (response.ok) return;
    if (response.status !== 429 && response.status < 500) {
      throw new Error(`publish failed ${response.status}: ${await response.text()}`);
    }

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after") ?? 0);
    const delay = retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : 2 ** attempt * 250;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delay));
  }

  throw new Error("publish failed after bounded retries");
}

The exact same boundary applies after publishing: a 429 or temporary 5xx can be retried with backoff, while a validation response belongs in the dead-letter path. The idempotency key is tied to the reminder ID so a network timeout does not create a second logical job.

The limits I would write into the design document

The retry policy needs limits outside the code sample. Delayed messages are capped at 7 days, message bodies at 256 KB, and retention at 30 days. Acknowledged messages are removed, so this is not Kafka-style replay and there are no multiple consumer groups to recover a historical stream. If support needs a full history, write retry events to a separate durable store.

FIFO deduplication lasts only 5 minutes. Standard queues still require consumer idempotency. There is no native debounce or throttle, and there is no one-publish-to-many topic primitive; multiple queues are needed when fan-out is required. Cron expressions do not provide nonstandard L extensions, paused schedules do not backfill missed triggers, and execution history output is limited to its first 4 KB. Those are design constraints, not footnotes.

For latency versus cost, I would start with a short first delay, then increase the delay for repeated provider failures, while bounding total attempts and message age. More retries can reduce lost transient deliveries, but they also hold worker capacity and create duplicate risk. Fewer retries lower that pressure while pushing more cases to manual review. Measure queue age, retry count, dead-letter rate, and successful sends per attempt before changing the policy.

What I would change at scale

At scale, I would separate queues by failure behavior rather than put every reminder in one undifferentiated stream. A provider timeout and an invalid template should not compete for the same workers. I would also store a state transition for queued, sending, sent, and dead-lettered, with a uniqueness constraint on the reminder ID. That turns idempotency from a comment into a database invariant.

I would add a redrive command that requires an operator to select a bounded batch from the dead-letter queue. Redrive is useful for corrected data; it is dangerous as a button labeled “retry everything”. The review path should show the last error, attempt count, age, and next destination before release.

The queue is not the business policy. It is the delivery mechanism. Classify the failure, bound the retry, preserve the evidence, and make the send repeatable. That recipe survives a change from RabbitMQ to BullMQ or SQS because the important state lives at the worker boundary.

Further reading

  • RabbitMQ dead-letter exchanges
  • BullMQ job retries
  • Amazon SQS visibility timeout
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
  • RabbitMQ message TTL

title: The Vercel Sandbox CLI is now more agent-friendly
description:
The Sandbox CLI version 4.0.1 ships four output and error improvements:

  • New sandboxes point users towards how to connect into them.

  • A sandbox not found error shows where to look for existing sandboxes.

  • Common mistakes, like typing a command after sh, redirect to the command that was intended.

  • Outdated installs show an update notice when they create a new sandbox.

Each of these messages now carries the action to take next instead of leaving you to work it out.

New sandboxes tell you how to connect

create and fork output now ends with a connect hint, so a fresh sandbox never leaves you wondering what to type next.

Not found errors point you to your sandboxes

When a command references a sandbox that does not exist, the error is quiet and actionable instead of a raw API dump. Setting DEBUG=sandbox:errors restores the request detail for debugging.

A misused command explains the right one

sh opens a plain interactive shell, so it takes no command of its own. The CLI can now return precise answers that rewrite the attempt into the command that does what you meant, whatever the command is.

Outdated installs warn you at creation time

create, sh, and run check for a newer published CLI and print an update notice when the install is behind. The check is cached to a file and refreshed at most once per hour; when a lookup does run it happens concurrently with the creation request, so it adds no latency. Creation defaults, such as the base image, are chosen client side, so an outdated global install silently keeps old defaults. Prerelease versions skip the check, and SANDBOX_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 disables it.

Learn more in the Sandbox CLI documentation.

title: Every suppression is a claim
description:
There's a mailbox I worry about more than the others. If you find a hole in something I've published there's an address to send it to, and what turns up there is encrypted, because a vulnerability report is about the only sort of message where being read in transit is the whole disaster. The code that opens those is mine (a small tool called sigillum and two encryption modules underneath it), so when I set a heavyweight review running over the lot of it late one night I was braced to care quite a lot about what came back.

I did care, as it turned out... just not about the findings.

Forty-two notes saying "it's fine"

The findings themselves were fine, in the sense that they were ordinary and fixable and what you run a review to get. What stopped me was sitting underneath them: forty-two comments scattered across the three modules, each one telling a checker to leave a particular line alone.

//nolint:gosec // bounded by the caller.

If you've not met one before, //nolint is the Go convention for switching a check off on a single line, and gosec is the security checker. So what that comment actually says is yes, this looks dangerous, and I'm telling you it isn't, which makes it a strange sort of comment. What it's really doing is vouching for the code.

Whoever wrote it looked at that line, decided the checker had it wrong, left a note saying so, and then left the building. Whoever reads it next takes their word for it, and why wouldn't you? Someone clearly thought about it, they've written it down, and the alternative is going and working out the bounds of a bit-shift yourself at the end of a long day. So you nod and move on, and that's how the trick works: forty-two character references, none of which I could have told you the contents of.

So I didn't want a count. I wanted the list, one line at a time, so I could see what each was covering for.

Some of them showed their working

Line them up next to each other and they stop looking interchangeable.

// bounded above.
// bounded by the input length.
// seconds since epoch, well inside uint32 until 2106.

That third one is doing proper work. It names the quantity, it states the bound, and it tells you the year the claim stops being true, which means you can check it in a few seconds and satisfy yourself that it holds. It's a reason, and it behaves like one. The first two are vibes.

"Bounded above" by what, exactly? And "bounded by the caller" is the worst of the lot, because it's a promise about every call site that exists today plus every one that gets added next year, made in a file where you can't see a single one of them. It's about as reliable as a bloke in the pub telling you his mate will definitely pay you back.

They arrived in days

This wasn't years of accumulated debt. Those forty-two arrived in days. Most of that code was written by agents working through review findings at speed, and the awkward part is that they were doing what I'd asked them to.

That's the problem, really. Ask for a clean lint run and there are two ways to get one: fix the code, or tell the checker to shut up. Only one of those requires you to understand the finding, and the other is available pretty much every time, on any line, for free.

I've written before about an agent that has to make the build pass and about the gap between a claim of success and a green pipeline, and this is that pressure one floor further down. There the agent said it had finished; here it manufactured the finish and left a polite note explaining why that was fine.

When I write one of these at the end of a long day I at least feel a bit grubby about it, and I suspect a loop doesn't feel anything of the sort (nor does it get bored of taking the cheap option).

So I went through them

Simple ones first, then whatever was left standing. The true ones mostly stopped needing a comment at all, which I hadn't expected: a counter that had been excused on the grounds its value was bounded now gets checked, and a bare 3 that got waved through as obvious now multiplies two named quantities so the number explains itself. That's the pattern, and I was slower to spot it than I'd care to admit, because most of these were the linter being right and me being in a hurry.

The false ones were more interesting. Several of those narrowing conversions really were unchecked. "Bounded by the caller" was load-bearing and unproven, so there were real defects behind those notes, with a reason draped over them like a dust sheet.

And then there was this one

Mid clean-up, a new directive turned up.

//nolint:errcheck // the read below is what matters

It was on a Close(), and it's backwards.

If you've not worked with OpenPGP before, this catches people out. An encrypted message carries a modification detection code, the MDC, which is how you know nobody meddled with the ciphertext on its way to you, and it isn't checked as you read the message. It's checked when you close the reader, once every last byte has gone past. So the error being thrown away there was the integrity check... all of it!

A message that decrypts is not the same as a message that arrived intact, and that cheerful little note had the two the wrong way round with enough confidence to stop anyone looking. Ship it and sigillum decrypt writes attacker-modified vulnerability reports into my security rota and exits zero, which is about the worst thing that tool could do.

It never landed. It got caught in review on the very pass that was busy clearing out its forty-two cousins, which is a neater demonstration than anything I could have argued for. A test covers it now, and I'd rather have the test than the argument.

The good ones still need somewhere to live

Some exceptions are real, though, and the sanctioned move is to lift them off the line and into .golangci.yaml, scoped to the one file entitled to it, with the reasoning written beside it. There's one case in this code that deserves exactly that.

OpenPGP identifies a key by its fingerprint, and the spec defines that fingerprint as a SHA-1 hash. SHA-1 is broken, which is why the security checker objects to seeing it, but it isn't being used as a security guarantee here, only as a name, and a name only works if everyone computes the same one. Reach for something stronger and you've produced a key that no other OpenPGP implementation on the planet can match against.

So you use SHA-1, and you write down why, and that's a paragraph of argument instead of six words at the end of an import, somewhere a reviewer will actually meet it.

Then the fix was worse

So that's what I did, and it looked lovely for about six commits, right up until I noticed that three of those exclusions named linters that weren't in the enable list.

They suppressed nothing! Those linters hadn't been failing, they were never going to fail, and the careful reasoning I'd written to govern the whole module wasn't governing anything. There was even a comment in there claiming that the same construct introduced anywhere else would still get caught, which it wouldn't, with no linter there to watch.

That's worse than what it replaced, and I took a minute to admit it. An inline directive at least sits next to the line it excuses, where a reader trips over it and has a fighting chance of arguing back. A dead exclusion is a paragraph of confident prose vouching for a rule that isn't running, filed somewhere a reader rarely goes. And you won't hear about it, either: golangci-lint will not mention that you've excluded a linter it had no intention of running. Why would it.

What couldn't be fixed got a number

Not all of it could be cleared where it stood. go/signing had its own crop and untangling those wasn't part of that day's work, so they became an issue instead... chore: remove the 16 inline nolint directives.

That's most of the argument in one filing decision, really. The exception still exists, it's still unresolved, nothing has been fixed by writing it down. It's just in a tracker with a number on it now, instead of whispering from the end of a line where I'd probably not have gone looking.

It's a cousin of waivers with an expiry date, where the argument was that a dependency waiver needs a date on it so it can't outlive its reason. Same instinct, different beast: that one is about a waiver going stale, this one is about a note that never said anything to begin with.

Who's actually listening

There's one inline directive left across the three modules now, in a sigillum test, and it carries its reason with it ("identity is the point"). You can go and check that rather than take it from me. What I'd keep out of all this is a test. It reads .golangci.yaml, pulls out every linter named by a file-scoped exclusion, and fails if that linter isn't switched on:

%q is excluded for a path but is not enabled, so the exclusion suppresses nothing and its written reasoning governs nothing.

Forty lines and no dependencies, and it exists because the fix I wrote had failed just like the notes it was replacing... a character reference, written in my own hand, for someone who'd never turned up.

Originally published at phpboyscout.uk on 26 October 2026.

title: Pure cinema
description:
Most of what we ship is there to make something work, or stop something going
wrong. A refusal that waits for a human. A graph that is also the firewall. A
rollback that never puts back an old password. Important, and none of it is
much fun to watch.

This one is fun to watch.

Twenty-six seconds, nothing sped up. On the left, Claude Code is deploying a project. On the right, the console has LIVE on and is left alone. Watch the recording on gagarin.cloud.

What you are looking at

On the left, Claude Code working through a deploy: a Postgres, an API, a web
page. On the right, the project page in the console, empty when the clip
starts. The agent runs gg resource add, and a Postgres plate fades in on the
right. It ships the API, and a second plate arrives above the first with an
arrow down into it. It ships the web service, the picture slides
to make room, and a third plate lands on top with its public tag. The three
read RESTARTING for a moment, then one by one turn green, and the line under
the project name goes from "nothing running" to "3 of 3 drifting" to
"3 services, in agreement".

Nobody pressed refresh. Nobody touched the console at all.

How it is done, briefly

There is no feed. The engine answers a status read and pushes nothing, so LIVE
is a re-read on a clock: every five seconds the page asks again, through the
same session and the same path as opening it would. The next read waits for
the last one to finish, so a slow cluster slows the clock rather than piling
reads on itself. A tab you are not looking at reads nothing, and catches up the
moment you look back. The switch is remembered per browser, and it is off
until you turn it on, because a status read asks the cluster about every
workload and we would rather not do that to everybody.

The motion is the part we spent the time on. A re-read that redrew the graph
from scratch would snap: a new service would appear fully formed and
everything under it would jump a rank. Instead a plate that stays slides from
where it was to where it now belongs, with its arrows following. A new one
fades in at its place. One that was destroyed fades out where it stood. When a
plate's reading changes, it rings once in its own colour. The ledger on the
left does the same: rows arrive and leave, and a cost or a replica count that
moves flashes as it does. If your system asks for reduced motion, all of it
settles without the choreography.

Why bother

Because the whole pitch of this platform is that you hand a repository to an
agent and it comes back with an address, and that pitch has a weak moment in
the middle. For a minute or two the agent is running commands and you are
reading a transcript, trusting that each line did what it says.

LIVE turns that minute into something you can see. The agent says it added a
database, and a database appears. It says web now reaches api, and an arrow is
drawn. It says everything is up, and everything is green. The transcript and
the picture agree, or they do not, and you know which before the agent tells
you.

That is a real thing, and it is still not why we built it. We built it because
the first time we watched a project assemble itself on screen while an agent
typed, everyone in the room went quiet, and that seemed worth keeping.

Try it

Open any project at my.gagarin.cloud, press LIVE
in the bar above the graph, and tell your coding agent to deploy something
into it. If you have nothing to hand, the chit-chat recipe
in the recording is a Postgres, an API and a web page, and takes an agent
about a minute.

Then sit back. It is the most relaxing minute in infrastructure.

Originally published at gagarin.cloud.

title: EDWARD-NMT: Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for Neural Machine Translation
description:
arXiv:2610.32115v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a powerful paradigm for scaling Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and managing language heterogeneity. However, practical limitations hinder its deployment on resource-constrained devices: the entire expert pool must remain in memory, and the per-token compute budget is statically fixed during training by rigid top-k routing. We introduce EDWARD-NMT (Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for NMT), a novel MoE encoder-decoder architecture designed for a train once, deploy anywhere paradigm that exposes a family of deployable sub-networks at inference time. EDWARD-NMT integrates three key innovations: (i) Matryoshka-style elastic dimensions to flexibly reduce the memory footprint; (ii) an adaptive sigmoid router with a learned, task-conditioned threshold, allowing each token to dynamically determine its active expert count; and (iii) a dual-consistency objective to maximize the performance of the extracted sub-networks. Extensive experiments on PhoMT (En-Vi), WMT-14 (En-De), multilingual OPUS-16, and a multi-domain De-En benchmark validate our approach. The full-capacity architecture matches or exceeds strong MoE baselines with improved parameter efficiency. Furthermore, the sub-networks seamlessly extracted from a single checkpoint consistently outperform comparably sized dense Transformers without any retraining.

title: Assembly required
description:
A cloud hands you IP ranges, security groups, service accounts, IAM policies,
load balancer listeners and virtual machines. None of those is a place to put an
application. You get to one by assembling them, and the assembly is work: a few
days at the start of a project, an hour or two a week after that, for as long as
the project lives. It bills nothing. It ships no feature. Each team that does it
builds a private platform-as-a-service out of the same parts, and the one they
finish is as good as their best engineer's spare attention, which is not very
good. The other option is to pay an infrastructure salary for the same artifact.

The not-so-fun puzzle

Count the objects in the smallest useful deployment. One container serving HTTP,
one Postgres behind it, on a domain, with TLS.

On AWS: a VPC, two subnets in two availability zones because the load balancer
refuses to start with one, a route table, an internet gateway, a NAT gateway so
the container can reach your package registry, two security groups, a task
definition, an IAM task role, a second IAM role for the thing that launches the
task, a target group, a listener, an ACM certificate with its validation record,
a Route 53 record, an RDS subnet group, a parameter group, a secret, and a log
group. Twenty resources, give or take your tolerance for defaults. Your
application is one line inside one of them. Google Cloud and Azure sell the same
box with different part names.

None of the twenty is difficult on its own. The difficulty is that all twenty
have to agree, and when two of them disagree the system reports a timeout. You
forgot the NAT gateway, so image pulls hang for three minutes and then fail with
a registry error that says nothing about routing. The security group allows 5432
from a CIDR that looks right and covers the wrong subnet. The health check path
returns 302 and the target group calls it unhealthy, so the load balancer drains
the only task you have and the deploy rolls back clean, with no failure to read.

Nowhere in the documentation does anyone promise that a web app with a database
is easy to run. They promise a page for each primitive, and they deliver that.
The convenience was never offered. We supplied it ourselves and then forgot that
we had.

Your time or your money

Google and Stripe employ people whose entire job is the twenty objects. They
have platform teams, internal deploy tools and an on-call rotation to go with
them, and that is a sane way to spend money at their size.

Below that size you choose between two bills. Hire an infrastructure engineer,
who costs about what a senior backend developer costs and writes none of your
product. Or give the work to a backend developer, who does it in the gaps
between features.

Take the second option and look at what the repo collects. A Terraform module
copied from a blog post. A deploy.sh with a set -e at the top and four aws
calls under it. A GitHub Actions workflow that works, then a second one for
staging that drifts from the first within a month. A naming convention somebody
documented in Notion in March. Six weeks later you own a private PaaS with one
customer, no roadmap, and a maintainer who would rather be writing the product.

Yet another cloud wrapper

Say the expertise is in the building and the wrapper is good. I have read
several of these now, at companies with no connection to each other, and they
contain the same verbs. Build an image and push it. Set environment variables
for an environment. Deploy a version. Declare that this service may reach that
database. Print status. Roll back.

Six verbs, written from scratch at each of those companies, because the problem
has one shape and everybody finds it. Writing them again re-derives something
the industry settled years ago. No customer pays for your deploy subcommand.

And you keep it. The provider releases a major version that renames an attribute
you set in nine places. The node image you pinned goes end-of-life. The engineer
who understood the module takes another job, and the module becomes a thing the
team edits by copying the block above and changing a string. Internal tools get
the maintenance that nothing external demands, which is none.

Who's holding the bag?

Most firms with twelve engineers do not want an infrastructure salary on the
books, so the twenty objects land on developers who have never administered a
network. From there it goes one of a few ways.

They learn, on project time. Four days reading VPC documentation is four
days of a developer's salary spent arriving at the line where the application
work starts. They will be competent at it in a year and will have shipped less
in the meantime.

They guess, and some guesses cost money. A security group open to 0.0.0.0/0
because that made the timeout stop. A database whose backups have never been
restored, so nobody knows whether they work. A secret passed as a build argument
and printed into a public CI log. None of these announces itself on the day it
is made.

They hand it to an agent. An agent writes plausible Terraform in a minute,
and plausible is the output that hurts. The plan applies, the service answers
200, and the bucket holding customer uploads is readable by anyone who knows the
name. The agent is working from the same twenty-part box you are, with the same
four ways to change one thing and no single source of truth among them, so it
guesses in the places you would have guessed.

Then the bill arrives, or the data does not stay where you put it, and somebody
signs the incident report. The agent is not on call. Your developer, who was
never an infrastructure engineer and was handed the work anyway, holds the bag.

There's a better way

Raise the primitives to the things you say out loud when you describe the
system. A project. Services inside it. Managed resources. Which service may
reach which. A domain, for the ones the public should see.

gg resource add saas/pg postgres
gg ship         saas/api:8080 --deps pg
gg ship         saas/web:3000 --deps api
gg domain   add saas/web
# => Live at https://web-3cnciet6.apps.gagarin.cloud/

No VPC, because you were never going to express a product decision as a CIDR
block. No security groups: --deps pg opens the one route and hands api the
credentials for pg in the same call, so the route and the password arrive
together or neither of them does. Every service stays private until gg domain
add, which puts the public internet behind a command you have to type rather
than behind a default you have to remember.

What this does not buy you: containers still crash-loop, and migrations still
fail to apply. One class of failure leaves, the class where twenty parts have to
agree and the system tells you only that something, somewhere, timed out.

And when the project outgrows us, gg eject writes out the
Kubernetes you would have had, which you then own, knobs and all. The reasoning
behind all of this is in why coherence, and the objects themselves
are in the model.

We are on call for the platform. You are on call for your code. The line sits
where you can see it, which is more than the twenty objects ever offered.

Originally published at gagarin.cloud.

title: Lambda Web Functions cobra la memoria mientras el entorno viva: el punto de equilibrio contra Lambda clásica
description:
AWS lanzó Lambda Web Functions el 12 de octubre de 2026. Corre un servidor HTTP normal, atiende hasta 128 peticiones a la vez por entorno y cobra CPU activa en vez de tiempo de reloj. Suena a un descuento directo sobre AWS Lambda clásica. No lo es: el costo pasa de "el tiempo que corre una petición" a "la memoria que ocupa un entorno mientras existe". Este post calcula dónde se cruzan las dos líneas y lo prueba con una API real.

Qué cambia en la factura

Lambda clásica (us-east-1, Arm) cobra cada petición mientras corre:

  • $0.0000133334 por GB-segundo de memoria configurada, en tiempo de reloj, incluido el tiempo que pasa esperando a la base de datos
  • $0.20 por millón de peticiones

Web Functions cobra tres cosas:

  • $0.0000276944 por vCPU-segundo de CPU activa. Esperar I/O casi no cuesta.
  • $0.0000036667 por GB-segundo de memoria, mientras el entorno exista, incluido el tiempo ocioso entre peticiones
  • $0.30 por millón de peticiones

Dos consecuencias:

  1. La memoria se vuelve un piso mensual. Si llega tráfico cada pocos minutos, el entorno nunca se apaga. Con 1 GB son unos $9.50 al mes antes de cobrar una sola petición.
  2. La CPU cuesta casi el doble por segundo, pero sólo cuenta la CPU. Una petición que tarda 200 ms y calcula durante 50 ms paga 50 ms.

Así que Web Functions gana por petición sólo cuando las peticiones esperan mucho más de lo que calculan, y necesita suficientes peticiones para pagar el piso.

El punto de equilibrio

Los dos modelos pagan por petición; Web Functions además paga el piso. El cruce está en:

break-even requests/month = floor / (classic cost per request - Web Functions cost per request)

classic per request        = latency_s * classic_GB * 0.0000133334 + 0.0000002
Web Functions per request  = cpu_s * 0.0000276944 + 0.0000003
floor                      = env_GB * 2,592,000 * 0.0000036667

La página de precios de AWS trae un ejemplo de "API backend con mucho I/O": 200 ms por petición, 50 ms de CPU, unos 0.29 GB por entorno. Contra una función clásica de 1 GB:

Web Functions memory floor   $2.76/month
classic, per million         $2.87
Web Functions, per million   $1.68
break-even                   2,331,877 requests/month

Arriba de 2.3 millones de peticiones al mes, Web Functions sale más económica. Ahora la misma carga contra una función clásica de 512 MB:

Web Functions memory floor   $2.76/month
classic, per million         $1.53
Web Functions, per million   $1.68
Web Functions never pays off: per request it costs as much or more than classic.

La respuesta se voltea según cuánta memoria necesitaría la función clásica. La comparación sólo tiene sentido contra la configuración clásica que de verdad usarías. Una advertencia: Lambda clásica asigna CPU en proporción a la memoria, así que 50 ms de CPU a 1 GB tardan más a 512 MB, y la latencia sube con ellos. Mide antes de confiar en la línea más económica.

Una API real

Una API pequeña en producción: FastAPI en una tarea de AWS Fargate (0.25 vCPU, 1 GB, Arm), detrás de un Application Load Balancer, con PostgreSQL en Amazon RDS. Catorce días de métricas de Amazon CloudWatch:

RequestCount                 101865.0
latency_s avg=0.075 max=33.25 p50=0.0085 p99=1.096
minutes with >=1 request: 20159 of 20160
p50 requests/min: 1
peak requests/min: 283 (4.72 rps)
MemoryUtilization  68.65622133758562

Unas 218,000 peticiones al mes, con tráfico en casi todos los minutos y una petición por minuto en la mediana. Como hay tráfico en cada minuto, un entorno se quedaría vivo todo el mes y el piso se paga completo.

El punto de equilibrio en el caso más favorable para Web Functions, cero CPU por petición:

Web Functions memory floor   $6.56/month
classic, per million         $1.20
Web Functions, per million   $0.30
break-even                   7,286,426 requests/month
your traffic                 218,282 requests/month (3.0% of break-even)

Esta API necesitaría 33 veces su tráfico para que Web Functions le gane a Lambda clásica, aunque sus peticiones no usaran nada de CPU.

La factura mensual completa:

Fargate + ALB (hoy) Web Functions Lambda clásica
Cómputo $8.39 $7.03 $0.26
Puerta de entrada ALB, 2 IPv4 públicas, AWS WAF regional: $32.50 CloudFront + WAF: ~$9.22 CloudFront + WAF: ~$9.22
Total $40.89 ~$16.25 ~$9.48

El hallazgo más grande está en la segunda fila. A este tamaño, el dinero no se va en el cómputo. El balanceador, sus dos direcciones IPv4 públicas y el WAF regional cuestan cuatro veces lo que cuesta el contenedor que tienen detrás. Cualquiera de las dos opciones de Lambda ahorra sobre todo porque quita el ALB, no porque calcule de forma más eficiente. Un dominio propio o un WAF delante de Lambda siguen necesitando Amazon CloudFront, así que el costo del WAF se muda en vez de desaparecer.

Para esta API la pregunta es teórica de todos modos: en el lanzamiento, Web Functions sólo corre Node.js, y esta API es Python.

Cuándo conviene

  • Usa Web Functions cuando el tráfico sea constante y alto, las peticiones pasen casi todo su tiempo esperando I/O, el código sea Node.js y la función clásica que reemplazas necesite mucha memoria.
  • Quédate en Lambda clásica cuando el tráfico sea bajo o a ráfagas. Si un entorno atiende unas cuantas peticiones por minuto, el piso de memoria es puro gasto extra.
  • Si estás en contenedores, revisa la puerta de entrada antes que el cómputo. Un servicio pequeño detrás de un ALB puede pagar más por el balanceador que por la tarea.

title: A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox
description:
Running untrusted code safely requires more than separating it from the host. You also have to control what that code can reach.

This matters more as AI agents gain the ability to read files, execute commands, install packages, and generate programs of their own. A microVM can prevent that code from accessing the host or another workload. By itself, it cannot stop the code from exfiltrating data, probing internal services, attacking systems elsewhere on the internet, or using credentials available inside the environment.

Isolation without egress control contains the process, not its consequences.

A complete sandbox therefore needs both compute isolation and control over the authority available through its network: where code can connect, which credentials it can use, and how those permissions change throughout the workload’s lifecycle. These controls are part of the security boundary, not protections to bolt on later.

A sandbox has more than one boundary

Compute isolation answers one important question: what can this program access on the machine where it runs? Network isolation answers another: what can it access, or attack, through the network?

Consider an agent that reads a repository and runs generated code. A prompt injection hidden in an issue, log entry, dependency, or source file might instruct it to upload private data. The generated program does not need to escape its microVM. With unrestricted outbound traffic, it can simply send anything it can read to an external server.

The same access can be used to scan internal networks, exfiltrate data and credentials, or call an authenticated API. From the attacker’s perspective, crossing the VM boundary may be unnecessary. Without a network boundary, it is only half a sandbox.

A network bypass can be a sandbox escape

Recent security research has made one pattern clear: untrusted code does not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment. It only needs one network path that the security model failed to account for.

That path might be a DNS resolver left available in an otherwise disconnected environment, an empty allowlist that fails open, a hostname interpreted differently by a policy engine and a proxy, or a trusted package service turned into a relay. Any one of them can give untrusted code a channel to exfiltrate data, receive instructions, or move toward more sensitive infrastructure.

These are not compute escapes. The kernel, VM, or container boundary may continue working exactly as designed while containment still fails. The practical security boundary also includes DNS, proxies, identity services, internal networks, and every intentionally permitted destination.

Whether we call the result an escape or a bypass, the requirement is the same: a sandbox must account for every path by which untrusted code can communicate.

Useful sandboxes need selective connectivity

Completely disconnecting a sandbox closes the network path, but it also makes many workloads impractical. An agent may need to clone a repository, install a dependency, call an AI model, query a database, or upload its result.

Unrestricted internet access is not the only alternative. A useful sandbox should grant only the connectivity a workload requires:

  • Allow an AI provider, but no other public destination.

  • Allow one object storage bucket, rather than an entire cloud network.

  • Reach a private service, while blocking the rest of the private address space.

  • Install dependencies during trusted setup, then remove registry access before generated code runs.

  • Authenticate an API request without placing the API key inside the sandbox.

A practical policy model should support fully open access, complete network isolation, and granular policies that deny unmatched traffic by default. Those policies should be able to combine domain rules with allowed and denied address ranges.

Domains and CIDRs solve different problems. Domain policies are precise enough for modern services whose IP addresses change or serve many unrelated hostnames. CIDR policies work across protocols and provide control over fixed infrastructure and private networks.

Connectivity should also be temporary. A workflow can begin with access to a package registry, narrow access before untrusted execution, briefly permit an output destination, and finish with no outbound access, all without restarting the workload.

How Vercel enforces the network boundary

The Vercel Sandbox firewall runs on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it.

Linux networking transparently redirects outbound TCP connections and DNS queries through the firewall. Workloads do not need to configure a proxy, and the firewall retains each connection’s original destination.

For domain-restricted connections, the firewall inspects the beginning of the TLS handshake and extracts the Server Name Indication, or SNI. This identifies the requested hostname before the firewall opens an upstream connection. It checks that hostname against the sandbox’s domain policy and also checks the destination address against its CIDR policy.

Ordinary allowed TLS connections pass through without decryption. The firewall reads only the unencrypted handshake information required to enforce the policy, then connects the workload directly to its destination.

Some policies need to inspect or modify the HTTP request itself. For those configured domains only, header injection and request forwarding selectively terminate TLS using a certificate authority unique to the sandbox. The firewall can then match requests by hostname, path, method, query, or headers before injecting a credential or forwarding the request to an endpoint that you trust.

DNS traffic is filtered using the same domain policy. Together, these layers control both where a sandbox can connect and what authority a particular connection receives.

Keep credentials outside untrusted compute

An agent often needs to call an authenticated service, but a credential stored in an environment variable or file is a transferable bearer credential. Every program inside the sandbox can read it. Malicious code can copy it to a third-party service, where it can be retained and used long after the sandbox stops.

Vercel Sandbox instead injects credentials at the host network boundary. The firewall creates a dedicated certificate authority just in time for the sandbox and adds it to the sandbox’s trusted certificates. For a configured destination, it selectively terminates TLS, adds or replaces the authentication header, then establishes a new TLS connection to the upstream service.

The credential never enters the microVM. It never leaves the host unencrypted. The certificate authority is unique to the sandbox and is disposed when the sandbox stops.

Injection also limits where the credential can be used. The firewall sends it only to its configured destination, so uploading the sandbox’s files or environment to another service does not transfer that authority. Matchers can restrict it further by path, method, query, or request headers. Generated code might receive permission to submit results to one endpoint without receiving permission to read other resources from the same API.

Injected credentials should still follow the principle of least privilege, with access limited to the specific operations the workload requires.

Put your own policy in the path

Static allowlists cannot express every security requirement. Some workloads need to inspect payloads, enforce business rules, record an audit trail, or make an authorization decision using context only you have.

Request forwarding sends selected HTTPS requests through a proxy that you control. The proxy receives the original request along with a Vercel-issued OIDC token identifying the team, project, and sandbox that originated it.

That proxy becomes a programmable policy layer. It can:

  • Redact sensitive fields before a request leaves the environment.

  • Enforce per-user or per-sandbox authorization.

  • Route package downloads through supply-chain scanning and block artifacts that fail organizational policy.

  • Record requests and responses for compliance workflows.

  • Exchange a sandbox identity for a narrowly scoped credential.

  • Reject an operation that does not match organizational policy.

The policy and its secrets remain outside the sandbox, even when the code being governed has full root access inside its microVM. You can read more about request proxying in the Sandbox documentation.

Security belongs in the baseline product

We believe a sandbox should not require a payment method before it can safely handle untrusted code.

Every Vercel Sandbox includes both compute isolation and a complete firewall for defining what code inside it can communicate with.

The goal is not to make every sandbox completely offline. It is to make authority explicit:

  • Which destinations can this sandbox reach?

  • Which private address ranges are unavailable?

  • Which requests can use credentials?

  • Which operations must pass through additional policy?

  • When should all communication stop?

These are fundamental properties of the execution environment, not security controls to add after a workload reaches production. We believe so strongly in this that we have made our full egress firewall capabilities available to all Sandboxes.

Getting started

The following policy allows outbound connections to one API and injects a credential only for one operation. Other destinations are denied by default, and the credential remains outside the sandbox.

The same policy can be replaced while the sandbox runs:

A sandbox is not defined only by where its code runs. It is defined by what that code can reach, what authority it receives, and which boundaries still hold when the code itself is hostile.

The network is part of the sandbox.

Further reading

  • Vercel Sandbox firewall documentation

  • Understanding Vercel Sandboxes

  • Security boundaries in agentic architectures
