title: How Much Do You Trust A Dog? Quantifying Hint-Following in Reasoning Language Models
description:
arXiv:2610.32055v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophancy, altering their answers to align with user suggestions even on objective factual and reasoning tasks. Yet the quantitative form of this influence--- and whether it is calibrated to source reliability--- remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate this behavior through hint-induced answer shifts on MMLU questions, evaluating prompts of the form ``[Source] thinks the answer is (X)''. We systematically vary the source to which the hint is attributed (a professor, a friend, or a dog) across three open-source model families, Qwen, Gemma, and SmolLM. We show that the change induced by the hint follows a predictable structure well-characterized by an exponential tilt: the hint induces an approximately constant mean shift in the hinted answer's log-odds, with question--target susceptibility largely shared across sources. To explore how this pattern can arise, we introduce a formal decomposition of the hint response and illustrate in controlled synthetic experiments how KL-regularized reward-based training reshapes both hinted and unhinted answer distributions. Finally, we evaluate whether this shift is calibrated to source reliability, finding that the log-odds shift persists even when the hint-giver is declared inaccurate or accompanied by explicit warnings not to trust the source, highlighting the vulnerability of LLMs to adversarial steering.

title: I Built a Neomorphic UI Library for Next.js Because Interfaces Deserve More Personality
description:
Most modern interfaces are built from familiar pieces.

Buttons, cards, inputs, dropdowns, dialogs. We have excellent libraries for all of them. Yet when you browse enough products, you start noticing something: many interfaces feel remarkably similar.

I wanted to explore a different visual direction.

That's why I built "baloot-neomorphic-ui" (https://github.com/sajjadcodes/baloot-neomorphic-ui), a reusable neomorphic UI component library for Next.js App Router and Tailwind CSS v4.

The idea was simple: take the soft depth of neomorphism and turn it into a practical component system developers can use in real applications.

Why neomorphism?

Neomorphism, sometimes called Soft UI, creates depth through subtle highlights and shadows. Instead of relying on strong borders or dramatic contrast, components appear to rise from or press into their surrounding surfaces.

Done well, the result feels calm, tactile, and distinctive.

But a visual concept is only the beginning. A design that looks beautiful in a mockup still needs to work as an actual interface.

Buttons need clear states. Forms need useful validation. Components need to behave consistently. And the design needs to work in both light and dark themes.

A design system should make consistency easier, not turn every new component into another styling problem.

From visual idea to reusable components

I built the library around that principle.

Rather than recreating the same styles and behaviors across projects, the library provides reusable components with a shared visual language.

It includes:

  • Form controls: inputs, textareas, selects, checkboxes, radio groups, switches, and sliders.
  • Navigation and layout: cards, tabs, breadcrumbs, sidebars, pagination, and tables.
  • Feedback components: alerts, snackbars, dialogs, progress indicators, and skeletons.

The library also includes theme tokens, allowing developers to customize the visual system instead of treating every component as an isolated design.

It is built for Next.js App Router projects using Tailwind CSS v4, with TypeScript support.

Design is more than shadows

Neomorphism has a weakness: subtle visual depth can become a usability problem when it makes interactive elements difficult to distinguish.

That trade-off matters.

A component library cannot focus exclusively on appearance. It also needs to consider accessible markup, keyboard interactions, visible focus feedback, disabled states, and reduced-motion preferences where relevant.

The goal isn't to make every element look beautiful at the expense of usability. It's to make the visual identity and the interaction design work together.

That's the difference between a collection of styled components and a library intended for real applications.

Try it in your next project

You can install the package with npm:

npm install baloot-neomorphic-ui

Explore the source code, installation instructions, component examples, and theme customization options in the repository:

GitHub: https://github.com/sajjadcodes/baloot-neomorphic-ui

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/baloot-neomorphic-ui

The library is an evolving project, and I'm interested in making it more useful as it grows.

One question for frontend developers

We have no shortage of component libraries. What we need isn't necessarily another library with more components.

Sometimes, we need a different design perspective.

When choosing a UI library, what matters most to you: visual identity, accessibility, customization, developer experience, or the speed of building an interface?

I'd be interested to hear what other developers prioritize — and what you think neomorphism gets right or wrong.

title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
description:
arXiv:2610.32110v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool actually did, even when the tool's computation is correct. We saw this happen in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users. Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces. We also recreated an unlabeled estimate caught in code review before release. We studied whether these formatters misled agents and verifiers and how much the repaired wording helps. We fed tool results to agents using two formatter versions: one with the key omissions and one with all missing details clearly stated. That difference alone changed what the agents claimed and what the verifiers accepted. Unsupported agent claims dropped substantially for three of the four failure types. In one test, verifiers went from accepting incorrect answers 90 out of 90 times to rejecting them 90 out of 90 times. A control showed the verifiers could catch the errors once they were given the missing facts and asked to judge correctness. We include the audit prompt we used with Codex and Claude Code in an exploratory demonstration, written with prior knowledge of our own system's defects. When pointed at an old version of our own system, it rediscovered the defects that were still live and surfaced twelve more we had not catalogued. When pointed at OpenClaw and Hermes, two of the best-known open-source agentic systems, it found warped formatters in both. We opened PRs to fix both, and the OpenClaw fix has already been merged. Practitioners can run the same prompt on their own systems today.

title: How to Route Node.js Text Summaries for Game Reviews: Cost and Data Boundaries
description:
For a game code review, a text summarization API cost comparison is incomplete unless it names the model and the data boundary together. The bill is only one part of the decision; the review can contain unreleased mechanics, exploit details, player identifiers, or security-sensitive implementation notes. A useful design therefore chooses a summarization model and a retention boundary together.

Short answer: keep the review record in a private, region-appropriate system, send the smallest redacted text needed for the summary, and make the structured response contract the thing you validate. Use a lightweight model for routine diffs, reserve a stronger model for ambiguous architectural changes, and measure each route before submitting a large batch. A gateway can make the provider behind that contract replaceable, but it does not turn an upstream provider into your data-retention or residency authority.

For the cost-preflight and model-routing slice, Infrai is worth testing because its single REST contract can keep a Node.js worker stable while the backend model changes. Limitation: it is not a substitute for a specialist provider's contractual residency or retention guarantee, so choose that specialist when those terms are the hard requirement.

What must the summary preserve?

Start with the output, not the model catalog. For a game code review, a summary that sounds fluent but drops a severity, file path, or remediation is a failed review artifact. I use a deliberately narrow result shape:

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class ReviewSummary:
    summary: str
    findings: list[dict]
    has_blocker: bool


REQUIRED_FINDING_KEYS = {"severity", "file", "line", "finding", "recommendation"}


def validate_review(payload: dict) -> ReviewSummary:
    if not isinstance(payload.get("summary"), str):
        raise ValueError("summary must be a string")
    findings = payload.get("findings")
    if not isinstance(findings, list):
        raise ValueError("findings must be a list")

    for finding in findings:
        if not isinstance(finding, dict):
            raise ValueError("each finding must be an object")
        missing = REQUIRED_FINDING_KEYS - finding.keys()
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(f"missing finding keys: {sorted(missing)}")

    return ReviewSummary(
        summary=payload["summary"],
        findings=findings,
        has_blocker=any(item["severity"] == "blocker" for item in findings),
    )

The validator is intentionally boring. It does not decide whether a finding is correct; it prevents a syntactically plausible answer from entering the review queue without the fields the game team uses. Keep the original diff and the validated result under separate retention policies. The summary is an index for humans, not a replacement for the evidence.

Which boundary changes the provider choice?

There are four questions I ask before comparing per-token rates.

First, which region may process the text? A model's advertised availability is not a contractual residency guarantee. Record the permitted region in the job metadata, route only to a provider that can satisfy it, and fail closed when the route is unknown. “The API returned 200” is not evidence of residency.

Second, how long may the processor retain the prompt and output? Your own object store, queue, logs, and provider account can each have different defaults. Set a deletion deadline for the transient payload, suppress prompt bodies in application logs, and ask each direct provider for its current retention terms before treating a model as suitable for private review material.

Third, who is the processor? A routing layer can normalize authentication, model selection, and response envelopes, while the selected model vendor still processes the text. The layer may be a useful control point, but it cannot grant a downstream vendor a promise that vendor has not made.

Fourth, can deletion be demonstrated? Delete the transient request from your store, expire the queue item, and retain an audit record containing identifiers and timestamps rather than the source text. Then document what deletion means at the direct provider. Backups and abuse-monitoring systems may have different lifetimes; do not collapse all of them into one checkbox.

This is the point where a cheap model can become the wrong model. A lower input rate does not compensate for a region or retention requirement it cannot satisfy.

How do model, text summarization, and API cost compare?

The cost comparison should be a preflight decision, not a number copied into a README. The available model catalog and cost comparison route can show current per-token options, while the estimate route lets a batch owner test the expected volume before processing thousands of diffs. Keep the decision record with the batch: model, estimated input and output tokens, permitted region, retention class, and schema version. The 2026 discovery snapshot lists 295 routes across 20 modules, but breadth is not permission to send every review to the same processor.

I treat this as a routing record, not a leaderboard.

The runtime below is Python because the interface needs to be explicit and easy to audit; the same record can be produced by a Node.js worker. It uses an environment key, an explicit method, a bounded retry for rate limiting, and a client-supplied request identifier. The code does not send a gateway authorization header to any returned URL, because no returned URL is part of this text workflow.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


def post_cost_compare(body: dict) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/cost/compare",
            headers={
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
                "Idempotency-Key": request_id,
            },
            json=body,
            timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt
            time.sleep(delay)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"request failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}"
            )
        return response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("rate limit retry budget exhausted")


def compare_for_review(input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int) -> dict:
    return post_cost_compare(
        {
            "input_tokens": input_tokens,
            "output_tokens": output_tokens,
        }
    )

Do not infer a winning model from the cheapest row alone. Run a small labeled set of ordinary diffs, security-sensitive diffs, and deliberately ambiguous changes. Check that severity and file references survive. A model that costs less per token but needs human correction on every third summary is not cheap in this workflow.

What do the real alternatives handle differently?

There is no universal cheapest choice because the useful comparison includes data terms, structured-output behavior, model quality, and operational coupling. At minimum, compare three real alternatives against the same redacted fixture.

Infrai is a reasonable place to run the preflight comparison when the team wants one REST API and one credential across model choices. Its public discovery surface is self-describing, so a worker can inspect the capability contract without first embedding a vendor-specific SDK; the selected provider still remains the processor for the text.

Option Useful fit Boundary or engineering question
OpenAI API Broad model selection and a familiar API surface for teams already using OpenAI clients Confirm the selected model's current data controls, region availability, and structured-output behavior for your account and workload
Anthropic Claude API Strong candidate for long, explanatory review context and careful human-facing summaries Verify context, retention, regional processing, and the exact structured response contract before routing proprietary diffs
Cohere API Worth testing when the review pipeline also needs retrieval or reranking around code and issue text Reranking and summarization are different jobs; validate the summary schema instead of assuming a retrieval result is a review finding
An OpenAI-compatible gateway Useful when one stable client contract should survive a provider change and per-call metadata matters The gateway boundary does not erase the selected vendor's processor, region, or retention obligations

The last row describes where Infrai can fit: the OpenAI-compatible surface and a plain REST interface let an existing client keep a stable integration while the backend model changes. One REST API is a concrete operating advantage here: a Node.js worker or Python worker can use HTTP without installing a separate SDK for every model provider. Capabilities expose vendor readiness rather than pretending every route is equally ready. That is useful for a worker that needs to inspect available models and record the route it selected.

The recommendation is specific: try Infrai for the model-selection and cost-preflight part of a game review workflow when a stable client contract and per-call cost metadata matter, then keep the private source-of-truth and deletion policy under your control. This angle matters because replacing the backend should not require rewriting the review queue. Infrai is the wrong choice when a direct specialist provider is the only party able to satisfy a hard residency or contractual-retention requirement.

How do you roll this out without leaking a review?

Make the rollout a boundary test. Begin with synthetic diffs and redacted fixtures. Add a request ledger containing a hash of the source, not the source itself; the selected model, region decision, policy version, response request ID, and deletion deadline. Never put raw prompts in exception messages. A timeout should identify a job, not reproduce a proprietary patch in a centralized log.

Next, run two paths in parallel on a small sample: the default lightweight model for routine summaries and a stronger candidate for complex analytical summaries. Compare field validity, blocker recall, and reviewer corrections. Keep the acceptance rule visible. For example, a response that omits a blocker is a rejection even if its prose is excellent.

Then enforce deletion as a job transition. Once the validated summary and audit metadata are committed, remove the transient prompt from the application store and queue. Ask the direct model provider what its own retention and deletion controls cover; do not claim that your local delete removed a remote copy.

Finally, make provider replacement an ordinary change. The schema, redaction policy, region allowlist, and audit fields should be independent of the selected vendor. Change one model at a time, replay the same labeled fixtures, and keep a rollback route that preserves the output contract. The provider can move. The contract stays put. If this boundary fits your system, start by inspecting the AI capability schema and verify the current route before sending production review text.

Sources

References:

  • OpenAI API data controls
  • Anthropic privacy center
  • Cohere Rerank documentation
  • Infrai discovery and capability documentation

title: How to Track Usage Metrics in a Multi-Tenant SaaS Application (Node.js, Redis & Postgres)
description:
How to Track Usage Metrics in a Multi-Tenant SaaS Application (Node.js, Redis & Postgres)

Sooner or later every SaaS team gets the same three questions: "How much is tenant X actually using?", "Can we enforce plan limits?", and "Why did this customer's bill change?"

If you have no usage metering by then, the answers come from log greps and guesswork. If you built it hastily, they come from numbers nobody trusts.

This is especially painful in automation products, where usage is bursty. One tenant's workflow can trigger 50,000 runs overnight while another triggers 12 all month.

In this tutorial you'll build a per-tenant usage tracking pipeline that is:

  • Accurate: every event is attributed to exactly one tenant
  • Cheap on the hot path: it adds microseconds to each request, not milliseconds
  • Queryable: you can power dashboards, quotas, and usage-based billing from the same data

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites
  • Step 1: Define what you meter
  • Step 2: Design a tenant-safe event schema
  • Step 3: Capture usage with API middleware
  • Step 4: Count in Redis, persist in Postgres
  • Step 5: Expose usage through an API
  • Step 6: Enforce quotas
  • Common pitfalls
  • Conclusion

Prerequisites

You'll get the most out of this guide if you have:

  • [ ] Node.js 18+ and basic Express knowledge
  • [ ] PostgreSQL 14+ (any managed instance works)
  • [ ] Redis 6+
  • [ ] A multi-tenant app where every request can be resolved to a tenant_id (via API key, JWT claim, or subdomain)

Note: The patterns here are language-agnostic. Node.js is used for the examples, but the same design works in Go, Python, or Java.

Step 1: Define what you meter

The most common mistake is metering everything. Start with a short list of billable or limit-relevant units. For an automation product, that might be:

Metric key What it counts Typical use
workflow.run Completed workflow executions Plan limits, billing
message.sent Outbound messages across channels Billing, abuse detection
api.request Authenticated API calls Rate limits, analytics
ai.tokens LLM tokens consumed Cost pass-through
seat.active Active users in the last 30 days Seat-based pricing

Two rules keep this list healthy:

  1. Every metric has an owner and a purpose. If nobody uses it for billing, limits, or product decisions, don't collect it.
  2. Metric keys are an API. Once customers see them on invoices or dashboards, renaming them is a breaking change.

Step 2: Design a tenant-safe event schema

Every usage event should be a small, immutable record. The schema below works for almost any product:

CREATE TABLE usage_events (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id     UUID        NOT NULL,
  metric        TEXT        NOT NULL,
  quantity      BIGINT      NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  idempotency_key TEXT      NOT NULL,
  occurred_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  metadata      JSONB       NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  UNIQUE (tenant_id, idempotency_key)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_usage_events_tenant_metric_time
  ON usage_events (tenant_id, metric, occurred_at DESC);

Why it looks this way:

  • tenant_id is NOT NULL and leads every index. Every query is tenant-scoped by default.
  • idempotency_key + a unique constraint gives you safe retries. Queues redeliver messages, and without this you will double-count.
  • quantity is a number, not an implied 1. Tokens, bytes, and batch sends all need it.
  • metadata is JSONB for non-billing context such as channel, workflow ID, and region.

For row-level isolation, add Postgres Row-Level Security so a bug in one query can't leak another tenant's data:

ALTER TABLE usage_events ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON usage_events
  USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.current_tenant')::uuid);

Then set app.current_tenant at the start of each request or transaction.

Step 3: Capture usage with API middleware

The goal is to record usage without slowing down the request. Resolve the tenant once, attach it to the request, and emit the event after the response is sent.

// middleware/usage.js
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { recordUsage } from "../usage/recorder.js";

export function trackApiUsage(req, res, next) {
  // tenant is resolved earlier by your auth middleware
  const tenantId = req.tenant?.id;
  if (!tenantId) return next();

  res.on("finish", () => {
    // Only count successful or client-billable requests
    if (res.statusCode >= 500) return;

    recordUsage({
      tenantId,
      metric: "api.request",
      quantity: 1,
      idempotencyKey: req.headers["x-request-id"] ?? randomUUID(),
      metadata: { route: req.route?.path, method: req.method },
    });
  });

  next();
}

For non-HTTP work like background jobs and workflow runs, call the same recordUsage function from the worker:

// workers/runWorkflow.js
await executeWorkflow(job.data);

await recordUsage({
  tenantId: job.data.tenantId,
  metric: "workflow.run",
  quantity: 1,
  // job.id is stable across retries, which makes it a perfect idempotency key
  idempotencyKey: `workflow.run:${job.id}`,
  metadata: { workflowId: job.data.workflowId },
});

Tip: Derive idempotency keys from something that is stable across retries (a job ID, a message ID), never from a timestamp or a fresh random value.

Step 4: Count in Redis, persist in Postgres

Writing one Postgres row per event works until it doesn't. A better pattern is a hot counter in Redis plus a durable event log:

  • Redis answers "how much has this tenant used this month?" in under a millisecond, which is what quota checks need.
  • Postgres is the source of truth for audits, invoices, and recomputation. 
// usage/recorder.js
import Redis from "ioredis";
import { usageQueue } from "./queue.js";

const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL);

const periodKey = (tenantId, metric, date = new Date()) => {
  const period = date.toISOString().slice(0, 7); // e.g. "2026-10"
  return `usage:${tenantId}:${metric}:${period}`;
};

export async function recordUsage(event) {
  const { tenantId, metric, quantity = 1 } = event;

  // 1. Hot path: atomic increment (microseconds)
  const key = periodKey(tenantId, metric);
  await redis.incrby(key, quantity);
  await redis.expire(key, 60 * 60 * 24 * 40); // keep ~40 days

  // 2. Durable path: hand off to a queue for batched persistence
  await usageQueue.add("persist", event, {
    attempts: 5,
    backoff: { type: "exponential", delay: 1000 },
    removeOnComplete: true,
  });
}

The consumer batches inserts and relies on the unique constraint for deduplication:

// usage/persist.js
import { pool } from "../db.js";

export async function persistBatch(events) {
  const values = [];
  const placeholders = events.map((e, i) => {
    const o = i * 6;
    values.push(
      e.tenantId, e.metric, e.quantity,
      e.idempotencyKey, e.occurredAt ?? new Date(), JSON.stringify(e.metadata ?? {})
    );
    return `($${o + 1}, $${o + 2}, $${o + 3}, $${o + 4}, $${o + 5}, $${o + 6})`;
  });

  await pool.query(
    `INSERT INTO usage_events
       (tenant_id, metric, quantity, idempotency_key, occurred_at, metadata)
     VALUES ${placeholders.join(",")}
     ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, idempotency_key) DO NOTHING`,
    values
  );
}

Keep Redis and Postgres honest

Redis counters can drift if a process crashes between the INCRBY and the queue write. Run a nightly reconciliation job that recomputes totals from Postgres and overwrites the Redis counters:

SELECT tenant_id, metric, SUM(quantity) AS total
FROM usage_events
WHERE occurred_at >= date_trunc('month', now())
GROUP BY tenant_id, metric;

Postgres wins every disagreement. Redis is a fast cache, not a ledger.

Step 5: Expose usage through an API

Customers (and your own dashboard) need to read usage. Pre-aggregate into daily rollups so charts stay fast as the event table grows:

CREATE TABLE usage_daily (
  tenant_id UUID NOT NULL,
  metric    TEXT NOT NULL,
  day       DATE NOT NULL,
  total     BIGINT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, metric, day)
);

-- Run hourly; safe to re-run
INSERT INTO usage_daily (tenant_id, metric, day, total)
SELECT tenant_id, metric, occurred_at::date, SUM(quantity)
FROM usage_events
WHERE occurred_at >= now() - interval '2 days'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ON CONFLICT (tenant_id, metric, day)
DO UPDATE SET total = EXCLUDED.total;

Then a tenant-scoped endpoint:

// routes/usage.js
router.get("/v1/usage", async (req, res) => {
  const { metric, from, to } = req.query;

  const { rows } = await pool.query(
    `SELECT day, total
       FROM usage_daily
      WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND metric = $2 AND day BETWEEN $3 AND $4
      ORDER BY day`,
    [req.tenant.id, metric, from, to]
  );

  res.json({ metric, data: rows });
});

Notice that tenant_id comes from req.tenant, never from a query parameter. This is the single most important rule in multi-tenant APIs.

Step 6: Enforce quotas

With a fast counter you can enforce plan limits at the edge of your API:

// middleware/quota.js
const PLAN_LIMITS = {
  free:   { "workflow.run": 1_000 },
  growth: { "workflow.run": 50_000 },
};

export function enforceQuota(metric) {
  return async (req, res, next) => {
    const limit = PLAN_LIMITS[req.tenant.plan]?.[metric];
    if (limit === undefined) return next(); // unlimited

    const used = Number(await redis.get(periodKey(req.tenant.id, metric))) || 0;

    res.set("X-Usage-Limit", String(limit));
    res.set("X-Usage-Remaining", String(Math.max(limit - used, 0)));

    if (used >= limit) {
      return res.status(429).json({
        error: "quota_exceeded",
        message: `Monthly limit for ${metric} reached.`,
      });
    }
    next();
  };
}

Two design choices worth making deliberately:

  • Soft vs. hard limits. Many products warn at 80%, notify at 100%, and block only well past the limit. Hard blocking an automation tenant mid-run can be worse than the overage.
  • Expose remaining quota in headers. Developers integrating with your API will thank you.

Common pitfalls

  1. Time zones. Store everything in UTC and decide up front what "month" means for billing. Per-tenant billing anchors cause real pain later.
  2. Double counting on retries. If your idempotency key isn't stable, your invoices will be wrong.
  3. Noisy-neighbor writes. One tenant's spike shouldn't delay everyone's metering. Use per-tenant rate limits and queue partitioning if needed.
  4. Unbounded metadata cardinality. Don't put user IDs or full URLs in labels you plan to group by.
  5. No backfill story. Keep raw events long enough to recompute totals when you fix a bug.
  6. Metering in the request path synchronously. If Postgres hiccups, your API shouldn't go down with it.

Conclusion

A reliable usage metering system doesn't need a heavyweight platform. The core ideas are:

  • Meter a small, intentional set of metrics
  • Make every event tenant-scoped and idempotent
  • Count fast in Redis, store durably in Postgres, and reconcile regularly
  • Serve dashboards from daily rollups
  • Enforce quotas with clear headers and graceful limits

We went through this exact process while building multi-channel automation at Botsailor, where per-tenant message and workflow volumes vary wildly. Getting the event schema right early saved us from a painful migration later.

Your turn: how do you handle usage metering in your SaaS: build it in-house, or use a billing platform? Share your approach in the comments.

title: Algolia joins the Vercel Marketplace
description:
You can now provision and manage Algolia directly from the Vercel Marketplace.

Algolia is a hosted search platform. You send it your content, it builds an index, and your app queries that index instead of your database. Results come back in milliseconds, with typo tolerance, synonyms, and facet counts built in.

Key capabilities:

  • Index product catalogs, documentation, or any other content

  • Add recommendations and AI ranking to surface the most relevant results

  • Point the Algolia Crawler at a Vercel domain to index your site automatically

  • Build search interfaces with Algolia's InstantSearch libraries

Installing adds your Algolia credentials to your project's environment variables; redeploy to pick them up. Algolia's agent skills install too, so your coding agent knows how to use the API out of the box.

Install Algolia on the Vercel Marketplace or with the Vercel CLI: vc i algolia.

title: X-Dubbing: Speech-to-Speech Translation under Temporal and Visual Constraints
description:
arXiv:2610.32042v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cross-lingual dubbing aims to convert source speech into target-language speech that remains synchronized with the original video. The key to this task is to produce a faithful translation that is naturally speakable within the source timing, which is non-trivial because languages differ in duration, rhythm, and articulation. In this paper, we propose X-Dubbing, which formulates the task as a joint problem of time-aware speech-to-text translation and video-aware text-to-speech. Specifically, our method consists of a Dubbing Translator that generates temporally structured scripts and a Voice Actor that renders them in synchrony with the source video, both grounded in a language-agnostic timing budget. We further refine the translator with dubbing-aware feedback from the synthesized speech, encouraging scripts that yield well-synchronized dubbing. This design requires no paired dubbing data, as the two components are trained on speech-text and monolingual audio-visual data respectively. Extensive experiments show that X-Dubbing outperforms recent baselines across diverse metrics, including isochrony and audio-visual correspondence.

title: Watermarking Diffusion Language Models with Learned Foresight and Balanced Bands
description:
arXiv:2610.32205v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Green-red watermarks favor tokens from a green list that a secret key derives from the preceding tokens. Diffusion language models, however, often choose a token before its preceding tokens, and the token later shapes its neighbors' green lists. Prior work therefore tilts each choice to raise the expected number of green tokens at its own and its neighbors' positions. Building on this objective, we first learn two components that prior work keeps fixed: vocabulary bands that serve as green lists, separate competing candidates and keep the null distribution exact, and a foresight predictor that estimates how each candidate shifts its neighbors' predictions. Second, we count green tokens as the detector does, once per distinct context-token pair, so repetition earns nothing. On WaterBench with LLaDA-8B-Instruct, each learned component raises the z-score at equal distortion, and their gains are nearly additive. With a strong watermark, ours detects at least 96% of responses at a 1% false-positive rate while matching the LLM-judge score of unwatermarked text. Ours also detects more responses on Dream and as many or more on code and question answering without a significant loss in task accuracy.

title: Profile-Driven User Simulation via Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Rewards for Task-Oriented Dialogues
description:
arXiv:2610.32435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Building Task-Oriented Dialogue (TOD) systems for high-value scenarios such as financial marketing requires large volumes of domain-specific dialogue data, which privacy regulations, annotation costs, and the need for expert labor make hard to obtain. User simulation offers a remedy, but existing methods target general-domain dialogue and exhibit two key limitations: insufficient modeling of domain-specific business processes and compliance constraints, and inadequate capture of the colloquial, spoken-language character of voice interactions. We propose ProfileSim, a profile-driven user simulation framework for financial marketing outbound calls. It jointly models user profiles---demographics and Big Five personality traits---and business profiles---intents reverse-engineered from real call logs---enabling fine-grained control over simulated behavior. The base model is fine-tuned on real voice dialogue data and refined by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with hierarchical rewards at the dialogue and utterance levels. Paired with a customer service agent integrating Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) constraints and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), ProfileSim achieves the highest colloquial naturalness, the strongest user profile adherence and the lowest agent score on long-tail intents among all evaluated user generators, while producing substantially shorter user utterances at comparable business compliance. The generated dialogue data is designed to support intent recognition training, agent evaluation, and rapid cold-start deployment.

title: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization
description:
arXiv:2610.32127v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a key technique for efficiently deploying large language models, as it compresses weights into low-bit representations without retraining. Existing PTQ solvers, including GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent, commit each weight block to a single codeword before its neighbors are considered, leaving near-optimal alternatives unexplored. In this work, we cast row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks, in which existing solvers correspond to a zero-temperature, hard-decision limit retaining only the top codeword per block. We propose Message-Passing Quantization (MPQ), which preserves soft posterior information across blocks during inference and commits to hard codewords only at the output stage. MPQ first uses vector approximate message passing to compute approximate blockwise posteriors, then refines a hard-decision initialization by exact block coordinate descent. Across 2-bit lattice and 3- and 4-bit scalar quantization on dense language models from Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, MPQ improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over strong hard-decision baselines, and composes favorably with preprocessing techniques such as activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/MPQ.

title: Deployments now show build cache size
description:
Deployment summaries now show the size of the build cache each deployment saved and how close it is to the limit for its build machine. The same information is in the CLI with vercel inspect on version 65.1.0 or newer, and in the get-deployment REST API endpoint.

Uploading the build cache is billable build time, and a cache that goes over the limit is discarded, so the next build starts without one.

This is on by default on all plans for deployments built on or after October 21. See the maximum build cache size for each build machine in the docs.

title: Can Test-Time Memory Evolution Outperform Test-Time Training for Scientific Discovery?
description:
arXiv:2610.32046v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent \emph{test-time training} (TTT) frameworks have enabled open-weight large language models (LLMs) to outperform inference-only frameworks powered by frontier models on scientific discovery tasks. However, TTT introduces additional computational cost for online weight updates during the discovery process, making computational efficiency an important consideration when scaling to larger models. This motivates us to explore an efficient \emph{test-time adaptation} method for scientific discovery. We introduce \emph{Test-Time Memory Evolution} (TTME), a plug-and-play test-time adaptation method, as an alternative to TTT. TTME continually updates the external memory by distilling the experience to guide subsequent discovery without updating model weights. To have a clean comparison, we evaluate TTME and TTT under the same discovery framework, replacing only the test-time adaptation method. Our evaluation shows that TTME outperforms TTT on all five mathematical tasks, while reducing computational cost by $82.8$-$84.6\%$ in FLOPs and $47.7$-$58.4\%$ in runtime. These results establish TTME as an effective and computationally efficient alternative to TTT in the evaluated discovery settings.

title: Multi-Class Log Loss Explained: Math, MLE & Python Code
description:
A comprehensive technical guide to Multi-Class Logarithmic Loss (Log Loss / Categorical Cross-Entropy): why lower loss indicates superior probabilistic calibration, how Maximum Likelihood Estimation requires the negative sign, why logarithms prevent floating-point underflow on large datasets, and how asymmetric penalties punish overconfident mispredictions.

1 · The Mathematical Formula & Variable Definitions

For a dataset containing N samples evaluated across C mutually exclusive classes, Multi-Class Logarithmic Loss is defined as:

$$L = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{c=1}^C y_{i,c} \ln(p_{i,c})$$

Every symbol and variable in this formulation serves a distinct mathematical role:

Symbol / Variable Domain / Value Formal Definition & Mathematical Purpose
N Positive integer Total number of observations or samples in the evaluation dataset.
C Integer $\ge 2$ Total number of discrete candidate classes in the classification task.
y_{i,c} {0, 1} Binary one-hot indicator: equals 1 if observation i belongs to class c, and 0 otherwise.
p_{i,c} (0.0, 1.0) Model's predicted probability that observation i belongs to class c, where $\sum_c p_{i,c} = 1.0$.
\ln Mathematical operator The natural logarithm (base $e \approx 2.71828$). In information theory, base 2 is often used, measuring loss in bits.

2 · Why is Lower Better?

In statistical learning, loss functions quantify the divergence between prediction and reality. Multi-class log loss is strictly lower is better due to two fundamental conventions:

  • The Target Value (Zero Loss): A theoretically perfect model assigns a probability of exactly 1.0 to the true class and 0.0 to all other classes. Because $\ln(1.0) = 0$, the resulting log loss for a perfect prediction is exactly 0.0. As predictions become less certain or more erroneous, the loss value grows toward positive infinity.
  • Minimization Convention in Optimization: Machine learning algorithms (such as stochastic gradient descent, Adam, or tree splitting criteria) are designed to minimize an objective cost function. Formulating log loss so that 0 represents perfection allows standard gradient descent algorithms to iteratively step downhill toward minimum error.

3 · Why the Negative Sign? From MLE to Gradient Descent

The negative sign at the front of the formula is required by the mathematical relationship between probabilities and logarithms:

  • Probabilities are Fractions Less Than or Equal to 1: Valid probabilities p satisfy $0 < p \le 1$. The natural logarithm of any fraction between 0 and 1 is strictly negative (for example, $\ln(0.5) \approx -0.693$, and $\ln(0.1) \approx -2.302$).
  • Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE): In classical statistics, generative and discriminative models are trained by maximizing the likelihood of observing the training data: $\max \prod_i P(y_i \mid x_i)$. Taking the natural logarithm converts this into maximizing the log-likelihood: $\max \sum_i \ln(P(y_i \mid x_i))$.
  • Flipping Maximization into Minimization: Because log-likelihood is negative, multiplying by -1 flips the sign from negative to positive. Maximizing the positive likelihood of the data is mathematically identical to minimizing the Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL). The negative sign transforms statistical MLE into a convex loss surface that gradient descent can minimize.

4 · Why the Need for a Logarithm?

The logarithm is not an arbitrary mathematical choice; it solves two practical challenges in computation and model calibration:

1. Converting Products into Sums (Preventing Numerical Underflow)

Assuming independent data points, the joint probability of an entire dataset is the product of individual probabilities:

$$P_{\text{joint}} = P_1 \times P_2 \times \dots \times P_N$$

When multiplying thousands of floating-point numbers smaller than 1.0 (such as $0.8^{1000}$), the result approaches zero so quickly that standard 64-bit IEEE floating-point numbers experience arithmetic underflow (the computer rounds the value to absolute zero).

Applying the logarithm exploits the logarithmic identity $\ln(a \cdot b) = \ln(a) + \ln(b)$. This transforms product chains into numerically stable sums of negative numbers that CPUs can accumulate without precision loss.

2. Penalty Amplification for Overconfident Mistakes

The logarithmic curve acts as an asymmetric penalty amplifier. Because $\lim_{p \to 0} \ln(p) = -\infty$, the loss penalty escalates steeply as the predicted probability for the true class approaches zero:

Predicted Probability for True Class p_{true} Instance Log Loss Penalty -\ln(p_{true}) Practical Model Diagnosis
0.99 0.01005 Near-perfect prediction with high confidence.
0.80 0.22314 Accurate prediction with moderate certainty.
0.50 0.69315 Uncertain coin-flip assignment.
0.10 2.30259 Significant error: model favored alternative classes.
0.01 4.60517 Severe mistake: model was 99% confident in wrong classes.
0.0001 9.21034 Catastrophic penalty: one such prediction can wreck a batch average.

5 · Worked Numerical Example: 3-Class Animal Classifier

Consider a 3-class image classification model evaluating an image containing a Cat across three possible categories: [Cat, Dog, Bird].

  • True Ground Truth Label: y = [1, 0, 0] (Class 0 is Cat).
  • Baseline Model Prediction: p = [0.80, 0.10, 0.10].

Applying the multi-class formula for this single sample:

$$\text{Loss} = - [ 1 \cdot \ln(0.80) + 0 \cdot \ln(0.10) + 0 \cdot \ln(0.10) ]$$
$$\text{Loss} = - [ -0.22314 + 0 + 0 ] = \mathbf{0.22314}$$

Now consider two alternative prediction scenarios on the exact same sample:

Scenario A: High-Confidence Correct Prediction

The model predicts P(Cat) = 0.95, P(Dog) = 0.03, P(Bird) = 0.02:

$$\text{Loss} = -\ln(0.95) \approx \mathbf{0.05129} \quad (\text{Lower is better})$$

Scenario B: Confident Mistake (Misclassified as Dog)

The model erroneously predicts that the animal is a Dog with 90% confidence, leaving only P(Cat) = 0.05:

$$\text{Loss} = -\ln(0.05) \approx \mathbf{2.99573} \quad (\text{Over 13x higher penalty than baseline})$$

Because the logarithm curves sharply toward infinity near zero, a single confident misprediction in Scenario B produces a penalty larger than twenty accurate predictions combined.

6 · Robust Python Implementation (NumPy & PyTorch)

In software engineering, implementing -np.log(p) directly is dangerous: if the model outputs a probability of exactly 0.0, np.log(0.0) produces -inf, poisoning the entire dataset score with NaN. To prevent this, standard implementations clip probabilities by an epsilon threshold (typically 1e-15):

import numpy as np

def multiclass_log_loss(y_true, y_pred, eps=1e-15):
    # Clip probabilities to [eps, 1 - eps]
    y_pred_clipped = np.clip(y_pred, eps, 1.0 - eps)

    # Renormalize rows so probabilities sum strictly to 1.0
    y_pred_clipped = y_pred_clipped / y_pred_clipped.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

    # Compute cross-entropy across all elements, normalized by sample count N
    loss = -np.sum(y_true * np.log(y_pred_clipped)) / y_true.shape[0]
    return float(loss)

# Verification with sample data
y_true = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0]])
y_pred = np.array([[0.80, 0.10, 0.10], [0.05, 0.90, 0.05]])
print(f"Log Loss: {multiclass_log_loss(y_true, y_pred):.5f}")
# Output: 0.16425

PyTorch Equivalent

In deep learning frameworks like PyTorch, nn.CrossEntropyLoss combines LogSoftmax and NLLLoss into a single numerically stable fused kernel, operating directly on unnormalized model logits:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Raw unnormalized model logits for 2 samples across 3 classes
logits = torch.tensor([[2.0, 0.5, 0.1], [-1.0, 3.2, 0.4]])

# Ground truth class indices (Class 0, Class 1)
targets = torch.tensor([0, 1])

criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
loss = criterion(logits, targets)
print(f"PyTorch Loss: {loss.item():.5f}")

7 · Practical Takeaways for Machine Learning Competitions

When competing on Kaggle or deploying probability models in production (such as our ongoing investigation in Pocket Data Science IX on Chatbot Arena LLM Evaluation), log loss demands distinct strategic behaviors:

  • Never Predict Absolute Certainty: Unless a physical law guarantees an outcome, never predict 1.0 or 0.0. If an outlier or annotation ambiguity reverses the label, a single zero probability will result in infinite loss.
  • Prior-Based Initialization: Initializing model biases or baseline logits to the natural logarithm of training class frequencies $\ln(p_c)$ guarantees optimal default calibration, preventing severe penalties on ambiguous queries.
  • Temperature & Platt Scaling: When ensembling deep learning models or tree-based boosters, apply post-processing probability calibration (such as temperature scaling or isotonic regression) to prevent overconfident softmax peaks.

title: When the browser doesn't tell you the keyboard is open
description:
Our bottom sheets worked everywhere we tested: Chrome, Samsung Internet, Firefox, Safari. Then we tried the default browser of a budget Redmi phone: the sign-in sheet sat under the on-screen keyboard, and the password field was invisible.

What was going on

The phone's default browser is a thin shell over Android System WebView. Since Android 15, apps that target SDK 35 are drawn edge-to-edge by default, and adjustResize no longer shrinks the window unless the app handles insets itself. Many small browser shells don't. So when the keyboard opens, the page gets nothing:

  • no resize on window;
  • no resize on visualViewport, and its height stays the same;
  • navigator.virtualKeyboard doesn't exist.

There is nothing to listen to. The keyboard covers the bottom 40% of the screen, and the page has no idea.

The fix: assume the worst after a short wait

If we can't detect the keyboard, we can detect that the browser failed to report it. A text field gets focus; on a phone, that almost always means the keyboard is coming. Wait a bit. If the visible height hasn't dropped, the browser is silent, and we move the sheet to the top of the screen, where the keyboard can't reach it.

(() => {
  const vv = window.visualViewport;
  // iOS reports the keyboard in every browser, and a script-focused field
  // doesn't raise it there, so the sheet would jump for nothing
  if (!vv || CSS.supports('-webkit-touch-callout', 'none')) return;
  const phone = matchMedia('(max-width:599px) and (pointer:coarse)');
  // full height = the largest we've seen; reset on rotation
  let full = vv.height;
  vv.addEventListener('resize', () => { full = Math.max(full, vv.height); });
  matchMedia('(orientation:portrait)')
    .addEventListener?.('change', () => { full = vv.height; });

  const field = el => el?.matches?.(
    'input:not([type=checkbox],[type=radio],[type=hidden]),textarea');
  const sheet = el => el?.closest?.('dialog.sheet[open]');

  document.addEventListener('focusin', e => {
    const d = sheet(e.target);
    if (!d || !field(e.target) || !phone.matches) return;
    setTimeout(() => {
      if (document.activeElement === e.target && vv.height > full * 0.85)
        d.classList.add('kb-top');
    }, 600);
  });
  document.addEventListener('focusout', e => {
    const d = sheet(e.target);
    // moving between fields of the same sheet keeps it on top
    if (d && !(sheet(e.relatedTarget) === d && field(e.relatedTarget)))
      d.classList.remove('kb-top');
  });
})();

.kb-top just flips the sheet: top: 0; bottom: auto, rounded corners at the bottom instead of the top, and swipe-to-close disabled, since there is nowhere to swipe it.

Why these numbers

  • 600 ms. Long enough for the keyboard animation to finish and for browsers that do report it to fire resize. Short enough that the person hasn't started typing blind.
  • 85%. A real keyboard takes 35–50% of a portrait screen. Toolbar show/hide changes the height by 5–10%. Anything above 85% of the full height means "no keyboard reported".
  • The largest height seen, not the current one. Opening the page with the address bar visible and then scrolling changes the baseline, so we keep the maximum.

This runs on Kinomig, a free movie site that a lot of people open on budget Android phones. If you've seen another browser that stays silent about the keyboard, I'd like to hear which one.

title: Design full test-space scenarios at once and delegate precised evidence-based exploratory testing to your AI
description:
You Can’t List Your Unknown Bugs, but You Can Model What Varies.

Combinatorics-Framework-JVM turns a model of settings, action histories and optional events into planned test cases, and keeps the experiment inspectable from design through evidence.

⚡️ Straight to the point for most impatient/busy-reader who respects human's work (let your AI read 'AI_DELEGATION.md' after dowloading the release, and it will answer you live): Combinatorics-Framework-JVM

“What kinds of bugs does my system under test have?”

It sounds like the obvious first question for any testing tool. It’s also the wrong one. If you could answer it, you’d already have the tests.

The defects that hurt are the ones nobody knew to name: a guest, a coupon and a repeated payment request, each fine alone and wrong together. AI coding assistants sharpen the problem. An assistant can implement the feature, generate the unit tests and explain why the code should work. It can’t tell you which interactions those tests exercised.

So don’t start from bugs. Start from three questions you can answer:

  • What varies? Settings, inputs, the order of actions, events that may or may not happen.
  • What must stay true? An invariant, such as “the same payment request creates at most one charge.”
  • How much am I willing to run? A bounded budget of cases you can actually inspect.

Bugs aren’t the input to that exercise. They’re the output.

Investigation, not diagnosis

Combinatorics-Framework-JVM is built for exactly that kind of investigational testing: a Java workbench with a desktop app (guif), a command line and an embedding API. You describe the variations, it generates test candidates, runs them through your configured runners and helps you examine the results. State a model, run a bounded experiment, read the evidence, refine the model, repeat.

It won’t discover unknown defects for you. It turns a test idea into a visible model, a bounded run and results another engineer can inspect.

Model the context, and the history

Take a small checkout:

What varies Choices
Customer Guest, registered
Payment method Card, wallet, cash on delivery
Channel Website, API
Pricing policy Current price, price captured earlier

That’s 24 static combinations. Run them all. Now add history: submit, time out, retry, a price change at different moments. The input values barely changed. The history did, and no parameter table shows it.

So the Framework models three kinds of variation separately:

  • Static context: account type, payment method, feature flags. Covering selection can reduce this part to a declared interaction strength.
  • Action sequences: what happens first, next and again, including order and repetition.
  • Sudden or optional events: a timeout, a duplicate request, a price change, including when it strikes and the case where it never does.

Sequences and sudden events are then crossed with every selected context, not squeezed into the same matrix. That stops you from flattening everything into interchangeable parameters and assuming you tested the histories that matter. For a workflow bug, the timeline deserves more attention than a big parameter matrix.

Constraints need the same care. An impossible combination can be excluded. A valid input the application should reject (cash on delivery over the API, say) deserves a negative test, not a deletion. The modeler decides which question a test answers. The generator can’t.

A model you can read in one minute

Two modes, three actions. Every candidate gets one mode and two different actions in a chosen order (AB, BA, AC, CA, BC, CB): 2 × 6 = 12 candidates. Save this as first-scenario.json:

{
  "spec_version": "1",
  "title": "Two modes and ordered pairs of actions",
  "slots": [
    {
      "sheet": "MODE",
      "alias": "choose_one",
      "raw": true,
      "values": ["safe", "fast"]
    },
    {
      "sheet": "OPS",
      "alias": "permute(2)",
      "flags": ["FW_Concatenator="],
      "raw": true,
      "values": ["A", "B", "C"]
    }
  ]
}

And these settings as first-scenario.properties:

cf.coverage.strength=0
cf.coverage.budget=0
cf.plan.autoPromoteSingleVerb=true

Then, with JDK 25 and fw-app.jar in your working folder:

java -Djava.awt.headless=true -jar fw-app.jar validate --scenario first-scenario.json --config first-scenario.properties
java -Djava.awt.headless=true -jar fw-app.jar plan --scenario first-scenario.json --config first-scenario.properties
java -Djava.awt.headless=true -jar fw-app.jar candidates --scenario first-scenario.json --config first-scenario.properties --limit 12

Validate, inspect the plan, read the candidates, all before anything runs. These are plain-text candidates for learning the model, not programs to execute.

Prefer spreadsheets? The classic workbook style (data sheets plus an FW_Seq control sheet) expresses the same model, and the wizard in guif guides a first scenario.

When order is the bug

A basic retry test submits a request twice with the same key and confirms that one order exists. Now change the history: the provider accepts the first request, its response times out, a confirmation arrives while the client is retrying, and the client tries again. Is there still exactly one charge and one order?

A small timeline model might include these histories:

History Events the harness controls
A Submit → success → retry the same request
B Submit → timeout → retry → confirmation
C Submit → timeout → confirmation → retry
D Submit → timeout → retry → retry → confirmation

The invariant: reusing a request key must never create a second charge or a second order. Check durable business state (charges, orders, how they relate), not just the final HTTP status.

One honest boundary: the Framework generates ordered choices, permutations, repetitions and optional events. It doesn’t control a thread scheduler or a remote payment provider. Your adapter has to make those events controllable: hold and release a callback, simulate a timeout, reset state. Once it does, you vary the histories without hand-copying a test method for every combination.

A planted defect, caught

(quick self-test)
You don’t have to take this on faith. The project’s manual ships a self-contained checkout demo whose stand-in system has a deliberately planted lost-order defect. validate, plan and candidates report 72 generated cases, 24 removed by one constraint and 48 executable. The full run ends with 44 PASS and 4 DOMAIN_FAIL, with no harness failures. The repo’s validation report records this on JDK 25 and a 0.1.0-SNAPSHOT build.

A larger showcase in the manual runs 4,128 generated Cucumber scenarios against an in-JVM checkout engine and 714 browser scenarios (Selenium, headless Firefox) against a dummy web shop, both with planted defects hiding in action order and event timing. A second run of each design gave the same verdict for every case.

Two things to notice:

  • A run that finds defects still exits with code 0. A failure is a result, not a crash, so read the verdicts. Keep product failures (DOMAIN_FAIL) apart from harness outcomes such as BROKEN, TIMEOUT and INFRA_FAIL.
  • Every defect here was planted. That shows the harness can see a fault, not that it finds ones nobody knows about. It’s why the manual says to calibrate the oracle with a known-failing case before trusting a model. The unknown bugs are what the experiment is for.

What comes back

Failures arrive as cases, not red lights: the candidate, its verdict, its measurements and the context to reproduce it. Checkpoints and exports keep the evidence, and triage groups failures into findings with representative witnesses. The documented “minimal witness” is the failing case with the least source in its group: a good place to start, not a proven mathematical minimum. Values associated with elevated failure rates are leads, not causes.

When nothing fails, you still get something: “within this model, at this strength, no violation observed.” That isn’t proof of absence. It’s a claim another engineer can inspect, challenge and extend.

What you bring, and what it doesn’t promise

The Framework generates and organizes. You make it real. The model and the invariant are yours: it doesn’t discover what must stay true (a far easier question than “what is broken?”, but not a free one). You also bring:

  • An adapter that connects candidates to your system and controls its state and dependencies.
  • An oracle: assertions that encode the invariant. A generated case without a meaningful check is just activity.
  • A controlled environment with a reset strategy, plus the judgment about which failures matter and what went untested.

And be honest about the limits:

  • Pairwise isn’t magic. It covers pairs of modeled values, not every three-way defect, action order or timing failure, and the selection is greedy, so it never claims a minimum suite. With fewer than three varying factors, every pair is already the whole space and nothing is reduced. Its value is that you can state what you selected and inspect it.
  • One verdict per case. The first failing check names the verdict and hides later ones, so report every check as a metric too.
  • No OS sandbox for Java. Java cases run inside the Framework’s own JVM with your permissions, so treat every run as code execution on your machine: use a dedicated workspace and keep production out until the adapter, assertions and side effects are clear. Python cases run as separate processes and can be sandboxed with bwrap or Docker.

The same machinery, for AI experiments

Prompts × retrieval strategies × thresholds is a combinatorial space too. Three retrieval strategies, two prompts and two thresholds make 12 configurations. Evaluate each on 50 questions, twice: 1,200 evaluations, not 12. Mind that arithmetic when a provider bills per request.

Multi-goal analysis, including a Pareto front, keeps cost and quality trade-offs visible instead of collapsing them into one early score. It describes what you measured, not the best system that could exist. Bring an evaluation method you trust, because there is no universal judge of LLM answers, and test the evaluator with a deliberately wrong answer. Generation is deterministic; a remote model isn’t, so record versions, settings and rate limits.

Hand your assistant an experiment, not a vibe

The model and the recorded evidence are files, so a second engineer, or a later assistant session, can pick them up without reconstructing a chat. Give your assistant evidence, not a symptom:

Here is the failing candidate (submit → timeout → retry → confirmation) and the two charge IDs it returned. The invariant is one request key, at most one charge. Propose a mechanism that fits this evidence, a focused change, and which existing cases would distinguish your explanation from the alternatives.

That asks for a testable claim instead of a guessed fix. Then rerun the same candidate and its surrounding histories against the change: if a repair fixes one sequence and breaks another, the regression stays visible.

The repo is built for this hand-off. The manual, AI_DELEGATION.md, is written for an AI operator acting for a human supervisor, and the desktop’s AI_delegation button copies its path for you to paste. Copying a path isn’t consent. The manual’s first rule is no agreement, no operation: the assistant needs your explicit yes, then must ask before it finalizes the design, executes any case (a smoke run comes first), builds or installs anything, or touches the network, files outside the agreed workspace or your system under test. It must report what it did and didn’t check, and never present a plausible explanation as an observed result. You stay the director, and the license makes that a condition.

Try it small

  • Pick a behavior you already understand, ideally a defect you’ve already fixed.
  • Write three or four factors, one troublesome sequence and one invariant.
  • Stay small enough to preview every candidate, and change one thing at a time.
  • Inject a fault into a local implementation. Does the scenario catch it? Fix it and rerun.
  • Save the scenario, run ID, checkpoint and evidence.

If you can express the behavior, understand the generated cases and recognize a useful failure, it fits. The manual itself rates a few situations as poor fits: one or two parameters, purely continuous spaces, no reliable oracle, and state you can’t reset. Use unit or property tests, fuzzing or an optimizer there, and keep the plain unit test whenever it already pins a defect down. Reach for a scenario model when the variations themselves are getting hard to track.

Requirements, status and license

  • First of all: AS IS..., no warranty
  • Requirements: JDK 25, a full JDK with the compiler rather than a bare JRE, because generated cases are compiled in memory. The core workflow needs no Python, no relational database and no containers. Python 3.11+ and the Python add-on are optional, for Python candidates.
  • Status: first public release (Oct 2026), one maintainer. It’s early-stage, so validate it on your own workload before it carries anything critical.

The case for it is specific. Interacting settings, action sequences and timed events get one shared model, the model becomes inspectable candidates, and the results stay available for review and retesting. For the bugs that live between individually working features, and for AI-assisted work that needs evidence rather than confidence, that’s worth a small trial.

Don’t ask it where your bugs are. Tell it what varies and what must stay true, then read what comes back.

P.S. You are a Scenario Test-space Architect/Designer (puzzle-items of any kind) and a supervisor of AI (who operates on "Combinatorics Framework" as a precise tool for all of these)

title: RootDown: Deploying and Benchmarking Models for Beet-Root Detection on Edge Devices
description:
arXiv:2610.32275v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quality inspection of sugar beets after harvest and storage is critical to preserve sugar content and ensure optimal processing efficiency. The transfer of harvested beets to field clamps or trucks provides an opportunity to visually inspect individual beets automatically on loader conveyors. However, this is a challenging task as the large number of beets causes partial overlap and occlusion, complicating both annotation and detection. In this work, we propose an end-to-end image-based pipeline for detecting partially occluded sugar beets in loading scenarios as a first step toward automated quality inspection. We introduce a dedicated benchmark and present an automatic annotation strategy that leverages the SAM 3 foundation model to generate bounding boxes. We compare models trained on manually annotated and automatically generated labels. Additionally, we investigate deployment considerations by benchmarking multiple inference configurations, including execution on an edge device, under realistic operational constraints regarding precision, inference time and power consumption. Our results show that, despite substantial occlusion and inherent annotation ambiguity, foundation-model-based labels can substitute for a substantial share of manual annotation, trading labeling effort for data volume at a modest accuracy cost. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a Raspberry Pi 5 equipped with a Hailo accelerator enables high-performance, low-power inference, making it a practical solution for mobile outdoor deployment.
