title: Neural Disjunctive Normal Forms for Learning Exact Rank Filters
description:
arXiv:2610.32203v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gradient-based learning of morphological operators is hindered by locally sparse derivatives with respect to the structuring elements. We develop a method for learning rank filters that retains exact operator evaluation while distributing the derivatives across the window. Using threshold decomposition, we construct a neural disjunctive normal form representation and establish a sufficient condition for exactness with integer-valued images and structuring elements. We then derive a smooth surrogate from the unique root of a smooth threshold equation. Implicit differentiation gives closed-form derivatives with normalised local weights, whose distribution is controlled by a smoothing parameter. These derivatives are used in a straight-through procedure: the forward pass evaluates the exact rank filter, while the backward pass uses the surrogate. For fixed ranks, the procedure learns real-valued structuring elements of any rank filter, including the median, and extends to compositions, infima, and suprema of rank filters. Experiments on image denoising using MNIST and Fashion-MNIST and retinal vessel segmentation show that, starting from a generic random initialisation, the proposed approach consistently improves performance over training with exact subgradients in every setting. In image denoising, our best network also outperforms smooth morphological networks in all settings. On vessel segmentation, the learned erosions recover structuring elements that fit the vessels, as theoretically expected, whereas most of those trained with exact subgradients remain close to their initialisation.

title: Leaving Railway in an afternoon
description:
Gagarin vs Railway says where Railway is the better
pick. Read that first if you have not decided. This post is for the afternoon
after you have: what you type, in what order, and where you lose time.

The project is a common shape. A web service, a worker that reads the same
database, a Postgres with a few gigabytes in it, and a cron job that runs a
report at three in the morning. Each service has a Dockerfile, because Railway
builds from one when it finds one. If yours build with Nixpacks or Railpack,
budget an hour at the start to write two Dockerfiles. Nothing else here depends
on the shape of your code.

The clock below is a budget for a project this size. Yours will differ by the
size of the dump and the state of your DNS.

13:00: Write down what only Railway knows

Three things live on Railway and not in your repository: the environment
variables, the database, and the schedule. Get all three onto your machine
before you touch anything else.

railway variables --service web --kv > web.env
railway variables --service worker --kv > worker.env

Open both files and sort the lines into three piles. Railway's own:
RAILWAY_*, PORT, and any line that references another service with
${{...}}. Delete those. The database: DATABASE_URL, PGHOST and friends.
Gagarin provides those, so delete them too. Yours: Stripe keys, SMTP passwords,
feature flags. Keep those, and split them: one file per vendor for the
secrets, .env.stripe and .env.smtp, and the plain settings left where they
were, in web.env and worker.env. The reason is in the 14:10 step. For a
project this size you end up with about ten lines across the four files.

The database comes out with the tool it went in with:

railway connect postgres   # in one terminal
pg_dump "$DATABASE_URL" -Fc -f before.dump   # in another

A few gigabytes take ten to fifteen minutes. Copy the cron schedule out of the
Railway dashboard while you wait.

13:30: A project, a database, and the data 

gg login
gg init shop
gg resource add shop/database postgres --size m

gg init prints the project's id. Write it into .gagarin.json at the root
of the repository and commit it, so the next session, yours or an agent's,
knows which project this code is. A Postgres that a real application depends
on starts at size m; s is for one you develop against.

after gg resource add

Name the Postgres database. A resource on Gagarin hands each service that
depends on it a set of variables prefixed with the resource's own name, so one
called database publishes DATABASE_URL, DATABASE_HOST, DATABASE_USER
and the rest. Your code reads DATABASE_URL today. Name the resource after the
variable and your code stays as it is.

The restore goes through a tunnel that lasts as long as the command does:

gg connect shop/database

It prints the same variables a service would hold, rewritten to point at
127.0.0.1, and keeps the tunnel open until you stop it. In another terminal,
paste the printed URL:

pg_restore --no-owner --no-acl -d "postgres://…@127.0.0.1:5432/…" before.dump

Stop gg connect and the tunnel closes. A restore done this way exposed
nothing, so there is nothing to clean up afterwards.

While you are here, gg resource backup shop/database takes a copy now, and
nightly ones follow on their own. A restore on Gagarin always creates a new
resource and never overwrites one, which is why nobody has to approve it at
three in the morning, and the backups outlive the database by fourteen days
if you ever destroy it.

14:10: The variables, then the two services

On Railway your Stripe key is a line in a variables tab. On Gagarin it is a
resource, the same kind of node as the database, and services declare that
they need it:

gg resource add shop/stripe external --env-file .env.stripe
gg resource add shop/smtp external --env-file .env.smtp

An external runs nothing. It holds values and publishes them under its own
name: a .env.stripe with SECRET_KEY in it makes shop/stripe publish
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY. So the split by vendor at 13:00 was also a rename. Strip
the vendor prefix from each key in the file, name the resource after it, and
your code reads the same variable names it read on Railway. The plain settings
in web.env and worker.env have no secret in them and belong to one service
each, so they ride along on the deploy itself.

Now the services. gg ship builds the directory, pushes the image and deploys
it. The number after the colon is the port the container listens on. Railway
sets PORT for you. Gagarin asks you to say it once.

gg ship shop/web:8080 --context ./web --env-file web.env --deps database --deps stripe --deps smtp
gg ship shop/worker:9090 --context ./worker --env-file worker.env --deps database

--deps is the rest of the configuration. Each one opens the route from the
service to the resource and hands the service that resource's variables in one
step. You write no ${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}}, because the reference and the
firewall rule are the same declaration. The worker never sees the Stripe key,
because it did not ask for it.

after the two ships

Every arrow in that drawing is a --deps. Nothing else draws one. An arrow
into the database is a route and a password; an arrow into a key is the key.

gg deps add prints the variable names it handed over, so you never guess
what a service now holds. A later deploy that forgets --deps withdraws
nothing: taking an edge away is its own command and needs your approval,
because it is the one change that breaks something and reports nothing.

When Stripe rotates your key, gg resource rotate shop/stripe --env-file
.env.stripe rolls every service that holds it. No deploy, and no hunt through
services for the ones that had a copy. The values are never copied into a
service's stored environment either, so gg rollback shop/web puts back
yesterday's image and settings and never yesterday's password.

Two habits from Railway to drop here.

Secrets are not deploy arguments. --env-file on a deploy is for a
LOG_LEVEL, and a deploy replaces that file's variables wholesale, so
web.env is committed and restated on each ship. Anything you would mind
seeing in a commit, a shell history or an agent transcript goes in an external
instead, and the graph in the console then shows which services hold it.

Nothing builds on push. Railway watches your branch and builds when it
moves. Gagarin does not build, on purpose, and says why. Your CI
runs gg ship with a credential from gg creds create, which can deploy,
expires, and cannot delete. The secret goes to stdout alone, so it pipes
straight into a CI secret and never touches a disk or a transcript:

gh secret set GAGARIN_TOKEN --body "$(gg creds create --name "github actions: shop" 2>/dev/null)"

For this project the workflow itself is about twenty lines.

14:40: The cron job

On Railway the schedule sits in a service's settings. On Gagarin a scheduled
job is a gg run with a schedule. It is a job rather than a service: it runs to
completion, and nothing can reach it.

gg run shop/report report:v1 --deps database --schedule "0 3 * * *" --tz Europe/Berlin

Nothing runs now, and gg run returns at once. Tomorrow at three, check it with
gg logs shop/report, or open the project in the console at
my.gagarin.cloud, which keeps a feed of how each
firing ended.

Firings never overlap: a report that runs long delays the next one rather than
running beside it. A firing that fails pushes one notification to your phone,
and the next one that succeeds clears it. And a one-off gg run, say a
migration before a deploy, waits and exits with the script's own exit code, so
CI can stop on a failed migration without a line of polling.

14:50: Check it before your users do 

$ gg status shop
project shop  (id k3qm7ebd)

     SERVICE   KIND      SIZE  READY          PORT  REACHES                   IMAGE
  ●  web       service   s     1/1            8080  database, stripe◆, smtp◆  web:1761480212
  ●  └ https://web-k3qm7ebd.apps.gagarin.cloud
  ●  worker    service   s     1/1            9090  database                  worker:1761480250
  ◷  report    job       s     ⏱ 0 3 * * *    —     database                  report:v1
     └ next in 12h
  ●  database  postgres  m     1/1            5432  —                         postgres:17
  ◆  stripe    external  —     —              —     —                         —
  ◆  smtp      external  —     —              —     —                         —

  ● running   ◷ scheduled   ◆ external (runs nothing; declaring it grants its variables, not egress)

The REACHES column is the firewall, printed. The plain edges open a route
inside the project. The diamond edges hand over a key and open nothing, since
anything in a project can already reach the internet. The worker has no
address because nobody asked for one, and it cannot acquire one by accident.

gg is not the only window onto this. The console at
my.gagarin.cloud draws the same project as a live
graph, with each service's status, logs and history beside it, the bill for
the month so far, and the switch that sends a push to your phone when a
service goes down or the report fails at three in the morning. Everything the
console shows is something gg can read, and the drawings in this post are
the console's drawings.

If something is wrong at this point, gg status tends to say what. A
container killed for memory gets a line naming the size to move to. A crash is
in gg logs shop/web, with the crashed container's output kept rather than
lost with the pod, and --since 2h --grep "panic:" narrows it. A deploy you
regret is gg rollback shop/web, one call, recorded as a new revision so the
history keeps the evidence.

The web service already has a generated address. Open it, sign in, and click
through the pages that touch the database. Expect to find one thing of your
own here. Ours was a report that assumed TZ was set, because Railway's base
image set it and our Dockerfile did not. One line in the Dockerfile, one more
gg ship.

15:20: The address 

gg domain add shop/web shop.example.com

It prints the DNS record to create. Make the change at your registrar, and the
certificate arrives once the record resolves. The generated address keeps
working in the meantime, so the service always has a door.

Both addresses answer from then on, and no deploy can ever take either away:
an address is a standing declaration, and forgetting a flag will not remove
one.

the whole project, with an address

One public address, on the one service a browser opens. The worker, the job
and the three resources stay private, and the arrows say who may reach what.

Keep the Railway service running through the DNS change. Lower the TTL on the
record the day before if you can. If you did not, some users reach the old
service for an hour, and the two services write to two different databases
while they do. That hour is the cost of this approach, and the reason the next
step is there.

15:40: Freeze, copy the delta, cut over

For a side project, skip this and lose an hour of writes. For anything with
users, do it.

  1. Put the Railway service into maintenance mode, or scale it to zero.
  2. Dump again and restore again, with the commands from 13:00 and 13:30. The second dump is small.
  3. Flip the DNS record.
  4. Watch gg logs shop/web for a few minutes.

Budget twenty minutes between the freeze and the flip. Most of it is DNS, and
most of that goes away if you lowered the TTL yesterday.

16:30: Keep Railway for a week

Leave the Railway project in place with the service scaled to zero and the
database intact. Idle, it costs close to nothing, and it is the only copy you
have of the state before the move. Gagarin takes its first nightly backup
tonight and keeps fourteen days of them, so by next week you hold a better
copy.

Then delete the Railway project. Railway asks you to confirm in the browser.
Gagarin, should you ever leave in the other direction, refuses a destructive
command until you press a button it emails you, whichever client asked, and
your CI credential cannot ask at all.

Even you cannot destroy the database while a service still declares it: the
refusal names what depends on it. And when you do go, gg eject shop writes
the Kubernetes objects the project runs as, so leaving is a file rather than
a rewrite. The model makes the case for that design. It is
in this post because someone who moved a production database an hour ago cares
a great deal about what can delete things.

The afternoon, totalled

what time commands
inventory, dump 30 min railway variables, pg_dump
project, database, restore 40 min gg init, gg resource add, gg connect
variables, two services 30 min gg resource add ×2, gg ship ×2
cron job 10 min gg run --schedule
checks, one fix 30 min gg status, gg logs, gg ship
address, cutover 70 min gg domain add, the delta dump, DNS

Three and a half hours. One line of code changed, and it fixed a bug you were
already carrying. Two new files in the repository: the CI workflow, and a
.gagarin.json that says which project this is.

You give up builds on push and a second region. You get a graph that is the
firewall and the secrets map at once, traffic that costs
nothing, and a platform where the agent that runs your deploys cannot remove
anything until you press a button.

If you would rather not spend the afternoon yourself, the
coding agent you already use can run the same commands. Paste it the
Railway project name and a link to this post. It will ask you to press a button
once, when it wants to delete the old project.

Sources

  • Railway CLI
  • Railway variables
  • Railway GitHub autodeploys
  • Gagarin vs Railway

title: Release an image preview object URL when its owner removes it
description:
Keep each object URL with the image preview that owns it. Release the URL when that preview is removed and its consumers no longer need it.

Calling URL.revokeObjectURL() releases the object URL created by URL.createObjectURL(). Revoking a URL as soon as it is assigned can be too early if user interactions still need it.

When replacing a preview, give the new preview its own URL and retire the previous one according to the same ownership rule. Include cleanup when the containing view is closed.

Reference: MDN revokeObjectURL()

title: Building a software factory for AI SDK
description:
The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once:

  • Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs

  • UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others

  • Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in

  • Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others

After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests.

That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow.

Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues.

Deciding what type of factory to build

Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions:

  • Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough

  • What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK

  • How to align automation and human effort to risk

Why not add more agents?

The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl.

All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle.

What kind of automation fits AI SDK?

Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle.

The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them.

How do we align automation and effort to risk?

For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk.

Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system.

To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project.

Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort:

  • Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification

  • Well-defined provider changes get focused validation

  • A new public API gets deep review

What we built

ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues and pull requests for AI SDK. Agents in the factory perform specific, reviewable tasks, like reproducing bugs, implementing features, and creating backports for older SDK versions. A human stays in control throughout the entire process, including merging every change.

We didn't ship the factory in one swing. We built it incrementally, starting at the beginning of the process with classification of issues as bugs, features, or documentation updates. That first step not only gave us more visibility into the shape of the backlog, but also passed helpful context to the other specialized agents we built later.

We prototyped multiple ways to build each new type of functionality, and in the process developed a set of guiding principles that shaped the architecture of the factory that went into production.

Build one agent per task

Once our classification agent reached a high level of accuracy, we focused on automating bug reproduction, fixes, and review of those fixes. We explored building a single agent equipped with skills for each step, but quickly realized that would come with a higher maintenance and troubleshooting burden over time.

Instead, we built a single agent for each specific task, making every new capability easier to reason about, test in isolation, and debug. Each one is scoped to a specific job, with its own prompts, context, and evals.

Today the factory has dedicated agents for every step in the flow:

  • Bug reproduction

  • Bug fixes

  • PR reviews

  • Backports

  • Documentation updates

  • Feature analysis

  • Feature implementation

Secure everything from the start

We implemented security with the second agent, because bug reproduction was the first step where the factory executed code based on content it didn't control.

A factory operating on a public repository has to assume attacker-controlled input: every issue, pull request, comment, and the links inside them are untrusted. Because successful open-source projects are high-value targets, threats range from malicious code changes and supply chain attacks to resource exhaustion, API key exfiltration, and prompt exfiltration.

Sandboxes are the foundation of our defense. Every agent in ai-sdk-factory runs inside an isolated Vercel Sandbox containing its code, its runtime, and only the secrets the agent's specific task needs. With those guardrails, untrusted content can shape what an agent proposes, but the damage any one task can do is contained to the sandbox.

We also built a shielding layer around the sandbox that controls what agents can reach over the network, blocking the paths an attacker would use to pull secrets out of the isolated environment.

The last line of defense is human review: nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team.

Build value locally, then move to the cloud

The first several agents we built for the factory ran through a local CLI. That enabled our team to iterate quickly as we noticed inaccuracies, felt friction, and prototyped different ideas.

Once multiple steps were running reliably through the CLI, we were ready to move the system onto managed infrastructure. ai-sdk-factory uses:

  • Vercel Functions for the API, workers, and webhook ingress

  • Vercel Queues for task execution

  • Vercel Blob for logs

  • Vercel Sandbox for the agent workspaces

  • Neon Postgres for factory data

Today, GitHub webhooks feed the issue queue, and as soon as they arrive workers automatically pull them and kick off agent runs in sandboxes. We also built a monitoring UI that tracks every run in parallel, and visualizes the queue for the team of reviewers.

Shipping software through our factory

On July 24, a community member asked for blocked-domain support in OpenAI web search, and the request became issue #17898. The following section explains every step the software factory went through to process the issue, open a pull request with an implementation of the feature, and ultimately backport the merged feature to v5 and v6 of the SDK.

Classification

The first agent that runs in the factory classifies issues and pull requests. In this case, the ai-sdk-factory bot commented on the issue and applied a label, identifying the type as Feature with high confidence. The agent included its rationale for the classification in the comment.

Analysis

After classification, the analysis agent runs. Agents in the factory don't make any assumptions about the technical validity of a feature request or bug, so the analysis agent wrote a probe to confirm the absence of support for blocked domains. issue-17898-type-probe.ts was generated and run, and failed with an error when it looked for blocked-domains and didn't find it.

The failing probe proved the feature was missing on main, and the agent included it in the analysis as evidence.

The analysis agent then used the results of its investigation to build out a spec for the feature: add an optional blockedDomains filter to the existing web-search tool and map it to the provider's blocked_domains field.

The agent also confirmed the spec fit the SDK's provider-adapter architecture and was backward compatible, and even scoped documentation changes.

Implementation

Another agent then implemented the spec and opened a pull request. The implementation agent ran a live end-to-end test, executing an OpenAI web search with wikipedia.org blocked and confirming the domain wasn't reachable. The test was included as additional evidence on the pull request.

Automated review

Next, a review agent scored the change, and when it didn't find any concerns, approved it. The agent rated the feature as fully implemented, with:

  • Side-effect risk: low

  • Performance risk: none

  • Backwards-compatibility risk: low

Human review

Finally, Lars read the chain of evidence from the agents, reviewed the code changes, and merged PR #18033 into main.

Backporting

Once Lars merged the initial PR, ai-sdk-factory opened additional PRs for two backports, #18035 for v6 and #18036 for v5. The v5 backport did not apply cleanly, so the factory agent labeled and committed the conflicted state, identified and validated a fix, and pushed it seventeen minutes later. After review, Lars merged both backport PRs.

Results

We are just over four weeks into running the software factory in production. Here are the results:

PRs merged to main

Between 25-35% of the PRs we merge on a weekly basis are now authored by ai-sdk-factory agents.

Backports

Factory PRs are above 50% of weekly merges to the v6 release line, and v5 looks similar. Backports used to be work we skipped because dealing with merge conflicts wasn't worth the effort. v5 and v6 get far better support now.

Issues

In July, over 75% of closed issues were closed by the factory.

Open issues fell from a peak of 1,022 in late June to 844 by early August, and open bugs are down roughly 25%.

The ai-sdk-factory runs in public, so you can see every pull request it has authored on the repo.

Improving the factory becomes the job

The most interesting part of running the factory is what happens when it fails. Every run ends one of four ways: success, flawed, blocked, or manual. Only success ships, so the rest are signal that re-enters the system as feedback.

  • A flawed run means an agent produced the wrong thing, and the fix is better prompts, better context, or a new eval case so the same mistake gets caught automatically next time

  • A blocked run means the environment was missing something, like a credential, a service, or a dependency, and the fix is provisioning it

  • A manual run marks a boundary we drew on purpose, and forces us to ask whether improvements in the factory justify removing it

Each of those fixes expands the automation boundary, and every week the factory can handle work that it couldn't be trusted with before.

Running the factory is the same discipline teams already apply to their test suites and pipelines, but pointed at the system that does the work, instead of the system that checks it. In a world where agents define the SDLC, improving the factory will become the standard engineering job.

title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
description:
arXiv:2610.31810v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.

title: SynthForge: fake test data with deterministic seeds, custom schemas, and SQL output
description:
Seeding a database with user1, user2, test@test.com works right up until your UI has to render a real-looking name, your demo needs 500 believable products, or your test suite needs the same dataset on every run, not a fresh snowflake each time.

SynthForge is a synthetic data API we built at DSP to fix that. It's live on RapidAPI with a free tier.

Predefined generators

Seven generators, up to 1,000 records per call: person, company, address, product, user, payment-card, and internet, covering names, safe emails, phones, job titles, SKUs, prices, usernames, IPs, UUIDs, and the rest of the usual test-data furniture.

Payment cards deserve a specific mention: numbers come only from the standard public test ranges (Visa 4242…, Mastercard 5555…, Amex, Discover), are Luhn-valid so your validators accept them, and every record is flagged "test_only": true. They will never work for a real purchase, by design.

The headline: bring your own schema

Describe the shape you want using any of 38 field generators, and get back exactly that shape:

curl -X POST https://synthforge.p.rapidapi.com/v1/generate/schema \
  -H "X-RapidAPI-Key: YOUR_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"schema": {"id": "uuid", "name": "product_name",
                  "price": "price", "city": "city", "zip": "zip_code"},
       "count": 2, "seed": 7}'

[{"id": "6513270e-269e-4d37-b2a7-4de452e6b438", "name": "Premium Lamp",
  "price": "395.03", "city": "North Loriville", "zip": "48432"},
 {"id": "81e74ef5-e8e2-4d94-8ed9-04759531985d", "name": "Modular Blender",
  "price": "59.99", "city": "North Christopher", "zip": "55311"}]

Output formats: JSON, CSV, or SQL INSERT statements, so generated data can go straight into a seed file.

Seeds make it deterministic

Every endpoint accepts a seed. Same seed, same data, byte for byte, seed 42 on the person generator gives you Margaret Johnson today, tomorrow, and in CI. That's the difference between a flaky fixture and a reliable one.

Locales are supported where they make sense (en_US, en_GB, de_DE, fr_FR, es_ES, ja_JP), and emails use safe, non-deliverable addresses.

Pricing

Every endpoint is available on every plan, including the free tier. All seven predefined generators and the custom schema endpoint are included from the start, with no Pro-only generators and no output format held back to force an upgrade. Upgrading simply gets you more requests per month: start free with 150 requests a month, move up to Pro at $4/month for 5,000, Ultra at $9/month for 20,000, or Mega at $24/month for 500,000. And since a single request can generate up to 1,000 records, even the free tier goes a long way. You pay for volume, not for access.

Try it: https://rapidapi.com/darksundarker/api/synthforge

What generator is missing for your use case? That's the v1.1 backlog, and it's being written by whoever asks.

title: Inventory expiry: how to test lots and FEFO before accepting the system
description:
Jonathan Perez · Nightly Software. Originally published October 7, 2026, and last updated on that date in the original guide. This cross-post was prepared with AI assistance to format and adapt that existing guide for DEV.

An expiry alert does not prove that an inventory system prevents shipping an expired lot. Before accepting the system, test the decision it makes, the quantities it changes and the evidence it preserves.

This guide uses one complete, synthetic exercise. It tests FEFO picking, reservations, a quarantined return, partial release, expiry and a repeated event. You can run the same sequence against the software you already use. Passing it depends on the product, version, configuration and operating rules being tested.

First define the dates and eligibility policy

FEFO means first expired, first out, but the date driving a particular system must be checked. The original guide used Odoo 19 documentation, reviewed October 7, 2026: its expiry documentation distinguishes expiry, best-before, removal and alert dates, and its FEFO strategy prioritizes the assigned removal date.

A warning and a picking block are separate controls. Write down these decisions before the demonstration:

  • Where the lot date comes from. Compare it with the label or supporting documentation. Receiving an older lot today must not silently give it a new life.
  • Which date orders picking. Specify expiry or removal date and a tie-breaking rule. If removal is earlier than expiry, test that difference.
  • When eligibility ends. Specify the date, time and time zone. Include any minimum remaining life required at delivery: a lot valid today may be unsuitable for a future shipment.
  • What happens to missing or corrected dates. Define review, permissions and a reason for the change. A missing date must not be silently treated as approval where the operation requires expiry tracking.

Agree these rules with receiving, picking and exception-approval staff. A column labelled “expiry” is not an acceptance test.

Keep physical stock separate from available stock

In this exercise:

available = on-hand - reserved - blocked

Reserved and blocked are distinct groups. A piece cannot be deducted twice. If a reserved lot becomes blocked, review the commitment and move the affected pieces into the appropriate group.

Quarantine is a block while a responsible person reviews returned goods or a discrepancy. The pieces may still be physically present. Quarantine does not mean disposal, and a warning alone does not move a quantity.

Test fixture: 100 pieces in three lots

These are invented test data, not customer records or project results. Keep the exercise date at October 7, 2026 when reproducing it.

The SKU is INS-01, measured in pieces, in one warehouse. The exercise blocks a lot from 00:00 on its expiry date, Mexico City time. No additional minimum remaining life applies. Removal and expiry dates are identical, and there are no initial reservations. These are explicit test assumptions, not universal inventory or Odoo defaults.

Lot Received Expiry and removal On-hand Blocked Available
V-01 Oct 2, 2026 Oct 7, 2026 20 20 0
P-01 Oct 6, 2026 Oct 10, 2026 30 0 30
C-01 Oct 1, 2026 Nov 1, 2026 50 0 50
C00 total 100 20 80

Order PED-45 needs 45 pieces. Reserve 30 from P-01, then 15 from C-01. C-01 arrived earlier but expires later. V-01 is already blocked and must not be used to complete the order.

Because expiry and removal dates coincide in this fixture, either date produces that order. If the dates differ in your configuration, repeat the test using the date that actually governs its strategy.

Run the whole event sequence

Step On-hand Reserved Blocked Available
C00: initial state on Oct 7 100 0 20 80
C01: reserve PED-45, using 30 P-01 + 15 C-01 100 45 20 35
C02: physically dispatch the 45 reserved pieces, SAL-45 55 0 20 35
C03: receive 5 returned P-01 pieces into quarantine, DEV-05 60 0 25 35
C04: resend DEV-05 without another physical receipt 60 0 25 35
C05: review releases 3; 2 remain blocked 60 0 22 38
C06: Oct 10 arrives; the 3 released pieces expire 60 0 25 35
C07: attempt to reserve 36; reject the request 60 0 25 35
C08: authorized physical removal of 20 V-01 pieces for disposal 40 0 5 35

Check the ledger after each event, rather than only the final dashboard total:

  1. Reservation is not dispatch. C01 changes the commitment, leaving 100 pieces physically present. C02 records their physical departure: 20 V-01 and 35 C-01 pieces remain.
  2. A return is not immediate availability. C03 receives five pieces, but all five enter quarantine. On-hand rises to 60; availability stays at 35.
  3. A repeated event is not another return. C04 represents the same DEV-05 receipt. It must retain the existing reference and balance, adding no pieces. A different return needs its own reference and evidence.
  4. Partial release needs an audit trail. C05 records who released three pieces, why and when, and why two remain blocked. The three released pieces are still eligible on October 7, so availability becomes 38.
  5. Time can change eligibility without changing physical stock. On October 10, those three pieces expire. Availability returns to 35. The two already in quarantine are not deducted a second time.
  6. Disposal needs a physical movement. C08 reduces on-hand and blocked stock by 20 each. It does not change the 35 available pieces. Keep the lot history; deleting a lot is not a substitute for recording its removal.

The final reconciliation is:

100 initial - 45 dispatched + 5 returned - 20 removed = 40 on-hand
40 on-hand - 0 reserved - 5 blocked = 35 available

Those 40 pieces are 35 C-01 pieces available and five P-01 pieces blocked. If the totals differ, keep the discrepancy open even if the screens look correct.

Inspect the return evidence

Record the product, lot, quantity, unit, original dispatch document and return reference before deciding what can be released. Changing an order status must neither recreate the goods nor renew their expiry date.

Under this exercise’s policy, the responsible person reviews the returned goods before releasing some, retaining a block or authorizing a physical removal. Preserve the original dispatch so the remaining distribution of that lot can be traced.

If your operation uses a different return policy, replace the assumptions in writing before running the tests. The fixture is a proposed acceptance model, not a statement that every inventory product behaves this way.

Turn the exercise into an acceptance checklist

Test Evidence to inspect
Receive lots in a different order from their expiry dates The eligible lot with earlier expiry/removal is selected first, even when received later.
Show an alert without relying on it as a block An expired lot cannot be reserved or picked under the agreed policy.
Put removal before expiry Priority and eligibility use the actual configured dates for the product and customer.
Cross the exact expiry boundary Check before and from the cutoff, including a reservation made the day before.
Omit or correct a lot date Visible review, authorized changes and a reason; preserve date history.
Split one order across lots Quantities and documents retain the actual lot for each dispatch.
Receive a return and release only part Only received goods increase on-hand; only approved, eligible goods increase availability.
Send the same event twice One receipt or dispatch, with the original reference and unchanged balance.
Request more than is available An explicit rejection or pending state; expired goods do not fill the gap.
Remove goods for disposal Authorized movement, reconciled balances and accessible lot history.

Run the sequence with the people who will receive and pick, on the intended devices. Keep event references, expected balances, screenshots and discrepancies. Compare the physical label with the lot selected in the system. After a correction, repeat the affected steps and verify their balances again.

Configure first, then decide whether to extend

Start with the system you already use: lot tracking, dates, removal strategy, permissions and blocking rules. If configuration passes the agreed tests, you may not need another system.

If sales, the warehouse and a customer portal show different balances, identify the missing integration or extension before replacing everything. The decision should follow demonstrated rules and reconciled evidence, rather than the presence of an expiry screen.

This is an operational acceptance exercise. It does not certify sanitary, tax or regulatory compliance, and it makes no claim that Nightly delivered these rules for a previous customer. The original publication date, source-review date and synthetic exercise dates remain October 7, 2026.

description:
arXiv:2610.31979v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Deepfakes increasingly undermine trust in digital media, yet existing detectors often struggle to generalize across unseen manipulation techniques, compression levels, and dataset shifts. Most approaches rely on RGB appearance, frequency-domain artifacts, or their combination, learning cues present in the final synthesized image. While effective in-distribution, such cues are frequently generator-specific and can diminish as synthesis models evolve. We argue that a complementary perspective can be obtained through implicit neural representations (INRs), which expose how an image is reconstructed rather than merely how it appears. By fitting an INR to an image and analyzing its internal activations, one can reveal reconstruction dynamics that are difficult to observe in the image domain alone and may capture more intrinsic differences between genuine and synthetic content. To this end, we propose Spectra, a deepfake detection framework that combines semantic visual representations with artifact-aware cues derived from INR reconstruction. Spectra extracts multi-level reconstruction heatmaps from image-specific INRs and jointly models them with semantic features through a bidirectional fusion mechanism. This enables direct interaction between image semantics and reconstruction artifacts, allowing the model to identify forgery cues that are less dependent on specific generation pipelines. Extensive experiments on multiple deepfake benchmarks demonstrate improved robustness and cross-dataset generalization, consistently outperforming detectors based solely on RGB appearance or semantic representations. Furthermore, we show that the proposed representation extends beyond deepfake detection to face presentation attack detection, highlighting its potential as a unified framework for facial attack detection.

title: The card number was in our error tracker, not our database
description:
We passed a PCI scoping review on the database side with no issues: no PANs stored, tokens only. Then someone searched our error tracker for a 6-digit BIN while debugging an unrelated decline and got hits.

The cause was boring. A JSON parse error in the checkout handler threw before validation, and the tracker's default integration attached the raw request body to the event. Anything a customer typed into the card field, when the payload was malformed, was stored in plaintext for 90 days. We found 41 events with full 16-digit numbers. All of them came from a mobile client version that sent a trailing comma.

What fixed it:

  1. Scrub at the SDK before send, not in the tracker's UI. Server-side scrubbing still means the data crossed the wire to a third party.
  2. Drop request bodies on payment routes entirely. Keep the route, status, and a request ID.
  3. Add a Luhn-pattern check to the log pipeline as a tripwire. It catches the next leak, not the first one.
  4. Same for reverse proxy access logs if you ever put card data in a query string. Don't.

The part that bothered me most: our scope diagram showed three boxes. The tracker wasn't one of them, because nobody thinks of it as a data store.

Where else have you found cardholder data you didn't expect: APM traces, support tool screenshots, analytics events?

Payneteasy handles this kind of payment flow for merchants and PSPs — see how it works.

title: meet catweb: a browser for windows (with a cat)
description:
so i have a browser now. it's called catweb, a pixel cat named tuft lives on the new tab page.

download: https://yupthatscole.github.io/catweb-releases/

what it is
catweb is a windows browser written in rust.

websites run on webview2, the same engine microsoft edge uses, so most sites just work. catweb draws everything around the page itself: tabs, address bar, menus, settings, downloads, and tuft.

there's also catweb native, a from-scratch rendering engine. it's an experimental side project, and tabs using it get an "Experimental" label. don't sign in to anything in those.

what it does
built-in ad and tracker blocking (easylist), toggle per site
tries https first, strips tracking junk from links
private tabs that forget everything when closed
tabs in the title bar, drag to reorder, reopen closed tabs (ctrl+shift+t)
address bar suggestions, bookmarks bar, history, downloads panel
imports your chrome bookmarks and history
themes and accent colors (default is "lavender soft")
updates itself and checks a signature before installing anything
silly settings, off by default. yes, the switches meow.
privacy
no accounts, no analytics, no telemetry. on its own, catweb only talks to:

github, once a day, to check for updates (can be turned off)
sites you visit, to grab their icons (never in private tabs)
microsoft smartscreen, for dangerous sites and downloads (on by default, can be turned off)
history and bookmarks stay on your pc. catweb doesn't save passwords.

it hasn't had an outside security audit, so i wouldn't use it for banking yet.

the smartscreen thing
catweb isn't code-signed (that costs money every year), so windows will warn you. click "More info", then "Run anyway".

if you want to check it first:

virustotal: https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/ea48b93c00d2345afdcbc42327ce868ffac0f0fcb33bd4c1df12320d2c864cec/detection
every release has a sha-256 checksum next to the download

what's next
a vpn/proxy option someday, making catweb native good enough for real sites.

bugs
found one? open an issue at https://github.com/yupthatscole/catweb-releases/issues and say what you did and what happened.

meow 🐈

title: Enterprise Guide to Linux Kernel Network Stack Tuning for 100GbE, BBR, and IRQ Affinity
description:
Originally published on the HostingPodium Enterprise Engineering Blog.

Free SRE & Developer Diagnostics: Test your stack live with our DMARC Record Checker, Generator & SPF/DKIM Validator, Free Website Speed & Core Web Vitals Checker, or explore all 9 Free Webmaster & Cloud Engineering Tools.

This guide details sysctl, BBR, and IRQ-affinity settings that let a Linux host sustain near line-rate on 100 GbE while keeping tail latency sub-50 µs.

Scope and audience

This guide assumes a Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 (or AlmaLinux 9) host equipped with a Mellanox ConnectX-6 100 GbE NIC. The target audience is senior platform engineers responsible for latency-sensitive, high-throughput services such as distributed databases, AI model serving, or video transcoding pipelines.

Baseline kernel parameters

Before any tuning, capture the default sysctl set. The following command produces a reproducible baseline:

sysctl -a | grep -E "net\.core|net\.ipv4|net\.ipv6" > baseline.sysctl

Typical defaults on RHEL 9 are shown in Table 1.

Parameter Default Recommended range
net.core.somaxconn 128 1024-4096
net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse 0 1
net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout 60 15-30
net.core.rmem_max 212992 4 MiB-16 MiB
net.core.wmem_max 212992 4 MiB-16 MiB
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem 4096 87380 6291456 4096 87380 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem 4096 16384 4194304 4096 16384 16777216

Core sysctl tuning for 100 GbE

High-throughput NICs generate thousands of interrupts per second. The kernel must be able to queue and dequeue packets without hitting socket buffer limits.

Increasing socket backlog

net.core.somaxconn controls the maximum length of the listen queue. For services that accept many concurrent connections, raise it to at least 4096.

# cat >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-network.conf
net.core.somaxconn = 4096

TIME_WAIT reuse

When a service performs rapid connection churn, the kernel can run out of available ports. Enabling tcp_tw_reuse permits reuse of sockets in TIME_WAIT state for new outbound connections.

net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1
net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout = 15

Socket buffer scaling

100 GbE links can sustain line-rate packet bursts that exceed the default 212 KB buffer. Raising rmem_max and wmem_max to 16 MiB gives the kernel headroom for large receive windows and TCP pacing.

net.core.rmem_max = 16777216
net.core.wmem_max = 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_rmem = 4096 87380 16777216
net.ipv4.tcp_wmem = 4096 16384 16777216

Disabling syncookies for controlled environments

If the deployment runs behind an authenticated edge, syncookies add unnecessary CPU cycles. Set net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 0, but retain it in public-facing zones.

net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 0

Enabling BBR congestion control

Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip time (BBR) replaces loss-driven algorithms with a model-based approach. It is well suited for data-center fabrics where packet loss is rare and latency variance dominates.

Kernel support check

RHEL 9 ships kernel 5.14, which includes BBR v2. Verify the algorithm list:

# sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control = cubic

If “bbr” is absent, install the latest kernel-rt or backport the module.

Activation steps 

# echo "bbr" > /etc/sysctl.d/99-bbr.conf
net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control = bbr
net.core.default_qdisc = fq
# sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-bbr.conf

Setting the default qdisc to fq (Fair Queuing) is required for BBR to receive accurate RTT samples.

Validation

Run a sustained iperf3 flow and inspect the congestion control state:

# iperf3 -c 10.0.0.2 -t 60 -P 4
# ss -tin | grep bbr

Typical output shows cwnd stabilizing around the BDP (Bandwidth-Delay Product) of the link.

Trade-offs

  • Pros: Higher steady-state throughput, lower queuing delay, predictable latency under moderate load.

  • Cons: BBR can be aggressive on shared links, potentially starving co-existing Cubic flows. In multi-tenant clusters, consider enabling BBR per-namespace rather than globally.

100 GbE NIC configuration

Linux treats the NIC as a collection of queues, each serviced by a dedicated interrupt vector. Proper ring-buffer sizing and IRQ affinity are mandatory to keep CPU utilization below 70 % at line rate.

Ring buffer sizing with ethtool

Default ring sizes on ConnectX-6 are 1024 descriptors. For 100 GbE, increase to 8192 or 16384 depending on expected burst size.

# ethtool -G eth0 rx 16384 tx 16384
# ethtool -g eth0
Ring parameters for eth0:
 Pre-set maximums: RX: 524288 TX: 524288
 Current hardware settings:
 RX: 16384 TX: 16384

IRQ distribution

Modern kernels expose one MSI-X vector per queue. Use irqbalance for baseline distribution, then pin critical queues to isolated cores.

# systemctl enable irqbalance && systemctl start irqbalance
# for i in /proc/irq/*/smp_affinity; do echo f > $i; done # naive example
# echo 0xFF > /proc/irq/45/smp_affinity # bind vector 45 to CPUs 0-7

Better practice is to reserve a NUMA-local CPU set (e.g., 0-15 on socket 0) and generate a bitmap accordingly. Example for a 32-core system:

# CPU_BITMAP=$(printf "%x" $(( (1 /proc/irq/45/smp_affinity

RPS/RFS for receive steering

When the NIC cannot deliver a dedicated interrupt per queue (e.g., virtualized environments), use Receive Packet Steering (RPS) and Receive Flow Steering (RFS) to spread packets across CPUs.

# echo 0xffff > /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-0/rps_cpus
# echo 3000 > /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-0/rps_flow_cnt

Performance validation runbook

The following checklist should be executed after any change to sysctl, BBR, or NIC settings.

  • Reload sysctl: sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-network.conf

  • Restart the affected service (e.g., systemctl restart myservice).

  • Run a baseline iperf3 test: iperf3 -c $SERVER -t 30 -P 8. Record throughput, jitter, and packet loss.

  • Collect kernel metrics with perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses -a -- sleep 30.

  • Verify BBR state: ss -tin | grep bbr.

  • Inspect IRQ distribution: cat /proc/interrupts | grep eth0.

  • Check for dropped packets: ethtool -S eth0 | grep drop.

  • If any metric deviates >5 % from the target, revert the last change and repeat.

Observability and security considerations

High-speed networking expands the attack surface. The following hardening steps are recommended.

TCP SYN protection 

net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 8192

eBPF tracing for latency spikes

Deploy a lightweight eBPF program that records tcp_probe events. The data can be streamed to Prometheus.

# cat /usr/share/bcc/tools/tcpconnect
# ./tcpconnect -p 80 -d 10

Monitoring BBR metrics

Export net_tcp_bbr_bw and net_tcp_bbr_min_rtt from the kernel via node_exporter or collectd to spot congestion mis-behaviour.

Comparison with alternative approaches

Table 2 contrasts the chosen stack with three common alternatives.

Aspect BBR + IRQ-affinity Cubic + default IRQ DCTCP + hardware offload
Throughput @ 100 GbE ≈99 % line rate ≈92 % line rate ≈95 % line rate (requires loss-aware switch)
Average RTT (µs) 30-45 55-80 40-60
CPU utilization ≈55 % ≈70 % ≈65 % (offload saves ~10 %)
Complexity Medium (sysctl + irq-pinning) Low High (switch config, DCTCP kernel patches)
Tenant fairness Potentially aggressive Balanced Balanced if ECN enabled

For isolated workloads where latency determinism outweighs raw bandwidth, BBR with dedicated IRQ affinity remains the most predictable configuration. In multi-tenant environments, Cubic or DCTCP may provide better fairness at the cost of higher tail latency.

Rollback procedure

All changes are stored in separate .conf files under /etc/sysctl.d. To revert:

# rm /etc/sysctl.d/99-network.conf /etc/sysctl.d/99-bbr.conf
# sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-default.conf # a minimal baseline file
# systemctl restart irqbalance
# ethtool -G eth0 rx 1024 tx 1024

After rollback, repeat the validation runbook to confirm that metrics have returned to pre-tuning values.

Summary

By raising socket buffers, enabling BBR, and pinning NIC queues to isolated CPUs, a Linux host can sustain near-line-rate traffic on a 100 GbE fabric while keeping 99th-percentile latency below 50 µs. The guide provides concrete configuration artifacts, a repeatable validation workflow, and a security checklist suitable for production deployment.

title: SAGE: A hybrid vision-language and geometry framework for work-zone pathway prediction under temporary traffic control
description:
arXiv:2610.31835v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporary traffic control redirects vehicles through work zones, requiring automated vehicles to connect an interpretation of the visible devices to a continuous passing path. Geometric predictors can provide several plausible paths, yet selecting the one consistent with the temporary control remains difficult. We propose SAGE (Semantic-to-Action Grounded Execution), a read-decide-execute-check framework that separates path construction, path preference, and control compliance within a shared candidate space. The central idea is to use a vision-language model's (VLM's) trajectory as a preference over intact geometric candidates. A role-decoupled generator constructs the candidates, and rank fusion combines each candidate's geometric score with its agreement with the VLM trajectory. Supervision structured around the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) trains SAGE-VLM to state the lane status and hazard side before its passage decision and trajectory. The predicted hazard side enters image-space predicates derived from MUTCD provisions, which support a final intervention bounded in score and displacement. On 2,306 real-world ROADWork validation episodes, the candidates include a path within 10 px of the human demonstration in 87% of episodes, yet selection regret accounts for 53% of the geometric ranker's error. SAGE reduces average and final displacement errors by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to the ranker, mostly in the far field, and hard-constraint violations by 37%. The trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator-selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to state-of-the-art VLM modules in accuracy, with a faster-responding VLM, and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/SAGE-page/.

title: Restyling a Legacy Website Without Touching Its HTML (or Breaking Its JS)
description:
You know the request: "Can you make our website look modern?" The site in question is years old. It has jQuery plugins bound to class names, a checkout nobody wants to touch, inline styles toggled by scripts written by someone who left long ago, and a CMS or backend that generates the markup.

WordPress sites are an especially common case. Many run a theme plus a long list of plugins for forms, shops, bookings, memberships, SEO and page building. Each plugin brings its own markup, styles and scripts. Together, they often represent years of work and a large investment in setup, content and customization. Their owners want a fresh look, but above all they need every one of those plugins to keep working.

A rebuild means migrating all of that and retesting everything. This post describes a different approach, the one behind AI Style Upgrade, a Chrome extension I built: leave the existing site exactly as it is, and ship the whole redesign as a layer on top.

Why restyles of legacy sites break things

Most breakage during a redesign doesn't come from the new look itself. It comes from the changes made to get there:

  • Changing the markup. Old scripts find elements by class names, ids and structure. Add a wrapper <div> or rename a class, and a dropdown stops opening, a slider stops sliding, or an analytics tag stops firing.
  • Overriding what scripts control. If a script shows a menu by setting style.display, a stylesheet that also sets display on that menu breaks it, even though the markup never changed.
  • Switching the WordPress theme. Plugins and page builders output their content into the theme's templates. A new theme can break shop pages, forms and carefully built layouts, and often means redoing customizations.
  • Touching the server. New templates, a theme migration or a new CMS put your integrations, database and URLs at risk, and changed URLs can cost search rankings.

The approach: a layer on top

AI Style Upgrade avoids all of these:

  • The HTML is never changed: no new tags or wrappers, and all class names and ids are kept.
  • Properties the site's own JavaScript or inline styles control are detected and left alone, so the features built on them keep working.
  • Nothing changes on the server: templates, CMS, database and URLs stay as they are.

On top of that, existing background images are preserved, text stays visible, and the design is built for both desktop and mobile, with no overlapping elements.

Deployment is two lines

The output is two static files: a stylesheet and a small script. Both go at the very beginning of <body>:

<body>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/ai314-cool-style.css">
  <script src="/ai314-cool-script.js"></script>
  <!-- your existing page content -->

The script is intentionally not deferred. It runs before the content below it renders, so the new design is active from the first paint, with no flash of the old style.

Rollback is just as simple: delete the two lines and the site is exactly as it was.

The workflow

The extension works with any AI chat assistant over the clipboard: it prepares a prompt, you paste it into the assistant, then you paste the answer back. For privacy, the AI never sees your real page. It gets a cleaned-up snapshot with styles and scripts stripped out and the text masked.

There are two paths:

  • New look: the AI suggests 30 design themes ranked by fit for your site. You pick one, then pick 1 of 5 color palettes for it. You preview the result on your own live site, in your browser only, and keep refining it with the AI.
  • Effects only: keep the current theme and just add effects and styling changes, without writing code.

What you can add goes beyond colors: a fixed menu that shrinks on scroll, fade-in on scroll, parallax layering, 3D tilt, flowing gradients, and layout changes such as three columns to two. You can also add static or animated effects to images you select on the page, for example steam rising from the schnitzels in a food photo, or a door in a picture that opens and closes.

The AI assistant is a separate service and isn't part of the extension. I get good results with Claude (claude.ai) on a Pro plan using Sonnet 5.5, but any assistant works.

A checklist before you ship any restyle

Whatever tool you use, or if you do it by hand, test these on the legacy site before going live:

  1. Menus and dropdowns: open and close each one, by mouse, touch and keyboard.
  2. Forms: submit with valid and invalid input, and check that validation messages still show and are readable.
  3. Checkout or sign-in: go through the whole flow, including error states.
  4. Third-party widgets: cookie banners, chat, maps, embedded video.
  5. Mobile: check the real breakpoints the site uses, not just one phone width.
  6. Accessibility: text contrast, visible focus outlines, and animations that respect prefers-reduced-motion.
  7. Images: background images and logos still visible, with nothing cropped or covered.

Where this approach stops

A style layer changes presentation, nothing else. It won't add features, restructure content, or fix a broken backend. If the project needs any of those, it's a real rebuild. But for the common case, a site that works fine and just looks old, leaving the site untouched removes most of the risk.

See it moving

Screenshots don't show scroll effects, menu animations or image effects. The before/after clips do:

Watch the before & after videos →

There's also a short video walkthrough of the extension.

Designing and testing are free. A one-time license per website is needed only when you deploy the stylesheet (details).

Cover image: before/after of a page from The University of Edinburgh. Modified for demonstration purposes. Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

I'd like to hear from anyone who has had to restyle a legacy site: what broke for you, and what would you want a tool like this to guard against?

title: DraMaze: A Multi-Agent Pipeline with Future-Aware Memory for Diverse Microdrama Script Generation
description:
arXiv:2610.32002v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid growth of microdramas has increased demand for high-quality script production. Long-form microdrama script generation with LLMs requires both diverse plot progression and long-range narrative coherence. Our observations reveal that candidate continuations increasingly concentrate on fewer narrative mechanisms as generation progresses, while conventional retrieval may reinforce trope reuse and overlook historical information essential to future plots. To address these challenges, we propose DraMaze, a multi-agent pipeline that explores diverse causal paths through trope memory-guided evolutionary tree search and mutation. It further constructs a Backward Narrative Dependency Tree to organize, retain, and retrieve historical memories based on future narrative goals. We also introduce MiDramaBench, a bilingual benchmark for evaluating script logic and creative quality across different script lengths, together with causal-pattern metrics for narrative repetition and diversity. Experiments show consistent improvements across three backbone LLMs. For 60-episode scripts of up to 60k words, DraMaze reduces causal-pattern repetition by 32.1% and achieves a Logic score of 82.5, outperforming the best-performing baseline by 8.5 points.

title: Developer Seeks Feedback on Open-Source Go SMTP Toolkit 'Raven,' Addresses AI-Generated Code Concerns
description:
Introduction to Raven: A Go SMTP Toolkit

In the ever-evolving landscape of email infrastructure, the Raven toolkit emerges as a comprehensive SMTP solution for Go developers. Born out of the necessity to support a commercial service, Raven addresses the critical need for a robust, modernized SMTP implementation that aligns with contemporary email transport and authentication protocols. The developer’s decision to open-source the core transport library is not just a gesture of goodwill but a strategic move to leverage community expertise for refinement and broader adoption.

At its core, Raven is designed to handle the complexities of SMTP, from RFC 5321 addr-spec parsing to streaming MIME traversal. The addr-spec parser, for instance, is a critical component that ensures compatibility with diverse email systems. It mechanically deconstructs email addresses into their constituent parts, validating syntax and structure. This process is essential because incorrect parsing can lead to delivery failures or security vulnerabilities, such as header injection attacks. By adhering strictly to RFC standards, Raven mitigates these risks, ensuring reliable email transport.

The toolkit’s support for modern mail transport protocols—DKIM, SPF, DMARC, and ARC—addresses the escalating demands of email security. These protocols work in tandem to authenticate email sources and prevent spoofing. For example, DKIM signs email headers, creating a cryptographic signature that is verified by the recipient’s server. This mechanism detects tampering during transit, ensuring the integrity of the message. Raven’s implementation of these protocols is not just a feature but a necessity in today’s threat landscape, where phishing and spoofing attacks are rampant.

One of Raven’s standout features is its provider-specific validation profiles. These profiles address the interoperability challenges posed by email providers like Gmail, which have unique validation rules. For instance, Gmail’s acceptance of equivalent email addresses (e.g., first.last+tag@gmail.com and firstlast@googlemail.com) is handled seamlessly by Raven. This feature is particularly useful in edge cases, such as when dealing with IP literal domains, which are often rejected by providers. By incorporating these profiles, Raven reduces the likelihood of delivery failures caused by provider-specific quirks.

The use of AI-generated code in Raven’s development is both a strength and a potential risk. On one hand, AI accelerates development, enabling the rapid implementation of complex features like SMTP extensions (e.g., PIPELINING, STARTTLS). On the other hand, AI-generated code can introduce subtle bugs or inefficiencies that are difficult to detect. The developer mitigates this risk through extensive testing and commercial service usage, which acts as a real-world stress test. However, the long-term maintainability of AI-generated code remains a concern, as it may lack the human intuition needed for edge-case handling. Developers considering Raven should weigh the trade-offs: if rapid development is prioritized, AI-generated code is optimal, but if long-term maintainability is critical, manual review and refactoring may be necessary.

Raven’s hardening through commercial service usage is a testament to its reliability and robustness. This process involves subjecting the library to high volumes of email traffic, which can expose performance bottlenecks or security vulnerabilities. For example, under high concurrency, the library’s handling of SMTP extensions like CHUNKING is tested to ensure it doesn’t degrade performance or consume excessive resources. This real-world testing is crucial because theoretical benchmarks often fail to capture the complexities of production environments.

In conclusion, Raven is a timely and critical tool for developers navigating the complexities of modern email infrastructure. Its open-source nature, combined with its robust feature set, positions it as a potential standard for SMTP implementations in the Go ecosystem. However, its success hinges on community engagement and feedback, which are essential for addressing edge cases and refining its capabilities. Developers should adopt Raven if they require a secure, efficient, and compliant SMTP solution, but they must also be prepared to contribute to its ongoing improvement, particularly in areas where AI-generated code may fall short.

The Role of AI in Raven's Development

The integration of AI-generated code in Raven’s development is a double-edged sword, offering both acceleration and potential pitfalls. By leveraging AI, the developer has rapidly implemented complex features like SMTP extensions (PIPELINING, STARTTLS) and modern authentication protocols (DKIM, SPF, DMARC). This approach has significantly reduced development time, allowing the library to address critical email transport and security needs in a timely manner. However, AI-generated code lacks the intuitive edge-case handling that human developers bring, which can lead to subtle bugs or inefficiencies. For instance, AI might misinterpret the nuances of RFC 5321 addr-spec parsing, potentially causing failures in email address validation under uncommon formats (e.g., quoted local parts with escaped characters).

To mitigate these risks, the developer has employed a rigorous testing framework, including a large test corpus and real-world stress testing via their commercial service. This dual-layer validation ensures that AI-generated code is hardened against typical failures, such as header injection attacks or protocol misimplementations. However, the long-term maintainability of AI-generated code remains a concern. Without human oversight, edge cases like provider-specific email quirks (e.g., Gmail’s handling of +tag addresses) could slip through, leading to compatibility issues. Here, community engagement becomes critical—human contributors can identify and patch these gaps, ensuring Raven’s sustainability.

The ethical dimension of AI involvement in open-source projects cannot be overlooked. While transparency about AI usage is commendable, it may deter contributions from developers who prioritize human-authored code. To counter this, the developer must actively demonstrate the robustness of AI-generated components through detailed documentation and test coverage. For example, the streaming MIME traversal feature, though AI-assisted, is validated against diverse email structures, ensuring it doesn’t break under large or nested MIME parts.

In summary, AI-generated code in Raven is a trade-off between speed and precision. When coupled with extensive testing and community collaboration, it becomes a viable strategy for accelerating development. However, without ongoing human oversight, the library risks becoming brittle in edge cases. The optimal approach is to use AI for initial feature implementation and rely on human review and community feedback for refinement. If AI is used without this balance, the library may fail to achieve widespread adoption due to perceived unreliability.

  • Rule for AI Integration in Open-Source Projects: If leveraging AI-generated code, pair it with extensive testing, transparent documentation, and active community engagement to address edge cases and maintain trust.

Community Engagement and Future Directions

The raven project, despite its reliance on AI-generated code, stands as a testament to the potential of blending automation with human oversight in software development. However, its success hinges on active community engagement to address edge cases, refine capabilities, and ensure long-term maintainability. Here’s how the developer plans to foster collaboration and steer the project’s evolution:

Incorporating Community Feedback

The developer acknowledges that AI-generated code, while accelerating development, may overlook edge cases or introduce subtle inefficiencies. To mitigate this, community feedback will be channeled into:

  • Edge-Case Refinement: Users encountering issues with complex email formats or provider-specific quirks (e.g., Gmail’s equivalent address handling) can submit patches or test cases. This ensures the RFC 5321 addr-spec parser and provider-specific validation profiles remain robust across diverse scenarios.
  • Protocol Hardening: Feedback on SMTP extensions like STARTTLS or CHUNKING will be prioritized to address security vulnerabilities or performance bottlenecks under high concurrency, leveraging the community’s real-world experience.

Roadmap for Future Enhancements

The developer has outlined a clear roadmap to expand raven’s capabilities while maintaining its core reliability:

  • Extended Protocol Support: Adding support for emerging protocols like MTA-STS and TLS Reporting to align with stricter email security standards, ensuring compliance with regulations like GDPR and CAN-SPAM.
  • Performance Optimization: Addressing streaming MIME traversal inefficiencies for very large emails (>50MB) by implementing parallel processing, reducing latency under high load.
  • AI Integration Refinement: Introducing a human review pipeline for AI-generated code, focusing on critical components like DKIM signature generation and SPF record validation, to minimize risks of misinterpretation.

How to Contribute or Benefit

The project’s sustainability depends on a symbiotic relationship between contributors and users:

  • For Contributors:
    • Submit patches for edge-case handling in the addr-spec parser or provider-specific profiles.
    • Enhance test coverage for AI-generated code, particularly in SMTP extensions like PIPELINING or BINARYMIME, to harden against failures.
    • Propose optimizations for high-concurrency scenarios, where the library’s performance may degrade due to resource contention.
  • For Users:
    • Leverage raven’s modern protocols (DKIM, SPF, DMARC) to build secure, compliant email systems, reducing risks of header injection attacks or spoofing.
    • Utilize provider-specific validation profiles to improve email deliverability, especially for services with strict validation rules like Gmail or Outlook.
    • Report issues with AI-generated code, such as unexpected behavior in SMTPUTF8 handling, to drive targeted improvements.

Optimal Strategy for Growth

The developer advocates for a balanced approach to AI integration: AI for initial feature implementation, followed by human review and community feedback. This strategy ensures:

  • Rapid Development: AI accelerates the implementation of complex features like SMTP extensions or DKIM signing.
  • Reliability: Rigorous testing and community scrutiny address edge cases, preventing failures in protocol misimplementations or security vulnerabilities.
  • Sustainability: Active community engagement mitigates the risk of long-term maintainability issues due to AI’s lack of intuition for edge cases.

Rule for Success: If leveraging AI-generated code, pair it with extensive testing, transparent documentation, and active community involvement to address edge cases and maintain trust.

By fostering this collaborative environment, raven can evolve into a widely adopted standard for SMTP implementations in the Go ecosystem, bridging the gap between traditional email transport and modern security practices.

title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
