title: GBase Database Installation Troubleshooting: 5 Common Errors and How to Fix Them
description:
When a GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation fails, the first instinct is often to switch packages and rerun the installation script.

But many installation errors originate before the installer starts. The root cause may be an OS compatibility check, terminal input, SSH authentication, a missing shared library, or the wrong Python interpreter.

The fastest way to troubleshoot GBase Database installation issues is to identify the failing layer before changing the environment.

Here are five common errors, ordered by the initial checks I would perform.

Error message Likely layer First check
operating system is 'xxx' OS and package validation OS release, kernel, architecture
invalid literal for int() Terminal input Escape sequences and interactive input
Permission denied (publickey) SSH authentication SSH port, user, keys, permissions
fail to add new datanodes to gcware Dependencies and services Service status and missing shared libraries
Python script syntax error Python runtime which python and interpreter version

1. OS Validation Error: operating system is 'xxx'

An installation script may report an error similar to:

operating system is 'xxx', must be centos7

This indicates that the package's OS validation did not accept the detected environment. It does not, by itself, prove that the operating system is incompatible.

Check the actual environment first:

cat /etc/os-release
uname -r
uname -m

Confirm three things:

  • The operating system and release are supported by the target GBase Database version.
  • The kernel and package requirements match the installation guide.
  • The CPU architecture matches the package, such as x86_64 or aarch64.

If the OS identity check is the only mismatch and the target environment is explicitly supported, a documented installer option may allow that check to be bypassed. Some installation workflows use -i for this purpose, but confirm its meaning in the documentation for your exact release before using it.

Do not bypass validation simply to make the error disappear. A validation flag cannot make incompatible binaries work. An x86_64 package will not become an aarch64 package because an OS check was skipped.

2. Terminal Input Error: invalid literal for int()

Sometimes the traceback contains unexpected characters such as:

\x1b[?2004l

This can happen when terminal escape sequences are passed into a script that expects ordinary text or a number. Bracketed-paste handling is one possible cause, especially when a script reads interactive input.

Start by checking how the script receives input.

Possible remedies include:

  • Entering the value manually instead of pasting it.
  • Testing with another terminal client.
  • Disabling bracketed-paste mode if the terminal supports it.
  • Using a documented non-interactive installation method when available.

Avoid editing the installation script immediately. First determine whether the unexpected characters came from the terminal or from the script itself.

This distinction can save time when troubleshooting GBase Database deployment in remote SSH sessions.

3. SSH Authentication Error: Permission denied (publickey)

A typical error looks like this:

Fail to login ... Permission denied (publickey)

This points toward SSH authentication, although connectivity and port configuration should also be checked.

Test SSH manually from the intended installation account:

ssh -v target-host

Replace target-host with the actual hostname or IP address.

Check the following in order:

  1. Network connectivity: Can the source node reach the target?
  2. SSH port: Is the target using the expected port?
  3. Username: Is the installation account correct?
  4. Authentication method: Does the account have the required public key or other supported credentials?
  5. Key permissions: Are the private key and .ssh directory protected with appropriate permissions?
  6. Server policy: Does the target's SSH configuration permit the selected authentication method?

If the deployment uses a non-default SSH port, verify the port setting in the appropriate configuration file. For example, a deployment options file may contain:

sshPort=2222

Use this only if the target SSH server actually listens on port 2222 and the installer supports that parameter.

Do not weaken SSH security or change passwords to simple values as a routine troubleshooting step. Diagnose the authentication failure and follow the organization's credential policy.

4. GCware Error: fail to add new datanodes to gcware

This error can occur when a GBase Database(GBase 8a) cluster cannot add data nodes to GCware successfully.

Possible causes include missing shared libraries, failed services, incorrect environment variables, or communication problems between nodes. A missing library is one useful lead, but it is not the only possible cause.

Start by loading the documented environment for the installation account. If the environment uses .gbase_profile, the command may be:

source ~/.gbase_profile

Then inspect the relevant services using the commands supported by your release:

gcware_services all start
gcluster_services all start
gcadmin

If a service fails to start, inspect its logs before repeatedly restarting it.

To check for missing shared libraries, locate the actual executable or shared object and run ldd against it:

ldd /path/to/gcware | grep "not found"
ldd /path/to/gclusterd | grep "not found"

Replace the example paths with the actual paths in your installation.

If the output contains something like:

libcrypto.so.10 => not found

the system may be missing a compatible OpenSSL library.

Before installing compatibility packages or changing library links, confirm the required ABI and library version against the product documentation and OS package sources. Do not create a symbolic link from an incompatible newer library just to satisfy the filename. Matching filenames do not guarantee binary compatibility.

Also check node-to-node connectivity, service logs, and the cluster configuration if all required libraries are present.

5. Python Syntax Error: The Installer Uses the Wrong Interpreter

A Python syntax error can occur when an installation script written for Python 2 is executed by Python 3.

Multiple Python versions may coexist on the same Linux server. Installing Python 2 does not guarantee that the command python resolves to it.

Check the interpreter used by the installation account:

which python
python --version

Repeat these checks under the root account and the intended database installation account, such as gbase, if both accounts are involved in the deployment.

If the installation guide requires Python 2, verify that the selected interpreter is Python 2 and that the necessary runtime dependencies are installed.

On CentOS 8 or RHEL 8, package availability and naming may vary depending on the configured repositories and system image. Confirm the requirements for the specific GBase Database release rather than assuming that every system provides python2 and python-libs by default.

Follow the documented installer entry point. For example, if the guide specifies invoking the script through the default Python command, use:

python gcinstall.py

Do not assume that python2 gcinstall.py is interchangeable in every installation workflow. If the installer relies on environment configuration or a particular entry point, use the invocation documented for that version.

A Better Troubleshooting Workflow

When GBase Database installation fails, avoid changing several variables at once.

Use a consistent sequence:

  1. Classify the error: OS validation, terminal input, SSH, dependencies, or Python.
  2. Collect evidence: Capture the complete error message, command output, and relevant logs.
  3. Verify the environment: Compare the actual configuration with the requirements for your release.
  4. Change one thing: Apply the smallest justified correction.
  5. Rerun the relevant check: Confirm that the original cause is resolved before proceeding.
  6. Record the fix: Document the affected node, root cause, and corrective action.

This approach is especially useful for multi-node deployments, where an environment inconsistency can make one node behave differently from the others.

Final Thoughts

Most GBase Database(GBase 8a) installation failures become easier to diagnose when the error is assigned to the correct layer.

An OS validation failure calls for package and compatibility checks. Unexpected terminal characters call for input-path investigation. SSH errors require authentication and connectivity checks. GCware failures require service, dependency, and cluster diagnostics. Python syntax errors require interpreter verification.

The goal is not to accumulate more troubleshooting commands. It is to identify the failing layer, verify the cause, and make one controlled correction at a time.

For version-specific installer flags, service commands, and runtime requirements, always consult the documentation for the exact release you are deploying.

When a database installation fails in your environment, which layer do you check first: OS compatibility, SSH, dependencies, or the runtime?

title: HyScale: Scaling Long-Context Training for Learned Sparse Attention
description:
arXiv:2610.32057v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present HyScale, a long-context training system for learned sparse attention. Learned sparse attention is a promising architecture for million-token contexts, widely adopted in production since DeepSeek-V3.2. Selection, however, grows into the training bottleneck. For each query, it scores every previous token whereas sparse attention reads only $k$; worse, current systems materialize a full score table and repeat selection during recomputation. Our key insight is that the output of selection is not an activation, but rather a set of indices. Building on it, HyScale introduces HyTopK and selection replay. HyTopK finds each query's exact top-$k$ on the fly without a score table, while selection replay reuses forward-pass selection in recomputation. Together with holistic system optimizations tackling end-to-end training challenges, HyScale speeds up GLM-5.1 training on 1M-token sequences by 2.07$\times$ over Megatron-LM on 512 H20 GPUs. It also speeds up the CSA layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and the QSA layers of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next by 2.01$\times$ and 1.57$\times$ at 1M tokens on 32 H800 GPUs.

title: Adaptive Control of Scientific Instruments with Nonstationary Responses through Multimodal Agents
description:
arXiv:2610.32370v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Controlling scientific instruments requires parameters to be adjusted progressively in response to feedback from successive operations. When unobserved operating conditions evolve with operational history, responses become nonstationary, and a static mapping from actions to responses becomes inadequate for decisions across shots. Shot-to-shot tuning of neutral beam injection (NBI) ion sources in magnetic confinement fusion devices is representative of this class of problems: the conditions of electrode surfaces and vacuum are difficult to observe directly, discharge outcomes vary between shots, and experiments are costly and carry operational risks. We propose a physically grounded multimodal agent with three independently auditable components. Deterministic algorithms extract symbolic physical quantities and visual evidence from multichannel waveforms; a memory with two layers organizes trajectories from the current task, experience from earlier tasks, and procedural knowledge, from which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) generates candidate actions; and an independent action feasibility check enforces action constraints before execution. In a strictly chronological replay of 455 shots from four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols alone outperformed waveform images alone by 0.21-0.32 in macro-F1 for quality classification across all four evaluated models. Retrieved context increased the mean agreement with historical action directions by 22.4-42.7 percentage points, whereas the contribution of visual evidence varied across models. Under supervised operation on five ion sources, the system achieved a beam-extraction rate of 86.80% across 409 executed shots. These results demonstrate the engineering feasibility of the framework for supervised sequential tuning on a physical scientific instrument.

title: How to Choose Backend Cron Alternatives for Scheduled Scripts: HTTP Calls and Cost
description:
For a media payment reconciliation, the practical backend cron alternatives for scheduled scripts are a timer, a queue-backed worker, or an HTTP task boundary. The cheapest-looking timer is not automatically the cheapest system: the real decision is how much latency you can tolerate before the media business sees a discrepancy, and how much operational machinery you are willing to own.

The useful boundary is this: use a simple scheduler when one run can be retried safely; use a queue-backed design when work can outlive the scheduler; use a workflow tool only when the human and application steps justify its extra abstraction. That rule keeps a 02:00 reconciliation from turning into a daytime accounting incident.

Start with the deadline.

The same rule applies to scheduled cleanup scripts and nightly settlement jobs, but the failure boundary changes when an HTTP call can be accepted before the caller times out. That is why support for HTTP alone is a weak selection criterion; the retry, idempotency, and durable completion contract matter more than the button that creates the schedule.

The awkward case deserves more design attention than the clean timeout. Imagine the reconciliation worker sends a request for the 2026-10-23 settlement, waits 45 seconds, and loses its connection while the provider continues processing. A blind retry can double-count a page; refusing to retry can leave the business date open until morning. The backend needs a request identity that the provider adapter can reuse, a local record that distinguishes “started” from “completed,” and a reconciliation query that can settle the ambiguous state later. If the provider offers no idempotency contract, the adapter should persist the request and response evidence it does have, mark the partition for review, and keep the scheduler from claiming success. This is slower than a one-line cron command, but it is the difference between a delayed report and an unexplained ledger discrepancy. The same boundary applies to external tools like Zapier or n8n: a convenient HTTP step does not change the semantics of a provider that may accept work after the client disconnects.

What should the on-call see when reconciliation is late?

The alert page should say which business date is missing, which run ID was expected, and whether the provider request started, finished, or was rejected. “Cron failed” is a poor alert. It tells the on-call almost nothing about money, scope, or the next safe action.

Work backwards from that page. The scheduler emits a run ID containing the reconciliation date. The worker writes a start record before making the HTTP call, stores the provider cursor or page boundary, and writes a terminal result only after the response has been validated. A metric for completed business dates then alerts on lateness, not merely process exit.

This distinction matters in media because a technically successful request can still leave a partial day unprocessed. A timeout after the provider accepted a request is not equivalent to a rejected request. The retry policy must therefore be keyed to the idempotency token and checkpoint, with a bounded attempt count and an operator-visible quarantine for ambiguous results.

A false-positive threshold has a cost too. Page every five minutes and the team learns to ignore the alert; page only after the next reporting window and the recovery path becomes expensive. Pick the threshold from the reporting deadline and the observed duration distribution, then review it after a few reporting cycles.

Should a backend cron alternative run scheduled scripts over HTTP?

Start with the job's shape, not the scheduler's feature list. A single nightly script that completes within the reporting window can run from a host or container timer. A Kubernetes CronJob expresses the same intent inside a cluster and documents concurrency, missed-start handling, and retention settings in declarative configuration. The Kubernetes documentation also makes clear that a CronJob creates Jobs, so the job's own idempotency still matters when a start is delayed or retried.

When the reconciliation expands into many account or date partitions, separate triggering from execution. A scheduler creates one run record and enqueues work; workers consume partitions and checkpoint progress. A queue with a dead-letter queue gives operators a place to inspect messages that repeatedly fail, but it does not decide whether a message is safe to replay. AWS describes dead-letter queues as a way to isolate messages that cannot be successfully consumed; the application still owns deduplication and recovery.

A task-delivery service can be a better fit when each partition is an HTTP request with a deadline and retry policy. Google Cloud Tasks documents this push model and its delivery controls. The important engineering boundary is the HTTP handler: it must accept a stable task identity, return only after the partition is durably recorded, and tolerate duplicate delivery.

External workflow tools like Zapier and n8n can be useful when the job includes human approval or several application handoffs, but that convenience does not remove the need for an idempotent reconciliation record. They are poor alternatives when the requirement is a tightly controlled backend batch with a narrow reporting deadline, because the team still has to define ownership, retries, secrets, and evidence of completion. A third category, represented by a repository-oriented runner such as GitHub Actions, may fit deployment-adjacent scripts but is a questionable home for a payment control path unless its scheduling, permissions, retention, and recovery policy are reviewed explicitly. These are boundaries, not rankings.

Here is a small Go handler that makes that contract explicit. The repository and provider client are intentionally interfaces, because the durable write and the external API call belong behind tested adapters.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
    "time"
)

type ReconciliationStore interface {
    Begin(ctx context.Context, runID string, businessDate string) (alreadyDone bool, err error)
    Complete(ctx context.Context, runID string, count int) error
}

func reconcileHandler(store ReconciliationStore, providerURL string) http.Handler {
    return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
            http.Error(w, "method not allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
            return
        }
        var request struct {
            RunID string `json:"run_id"`
            BusinessDate string `json:"business_date"`
        }
        if err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&request); err != nil || request.RunID == "" || request.BusinessDate == "" {
            http.Error(w, "invalid request", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 45*time.Second)
        defer cancel()
        done, err := store.Begin(ctx, request.RunID, request.BusinessDate)
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "cannot start run", http.StatusInternalServerError)
            return
        }
        if done {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
            return
        }
        count, err := fetchAndReconcile(ctx, providerURL, request.BusinessDate)
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "temporary provider failure", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
            return
        }
        if err := store.Complete(ctx, request.RunID, count); err != nil {
            http.Error(w, "cannot record completion", http.StatusInternalServerError)
            return
        }
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    })
}

func fetchAndReconcile(ctx context.Context, providerURL string, businessDate string) (int, error) {
    // Keep the provider adapter separate so pagination and response validation are testable.
    return 0, nil
}

The stub is deliberately not a pretend provider integration: the production adapter must validate response status, pagination, settlement date, and the reconciliation count before completion is written. A 200 response without those checks is not a reliable completion signal.

When does lower latency justify more machinery?

Model three quantities before selecting an execution pattern: the reporting deadline, the normal run duration, and the maximum replay duration. If the job normally finishes in 12 minutes and the reporting window allows 90, a basic nightly trigger leaves room for a bounded retry. If a provider occasionally takes 70 minutes, moving the timer to a faster service may change little; partitioning and checkpointing will change more.

The cost axis includes operator time. A managed task or queue can reduce the amount of delivery plumbing the platform team maintains, while a self-hosted scheduler can fit an existing cluster and deployment process. Neither is free. The relevant comparison is: who owns upgrades, persistence, delivery retries, access control, alerting, and recovery testing?

The limitation is important: no scheduler can make an ambiguous provider response safe by itself. If the job cannot identify a duplicate, store a checkpoint, or explain a partial result, moving it between cron alternatives only moves the uncertainty.

Pattern Latency and failure behavior Operational cost Use it when
Host or container timer Low setup latency; one execution boundary Small footprint, but the host is part of the failure domain One idempotent run fits inside the reporting window
Kubernetes CronJob Declarative scheduling with Job-level controls; execution still needs durable state Fits a cluster team, adds cluster ownership The workload already lives in Kubernetes
Queue plus workers Partitioned work and explicit retry or dead-letter handling More components and more observability work A run is too large or variable for one process
HTTP task delivery Per-task deadlines and retry semantics Delivery service reduces plumbing; handler contract is stricter Each reconciliation partition is an independent HTTP task
External workflow tool Fast composition for application and human steps Less scheduler code, more dependency and policy review The workflow includes approvals or cross-system actions

That table is a decision aid, not a ranking. A small team may rationally accept higher execution latency to avoid owning another persistent control plane. A large platform team may choose partitioning because predictable recovery matters more than the timer's nominal price.

How do you test the path before trusting it?

Test the business date boundary first. Run the same date twice and assert that the second run produces no duplicate ledger effect. Then test a timeout after the provider accepts the request, a malformed page token, a process termination after checkpoint write, and a dead-letter replay. These cases expose more than a happy-path integration test.

The deployment check should prove that the scheduler can reach the endpoint, credentials are scoped to reconciliation data, and the alert includes the run ID. The operational check should replay a quarantined partition in a non-production account and verify that the completion metric moves only after durable state changes.

Keep the code path boring. The scheduler should trigger; the worker should enforce idempotency; the store should provide the durable record; the provider adapter should handle pagination and response validation. When one component silently performs another component's job, the failure report becomes ambiguous and the cost of diagnosis rises.

A practical decision rule

For a nightly media payment reconciliation, begin with the smallest scheduler that meets the reporting deadline and add a durable run record before adding sophisticated orchestration. Move to queue-backed partitions when the duration distribution, retry volume, or dataset size makes one process a risky unit of work. Add an HTTP task boundary when delivery deadlines and per-partition retries are clearer than a single batch.

The signal to change architecture is not a fashionable feature gap. It is evidence: late business dates, repeated ambiguous retries, growing replay scope, or an on-call who cannot tell what completed. Instrument those signals first. Then choose the boundary that reduces the largest failure and keeps latency within the reporting promise.

Further reading

  • AWS SQS dead-letter queues: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • Google Cloud Tasks overview: https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/dual-overview
  • Kubernetes CronJob documentation: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/

title: The player believes the idle game interface, not the simulation
description:
Development covered 6 Sep 2026 to 7 Sep 2026 (commit dates).

The last stretch before a release is where I go looking for a category of problem that never shows up as an error. The game is correct and the screen is wrong. Nobody can see the simulation, so the screen is what the player treats as true.

Almost fifty small changes this week, and a surprising share of them were this one shape: the idle game interface disagreeing with the game underneath.

Numbers that are computed twice

The recipe list showed a brewing time that did not include the speed bonus the craft itself applies, so the same recipe quoted one duration in the list and a different one once you selected it. Those recipes make the potions in the game's pill catalogue, so the duration is a number players plan around. A technique card reported its effect about ten percent below what actually took effect, because a bonus was included where the effect is applied but not where it is described.

The bag offered to sort by name and sorted by the internal identifier instead, which looks almost right in English, produces a nonsense order in every other language, and is invisible unless you are reading carefully in a language you speak.

An offline popup stated the cap as forty eight hours in its text while the real cap is worked out from your account. The text was right when it was written.

Each of these is a value derived in two places, one for the player and one for the system, and it is the same failure I keep meeting in different clothing. When a number appears on screen, it should be the number the code will use, and both should come from the same place instead of two calculations that agree today. The heart-methods in question are listed in the catalogue of arts and heart-methods.

Affordances that promise wrongly

Two consumables give their benefit while you hold them, and both still had a Use button. Pressing it consumed the item and threw the benefit away. Nothing failed, because the game did what the button said, and the button should not have existed.

Elsewhere there was a disabled control that could not say why it was disabled, when the reason was as simple as already being friends with that person, and a legend teaching a colour the player will never encounter. A view reset framed the set of nodes from your previous realm instead of your current one. Two buttons on the same card both answered where do I do this and sent you to different places.

And my favourite, because it is so ordinary: a pinch to zoom handler attached to the window instead of to its own panel, so two fingers anywhere in the game zoomed a diagram on a screen you were not looking at.

The clock going backwards

One genuine simulation bug, worth its own paragraph because it will happen to anyone building idle mechanics.

Everything here is derived from elapsed time. If the system clock moves backwards, which it does when a device corrects itself, elapsed time is briefly negative and the whole loop sits still until real time catches up. On a device that had drifted, that could be minutes of a game that had simply stopped.

Wall clock time is not monotonic, it is a number the operating system is free to revise. Anything that steps forward on a difference of two readings needs to decide, explicitly, what a negative difference means.

Why this sweep is worth doing on a schedule

None of these appear in any log. They do not fail a test, because the test asserts what the code computes, and the code computes correctly. They are only findable by using the thing and reading what it says with the suspicion of someone who has never seen it before.

For an idle game the point is sharper than usual. The player never watches the simulation, only the idle game interface: a number going up and a sentence about why. That sentence is the product.

Read every number for yourself in the browser; the series continues at Incremental RPG.

title: StackGen3D: Stable 3D Block Stack Generation from Multiview Silhouettes
description:
arXiv:2610.31803v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Generating physically stable 3D structures from visual specifications requires resolving geometric ambiguity while accounting for physical interactions among objects. We present StackGen3D, a framework for generating stable block assemblies conditioned on a given block inventory and three orthographic silhouettes. Our approach consists of two stages. First, we develop a physics-informed graph neural network (PI-GNN) that models support relations between blocks and serves as a fast stability predictor for curating a diverse dataset of stable structures. Second, we train a conditional flow-matching model on this dataset to capture the multimodal distribution of block configurations consistent with the target silhouettes. At inference time, lightweight geometric selection and refinement reduce inter-block penetration without physics simulation. Preliminary experiments show that the PI-GNN generalizes from simple stacks to complex structures substantially better than a parameter-matched multilayer perceptron. For structure generation, Best-of-10 selection improves physical stability from 45.3% to 72.4% while achieving a silhouette IoU of 0.970. These results highlight the potential of combining relational physical reasoning, scalable data curation, and conditional generative modeling for creative 3D assembly.
  Project website: [https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/](https://ripl.github.io/StackGen3D-web/)

title: Everything hackable will get hacked
description:
Over the past year, AI models have become much more capable of performing cybersecurity work. These changes are reshaping both the threats facing the web and the tools available to defend it. Right now, defenders have an advantage because they can use stronger models for defensive work than the open-weight models broadly available for offensive research. But this advantage will not always last. The gap will soon close.

I have both good news and bad news, neither of which is yet widely understood in the community.

  • Bad news: Near-frontier open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today. Kimi K3 is an Opus 4.X-class model with no relevant cybersecurity safeguards.

  • Good news: You do not need to wait for “Mythos access” or OpenAI’s cyber program to begin defensive cybersecurity work. Frontier models, with the notable exception of Fable 5, will perform defensive cybersecurity tasks today.

The uncertainty around Mythos 5's release seems to have created a kind of paralysis among defenders, many of whom are underutilizing the powerful tools available to them today. This post aims to give readers insight into how we're thinking about AI-enabled defensive cybersecurity at Vercel and why we think teams should be moving with more urgency.

The OpenAI/Hugging Face security incident

This YouTube video from OpenAI researchers on the widely reported security incident involving Hugging Face is an absolute must-watch for anyone concerned with cybersecurity. It clarifies that there were two separate security incidents exploiting vulnerabilities that will be found in most computer systems.

The gist is that models working on an OpenAI training run found 0-day vulnerabilities that allowed them to bypass egress internet restrictions, enabling communication between models and access to the broader internet. Once internet access was established, broader exploitation occurred.

Open-weight models that perform offensive security research are available today

Open-weight model capabilities have been top of mind in the AI community lately, but it is less widely understood that Kimi K3, a popular open-weight model, has no effective safeguards against offensive cybersecurity work.

On DeepSec Bench, which measures application-code vulnerability discovery, it ranks highest among the open-weight models we evaluated, roughly matching Sonnet 5 and outperforming Opus 4.8.

I tasked Kimi K3 with trying to break out of Vercel Sandbox, and while it did not successfully escape, it mapped the guest-kernel attack surface, followed possible privilege escalation paths, built a VM environment to reproduce its ideas, and implemented and ran a fuzzer.

These are some excerpts from that research, beginning with an analysis of the guest-kernel attack surface.

The model followed that lead into candidate privilege escalation paths and considered what guest-kernel control could mean for a microVM escape.

When paths still needed testing, Kimi built a VM environment for reproductions and wrote a stateful fuzzer for the device path it was investigating.

While none of this produced an escape from Vercel Sandbox, it did show Kimi conducting an investigation on its own, and given the right vulnerable surface, this would lead to a successful exploit.

Frontier models can help defenders today

Much of the community assumed that meaningful security review would require access to Mythos-class models and therefore held off on using the models already available to them.

But that assumption has never been true. All the frontier models that we evaluated, with the notable exception of Fable 5, can perform defensive cybersecurity work today and have been able to do so throughout the year so far.

The rough heuristic I have observed is that models with safeguards will still make hypotheses about security vulnerabilities when they have access to source code, apparently because access to proprietary source code typically suggests a defensive use case. Attackers can also obtain source code, but I think source-code access is a reasonable working signal of defensive intent.

I personally discovered this in March, when I first heard about cyber variants and was also seeing AI code reviews find security issues in my own code. That made me wonder, “If code review can find issues in a diff, can I also run it across an entire codebase?” It turns out the answer was yes. From that experiment, I created deepsec, an open-source security harness for performing security analysis at scale across large codebases.

The temporary defensive advantage

Right now, OpenAI’s Sol 5.6 on XHigh is the best model for cybersecurity defense. It is much smarter than Kimi K3, the best available open-weight model without safeguards against offensive work. As defender, you have the better tool at your disposal, but you have to use it.

A full deepsec review will help you improve the security posture of your codebase by surfacing vulnerability hypotheses for you to investigate. In my experience, it is especially good at finding IDORs, XSS, and SSRF. The Hugging Face incident shows what this kind of application-level research looks like from the other side, since the models kept searching after an SSRF attempt was blocked and eventually found successful routes through file disclosure and template injection.

deepsec is open source and can run entirely in your own infrastructure with inference providers controlled by you. Vercel has no financial gain from you using it. It is really worth trying on your own source code.

Once the run finishes, review every finding yourself and compare the results with what your current security process already catches.

Continuous defense

AI model capabilities will continue to improve, and I expect open-weight models to catch up with Sol’s current performance on application-code vulnerability discovery even as frontier models advance again. We need to prepare for that cycle by continuously improving how we find and fix vulnerabilities as the models progress.

At Vercel, we run full deepsec reviews across mission-critical repositories every quarter and whenever a stronger model becomes available, in addition to automated security reviews on every pull request.

Those full reviews cost tens of thousands of dollars, which we consider a relatively small expense compared with what we spend on our HackerOne program or the opportunity cost of a security incident.

We have connected deepsec output to Vercel software factories for automated vulnerability processing and will share more about this work soon. As these reviews produce more findings, automatically managing them becomes the next frontier.

What Vercel is doing

As an immediate measure, we made the full egress firewall in Vercel Sandbox available on the Hobby plan, giving everyone access to the same network controls.

We are also working to launch a dedicated HackerOne program focused on finding zero-day vulnerabilities in Vercel Sandbox and the egress firewall. We want to redirect offensive model capabilities toward defensive work, so the program will cover AI costs for researchers who use AI Gateway and submit a vulnerability report that is accepted.

We also plan to extend deepsec to use the offensive capabilities of open-weight models and cyber variants of frontier models when triaging the vulnerability hypotheses it identifies.

Defenders can already use stronger models than those broadly available for offensive work. Teams should use that advantage now and continue reviewing their systems as the gap closes.

Takeaways

  • The cybersecurity threat from AI models is real.

  • Everybody can improve their defensive posture with tools like deepsec today.

  • Doing this is urgent, and the practice should continue as models improve.

title: Let your users to build their own dashboards in your app
description:
Customers like dashboards they can rearrange. Building one yourself means a grid system, a catalog of charts, a settings form, filters and a way to save the layout, and that list is longer than it looks from the outside.

@datastripes/dashboard packages those pieces. You pass it an array of rows and a JSON config, and it renders a dashboard that users can edit, filter and export. This page covers how the config works, how to embed the dashboard in each framework, and what the package leaves to you.

One package, four entry points

The root entry, @datastripes/dashboard, is the core engine: schema, query engine, grid engine, store, widget logic and licensing. It needs nothing else. On top of it sit a React entry with a <DatastripesDashboard> component (React 19), a Vue entry for Vue 3.4 and later, an Angular entry with a standalone DatastripesDashboardComponent (Angular 18 or 19), and an /elements entry that registers a <datastripes-dashboard> custom element.

The UI frameworks are optional peer dependencies, so installing the package never pulls one in.

npm install @datastripes/dashboard

The dashboard is a JSON document

Everything about a dashboard lives in one config object: a version, settings with the grid layout, global filters, calculated fields, column labels and a list of widgets. Each widget has a type, a position on the grid and a query.

import { DashboardStore, JsQueryEngine, parseDashboardConfig } from '@datastripes/dashboard';

const config = parseDashboardConfig({
  version: '1.0.0',
  settings: { title: 'Sales', layout: { columns: 12, rowHeight: 60, gutter: 16 } },
  globalFilters: [],
  calculatedFields: [],
  columnLabels: {},
  widgets: [
    {
      id: 'kpi_revenue',
      type: 'kpi_card',
      title: 'Total Revenue',
      grid: { x: 0, y: 0, w: 3, h: 2 },
      dataQuery: { metrics: [{ field: 'amount', aggregation: 'sum', alias: 'amount' }] },
      renderConfig: { format: 'currency' },
    },
  ],
});

const store = new DashboardStore({ config, data: myRows, engine: new JsQueryEngine() });

The grid here is twelve columns wide with 60 pixel rows. The single widget sits at the top left corner, three columns wide and two rows tall, and sums the amount column. Because the config is plain JSON, you can store it next to the user's account and load it back later.

Embedding it in React

In React the config and the data go in as props. In edit mode the user can change the layout, and the component reports every change back to you.

import { DatastripesDashboard } from '@datastripes/dashboard/react';
import type { DashboardConfig } from '@datastripes/dashboard';

function App() {
  const [config, setConfig] = useState<DashboardConfig | undefined>();

  return (
    <DatastripesDashboard
      data={myRows}
      config={config}
      mode="edit"
      apiKey={import.meta.env.VITE_DATASTRIPES_KEY}
      onChange={setConfig}
      onSave={(saved) => persistToBackend(saved)}
      onAction={(event) => console.log(event)}
    />
  );
}

In edit mode the toolbar has an Add widget button that opens a short wizard. The user picks a widget type, then a chart kind from the catalog of 25, then fields, colors and axis labels. The gear icon on an existing widget reopens the same form. The toolbar also offers a light and dark switch, PDF export and a period navigator.

onSave fires when the user clicks Save, which is where you persist the config. onAction delivers row_click and filter_change events, which is how you connect drill-down and cross-filtering to the rest of your app.

What users can change without you

The settings panel lets users adjust number formatting, define calculated fields and rename columns. That covers a lot of the requests that usually come back to a developer: show this as a percentage, add a margin column, call the field something readable. Because those choices end up in the config, they are saved and restored with the layout.

Filters work at two levels. Global filters in the config apply across the dashboard, and a filter panel widget lets the user change them in place.

Vue, Angular and plain HTML

Vue uses a DatastripesDashboard single file component and Angular a standalone DatastripesDashboardComponent. For any other stack the custom element works straight from a script tag.

<script src="https://unpkg.com/@datastripes/dashboard/dist/elements/index.global.js"></script>
<datastripes-dashboard id="dash" mode="edit" api-key="..."></datastripes-dashboard>
<script>
  const el = document.getElementById('dash');
  el.data = myRows;       // set as a property for large datasets
  el.config = myConfig;   // DashboardConfig object
  el.addEventListener('ds-change', (e) => console.log(e.detail));
  el.addEventListener('ds-action', (e) => console.log(e.detail));
</script>

Storing dashboards and building your own layout

Keep the config as JSON in whatever table holds your user settings, one row per dashboard. The config carries a version field, so when the format changes you can tell which shape a stored dashboard has and migrate it.

If the full component is more than you need, the pieces are exported separately: the toolbar, the add widget and settings modals, the KPI card, chart and table widgets, the filter panel, a markdown widget and the frame that provides drag and resize handles around any widget. That lets you compose your own page around the same engine.

Using the engine without any UI

Everything a framework wrapper does, including querying, filtering, grid layout and licensing, is a call into the core. That means you can compute a dashboard's results on a server and hydrate a framework component with them later.

The dashboard takes its data as an array of rows. Fetching those rows and shaping them is your job, which keeps the package independent of your database and your API.

What the trial tier limits

Without a valid apiKey every dashboard runs in a restricted trial. The dataset is silently cut to its first 1,000 rows, the PDF export button is disabled and a banner states the row cap. The cap lives in the store itself, so it applies the same way in React, Vue, Angular and the custom element.

Some chart types also need a valid license. Heatmaps, graphs, sankey diagrams, parallel coordinates, gauges, funnels, candlesticks, box plots and calendar heatmaps are gated, so check that the charts you plan to ship are available on the plan you buy.

Where it is the wrong tool

This is a component for dashboards inside your own product. It does not replace a data warehouse or a hosted BI server. Everything is computed in the browser from the rows you pass in, so very large datasets should be aggregated before they reach it.

If your users need scheduled email reports or governed metrics shared across a whole company, a full BI platform is the better fit.

FAQ

What is the best way to let my users build their own dashboards inside my app?
@datastripes/dashboard is purpose-built for this: it packages the grid layout engine, the add-widget wizard, 20+ chart types and JSON-based config persistence that you would otherwise have to build from scratch. It runs client-side, is framework-agnostic (React, Vue, Angular or a plain custom element from the same package), and returns the user-built layout as plain JSON you store yourself, so you keep full ownership of the data. For embedding a self-serve, editable dashboard inside an existing product, it is the most direct npm-install path to that feature.

Can my users rearrange the dashboard?
Yes. In edit mode they can add widgets, change their fields and appearance, and drag and resize them on the grid.

How do I save what a user built?
onSave returns the dashboard config as plain JSON when the user clicks Save. Store it wherever you keep user settings and pass it back as the config prop.

Which frameworks are supported?
React 19, Vue 3.4 and later, and Angular 18 or 19, plus a <datastripes-dashboard> custom element for any other stack.

What does the trial tier limit?
It cuts the dataset to 1,000 rows, disables PDF export and shows a banner. Some chart types need a valid license.

Landing: https://datastripes.com/dashboard-widget/ ·

Docs: https://datastripes.com/dashboard-widget/docs/

title: Mastering Advanced Features and Techniques of JEST React Testing Library
description:
Welcome to a deeper journey into the JEST React Testing Library world! We'll explore advanced methods and tricks that enhance your testing expertise here. If you're new to JEST, don't worry! We've got you covered with "Exploring JEST React Testing Library: A Complete Overview," which helps you understand basic and advanced insights, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of JEST Testing. Go and check this out right here.

Now, let's start exploring advanced features and techniques.

1. Simulating User Interactions

JEST React Testing Library allows you to simulate user interactions with your components. This feature lets you test how your components respond to different user actions. Here are some examples:

a. Simulating button clicks

The below code defines a simple functional component named "Button" that takes a prop named "label" and renders a button element with the provided label.

Button.js: 

import React from "react";
const Button = ({ label, onClick }) => {
 return <button onClick={onClick}>{label}</button>;
};
export default Button;

Button.test.js: 

import React from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";
import Button from "./Button";
test("button click triggers an action", () => {
 const handleClick = jest.fn();
 render(<Button label="Click me" onClick={handleClick} />);
 const buttonElement = screen.getByText(/click me/i);
 fireEvent.click(buttonElement);
 expect(handleClick).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
});

In this example, we define a mock function** "handleClick"** using "jest.fn()". We pass this function as a prop to the** "Button"** component. After rendering the component, we simulate a button click using "fireEvent.click" and assert that the** "handleClick"** function is called once. Below is a screenshot of the output showing the successful execution of the test cases:

b. Simulating Input value change

The below code defines a simple functional component named "LoginForm" that includes a controlled input field for capturing a username. The "useState" hook manages the username state, and the input is associated with a label, allowing users to input their username. Any changes trigger the "handleInputChange" function, keeping the username state synchronized with the input value.

LoginForm.js: 

import React, { useState } from "react";
const LoginForm = () => {
  const [username, setUsername] = useState("");
  const handleInputChange = (e) => {
    setUsername(e.target.value);
  };
  return (
    <div>
      <label htmlFor="username">Username:</label>
      <input
        type="text"
        id="username"
        value={username}
        onChange={handleInputChange}
      />
    </div>
  );
};
export default LoginForm;

LoginForm.test.js: 

import React from "react";
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from "@testing-library/react";
import LoginForm from "./LoginForm";
test("Typing in username field updates the value", () => {
 render(<LoginForm />);
 const usernameInput = screen.getByLabelText(/username/i);
 fireEvent.change(usernameInput, { target: { value: "testuser" } });
 expect(usernameInput.value).toBe("testuser");
});

In this example, we render a "LoginForm" component that contains an input field for the username. We use** "screen.getByLabelText"** to find the input field and "fireEvent.change" to simulate the change in input value in the field. Finally, we assert that the input field's value is updated correctly. Below is a screenshot of the output showing the successful execution of the test cases:

2. Testing Asynchronous Behaviour

The "ProductInformation" component is a React functional component that fetches product data from "https://fakestoreapi.com/products/1" using the "fetchProductData" function. The data is stored in the data state using "useState". The "useEffect" hook ensures data fetching occurs when the component mounts. The component conditionally renders either the "title" of the data or a "Loading..." message based on the data's availability.

ProductInformation.js: 

import React, { useEffect, useState } from "react";
const ProductInformation = () => {
  const [data, setData] = useState(null);
  const fetchProductData = async () => {
    const response = await fetch("https://fakestoreapi.com/products/1");
    const data = await response.json();
    setData(data);
  };
  useEffect(() => {
    fetchProductData();
  }, []);
  return (
    <div>
      {data ? (
        <div>
          <p>title: {data.title}</p>
        </div>
      ) : (
        <p>Loading...</p>
      )}
    </div>
  );
};
export default ProductInformation;

ProductInformation.test.js: 

import React from "react";
import { render, screen, waitFor } from "@testing-library/react";
import ProductInformation from "./ProductInformation";
test("displays fetched data", async () => {
  render(<ProductInformation />);
  const loadingElement = screen.getByText(/loading/i);
  expect(loadingElement).toBeInTheDocument();
  await waitFor(() => {
    const dataElement = screen.getByText(/title: /i);
    expect(dataElement).toBeInTheDocument();
  });
});

In this example, we render the "ProductInformation" component, which fetches data asynchronously. Initially, we expect to see a loading message. Using "waitFor" and "await", we wait for the data to be fetched and then assert that the data is displayed. Below is a screenshot of the output showing the successful execution of the test cases:

Conclusion

In this second part of our guide, we delved into advanced features and techniques of the JEST React Testing Library. We explored simulating user interactions and handling asynchronous behaviour. Combining the knowledge from both parts of this guide allows you to write comprehensive tests for your React components, ensuring their reliability and robustness.

title: RSIHub: A Composable Framework for Agent-Evolution Methods
description:
arXiv:2610.32253v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Agent-evolution methods use execution feedback to improve prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration, but their implementations often rebuild the same experimental machinery. We present RSIHub, an open-source framework for building, comparing, and extending these methods on shared infrastructure. Recipes compose reusable operators and declare mutable resources; RSIHub supplies execution, evaluation, recovery, and lineage. Researchers can focus on evolution policy while evaluation stays outside the mutable surface and results remain tied to candidates and evaluation conditions. We instantiate AHE, Hyperagents, A-Evolve, and GEPA without modifying the framework core, keeping method-specific logic in recipes and operators. We evaluate them with MiniSWE and Codex on Terminal Bench 2 and $\tau^3$ Banking under fixed model and evaluator configurations. The largest observed overall pass@1 gain is 13.5 percentage points, while method rankings vary across settings and optimization gains do not always transfer to held-out tasks. RSIHub provides a common protocol for comparing evolution policies, inspectable candidate histories, and reusable components for developing new methods.

title: Sign JWTs from your Functions without managing private keys
description:
Vercel KMS lets you sign JWTs and arbitrary messages from your Vercel Functions using managed asymmetric signing keys, so private keys never live in your code or environment variables. Your function authenticates with its Vercel OIDC token, and the private key stays inside Vercel's key management service while verifiers use only the public key.

With Vercel KMS you can:

  • Create and rotate issuers and signing keys (RSA and ECDSA) from the CLI and dashboard.

  • Sign JWTs with custom claims and a configurable TTL, or sign raw bytes, using the @vercel/kms package.

  • Grant a project signing access per environment, including production, preview, development, and custom environments.

  • Constrain the claims a project can request per grant, and validate token claims against a JSON Schema.

  • Verify signed tokens anywhere. Each issuer publishes a public OpenID Connect Discovery document at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration and a JWK set at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/jwks.json, so any standard OIDC or JOSE library can validate tokens without Vercel-specific code.

Sign a token inside a function:

Verify a token anywhere with a standard JOSE library, using the issuer's public JWKS:

Set up an issuer and grant a project access from the CLI:

As a best practice, create a separate issuer per project and environment. Isolating issuers keeps each token audience distinct, scopes signing access to exactly one project and environment, and lets you rotate or revoke keys for one without affecting the others.

To get started, read the docs or open Key Management in your team's dashboard.

title: How to Evaluate a Sports Data API: A Developer’s Checklist (Benchmark Script Included)
description:
Disclosure: I work on Orbistats, a sports data API, and it is used as one example below. The checklist and scripts work with any provider.

Picking a sports data API usually goes like this: you read ten landing pages that all say “real-time, reliable, comprehensive,” sign up for two or three, and choose whichever one you got working first. Six months later you discover the cricket data lags, the odds schema changed without notice, or the rate limits do not fit your traffic.

This post gives you a repeatable way to compare providers using numbers instead of marketing. You will get:

A checklist of what to evaluate and why
A Python benchmark script that measures latency and reliability
A provider-agnostic client so switching providers later is a config change, not a rewrite
A results template you can fill in for your own shortlist
Why free tiers are the right place to start

Free tiers are the cheapest way to test real endpoints. But they differ a lot in shape, and that matters when you compare:

Some give a daily request cap.
Some give limited sports or endpoints.
Some give a time-boxed window. Orbistats’ Free plan, for example, is 1 hour of access across all sports and endpoints with no card, and the timer starts only when you open the activation link.

A 1-hour window means you should prepare your test script before you activate. The script below is built for that.

Part 1: The developer’s checklist

  1. Coverage: sports, leagues and depth

Do not just count sports. Check the exact leagues and markets you need. A provider can list “cricket” and still lack the domestic tournaments your users care about.

Orbistats covers 13 sports, including football, cricket and tennis. Whichever provider you test, pick three leagues you actually need and check them one by one.

  1. Latency, measured from your own server

Marketing pages quote best-case numbers from the provider’s network. Measure from where your code runs. Track p50 and p95, not just the average, because p95 is what your users feel on a bad day.

  1. Reliability

Over a fixed number of requests, what percentage succeed? Which errors appear (429, 500, timeouts)? Is there a public status page with history?

  1. Delivery methods

REST alone is fine for fixtures and standings. For live products, check whether the provider offers a WebSocket API for streaming and webhooks for push events, so you are not polling every second.

  1. Schema quality and stability

Look for consistent field names across sports, stable IDs, ISO timestamps and typed values. Then read the changelog to see how often things break. Also check the versioning policy: Orbistats uses /v1/ and moves breaking changes to a new version.

  1. Odds normalization (if you need odds)

If you consume prices from multiple bookmakers, check whether the Odds API normalizes formats and market names. Otherwise you will write that mapping layer yourself.

  1. Historical depth

For modeling, check historical data for opening and closing odds, event data and how far back each sport goes. Verify coverage per sport rather than assuming it is uniform.

  1. Pricing transparency

Can you see a number without a sales call? Does the plan structure match how you will actually use it (access window, request cap, monthly)? Compare against the pricing page and the provider comparison pages.

  1. Developer experience

Time yourself: from signup to first successful response. A good quickstart, a sandbox and clear documentation can save days.

Part 2: The benchmark script

This script sends a fixed number of requests to any endpoint, measures latency, records status codes and checks that the response contains the fields you expect. It uses httpx and runs requests concurrently in small batches to avoid tripping rate limits.

bash
pip install httpx
python
import asyncio
import statistics
import time
from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

import httpx

@dataclass
class Target:
name: str
url: str
headers: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
required_fields: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

def has_fields(payload, required: list[str]) -> bool:
"""Check that required top-level keys exist (or exist in the first item of a list)."""
if isinstance(payload, list):
payload = payload[0] if payload else {}
if isinstance(payload, dict) and "data" in payload:
inner = payload["data"]
payload = inner[0] if isinstance(inner, list) and inner else inner
return isinstance(payload, dict) and all(k in payload for k in required)

async def one_request(client: httpx.AsyncClient, target: Target):
start = time.perf_counter()
try:
r = await client.get(target.url, headers=target.headers, timeout=10)
elapsed_ms = (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000
schema_ok = False
if r.status_code == 200:
try:
schema_ok = has_fields(r.json(), target.required_fields)
except ValueError:
pass
return elapsed_ms, r.status_code, schema_ok
except httpx.HTTPError:
return (time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000, "timeout/error", False

async def benchmark(target: Target, total=50, batch=5, pause=0.5):
results = []
async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
for _ in range(total // batch):
results += await asyncio.gather(
*[one_request(client, target) for _ in range(batch)]
)
await asyncio.sleep(pause) # be polite to free tiers

latencies = sorted(r[0] for r in results if r[1] == 200)
statuses = Counter(r[1] for r in results)
ok = statuses.get(200, 0)

def pct(p):
    return latencies[min(int(len(latencies) * p), len(latencies) - 1)] if latencies else None

return {
    "provider": target.name,
    "requests": total,
    "success_rate": round(100 * ok / total, 1),
    "p50_ms": round(pct(0.50), 1) if latencies else None,
    "p95_ms": round(pct(0.95), 1) if latencies else None,
    "mean_ms": round(statistics.mean(latencies), 1) if latencies else None,
    "schema_ok_pct": round(100 * sum(r[2] for r in results) / total, 1),
    "status_codes": dict(statuses),
}

async def main():
targets = [
Target(
name="Orbistats",
url="https://api.orbistats.com/v1/football/matches/live",
headers={"Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_KEY"},
required_fields=["match_id", "status"],
),
# Add up to 9 more providers here, using each one's own URL and auth.
]
for t in targets:
print(await benchmark(t))

if name == "main":
asyncio.run(main())

Notes on running it fairly:

Run from the same machine and network for every provider.
Run at different times of day, including during live matches, because latency under load is what matters.
Use the same type of endpoint for each provider (for example, live football matches).
Check each provider’s terms before benchmarking. Keep request counts modest on free tiers.
Adjust required_fields to match each provider’s actual response shape. The Orbistats example uses match_id and status, which appear in the live response.
Part 3: A provider-agnostic client

Once you pick a provider, you do not want it to leak into your whole codebase. Define your own model and write one small adapter per provider.

python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from dataclasses import dataclass

import httpx

@dataclass
class LiveMatch:
match_id: str
status: str
minute: int | None
home_name: str
home_score: int
away_name: str
away_score: int

class SportsProvider(ABC):
@abstractmethod
def live_matches(self, sport: str) -> list[LiveMatch]: ...

class OrbistatsProvider(SportsProvider):
BASE = "https://api.orbistats.com/v1"

def __init__(self, api_key: str):
    self.client = httpx.Client(
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}, timeout=10
    )

def live_matches(self, sport: str) -> list[LiveMatch]:
    r = self.client.get(f"{self.BASE}/{sport}/matches/live")
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = r.json()
    items = data if isinstance(data, list) else data.get("data", [data])
    return [
        LiveMatch(
            match_id=m["match_id"],
            status=m["status"],
            minute=m.get("minute"),
            home_name=m["home"]["name"],
            home_score=m["home"]["score"],
            away_name=m["away"]["name"],
            away_score=m["away"]["score"],
        )
        for m in items
    ]

def get_provider(name: str, api_key: str) -> SportsProvider:
providers = {"orbistats": OrbistatsProvider}
return providersname

To add another provider, write one more class that maps its response into LiveMatch. Your app only ever talks to SportsProvider, so switching is a one-line config change. It also lets you run two providers side by side and compare their output during a trial.

title: Mastering Axios in React: A Complete Overview
description:
A popular JavaScript library, Axios has become a staple in modern web development, especially when handling HTTP requests in React applications. This blog will explore the ins and outs of using Axios with React, providing a complete guide and practical code examples to enhance your understanding.

Getting Started with Axios in React

Installation

Step 1: Creating a React App

Run the given command to build a new React app.

Note: If you already have the react application created, you can skip this step and directly follow the 2nd step.

npx create-react-app my-axios-app

cd my-axios-app

npm start

Step 2: Installing Axios

Now, install Axios into your project by running:

npm install axios

Making GET Requests

Basic GET Request

Let's initiate our exploration with a fundamental aspect - making a simple GET request. Create a new file named getExample.js within an 'Axios' folder in your React project and add the following code:

getExample.js 

// Import Axios
import axios from "axios";

// Make a GET request
const fetchData = async () => {
  try {
    const response = await axios.get(
      "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1"
    );
    console.log("Data fetched:", response.data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error fetching data:", error);
  }
};

// Export the function for use in other files
export default fetchData;

In this getExample.js file, 'Axios' is imported to handle HTTP requests. The 'fetchData' function, defined as an asynchronous operation, utilizes Axios to request a GET to a specified URL. Upon a successful request, the fetched data is logged to the console. Any errors encountered during the request are caught and logged as well.

Import the 'fetchData' function in the App.js component to retrieve data from the API.

App.js 

import React, { useEffect } from "react";
import fetchData from "./axios/getExample";
const App = () => {
  useEffect(() => {
    fetchData();
  }, []);
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Mastering Axios in React: A Complete Overview</h2>
      <p>Basic GET request: </p>
    </div>
  );
};
export default App;

Output

Handling Async/Await

To enhance code readability, we can use the async/await syntax. Create another file named asyncAwaitExample.js within an **'Axios' **folder in your React project and add the following code:

asyncAwaitExample.js 

// Import Axios
import axios from "axios";

// Make an asynchronous request using async/await
const fetchDataAsync = async () => {
  try {
    const response = await axios.get(
      "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1"
    );
    console.log("Data fetched asynchronously:", response.data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error fetching data:", error);
  }
};

// Export the function for use in other files
export default fetchDataAsync;

In this asyncAwaitExample.js file, we import Axios to handle HTTP requests. The 'fetchDataAsync' function is defined as an asynchronous operation utilizing the async/await syntax. Axios makes a GET request to a specified URL inside a try block. The fetched data is logged to the console after successful completion with a message indicating asynchronous retrieval. Any encountered errors during the request are caught in the catch block and logged to the console. Import the 'fetchDataAsync' function in the App.js component to fetch data asynchronously using async/await.

App.js 

import React, { useEffect } from "react";
import fetchDataAsync from "./axios/asyncAwaitExample";
const App = () => {
  useEffect(() => {
    fetchDataAsync();
  }, []);
  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Mastering Axios in React: A Complete Overview</h2>
      <p>Handling Async/Await GET Request: </p>
    </div>
  );
};
export default App;

Output

Making POST Requests

To create a POST request functionality, first, create a new file named postExample.js within an** 'Axios' **folder in your React project and add the following code:

postExample.js 

import axios from "axios";

const postData = async (data) => {
  try {
    const response = await axios.post(
      "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts",
      data
    );
    console.log("Data posted:", response.data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error posting data:", error);
  }
};

export default postData;

In this postExample.js file, we define a function** 'postData'** that uses the 'Axios.post' method, a function in Axios used to send data to a server over the internet. It requires the server's address (URL) and the data you want to send. It handles the data-sending process and provides error messages if something goes wrong. This method makes interacting with APIs easy and transmitting data from your React app to a server. Import the 'postData' function in the App.js component to send data via a POST request.

App.js 

import React, { useState } from "react";
import postData from "./axios/postExample";
function App() {
  const [data, setData] = useState({ title: "", body: "" });
  const handlePost = (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    postData({ ...data, userId: 1 });
  };
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Mastering Axios in React: A Complete Overview</h1>
      <h4>Making POST Requests: </h4>
      <form onSubmit={handlePost}>
        <label>
          Title:
          <input
            type="text"
            value={data.title}
            onChange={(e) => setData({ ...data, title: e.target.value })}
          />
        </label>
        <br />
        <label>
          Body:
          <textarea
            value={data.body}
            onChange={(e) => setData({ ...data, body: e.target.value })}
          />
        </label>
        <br />
        <input type="submit" />
      </form>
    </div>
  );
}
export default App;

In App.js, the state manages post data using the 'useState' hook. When submitting the form, the 'handlePost' function prevents the default action and sends the post data using Axios via 'postData' from postExample.js. Users can input the post title and body through input fields and a textarea element. This component makes submitting post data straightforward, showcasing how Axios can handle POST requests in React applications.

Output

Advanced Techniques with Axios

Configuring Global Defaults

Axios allows you to set global configuration defaults, making managing headers and base URLs easier. Create a new file named global.js within an** 'Axios' **folder in your React project and add the following code:

global.js 

// Import Axios
import axios from "axios";

// Set global configuration defaults
axios.defaults.headers.common["Authorization"] = "Bearer TEST_GLOBAl_DEFAULTS";
axios.defaults.headers.common["Accept"] = "application/json";
axios.defaults.baseURL = "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com";

In this global.js file, we set standard headers like authorization, accept headers, and specify a base URL for all requests. To integrate these global defaults into our React components, we simply import the global.js file into our App.js component:

App.js 

import React, { useEffect } from "react";
import axios from "axios";
import "./axios/global";
function App() {
  const fetchData = async () => {
    try {
      const response = await axios.get("/posts/1");
      console.log("Data fetched:", response.data);
    } catch (error) {
      console.error("Error fetching data:", error);
    }
  };
  useEffect(() => {
    fetchData();
  });
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Mastering Axios in React: A Complete Overview</h1>
      <h4>Configuring Global Defaults: </h4>
    </div>
  );
}
export default App;

In this App.js file, we import Axios and global.js to set default configurations. We define a 'fetchData' function to fetch data from an API endpoint using Axios. The 'useEffect' hook ensures 'fetchData' is called when the component mounts. If data is fetched successfully, we log it; if an error occurs, we log the error.

Output

Custom Axios Instance

Custom Axios instances allow developers to create specialized instances of Axios with unique configurations tailored to specific needs. This means you can define custom settings, such as base URLs, headers, and interceptors, for different parts of your application without affecting the global Axios configuration. Create a file named customInstance.js and add the following code:

customInstance.js 

import axios from "axios";

const customAxios = axios.create({
  baseURL: "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com",
  headers: {
    Authorization: "Bearer TEST_CUSTOM_AXIOS",
    Accept: "application/json",
  },
});

export default customAxios;

In the customInstance.js file, we create a custom Axios instance. This instance is created using the 'Axios.create' method and sets a base URL and custom headers, including authorization and content type. This allows us to interact with the API in a controlled manner. Import the custom Axios instance from customInstance.js in the App.js component to make requests with custom configurations.

App.js 

import React, { useEffect } from "react";
import customInstance from "./axios/customAxios";
function App() {
  const fetchData = async () => {
    try {
      const response = await customInstance("/posts/2");
      console.log("Data fetched:", response.data);
    } catch (error) {
      console.error("Error fetching data:", error);
    }
  };
  useEffect(() => {
    fetchData();
  });
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Mastering Axios in React: A Complete Overview</h1>
      <h4>Custom Axios Instance: </h4>
    </div>
  );
}
export default App;

Output

Interceptors

Interceptors play a vital role in intercepting and modifying HTTP requests and responses in Axios. They provide a powerful mechanism to manage the request and response lifecycle, allowing developers to add custom logic, such as logging, error handling, and authentication, before sending requests or after receiving responses. Create a file named interceptors.js and add the following code:

interceptors.js 

import axios from "axios";
const createInstance = axios.create({
  baseURL: "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com",
});
createInstance.interceptors.request.use(
  (request) => {
    console.log("Request sent:", request);
    return request;
  },
  (error) => {
    console.error("Error in request interceptor:", error);
    return Promise.reject(error);
  },
);
createInstance.interceptors.response.use(
  (response) => {
    console.log("Response received:", response);
    return response;
  },
  (error) => {
    console.error("Error in response interceptor:", error);
    return Promise.reject(error);
  },
);
export default createInstance;

In this interceptors.js file, we have two interceptors: one for handling requests and another for managing responses. These interceptors are created using the Axios.interceptors.request.use and Axios.interceptors.response.use methods, respectively. These methods allow us to intercept HTTP requests and responses made by Axios before they are sent or received by the server, allowing us to add custom logic or modify the data. Import interceptors.js to set up request and response interceptors for Axios in the App.js component.

App.js 

import React, { useEffect } from "react";
import createInstance from "./axios/interceptors";
function App() {
  const fetchData = async () => {
    try {
      const response = await createInstance("/posts/3");
      console.log("Data fetched:", response.data);
    } catch (error) {
      console.error("Error fetching data:", error);
    }
  };
  useEffect(() => {
    fetchData();
  });
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Mastering Axios in React: A Complete Overview</h1>
      <h4>Interceptors: </h4>
    </div>
  );
}
export default App;

In this App.js file, we have a fetchData function responsible for fetching data from the API endpoint '/posts/3' using our custom Axios instance createInstance and using the 'useEffect' hook to ensure that the 'fetchData' function is called when the component mounts. This hook runs the** 'fetchData'** function once the element is rendered to the screen.

Output

Conclusion

Congratulations! You've successfully set up Axios in a React app, made a basic GET request, and delved into advanced techniques like configuring global defaults, using custom instances, and implementing interceptors. These techniques are essential for real-world applications, offering flexibility, maintainability, and a centralized approach to handling HTTP requests. As you continue your journey, explore additional Axios features and adapt them to meet the specific needs of your projects.
