title: AI Needs Better Batteries. Better Batteries Need AI
description:
From iron-air batteries to CO₂ storage, the next energy breakthrough may be coordinating electricity and computation—not just inventing a better battery

Training a model is a computing problem.

Keeping its infrastructure powered through a windless night, a demand spike, or several days of weak renewable generation is an energy problem.

Increasingly, those two problems belong in the same architecture.

AI can help improve how energy storage is designed and operated. Energy storage can help supply the electricity that AI infrastructure needs. Between them sits a third opportunity: software that coordinates when electricity is stored, when it is released, and when flexible computation runs.

The most interesting connection is not an LLM attached to a battery dashboard.

It is coordination.

Two directions of innovation—and a missing middle

The relationship between AI and energy storage runs in two directions:

AI → Energy storage
Better models, experiments, forecasts, and operating decisions

Energy storage → AI
Electricity available beyond the moment it is generated

Both directions already have concrete examples.

Researchers at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory have combined neural networks with physical models to study redox flow battery performance. Google, meanwhile, has announced a collaboration with Energy Dome to support long-duration storage deployment. pnnl

But the missing middle is where things become especially interesting for developers:

Forecast renewable generation
            ↓
Estimate available storage
            ↓
Understand computing deadlines
            ↓
Optimize energy and workload schedules together
            ↓
Execute within explicit operating constraints

Instead of treating a data center as an inflexible electricity consumer and a battery as an isolated asset, we can investigate them as parts of a coordinated system.

First, stop treating every battery as the same product

“How long can it supply power?” is a different question from “How efficiently does it return stored electricity?”

And neither question tells us everything about lifetime, operating cost, deployment constraints, or maintenance.

The technologies entering this discussion are also more diverse than the word battery suggests:

Technology Example company Storage mechanism
Iron–air Form Energy Electrochemical storage
Vanadium flow Invinity Electrochemical storage using circulating electrolytes
Aqueous zinc Eos Zinc-based electrochemical storage
CO₂ storage Energy Dome A thermomechanical cycle
Advanced compressed air Hydrostor Compressed-air energy storage
Liquid air Highview Power Air liquefaction and subsequent energy recovery

These are different engineering systems, not interchangeable versions of one device. formenergy

Their intended time horizons differ, too. Energy Dome describes an 8–24-hour operating envelope, while Form Energy targets approximately 100 hours of discharge. blog

That creates a software problem: how should resources with different capabilities work together?

1. AI can improve the models behind storage

A storage controller needs some representation of the equipment it operates.

How much usable energy remains? How will performance change with temperature? What happens if operating conditions shift?

One promising approach combines physical modeling with machine learning rather than asking a neural network to learn everything from scratch.

A PNNL study coupled a deep neural network with a multiscale redox flow battery model. It investigated variable electrolyte inlet velocity to reduce pumping power, with a small reduction in discharge power. This was a modeling result—not proof of performance in a particular commercial product. pnnl

The distinction matters.

“AI improved a simulated operating strategy” is a useful research result.

“AI has solved commercial battery efficiency” is a different claim.

Where this could go next

The following are project directions, not claims about what the named companies currently deploy:

  • For flow batteries: estimate internal conditions and investigate pump scheduling.
  • For iron–air systems: model usable energy and plan reserves across several days.
  • For zinc batteries: investigate charging strategies and detect abnormal behavior.
  • For CO₂, compressed-air, and liquid-air systems: develop fast surrogate models for operating-point optimization.

Each proposal needs equipment-specific data, physical constraints, and validation.

A model that works for one storage chemistry does not automatically transfer to another.

2. AI can help decide which experiment to run next

Improving storage also means improving materials and manufacturing processes.

Here, the useful question is not simply:

Can a model predict a material property?

It is:

Which experiment should we run next to learn something valuable?

That creates a feedback loop:

Propose conditions
        ↓
Run experiment
        ↓
Measure outcome
        ↓
Update model and uncertainty
        ↓
Select the next experiment

Researchers at PNNL and the University of Washington demonstrated an autonomous experimental workflow for optimizing the synthesis of fluorenone derivatives relevant to redox flow batteries. Using Bayesian optimization over factors including concentration, reaction time, and temperature, the workflow identified 11 conditions with synthesis yields above 90%. pnnl

That percentage describes chemical synthesis yield.

It does not describe battery efficiency.

This is exactly the kind of distinction good technical communication must preserve: AI may improve one step in a development pipeline without solving the entire energy-storage problem.

3. The larger opportunity is deciding when to use what

Imagine a hypothetical system with:

  • Wind and solar generation.
  • A storage resource intended for shorter-duration cycling.
  • Another intended for multiday energy delivery.
  • A data center with both urgent and deferrable workloads.

A simplistic strategy might discharge whichever storage asset currently looks cheapest.

A better research question asks what that decision does to the next several days.

Should the system preserve long-duration reserves because low renewable production is likely tomorrow?

Should it run a flexible computing job now, while electricity is abundant?

Should it keep additional reserves because the forecast is unusually uncertain?

These are connected decisions.

A proposed architecture could separate them into distinct layers:

Telemetry and external data
            ↓
Probabilistic forecasting
            ↓
Equipment state estimation
            ↓
Constrained optimization
            ↓
Validated operating schedule
            ↓
Execution and monitoring

Not every layer needs AI.

For an initial implementation, I would use machine learning for forecasting and state estimation, then pass those outputs to an optimizer with explicit constraints.

The optimizer should account for limits such as:

  • Available energy.
  • Charging and discharging power.
  • Equipment operating boundaries.
  • Required reserves.
  • Computing deadlines.
  • Restrictions on grid import and export.

The LLM, if included, belongs in an interface or analysis layer—not as an unrestricted actuator.

4. Storage is also becoming infrastructure for AI

The connection is not only theoretical.

Google’s Energy Dome announcement describes using storage to shift clean electricity across 8–24 hours, bridging the gap between when renewable power is generated and when it is needed. blog

Separately, reporting on Google’s Minnesota data-center arrangement describes planned Form Energy storage of 300 MW and 30 GWh. These are announced project specifications, not evidence that the full installation is already operating. trellis

Power and energy are different quantities:

  • MW describes the rate at which electricity can be delivered.
  • MWh or GWh describes how much energy can be delivered over time.

For the announced figures, 30 GWh divided by 300 MW corresponds to 100 hours at rated power.

That is a different planning horizon from shifting electricity across an evening.

It also suggests a compelling software research direction: coordinate storage dispatch with computing schedules.

5. Build an experiment, not an “AI-powered” label

A useful first project does not need a physical battery or access to a hyperscale data center.

Start with a simulation.

Define the system

Use time series for:

  • Renewable generation.
  • Electricity prices.
  • Inflexible demand.
  • Flexible computing jobs and their deadlines.

Add two storage models with different durations, efficiencies, and operating constraints.

Keep the assumptions explicit. A generic storage model should not be presented as an accurate digital twin of a proprietary product.

Compare meaningful baselines

Test at least three strategies:

  1. A rule-based controller.
  2. A forecast-based optimizer.
  3. Joint energy-and-compute scheduling with uncertainty-aware forecasts.

This prevents a weak evaluation in which an elaborate AI system only competes against an obviously poor baseline.

Measure the whole outcome

Track:

  • Electricity cost.
  • Unserved demand.
  • Missed computing deadlines.
  • Storage losses.
  • Constraint violations.
  • Sensitivity to forecast errors.

Do not celebrate a lower electricity bill if the system achieves it by missing critical workloads or exhausting reserves.

For developers interested in flow-battery modeling, PNNL’s open-source EZBattery provides a physics-based starting point for simulating concentrations, potentials, and cycling performance. It is not itself an AI controller or a complete microgrid simulator. github

The breakthrough may be between the components

Better materials matter.

Better storage hardware matters.

But a system can also improve because its components stop making decisions in isolation.

A storage controller should understand the consequences of using energy now rather than later. A workload scheduler can be designed to account for electricity availability—not just processor availability.

That is the opportunity worth investigating: not a battery that “thinks,” but an architecture that coordinates energy and computation under real constraints.

The strongest result will not be an impressive dashboard or a persuasive chatbot.

It will be a reproducible experiment showing that the same resources can deliver more reliable service, meet computing deadlines, or reduce cost—without hiding the trade-offs.

title: Vercel Connect adds observability support
description:
Vercel Connect now gives teams line-level visibility into the token lifecycle. See who created a token, what app or project used it, when, and whether it is still active.

Every connector's detail page includes a new Observability tab:

  • Runtime events: Every token request, authorization, refresh, revocation, and trigger delivery, filterable by type.

  • Correlation IDs: Stable tokenId and authorizationId values link each token's events, so you can match Connect events to your own systems.

  • Activity: The Activity filter button opens the Activity page pre-filtered to the connector's configuration events, so you can see when and how it changed.

Connect observability is available on all plans. Events are retained for 12 hours on Hobby, 3 days on Pro, and 30 days on Enterprise. To retain events longer, forward them to a custom webhook endpoint by adding a Drain on Pro and Enterprise plans. Enterprise teams also get role-based access control and audit logs.

Get started in the Observability tab on a connector, or read the documentation.

title: Beyond On-Policy vs. Off-Policy: At What Level Should LLM Agent Distillation Follow the Student?
description:
arXiv:2610.31918v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Distilling interactive LLM agents requires choosing between teacher-generated demonstrations and student-generated experience, corresponding broadly to off-policy and on-policy distillation. While both have proven effective, we argue that this distinction is inherently hierarchical: the policy that induces an interaction history need not be the same as the policy that generates the token prefix of the current action. We introduce a hierarchical agent distillation framework that formalizes these two levels of on-policiness and enables explicit control over their pairing, mixture proportions, and training schedule. We study this problem through self-distillation, where a frozen teacher has access to task guidance unavailable to the student, and conduct a three-stage controlled study across three models and four interactive environments. We find that student-induced histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone training signal, whereas following the student at both levels generally performs worst. Nevertheless, fully on-policy data becomes beneficial when incorporated into a mixture with other configurations. Moreover, mixtures with identical teacher/student proportions at each level can yield substantially different performance, showing that how the two levels are paired matters beyond the overall amount of on-policy data. Finally, front-loading fully teacher-generated contexts and delaying fully on-policy contexts improves over a static mixture. These findings provide practical principles for deciding where, how much, and when agent distillation should follow the student.

title: FSVL: Taxonomic Fast-Slow Vision-to-Language Collaborative Framework for Interpretable Confusable Fish Species Identification and Knowledge Generation in the Middle Yangtze River
description:
arXiv:2610.31880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Yangtze River Basin is a critical region for freshwater biodiversity conservation. The implementation of the Yangtze River Ten-Year Fishing Ban has increased the importance of effective aquatic biodiversity monitoring and species-level identification. However, fine-grained identification of closely related freshwater fish species remains challenging due to subtle morphological differences. Existing deep learning methods often struggle to balance classification accuracy and inference efficiency, while LLMs may generate unsupported information when producing specialized biological knowledge. To address these challenges, this study proposes FSVL, a fast-slow dual-pathway framework integrating visual recognition with LLM-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). A lightweight ResNet50 fast path performs preliminary classification across 51 fish species in the Middle Yangtze River Basin and routes predefined groups of easily confused species to a slow path for refined identification. Guided by taxonomic criteria, the slow path uses YOLOv8n to detect key morphological regions, including the head, dorsal fin, and tail, leveraging morphometric and outline traits to improve discrimination among closely related species. The framework further integrates a retrieval-enhanced Qwen3-14B backend, using soft tokens and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for parameter-efficient domain knowledge generation. On the evaluated test set of 607 images, the fast classifier achieved 99.67% accuracy, whereas the cascade corrected the two errors, yielding 100.00% overall accuracy; further validation on independent specimens and external conditions remains needed. Across 255 knowledge generation samples, scientific name accuracy rises from 91.37% to 100.00%, genus accuracy from 90.20% to 98.82%, and ROUGE-L from 0.335 to 0.655, supporting intelligent biodiversity monitoring and fisheries management.

title: Implementing Email Functionality with Nodemailer in Node.js
description:
In the contemporary digital landscape, the automated transmission of emails has become an integral aspect of web application development. Be it for dispatching notifications, distributing newsletters, or executing password resets, the integration of email functionality into Node.js applications holds significant importance. Thankfully, Node.js provides Nodemailer, an efficient library that enhances the email-sending experience. This tutorial investigates how to utilize Nodemailer to effortlessly dispatch emails from your Node.js application.

Prerequisites for Nodemailer

Before delving into Nodemailer utilization, ensure the following prerequisites are fulfilled:

  • Confirm the correct installation and configuration of js and npm on your system.
  • Possess foundational knowledge in JavaScript and Node.js.

Setting Up the Node.js Application

Begin by establishing a rudimentary Node.js application. Navigate to your project directory and adhere to the following steps:

Create a new directory for your project

mkdir nodemailer-demo

cd nodemailer-demo

Initialize a fresh Node.js project

npm init -y

Initialize a fresh Node.js project

Procure the requisite dependencies by executing the following commands:

1. Install Express

Express, a swift, adaptable, and lightweight web framework tailored for Node.js, furnishes a comprehensive toolkit for erecting web applications and APIs. It encompasses functionalities like routing, middleware integration, and support for template engines. In our context, Express is employed to establish the server, delineate routes, and handle HTTP requests.

To install Express, execute the following command:

npm install express

2. Install Body-parser

Body-parser, a middleware for Express.js, extracts the entire body segment of an incoming request stream, thereby exposing it on req.body. This middleware facilitates the parsing of incoming request bodies before they reach designated handlers, rendering them accessible via the req.body property. Body-parser is instrumental in parsing form data dispatched via POST requests.

To install Body-parser, utilize the ensuing command:

npm install body-parser

3. Install Nodemailer

Nodemailer, a dedicated Node.js module, streamlines the process of sending emails within applications. It furnishes a user-friendly API for dispatching emails employing diverse email services and protocols. Nodemailer is instrumental in sending dynamic emails from Node.js applications.

To integrate Nodemailer, execute the ensuing command:

npm install nodemailer

Create and Configure app.js

Create a file named app.js within your project directory. This file will serve as the primary entry point for the application. Within app.js, the Express server will be instantiated, routes will be established, and email-sending functionality utilizing Nodemailer will be managed.

The following is an illustrative code snippet for app.js:

app.js 

const express = require("express");
const nodemailer = require("nodemailer");
const bodyParser = require("body-parser");
const app = express();
// Middleware to parse form data
app.use(bodyParser.urlencoded({ extended: true }));
// Define transporter object using SMTP transport
const transporter = nodemailer.createTransport({
  service: "Gmail",
  auth: {
    user: "your-email@gmail.com",
    pass: "your-password",
  },
});
// Route to serve the HTML form
app.get("/", (req, res) => {
  res.send(`
 <h2>Send Email</h2>
 <form action="/send-email" method="post">
 <label for="recipient">Recipient Email:</label><br>
 <input type="email" id="recipient" name="recipient" required><br><br>
 <label for="subject">Subject:</label><br>
 <input type="text" id="subject" name="subject" required><br><br>
 <label for="content">Email Content:</label><br>
 <textarea id="content" name="content" rows="4" required></textarea><br><br>
 <button type="submit">Send Email</button>
 </form>
 `);
});
// Route to handle form submission
app.post("/send-email", (req, res) => {
  const { recipient, subject, content } = req.body;
  // Define email content
  const mailOptions = {
    from: "your-email@gmail.com",
    to: recipient,
    subject: subject,
    html: content,
  };
  // Send email
  transporter.sendMail(mailOptions, (error, info) => {
    if (error) {
      console.error("Error occurred:", error.message);
      res.send("Error occurred while sending email.");
    } else {
      console.log("Email sent successfully!");
      res.send("Email sent successfully!");
    }
  });
});
// Start the server
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000;
app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Server is running on port ${port}`);
});

Explanation of app.js Code

Express Setup: Import the Express module and instantiate an Express application.

Middleware: Employ the body-parser middleware to parse form data dispatched via POST requests.

Nodemailer Configuration: Define a transporter object utilizing SMTP transport. Substitute your-email@gmail.com and 'your-password' with your email credentials. This transporter object facilitates email dispatch.

Routes: Define two routes—one for serving the HTML form ('/') and another for handling form submission ('/send-email'). The HTML form is dispensed upon visiting the root URL, while the form submission route manages the POST request sent upon submission.

Server Initialization: Initiate the Express server and listen on a designated port (3000 by default).

Understanding the nodemailer.createTransport Method

The nodemailer.createTransport method is instrumental in crafting a transporter object that specifies the methodology for sending emails. It accepts an options object, delineating the email service, authentication credentials, and additional transport options.

In our scenario, SMTP transport is employed for dispatching emails via a Gmail account. The Gmail service is designated as the service option, while authentication is executed utilizing the username and password associated with the Gmail account. The auth object encompasses the user (email address) and pass (password) properties.

const transporter = nodemailer.createTransport({
    service: 'Gmail',
    auth: {
        user: 'your-email@gmail.com',
        pass: 'your-password'
    }
});

Invocation of nodemailer.createTransport yields a transporter object tailored for dispatching emails via the specified email service and authentication credentials. This transporter object is subsequently employed for sending emails within our application. Note on Addressing "Invalid Login" Error: Encountering an "Invalid login" error typically implies rejection of login credentials by the email service provider. In such instances, generating an app password for the email account and utilizing it within the nodemailer.createTransport function, instead of the conventional password, usually resolves the authentication conundrum.

Executing the Node.js Application

To execute the app.js file and commence your Node.js application, execute the subsequent command in your terminal:

node app.js

This command triggers the execution of the app.js **file via **Node.js, launching the Express server and rendering your application accessible at the designated port. Ensure you execute this command within the root directory of your project.

Upon execution, a message indicating the server's operational status on the specified port, as defined within your app.js file, should manifest. Access your application by visiting http://localhost:3000 through your web browser.

Output

Conclusion

Nodemailer emerges as a potent and adaptable library, streamlining the process of email dispatch from Node.js applications. This guide has expounded on the fundamental steps of Nodemailer setup and email dispatch employing a Gmail account. Nonetheless, Nodemailer boasts support for various email services and proffers various advanced features, encompassing HTML content, attachments, and more. I encourage delving into the official.

title: İş teslim edildikten sonra "olmamış" cevabını almak üzerine
description:
Geçen ay küçük bir çeviri işi aldım, üç sayfalıktı. Teslim etmeden önce sordum: "Bu işin iyi olduğunu nereden anlayacağız?" Cevap şuydu: "Profesyonelce olsun, gerisi önemli değil."

Üç gün çalıştım, teslim ettim. Gelen cevap tek satırdı: "Beklediğim gibi olmamış." Neyin beklediği gibi olmadığını sorduğumda net bir şey çıkmadı. Sonunda iş iptal oldu. Ben üç günümü kaybettim, karşı taraf da yeni birini arama süresini. Kimse kötü niyetli değildi; sadece işin başında "iyi"nin ne demek olduğunu hiç konuşmamıştık.

Bir süredir bunun sadece benim başıma gelmediğini sanmıyorum. Sorun genelde işin kalitesi değil, ölçütün iş bitmeden önce yazılmamış olması.

Geçenlerde bir arkadaşım Base ağında Verdikta diye bir protokolden bahsetti. İlk duyduğumda "yine bir kripto projesi" dedim, ama işin mantığı beni durdurdu.

Verdikta'da olan şu: işi veren kişi parayı baştan bir akıllı sözleşmeye kilitliyor. Yani para ortada duruyor, iş bitmeden kimseye geçmiyor. Yanına bir de değerlendirme listesi ekliyor: bu işte neyin zorunlu olduğu, neyin sadece puan getirdiği ve kaç puanın "yeterli" sayıldığı. Liste işe başlamadan IPFS'te yayınlanıyor. Ardından Base zincirine yazılıyor, yani sonradan değiştirilemiyor, geri alınamıyor.

Sonra bağımsız yapay zekâ düğümlerinden oluşan bir jüri bu listeye göre değerlendiriyor. Önemli olan kısım şu: sadece "geçti" ya da "kaldı" demiyorlar, her maddeye ayrı puan veriyorlar ve bu puanlar herkesin görebileceği şekilde açık. Yani işi yapan kişi nerede kaç puan kaybettiğini görebiliyor.

Bir de şu var: eşiği ilk geçen teslimat bütün parayı alıyor. Son güne kadar bekleyip "en güzelini" seçme durumu yok. Platform herhangi bir komisyon almıyor; işi teslim eden kişi yalnızca jürinin çalışması için yaklaşık 0,00024 ETH kadar bir ön tutar yatırıyor, kullanılmayan kısmı iade ediliyor. Kimse eşiği geçemezse para işi verene dönüyor.

Bunları yazarken abartmak istemiyorum. Makine hâlâ makine: zevk, ton, "bu metin kulağa hoş geliyor mu" gibi ölçütü olmayan işlerde bir insan kadar isabetli olmayabilir. Edebi çeviri, pazarlama metni, arayüz yazısı gibi işler bence hâlâ insan işi. Zincire kazınmış olsa bile kötü yazılmış bir liste kötü liste kalır; o zaman iyi iş de duvara çarpıyor. Bence bu sistem, ürün ve ölçütler net ve ölçülebilir olduğunda en iyi sonuç veriyor.

title: An Agentic Approach with Evidence-Grounded Verification for Multimodal Emotion Reasoning in Conversation
description:
arXiv:2610.31685v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM-based multimodal emotion reasoning systems perform well on standard benchmarks, but improving them through instruction tuning can be computationally expensive. Agentic pipelines built from frozen models avoid this cost, but introduce a different challenge: when a prediction is wrong, the system must identify which agent or stage caused the error. We address this problem with an agentic framework for traceable multimodal emotion reasoning and prompt-space adaptation. Modality-specific perception agents analyze visual, acoustic, and lexical inputs and post evidence-cited observations to a shared board. An integration agent combines these observations with retrieved multimodal examples to produce an emotion description, label set, and supporting citations, while an MLLM critic can request one revision before the output is finalized. For incorrect predictions, a separate evidence-grounded verification stage applies deterministic checks to verify that cited evidence and references are valid, and an entailment check to determine whether the final claims are supported by that evidence. Detected failures are then grouped by the responsible component and failure type, converted into targeted prompt patches, and accepted only after validation on a held-out set. This adapts the agent prompts without updating model weights. On the MER2025 dataset, targeted prompt adaptation outperforms the frozen static pipeline on all four MLLMs, ranging from 2B to 38B parameters, and matches or outperforms undifferentiated reflection baselines on each of them: VideoLLaMA3-2B, Phi-3.5-vision-instruct, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, and InternVL2.5-38B. It improves F-score by 0.6--2.2 points depending on the backbone, including an increase from 52.3 to 54.5 on Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

title: Firefox Dark Mode: OS Level, prefers-color-scheme, Extensions, and New Tab
description:
Dark mode has become a mainstream expectation — most apps support it, most operating systems default to it or offer it prominently. Firefox has several layers of dark mode support, and understanding how they interact makes a difference in how consistent the experience is.

Layer 1: OS-Level Dark Mode

When you enable dark mode in Windows or macOS, Firefox respects it for its own UI: the toolbar, tabs, and settings panels go dark automatically.

This doesn't affect web pages by default — most websites have their own light/dark mode implementation that's separate from the OS setting.

Layer 2: Website Dark Mode (prefers-color-scheme)

Well-implemented websites check the prefers-color-scheme CSS media query and serve a dark-mode version when it's set to dark. This is the "right" way websites handle dark mode.

You can test whether a site supports this via Firefox DevTools: Responsive Design Mode → Sun/Moon icon to simulate light or dark preference.

Sites that don't implement prefers-color-scheme will always appear in their default (usually light) theme.

Layer 3: Firefox's Built-In Override

Firefox has a setting (Settings → Colors section) to force dark backgrounds on websites that don't support prefers-color-scheme. This uses Firefox's own CSS to apply a dark background to all pages.

This is hit-or-miss — some sites look fine, others have broken contrast or unreadable text because the override can't predict what colors a site uses.

Layer 4: Dark Mode Extensions

For consistent dark mode across all websites, a content-script extension is the reliable approach.

Dark Reader is the most popular. It analyzes each page and applies a dark theme based on the site's existing color palette. Results are generally good. It has CPU/memory overhead because it runs analysis on every page.

NightOwl (Firefox AMO) takes a different approach — it injects a CSS filter across all pages rather than doing per-page color analysis. It's lighter-weight but produces more uniform (less site-adapted) results. Good for people who want dark mode everywhere without configuration.

Layer 5: New Tab Extensions

New tab replacements like Weather & Clock Dashboard have their own dark/light mode toggle, independent of both the OS setting and web page dark mode. Since new tab is an extension page (not a regular web page), regular dark mode extensions don't apply to it.

Weather & Clock Dashboard's toggle is in the top corner of the new tab. It remembers your preference across sessions.

The Recommended Setup

For the most consistent dark mode experience:

  1. Enable OS dark mode
  2. Install Dark Reader or NightOwl for sites that don't support prefers-color-scheme
  3. Set your new tab extension to dark mode manually

This covers:

  • Firefox UI ✅
  • Modern sites that support the media query ✅
  • Older/unconfigured sites (via extension) ✅
  • New tab page ✅

The only gaps are PDFs (Firefox's built-in PDF viewer doesn't respect dark mode) and about: pages (Firefox internal pages have their own dark mode separate from all of this).

title: Adding Architecture Tests Without Taking on Every Violation at Once
description:
A team can usually agree that ordering should use the payments API without knowing how payments is implemented. Keeping that agreement intact over several years of ordinary feature work takes a little more care. An import is easy to add, and the compiler has never attended the architecture meeting.

In an existing Java application, the awkward part of introducing architecture tests is often deciding what to do with the failures. Turning on every rule at once can leave the team with a substantial new backlog and a build nobody is keen to open.

I would start with one boundary whose responsibilities are clear enough to discuss. Here is a small example of how to do that, followed by the decisions I would make before putting the check into a shared build.

Agree on the dependency first

Suppose ordering needs to request a payment. Payments exposes an interface:

// src/main/java/com/shop/payments/api/PaymentGateway.java
package com.shop.payments.api;

public interface PaymentGateway {
    void pay();
}

The implementation belongs inside payments:

// src/main/java/com/shop/payments/internal/PaymentGatewayImpl.java
package com.shop.payments.internal;

import com.shop.payments.api.PaymentGateway;

public class PaymentGatewayImpl implements PaymentGateway {
    @Override
    public void pay() {}
}

The empty method keeps payment processing out of the example. We are interested in who depends on the implementation, so there is no need to introduce a payment provider just to give the build something to object to.

Ordering currently imports the implementation directly:

// src/main/java/com/shop/ordering/internal/OrderService.java
package com.shop.ordering.internal;

import com.shop.payments.internal.PaymentGatewayImpl;

public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGatewayImpl payments;

    public OrderService(PaymentGatewayImpl payments) {
        this.payments = payments;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        payments.pay();
    }
}

All of this compiles. The class is public, and Java gives a package named internal no special protection. If the implementation needs to be public for use across packages within payments, another module can reach it too.

Before writing the test, agree on the restriction with the team: ordering may depend on the payments API, while payment implementation types remain private to the payments module. If that agreement is still contested, a failing build is a rather inconvenient place to hold the discussion.

Put one restriction into a test

The example uses Modulith Rules, an open-source library I maintain that provides pre-built ArchUnit rules. The core works without Spring and is added in test scope. You will need Java 17 or newer, with these dependencies:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.modularmonolith</groupId>
    <artifactId>modulith-rules-core</artifactId>
    <version>0.2.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
    <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
    <version>6.1.2</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Register the two modules and select the internal-package rule:

// src/test/java/com/shop/architecture/ArchitectureTest.java
package com.shop.architecture;

import com.tngtech.archunit.core.importer.ClassFileImporter;
import io.modulith.rules.ModulithRules;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class ArchitectureTest {
    @Test
    void modulesDoNotAccessEachOthersInternals() {
        var classes = new ClassFileImporter().importPackages("com.shop");

        ModulithRules.forPackage("com.shop", "ordering", "payments")
            .boundaryRules()
            .internalsShouldNotBeAccessedFromOutside()
            .check(classes);
    }
}

The configuration derives com.shop.ordering and com.shop.payments from the root package and module names. The rule checks access across those registered modules, using the library's internal-package conventions.

With the direct implementation dependency, the test fails and identifies access from OrderService to PaymentGatewayImpl. That gives us a specific dependency to review, along with the code that introduced it.

Make the smallest useful change

Ordering already has an interface it can use, so change its import, field type and constructor parameter:

package com.shop.ordering.internal;

import com.shop.payments.api.PaymentGateway;

public class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway payments;

    public OrderService(PaymentGateway payments) {
        this.payments = payments;
    }

    public void placeOrder() {
        payments.pay();
    }
}

The architecture test now passes. The application still needs to supply a payment implementation when it is assembled, through its composition root or dependency injection configuration. That wiring is a separate concern from the dependency we have just removed from ordering.

The complete example contains Maven projects for both versions. Run mvn test in boundary-example/before to see the violation, then in boundary-example/after to see the same test pass.

Decide what to do with existing violations

In a larger codebase, the first run may find several dependencies that cross this boundary. Read them before deciding how to respond. Some may be straightforward mistakes; others may support behaviour that will take more work to untangle.

I would record the dependencies that need a migration, identify who owns that work, and choose a scope the team can reasonably bring into compliance. A focused check is useful when everyone understands which part of the system it covers and which dependencies still need attention.

If a violation needs to remain temporarily, keep that decision explicit and reviewable. Quietly leaving a module out of the configuration can make the test pass, but it also removes the protection people may assume they have. A migration plan should make those gaps visible.

Once the selected boundary is in a state the team accepts, run the test in CI alongside the existing tests. Future changes can then bring the same dependency decision back into review while the code is still fresh in somebody's mind.

Give a green result some context

The test imports classes under com.shop, but these module rules govern the registered module packages. Classes outside them are ignored. Register the modules you intend to inspect, and check the package names carefully.

The selected rule also matters. The example protects internals; it does not apply every policy in the library. allRules() groups allowed dependencies, internal-package protection and cycle detection. allCoreRules() adds API-only access and communication-contract checks.

Some settings are deliberately permissive. An empty allowedDependencies list leaves a module unrestricted by that rule, and API-only access skips target modules with no configured API packages. The documentation describes these defaults, which deserve a read before a green build becomes evidence in a design discussion.

I would also introduce a deliberate violation before trusting the check. If a known bad dependency passes, investigate the registration and selected policy while the example is still small enough to understand.

Keep the wider design in view

Two modules can pass a Java dependency test while sharing a database table that forces them to change together. Static checks also tell us little about what happens when an event consumer crashes after performing part of its work. Data ownership and failure handling still need their own decisions and tests.

If you already use Spring Modulith, check its existing verification first. ApplicationModules.verify() already checks module cycles, internal access and explicitly allowed dependencies, and it can run during tests. An additional library should earn its place through a policy you need or a framework-independent core.

The Modulith Rules documentation covers configuration and rule behaviour, and the repository includes a wider example application.

A useful first check protects a decision the team understands and can maintain. Start there, verify that it catches a dependency you know should fail, and let the next boundary earn its place in the build.

title: Mining Frames: Association Rule Mining as an Unsupervised Framework for News Framing Detection
description:
arXiv:2610.31874v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational framing analysis is dominated by supervised classifiers that require large annotated corpora and predefined frame taxonomies, limiting their use for non-English languages, novel events, and low-resource settings. This paper presents Association Rule Mining (ARM) as an unsupervised, annotation-free framework for news framing detection. Each document or sentence is treated as a transaction of lexical items, and high-lift co-occurrence rules are read as candidate framing signals (Gamson and Modigliani's condensing symbols), confirmed in context by journalist-researchers. The primary validation is Framing Gaza: 25,512 English-language articles from 16 US, UK, French, and German outlets covering the first year of the Gaza war (October 2023 to October 2024), analyzed with Apriori (mlxtend), platform-weighted support, POS-filtered n-grams, and lift-based scoring. ARM inductively surfaces interpretable patterns without predefined categories: a cross-platform military frame, {israeli, strike} to {kill}, appears as a closed rule in 14 of 16 outlets, and a month-by-month analysis recovers event-driven framing pivots (e.g., the April 2024 World Central Kitchen strike) with no prior event labeling. A systematic headline-body divergence is identified, with headlines carrying concentrated, high-lift editorial framing and body text reproducing institutional, procedural language. A methodological validation on the Seven Days project (1,575 Arabic articles on the 2026 Iran war) shows that FP-Growth enables sentence-level analysis with far lower memory overhead. Findings were validated through editorial uptake: two published investigative stories (Daraj Media; Saheeh Masr). Preprocessing code is released openly; the full pipeline is documented but withheld to preserve operational deployability.

title: PlugThis vs Ctruh Studio: Which AI Tool Is Better?
description:
⚡

Executive Verdict: PlugThis vs Ctruh Studio (2026)

  • PlugThis Advantage: PlugThis stands out for Teams evaluating AI Automation software and comparing official feature positioning.
  • Ctruh Studio Advantage: Ctruh Studio is superior for Teams evaluating AI Automation software and comparing official feature positioning.
  • Workflow & Usability: PlugThis provides faster setup and lighter onboarding, whereas Ctruh Studio accommodates more complex multi-seat pipelines.
  • Which One to Pick: Choose PlugThis for speed and solo workflows; select Ctruh Studio if your organization requires team-wide scaling.

Introduction

Comparing PlugThis and Ctruh Studio is a useful exercise, but it comes with an important caveat: despite both being filed under the broad "AI Automation" category, they solve fundamentally different problems. PlugThis is a Chrome extension builder that turns plain-English descriptions into working Manifest v3 extensions. Ctruh Studio is a no-code platform for building AR try-ons, 3D product visualizers, configurators, virtual stores, and AI-generated creatives in the browser.

In other words, this is less a "which is better" question and more a "which one matches your workflow" question. A developer or founder who needs a functional browser extension shipped in a day will find little use for a 3D configurator platform, and an e-commerce team building AR product experiences will not solve that problem with an extension generator.

This review is written from a practitioner's perspective. It draws strictly on verified public positioning for both tools, flags where details still require manual verification, and avoids inventing pricing or feature specifics that are not confirmed. Where plan details, usage limits, or integration depth are unknown, we say so plainly and direct you to the official websites.

The goal is to give you a realistic decision framework: what each tool actually does, where each fits in a real workflow, and how to choose between them—or whether you need a third option entirely.

PlugThis Core Capabilities

PlugThis is positioned as an AI-powered Chrome extension builder. The core promise, per its official summary, is straightforward: describe what you want in plain English and receive a working Manifest v3 extension in under two minutes—no coding required, with real code and a real backend ready for the Chrome Web Store.

Key Features

  • AI built-in: The build process is driven by natural-language prompts rather than a visual editor or hand-written code.
  • Plain English in, working extension out: You describe the extension's behavior; the tool generates functional output.
  • Real code and real backend: The output is positioned as production-oriented—Manifest v3 compliant and structured for Chrome Web Store submission—not a mockup.
  • Fast iteration: The provided workflow context describes an extension working within 2–3 prompts, then polished with assets and submitted.
  • Official summary: "Chrome extension builder powered by AI. Describe what you want, get a working Manifest v3 extension in under 2 minutes. No coding. Real back[end]."

Realistic Use Cases

The strongest verified signal comes from the Indexly case context: Chetan Giridhar, founder of Indexly (an SEO and AI-search-visibility platform), built a companion extension ("Indexly Vault") for his customers. Per the provided facts, the extension was working in 2–3 prompts, then polished with assets and submitted to the Chrome Web Store—ready in a day.

That maps to concrete practitioner scenarios:

  1. SaaS companion extensions: A product team wants a lightweight browser extension that connects customers to its web app.
  2. Internal tooling: A team needs a quick extension for a repetitive browser task without allocating engineering sprint time.
  3. Rapid validation: A founder wants to test whether an extension idea has traction before investing in a full build.

Where to Be Careful

  • Feature availability, usage limits, integrations, and plan details are not confirmed in the verified facts and require manual verification on the official site.
  • The summary above is based on public website extraction; treat capability claims as positioning until you test them against your specific extension requirements (permissions, API calls, store compliance).

Ctruh Studio Core Capabilities

Ctruh Studio occupies a different lane entirely. Its official summary describes a no-code, in-browser platform for creating AR try-ons, 3D product visualizers and configurators, virtual stores, and AI creatives.

Key Features

  • AR try-on experiences: Positioned for retail and product visualization use cases where customers preview items.
  • 3D product visualizers and configurators: Interactive 3D presentation of products, with configuration options.
  • Virtual stores: Browser-based immersive storefront experiences.
  • AI creatives: AI-assisted generation of marketing or product creative assets.
  • No-code, in-browser: The workflow runs in the browser without a coding requirement.
  • Official summary: "Create AR try-ons, 3D Product visualizers & configurators, virtual stores & AI creatives in-browser with Ctruh Studio. No code."

Realistic Use Cases

Ctruh Studio's positioning points toward commerce and marketing teams rather than developer tooling:

  1. E-commerce product pages: Adding AR try-on or 3D configurators to reduce return rates and improve conversion.
  2. Virtual showrooms: Building immersive storefronts for campaigns, launches, or B2B sales.
  3. Marketing asset production: Using AI creatives to support campaigns around the 3D/AR experiences.

Where to Be Careful

  • Feature availability, usage limits, integrations, and plan details require manual verification—the verified facts do not confirm specifics.
  • The positioning is based on public website extraction and should be reviewed before approval or procurement decisions.
  • "No code" claims should be tested against your actual complexity requirements (asset pipelines, hosting, analytics).

Head-to-Head Comparison

The table below compares the two tools strictly against verified public positioning. Where a fact is unconfirmed, it is marked accordingly rather than estimated.

Dimension PlugThis Ctruh Studio
Category AI Automation (Chrome extension builder) AI Automation (AR/3D commerce builder)
Core Output Working Manifest v3 Chrome extension with real code and backend AR try-ons, 3D visualizers/configurators, virtual stores, AI creatives
Primary Input Method Plain-English prompts No-code in-browser builder
Coding Required No coding (per official summary) No code (per official summary)
Speed Claim Working extension in under 2 minutes; 2–3 prompts per case context Not specified in verified facts
Deployment Target Chrome Web Store In-browser experiences (web)
Typical Buyer SaaS founders, product teams, internal tooling owners E-commerce, retail, and marketing teams
Integrations Requires manual verification Requires manual verification
Usage Limits Requires manual verification Requires manual verification
Pricing Check the official website for the latest pricing. Check the official website for the latest pricing.
Best For Teams evaluating AI Automation software for extension-building workflows Teams evaluating AI Automation software for AR/3D commerce workflows

Feature-by-Feature Notes

  • On output format: PlugThis produces a distributable software artifact (an extension). Ctruh Studio produces interactive experiences. These are not substitutes; overlap is minimal.
  • On speed: PlugThis makes an explicit speed claim (under two minutes; 2–3 prompts per the Indexly context). Ctruh Studio's verified facts include no comparable build-time claim, so no comparison is possible without testing.
  • On pricing: Neither tool has confirmed pricing in the verified facts. Check the official website for the latest pricing for both before budgeting.
  • On verification status: Both fact sets are based on public website extraction and flagged for human review. Treat all capability claims as directional until you run a hands-on trial.

Workflow Fit: How Each Tool Slots In

PlugThis workflow (extension build):

  1. Define the extension's purpose and required permissions in plain English.
  2. Prompt PlugThis and iterate (the case context suggests 2–3 prompts to a working build).
  3. Review the generated code and backend behavior against your requirements.
  4. Add branding assets and polish.
  5. Submit to the Chrome Web Store.

Ctruh Studio workflow (AR/3D experience):

  1. Prepare product assets (3D models, imagery) for the experience type you need.
  2. Build the try-on, configurator, or virtual store in the browser without code.
  3. Generate supporting AI creatives for the campaign or product page.
  4. Review output quality and embed/deploy per the platform's (to-be-verified) deployment options.

If your roadmap involves both—say, a companion extension and an AR product page—these tools are complementary rather than competitive. Teams needing broader automation orchestration between systems should also evaluate general-purpose platforms such as Zapier, Latenode AI Workflow Builder, or Albato AI, which sit in a different layer than either tool here.

Pros and Cons Summary

PlugThis

Pros:

  • Official positioning suggests PlugThis is built for AI Automation workflows.
  • The product page provides enough workflow context for a first-pass research snapshot.
  • Official summary: Chrome extension builder powered by AI—describe what you want, get a working Manifest v3 extension in under 2 minutes, no coding, real backend.
  • Documented case context (Indexly) shows a working extension in 2–3 prompts, ready in a day.

Cons:

  • Feature availability, usage limits, integrations, and plan details still require manual verification.
  • The facts draft is based on public website extraction and should be reviewed before approval.

Ctruh Studio

Pros:

  • Official positioning suggests Ctruh Studio is built for AI Automation workflows.
  • The product page provides enough workflow context for a first-pass research snapshot.
  • Official summary: create AR try-ons, 3D product visualizers and configurators, virtual stores, and AI creatives in-browser—no code.

Cons:

  • Feature availability, usage limits, integrations, and plan details still require manual verification.
  • The facts draft is based on public website extraction and should be reviewed before approval.

Direct Side-by-Side

PlugThis Ctruh Studio
Primary strength Fast, prompt-driven extension generation with real code No-code AR/3D commerce experiences in-browser
Primary limitation Unverified limits, integrations, and pricing Unverified limits, integrations, and pricing
Decision blocker Confirm store-compliance and backend fit Confirm asset pipeline and deployment fit

Final Verdict: Which One Should You Choose?

There is no universal winner here because the tools do not compete for the same job. Choose based on the artifact you need to ship.

Choose **PlugThis if:**

  • You need a Chrome extension—a companion tool, internal utility, or customer-facing browser tool—and want it built from plain-English prompts.
  • You value speed to a Chrome Web Store submission and are comfortable reviewing generated code and backend behavior.
  • You are a SaaS founder, product manager, or ops lead who wants to validate an extension idea without an engineering sprint.
  • Your team already has web infrastructure and just needs the extension layer.

Choose **Ctruh Studio if:**

  • You need AR try-ons, 3D product configurators, virtual stores, or AI creatives for commerce or marketing.
  • Your buyers or customers are the audience—product pages and immersive storefronts are the goal, not developer tooling.
  • You want a no-code, in-browser workflow for 3D/AR assets rather than a code-generating tool.

Consider neither (or both plus orchestration) if:

  • Your real need is connecting existing apps and automating data flows—evaluate Zapier, Albato AI, or Latenode AI Workflow Builder instead.
  • You need founder-level or operational tooling beyond these categories—tools like Locus Founder or ModuleX may be worth a parallel look.

Before committing either way, verify pricing, usage limits, and integrations directly on each official site—check the official website for the latest pricing—and run a hands-on trial against one real project. Both fact sets here are directional snapshots, not procurement-grade specifications.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are PlugThis and Ctruh Studio direct competitors?
No. PlugThis builds Chrome extensions from plain-English prompts, while Ctruh Studio creates AR try-ons, 3D visualizers, virtual stores, and AI creatives in-browser. Both sit under AI Automation, but they produce different artifacts and serve different teams, so they are rarely evaluated for the same project.

Does PlugThis require coding to build an extension?
Per its official summary, no. You describe what you want in plain English and receive a working Manifest v3 extension with real code and a real backend, ready for the Chrome Web Store. The documented Indexly case had an extension working within 2–3 prompts, polished and submitted in about a day.

Does Ctruh Studio require coding for AR and 3D experiences?
Per its official summary, no—Ctruh Studio is positioned as a no-code, in-browser platform for AR try-ons, 3D product visualizers and configurators, virtual stores, and AI creatives. title: Free Lunch for LLMs Confidence: The RL Critic Already Knows
description:
arXiv:2610.31820v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reliable confidence estimation is essential for trustworthy deployment of large language models (LLMs), but dedicated confidence training stage requires additional data and compute. We ask a fundamental question: what prediction problem does confidence training actually solve? Inspired by prior work on external confidence estimation, we compare self- and external estimators of comparable capacity trained on the same (question, response, correctness) triples. We show that an external model trained solely on a policy's behavioral traces can estimate the policy's confidence as accurately as the policy itself, without accessing the policy's internal representations. This points to a deeper connection with value function learning in reinforcement learning (RL): under a correctness-based outcome, we prove that confidence estimation and critic training are equivalent, both predicting the likelihood that a policy's response will be correct from its trajectory. A simple consequence follows: for LLMs trained with value-based RL, the existing critic can be reused as an off-the-shelf confidence estimator with no additional training or data. The policy remains unchanged, so its task performance is preserved, and the critic provides confidence throughout generation, including intermediate reasoning steps. Across math, code, tool calling, and general reasoning spanning a dozen domains, the reused critic is the best confidence estimator on every in-distribution split and the best-calibrated on 14 of 16, without hurting the task performance.

title: Forging Emotions: a deep learning experiment on emotions and art
description:
arXiv:2610.32163v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Affective computing is an interdisciplinary field that studies computational methods that relate to or influence emotion. These methods have been applied to interactive media artworks, but they have focused on affect detection rather than affect generation. For affect generation, computationally creative methods need to be explored that have recently been driven by the use of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), a deep learning method. The experiment presented in this paper, Forging Emotions, explores the use of visual emotion datasets and the working processes of GANs for visual affect generation, that is, for generating images that can convey or trigger specified emotions. This experiment concludes that the methodology used so far by computer science researchers to build image datasets for describing high-level concepts such as emotions is insufficient and proposes utilizing emotional networks of associations according to psychology research. Forging Emotions also concludes that to generate affect visually, merely corresponding to basic psychology findings, such as bright or dark colours, does not seem adequate. Therefore, research efforts should aim to understand the structure of trained GANs and compositional GANs in order to produce genuinely novel compositions that can convey or trigger emotions through the subject matter of generated images.

title: Enterprise Managed Users is now generally available
description:
Enterprise Managed Users (EMU) gives organizations full control over the Vercel accounts tied to their verified domains. It makes the organization's identity provider the single source of truth for authentication and account lifecycle, so accounts on company domains are governed centrally rather than owned by individuals.

Now generally available

  • IdP-enforced sign-in: Managed users sign in through SAML SSO only. All other login methods, including email OTP, GitHub, Google, and GitLab, no longer work for managed accounts.

  • SCIM provisioning & lifecycle: Directory Sync creates, updates, and deprovisions managed users automatically, keeping accounts in sync with your IdP.

  • Owned by your organization: Profile settings are managed through your IdP rather than by the individual.

  • Self-serve enablement: Turn EMU on for a verified domain in Team Settings under Security & Privacy, and extend it across multiple eligible teams in a single step.

Requires an Enterprise plan, enforced SAML SSO, active Directory Sync, and at least one verified domain.

In Beta, available on request

  • Hobby team transition: Members with an existing personal account on a newly managed domain are guided to add a personal email (keeping their hobby projects) or delete the account, then continue to their work through SSO.

  • Automatic conversion: Personal accounts with no content or activity are archived automatically, and their owners land in a new managed account at their next SSO sign-in.

To request access, contact your account team.

Learn more in the Enterprise Managed Users and Hobby team transition docs.
